q: Immediately after an esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD), which nursing action has the highest priority?
o: Offer cool fluids to soothe the throat
Assess for return of the gag reflex before giving anything by mouth
Encourage the client to cough forcefully
Ambulate the client in the hall
r: The client is kept NPO until the gag reflex returns to prevent aspiration after throat anesthetic and sedation. A sore throat is expected, but nothing is given by mouth until the gag reflex is confirmed.

q: What is the most reliable method to confirm correct placement of a newly inserted NG tube before its first use?
o: Auscultate air injected into the tube
Radiographic (X-ray) confirmation
Aspirate and check gastric pH
Ask the client to speak
r: X-ray is the gold standard to confirm initial placement before first use. pH testing (≤5) helps with ongoing verification, but auscultating an air bolus is NOT an acceptable method.

q: A client is receiving continuous enteral tube feedings. Which interventions reduce the risk of aspiration? Select all that apply.
o: Keep the head of the bed elevated 30–45°
Verify tube placement before feeding
Check gastric residual volume per policy
Keep the client lying flat during the feeding
Flush the tube with water per protocol
r: Aspiration prevention is the #1 priority: HOB up 30–45°, verify placement, check residuals, and flush per policy. Lying the client flat increases aspiration risk and is incorrect.

q: Which instruction is correct when teaching a client with dumping syndrome after gastric surgery?
o: Drink fluids with every meal
Eat high-simple-carbohydrate meals
Lie down after eating
Sit fully upright for 2 hours after meals
r: Lying down (recumbent) after meals slows gastric emptying. Teaching also includes small frequent meals, high protein, LOW simple carbs, and NO fluids with meals (drink between meals).

q: A client reports epigastric pain that occurs 2–3 hours after meals and during the night, and is relieved by eating. This is most characteristic of a:
o: Gastric ulcer
Duodenal ulcer
Esophageal varix
Hiatal hernia
r: Duodenal ulcer pain occurs 2–3 hours after meals/at night and is RELIEVED by food. Gastric ulcer pain occurs WITH or soon after eating and food worsens it.

q: Which findings suggest a perforated peptic ulcer? Select all that apply.
o: Sudden, severe abdominal pain
Rigid, board-like abdomen
Rebound tenderness
Increased appetite and hyperactive bowel sounds
Tachycardia and hypotension
r: Perforation causes sudden severe pain, a rigid board-like abdomen, rebound tenderness, and signs of shock (tachycardia, hypotension). Bowel sounds decrease/absent — increased appetite is not expected.

q: After a total gastrectomy, the nurse anticipates the client will require lifelong:
o: Oral iron supplements
Vitamin B12 injections
Potassium supplements
Pancreatic enzymes
r: Removal of the stomach eliminates intrinsic factor (from parietal cells), which is required to absorb vitamin B12. This causes pernicious anemia, requiring lifelong B12 injections.

q: A nurse is teaching a client with GERD how to control reflux at home. Which pairing of instructions is correct?
o: Lie flat for 2 to 3 hours after meals — avoid caffeine, chocolate, peppermint, and fatty or fried foods
Lie down with the head of the bed flat after meals — avoid high-fiber foods and drink whole milk between meals
Stay upright 2 to 3 hours after meals — avoid caffeine, chocolate, peppermint, and fatty or fried foods
Stay upright 2 to 3 hours after meals — sip peppermint tea and eat chocolate at bedtime to soothe the stomach
r: STAYING UPRIGHT 2–3 HOURS AFTER MEALS AND ELEVATING THE HOB REDUCE REFLUX. Trigger foods (caffeine, chocolate, peppermint, fatty/fried/spicy foods, alcohol) should be avoided. Lying down after eating raises intra-abdominal pressure and worsens reflux, so any option that has the client recline after meals is wrong.

q: Chronic GERD can progress to Barrett esophagus, which is clinically significant because it:
o: Always resolves with antacids
Increases the risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma
Is a contagious bacterial infection
Directly causes duodenal ulcers
r: Barrett esophagus is metaplastic change from chronic acid exposure and is a premalignant condition that raises the risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma; it requires surveillance endoscopy.

q: Which assessment is the priority in the immediate postoperative period after a radical neck dissection?
o: Pain level
Airway patency
Nutritional status
Body image concerns
r: Airway is the priority — edema can obstruct the airway. Keep the HOB elevated to reduce swelling and support drainage; also monitor flaps/drains and for carotid rupture.

q: The most common cause of chronic gastritis and peptic ulcer disease is:
o: Emotional stress alone
Helicobacter pylori infection
Caffeine intake
Lactose intolerance
r: H. pylori and NSAID use are the two leading causes of gastritis and PUD. H. pylori is treated with combination (triple) therapy including antibiotics and a PPI.

q: Which is the hallmark presenting symptom of esophageal cancer?
o: Sudden weight gain
Progressive dysphagia with unintentional weight loss
Bright red bloody diarrhea
Isolated mild heartburn
r: Progressive dysphagia (solids, then liquids) with weight loss is the classic presentation. It is often diagnosed late, so new/worsening dysphagia should always be evaluated.

q: A client on continuous NG suction is at greatest risk for which acid-base and electrolyte imbalance?
o: Metabolic acidosis with hyperkalemia
Metabolic alkalosis with hypokalemia
Respiratory acidosis
Respiratory alkalosis
r: Continuous NG suction removes acidic gastric contents, causing metabolic alkalosis and loss of potassium (hypokalemia). Strict I&O monitoring is essential.

q: Which instruction is appropriate for a client with a hiatal hernia?
o: Lie down immediately after eating
Eat three large meals daily
Eat small, frequent meals and avoid tight clothing
Increase caffeine and carbonated beverages
r: Small frequent meals, staying upright after eating, elevating the HOB for sleep, weight loss, and avoiding tight clothing and trigger foods reduce reflux symptoms.

q: Which are the greatest risk factors for oral and oropharyngeal cancer?
o: High dairy and gluten intake
Tobacco and alcohol use
Excess caffeine
Chronic NSAID use
r: Tobacco (all forms) and alcohol are the leading risk factors and act synergistically; HPV and sun exposure (lip) also contribute. A non-healing mouth sore is a warning sign.

q: A client with suspected appendicitis suddenly reports that the severe pain is gone. The nurse recognizes this may indicate:
o: The appendix is healing
Rupture (perforation) of the appendix
Effective pain control
Simple constipation
r: Sudden relief of pain in appendicitis suggests the appendix has ruptured. Diffuse pain then returns as peritonitis develops — this is an emergency and must be reported.

q: Which interventions are CONTRAINDICATED in a client with suspected appendicitis? Select all that apply.
o: Applying heat to the abdomen
Administering an enema
Giving a laxative
Keeping the client NPO
Starting IV fluids
r: Heat, enemas, and laxatives can increase peristalsis/pressure and cause rupture — all contraindicated. Keeping the client NPO and starting IV fluids are appropriate and expected.

q: The next bag of TPN is not yet available from the pharmacy. The nurse should:
o: Stop the infusion and flush the line
Hang dextrose 10% in water (D10W)
Run normal saline wide open
Slow the empty bag to keep-vein-open
r: To prevent rebound hypoglycemia, hang D10W (or per policy) until the next TPN bag arrives — never abruptly stop TPN.

q: Which actions reflect safe administration of total parenteral nutrition (TPN)? Select all that apply.
o: Use a dedicated central line
Change the tubing and bag every 24 hours
Monitor blood glucose regularly
Increase the rate to 'catch up' if behind
Infuse via an electronic infusion pump
r: TPN uses a dedicated central line, tubing/bag changed q24h, regular glucose monitoring, and a pump. Never speed up or slow down to catch up — it causes glucose swings.

q: During an episode of acute diverticulitis, the appropriate diet is:
o: High fiber started immediately
Clear liquids / low fiber with bowel rest
High roughage with nuts and seeds
A full regular diet
r: Acute diverticulitis is treated with bowel rest — clear liquids/low fiber (NPO if severe), then gradual advancement. HIGH fiber is for prevention (diverticulosis), not the acute flare.

q: A client with ulcerative colitis develops abdominal distension, fever, and tachycardia with decreased bowel sounds. The nurse suspects:
o: Hemorrhoids
Toxic megacolon
Dumping syndrome
Appendicitis
r: Toxic megacolon is a life-threatening complication of UC — marked distension, fever, and tachycardia with risk of perforation. It must be reported immediately.

q: A colonoscopy is contraindicated during which condition?
o: Routine colorectal screening
Acute diverticulitis
Work-up of unexplained anemia
Polyp surveillance
r: During acute diverticulitis, colonoscopy (and enemas) are contraindicated due to perforation risk. It is performed later, after the inflammation resolves.

q: Which finding would NOT be expected in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)?
o: Abdominal pain relieved by defecation
Bloating
Alternating diarrhea and constipation
Bloody stools with weight loss
r: IBS is a functional disorder with NO structural damage — bleeding, weight loss, or fever are red flags that point to IBD or another organic disease and warrant work-up.

q: The only effective treatment for celiac disease is:
o: A low-fat diet
A lifelong strict gluten-free diet
A course of antibiotics
Lactose avoidance
r: Celiac disease is an autoimmune reaction to gluten. A lifelong strict gluten-free diet (no wheat, barley, rye) is the only treatment; even small amounts damage the intestinal villi.

q: Which pairing correctly contrasts the presentation of a small bowel obstruction with that of a large bowel obstruction?
o: Small bowel obstruction — early, profuse vomiting; large bowel obstruction — marked abdominal distension
Small bowel obstruction — early vomiting with marked distension; large bowel obstruction — late vomiting with minimal distension
Small bowel obstruction — vomiting that is late or absent; large bowel obstruction — minimal abdominal distension
Small bowel obstruction — marked abdominal distension; large bowel obstruction — early, profuse vomiting
r: SBO: EARLY, PROFUSE VOMITING (may be bilious/fecal) WITH LESS DISTENSION. LBO: VOMITING IS LATE/ABSENT WITH MARKED DISTENSION. Both are managed with NPO + NG decompression. Marked distension with little or no vomiting points to the large bowel, not the small bowel.

q: Priority management of a mechanical bowel obstruction includes:
o: A high-fiber diet
NPO status with NG decompression
Oral laxatives
Ambulation with enemas
r: Bowel obstruction is managed with NPO, NG tube decompression, IV fluids and electrolyte replacement, and monitoring for strangulation/perforation while awaiting possible surgery.

q: Which finding is most associated with left-sided colorectal cancer?
o: Sudden weight gain
Narrow 'pencil-shaped' stools and a change in bowel habits
Bright red hematemesis
Jaundice and clay-colored stools
r: Left-sided lesions narrow the lumen, causing pencil-shaped stools and changes in bowel habits. A change in bowel habits and rectal bleeding should always be investigated.

q: Which are priorities for a client with an acute GI bleed? Select all that apply.
o: Establish two large-bore IV lines
Monitor vital signs for signs of shock
Keep the client NPO
Provide a large meal to maintain strength
Prepare for endoscopy to locate the bleed
r: Airway/breathing/circulation first: two large-bore IVs, fluids/blood, monitor for shock, keep NPO, and prepare for endoscopy. Feeding a large meal is inappropriate during an active bleed.

q: Compared with a colostomy, an ileostomy places the client at greater risk for:
o: Constipation
Dehydration and electrolyte imbalance
Very formed stool
Rectal bleeding
r: Ileostomy output is liquid, constant, and enzyme-rich, so dehydration, electrolyte loss, and peristomal skin breakdown are key risks. Increased fluids and electrolytes are taught.

q: A healthy, newly created stoma should appear:
o: Pale and dry
Pink to red and moist
Dark purple
Black
r: A healthy stoma is pink/red and moist. Pale suggests poor perfusion; dark purple or black indicates ischemia/necrosis and must be reported immediately.

q: Which statement correctly matches the diet to the stage of diverticular disease?
o: Diverticulosis — clear liquids until the pouches resolve; acute diverticulitis — regular diet as tolerated
Diverticulosis — high-fiber diet to prevent flares; acute diverticulitis — high-fiber diet with added bran
Diverticulosis — low-fiber or clear-liquid diet; acute diverticulitis — high-fiber diet to prevent flares
Diverticulosis — high-fiber diet to prevent flares; acute diverticulitis — low-fiber or clear-liquid diet for bowel rest
r: DiverticulOSIS (pouches, prevention) → HIGH FIBER ON. DiverticulITIS (acute inflammation) → FIBER OFF / bowel rest, then rebuild fiber after healing. Adding bran during an acute flare would worsen the inflammation rather than prevent it.

q: A rigid, board-like abdomen with rebound tenderness and absent bowel sounds most likely indicates:
o: Constipation
Peritonitis
Irritable bowel syndrome
Internal hemorrhoids
r: These are classic signs of peritonitis, a life-threatening emergency from perforation/leak. Management includes NPO, NG decompression, IV fluids/antibiotics, and surgery.

q: Which points should the nurse include when teaching a client to prevent constipation? Select all that apply.
o: Increase dietary fiber gradually
Increase fluid intake
Increase physical activity
Ignore the urge to defecate until convenient
Establish a regular toileting routine
r: Fiber, fluids, activity, responding to the urge, and a regular routine prevent constipation. Ignoring the urge worsens constipation and promotes straining.

q: A client has Clostridioides difficile–associated diarrhea. Which precautions are required?
o: Alcohol-based hand rub only
Contact precautions with soap-and-water hand hygiene
Standard precautions only
Airborne precautions
r: C. difficile spores are not killed by alcohol gel — use contact precautions and wash hands with soap and water. Priorities also include fluid/electrolyte balance and skin care.

q: Which finding in a client with an abdominal hernia requires immediate attention?
o: A reducible bulge that appears with coughing
A bulge that flattens when lying down
Severe pain with a firm, tender, non-reducible bulge
Mild discomfort when lifting
r: A firm, tender, non-reducible bulge with severe pain suggests strangulation (blood supply cut off) — a surgical emergency, often with signs of bowel obstruction.

q: A client is scheduled for an esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD). Which action is most important for the nurse to confirm before the procedure?
o: Confirm the client has been NPO for at least 8 hours
Encourage the client to eat a high-fiber meal
Administer a cleansing enema
Have the client ambulate in the hallway
r: NPO status prevents aspiration and allows clear visualization of the upper GI mucosa; the other actions are irrelevant to EGD preparation.

q: Following an EGD, which assessment finding must the nurse verify before allowing the client to eat or drink?
o: Return of the gag reflex
Presence of bowel sounds
Ability to void
Stable temperature
r: The throat is anesthetized for the scope, so the gag reflex must return before oral intake to prevent aspiration.

q: After inserting a nasogastric tube, which method is the most reliable for confirming correct placement before initiating feedings?
o: Radiographic (X-ray) confirmation
Auscultating air injected into the tube
Placing the tube tip in water to check for bubbling
Measuring the external tube length only
r: X-ray is the gold standard for verifying NG tube placement; auscultation and bubbling are unreliable and unsafe indicators.

q: Which intervention best reduces the risk of aspiration during nasogastric tube feedings?
o: Elevate the head of the bed 30 to 45 degrees
Position the client flat during the feeding
Administer the feeding as rapidly as possible
Withhold all water flushes
r: Elevating the head of the bed uses gravity to reduce reflux and aspiration; lying flat and rapid infusion increase aspiration risk.

q: To maintain patency of an enteral feeding tube, which action should the nurse take?
o: Flush the tube with 30 mL of water before and after feedings
Instill carbonated cola to dissolve residue
Crush and add enteric-coated tablets to the formula
Clamp the tube between feedings without flushing
r: Routine water flushes before and after feedings prevent clogging; cola is not evidence-based and enteric-coated tablets should never be crushed.

q: The nurse must give several oral medications through a client's feeding tube. Which action is correct?
o: Flush the tube with water between each medication
Crush sustained-release capsules and mix them together
Combine all medications in one syringe
Add the medications directly into the feeding formula bag
r: Medications are given separately with water flushes between them to prevent interactions and clogging; sustained-release forms must not be crushed.

q: When teaching a client about preventing dental caries, which instruction should the nurse include?
o: Limit sugary foods and brush with fluoride toothpaste
Rinse with a sugar-sweetened mouthwash daily
Brush only once weekly to avoid enamel wear
Avoid dental checkups unless pain occurs
r: Reducing dietary sugar and using fluoride are the cornerstones of caries prevention; the other options promote decay or delay care.

q: Which intervention should the nurse include in the plan of care for a client with sialadenitis?
o: Encourage hydration and use of sialagogues such as sour candies
Restrict all oral fluids to rest the gland
Apply cold compresses and massage away from the gland
Discourage mouth care to reduce stimulation
r: Hydration, sialagogues, warm compresses, gland massage, and good oral hygiene promote salivary flow and resolve sialadenitis; fluid restriction worsens it.

q: Which factor places a client at greatest risk for oropharyngeal cancer?
o: Combined tobacco and alcohol use
A high-fiber diet
Frequent dental cleanings
Chewing sugar-free gum
r: Tobacco and alcohol (and HPV) are the leading risk factors for oropharyngeal cancer and act synergistically; the other options are protective or neutral.

q: Which assessment is the nursing priority during the immediate postoperative period following a radical neck dissection?
o: Airway patency and respiratory status
Bowel sounds
Urine color
Calf tenderness
r: Edema, bleeding, and secretions can compromise the airway after neck surgery, making airway and breathing the top priority.

q: A client with achalasia reports difficulty swallowing. Which statement about achalasia is accurate?
o: The lower esophageal sphincter fails to relax, causing dysphagia to both solids and liquids
Only solid foods cause difficulty swallowing
It results from excessive gastric acid production
It is permanently cured with antacids
r: In achalasia the LES does not relax and esophageal peristalsis is impaired, producing dysphagia for both solids and liquids.

q: Which instruction should the nurse give a client with a hiatal hernia to reduce symptoms?
o: Eat small, frequent meals and avoid lying down for about 1 hour after eating
Lie down immediately after meals
Eat one large meal in the evening
Wear a tight abdominal binder
r: Small frequent meals and remaining upright after eating reduce reflux; large meals, recumbency, and abdominal pressure worsen symptoms.

q: Which food should the nurse advise a client with GERD to avoid?
o: Chocolate
Oatmeal
Baked chicken
Plain white rice
r: Chocolate relaxes the lower esophageal sphincter and promotes reflux; the other foods are low in fat and reflux-friendly.

q: The nurse teaches a client about omeprazole for GERD. Which instruction is correct?
o: Take the medication 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast
Take it only when heartburn occurs
Take it immediately after the largest meal
Crush the capsule and dissolve it in cola
r: Proton pump inhibitors work best taken before the first meal so acid pumps are inhibited during eating; they are scheduled, not as-needed, drugs.

q: A client with long-standing GERD is diagnosed with Barrett esophagus. How should the nurse explain this condition?
o: Normal squamous cells are replaced by columnar cells, a premalignant change
It is a benign condition requiring no follow-up
It means the GERD has been cured
It is an acute infection of the esophagus
r: Barrett esophagus is metaplasia of normal squamous epithelium to columnar epithelium and is a premalignant change requiring surveillance.

q: Which is the most common initial manifestation of esophageal cancer?
o: Progressive dysphagia, first with solids then with liquids
Sudden severe hematemesis
Painless jaundice
Projectile vomiting
r: Esophageal cancer typically presents with progressive dysphagia and weight loss as the tumor narrows the lumen.

q: The nurse explains that an EGD allows the provider to do which of the following?
o: Directly visualize and biopsy the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum
Examine the colon and rectum
Measure liver enzyme levels
Image the biliary ducts only
r: EGD is direct endoscopic visualization of the upper GI tract that also permits biopsy; it does not evaluate the colon or biliary tree.

q: When irrigating a nasogastric tube used for gastric decompression, which solution should the nurse use?
o: Normal saline
Sterile water
Tap water with added potassium
Half-strength hydrogen peroxide
r: Isotonic normal saline is used to irrigate NG tubes to avoid electrolyte depletion that hypotonic water can cause with gastric suction.

q: Which finding at a gastrostomy tube site should the nurse report as a sign of infection?
o: Redness, warmth, and purulent drainage around the site
A small amount of clear serous drainage on insertion day
Intact skin with no drainage
The external bumper resting lightly against the skin
r: Erythema, warmth, and purulent drainage indicate infection and require reporting; small serous drainage and intact skin are expected.

q: Which is a potential complication of chronic, untreated GERD?
o: Esophageal stricture
Gallstones
Diverticulitis
Acute appendicitis
r: Chronic acid exposure leads to esophagitis, stricture, and Barrett esophagus; the other conditions are unrelated to reflux.

q: A client who had a radical neck dissection suddenly has bright red bleeding from the surgical site. What is the nurse's immediate action?
o: Apply direct pressure to the site and call for emergency help
Document and reassess in 15 minutes
Offer the client oral fluids
Leave to gather supplies before intervening
r: Bright red bleeding may signal carotid artery rupture, a surgical emergency requiring immediate direct pressure and summoning help.

q: Which condition most increases a client's risk for developing esophageal adenocarcinoma?
o: Barrett esophagus
Lactose intolerance
Occasional gastritis
Appendicitis
r: Barrett esophagus is a premalignant metaplasia that markedly raises the risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma.

q: Which statement accurately describes a sliding hiatal hernia?
o: The gastroesophageal junction and part of the stomach slide up into the thorax
The junction stays in place while the fundus rolls up beside the esophagus
The entire stomach herniates and twists in the chest
It never causes reflux symptoms
r: In a sliding (type I) hiatal hernia the gastroesophageal junction and upper stomach move above the diaphragm; a paraesophageal hernia is the rolling type.

q: Which intervention helps prevent parotitis in an older postoperative client?
o: Encourage adequate hydration and frequent oral hygiene
Restrict fluids to rest the glands
Provide only a bland diet requiring no chewing
Withhold mouth care to reduce stimulation
r: Hydration, oral care, and chewing stimulate salivary flow and prevent stasis that leads to parotitis; dehydration and poor oral care promote it.

q: Which finding should the nurse recognize as an early warning sign of oral cancer?
o: A painless oral ulcer or leukoplakia that does not heal
Bright red gums after flossing
Temporary tongue soreness after eating citrus
Occasional morning bad breath
r: A nonhealing oral lesion or leukoplakia is a classic early sign of oral cancer and warrants evaluation; the other findings are benign.

q: A client with a complete esophageal obstruction is at greatest risk for which complication?
o: Aspiration of saliva and secretions
Constipation
Urinary retention
Hyperglycemia
r: When the esophagus is obstructed, the client cannot swallow saliva, creating a high risk for aspiration and airway compromise.

q: What is the recommended follow-up for a client diagnosed with Barrett esophagus?
o: Periodic surveillance endoscopy with biopsies
Annual colonoscopy
Monthly barium enema
No further follow-up is needed
r: Because Barrett esophagus is premalignant, periodic surveillance EGD with biopsy is done to detect dysplasia or early cancer.

q: The nurse is teaching a client with GERD about lifestyle modifications. Which instructions should be included? Select all that apply.
o: Elevate the head of the bed on 6- to 8-inch blocks
Avoid eating within 2 to 3 hours of bedtime
Lose weight if overweight
Lie down after meals to aid digestion
Reduce caffeine and alcohol intake
Wear tight-fitting clothing around the waist
r: Elevating the head of the bed, avoiding late meals, weight loss, and reducing caffeine and alcohol decrease reflux; lying down and tight clothing increase intra-abdominal pressure and reflux.

q: Which nursing actions are appropriate when caring for a client with a nasogastric tube for decompression? Select all that apply.
o: Verify placement before use
Provide frequent oral and nasal care
Secure the tube to avoid pressure on the nares
Irrigate with normal saline as ordered
Permanently clamp the tube when drainage slows
Keep the head of the bed flat at all times
r: Confirming placement, oral and nasal care, protecting the nares, and saline irrigation are correct; clamping decompression tubes and keeping the client flat are unsafe.

q: Which interventions reduce the risk of aspiration in a client receiving continuous tube feedings? Select all that apply.
o: Keep the head of the bed elevated at least 30 degrees
Verify tube placement per protocol
Monitor for signs of intolerance such as abdominal distension
Lay the client flat during feedings
Assess gastric residual per facility policy
Infuse the feeding as a rapid bolus each hour
r: Head-of-bed elevation, placement verification, monitoring tolerance, and checking residuals prevent aspiration; lying flat and rapid bolusing increase the risk.

q: Which interventions are appropriate in the postoperative care of a client following a radical neck dissection? Select all that apply.
o: Monitor airway patency and respiratory status
Position in semi-Fowler to reduce edema and promote drainage
Assess surgical drains for amount and character of output
Keep emergency airway equipment at the bedside
Encourage vigorous neck range-of-motion immediately
Monitor for signs of carotid artery rupture
r: Airway monitoring, semi-Fowler positioning, drain assessment, bedside airway equipment, and watching for carotid rupture are essential; vigorous immediate neck ROM stresses the suture line and is contraindicated.

q: Which factors increase a client's risk for dental caries? Select all that apply.
o: Frequent intake of sugary or sticky foods
Inadequate fluoride exposure
Poor oral hygiene
Xerostomia (dry mouth)
Drinking plain water between meals
Regular use of fluoride toothpaste
r: Dietary sugar, low fluoride, poor hygiene, and dry mouth promote decay; plain water and fluoride toothpaste are protective.

q: Which are risk factors for esophageal cancer? Select all that apply.
o: Chronic GERD and Barrett esophagus
Heavy alcohol use
Tobacco use
Obesity
High intake of fresh fruits and vegetables
Regular physical activity
r: Chronic reflux with Barrett changes, alcohol, tobacco, and obesity raise esophageal cancer risk; a diet high in produce and activity are protective.

q: Which clinical manifestations are commonly associated with a hiatal hernia? Select all that apply.
o: Heartburn (pyrosis)
Regurgitation
Dysphagia
Feeling of fullness after eating
Painless rectal bleeding
Chronic watery diarrhea
r: Hiatal hernia commonly causes heartburn, regurgitation, dysphagia, and postprandial fullness; rectal bleeding and diarrhea are not typical features.

q: GERD results from an incompetent structure and produces a classic hallmark symptom. Which pairing is correct?
o: Incompetent pyloric sphincter — pyrosis (heartburn)
Incompetent lower esophageal sphincter — pyrosis (heartburn)
Incompetent upper esophageal sphincter — projectile vomiting
Incompetent lower esophageal sphincter — melena
r: A weak or incompetent LOWER ESOPHAGEAL SPHINCTER allows gastric contents to reflux, producing PYROSIS (HEARTBURN) as the classic symptom. The pyloric sphincter guards the stomach outlet and is not the structure involved in GERD.

q: Before starting an intermittent nasogastric feeding, which pairing of client position and placement verification is correct?
o: High-Fowler position — auscultate over the epigastrium while injecting air into the tube
Trendelenburg position — auscultate over the epigastrium while injecting air into the tube
High-Fowler position — check the pH of the gastric aspirate
Supine position — check the pH of the gastric aspirate
r: HIGH-FOWLER POSITIONING REDUCES ASPIRATION RISK, AND CHECKING ASPIRATE pH IS A RELIABLE BEDSIDE METHOD TO HELP CONFIRM GASTRIC PLACEMENT. Auscultating injected air is no longer considered a reliable way to verify tube placement.

q: Which pairing correctly describes how the throat is prepared for an EGD and the related nursing precaution afterward?
o: Topical local anesthetic spray — offer clear liquids as soon as the client is awake and alert
Topical antiseptic spray — keep the client NPO for a full 24 hours after the procedure
Intravenous paralytic agent — keep the client NPO until the gag reflex returns
Topical local anesthetic spray — keep the client NPO until the gag reflex returns
r: A TOPICAL LOCAL ANESTHETIC SUPPRESSES THE GAG REFLEX, SO THE CLIENT MUST REMAIN NPO UNTIL IT RETURNS to prevent aspiration. Being awake and alert is not enough — the gag reflex itself must return before anything is given by mouth.

q: A client with a duodenal ulcer describes the typical pain pattern. Which statement is most characteristic of duodenal ulcer pain?
o: Burning pain 30 to 60 minutes after eating that worsens with food
Gnawing pain 2 to 3 hours after meals that is relieved by eating
Pain only during the act of swallowing solid foods
Constant left-sided pain unrelated to meals
r: Duodenal ulcer pain classically occurs 2 to 3 hours after meals and at night, and is relieved by food or antacids because food buffers the acid. Gastric ulcer pain typically worsens with eating.

q: A client with a gastric ulcer is being taught about the pain pattern. The nurse explains that gastric ulcer pain typically:
o: Is relieved promptly by eating a meal
Occurs 30 to 60 minutes after eating and may worsen with food
Awakens the client between 1 and 2 AM every night
Is completely absent when the stomach is empty
r: Gastric ulcer pain usually occurs 30 to 60 minutes after eating and is often aggravated by food, which is why clients may lose weight. Nighttime pain relieved by food is more typical of duodenal ulcers.

q: A client with an upper GI bleed vomits bright red blood. The nurse documents this finding using which term?
o: Melena
Hematochezia
Hematemesis
Steatorrhea
r: Hematemesis is the vomiting of blood and is more commonly associated with gastric ulcers. Melena (black, tarry stools) reflects digested blood and is more common with duodenal ulcers.

q: A client with a bleeding duodenal ulcer is most likely to present with which stool finding?
o: Bright red blood coating the stool
Black, tarry stools (melena)
Clay-colored stools
Green, mucus-filled stools
r: Melena, or black tarry stools, results from blood digested during transit through the GI tract and is more characteristic of duodenal ulcer bleeding. Hematemesis is seen more often with gastric ulcers.

q: A client suddenly develops severe, sharp midepigastric pain and a rigid, boardlike abdomen. The nurse suspects which complication of peptic ulcer disease?
o: Dumping syndrome
Pyloric obstruction
Perforation
Pernicious anemia
r: Sudden severe pain with a rigid, boardlike abdomen indicates perforation and peritonitis, a surgical emergency. This requires immediate notification of the provider.

q: A client reports frequent use of NSAIDs for chronic joint pain. The nurse explains that NSAIDs contribute to gastritis and ulcers primarily by:
o: Increasing production of protective mucus
Inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis that protects the gastric mucosa
Neutralizing gastric acid
Slowing gastric emptying
r: NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase and reduce prostaglandin synthesis, decreasing the protective mucus and bicarbonate barrier of the gastric mucosa. This makes the mucosa vulnerable to acid injury.

q: A client is diagnosed with Helicobacter pylori-associated gastritis. The nurse anticipates a treatment regimen that includes:
o: A single antibiotic for 3 days
A proton pump inhibitor combined with two antibiotics
Lifelong corticosteroid therapy
An antacid taken only as needed
r: H. pylori infection is treated with combination therapy, typically a PPI plus two antibiotics (such as clarithromycin and amoxicillin) for 10 to 14 days. A single antibiotic promotes resistance and is inadequate.

q: Which client is at greatest risk for developing acute gastritis?
o: A client who eats small frequent meals
A client who drinks large amounts of alcohol and takes daily aspirin
A client who takes a daily multivitamin
A client with a high-fiber diet
r: Alcohol and aspirin are direct irritants to the gastric mucosa and are common causes of acute gastritis. Small frequent meals and fiber are not risk factors.

q: A client with chronic atrophic gastritis develops pernicious anemia. The nurse understands this occurs because the stomach fails to produce:
o: Hydrochloric acid only
Intrinsic factor needed to absorb vitamin B12
Pepsinogen for protein digestion
Gastrin for acid regulation
r: Chronic gastritis destroys the parietal cells that secrete intrinsic factor, which is required for vitamin B12 absorption in the ileum. Without intrinsic factor, B12 cannot be absorbed and pernicious anemia results.

q: A client with pernicious anemia asks how the condition will be treated. The nurse's best response is:
o: You will take oral iron tablets with each meal.
You will need lifelong vitamin B12 injections.
A short course of antibiotics will cure it.
Increasing dietary folic acid will resolve it.
r: Because pernicious anemia results from lack of intrinsic factor, oral B12 cannot be absorbed, so lifelong intramuscular B12 replacement is required. Iron and folic acid do not correct a B12 deficiency.

q: Which neurologic finding should the nurse expect in a client with untreated pernicious anemia?
o: Bilateral hand tremors relieved by rest
Numbness and tingling (paresthesias) of the hands and feet
Sudden one-sided facial droop
Seizure activity
r: Vitamin B12 deficiency affects myelin, producing paresthesias of the extremities, gait problems, and impaired proprioception. These neurologic changes distinguish B12 deficiency from other anemias.

q: The nurse assessing a client with pernicious anemia would expect the tongue to appear:
o: Coated and white
Beefy red, smooth, and sore
Black and hairy
Pale with deep fissures only
r: Glossitis with a smooth, beefy-red, sore tongue is a classic finding in pernicious anemia due to B12 deficiency. This reflects atrophy of the papillae.

q: A client who had a partial gastrectomy reports weakness, dizziness, sweating, and palpitations 20 minutes after eating. The nurse recognizes these as signs of:
o: Late dumping syndrome
Early dumping syndrome
Bile reflux gastritis
Afferent loop syndrome
r: Early dumping syndrome occurs 15 to 30 minutes after eating when hypertonic chyme rapidly enters the jejunum, pulling fluid into the bowel and causing vasomotor symptoms. Late dumping involves reactive hypoglycemia 1 to 3 hours after eating.

q: Which dietary instruction should the nurse give to a client with dumping syndrome?
o: Drink large amounts of fluid with each meal
Eat three large high-carbohydrate meals daily
Eat small, frequent meals that are high in protein and low in simple sugars
Sit upright for two hours after each meal
r: Clients with dumping syndrome should eat small, frequent meals high in protein and fat and low in simple carbohydrates to slow gastric emptying. Fluids should be taken between rather than with meals, and lying down after eating helps.

q: A client with dumping syndrome asks about fluid intake. The nurse should instruct the client to:
o: Drink at least 8 ounces of water with every meal
Avoid fluids with meals and drink between meals instead
Drink concentrated fruit juices for quick energy
Limit total daily fluids to 500 mL
r: Fluids taken with meals speed gastric emptying and worsen dumping symptoms, so fluids should be consumed between meals. Concentrated sugars should also be avoided.

q: A client with dumping syndrome experiences sweating, tremor, and confusion about 2 hours after eating. The nurse attributes this late dumping symptom to:
o: Rapid rise in blood glucose
Reactive hypoglycemia from excess insulin release
Dehydration from vomiting
Gastric acid rebound
r: Late dumping syndrome occurs 1 to 3 hours after eating when a rapid carbohydrate load triggers excessive insulin secretion, leading to reactive hypoglycemia. Symptoms include sweating, shakiness, and confusion.

q: Which early clinical manifestation of gastric cancer makes early detection difficult?
o: Severe hematemesis
Vague symptoms such as indigestion and early satiety
Boardlike rigid abdomen
Projectile vomiting
r: Gastric cancer often produces vague, nonspecific early symptoms such as indigestion, early satiety, and anorexia, which delays diagnosis. More dramatic signs appear only in advanced disease.

q: During assessment of a client with suspected advanced gastric cancer, the nurse palpates an enlarged, hard lymph node in the left supraclavicular area. The nurse recognizes this as:
o: Rovsing sign
Virchow node
McBurney point
Cullen sign
r: An enlarged left supraclavicular node (Virchow node) is a classic sign of metastatic gastric cancer. It reflects spread of disease through the thoracic duct.

q: Which factor in a client's history increases the risk for gastric cancer?
o: A diet high in fresh fruits and vegetables
Chronic H. pylori infection and a diet high in smoked or salted foods
Regular aerobic exercise
Lifelong vegetarian diet
r: Chronic H. pylori infection, pernicious anemia, and diets high in smoked, salted, or nitrate-containing foods are established risk factors for gastric cancer. Fruits and vegetables are protective.

q: After a total gastrectomy, the nurse teaches the client that lifelong supplementation will be required for which vitamin?
o: Vitamin C
Vitamin B12
Vitamin K
Vitamin D
r: Total gastrectomy removes the parietal cells that produce intrinsic factor, so the client can no longer absorb vitamin B12 and needs lifelong parenteral B12. Without it, the client develops pernicious anemia.

q: A client returns from a partial gastrectomy with an NG tube. Four hours postoperatively the nurse notes the drainage has changed from bright red to dark brown. The nurse should:
o: Immediately irrigate the tube with cold saline
Recognize this as an expected finding and continue monitoring
Reposition the NG tube to increase drainage
Clamp the tube and notify the surgeon
r: Drainage is expected to be bright red in the first several hours and then darken to brown within about 24 hours as bleeding subsides. The nurse should not reposition or irrigate the NG tube after gastric surgery without a specific order.

q: A client's NG tube stops draining after a subtotal gastrectomy. What is the nurse's priority action?
o: Advance the NG tube 5 cm into the stomach
Reposition or manipulate the tube at the suture line
Notify the surgeon rather than repositioning the tube
Remove the tube and replace it with a new one
r: After gastric surgery the NG tube must not be repositioned or manipulated because it could disrupt the suture line. The nurse should notify the surgeon, who will reposition the tube if needed.

q: A client is prescribed sucralfate (Carafate) for a duodenal ulcer. The nurse instructs the client to take it:
o: With meals and at bedtime
1 hour before meals and at bedtime on an empty stomach
Only when pain occurs
Immediately after taking an antacid
r: Sucralfate forms a protective barrier over the ulcer and works best on an empty stomach, taken 1 hour before meals and at bedtime. Antacids should be separated by at least 30 minutes because they can interfere with its action.

q: A client taking omeprazole for peptic ulcer disease asks how the medication works. The nurse explains that proton pump inhibitors:
o: Neutralize acid already in the stomach
Block the final step of gastric acid production
Coat the ulcer with a protective gel
Kill H. pylori bacteria directly
r: Proton pump inhibitors irreversibly block the H+/K+ ATPase (proton pump) of the parietal cells, the final step in acid secretion. This markedly reduces gastric acid production.

q: A client with acute gastritis is NPO and reports nausea. As symptoms subside, the nurse anticipates the diet will progress by first introducing:
o: A high-fat, spicy meal
Clear liquids, then bland solids as tolerated
Caffeinated beverages
Carbonated soft drinks
r: After acute gastritis, the diet is advanced gradually beginning with clear liquids and progressing to bland foods as tolerated. Irritants such as spicy foods, caffeine, and alcohol are avoided.

q: The nurse is teaching a client with peptic ulcer disease about lifestyle and dietary modifications. Which instructions should be included? Select all that apply.
o: Avoid caffeine, alcohol, and smoking
Take NSAIDs on an empty stomach for faster relief
Eat regular meals and avoid skipping meals
Report black, tarry stools to the provider
Use aspirin freely for any pain
Manage stress with relaxation techniques
r: Clients with PUD should avoid gastric irritants (caffeine, alcohol, smoking, NSAIDs, and aspirin), eat regular meals, manage stress, and report signs of bleeding such as melena. NSAIDs and aspirin worsen mucosal injury and should not be taken freely.

q: A nurse is teaching a client with dumping syndrome after gastrectomy. Which statements should be included in the teaching? Select all that apply.
o: Lie down for 20 to 30 minutes after eating
Increase intake of simple sugars and concentrated sweets
Eat small, frequent meals throughout the day
Drink fluids between meals rather than with meals
Increase protein and fat in the diet
Consume high-carbohydrate liquids with each meal
r: Dumping syndrome is managed by lying down after meals, eating small frequent meals high in protein and fat, and separating fluids from meals. Simple sugars and concentrated carbohydrates should be avoided because they worsen rapid gastric emptying.

q: Which nursing interventions are appropriate for a client immediately following a subtotal gastrectomy? Select all that apply.
o: Monitor NG drainage for color and amount
Reposition the NG tube every 4 hours for patency
Assess for signs of dumping syndrome when feedings resume
Encourage early ambulation to prevent complications
Splint the incision during coughing and deep breathing
Keep the client flat without a pillow for 48 hours
r: Postoperative gastrectomy care includes monitoring NG drainage, assessing for dumping syndrome, promoting ambulation, and splinting the incision during coughing. The NG tube must not be repositioned because it can disrupt the suture line.

q: Which clinical manifestations would the nurse expect in a client with pernicious anemia? Select all that apply.
o: Beefy, red, sore tongue
Paresthesias of the hands and feet
Pallor and fatigue
Increased appetite with weight gain
Difficulty with balance and gait
Bright red rectal bleeding
r: Pernicious anemia from B12 deficiency causes glossitis, paresthesias, pallor, fatigue, and neurologic changes such as impaired balance and gait. Weight gain and rectal bleeding are not features of this condition.

q: The nurse is identifying causes of acute gastritis. Which factors can precipitate acute gastritis? Select all that apply.
o: Chronic NSAID use
Excessive alcohol intake
H. pylori infection
Ingestion of a corrosive substance
Daily intake of dietary fiber
Severe physiologic stress such as burns
r: Acute gastritis can be caused by NSAIDs, alcohol, H. pylori, corrosive substances, and severe stress (which can produce stress-related mucosal disease). Dietary fiber does not cause gastritis.

q: A client with peptic ulcer disease is at risk for complications. Which findings should the nurse recognize as signs of a possible GI bleed? Select all that apply.
o: Coffee-ground emesis
Black, tarry stools
Hypotension and tachycardia
Bright pink, well-perfused mucous membranes
Decreasing hemoglobin and hematocrit
Increased blood pressure with bradycardia
r: GI bleeding is indicated by coffee-ground emesis, melena, hypotension, tachycardia, and falling hemoglobin and hematocrit. Increasing blood pressure with bradycardia and well-perfused mucosa are not signs of active bleeding.

q: Which factors are associated with an increased risk of gastric cancer? Select all that apply.
o: Chronic H. pylori infection
History of pernicious anemia
Diet high in smoked and salted foods
Regular consumption of fresh fruits and vegetables
Smoking
Family history of gastric cancer
r: Risk factors for gastric cancer include chronic H. pylori infection, pernicious anemia, diets high in smoked or salted foods, smoking, and family history. Diets rich in fresh fruits and vegetables are protective.

q: A client reports epigastric pain that occurs 2 to 3 hours after eating and is relieved by food. Which pairing of ulcer type and typical bleeding presentation is correct?
o: Duodenal ulcer — melena
Duodenal ulcer — hematemesis
Gastric ulcer — melena
Gastric ulcer — hematemesis
r: DUODENAL ULCER PAIN OCCURS 2 TO 3 HOURS AFTER MEALS AND IS RELIEVED BY FOOD, AND ITS BLEEDING TYPICALLY PRESENTS AS MELENA. Gastric ulcers are more often associated with hematemesis, so choosing hematemesis pairs the duodenal ulcer with the gastric ulcer's usual bleeding pattern.

q: Pernicious anemia develops when the stomach fails to secrete a substance that is required for absorption of a specific nutrient in the ileum. Which pairing is correct?
o: Hydrochloric acid — vitamin B12
Intrinsic factor — vitamin B12
Intrinsic factor — folic acid
Pepsinogen — iron
r: INTRINSIC FACTOR, SECRETED BY GASTRIC PARIETAL CELLS, IS ESSENTIAL FOR ABSORPTION OF VITAMIN B12 IN THE TERMINAL ILEUM. Loss of intrinsic factor leads to B12 deficiency and pernicious anemia. Folic acid does not require intrinsic factor for its absorption.

q: Which pairing correctly describes the timing of early dumping syndrome and the mechanism that causes it?
o: 1 to 3 hours after eating — a reactive release of insulin producing hypoglycemia
15 to 30 minutes after eating — rapid emptying of hypotonic chyme into the jejunum
2 to 3 hours after eating — rapid emptying of hypertonic chyme into the jejunum
15 to 30 minutes after eating — rapid emptying of hypertonic chyme into the jejunum
r: EARLY DUMPING SYNDROME OCCURS 15 TO 30 MINUTES AFTER EATING WHEN HYPERTONIC CHYME RAPIDLY ENTERS THE JEJUNUM, drawing fluid into the bowel lumen. This fluid shift produces vasomotor and GI symptoms. Symptoms appearing 1 to 3 hours after eating from a reactive insulin release describe LATE dumping, not early.

q: A patient is scheduled for a colonoscopy in the morning. Which instruction should the nurse include in the pre-procedure teaching?
o: Eat a high-fiber breakfast the morning of the test
Drink the prescribed bowel-cleansing solution until stool is clear yellow liquid
Take all routine medications with a full glass of milk
Maintain a regular diet until midnight before the procedure
r: Adequate bowel prep is confirmed when rectal effluent is clear to light-yellow liquid, ensuring the mucosa can be visualized. A clear liquid diet, not solids or fiber, is required before the test.

q: Two hours after a colonoscopy with moderate sedation, which finding requires the nurse to notify the provider immediately?
o: Passing a moderate amount of flatus
Firm, distended abdomen with rigidity and severe pain
Feeling drowsy and slightly groggy
Small amount of blood on the first bowel movement
r: A rigid, distended, painful abdomen suggests bowel perforation, a serious complication of colonoscopy that requires immediate intervention. Flatus, mild drowsiness, and minimal bleeding are expected.

q: The nurse reviews the chart before a scheduled colonoscopy. Which finding is a contraindication to the procedure?
o: History of diverticulosis
Suspected acute diverticulitis with peritoneal signs
Family history of colorectal cancer
Chronic constipation
r: Colonoscopy is contraindicated during acute diverticulitis or suspected perforation/peritonitis because insufflation and scope advancement increase perforation risk. Diverticulosis and cancer history are common indications.

q: A patient is receiving total parenteral nutrition (TPN) through a central line. Which nursing action ensures safe administration?
o: Piggyback antibiotics into the TPN line to save access
Use the TPN lumen exclusively for the nutrition solution
Slow the rate to make up doses if the bag runs behind
Change the bag every 72 hours to reduce cost
r: TPN requires a dedicated line or lumen to prevent incompatibilities and infection; no other medications or infusions should share it. Bags and tubing are changed every 24 hours.

q: While a central line dressing is being changed, the patient suddenly becomes dyspneic, anxious, and hypotensive. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Place the patient in high-Fowler position
Turn the patient to the left side in Trendelenburg position
Increase the TPN infusion rate
Apply a warm compress to the insertion site
r: These are signs of air embolism; positioning the patient on the left side in Trendelenburg traps air in the right atrium away from the pulmonary outflow tract. Oxygen and provider notification follow.

q: A severely malnourished patient is started on TPN. On day two the patient develops muscle weakness, confusion, and a serum phosphate of 1.2 mg/dL. The nurse recognizes this as:
o: Refeeding syndrome
Air embolism
Catheter sepsis
Rebound hypoglycemia
r: Refeeding syndrome occurs when nutrition is reintroduced too quickly, causing intracellular shifts of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium. TPN should be advanced slowly with close electrolyte monitoring.

q: The next bag of TPN is not yet available from the pharmacy and the current bag has finished. Which action should the nurse take to prevent hypoglycemia?
o: Flush the line with normal saline and wait
Hang 10% dextrose (D10W) at the same rate until TPN arrives
Discontinue the infusion and clamp the line
Give the patient a carbohydrate snack by mouth
r: Abrupt cessation of high-dextrose TPN can cause rebound hypoglycemia, so D10W is infused at the same rate until the next bag arrives. This maintains a steady glucose supply.

q: A patient with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) asks the nurse to explain the disorder. Which statement is most accurate?
o: IBS is an autoimmune disease that destroys the intestinal lining
IBS is a functional disorder with no structural or inflammatory damage
IBS commonly causes rectal bleeding and unintentional weight loss
IBS always progresses to colon cancer without surgery
r: IBS is a functional GI disorder characterized by altered motility and abdominal pain without structural, inflammatory, or biochemical abnormalities. Bleeding and weight loss are red flags that suggest another diagnosis.

q: A patient newly diagnosed with celiac disease asks how long the diet must be followed. The nurse's best response is:
o: Only until symptoms resolve
For six months, then gluten can be reintroduced slowly
A strict gluten-free diet must be followed for life
Only when experiencing diarrhea
r: Celiac disease requires lifelong elimination of gluten because any exposure triggers immune-mediated damage to the small intestinal villi. There is no cure other than permanent dietary avoidance.

q: A patient with suspected appendicitis reports increasing right lower quadrant pain. Which intervention should the nurse avoid?
o: Keeping the patient NPO
Applying a heating pad to the abdomen
Positioning the patient with knees flexed
Monitoring vital signs frequently
r: Heat, enemas, and laxatives are contraindicated in appendicitis because they increase circulation and peristalsis, raising the risk of rupture. The patient is kept NPO in preparation for possible surgery.

q: A patient with appendicitis who was in severe pain suddenly reports that the pain has stopped. How should the nurse interpret this change?
o: The appendicitis has resolved on its own
The appendix may have ruptured
The pain medication is finally working
The diagnosis was incorrect
r: A sudden cessation of pain in appendicitis often signals rupture, after which diffuse peritonitis and worsening symptoms typically follow. This is an emergency requiring immediate notification of the provider.

q: Which assessment finding is most characteristic of peritonitis?
o: Soft, nontender abdomen with active bowel sounds
Board-like rigid abdomen with rebound tenderness
Hyperactive bowel sounds and loose stools
Localized pain relieved by eating
r: Peritonitis produces a rigid, board-like abdomen with rebound tenderness, guarding, and absent bowel sounds from paralytic ileus. It is a life-threatening inflammation of the peritoneal cavity.

q: A patient with diverticulosis (without inflammation) asks about diet. Which recommendation is appropriate?
o: Follow a low-residue, low-fiber diet
Increase dietary fiber and fluid intake
Remain on clear liquids indefinitely
Avoid all whole grains permanently
r: For diverticulosis without acute inflammation, a high-fiber diet with adequate fluids promotes regular bowel movements and reduces intraluminal pressure. This helps prevent progression to diverticulitis.

q: A patient is admitted with acute diverticulitis. Which diet order does the nurse anticipate during the acute phase?
o: High-fiber diet with bran
Clear liquids or NPO to rest the bowel
Regular diet as tolerated
High-residue diet with raw vegetables
r: During acute diverticulitis the bowel is rested with NPO status or clear liquids, then advanced to low-fiber foods as inflammation subsides. High fiber is reintroduced only after recovery.

q: Which position will the nurse assist the patient into at the start of a colonoscopy?
o: Prone with arms above the head
Left lateral (Sims) position with knees drawn up
Supine with legs fully extended
High-Fowler position
r: The left lateral (Sims) position with knees flexed allows the scope to be advanced through the sigmoid colon and is the standard starting position. The patient may be repositioned as the scope advances.

q: A patient receiving TPN should have which laboratory value monitored most closely for the common metabolic complication?
o: Serum blood glucose
Serum amylase
Urine specific gravity
Serum bilirubin
r: Hyperglycemia is the most common metabolic complication of the high dextrose concentration in TPN, so blood glucose is monitored frequently. Insulin may be added or given per sliding scale.

q: Which dietary teaching is appropriate for a patient with IBS and constipation-predominant symptoms?
o: Eliminate all fiber from the diet
Gradually increase soluble fiber and fluids
Drink large amounts of caffeinated beverages
Consume carbonated drinks with meals
r: Gradually increasing soluble fiber and fluid intake helps manage constipation-predominant IBS, while gas-producing foods, caffeine, and carbonated drinks are limited. Trigger foods vary and are identified individually.

q: A patient with celiac disease is reading food labels. Which grain must be avoided?
o: Rice
Corn
Barley
Quinoa
r: Barley contains gluten, as do wheat and rye, and must be strictly avoided in celiac disease. Rice, corn, and quinoa are naturally gluten-free alternatives.

q: When assessing a patient with suspected appendicitis, the nurse locates McBurney point at which location?
o: Left upper quadrant near the spleen
Midway between the umbilicus and the right anterior iliac spine
Directly over the umbilicus
Right upper quadrant below the ribs
r: McBurney point, located about one-third the distance from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus, is the classic site of maximal tenderness in appendicitis. Rebound tenderness may also be present here.

q: A postoperative patient develops peritonitis. Which nursing action is the priority?
o: Encourage ambulation to relieve gas
Maintain NPO status and prepare for IV fluids and antibiotics
Offer a high-fiber meal
Apply heat to the abdomen for comfort
r: Peritonitis management focuses on bowel rest with NPO status, fluid resuscitation, and IV antibiotics to control infection and prevent septic shock. Nasogastric decompression is often added.

q: Which complication should the nurse monitor for in a patient with acute diverticulitis?
o: Villous atrophy
Perforation and peritonitis
Gluten intolerance
Air embolism
r: An inflamed diverticulum can perforate, leading to abscess, peritonitis, or fistula formation. Signs of worsening pain, fever, and abdominal rigidity require immediate attention.

q: Which patient teaching helps prevent complications of diverticulosis?
o: Strain during bowel movements to fully empty
Eat a high-fiber diet and drink plenty of fluids daily
Use laxatives every day
Limit physical activity
r: A high-fiber diet, adequate hydration, and regular exercise keep stool soft and lower colonic pressure, reducing the chance of diverticular inflammation. Straining and chronic laxative use raise intraluminal pressure.

q: Which statement by a patient indicates the bowel prep for colonoscopy has been adequate?
o: My last stool was brown and formed
My rectal output is now clear yellowish liquid
I still have some solid stool but feel done
I stopped the solution because I felt full
r: Clear to yellow watery output indicates the colon is sufficiently cleansed for visualization. Remaining solid or brown stool means prep is incomplete and may require additional solution.

q: How often should the nurse change the TPN tubing and filter to reduce infection risk?
o: Every 8 hours
Every 24 hours
Every 72 hours
Once weekly
r: Because TPN is a rich medium for bacterial and fungal growth, the tubing, filter, and bag are changed every 24 hours. Strict aseptic technique is used at all times.

q: A patient with diarrhea-predominant IBS is prescribed a medication. Which additional teaching point should the nurse emphasize?
o: Report any new rectal bleeding or unexplained weight loss
Expect the medication to cure the disorder permanently
Fever is a normal part of IBS flares
Increase caffeine intake to regulate the bowel
r: Rectal bleeding, weight loss, and fever are not features of IBS and warrant further evaluation for organic disease. IBS is managed, not cured, through diet, stress reduction, and symptom-targeted medications.

q: Which long-term complication is a patient with poorly controlled celiac disease at risk for?
o: Malabsorption with iron and vitamin deficiencies
Rebound hyperglycemia
Air embolism
Increased gluten tolerance over time
r: Ongoing villous atrophy impairs nutrient absorption, leading to anemia, osteoporosis, and vitamin deficiencies. Strict gluten avoidance allows the mucosa to heal and prevents these complications.

q: Which diagnostic finding supports a diagnosis of appendicitis?
o: Decreased white blood cell count
Elevated white blood cell count with left shift
Low serum glucose
Elevated serum amylase only
r: Appendicitis typically causes leukocytosis with a left shift reflecting acute inflammation, and CT imaging confirms an enlarged appendix. A normal or low WBC would be atypical.

q: Which vital sign trend would the nurse expect as peritonitis progresses toward septic shock?
o: Rising blood pressure and bradycardia
Tachycardia, fever, and falling blood pressure
Normal temperature and slow respirations
Bradypnea with hypertension
r: As peritonitis advances, the patient develops tachycardia, fever, hypotension, and rapid shallow breathing consistent with sepsis. Prompt fluid resuscitation and antibiotics are essential.

q: The nurse is teaching a patient preparing for a colonoscopy. Which instructions should be included? Select all that apply.
o: Begin a clear liquid diet the day before the procedure
Avoid red or purple liquids during the prep
Complete the entire bowel-cleansing solution as prescribed
Eat a steak dinner the night before
Arrange for someone to drive you home after sedation
Continue taking iron supplements up to the procedure
r: Clear liquid diet, avoiding red/purple dyes that mimic blood, completing the prep, and arranging a driver after sedation are all correct. Solid food and iron (which darkens stool and coats the mucosa) should be stopped before the test.

q: Which complications should the nurse monitor for in a patient receiving TPN through a central line? Select all that apply.
o: Hyperglycemia
Catheter-related bloodstream infection
Air embolism
Refeeding syndrome
Gluten sensitivity
Fluid overload
r: Hyperglycemia, infection, air embolism, refeeding syndrome, and fluid overload are all recognized TPN complications. Gluten sensitivity is unrelated to intravenous nutrition.

q: Which self-management strategies should the nurse teach a patient with IBS? Select all that apply.
o: Identify and avoid personal trigger foods
Practice stress-reduction techniques
Eat regular, unhurried meals
Increase intake of gas-producing foods
Keep a food and symptom diary
Maintain adequate fluid intake
r: Avoiding triggers, managing stress, eating regularly, tracking symptoms, and staying hydrated all help control IBS. Gas-producing foods worsen bloating and should be limited.

q: Which foods should a patient with celiac disease avoid? Select all that apply.
o: Whole wheat bread
Barley soup
Rye crackers
Fresh apples
Regular pasta
Grilled chicken
r: Wheat, barley, and rye all contain gluten, so bread, barley soup, rye crackers, and regular pasta must be avoided. Fresh fruit and plain grilled meats are naturally gluten-free.

q: Which clinical manifestations would the nurse expect in a patient with acute appendicitis? Select all that apply.
o: Periumbilical pain that shifts to the right lower quadrant
Rebound tenderness at McBurney point
Low-grade fever
Anorexia and nausea
Painless rectal bleeding
Chronic weight loss over months
r: Migrating RLQ pain, rebound tenderness, low-grade fever, and anorexia with nausea are classic appendicitis findings. Painless bleeding and chronic weight loss are not features of acute appendicitis.

q: Which findings support a diagnosis of peritonitis? Select all that apply.
o: Rigid, board-like abdomen
Rebound tenderness
Absent or diminished bowel sounds
Fever and tachycardia
Increased appetite
Abdominal guarding
r: Rigidity, rebound tenderness, absent bowel sounds, fever, tachycardia, and guarding all indicate peritoneal inflammation. Appetite is lost, not increased, in peritonitis.

q: A patient is recovering from acute diverticulitis and the inflammation has resolved. Which dietary instructions should the nurse give as the diet advances? Select all that apply.
o: Begin with clear liquids during the acute flare
Progress to low-fiber foods as symptoms improve
Gradually add high-fiber foods after full recovery
Eat nuts and popcorn during the acute phase
Increase fluid intake as fiber is added
Return to a high-fiber diet immediately during the flare
r: Acute diverticulitis is managed with bowel rest, then low fiber, then gradual return to high fiber with increased fluids once healed. High fiber, nuts, and popcorn are avoided during the acute inflammatory phase.

q: Which measures help prevent the progression of diverticulosis to diverticulitis? Select all that apply.
o: Consume a diet high in fiber
Drink adequate fluids each day
Engage in regular physical activity
Use daily stimulant laxatives routinely
Avoid straining during defecation
Maintain a healthy body weight
r: High fiber, hydration, exercise, avoiding straining, and healthy weight all lower colonic pressure and prevent inflammation. Routine daily laxative use is not recommended for prevention.

q: A nurse is planning nutrition for two clients: one with diverticulosis and one with acute diverticulitis. Which client-to-diet pairing is correct?
o: Diverticulosis — permanent low-residue diet; acute diverticulitis — regular diet as tolerated
Diverticulosis — clear liquids or NPO for bowel rest; acute diverticulitis — high-fiber diet
Diverticulosis — high-fiber diet; acute diverticulitis — clear liquids or NPO for bowel rest
Diverticulosis — high-fiber diet; acute diverticulitis — high-fiber diet with added bran
r: Diverticulosis without inflammation is managed with HIGH FIBER to reduce colonic pressure, while ACUTE DIVERTICULITIS REQUIRES BOWEL REST until the inflammation resolves. The diets are essentially opposite. Fiber is added back only after the acute inflammation has healed.

q: The next bag of TPN is delayed and the current bag is nearly empty. Which pairing of nursing action and rationale is correct?
o: Hang 0.9% sodium chloride at the same rate — to prevent rebound hypoglycemia
Hang D10W at the same rate — to prevent rebound hypoglycemia
Stop the infusion and flush the line — to prevent rebound hyperglycemia
Hang D10W at the same rate — to prevent fluid volume overload
r: Abruptly stopping high-dextrose TPN can cause REBOUND HYPOGLYCEMIA, SO D10W IS INFUSED AT THE SAME RATE until the next bag is available. This maintains a stable glucose level. Normal saline contains no dextrose and would not prevent the fall in blood glucose.

q: A client being observed for appendicitis suddenly reports that the abdominal pain has stopped. Which pairing of finding and interpretation is correct?
o: Sudden relief of pain — rupture (perforation) of the appendix, requiring immediate provider notification
Sudden increase in pain — rupture (perforation) of the appendix, requiring immediate provider notification
Sudden relief of pain — the appendiceal obstruction has cleared on its own, so surgery can be delayed
Sudden relief of pain — the inflammation is resolving, so the nurse can continue routine monitoring
r: A SUDDEN RELIEF OF PAIN IN APPENDICITIS OFTEN SIGNALS THAT THE APPENDIX HAS RUPTURED, which is soon followed by diffuse peritonitis. This constitutes a surgical emergency. Reading the pain relief as improvement is the classic trap and delays urgent care.

q: A nurse reviews the pathology of a client newly diagnosed with Crohn disease. Which statement best describes the typical pattern of intestinal involvement?
o: Continuous inflammation beginning at the rectum
Skip lesions that can occur anywhere from mouth to anus
Inflammation limited to the mucosal layer of the colon
Involvement restricted to the sigmoid colon
r: Crohn disease produces discontinuous skip lesions that may affect any part of the GI tract from mouth to anus, unlike the continuous colonic pattern of ulcerative colitis.

q: Which feature distinguishes the inflammation of Crohn disease from that of ulcerative colitis?
o: It involves only the innermost mucosal layer
It extends through the entire bowel wall (transmural)
It never leads to fistula formation
It is always confined to the rectum
r: Crohn inflammation is transmural, involving all layers of the bowel wall, which predisposes to fistulas, strictures, and abscesses; UC inflammation is limited to the mucosa and submucosa.

q: A client with ulcerative colitis is most likely to report which characteristic stool pattern?
o: Steatorrhea with foul-smelling fatty stools
Frequent bloody, mucus-containing diarrhea
Ribbon-like constipated stools
Clay-colored stools
r: Ulcerative colitis classically causes frequent bloody diarrhea with mucus because of continuous mucosal ulceration of the colon and rectum.

q: A client with severe ulcerative colitis develops abdominal distention, fever, tachycardia, and a rigid abdomen. The nurse suspects which life-threatening complication?
o: Toxic megacolon
Diverticulitis
Appendicitis
Internal hemorrhoids
r: Toxic megacolon is massive colonic dilation with systemic toxicity that can lead to perforation and is a feared complication of ulcerative colitis.

q: A client asks whether surgery will cure their Crohn disease. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
o: Removing the colon completely cures Crohn disease.
Surgery does not cure Crohn disease because it can recur anywhere in the GI tract.
Surgery is never used for Crohn disease.
A single operation permanently eliminates all inflammation.
r: Because Crohn disease can affect any segment of the GI tract, surgery relieves complications but is not curative, and disease often recurs at anastomotic sites.

q: Which statement about surgical treatment of ulcerative colitis is correct?
o: Total proctocolectomy is considered curative
Surgery only worsens the disease
Ulcerative colitis cannot be treated surgically
Partial resection eliminates all recurrence in Crohn disease
r: Because ulcerative colitis is confined to the colon and rectum, a total proctocolectomy removes the diseased tissue and is curative.

q: A client with an acute exacerbation of Crohn disease is prescribed dietary teaching. Which recommendation is most appropriate during a flare?
o: A high-fiber, high-residue diet
A low-residue, high-protein, high-calorie diet
A high-fat diet to increase calories
Unlimited raw fruits and vegetables
r: During an IBD flare a low-residue, high-protein, high-calorie diet reduces bowel stimulation while meeting increased nutritional needs; high-fiber and raw produce worsen symptoms.

q: A client with a suspected small bowel obstruction is assessed. Which manifestation would the nurse expect early in the course?
o: Profuse, early vomiting
Marked distention with minimal vomiting
Ribbon-like stools
Absence of any cramping pain
r: Small bowel obstruction causes early and often profuse vomiting with minimal distention, whereas large bowel obstruction produces significant distention with later, feculent vomiting.

q: A client with a high small bowel obstruction has been vomiting for two days. Which acid-base imbalance is most likely?
o: Metabolic alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis
Respiratory alkalosis
Respiratory acidosis
r: Loss of hydrochloric acid from persistent vomiting of gastric contents in a high SBO leads to metabolic alkalosis.

q: A nasogastric tube is placed for a client with a bowel obstruction. What is the primary purpose of the tube?
o: To provide enteral nutrition
To decompress the bowel by removing gas and fluid
To administer a bowel prep
To measure gastric pH hourly
r: An NG tube attached to suction decompresses the GI tract by removing accumulated gas and fluid proximal to the obstruction, relieving distention and vomiting.

q: Which finding best supports a diagnosis of paralytic (functional) ileus rather than a mechanical obstruction?
o: High-pitched, hyperactive bowel sounds
Absent or hypoactive bowel sounds without a physical blockage
A palpable tumor at the obstruction site
Visible peristaltic waves
r: Paralytic ileus results from loss of peristalsis (often after surgery, opioids, or hypokalemia) and produces absent or diminished bowel sounds without a mechanical blockage.

q: Compared with a small bowel obstruction, a large bowel obstruction more commonly presents with which feature?
o: Rapid onset of severe vomiting
Gradual onset with pronounced abdominal distention
Early metabolic alkalosis
Minimal change in bowel elimination
r: Large bowel obstruction typically has a gradual onset with marked distention and constipation, and vomiting, if present, occurs late and may be feculent.

q: Which condition is the most common cause of a mechanical small bowel obstruction?
o: Postoperative adhesions
Hypokalemia
Opioid analgesic use
Recent general anesthesia
r: Adhesions from previous abdominal surgery are the most common cause of mechanical small bowel obstruction; hypokalemia, opioids, and anesthesia cause functional paralytic ileus.

q: A client reports narrow, pencil-shaped stools and a recent change in bowel habits. These findings are most concerning for cancer in which location?
o: The left (descending or sigmoid) colon
The stomach
The small intestine
The gallbladder
r: Left-sided colorectal tumors narrow the lumen and produce pencil-thin stools and altered bowel habits, whereas right-sided lesions more often cause occult bleeding and anemia.

q: Which symptom is often the earliest warning sign of colorectal cancer that the nurse should teach clients to report?
o: A persistent change in bowel habits
Sudden weight gain
Increased appetite
Bright yellow sclera
r: A persistent change in bowel habits, along with blood in the stool, is a classic early warning sign of colorectal cancer that warrants evaluation.

q: According to current guidelines, at what age should an average-risk adult begin screening for colorectal cancer?
o: Age 30
Age 45
Age 60
Age 70
r: Current guidelines recommend average-risk adults begin colorectal cancer screening at age 45, with colonoscopy the gold-standard test.

q: A provider orders a carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) level for a client with colorectal cancer. What is the primary use of this test?
o: To definitively diagnose colorectal cancer
To monitor treatment response and detect recurrence
To determine blood type before surgery
To measure liver enzyme function
r: CEA is a tumor marker used to monitor response to therapy and detect recurrence rather than to diagnose colorectal cancer, since it can be elevated in other conditions.

q: A nurse is caring for a client with a new sigmoid colostomy. Which stoma finding requires immediate notification of the provider?
o: A moist, beefy-red stoma
A dusky, dark purple stoma
Slight bleeding when cleaning the stoma
A stoma protruding slightly above the skin
r: A healthy stoma is pink to beefy-red and moist; a dusky, purple, or black stoma indicates ischemia or necrosis and must be reported immediately.

q: A client presents vomiting bright red blood. This finding, called hematemesis, indicates bleeding from which portion of the GI tract?
o: Upper GI tract (above the ligament of Treitz)
Lower GI tract
Sigmoid colon
Rectum only
r: Hematemesis reflects an upper GI source such as the esophagus, stomach, or duodenum, proximal to the ligament of Treitz.

q: A client passes black, tarry, foul-smelling stools. The nurse documents this as melena and recognizes it most commonly indicates:
o: A lower GI bleed in the rectum
An upper GI bleed with digested blood
Ingestion of a high-fiber meal
Normal stool coloration
r: Melena is black, tarry stool produced when blood from an upper GI source is digested as it passes through the intestines.

q: The passage of bright red blood from the rectum (hematochezia) most typically indicates bleeding from which source?
o: The lower GI tract
The stomach
The esophagus
The duodenum
r: Hematochezia, bright red blood per rectum, usually indicates a lower GI source such as the colon or rectum, though a brisk upper GI bleed can also cause it.

q: A client with an acute upper GI bleed is pale, diaphoretic, and hypotensive. Which intervention is the nurse's priority?
o: Obtain a detailed diet history
Establish two large-bore IV access sites for fluid resuscitation
Schedule an outpatient colonoscopy
Administer an oral iron supplement
r: The priority in an active GI bleed with signs of shock is airway, breathing, and circulation; establishing two large-bore IVs allows rapid fluid and blood replacement.

q: Which set of findings in a client with a GI bleed indicates hypovolemic shock?
o: Bradycardia and hypertension
Tachycardia, hypotension, cool clammy skin, and restlessness
Flushed warm skin and bounding pulses
Slow deep respirations and pink skin
r: Hypovolemic shock from blood loss produces tachycardia, hypotension, cool clammy skin, decreased urine output, and altered mental status such as restlessness.

q: Which condition is a common cause of an upper GI bleed?
o: Peptic ulcer disease
Diverticulosis of the sigmoid colon
Internal hemorrhoids
Colorectal polyps
r: Peptic ulcer disease and esophageal varices are leading causes of upper GI bleeding; diverticulosis, hemorrhoids, and polyps are lower GI sources.

q: A nurse is teaching about ulcerative colitis. Which characteristics are associated with this disorder? Select all that apply.
o: Continuous inflammation of the colon and rectum
Inflammation limited to the mucosa and submucosa
Skip lesions from mouth to anus
Frequent bloody diarrhea
Curable by total proctocolectomy
Common fistula and stricture formation
r: Ulcerative colitis causes continuous mucosal inflammation of the colon and rectum with bloody diarrhea and is cured by colectomy; skip lesions and fistulas are features of Crohn disease.

q: Which findings are characteristic of Crohn disease? Select all that apply.
o: Transmural inflammation of the bowel wall
Can involve any area from mouth to anus
Fistulas and strictures are common
Surgery is curative
Cobblestone appearance of the mucosa
Bleeding is always more severe than in ulcerative colitis
r: Crohn disease is transmural, can affect any part of the GI tract, and commonly causes fistulas, strictures, and a cobblestone mucosal appearance; it is not cured by surgery and bleeds less than UC.

q: A client is admitted with a small bowel obstruction. Which findings does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
o: Early, frequent vomiting
Colicky, cramping abdominal pain
High-pitched bowel sounds proximal to the obstruction
Metabolic alkalosis from vomiting
Passage of large amounts of normal stool
Dehydration and electrolyte imbalance
r: Small bowel obstruction causes early vomiting, cramping pain, high-pitched bowel sounds above the blockage, and fluid or electrolyte loss with metabolic alkalosis; obstipation, not normal stools, occurs.

q: Which factors increase a client's risk for developing colorectal cancer? Select all that apply.
o: Age older than 50
Diet high in red and processed meats
Long-standing inflammatory bowel disease
Family history of colorectal cancer
High intake of dietary fiber
Regular physical activity
r: Older age, high red or processed meat intake, chronic IBD, and family history raise colorectal cancer risk, whereas high fiber intake and physical activity are protective.

q: A client is admitted with an active upper GI bleed. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Establish two large-bore IV lines
Monitor vital signs frequently for signs of shock
Prepare to administer isotonic fluids and blood products
Encourage a large oral meal to maintain strength
Assess stools and emesis for blood
