Insert a nasogastric tube as ordered
r: Priorities in an acute GI bleed include large-bore IV access, frequent hemodynamic monitoring, fluid and blood replacement, monitoring output for blood, and NG placement; the client is kept NPO, not fed.

q: A nurse teaches a client about caring for a new colostomy. Which statements indicate correct understanding? Select all that apply.
o: A healthy stoma should look pink or beefy-red and moist.
I should report a stoma that turns dark purple or black.
I will empty the pouch when it is about one-third to one-half full.
The skin around my stoma should be kept clean and dry.
A little bleeding when I clean the stoma can occur because it is vascular.
A dusky, dark stoma is normal and needs no attention.
r: A healthy stoma is pink or red and moist, minor bleeding with cleaning is normal, and the pouch is emptied when one-third to one-half full; a dusky or black stoma signals ischemia and must be reported.

q: Which pairing correctly contrasts the pattern of inflammation in Crohn disease with that in ulcerative colitis?
o: Crohn disease — continuous mucosal inflammation confined to the colon and rectum; ulcerative colitis — transmural inflammation with skip lesions anywhere in the GI tract
Crohn disease — transmural inflammation confined to the colon and rectum; ulcerative colitis — mucosal skip lesions anywhere in the GI tract
Crohn disease — mucosal inflammation with skip lesions; ulcerative colitis — continuous transmural inflammation
Crohn disease — transmural inflammation with skip lesions anywhere in the GI tract; ulcerative colitis — continuous mucosal inflammation confined to the colon and rectum
r: CROHN DISEASE IS TRANSMURAL WITH DISCONTINUOUS SKIP LESIONS ANYWHERE IN THE GI TRACT, WHILE ULCERATIVE COLITIS IS CONTINUOUS MUCOSAL INFLAMMATION CONFINED TO THE COLON AND RECTUM. Depth is the discriminator: mucosa only points to UC, full thickness points to Crohn.

q: A client has a high small bowel obstruction. Which pairing of expected acid-base imbalance and vomiting pattern is correct?
o: Metabolic alkalosis — vomiting occurs late in the course or not at all
Metabolic alkalosis — vomiting occurs early in the course
Respiratory alkalosis — vomiting occurs late in the course or not at all
Metabolic acidosis — vomiting occurs early in the course
r: A high SBO produces EARLY VOMITING WITH LOSS OF ACIDIC GASTRIC CONTENTS, LEADING TO METABOLIC ALKALOSIS; large bowel obstructions vomit late if at all. Losing acid raises the pH, so acidosis is the wrong direction for this client.

q: Which pairing of GI bleeding term and its description is correct?
o: Melena — vomiting of blood from an upper GI source; hematemesis — black, tarry stool from digested blood
Hematemesis — vomiting of blood from an upper GI source; hematochezia — black, tarry stool from digested blood
Hematemesis — vomiting of blood from an upper GI source; melena — black, tarry stool from digested blood
Occult blood — vomiting of blood from an upper GI source; melena — bright red blood passed rectally
r: HEMATEMESIS IS VOMITED BLOOD FROM AN UPPER GI SOURCE, AND MELENA IS BLACK TARRY STOOL from digested upper GI blood. Hematochezia is a look-alike term but means bright red blood passed rectally, usually from a lower GI source.

q: A client reports having a hard, dry bowel movement every 4 to 5 days with straining. Which dietary recommendation should the nurse prioritize?
o: Increase intake of dietary fiber and water
Limit fluids to reduce bloating
Add more refined white bread and rice
Avoid fruits and raw vegetables
r: Increasing fiber and fluid intake adds bulk and softens stool, promoting normal peristalsis and easier evacuation.

q: A nurse is teaching a client about safe long-term management of chronic constipation. Which laxative type is generally safest for daily use?
o: Stimulant laxatives such as bisacodyl
Bulk-forming agents such as psyllium
Saline osmotic agents such as magnesium citrate
Mineral oil lubricant laxatives
r: Bulk-forming laxatives most closely mimic normal physiologic elimination and are preferred for long-term use, while stimulants can cause dependence.

q: A client has had frequent watery stools for 3 days. Which laboratory finding does the nurse most expect?
o: Hyperkalemia
Hypokalemia
Metabolic alkalosis
Hypernatremia
r: Prolonged diarrhea causes loss of potassium and bicarbonate in stool, leading to hypokalemia and metabolic acidosis.

q: A client is diagnosed with Clostridioides difficile infection. Which infection control measure is most appropriate?
o: Place the client on airborne precautions
Use alcohol-based hand rub after client contact
Perform hand hygiene with soap and water
Wear an N95 respirator when entering the room
r: C. difficile spores are not killed by alcohol-based sanitizer, so hand washing with soap and water plus contact precautions is required.

q: Which personal protective equipment does the nurse don before entering the room of a client with C. difficile?
o: Gown and gloves
N95 respirator and goggles
Gloves only
Surgical mask and gown
r: Contact precautions for C. difficile require a gown and gloves to prevent spore transmission on hands and clothing.

q: A nurse is caring for an older adult with fecal incontinence. Which intervention best protects skin integrity?
o: Apply a moisture barrier cream after cleansing
Use an indwelling urinary catheter
Restrict oral fluids to reduce stooling
Leave the perineal area open to air only
r: Cleansing promptly and applying a moisture barrier protects the perineal skin from breakdown caused by frequent exposure to stool.

q: A client with painful external hemorrhoids asks how to relieve discomfort at home. Which measure should the nurse recommend?
o: Sitting for long periods on a firm surface
Warm sitz baths several times daily
Using a strong stimulant laxative each morning
Applying ice packs for 20 minutes every hour indefinitely
r: Warm sitz baths increase blood flow, relax the anal sphincter, and relieve pain and swelling associated with hemorrhoids.

q: On a urine dipstick, what does a POSITIVE nitrite result indicate?
o: Absence of infection
Bacterial conversion of nitrates (UTI)
Dehydration
Kidney failure
r: Positive nitrites reflect bacteria converting urinary nitrates → nitrites — highly accurate for a UTI.

q: A specific gravity of 1.035 (normal 1.005–1.030) indicates the urine is:
o: Dilute
Normal concentration
Concentrated
Infected
r: Higher specific gravity = more concentrated urine (e.g., dehydration). Lower = dilute.

q: Which interventions support PSYCHOSOCIAL integrity for a client with functional incontinence? (SATA)
o: Involve client in scheduling toileting routines
Recommend complete social isolation
Use respectful, non-judgmental communication
Offer assistive devices to reach the bathroom
Minimize discussion to avoid discomfort
r: Promote autonomy, dignity, and trust. Isolation and ignoring the issue harm psychosocial health.

q: A client with CKD on erythropoietin develops which finding that indicates a COMPLICATION of therapy?
o: Potassium 3.5
Hemoglobin 11
Respiratory rate 16
r: EPO thickens blood → hypertension and clotting (DVT/PE/stroke). Rising Hgb is the expected effect, not a complication.

q: Which findings are expected with URGE incontinence? (SATA)
o: Sudden strong desire to void then involuntary loss
Small leakage with coughing/sneezing
Frequency and dysuria
Waking to urinate at night
Incomplete emptying despite voiding
r: Only the sudden-urge-then-loss describes urge incontinence. The others are stress, UTI, and overflow.

q: CKD client with 4+ edema, lung crackles, SOB, BP 178/98. Priority intervention?
o: Increase fluid intake
Give potassium supplements
Position supine
Administer prescribed loop diuretic
r: This is fluid overload affecting breathing (ABCs). Diuresis is the priority; the others worsen it.

q: Autosomal dominant PKD — which findings does the nurse expect?
o: Bradycardia and dry skin
Flank pain and hematuria
Jaundice and clay-colored stools
Petechiae and bleeding gums
r: Enlarging, blood-filled cysts cause flank pain and hematuria. The distractors point to thyroid, biliary, and platelet problems.

q: Discharge teaching on fluid overload in CKD — which statement needs MORE teaching?
o: I'll weigh myself daily for sudden gain
I can drink all I want as long as I avoid salty foods
I'll report ankle swelling or trouble breathing
I'll follow my prescribed fluid restriction
r: CKD clients need fluid restriction; unlimited fluids overload weak kidneys even without salt.

q: Assessing an AV graft before HD: no palpable thrill and no audible bruit. Priority action?
o: Reassess in 30 minutes
Apply warm compress and hand exercises
Notify the provider immediately
Proceed with dialysis using the graft
r: Absent thrill/bruit = clotted access = emergency. Notify the provider; the site cannot be used.

q: Which are risk factors for developing a UTI/cystitis? (SATA)
o: Recent cystoscopy
Adequate daily fluid intake
Shorter urethra than males
Urinating immediately after sex
Wiping back to front
History of diabetes mellitus
r: Instrumentation, short female urethra, back-to-front wiping, and glucosuria raise risk. Hydration and post-coital voiding are protective.

q: Which interventions reduce the risk of CAUTI? (SATA)
o: Prophylactic antibiotics
Keep bag below bladder level
Monitor for fever
Routine catheter irrigation
Remove catheter as soon as not needed
Keep tubing straight/unkinked
Perineal care every shift & PRN
r: Bundle = bag below bladder, early removal, no kinks, peri-care. Prophylactic antibiotics and routine irrigation are NOT done; monitoring fever detects but doesn't prevent.

q: Client with severe pain, nausea, and hematuria — which finding indicates RENAL COLIC?
o: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back
RUQ pain after a fatty meal
Severe sharp flank pain radiating to the groin
Central abdominal pain with distension and vomiting
r: Renal colic = flank pain radiating to the groin. Distractors suggest pancreatitis, cholecystitis, and bowel obstruction.

q: Client on peritoneal dialysis — which findings suggest PERITONITIS? (SATA)
o: Cloudy dialysate outflow
Abdominal pain/tenderness
Elevated WBC count
Clear, straw-colored dialysate
Fever
Bradycardia
Nausea and vomiting
r: Cloudy outflow, abd pain, ↑WBC, fever, N/V indicate peritonitis. Straw-colored outflow is normal; expect tachycardia, not bradycardia.

q: Why do CKD clients receive erythropoietin instead of iron or B12/folate for anemia?
o: They are iron deficient
Their kidneys can't produce erythropoietin
They have B12 deficiency
They need folate for RBCs
r: CKD anemia is from loss of the hormone erythropoietin, not a nutrient deficiency.

q: A client with heart failure needs dialysis. Why might an AV fistula be a poor choice?
o: It clots too easily
The high-flow shunt overworks a weak heart
It causes hyperkalemia
It can't filter potassium
r: An AV fistula adds a high-flow circuit the heart must pump; in HF this worsens failure, so PD is often preferred.

q: Which lab is the MOST accurate marker of kidney function?
o: BUN
Creatinine
Sodium
Specific gravity
r: Creatinine (and GFR) best reflect kidney function; BUN is affected by dehydration, diet, and bleeding.

q: A nurse reviews labs for a client in renal failure. Which electrolyte finding is expected?
o: Hypokalemia
Hyperkalemia
Hypophosphatemia
Hypercalcemia
r: Failing kidneys retain potassium and phosphate and lose calcium → hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia.

q: Renal failure most commonly causes which acid-base imbalance?
o: Metabolic acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis
Respiratory acidosis
Respiratory alkalosis
r: Kidneys can't excrete H⁺ or retain bicarbonate → metabolic acidosis.

q: Which are functions of the kidney? (SATA)
o: Activate vitamin D (calcitriol)
Produce erythropoietin
Regulate blood pressure
Produce insulin
Acid-base balance
r: Kidneys handle vitamin D activation, EPO, BP/renin, fluid/electrolytes, and acid-base. Insulin is pancreatic.

q: The primary clinical manifestation of bladder cancer is:
o: Dysuria
Gross, painless hematuria
Flank pain
Fever
r: Painless gross hematuria is the hallmark; smoking is the top risk factor.

q: After intravesical BCG immunotherapy for bladder cancer, the agent is:
o: Given IV over 1 hour
Instilled into the bladder and retained ~2 hours
Injected into the tumor
Taken orally daily
r: BCG is instilled into the bladder and held about 2 hours to prevent cancer recurrence.

q: Which urine finding is classic for post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?
o: Clear, dilute urine
Cola/reddish-brown urine
Glucosuria
Ketonuria
r: Glomerular inflammation causes hematuria → cola-colored urine, plus HTN, edema, and oliguria.

q: Which are part of the nephrotic syndrome picture? (SATA)
o: Massive proteinuria
Hypoalbuminemia
Edema
Hyperlipidemia
Polycythemia
r: Nephrotic syndrome = heavy proteinuria, low albumin, edema, and hyperlipidemia.

q: During the OLIGURIC phase of AKI, the nurse monitors most closely for:
o: Hypokalemia
Hyperkalemia and fluid overload
Dehydration
Hypoglycemia
r: Low urine output → potassium and fluid retention; hyperkalemia is life-threatening.

q: Which type of AKI results from prolonged hypotension or volume depletion?
o: Prerenal
Intrarenal
Postrenal
Functional
r: Prerenal AKI is from reduced perfusion; restoring volume early can reverse it before CKD develops.

q: A client with CKD has skin findings of urea crystals. This is called:
o: Uremic frost
Caput medusae
Asterixis
Spider angioma
r: Uremic frost = urea crystals on the skin from severe uremia in CKD.

q: Dietary teaching for CKD includes limiting which? (SATA)
o: Protein
Potassium
Phosphate
Sodium
Complex carbohydrates
r: Limit protein, K⁺, phosphate, Na⁺, and Mg; complex carbs are encouraged for calories.

q: Which client is the BEST candidate for peritoneal dialysis over hemodialysis?
o: A client with recent abdominal surgery
A client with heart failure
A client with peritonitis
A client with extensive abdominal adhesions
r: PD is gentler hemodynamically — good for HF. Abdominal pathology contraindicates it.

q: A hemodialysis client develops headache, nausea, and confusion during treatment. This suggests:
o: Disequilibrium syndrome
Air embolism
Hypoglycemia
Infection
r: Rapid solute/fluid shifts cause cerebral edema → disequilibrium syndrome; slow the exchange rate.

q: Warming peritoneal dialysate is done by:
o: Microwaving it
Using a warming device/dry heat (never microwave)
Adding hot water
Refrigerating then thawing
r: Warm dialysate with a designated warmer; never microwave (uneven heating/burns).

q: The HIGHEST nursing priority for a client with polycystic kidney disease is:
o: Pain control with NSAIDs
Controlling blood pressure
Fluid loading
Strict bed rest
r: BP control protects remaining kidney function; avoid NSAIDs (nephrotoxic).

q: A client passing a calcium oxalate stone should AVOID:
o: White bread
Spinach, chocolate, and black tea
Lean chicken
Apples
r: Oxalate-rich foods (spinach, cocoa/chocolate, black tea, beets, strawberries) promote oxalate stones.

q: After extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL), the nurse teaches the client to expect:
o: No urine changes
Hematuria and bruising at the site
Permanent flank numbness
Anuria for 24 hours
r: Hematuria and bruising are normal after ESWL; strain all urine for fragments.

q: Highest priority post-op assessment after a renal biopsy is:
o: Bowel sounds
Bleeding/hemorrhage
Pupil response
Capillary refill in toes
r: The kidney is highly vascular — monitor for hemorrhage and hematuria after biopsy.

q: Which signs point to pyelonephritis rather than simple cystitis? (SATA)
o: Flank/CVA tenderness
High fever and chills
Nausea and vomiting
Mild suprapubic discomfort only
r: Upper-tract (kidney) infection adds flank pain, high fever, chills, and N/V; risk of sepsis.

q: A new ileal conduit stoma should appear:
o: Pale and dry
Pink/red and moist
Dusky blue
Black
r: Healthy stoma = pink/red and moist. Dusky/dark = ischemia — report it. Mucus in urine is normal.

q: Normal BUN range?
o: 3–8 mg/dL
8–20 mg/dL
30–50 mg/dL
60–90 mg/dL
r: BUN ~8–20 mg/dL (some texts 10–20).

q: Creatinine above which value generally signals impaired kidneys?
r: Roughly >1.3 mg/dL suggests reduced kidney function ('critical kidney lab').

q: Urine output that signals kidney distress is:
o: <30 mL/hr
60 mL/hr
100 mL/hr
120 mL/hr
r: <30 mL/hr (or <0.5 mL/kg/hr) indicates inadequate perfusion/output.

q: Which dipstick pair is most consistent with a UTI?
o: Glucose + ketones
Leukocyte esterase + nitrites
Bilirubin + protein
pH + specific gravity
r: Leukocyte esterase (WBCs) + nitrites (bacteria) = UTI.

q: Thrill and bruit over an AV fistula indicate:
o: Infection
Clotting
Patency (good blood flow)
Rupture
r: Palpable thrill + audible bruit = patent, functioning access.

q: Best long-term way to prevent kidney stones?
o: Limit all calcium
Drink large amounts of water daily
Bed rest
High-protein diet
r: Generous water intake dilutes urine and prevents stone formation.

q: #1 and #2 causes of CKD?
o: Smoking and alcohol
Diabetes and hypertension
Infection and trauma
Cancer and stones
r: Diabetes is #1, hypertension #2.

q: Which lab is the MOST liver-specific marker of hepatocellular injury?
o: AST
ALT
ALP
Amylase
r: ALT is more specific to the liver than AST; both rise in hepatitis.

q: A rise in which lab best explains hepatic encephalopathy?
o: Bilirubin
Ammonia
Albumin
Amylase
r: The failing liver can't convert ammonia to urea → ammonia crosses the BBB causing encephalopathy.

q: Lactulose is titrated to achieve:
o: No bowel movements
2–3 soft stools per day
Watery diarrhea
One hard stool weekly
r: Lactulose traps and excretes ammonia in stool; goal is 2–3 soft stools/day.

q: Which are manifestations of cirrhosis? (SATA)
o: Jaundice
Ascites
Asterixis
Spider angiomas
Bradycardia
r: Cirrhosis produces jaundice, ascites, asterixis, spider angiomas, palmar erythema, bruising. Bradycardia isn't typical.

q: Priority for a client with ruptured esophageal varices?
o: Administer lactulose
Maintain airway and control hemorrhage
Encourage oral fluids
Give a high-protein meal
r: Bleeding varices are a life-threatening emergency — airway protection and hemorrhage control (octreotide, banding) come first.

q: Before a paracentesis, the nurse should:
o: Have the client void
Place the client flat
Give a laxative
Restrict the client to bed for 24 h first
r: Emptying the bladder lowers the risk of bladder puncture during paracentesis.

q: Which diuretic is preferred for cirrhotic ascites?
o: Furosemide alone
Spironolactone
Mannitol
Hydrochlorothiazide
r: Spironolactone (K⁺-sparing, anti-aldosterone) is first-line for ascites, often with a loop diuretic.

q: Which hepatitis virus is bloodborne with NO vaccine available?
o: Hepatitis A
Hepatitis B
Hepatitis C
Hepatitis E
r: Hep C is bloodborne and has no vaccine (but is curable with antivirals). A and B have vaccines.

q: Which hepatitis types are transmitted fecal-orally? (SATA)
o: Hepatitis A
Hepatitis B
Hepatitis C
Hepatitis E
r: A and E spread fecal-orally (the 'vowels' from the alimentary tract); B, C, D are bloodborne.

q: Classic risk profile for gallstones (cholelithiasis) — the '4 F's':
o: Fever, Fatigue, Flank, Fluid
Female, Forty, Fat, Fertile
Fast, Firm, Flat, Full
Frequent, Foamy, Flank, Fever
r: Female, Forty (40+), Fat (obesity), Fertile (multiparity/estrogen).

q: A positive Murphy's sign indicates:
o: Pancreatitis
Cholecystitis
Appendicitis
Cirrhosis
r: Inspiratory arrest on RUQ palpation = Murphy's sign = cholecystitis.

q: Which lab is MOST specific for acute pancreatitis?
o: Amylase
Lipase
ALT
Bilirubin
r: Lipase is more specific and stays elevated longer than amylase.

q: The cornerstone of managing acute pancreatitis is to:
o: Feed a high-fat diet
Keep the client NPO to rest the pancreas
Encourage large meals
Give pancreatic enzymes IV
r: NPO (± NG suction) reduces enzyme stimulation and rests the pancreas; add IV fluids and pain control.

q: Periumbilical bruising (Cullen's sign) and flank bruising (Grey Turner's sign) suggest:
o: Mild cholecystitis
Hemorrhagic pancreatitis
Hepatitis A
Simple gallstones
r: These bruising signs indicate severe/hemorrhagic pancreatitis.

q: Pancreatic enzyme replacement (pancrelipase) should be taken:
o: At bedtime only
With every meal and snack
Once a week
On an empty stomach
r: Enzymes must be taken with food to aid digestion/absorption; don't crush enteric-coated forms.

q: A major complication to monitor for AFTER an ERCP is:
o: Pancreatitis
Stroke
Deep vein thrombosis
Hyperglycemia
r: Post-ERCP pancreatitis is the key risk (severe pain, ↑ amylase/lipase); also watch perforation/bleeding and gag reflex.

q: After laparoscopic cholecystectomy, a common expected complaint is:
o: Severe flank pain
Right shoulder pain from CO₂ gas
Bloody urine
Loss of taste
r: CO₂ insufflation irritates the diaphragm → referred right shoulder pain; ambulation helps.

q: A client with a T-tube after open cholecystectomy — the drainage bag should be:
o: Above the gallbladder level
Below the gallbladder level
Clamped at all times
Irrigated hourly
r: Keep the T-tube below the surgical site for gravity drainage; record output and protect skin.

q: Which vitamins are commonly deficient in chronic liver disease? (SATA)
o: Vitamin A
Vitamin D
Vitamin K
Vitamin E
Vitamin C
r: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) need bile for absorption; vitamin K deficiency worsens bleeding.

q: Yellowing of skin/sclera from high bilirubin is called:
o: Cyanosis
Jaundice
Pallor
Erythema
r: Jaundice = elevated bilirubin.

q: The flapping hand tremor of hepatic encephalopathy is:
o: Asterixis
Clonus
Fasciculation
Chvostek's sign
r: Asterixis = flapping tremor from elevated ammonia.

q: Dilated, fragile veins in the esophagus that can hemorrhage are:
o: Hemorrhoids
Esophageal varices
Spider angiomas
Caput medusae
r: Portal hypertension causes esophageal varices that can rupture.

q: Which gut antibiotic is added to lactulose for encephalopathy?
o: Vancomycin
Rifaximin
Ceftriaxone
Metronidazole
r: Rifaximin reduces ammonia-producing gut bacteria.

q: Pancreatitis pain classically radiates to the:
o: Right shoulder
Back
Groin
Jaw
r: Epigastric/LUQ pain radiating to the back, worse after eating, relieved leaning forward.

q: Fatty, foul-smelling, floating stools from fat malabsorption are called:
o: Melena
Steatorrhea
Hematochezia
Tenesmus
r: Steatorrhea = fat in stool, seen in pancreatic/biliary disease.

q: Cholelithiasis means:
o: Inflammation of the gallbladder
Gallstones
Liver scarring
Bile duct cancer
r: Cholelithiasis = gallstones; cholecystitis = gallbladder inflammation.

q: Case 9A · Mrs. Alvarez, 68, has end-stage kidney disease and dialyzes 3×/week through a left-arm AV fistula. Which finding is the BEST sign the fistula is patent?
o: Strong palpable thrill and audible bruit
Absent pulse distal to the site
Cool, pale fingers on that hand
No sound heard over the site
r: A patent fistula has a palpable thrill (buzz) and audible bruit (whoosh). Absent thrill/bruit or poor distal perfusion signals clotting/complication.

q: Case 9B · Mrs. Alvarez (68) has end-stage kidney disease and dialyzes through a LEFT-arm AV fistula. Which action by a new nurse requires immediate intervention?
o: Placing the blood pressure cuff on the LEFT arm
Drawing blood from the right arm
Palpating the fistula for a thrill
Auscultating the fistula for a bruit
r: Never take BP, start IVs, or draw blood in the fistula arm — pressure can clot or rupture the access. Use the other arm.

q: Case 9C · Mrs. Alvarez (end-stage kidney disease) is 30 minutes into hemodialysis when she develops a headache, nausea, and confusion. The nurse suspects:
o: Disequilibrium syndrome
Air embolism
Hypoglycemia
A urinary tract infection
r: Rapid solute/fluid shifts pull water into brain cells → dialysis disequilibrium syndrome (HA, N/V, confusion, late seizures). Slow the exchange rate.

q: Case 9D · Mrs. Alvarez has end-stage kidney disease. Which lab findings would the nurse EXPECT? (SATA)
o: Elevated creatinine
Elevated potassium
Low hemoglobin
Low phosphorus
Elevated calcium
r: ESKD → ↑creatinine, ↑K⁺, ↑phosphorus, ↓calcium, and ↓hemoglobin (low erythropoietin). Phosphorus is high and calcium low — not the reverse.

q: Case 9E · Mr. Boyd is admitted after severe GI bleeding: BP 84/50, HR 122, urine output 15 mL/hr. Which type of acute kidney injury is most likely?
o: Prerenal
Intrarenal
Postrenal
Chronic
r: Hypovolemia/hypotension reduces kidney perfusion = prerenal AKI. Restoring volume early can reverse it before intrinsic damage.

q: Case 9F · Mr. Boyd developed acute kidney injury after severe GI bleeding and is now oliguric. Which value is the most immediate life threat?
o: Potassium 6.8 mEq/L
Sodium 138 mEq/L
Calcium 9.0 mg/dL
Hemoglobin 12 g/dL
r: Hyperkalemia (6.8) can cause fatal dysrhythmias — the priority in the oliguric phase. Watch telemetry for peaked T waves.

q: Case 9G · Mr. Boyd (AKI, oliguric phase after GI bleeding) shows tall, peaked T waves on the monitor. This reflects:
o: Hyperkalemia
Hypokalemia
Hypercalcemia
Hyponatremia
r: Peaked T waves are the classic ECG sign of hyperkalemia, common in the oliguric phase of AKI.

q: Case 9H · Ms. Chen has sudden severe flank pain radiating to the groin, hematuria, and vomiting. Which nursing actions are appropriate? (SATA)
o: Strain all urine
Administer prescribed analgesia
Encourage increased fluid intake
Restrict all fluids
Save any stone passed
r: Renal colic care: strain all urine and save stones, treat pain, and push fluids (~3 L/day) to help the stone pass. Fluids are encouraged, not restricted.

q: Case 9I · Ms. Chen passed a calcium oxalate stone. Which menu choice shows she understood the diet teaching?
o: Spinach salad with iced black tea
Baked chicken, rice, and an apple
Chocolate cake with strawberries
Beet salad with cocoa dressing
r: Oxalate stones: avoid spinach, black tea, chocolate/cocoa, beets, and strawberries. The chicken/rice/apple meal is low-oxalate.

q: Case 9J · An 82-year-old with a chronic indwelling catheter becomes acutely confused with T 101.8°F and HR 108. What does the nurse suspect FIRST?
o: Catheter-associated UTI / urosepsis
Normal aging
Dementia progression
Dehydration only
r: New confusion + fever in a catheterized older adult = CAUTI until proven otherwise; UTIs are a leading cause of sepsis in elders. Obtain a UA/culture and treat.

q: A client with CKD is scheduled for a CT with IV contrast. Which routine medication does the nurse plan to hold around the procedure?
o: Metformin
Acetaminophen
Calcium carbonate
Docusate
r: Hold metformin ~48 h around iodinated contrast (lactic-acidosis risk); contrast is nephrotoxic — hydrate and check renal function.

q: Which client on the medical unit should the nurse assess FIRST?
o: A CKD client with potassium 6.5 mEq/L
A client with mild dysuria awaiting a UA
A stone client whose pain is now controlled
A dialysis client with a well-healed fistula
r: Potassium 6.5 is a life-threatening dysrhythmia risk — circulation/ABC priority over the stable clients.

q: A client in the diuretic phase of AKI is producing 4 L of urine per day. The nurse monitors most closely for:
o: Fluid volume deficit and hypokalemia
Fluid overload
Worsening hyperkalemia
Metabolic alkalosis
r: Large output in the diuretic phase risks dehydration and potassium loss — replace fluids/electrolytes and watch for hypotension.

q: A client with CKD asks which over-the-counter medicine is safe for a headache. The best answer is:
o: Ibuprofen
Naproxen
Acetaminophen
Aspirin
r: NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin) are nephrotoxic and avoided in CKD; acetaminophen within limits is preferred.

q: The glomerular filtration rate the nurse wants to see is:
o: Greater than 90 mL/min
60 mL/min
30 mL/min
Less than 15 mL/min
r: GFR >90 = healthy filtering; <15 signals the need for dialysis.

q: Case 10A · Mr. Freeman, 45, arrives after an acetaminophen overdose: nausea, RUQ pain, confusion, BP 108/66, elevated INR and AST/ALT. His confusion is most likely due to:
o: Elevated ammonia (hepatic encephalopathy)
Low blood glucose only
Opioid sedation
Hypercalcemia
r: A failing liver can't convert ammonia to urea → ammonia crosses the blood-brain barrier, causing hepatic encephalopathy.

q: Case 10B · Mr. Freeman has acute liver failure from an acetaminophen overdose and is now confused (hepatic encephalopathy). Which medication does the nurse anticipate to treat it?
o: Lactulose
Furosemide
Warfarin
Metformin
r: Lactulose traps ammonia in the gut for excretion; titrate to 2–3 soft stools/day (rifaximin may be added).

q: Case 10C · Mr. Freeman (45) is admitted after an acetaminophen overdose. What is the antidote?
o: Acetylcysteine
Naloxone
Flumazenil
Vitamin K
r: Acetylcysteine is the acetaminophen antidote and is most effective when given early.

q: Case 10D · Mr. Freeman has acute liver failure from an acetaminophen overdose; his INR is now 2.8. The priority nursing concern is:
o: Bleeding risk
Constipation
Hypertension
Hyperglycemia
r: A damaged liver makes fewer clotting factors → high INR/PT and bleeding risk. Start bleeding precautions; vitamin K may be given.

q: Case 10E · Mr. Freeman has acute liver failure after an acetaminophen overdose. Which findings would the nurse expect? (SATA)
o: Jaundice
Elevated AST and ALT
Elevated ammonia
Low INR
Risk of hypoglycemia
r: Liver failure → jaundice, ↑AST/ALT, ↑ammonia, and hypoglycemia risk (impaired glycogen release). INR is HIGH, not low.

q: Case 10F · Mr. Diaz has cirrhosis and suddenly vomits a large amount of bright red blood. The nurse's FIRST priority is to:
o: Maintain the airway and support circulation with fluids/blood products
Administer lactulose
Give a high-protein meal
Encourage oral fluids
r: Ruptured esophageal varices = life-threatening hemorrhage. Stabilize airway and BP (fluids, blood, vasoactive drugs) before definitive banding/ligation.

q: Case 10G · Mr. Diaz has cirrhosis with tense ascites, SpO₂ 91%, and dyspnea. The nurse's priority is to:
o: Address respiratory status (raise the head of bed, prepare for paracentesis)
Restrict all fluids to 500 mL
Place him flat and supine
Give a stool softener
r: Ascites pushes on the diaphragm — respiratory compromise is the priority. Semi-Fowler's helps; paracentesis relieves the pressure.

q: Case 10H · Mr. Diaz has cirrhosis with ascites. Which diuretic does the nurse anticipate for his ascites?
o: Spironolactone
Mannitol
Hydrochlorothiazide alone
Acetazolamide
r: Spironolactone (aldosterone antagonist, potassium-sparing) is first-line for cirrhotic ascites, often with a loop diuretic and sodium restriction.

q: Case 10I · Mr. Diaz (cirrhosis with ascites) has just had a large-volume paracentesis. Immediately afterward, which is given to prevent hypotension?
o: IV albumin
IV potassium
An oral protein shake
A bolus of dextrose
r: Removing large volumes of ascitic fluid can drop intravascular volume/BP; IV albumin helps hold fluid in the vessels.

q: Case 10J · Ms. Ortiz, a 40-year-old obese mother of four, has RUQ pain radiating to the right shoulder after fried food and a positive Murphy's sign. The most likely diagnosis is:
o: Cholecystitis
Pancreatitis
Appendicitis
Hepatitis A
r: RUQ pain to the right shoulder after fatty food + positive Murphy's sign = cholecystitis; she fits the classic 'F' risk profile.

q: Case 10K · Ms. Ortiz was treated for gallstones and returns from an ERCP. Which is the priority assessment?
o: Signs of pancreatitis and return of the gag reflex
Pupil size
Calf tenderness
Deep tendon reflexes
r: Post-ERCP pancreatitis is the key complication (severe pain, ↑amylase/lipase); also confirm the gag reflex returns before food/fluids after sedation.

q: Case 10L · After her laparoscopic cholecystectomy (for gallstones), Ms. Ortiz reports right shoulder pain. The best nursing response is:
o: This is from the CO₂ gas used in surgery; walking and position changes help it pass
This means the surgery failed
We need to call a rapid response
You are having a heart attack
r: Insufflated CO₂ irritates the diaphragm → referred shoulder pain; ambulation and repositioning relieve it. It's expected, not an emergency.

q: Case 10M · Mr. Nguyen has acute pancreatitis with severe boring epigastric pain radiating to the back. Which position gives the most relief?
o: Sitting up and leaning forward (or fetal)
Flat and supine
Trendelenburg
Prone
r: Leaning forward, fetal, or sitting up eases pancreatic pain; lying flat worsens it.

q: Case 10N · Mr. Nguyen has acute pancreatitis (severe epigastric pain radiating to the back). What is the priority intervention?
o: Keep NPO to rest the pancreas (with IV fluids)
Offer clear liquids and ice chips
Encourage a high-fat meal
Give oral pancreatic enzymes now
r: NPO (± NG suction) stops stimulating enzyme release and rests the pancreas; even ice chips can trigger pain. Provide IV fluids and pain control.

q: Case 10O · Mr. Nguyen, who has acute pancreatitis, develops bruising around the umbilicus and along the flanks. This indicates:
o: Hemorrhagic pancreatitis (Cullen's and Grey Turner's signs)
Clinical improvement
A reaction to heparin only
Normal post-op change
r: Cullen's (periumbilical) and Grey Turner's (flank) bruising signal hemorrhagic/necrotizing pancreatitis — a serious deterioration.

q: Case 10P · Mr. Nguyen is admitted with acute pancreatitis (severe epigastric pain radiating to the back). Which findings are expected? (SATA)
o: Elevated lipase
Elevated amylase
Hypocalcemia
Hyperglycemia
Hyperkalemia
r: Pancreatitis → ↑lipase/amylase, hypocalcemia (check Chvostek/Trousseau), and hyperglycemia (islet damage). Potassium isn't characteristically elevated.

q: A client with chronic pancreatitis is prescribed pancrelipase. The nurse teaches to take it:
o: With every meal and snack, swallowed whole
At bedtime on an empty stomach
Only when pain occurs
Crushed in a hot drink
r: Enzyme replacement is taken with all meals/snacks to aid digestion; don't crush enteric-coated forms — follow with a full glass of water.

q: A nurse cares for a client with an open cholecystectomy and a T-tube. Which action is correct?
o: Keep the drainage bag below the surgical site
Clamp the tube continuously
Irrigate the tube every hour
Keep the bag above the gallbladder level
r: Position the T-tube to gravity-drain below the site; record bile output and protect the skin. It typically stays 2–4 weeks.

q: A nursing student asks how gallstones are detected before they cause symptoms. The best answer is:
o: Imaging such as ultrasound or CT — no blood test detects stones
A fasting amylase level
A urine dipstick
A stool guaiac test
r: Gallstones are found on imaging (ultrasound first); there is no lab test for them, so they're often silent until they obstruct a duct.

q: Which teaching points are appropriate for a client recovering from viral hepatitis? (SATA)
o: Avoid all alcohol
Eat small, frequent high-calorie meals
Use proper hand hygiene
It's fine to skip precautions once you feel well
Rest to allow liver regeneration
r: Hepatitis care: no alcohol, small frequent high-cal/high-carb meals, hand hygiene/safe practices, and rest. People can be contagious without symptoms, so precautions still matter.

q: A nurse must infuse esmolol 45 mcg/kg/min for a client weighing 59 kg. Available: esmolol 2500 mg in 250 mL D5W. What rate should the pump deliver? (round to the nearest tenth)
o: 1.6 mL/hr
15.9 mL/hr
159 mL/hr
6.4 mL/hr
r: Dimensional analysis: 45 mcg/kg/min × 59 kg × (1 mg/1000 mcg) × (250 mL/2500 mg) × (60 min/1 hr) = 15.9 mL/hr.

q: A client in renal failure develops metabolic acidosis because the kidneys can't excrete acid. Which compensatory finding does the nurse expect?
o: Slow, shallow breathing
Rapid, deep (Kussmaul) respirations
Bradycardia
Hypoventilation
r: The lungs compensate by blowing off CO₂ — rapid, deep Kussmaul respirations (respiratory alkalosis compensating for the metabolic acidosis).

q: Why are ACE inhibitors and ARBs frequently prescribed for clients with diabetes or CKD?
o: They raise potassium
They protect the glomeruli and slow kidney damage
They rapidly raise the GFR
They replace erythropoietin
r: Beyond lowering BP, ACE inhibitors/ARBs are renoprotective — they lower glomerular pressure and slow progression of kidney damage.

q: A normal, healthy urinalysis should be:
o: Cloudy with protein
Clear and colorless with no protein, glucose, or blood
Dark amber with ketones
Positive for nitrites
r: Normal urine is clear and colorless — a UA should be 'boring': no protein, glucose, ketones, blood, or nitrites.

q: A positive heme result on a urine dipstick may indicate blood OR:
o: Myoglobin from rhabdomyolysis
Excess glucose
Bilirubin
Ketones
r: Heme reflects RBCs (blood) or myoglobin released when muscle breaks down (rhabdomyolysis).

q: A diabetic client is found to have albumin (protein) in the urine. This most likely indicates:
o: A normal finding
Early kidney (glomerular) damage
Simple dehydration
A bladder infection
r: Microalbuminuria signals early glomerular damage — protein leaking through a damaged filter as diabetes injures the kidney.

q: The thrill and bruit felt and heard over an AV fistula are caused by:
o: Infection
Turbulent blood flow where the artery joins the vein
A forming clot
Low blood pressure
r: Joining a high-pressure artery to a low-pressure vein creates turbulent flow — the palpable thrill and audible bruit that confirm patency.

q: Why is forcing oral fluids NOT done immediately for a client with acute renal colic and an obstructing stone?
o: It dilutes the blood
Fluid can back up and worsen hydronephrosis behind the obstruction
It causes hyperkalemia
It has no effect at all
r: Until size and location are known, pushing fluids raises pressure and hydronephrosis behind the blocked ureter. Generous fluids are for PREVENTION, not acute obstruction.

q: Which imaging test best identifies the exact size and location of a ureteral stone?
o: Chest x-ray
CT scan
EEG
Echocardiogram
r: A CT scan pinpoints stone size and location (ultrasound is an alternative). First-time stones are strained and sent for analysis.

q: On a renal matrix, which condition is described by SUDDEN decreased renal function after hypotension or dehydration?
o: Chronic kidney disease
Acute kidney injury
Pyelonephritis
Nephrotic syndrome
r: AKI is the sudden, often reversible drop from poor perfusion; CKD is gradual, and pyelonephritis is usually one-sided so overall function is preserved.

q: In a renal matrix, which condition is MOST likely to progress to sepsis if untreated?
o: Acute kidney injury
Chronic kidney disease
Pyelonephritis
Nephrotic syndrome
r: Pyelonephritis is a bacterial kidney infection that can seed the bloodstream → urosepsis; AKI and CKD are not infectious.

q: Cloudy urine is most often caused by:
o: Dehydration
White blood cells/pus from infection
Excess vitamin C
A high-protein diet
r: WBCs (pus) make urine cloudy — a sign of infection.

q: Which items are common bladder irritants to limit with an irritable bladder or recurrent UTIs?
o: Water and herbal tea
Caffeine, alcohol, citrus, and spicy foods
Plain rice and bananas
Milk and bread
r: Caffeine (coffee/tea/cola), alcohol, citrus, and spices irritate the bladder.

q: Spider angiomas and palmar erythema in cirrhosis result from:
o: High ammonia
The liver failing to metabolize estrogen
Low bilirubin
Excess clotting factors
r: A damaged liver can't break down estrogen; the excess drives vascular skin changes (spider angiomas, palmar erythema).

q: For a client undergoing a large-volume paracentesis, the best position is:
o: Flat and supine
Upright / high-Fowler's or sitting at the edge of the bed
Trendelenburg
Prone
r: Sitting upright lets ascitic fluid pool low, away from organs. Have the client void first (avoid bladder puncture) and give albumin after.

q: The nuclear scan that evaluates gallbladder and biliary-duct patency after IV contrast is the:
o: HIDA scan
EEG
KUB x-ray
Barium swallow
r: A HIDA scan assesses bile flow and patency of the biliary tree.

q: A client with cirrhosis has an NG tube draining bright red blood, and H&H are falling. Because blood is a protein source, which lab change does the nurse ALSO expect once the blood is removed from the gut?
o: Increased serum ammonia
Decreased serum ammonia
Increased serum albumin
Decreased creatinine
r: Gut bacteria break down blood (protein) into ammonia. Removing the blood lowers ammonia production — important for preventing hepatic encephalopathy.

q: While taking the BP of a client with acute pancreatitis, the nurse sees a carpal spasm (positive Trousseau sign). What does this indicate, and why is it the priority?
o: Hyperkalemia — cardiac risk
Hypocalcemia — can cause seizures and dysrhythmias
Hypoglycemia — mental status change
Hypernatremia — fluid shift
r: A positive Trousseau (or Chvostek) sign signals hypocalcemia, common in acute pancreatitis, and takes priority over the expected pain.

q: Before a scheduled hemodialysis session, which electrolyte imbalance should the nurse anticipate in a client with chronic kidney disease?
o: Hypocalcemia
Isolated hypophosphatemia
Hypernatremia
Hypokalemia
r: CKD → chronic hyperphosphatemia lowers calcium and impairs vitamin D activation → hypocalcemia. (Sodium and potassium tend to run HIGH before dialysis.)

q: Which ECG changes are characteristic of hyperkalemia in a client with renal failure?
o: Flattened T waves and U waves
Tall, peaked T waves with a widening QRS
ST elevation only
A shortened PR interval
r: Hyperkalemia produces tall, peaked T waves and, as it worsens, a widening QRS — keep the client on telemetry.

q: Which urinalysis finding can be a NORMAL variant in an otherwise healthy 80-year-old man?
o: Large glucose and ketones
Slight protein with asymptomatic bacteriuria and pyuria
Gross hematuria
3+ proteinuria
r: Older adults commonly show slight proteinuria and asymptomatic bacteriuria/pyuria from kidney aging and incomplete bladder emptying.

q: Which findings are commonly associated with end-stage renal disease?
o: Hypokalemia and low lipids
Hyperkalemia and elevated serum lipids
Hypernatremia and low phosphate
Metabolic alkalosis
r: ESRD retains potassium and is associated with elevated serum lipids (plus hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, metabolic acidosis, and anemia).

q: A client taking an ACE inhibitor for hypertension reports a new dry cough. What should the nurse advise?
o: Stop the drug immediately
Keep taking it until seen by the provider — a dry cough is a known side effect, and stopping antihypertensives abruptly risks rebound hypertension
Double the dose
Ignore it permanently
r: Dry cough is a common ACE-inhibitor effect, not an emergency; don't stop antihypertensives abruptly. The provider may switch to an ARB.

q: What is the normal range for urine specific gravity?
r: Normal specific gravity is ~1.005–1.030; higher = concentrated (dehydration), lower = dilute.

q: A nurse inserts a urinary catheter in a female client but sees no urine return. What should the nurse do NEXT?
o: Notify the provider about an obstruction
Leave the first catheter in place and insert a NEW sterile catheter, using the first as a landmark
Clamp and recheck in 60 minutes
Pull back and redirect the same catheter
r: No return usually means the catheter is in the vagina. Leave it as a landmark and insert a new sterile catheter into the urethra.

q: IV insulin (with dextrose) is given to a client with renal failure and hyperkalemia because insulin:
o: Raises serum potassium
Shifts potassium into the cells, temporarily lowering serum potassium
Removes potassium from the body
Has no effect on potassium
r: Insulin drives potassium into cells — a temporary emergency measure (given with dextrose to prevent hypoglycemia). Kayexalate/dialysis actually remove potassium.

q: Which discharge instruction is correct for a client with a new ostomy (ileostomy or urinary diversion)?
o: Replace the appliance every day
Irrigate the stoma with warm tap water
Change the pouch when the seal is broken to protect the skin
No peristomal skin care is needed
r: Change the pouch when the seal loosens or leaks to prevent skin breakdown from output; daily changes are excessive and irritating.

q: Which outcome best supports psychosocial adjustment for a client with a new ostomy?
o: Reduce dietary fat to 10% within 6 weeks
Attend an ostomy support group within 2 weeks
Irrigate perfectly within 1 week
Have formed stool within 1 month
r: Attending a support group is attainable, measurable, and aids the difficult emotional adjustment to an ostomy.

q: A client is admitted with severe acute diverticulitis. Which nursing intervention is the HIGHEST priority?
o: Obtain a stool specimen
Place the client on NPO status to rest the bowel and reduce perforation/peritonitis risk
Assess temperature
Ambulate the client
r: NPO rests the bowel and lowers the risk of perforation and peritonitis — the priority in severe diverticulitis.

q: A client with an acute small-bowel obstruction develops a temperature of 102°F. Why is this the priority to report?
o: It is an expected finding
A sudden fever suggests peritonitis and needs immediate provider notification
It indicates simple dehydration
It reflects normal cramping
r: A sudden temperature spike signals peritonitis (a serious complication); cramping and dry mucous membranes are lower priority.

q: A community health nurse is teaching older adults how to prevent electrolyte imbalances. Which teaching point is most effective?
o: Drink water only when you feel thirsty
Limit fluid intake to 1,000 mL per day
Maintain adequate hydration, especially during hot weather
Replace sports drinks with water for all hydration needs
r: Older adults have a blunted thirst response, so 'drink only when thirsty' fails them. Prevention needs intentional hydration, especially when sick or hot. Watch absolutes ('only,' 'all') — usually wrong.

q: A nurse documents intake over 12 hours: 1 cup coffee, 2 cups water, 3 tbsp ice, plus 120 mL emesis. IV intake equals urine output. What is the fluid balance?
r: Ice counts as HALF volume: 3 tbsp = 45 mL to 22.5 mL. Intake = 240 + 480 + 22.5 = 742.5 mL. Output = 120 mL emesis (IV in and urine out cancel). Balance = 742.5 - 120 = +622.5 mL.

q: A client had major abdominal surgery with significant blood loss: BP 90/50, HR 120, cool clammy skin. Which IV fluid is most appropriate for immediate volume resuscitation?
o: 0.45% normal saline (half NS)
5% dextrose in water (D5W)
0.9% normal saline (NS)
5% dextrose in 0.45% NS (D5 half-NS)
r: Use an isotonic fluid (0.9% NS) for acute blood loss and hypotension — it stays intravascular to restore volume. Hypotonic and dextrose fluids leave the bloodstream too fast. Above 0.9% = hypertonic, below = hypotonic.

q: After a marathon, a client has diaphoresis and weakness. Sodium 129 (135-145), potassium 3.6 (3.5-5.0). Which prescriptions should the nurse anticipate? (SATA)
o: Administer 0.9% sodium chloride IV
Initiate seizure precautions
Provide high-sodium foods
Administer potassium chloride IV
Administer 0.45% sodium chloride IV
Closely monitor intake and output
r: The problem is hyponatremia (Na 129); potassium is normal, so don't treat it. Correct what's abnormal: 0.9% NS and high-sodium foods raise sodium; seizure precautions because low sodium risks seizures; monitor I&O. Skip KCl and hypotonic 0.45% NS.

q: A client with a history of hyperkalemia needs teaching on foods to AVOID. Which should be included? (SATA)
o: Avocado
Banana
Lettuce
Potato
Apple
Orange
r: High-potassium foods to limit: avocado, banana, potato (very high), and orange. Lettuce and apple are low in potassium. Clients in renal failure or on ACE inhibitors/spironolactone must especially watch intake.

q: A nurse cares for a terminally ill, competent client whose family insists on aggressive treatment. The client says, 'I just want to be done and be comfortable.' Best response?
o: I understand, but you'll have to convince your family
Let's talk to the provider about what you want your care to be
You should listen to your family, since they care about you
I'll inform your family that you want to stop all treatments
r: A competent client is the decision-maker for their own care. Support autonomy by connecting them with the provider — not acting as an intermediary, overriding them, or speaking for them. Family decides only if the client cannot.

q: A client with diabetes cries: 'I cannot stand giving myself these shots for the rest of my life.' Best nurse response?
o: If you don't give the insulin, you'll be at greater risk for complications
We can teach a family member to give the shot so you don't have to
I can arrange a home health nurse to give the shots every day
What is it about giving yourself the insulin shots that bothers you?
r: For emotional distress, explore feelings with an open-ended question rather than threatening, shifting responsibility, or giving unrealistic fixes. Understanding the specific fear lets you address it — mind and body health are linked.

q: A client with chronic pain is tired of taking medications. Which NON-pharmacologic interventions are appropriate? (SATA)
o: Tell the client they need less medication
Lead the client through guided imagery
Instruct the client in relaxation breathing techniques
Offer ibuprofen 600 mg PO
Apply ice to areas with impaired circulation
Distract the client with music or television
r: The client wants non-drug options, so eliminate medication answers. Guided imagery, relaxation breathing, and distraction reduce sympathetic activation and help chronic pain. Never apply ice to impaired-circulation areas — vasoconstriction can injure tissue.

q: A client with severe pancreatitis develops carpopedal spasms the next day. Which lab finding is the most likely cause?
o: Hypocalcemia
Hyperkalemia
Hypoalbuminemia
Hypermagnesemia
r: Carpopedal spasm (Trousseau sign) signals hypocalcemia. In severe pancreatitis, calcium is drawn to inflamed tissue (fat saponification), dropping serum calcium. Spasms/tingling: think calcium first (Chvostek = facial twitch, Trousseau = hand spasm).

q: A client with severe pancreatitis is assessed for Grey Turner sign. Which statements are accurate? (SATA)
o: It appears as ecchymosis (bruising) on the flanks
It warrants monitoring for Cullen sign (periumbilical bruising) too
It develops within a few hours of symptom onset
It may result in hypotension and shock
It describes the pain associated with pancreatitis
r: Grey Turner = flank ecchymosis from retroperitoneal bleeding in hemorrhagic pancreatitis; Cullen = periumbilical bruising, so monitor both. It does NOT appear within hours (a late, severe finding). Major internal bleeding can cause hypotension/shock. It reflects bleeding, not pain.

q: For a client with acute hemorrhagic pancreatitis showing Cullen and Grey Turner signs, which action is the FIRST priority?
o: Initiate IV fluid resuscitation
Administer pain medication
Notify the provider of signs of internal bleeding
Prepare for possible surgical intervention
r: Order: (1) notify provider of internal bleeding (triggers orders for transfusion/fluids); (2) IV fluid resuscitation for hypotension; (3) monitor VS and urine output to guide adjustments; (4) pain medication; (5) prepare for possible surgery.

q: While giving a gastrostomy (G-tube) feeding, the nurse notices formula is not flowing as expected. Priority action?
o: Flush the G-tube with warm water
Reposition the client to left Sims
Stop the feeding and notify the provider
Look for kinks or pinches in the G-tube tubing
r: Start least-invasive/simplest: check for kinks or pinches. Flushing is reasonable but not first; stopping and notifying the provider is premature before ruling out a mechanical cause. Never use cola/coffee to unclog (a myth that worsens clumping).

q: A client has an upper GI bleed. Which assessment finding requires immediate intervention?
o: Dark, concentrated urine with high specific gravity
Heart rate 110 with blood pressure 88/56
Pallor with mild epigastric pain
Positive fecal occult blood with loose brown stool
r: Unstable vital signs come first (ABCs). HR 110 + BP 88/56 signals hypovolemia/hemorrhagic shock — life-threatening with a bleed you can't directly see. The others are concerning but not immediately life-threatening.

q: A care plan for a client with chronic upper respiratory issues includes psychosocial interventions. Which best reflects how psychosocial factors influence management?
o: Recommend social isolation to reduce trigger exposure
Promote smoking cessation through individualized behavioral counseling
Encourage alcohol use to manage stress and improve sleep
Advise limiting physical activity to avoid respiratory strain
r: Psychosocial questions focus on emotional wellbeing and healthy coping, not fixing the disease. Behavioral counseling supports the whole person. Social isolation, alcohol as coping, and activity restriction are all harmful red-flag options.

q: A client has anxiety, pleuritic chest pain, yellow-tinged sputum, fever, and shortness of breath. Priority nursing action?
o: Notify the healthcare provider
Administer PRN acetaminophen
Place the client in high Fowler's position
Provide supplemental oxygen
r: The picture suggests pneumonia. High Fowler's is the fastest, simplest way to improve breathing (diaphragms descend, O2 rises) — an ABC priority. Fever and notifying the provider are lower priority; oxygen is tempting but no O2 sat is given and repositioning acts immediately.

q: A ventilated client in acute respiratory failure has SaO2 88%, RR 32, is agitated and pulling at the ET tube, and ventilator alarms are sounding. Highest priority?
o: Administer prescribed sedation to reduce agitation
Reassure the client and explain the ventilator's purpose
Silence the ventilator alarm and assess the tubing
Assess the client's breathing and airway status immediately
r: With hypoxemia, tachypnea, agitation, and alarms, assess breathing/airway first (ABCs). Don't just sedate (masks a low O2 sat), don't merely reassure, and don't silence the alarm without assessing. Abnormal vitals demand direct assessment.

q: A COPD client in acute respiratory failure trends over 4 hours: falling O2 sat, rising RR, worsening mental status, ABGs pH 7.35 to 7.28, CO2 50 to 60, O2 70 to 58. Which trend most indicates the need for intubation?
o: Decreasing PaO2
Decreasing pH
Increasing respiratory rate
Increasing PaCO2
r: Rising PaCO2 is the strongest indicator: inability to clear CO2 defines respiratory failure, drives the falling pH (respiratory acidosis), and leads to CO2 narcosis (loss of consciousness, can't protect airway). Low PaO2 can often be treated with oxygen, so it's less definitive.

q: A client with a spontaneous pneumothorax has a chest tube on a closed water-seal system. The nurse notes no bubbling or tidaling and increasing shortness of breath. Which are APPROPRIATE interventions? (SATA)
o: Check the tubing for kinks or occlusions
Notify the healthcare provider
Encourage ambulation to promote lung expansion
Document findings as expected post-op progress
Lower the drainage system to the floor
Assess for signs of tension pneumothorax
r: No tidaling/bubbling with worsening SOB suggests obstruction or developing tension pneumothorax: check tubing for kinks, notify the provider, assess for tension pneumothorax. Do NOT dismiss it as expected, lower the system to the floor, or prioritize ambulation in acute distress.

q: A client is in an acute asthma exacerbation and is short of breath. Priority intervention?
o: Obtain a stat chest x-ray
Administer a short-acting beta agonist (albuterol)
Prepare the client for an arterial blood gas
Administer an IV corticosteroid
r: Open the airways first: a short-acting beta agonist (albuterol) rapidly reverses bronchoconstriction. A chest x-ray won't help acutely, an ABG can wait, and IV corticosteroids take 6-12 hours (given but not first). Albuterol is the #1 rescue for asthma and COPD.

q: After a cardiac catheterization, the nurse sees a rapidly expanding hematoma at the access site and a drop in BP. Which action should the nurse implement FIRST?
o: Give anti-anxiety medication and oxygen
Apply a pressure dressing and give PRN pain medication
Place in high Fowler's and apply an ice pack
Outline the hematoma with a pen and apply manual pressure over the site
r: A rapidly expanding hematoma after arterial puncture needs direct control: apply manual pressure and outline the hematoma to track expansion. High Fowler's could worsen it (stay supine post-cath); the other options don't control active arterial bleeding as effectively.

q: A client has symptomatic sinus bradycardia with a heart rate of 42. Which interventions are appropriate? (SATA)
o: Administer atropine as ordered
Prepare for transcutaneous pacing
Place the client in Trendelenburg position
Monitor blood pressure and level of consciousness
Administer amiodarone as ordered
Ensure IV access is established
r: 'Symptomatic' means the slow rate is impairing perfusion, so act. Atropine (chemical) and transcutaneous pacing (physical) speed the rate; monitor BP/LOC for perfusion and ensure IV access. Trendelenburg isn't indicated; amiodarone treats tachydysrhythmias, not bradycardia.

q: A monitor strip shows an irregularly irregular rhythm with a fibrillating baseline and no identifiable P waves. Which rhythm is this most likely?
o: Sinus tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia
Atrial fibrillation
Ventricular fibrillation
r: Absent P waves with a fibrillating baseline and irregularly irregular response = atrial fibrillation. Sinus tach is regular with P waves; V-tach has wide tombstone QRS; V-fib has no organized waveforms (chaotic).

q: A client has developed atrial fibrillation. Which medications may be in the treatment plan? (SATA)
o: Warfarin
Metformin
Diltiazem
Digoxin
Lisinopril
Apixaban
Amiodarone
Rivaroxaban
r: AFib care targets stroke prevention (anticoagulants: warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban) and rate/rhythm control (diltiazem and digoxin slow the rate; amiodarone maintains rhythm). Metformin and lisinopril don't treat the rhythm itself.

q: A client with a new ICD asks, 'How will I know if my device is working properly?' Best nurse response?
o: You may feel a mild shock occasionally, which means it's working
You'll need weekly clinic visits for the first month
Scheduled follow-ups and remote monitoring will track its performance
If you don't feel anything, it's working
r: Remote monitoring plus scheduled follow-ups is the standard, accurate way ICDs are tracked. Feeling a shock is NOT a normal sign of function — it means a dangerous rhythm was detected (or a malfunction). The other options are inaccurate.

q: A client had a total hip replacement yesterday. Which intervention is MOST effective in preventing venous thromboembolism (VTE)?
o: Elevate the affected extremity every 4 hours
Encourage adequate hydration
Implement early ambulation
Apply elastic stockings when the client is in bed
r: Early ambulation is the gold standard — it directly counters venous stasis (Virchow's triad) by promoting venous return. Hydration and stockings are more passive; elevation addresses edema, not clots. For 'most effective,' pick the greatest physiologic benefit.

q: Order: metoprolol 50 mg PO. Available: 25 mg tablets. How many tablets?
o: 1 tablet
2 tablets
3 tablets
0.5 tablet
r: 50 mg ÷ 25 mg/tab = 2 tablets. (Desired ÷ Have.)

q: Order: amoxicillin 500 mg PO. Available: 250 mg/5 mL. How many mL?
o: 5 mL
10 mL
15 mL
2.5 mL
r: (500 ÷ 250) × 5 mL = 10 mL. (Desired ÷ Have × Quantity.)

q: Infuse 1000 mL NS over 8 hours. What rate in mL/hr?
o: 100 mL/hr
125 mL/hr
150 mL/hr
80 mL/hr
r: 1000 mL ÷ 8 hr = 125 mL/hr.

q: Infuse 1000 mL over 8 hr with a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL. Rate in gtt/min?
o: 21 gtt/min
31 gtt/min
42 gtt/min
15 gtt/min
r: 125 mL/hr ÷ 60 min × 15 gtt/mL = 31.25 → 31 gtt/min.

q: A microdrip set (60 gtt/mL) runs at 80 mL/hr. Rate in gtt/min?
o: 40 gtt/min
60 gtt/min
80 gtt/min
20 gtt/min
r: With a 60 gtt/mL set, gtt/min = mL/hr. So 80 mL/hr = 80 gtt/min.

q: Dopamine 5 mcg/kg/min for an 80 kg client. Bag: 400 mg in 250 mL. Rate in mL/hr?
o: 12 mL/hr
15 mL/hr
18 mL/hr
24 mL/hr
r: Dose = 5 × 80 = 400 mcg/min = 24 mg/hr. Concentration = 400/250 = 1.6 mg/mL. 24 ÷ 1.6 = 15 mL/hr.

q: Heparin 18 units/kg/hr for an 80 kg client. Bag: 25,000 units/250 mL. Rate in mL/hr?
o: 14.4 mL/hr
18 mL/hr
25 mL/hr
144 mL/hr
r: Dose = 18 × 80 = 1440 units/hr. Concentration = 25,000/250 = 100 units/mL. 1440 ÷ 100 = 14.4 mL/hr.

q: Convert 0.5 mg to micrograms (mcg).
o: 5 mcg
50 mcg
500 mcg
5000 mcg
r: 1 mg = 1000 mcg, so 0.5 mg × 1000 = 500 mcg. (Larger→smaller unit: multiply.)

q: Convert 250 mcg to milligrams (mg).
o: 2.5 mg
25 mg

q: A client weighs 154 lb. What is the weight in kg?
o: 70 kg
68 kg
154 kg
338 kg

q: A child weighs 44 lb. Weight in kg?
o: 20 kg
22 kg
44 kg
97 kg

q: Order: 2 teaspoons of a liquid. How many mL should the nurse give?
o: 2 mL
5 mL
10 mL
15 mL
r: 1 tsp = 5 mL, so 2 tsp × 5 = 10 mL.

q: Order: 12 units regular insulin. Available: 100 units/mL. How many mL? (No insulin syringe available.)
o: 1.2 mL
12 mL
r: 12 ÷ 100 = 0.12 mL. (Best practice: always use an insulin syringe.)

q: Order: heparin 5000 units SC. Available: 10,000 units/mL. How many mL?
o: 0.5 mL
1 mL
2 mL

q: Order: cefazolin 1 g IV. Reconstituted to 250 mg/mL. How many mL?
o: 2 mL
4 mL
8 mL
10 mL

q: Order: 10 mg/kg for a 25 kg child. What is the total dose?
o: 100 mg
250 mg
2.5 mg
25 mg
r: 10 mg/kg × 25 kg = 250 mg.

q: Order: 30 mg/kg/day divided every 8 hr for a 24 kg child. Dose per administration?
o: 240 mg
720 mg
80 mg
360 mg
r: 30 × 24 = 720 mg/day ÷ 3 doses (q8h) = 240 mg per dose.

q: Order: digoxin 0.125 mg PO. Available: 0.25 mg tablets. How many tablets?
o: 0.5 tablet
2 tablets
1 tablet
0.25 tablet
r: 0.125 ÷ 0.25 = 0.5 tablet (a scored tablet may be halved).

q: Order: 1.5 g of a medication. Available: 500 mg tablets. How many tablets?
o: 2 tablets
3 tablets
1.5 tablets
4 tablets

q: Infuse 50 mL over 30 minutes. What rate in mL/hr does the pump need?
o: 50 mL/hr
100 mL/hr
150 mL/hr
25 mL/hr

q: 1000 mL is infusing at 125 mL/hr. How many hours will it take?
o: 6 hr
8 hr
10 hr
12 hr

q: How many grams of dextrose are in 1000 mL of D5W?
o: 5 g

q: Infuse 500 mL over 4 hr with a 20 gtt/mL set. Rate in gtt/min?
o: 25 gtt/min
42 gtt/min
31 gtt/min
60 gtt/min

q: A 20 kg child is ordered 400 mg/day. Safe range is 15–25 mg/kg/day. What should the nurse do?
o: Hold — the dose is too high
Hold — the dose is too low
Administer — the dose is within the safe range
Give half the dose
r: Safe range = 15×20 to 25×20 = 300–500 mg/day. 400 mg falls within range → safe to administer.

q: Which dressing is most appropriate for a stage 2 pressure injury (shallow, partial-thickness, open)?
o: Dry gauze changed twice daily
Hydrocolloid dressing
Wet-to-dry gauze
No dressing; leave open to air
r: A stage 2 injury needs a moist wound environment — a hydrocolloid (or thin foam/film) supports healing. Dry and wet-to-dry dressings damage new tissue.

q: Which task can the nurse safely delegate to assistive personnel (AP)?
o: Assessing a newly admitted client
Teaching a client to self-inject insulin
Measuring routine vital signs on a stable client
Evaluating a client's response to a new medication
r: AP may perform routine, standardized tasks on stable clients (VS, ADLs, ambulation). Assessment, teaching, and evaluation cannot be delegated.

q: Which action is appropriate when initiating seizure precautions?
o: Insert a padded tongue blade if a seizure begins
Apply wrist restraints
Pad the side rails and keep suction and oxygen available
Keep the bed in the highest position
r: Pad side rails, keep bed low, and have suction/O2 ready. Never put anything in the mouth or restrain a seizing client.

q: A client has Clostridioides difficile (C. diff). Which is correct?
o: Airborne precautions with an N95
Alcohol-based hand rub is sufficient
Contact precautions with soap-and-water handwashing
Droplet precautions only
r: C. diff requires contact precautions, and hands must be washed with soap and water — alcohol rubs do not kill the spores.

q: When a fire is discovered in a client's room, the nurse's FIRST action is to:
o: Pull the fire alarm
Rescue (remove) clients in immediate danger
Extinguish the fire
Close all the doors
r: RACE: Rescue first — move clients in immediate danger — then Alarm, Contain, Extinguish.

q: Which is required for a client in wrist restraints?
o: Tie the restraint to the side rail
Assess circulation every 4 hours
A time-limited provider order, with release and circulation checks at least every 2 hours
Apply restraints to all four limbs routinely
r: Restraints need a time-limited order; secure to the bed frame (not rails), and release/reposition with skin and circulation checks at least q2h.

q: Essential teaching for a client using home oxygen:
o: It is fine to smoke in a different room
Keep oxygen away from open flames and avoid petroleum-based products
Extension cords are fine for the concentrator
Store the tank lying in direct sunlight
r: Oxygen supports combustion — no smoking/flames nearby, and avoid petroleum products (e.g., Vaseline) near the face.

q: The purpose of medication reconciliation on admission is to:
o: Ensure correct billing
Obtain an accurate list of ALL current medications (prescription, OTC, supplements) to prevent discrepancies
Automatically discontinue all home medications
Determine the client's insurance
r: Med reconciliation compiles a complete, accurate medication list to prevent errors and omissions across care transitions.

q: Which laboratory value requires immediate provider notification?
o: Potassium 4.0 mEq/L
Sodium 140 mEq/L
Potassium 6.8 mEq/L
Hemoglobin 13 g/dL
r: Potassium 6.8 is critically high (normal 3.5–5.0) → risk of lethal dysrhythmias; report immediately.

q: Which findings indicate malnutrition?
o: Weight gain and high energy
Brittle hair and a low prealbumin
Albumin 4.2 g/dL
Elevated lymphocyte count
r: Low prealbumin/albumin, brittle hair, muscle wasting, and poor wound healing indicate malnutrition.

q: Priority intervention to prevent complications after abdominal surgery:
o: Strict bed rest for 48 hours
Incentive spirometry and early ambulation
Withhold all pain medication
Start a high-fiber diet immediately
r: Early ambulation + incentive spirometry prevent the big post-op risks (atelectasis/pneumonia and VTE).

q: When should discharge planning for a newly diagnosed client with diabetes begin?
o: The day of discharge
On admission
After the first insulin dose
At the first outpatient visit
r: Discharge planning begins on admission to allow time for teaching and coordination.

q: Which situation is a violation of EMTALA?
o: Stabilizing, then transferring with consent
Refusing to screen or stabilize a client with an emergency condition because they have no insurance
Providing a medical screening exam to everyone
Transferring a stabilized client appropriately
r: EMTALA requires a medical screening exam and stabilization of emergency conditions regardless of ability to pay.

q: Correct technique for an intradermal injection (e.g., PPD)?
o: Deltoid at a 90° angle
Inner forearm at a 5–15° angle, forming a small wheal/bleb
Vastus lateralis at 45°
Abdomen at 90°
r: Intradermal injections go into the inner forearm at 5–15°, raising a small wheal; read a PPD at 48–72 h.

q: A client on IV fluids develops crackles, dyspnea, and a bounding pulse. Priority action?
o: Increase the infusion rate
Slow the IV to keep-vein-open and raise the head of the bed
Lay the client flat
Discontinue the IV entirely
r: These are signs of fluid overload — slow the IV to KVO, raise HOB to ease breathing, notify the provider, anticipate a diuretic.

q: The greatest life-threatening risk of immobility is:
o: Constipation
A pressure injury
Venous thromboembolism (DVT that can become a PE)
Muscle atrophy
r: Venous stasis → DVT → pulmonary embolism is the greatest life-threatening hazard of immobility; prevent with early mobility/prophylaxis.

q: Which intervention is appropriate for a client with dysphagia?
o: Offer thin liquids to ease swallowing
Sit upright at 90°, use a chin-tuck, and thicken liquids
Have the client lie flat while eating
Encourage talking during meals
r: Aspiration precautions: upright 90°, chin-tuck, thickened liquids, small bites, no distractions.

q: Before an intermittent enteral (NG/G-tube) feeding, the nurse should FIRST:
o: Flush the tube with cola
Verify tube placement and elevate the HOB 30–45°
Instill the feeding rapidly
Position the client flat
r: Confirm placement and raise the HOB to prevent aspiration before every intermittent feeding; check residual per policy.

q: Which preoperative finding should the nurse report to the provider before surgery?
o: Blood pressure 122/78
Potassium 2.9 mEq/L
The client has been NPO since midnight
A signed operative consent is on the chart
r: Potassium 2.9 (hypokalemia) increases risks of dysrhythmias and prolonged anesthesia effects — report before surgery.

q: A client with a new urinary diversion says, 'I'll never feel normal again.' The best nurse response is:
o: You'll get used to it soon
Tell me more about what worries you most
Most people adjust just fine
Let's not focus on the negative
r: Therapeutic communication explores the client's feelings with an open-ended response rather than dismissing or minimizing them.

q: A client who recently had a colostomy created says they feel anxious and overwhelmed about managing the bag, and they are worried about their body image, the impact on daily life, and how other people will see them. Which statement by the nurse is most appropriate?
o: “Here are some detailed instructions on how to care for a colostomy — they will help you manage it better.”
“I encourage you to join a support group for people with colostomies. It can help to talk with others who understand what you are going through.”
“You’re going to be fine. Everybody feels this way at first, but you will adjust over time once things settle down.”
“Why is your body causing you this much mental distress?”
r: This looks like a colostomy question, but it is really a THERAPEUTIC COMMUNICATION question — the client gave you feelings, not a clinical problem. Work by elimination: (1) is accurate but jumps straight to teaching and never touches the feelings. (3) “You’re going to be fine” is FALSE REASSURANCE — never therapeutic; your definition of “fine” may not be theirs. (4) starts with “Why,” which always reads as judgmental — never therapeutic. That leaves (2), which acknowledges the feeling and points toward real support. A note from lecture: she didn’t love (2) at first (it can feel like passing the buck), but once the other three are ruled out it is clearly the most therapeutic option.

q: A nurse is discharging a client hospitalized for ACUTE diverticulitis. Which dietary recommendation should the nurse emphasize to support healing during the acute inflammatory phase?
o: Begin a high-fiber diet immediately to promote bowel regularity
Follow a clear liquid diet and gradually advance as tolerated
Increase raw fruits and vegetables to reduce inflammation
Consume whole grains and legumes to restore gut flora
r: ACUTE flare = bowel rest. Clear liquids first, then advance to LOW fiber, and only return to a HIGH-fiber diet once the diverticulitis has resolved (high fiber is for preventing new diverticula long-term, not for treating a flare). Test-taking shortcut: options 1, 3, and 4 are all essentially “high fiber” — when three answers say the same thing, they can’t all be right, so cross them off. An analogy from lecture: a loofah is fine on intact skin, but you’d never scrub an inflamed rash with it — same logic inside an inflamed bowel. This applies to Crohn’s flares too.

q: A nurse is caring for several clients with inflammatory bowel disease. Which clinical manifestation is associated with CROHN’S DISEASE rather than with ulcerative colitis?
o: Mouth sores
Bloody diarrhea
Rectal bleeding
Tenesmus
r: Crohn’s can inflame ANYWHERE from MOUTH TO ANUS — so aphthous mouth ulcers are possible with Crohn’s and impossible with UC, which is limited to the colon. Bloody diarrhea and rectal bleeding are more common in UC but can occur in Crohn’s colitis, so neither is exclusive (and notice how similar those two options are — a hint they’re both wrong). Tenesmus (the feeling of incomplete emptying) points to rectal inflammation, which is classic UC.

q: A nurse is caring for a client hospitalized with acute diverticulitis. To reduce the risk of COMPLICATIONS, which nursing interventions should the nurse implement? Select all that apply.
o: Maintain the client on a clear liquid diet
Encourage frequent ambulation
Monitor for signs of peritonitis
Administer prescribed antibiotics
Apply a heating pad to the abdomen
r: Read the stem carefully — it asks what prevents COMPLICATIONS, not what feels nice. Clear liquids rest an inflamed, possibly strictured bowel and reduce obstruction risk. Monitoring for peritonitis catches a ruptured diverticulum early — know the cues: ABDOMINAL RIGIDITY, GUARDING, REBOUND TENDERNESS. Antibiotics prevent progression to abscess and peritonitis. Ambulation increases peristalsis when you want bowel rest (and prevents DVT, not a diverticulitis complication). Heat causes VASODILATION, bringing more blood to already-inflamed tissue. A rule from lecture: whenever an option involves heat or cold, ask what it does physiologically — heat vasodilates, cold vasoconstricts — rather than memorizing a list.

q: A nurse is teaching a client about the potential complications of frequent laxative use. Which should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Electrolyte imbalances
Dehydration
Increased risk of colon cancer
Bowel dependence
Impaired absorption of medications
r: Frequent laxative use → diarrhea → fluid and electrolyte losses (especially K⁺ and Na⁺) and dehydration. The bowel also becomes DEPENDENT: stop the laxative and peristalsis stalls, causing REFLEX CONSTIPATION, which drives the client right back to laxatives. Speeding transit through the small intestine means drugs and nutrients have less time to be absorbed. There is NO established link between laxative use and colon cancer.

q: A 38-year-old client with peritonitis is admitted to a med-surg unit. Day 1 → Day 2 → Day 3: BP 120/80 → 118/78 → 125/76; HR 95 → 105 → 110; RR 22 → 24 → 26; SpO₂ 94% → 90% → 86%; Temp 100.4°F → 101.2°F → 102°F; Pain 4/10 localized → 7/10 generalized → 10/10 radiating to the shoulder; WBC 12,000 → 14,000 → 16,000. Based on the TRENDS, what clinical judgment should the nurse make?
o: The client’s condition is improving — continue current treatment
The client’s condition is stable — no changes needed
The client’s condition is worsening — intervention is required
The client’s condition is resolved — prepare for discharge
r: Every single trend is moving the wrong way: rising HR, rising RR, FALLING SpO₂ (94 → 86%), climbing fever, pain going from 4/10 localized to 10/10 generalized and radiating, and a WBC climbing 12k → 16k. A near-normal blood pressure does not reassure you when everything else is deteriorating. The peritoneum is a STERILE lining — like sterile plastic wrap around the abdominal contents — so bacteria there (from a perforated ulcer or a leaking diverticulum) is a SURGICAL EMERGENCY. On trend items, don’t judge single values; read each row left to right.

q: A nurse is caring for a client with an acute exacerbation of ulcerative colitis. Several interventions are prescribed. What should the nurse prioritize to address the client’s IMMEDIATE needs?
o: Monitor fluid and electrolyte balance closely
Administer corticosteroids as prescribed
Provide emotional support and stress management techniques
Monitor for signs of complications
r: All four are correct actions — the question is which is IMMEDIATE. A UC flare means profuse, often bloody diarrhea, dumping sodium, potassium, and volume fast enough to cause circulatory collapse. That is the ABC/circulation threat you can act on right now. Steroids matter but take time; emotional support is ongoing; monitoring for complications is important but complications may never develop. A tiebreaker for “priority” items: ask which one could kill the client the FASTEST.

q: A nurse is assessing a client who is 2 days post-operative following creation of an ILEOSTOMY. Which assessment finding requires IMMEDIATE notification of the healthcare provider?
o: The stoma is moist and pink with a small amount of serosanguineous drainage
The client reports passing liquid stool into the ostomy bag regularly
The stoma appears dusky and has had minimal output over the last 8 hours
The peristomal skin is slightly reddened but intact
r: A DUSKY stoma suggests ischemia or necrosis — the blood supply is failing — and 8 hours with almost no output from an ileostomy (which should drain liquid stool steadily) suggests obstruction. Together that’s an emergency. A moist pink stoma is normal; serosanguineous (yellow, blood-tinged) drainage is expected post-op — purulent drainage would signal infection. Liquid stool from an ileostomy is exactly what you expect, since it is proximal in the GI tract. Slight peristomal redness is worth watching, not an urgent call. A test-taking trick for “notify the provider” items: picture calling at 3 AM — which finding earns a “thank you, I’ll be right there” instead of “that could have waited until morning”?

q: A nurse is preparing to administer a medication 6 mg/kg/day PO, divided into equal doses every 12 hours, to a client who weighs 44 lb. Available: elixir 20 mg/5 mL. How many mL should the nurse administer PER DOSE?
o: 7.5 mL
12 mL
15 mL
30 mL
r: Step 1 — convert: 44 lb ÷ 2.2 = 20 kg. (Logic check: pounds is always the BIGGER number, so going lb → kg you must divide.) Step 2 — daily dose: 6 mg × 20 kg = 120 mg/day. Step 3 — DON’T STOP HERE: q12h means 2 doses/day, so 120 ÷ 2 = 60 mg per dose. Step 4 — Desired ÷ Have × Quantity: 60 ÷ 20 × 5 = 15 mL. Logic check: the dose you want (60 mg) is 3× what’s in 5 mL (20 mg), so your answer must be 3× 5 mL. The most common error on this item is answering 30 mL — the DAILY volume — instead of the per-dose volume.

q: A nurse is leading a community education session on colorectal cancer prevention. Which risk factors should the nurse identify as significant? Select all that apply.
o: Regular use of tobacco products
Diet high in red meat
Family history of colorectal cancer
Frequent drinking of alcohol
Diet high in raw fruits and vegetables
r: Smokers swallow carcinogens, raising both gastric and colorectal cancer risk. Red meat stimulates BILE secretion, and bile is irritating to the colon lining over years to decades. Family history matters enough that some inherited syndromes lead people to elect a prophylactic colectomy — those families can develop colon cancer in their 30s. Alcohol is now firmly on the risk list. Raw fruits and vegetables are PROTECTIVE — bulking, high fiber, and they don’t drive bile secretion — so option 5 lowers risk rather than raising it.

q: A nurse is preparing to administer 0.9% sodium chloride 500 mL over 30 minutes. The nurse should set the IV pump to deliver how many mL/hr?
o: 250 mL/hr
500 mL/hr
1,000 mL/hr
1,500 mL/hr
r: The fluid type is irrelevant — the math is identical for NS, LR, or D5W. Easiest route: 30 minutes is HALF an hour, so double both sides — 500 mL/30 min = 1,000 mL/60 min = 1,000 mL/hr.
