Or work it out: 500 ÷ 30 = 16.667 mL/min × 60 min = 1,000 mL/hr. Ratio and dimensional analysis get you the same place — use whichever method your brain trusts. Don’t be thrown by a rate larger than the bag volume; that’s just the hourly rate the pump needs.

q: A client presents to the ED with severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and abdominal distension. The client has a history of MULTIPLE abdominal surgeries. Which is the priority nursing intervention?
o: Insert a nasogastric tube
Administer oral fluids
Encourage ambulation
Prepare for a paracentesis
r: Pull the cues from the stem: pain + vomiting + DISTENSION = bowel obstruction, and a history of multiple abdominal surgeries means ADHESIONS, which are the classic cause of recurrent obstruction. An NG tube DECOMPRESSES the GI tract by suctioning out air and fluid — uncomfortable to place, but it relieves the distension and vomiting. Oral fluids are pointless when the client is vomiting behind an obstruction. Ambulation increases peristalsis against a blockage and isn’t realistic in severe pain. Paracentesis drains ASCITES — that’s a cirrhosis intervention, and this client has distension from gas and fluid trapped in bowel, not free peritoneal fluid.

q: A nurse is caring for a client receiving total parenteral nutrition (TPN) through a central line. Which nursing interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Verify the TPN bag label and prescription with a second nurse
Administer medications through the TPN line to reduce line access
Monitor daily weights and intake/output
Change the TPN tubing, bag, and filter every 48 hours
Monitor blood glucose levels every 4 hours
Use IV tubing with a filter only if lipids are included
Have 10–20% dextrose available if the next TPN bag is delayed
Flush the TPN line with saline before and after use
r: Independent double-check applies to high-alert therapies — yes. Daily weights and I&O track fluid and nutritional response — yes. Glucose q4h — yes, because TPN delivers a heavy carbohydrate load and causes HYPERglycemia. Keeping dextrose available — yes: if TPN stops abruptly the client’s already-elevated insulin keeps working and they crash into HYPOglycemia. The wrong ones: TPN needs a DEDICATED lumen (a central line has several — just don’t share the TPN one). Tubing and bag change is every 24 HOURS, not 48 — this is essentially IV food and it grows bacteria. A filter is ALWAYS used, not just with lipids. Flushing before and after “use” only applies to intermittent (usually home) TPN — standard hospital TPN runs continuously, so there is no before or after. Advice from lecture on that last one: if you’ve never heard of it, leave it unselected.

q: A nurse is assessing a client with a suspected bowel obstruction. Which findings are most consistent with a LARGE bowel obstruction rather than a small bowel obstruction? Select all that apply.
o: Significant lower abdominal distension
Diarrhea leaking around an impaction
Only minor fluid and electrolyte imbalance
Profuse vomiting with a fecal odor
Severe metabolic alkalosis
High-pitched (tympanic) bowel sounds above the obstruction
r: The whole distinction comes down to one idea: a SMALL bowel obstruction can decompress itself by VOMITING; a large bowel obstruction cannot, because the ileocecal valve blocks backflow. So LARGE bowel → marked lower abdominal distension, stool impaction with liquid diarrhea leaking around it, and only mild fluid/electrolyte disturbance. SMALL bowel → profuse feculent vomiting, and losing gastric acid produces METABOLIC ALKALOSIS with rapid dehydration and electrolyte loss. High-pitched tympanic bowel sounds above the blockage and obstipation occur in BOTH, so they don’t help you tell them apart — which is exactly why they’re in the option list.

q: A nurse is teaching a client about hernia care. Which interventions apply to PREOPERATIVE hernia care? Select all that apply.
o: Wear a truss pad during waking hours
Avoid lifting objects greater than 10 pounds
Prevent constipation with fiber and fluids
Apply ice to the incision site
Rest for several days
Inspect and report redness or swelling
r: A truss supports the weakened abdominal wall and is worn while UPRIGHT (lying down already relieves the pressure) — it’s preoperative only, since the repair makes it unnecessary. Avoiding heavy lifting and preventing constipation both apply BEFORE and AFTER surgery: before, straining and lifting can push the hernia out and cause a STRANGULATED hernia; after, the same forces threaten the repair with dehiscence. Ice to the incision, resting several days, and watching for redness or swelling all presuppose an incision — those are post-op only. Teach the client that a hernia they cannot push back in, especially with severe pain, is a STRANGULATED hernia and an emergency. Risk factors: male, older age, chronic constipation, chronic cough (COPD), and heavy lifting.

q: A 45-year-old presents with 2 days of abdominal pain, decreased appetite, and nausea. Assessment: pain 8/10 in the LEFT lower quadrant, abdomen tender to palpation, temperature 101.6°F, HR 116, BP 108/64, WBC 17,800. The patient reports that every bump in the car on the way in made the pain worse. Which condition is the nurse most likely seeing?
o: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)
Acute appendicitis
Acute diverticulitis
Colon cancer
r: LEFT LOWER QUADRANT PAIN + FEVER + LEUKOCYTOSIS = LOCALIZED INFLAMMATION OF DIVERTICULITIS — that combination should go 'ding ding ding' in your brain. IBS is out because IBS has NO fever and NO leukocytosis (IBS hurts, but it doesn't harm). Appendicitis localizes to the RIGHT lower quadrant, so location alone removes it. Colon cancer develops gradually and is unlikely to present acutely with fever and a WBC of 17,800, and Crohn's would usually bring chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and recurrent symptoms.

q: The provider writes several orders for the patient with acute diverticulitis (temp 101.6°F, WBC 17,800, pain 8/10). Which order should the nurse complete FIRST?
o: Begin patient education about a high-fiber diet
Administer the prescribed IV antibiotics
Administer the prescribed IV antiemetic
Obtain consent for a colonoscopy
r: The fever and elevated white blood cells tell you there is A BACTERIAL INFECTION THAT MUST BE TREATED FIRST — treating the infection is the life-saving, ABC-level action. Use trick: ask yourself what happens to my patient if I choose the wrong priority — the inflamed diverticulum keeps filling with bacteria, an abscess forms, the bowel perforates, peritonitis, sepsis, death — you already know that, which means you already know the right answer. The antiemetic and teaching improve comfort and understanding but do not stop the infection, and teaching is never the priority in an acute infection. A colonoscopy is not safe on an acutely inflamed bowel wall because the scope can poke through and perforate it.

q: Twelve hours after admission for acute diverticulitis, the nurse reassesses the patient. Which finding is MOST concerning?
o: Pain has decreased from 8/10 to 4/10
Temperature has decreased from 101.6°F to 99°F
The patient reports the abdominal pain is completely gone, but the abdomen is now rigid and distended
The patient is asking when a regular diet can be resumed
r: SUDDEN, COMPLETE RELIEF OF PAIN WITH A RIGID, BOARD-LIKE, DISTENDED ABDOMEN MEANS THE BOWEL PERFORATED AND GI CONTENTS HAVE LEAKED INTO THE PERITONEUM — this is peritonitis and it is an emergency. A rigid, board-like abdomen is THE one assessment finding that should immediately make you think peritonitis; the muscles go hard to guard the inflamed organs underneath. Pain dropping from 8/10 to 4/10 and a temperature falling toward normal are expected improvements from the IV antibiotics and analgesia. Sudden relief of pain is always a red flag — it is the same trap as the appendicitis patient whose pain 'gets much better' right after the appendix ruptures.

q: The nurse finds the diverticulitis patient with a rigid, board-like, distended abdomen, HR 128, BP 88/52, and a temperature of 102.4°F. What is the nurse's priority action?
o: Give the ordered oral pain medication and reassess in one hour
Notify the provider immediately and prepare for emergency surgery while starting rapid IV fluid resuscitation and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
Encourage ambulation in the hallway to stimulate bowel motility
Position the patient in high Fowler's and start clear liquids to test tolerance
r: WHEN THE BOWEL PERFORATES, IT IS NOT JUST THE BOWEL ANYMORE — IT IS THE ENTIRE BODY, so the patient needs immediate provider notification, rapid IV fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and emergency surgery, with continuous vitals and oxygen if the ABCs change. Oral pain medication and 'reassess in an hour' delay the only intervention that saves this patient, and this rigid abdomen with a rising heart rate and falling blood pressure is already showing you SIRS criteria heading toward sepsis. Ambulating or feeding this patient is unsafe — an angry, perforated bowel needs to sleep and the patient must stay NPO for surgery. Remember the chain: perforation → peritonitis → sepsis → shock → death if nothing is done.

q: the course teaches, 'If you delay the priority intervention, what complication are you allowing to happen?' For a patient with a bowel obstruction, which chain of complications is the nurse allowing?
o: Ischemia → necrosis → perforation → sepsis
Fistula formation → abscess → sepsis
Toxic megacolon → ulceration → sepsis
Metastasis → obstruction → perforation
r: IN A BOWEL OBSTRUCTION, BLOOD FLOW IS COMPROMISED FIRST — ISCHEMIA LEADS TO DEAD TISSUE (NECROSIS), WHICH PERFORATES, WHICH SEEDS THE PERITONEUM AND ENDS IN SEPSIS. The fistula → abscess → sepsis chain belongs to Crohn's disease, and toxic megacolon with ulceration belongs to ulcerative colitis. The metastasis chain is colorectal cancer, which leads to obstruction and then to perforation or metastasis. Every one of these chains ends in the same place, which is exactly why the instructor says different diseases share the same complication and the same treatment.

q: Which patient is MOST likely to require total parenteral nutrition (TPN)?
o: A patient with IBS and occasional constipation
A patient recovering from an uncomplicated appendectomy who is tolerating clear liquids
A patient with severe Crohn's disease with multiple fistulas and prolonged bowel rest
A patient who has been NPO for 8 hours in preparation for a colonoscopy
r: TPN IS USED WHEN THE GI TRACT CANNOT BE SAFELY USED — severe Crohn's with multiple fistulas is an angry, ticked-off bowel that needs to sleep, so nutrition must bypass the gut entirely and go through a central line. Even if the question never said 'prolonged bowel rest,' severe Crohn's with multiple fistulas alone tells you the bowel is on rest and the patient still needs nutrition. The IBS patient and the appendectomy patient tolerating clear liquids both have a working gut — use the gut, whether by mouth or tube feeding. Being NPO for 8 hours before a procedure is not starvation and does not require TPN; TPN is not given because the patient is hungry or because it is convenient, and it can be continued for weeks or even a lifetime when needed.

q: A patient's TPN bag is nearly empty and the replacement bag has not yet arrived from pharmacy. Which action by the nurse is correct?
o: Abruptly discontinue the TPN and flush the central line with normal saline
Notify the provider and pharmacy and follow the order to hang a dextrose-containing solution until the new bag arrives
Borrow the TPN bag prepared for another patient on the unit who has similar additives
Slow the current bag to a keep-vein-open rate so it lasts until the new bag arrives
r: NEVER ABRUPTLY STOP TPN — STOPPING ALL OF THAT SUGAR AT ONCE CAUSES REBOUND HYPOGLYCEMIA, so a dextrose-containing solution is hung to bridge the gap until the patient's own bag arrives. Hanging another patient's bag is a MED ERROR: every TPN bag is mixed in pharmacy for one specific patient with that patient's name on it, which is also why a second nurse must verify the bag before it is hung. Slowing the infusion to a trickle is not a safe workaround either, because infusing TPN too slowly gives inadequate nutrition and can also drop the blood glucose. The nurse does not stop or pause a TPN infusion on her own unless she is working with the line itself or suspects a clot or migration.

q: A nurse caring for a patient receiving TPN through a central line meets resistance when attempting to flush and notes the infusion has become sluggish; the external catheter length appears longer than documented. What should the nurse do?
o: Apply firm pressure with a syringe to push the occlusion through and restore flow
Stop the infusion, assess the catheter, and notify the provider without forcing a flush
Continue the TPN at the current rate because stopping it causes rebound hypoglycemia
Increase the infusion rate to keep the line open until the provider rounds
r: SUSPECTED OCCLUSION, THROMBOSIS, OR CATHETER MIGRATION IS THE ONE SITUATION WHERE THE NURSE STOPS A TPN INFUSION WITHOUT WAITING FOR A PROVIDER ORDER, because this risk outweighs the risk of rebound hypoglycemia. Do NOT force a flush — the central line tip sits at the heart, so popping a clot loose sends it straight there, and forcing air or a displaced catheter risks an air embolism. Continuing or speeding up the infusion into a migrated or occluded line pushes concentrated TPN into the wrong space and delays recognition. Stop the infusion, inspect the catheter, and notify the provider.

q: Which assessment findings in the 45-year-old with 2 days of abdominal pain support acute diverticulitis rather than IBS or appendicitis? Select all that apply.
o: Temperature of 101.6°F
WBC of 17,800
Pain localized to the LEFT lower quadrant
Pain that intensifies with every bump in the car
Cramping that is relieved after a bowel movement
Alternating constipation and diarrhea with normal labs and a normal colonoscopy
r: FEVER PLUS LEUKOCYTOSIS PLUS LEFT LOWER QUADRANT PAIN IS THE DIVERTICULITIS PICTURE — infection plus localized inflammation in the left colon. Pain worsening with every bump in the car tells you there is peritoneal irritation, which is a red flag that this inflammation is reaching the lining. Cramping relieved by a bowel movement, alternating constipation and diarrhea, and normal diagnostics are the classic IBS description — IBS is irritated but structurally normal, with no fever and no leukocytosis. Right lower quadrant pain would have pointed you to appendicitis instead.

q: the course asks the class, 'If you delay the priority intervention, what complication are you allowing to happen?' Which complication chains are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Appendicitis → rupture → peritonitis → sepsis
Diverticulitis → perforation → peritonitis → sepsis
Crohn's disease → fistulas → abscess → sepsis
Ulcerative colitis → toxic megacolon → ulceration/perforation → sepsis
IBS → perforation → peritonitis → sepsis
Celiac disease → toxic megacolon → peritonitis → sepsis
r: DIFFERENT DISEASES, SAME ENDING — SOMETHING RUPTURES OR PERFORATES, GI CONTENTS LEAK WHERE THEY DO NOT BELONG, AND THE PATIENT GOES TO PERITONITIS AND THEN SEPSIS. Appendicitis and diverticulitis both perforate; Crohn's tunnels into fistulas that abscess; ulcerative colitis dilates into toxic megacolon that ulcerates and perforates; colorectal cancer obstructs and then perforates or metastasizes. IBS does NOT belong on this list — IBS hurts but does not harm, the bowel is structurally normal, and it does not perforate. Celiac disease damages the villi of the small intestine and causes malabsorption, not toxic megacolon.

q: Which nursing actions are required for a patient receiving TPN through a central line? Select all that apply.
o: Have a second nurse verify the TPN bag against the order before hanging it
Monitor blood glucose per protocol
Obtain daily weights and strict intake and output
Scrub the central line port vigorously every single time before connecting, and scrub it again if you looked away from it
If the patient's own bag is unavailable, hang a bag mixed for another patient with the same additives
Discontinue routine blood glucose checks once the infusion rate has been stable for 24 hours
r: TPN IS ICU-LEVEL THERAPY THAT GOES STRAIGHT INTO THE BLOODSTREAM — every carb, electrolyte, vitamin, and gram of protein is systemic, so it demands a second-nurse bag verification, glucose monitoring, daily weights, and I&O. Hanging the wrong bag is a med error, which is exactly why a second nurse verifies it; each bag is mixed in pharmacy with your patient's name on it. Glucose checks continue for the duration of therapy because carbs are going directly into the blood and the patient can swing hyperglycemic or hypoglycemic at any point. Be the nurse who is fanatical about scrubbing that port every single time — a central line infection is preventable, and sepsis from a dirty port can kill your patient.

q: A patient receiving TPN has a blood glucose of 348 with increased thirst, frequent urination, and dry mouth. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Administer insulin if it is prescribed
Verify the infusion rate and slow the infusion
Notify the provider, as the glucose concentration in the TPN may need to be adjusted
Immediately stop the TPN infusion and remove the tubing
Increase the infusion rate to flush the excess glucose through faster
Document the value as an expected TPN finding and recheck in 8 hours
r: A GLUCOSE OF 348 WITH THIRST, POLYURIA, AND DRY MOUTH IS TPN-INDUCED HYPERGLYCEMIA, USUALLY BECAUSE THE INFUSION IS RUNNING TOO FAST OR THE BAG CONTAINS TOO MUCH GLUCOSE. The nurse gives insulin if prescribed, verifies and slows the rate, and notifies the provider so the formula can be adjusted. Do NOT abruptly stop the infusion — that causes rebound hypoglycemia; the infusion is only stopped without an order when a clot or catheter migration is suspected. Increasing the rate would worsen the hyperglycemia and risk fluid overload, and hyperglycemia is never an expected finding to simply document and ignore.

q: A 45-year-old is admitted with left lower quadrant pain, fever of 101.6 F, a WBC of 17,800, and an abdomen that is tender to palpation. The provider suspects acute inflammation of the bowel wall. Which diagnostic test should the nurse anticipate FIRST?
o: CT scan of the abdomen
Colonoscopy, since it is the test of choice for the lower GI tract
Upper endoscopy (EGD)
Fecal occult blood test (FOBT)
r: Colonoscopy IS normally the test of choice for the lower GI tract because it is the only study that lets you look directly at the colon and rectum for polyps, bleeding, tumors, diverticula, ulcers, and obstructions. But as the instructor put it, sometimes the best diagnostic isn't the safest: PUSHING A SCOPE PAST AN ACUTELY INFLAMED BOWEL WALL CAN PERFORATE IT, so the less invasive CT comes first. An EGD is the wrong end of the GI tract entirely (esophagus, stomach, duodenum). FOBT only detects hidden blood and tells you nothing about an inflamed bowel wall.

q: A client with fatigue, pale skin, and a low hemoglobin has no visible blood in the stool. The fecal occult blood test (FOBT) comes back positive. What does this result tell the nurse?
o: The client has colorectal cancer
Blood is present in the stool — that is all
The bleeding is coming from the lower GI tract
The client has an upper GI ulcer
r: FOBT ANSWERS ONLY ONE QUESTION: IS BLOOD PRESENT? It does not tell you why the client is bleeding, where the bleeding is, or what disease they have. That is why the next step is a colonoscopy — FOBT asks 'is there blood?' and colonoscopy asks 'where is it coming from?' Naming a specific disease from an FOBT result is jumping past the data you actually have, and the test cannot localize bleeding to the upper or lower tract.

q: A client is scheduled for a colonoscopy tomorrow. Which nursing actions are appropriate before the procedure? Select all that apply.
o: Verify that informed consent has been obtained before the scope is inserted
Teach the client how to take the prescribed bowel prep and confirm it is completed
Establish IV access
Educate the client that sedation will be used during the procedure
Give the client a full breakfast the morning of the procedure to prevent hypoglycemia
Withhold all teaching until after the procedure because sedation causes amnesia
r: Before we put a scope in a patient: CONSENT, BOWEL PREP, IV ACCESS, AND SEDATION TEACHING. The bowel prep matters because the only way the provider can see the walls is if the colon is cleaned out, and a lot of the nurse's job here is education — making sure the prep is done correctly. Feeding the client defeats the prep and violates pre-sedation NPO safety. Teaching must happen BEFORE sedation, when the client can actually understand and consent.

q: Mrs. Garcia is 78 years old, post-op day 4 after hip surgery. She has had no bowel movement in 6 days and says 'I feel fine.' Her abdomen is mildly distended, she is receiving opioids every 4 hours, drinks very little water, has hypoactive bowel sounds, and has a small amount of liquid stool in her brief this morning. Which condition is most likely?
o: Mechanical bowel obstruction
Ulcerative colitis
Fecal impaction with constipation
Viral gastroenteritis
r: Constipation happens because stool is TOO DRY, TOO SLOW, OR BLOCKED — and Mrs. Garcia has all three drivers: opioids (a top cause of post-op constipation), poor fluid intake (the colon pulls even more water out, hardening the stool), and hypoactive sounds (slow motility). THE LIQUID STOOL IS NOT DIARRHEA — IT IS OVERFLOW LEAKING AROUND A HARD IMPACTION. A mechanical obstruction would show severe pain, vomiting, marked distention, and early high-pitched sounds; ulcerative colitis presents with frequent bloody diarrhea, not hard stool; gastroenteritis brings vomiting, fever, and hyperactive sounds.

q: Which assessment findings best support the nurse's conclusion that Mrs. Garcia has a fecal impaction with constipation? Select all that apply.
o: No bowel movement for 6 days
Hypoactive bowel sounds
A small amount of liquid stool in her brief
The client's statement 'I feel fine'
High-pitched, hyperactive bowel sounds
Temperature of 101.6 F
r: Three findings tie this together: six days without a stool means stool has sat in the colon long enough for more water to be absorbed and harden it, hypoactive sounds mean slow intestinal motility, and the liquid stool is OVERFLOW DIARRHEA LEAKING AROUND THE HARD IMPACTED STOOL. Students often reject impaction the moment they see liquid stool — that is exactly the trap. 'I feel fine' is subjective and does not support any pathology, and high-pitched sounds and fever point toward obstruction or infection rather than impaction.

q: Which nursing interventions are most appropriate for Mrs. Garcia's fecal impaction with constipation? Select all that apply.
o: Review the opioid regimen with the provider for a bowel regimen or dose adjustment
Encourage increased oral fluid intake
Schedule toileting after meals to take advantage of the gastrocolic reflex
Assist the client to ambulate in the hallway
Administer loperamide for the liquid stool
Keep the client NPO on strict bed rest and restrict fluids
r: TREAT THE CAUSE, NOT JUST THE SYMPTOM: if opioids are contributing, the regimen needs adjusting or a bowel regimen added. Fluids rehydrate the colon and loosen stool, the bowel likes routine so sitting on the toilet after meals uses the gastrocolic reflex to naturally stimulate a movement, and walking helps constipation. Loperamide is a diarrhea drug that SLOWS the bowel — a very bad choice here because the liquid stool is overflow, not true diarrhea. NPO and bed rest are for bowel rest; this bowel needs to be woken up, and restricting fluids makes the stool harder.

q: Weeks after her constipation resolved, Mrs. Garcia returns reporting 8 to 10 stools a day with blood mixed in, cramping before bowel movements, weight loss, and fatigue. She states 'this is different than when I was constipated.' Hemoglobin is 10.1, CRP is elevated, and albumin is low. What is most likely occurring?
o: Recurrent fecal impaction with overflow leakage
Irritable bowel syndrome
An inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) flare
Viral gastroenteritis
r: This is an entirely different picture in the same patient. INFLAMED BOWEL TISSUE BLEEDS EASILY — that is why blood is mixed with the stool, and blood is what separates this from constipation with overflow. The weight loss reflects nutrients not being absorbed plus avoiding food because eating worsens symptoms, and the elevated CRP tells you inflammation is occurring somewhere; the low albumin and hemoglobin of 10.1 back that up. Loose stool alone could be food poisoning, viral illness, IBS, or overflow — but IBS has no blood, no weight loss, and normal labs, and gastroenteritis is acute with fever and hyperactive sounds.

q: Which diagnostic tests will help confirm inflammatory bowel disease in Mrs. Garcia? Select all that apply.
o: Colonoscopy with biopsy
C-reactive protein (CRP)
Complete blood count (CBC)
Fecal occult blood test (FOBT)
H. pylori testing
Upper endoscopy (EGD)
r: COLONOSCOPY WITH BIOPSY IS THE GOLD STANDARD because it both visualizes the inflammation and obtains tissue. CRP shows inflammation and is useful for monitoring disease activity, and the CBC is the one students skip — with blood in the stool you absolutely worry about anemia from blood loss, plus you can check the white count. FOBT is unnecessary here: it only tells you whether blood is present, and this blood is already VISIBLE. H. pylori and an upper endoscopy both belong to the upper GI tract (esophagus, stomach, duodenum) — wrong part of the body for these symptoms.

q: While awaiting confirmation of Mrs. Garcia's IBD diagnosis, which set of nursing priorities is most important?
o: Maintain hydration, support nutrition, and monitor stool frequency and characteristics
Restrict oral fluids to decrease the number of stools
Administer an antidiarrheal to stop the bloody diarrhea immediately
Keep the client NPO and withhold all assessment until the biopsy results return
r: THE THREE PRIORITIES WHILE AWAITING DIAGNOSIS ARE HYDRATION, NUTRITION, AND STOOL MONITORING. Diarrhea causes rapid fluid loss, so you watch blood pressure, heart rate, and urine output; an inflamed bowel absorbs nutrients poorly, so you follow weight, albumin, and protein intake; and tracking stool frequency, blood, and changes over time is how you know whether treatment is working. Restricting fluids in a client already losing 8 to 10 stools a day accelerates dehydration, and you never stop assessing while waiting on a result.

q: A client was recently diagnosed with celiac disease. Which assessment finding best indicates that the client is NOT effectively managing the disease?
o: Occasional abdominal cramping after a stressful day at work
Progressive weight loss with new iron and fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies
The client reports reading the label on every packaged food
One loose stool after eating a large salad
r: THE REAL PROBLEM IN CELIAC DISEASE IS MALABSORPTION — not the diarrhea and not the abdominal pain. Gluten triggers the immune system to attack the small intestine, and over time the VILLI, where absorption actually happens, become flattened and gone; no villi means no absorption, so the body shows it as weight loss, vitamin deficiencies, fatigue, and malnutrition. This can look like a nutrition question, and that is the point. Label reading is exactly the behavior you want, since DIET IS THE ONLY TREATMENT — you cannot repair the damage, but you can remove the gluten that causes it.

q: An 82-year-old client tells the nurse she has been leaking stool for several months but has not mentioned it because 'that's just what happens when you get old.' What is the nurse's best action?
o: Reassure the client that some stool leakage is expected with aging
Apply protective briefs and limit her fluid intake to reduce episodes
Assume a weak pelvic floor and begin teaching pelvic floor exercises
Assess for an underlying cause, including impaction with overflow, weak muscles, nerve problems, or an inflamed bowel with diarrhea
r: FECAL INCONTINENCE IS NOT A NORMAL PART OF AGING — if a client has it, you investigate further and ask more questions rather than dismissing it. The four causes to remember are full (overflow around constipation or impaction), weak muscles (sphincter or pelvic floor after childbirth, rectal surgery, or pelvic floor disorder), disconnected nerves (stroke, dementia, spinal cord injury, MS, diabetes), and inflamed bowel with diarrhea (IBD, radiation injury). The approach is find, fix, protect, teach — find the cause first, which is why a rectal exam makes sense to look for a blockage. Limiting fluids worsens constipation, and starting exercises before identifying the cause treats a diagnosis you have not made.

q: Mrs. Lewis is a 39-year-old with a long history of IBS: alternating constipation and diarrhea, cramping relieved after a bowel movement, symptoms worse with stress, and a normal colonoscopy and labs. She now returns reporting new bloody stools and unexplained weight loss. How should the nurse interpret this?
o: This is expected because IBS alternates between constipation and diarrhea
These are red flags that the problem is no longer consistent with IBS and require further evaluation
This is an IBS flare triggered by stress at work
This is a common side effect of psyllium therapy
r: NEW BLOODY STOOLS AND UNEXPLAINED WEIGHT LOSS ARE NEVER IBS. As the instructor framed it, IBS hurts but it doesn't harm — IBS is irritated but structurally normal, with a normal colonoscopy and normal labs, while IBD is inflamed and damaged, and inflamed bowel tissue bleeds easily. Stress does trigger IBS, but it does not cause bleeding or weight loss. Alternating constipation and diarrhea is classic IBS; blood and weight loss are not, and once you have evidence the bowel is injured or inflamed you go IBD over IBS.

q: The provider is considering alosetron for a client whose severe diarrhea-predominant IBS has not responded to other therapies. Which consideration is most important for the nurse to understand?
o: Alosetron is first-line for any IBS client with diarrhea
Alosetron is used for IBS with constipation because it increases fluid in the intestines
Alosetron is reserved for severe IBS that has failed other treatments because it can cause ischemic colitis
Alosetron cures IBS by resolving the underlying bowel inflammation
r: ALOSETRON IS USED ONLY FOR SEVERE, REFRACTORY IBS BECAUSE IT CAN CAUSE ISCHEMIC COLITIS — an ischemic bowel is a far worse problem than the symptom you were treating. IBS meds match the bowel pattern: for diarrhea you slow the bowel with loperamide (Imodium) or bulk with psyllium; for constipation you soften and move stool with fiber supplements or lubiprostone, which increases fluid in the intestines. Nothing here cures IBS — treatment is about control, not cure, and IBS has no inflammation to resolve because the bowel is structurally normal.

q: A nurse is teaching a client who was newly diagnosed with diverticulosis after a routine colonoscopy. The client has no fever, no pain, and a normal white blood cell count. Which instruction should the nurse include?
o: Follow a low-fiber, low-residue diet from now on to keep the pouches empty
Increase dietary fiber and fluids and avoid straining during bowel movements
Begin taking an antibiotic at the first sign of abdominal cramping
Limit walking and other activity so the pouches do not rupture
r: OSIS MEANS THE POUCHES ARE THERE BUT ARE NOT INFLAMED - there is no infection to treat yet. Remember: pouches are peaceful until poop gets trapped and pouches pop, so the whole goal in diverticulOSIS is fiber, fluids, and movement to prevent constipation, straining, and the pressure that traps stool. Low fiber/low residue is the diet for ACUTE diverticulITIS, not for the quiet pouches; antibiotics treat an established infection, not cramping; and activity actually helps move stool, so restricting it makes constipation worse.

q: A client hospitalized with acute diverticulitis is receiving IV antibiotics and asks the nurse, "When can I go back to the high-fiber diet my doctor told me to eat?" Which response by the nurse is best?
o: "Stay on high fiber now - it will push the stool out of the pouches faster."
"You will be on a low-fiber, low-residue diet while the infection is treated, and go back to high fiber once it has resolved."
"High fiber is never recommended again once you have been diagnosed with diverticular disease."
"You will need clear liquids only for the next several months to keep the bowel at rest."
r: DURING ACUTE DIVERTICULITIS THE DIET IS LOW FIBER / LOW RESIDUE, AND HIGH FIBER RESUMES ONLY AFTER THE INFLAMMATION RESOLVES. The instructor's image says it best - would you rather rub a scraped knee or leave it alone to heal? Low residue is smooth and easy to pass so nothing scrapes or gets stuck while the angry bowel sleeps. Pushing fiber now irritates the inflamed bowel, but permanently avoiding fiber is also wrong, because once the itis becomes an osis again the client needs high fiber to prevent the constipation and straining that started the whole problem.

q: A client being treated for diverticulitis reports that stool and gas are now draining from an abnormal opening between the bowel and the bladder. The nurse recognizes this as which complication?
o: Abscess
Fistula
Bowel obstruction
Perforation with peritonitis
r: A FISTULA IS AN ABNORMAL TUNNEL THAT DEVELOPS BETWEEN ORGANS, which is exactly what stool draining from bowel into bladder describes. An abscess is infection walled off and trapped inside the pouch; an obstruction happens when the inflammation swells enough to stop things from flowing through; and perforation is the pouch actually popping, which spills bowel contents into the abdomen and produces peritonitis with a rigid board-like abdomen - the client here is not describing that. Abscess, fistula, obstruction, bleeding, and perforation are the five complications that come from pouches that pop.

q: A nurse is caring for a client admitted with acute diverticulitis. Which assessment finding requires immediate action?
o: Left lower quadrant tenderness with a temperature of 100.8 F (38.2 C)
White blood cell count of 13,000/mm3
Rigid, board-like abdomen with a blood pressure of 86/48 and a heart rate of 124
Report of no bowel movement for the past two days
r: A RIGID, BOARD-LIKE ABDOMEN IS THE CLASSIC SIGN OF PERITONITIS, AND PERITONITIS IS ALWAYS AN EMERGENCY. That is the pouch popping and spilling stool and bacteria into a sac that is supposed to be sterile, and the hypotension plus tachycardia say this client is deteriorating toward sepsis. Left lower quadrant pain, low-grade fever, leukocytosis, and constipation are all expected with diverticulitis itself - the reason the nurse watches vital signs is precisely to catch the fever, tachycardia, and hypotension that mean it is no longer just diverticulitis.

q: A client admitted with acute diverticulitis is suspected of having a ruptured diverticulum and is now developing peritonitis. Which nursing interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Keep the client NPO
Administer IV broad-spectrum antibiotics as prescribed
Begin IV fluid replacement
Prepare the client for possible surgery
Encourage frequent ambulation before the client is stabilized
Provide a high-fiber diet to move trapped stool through the bowel
r: THE BOWEL HAS RUPTURED, SO IT MUST REST (NPO), THE SPILLED BACTERIA MUST BE COVERED (IV BROAD-SPECTRUM ANTIBIOTICS), THE LOST FLUID MUST BE REPLACED (IV FLUIDS), AND THE HOLE MUST BE CLOSED (SURGERY). Antibiotics cannot close a hole - surgery is the only way to fix something that has popped, burst, or ruptured inside the body. Ambulation is wrong because this client is not stable, and any oral intake, especially fiber, is wrong because the angry bowel needs to sleep, not digest.

q: A nurse is assessing four clients with inflammatory bowel disease. Which client is MOST likely experiencing ulcerative colitis?
o: A client with mouth ulcers, non-bloody diarrhea, and a 20-pound unintentional weight loss
A client with left lower quadrant cramping, bloody diarrhea, and urgency with blood and mucus
A client with right lower quadrant pain, a fistula, and fat malabsorption
A client whose colonoscopy showed patchy areas of inflammation with healthy bowel in between
r: ULCERATIVE COLITIS = COLON ONLY, SO THE PAIN IS LEFT LOWER QUADRANT AND THE DIARRHEA IS BLOODY WITH URGENCY AND MUCUS. The C in colitis is the reminder: colitis stays in the colon, the inflammation is on the surface/inner lining, and those surface ulcers bleed into the stool. Every other option is Crohn's, which CRAWLS anywhere from mouth to anus through ALL layers - mouth sores, non-bloody diarrhea and weight loss, right lower quadrant pain with fistulas and malabsorption from the small intestine, and skip lesions.

q: A nurse is reviewing the colonoscopy report of a client diagnosed with ulcerative colitis. Which finding is expected?
o: Skip lesions with areas of healthy bowel in between
Continuous inflammation beginning in the rectum and extending through the colon
Fistulas between loops of small bowel
Patchy inflammation involving all layers of the bowel wall throughout the GI tract
r: UC IS CONTINUOUS AND STARTS IN THE RECTUM, THEN SPREADS UP THROUGH THE COLON WITHOUT SKIPPING. Colitis = colon, surface only, one unbroken stretch of inflamed inner lining. Skip lesions, fistulas, and transmural inflammation anywhere in the GI tract all belong to Crohn's, which crawls and craters through the entire bowel wall - that is exactly why Crohn's tunnels and UC bleeds.

q: A nurse is teaching a community group about ulcerative colitis. Which client has the GREATEST risk for developing this disease?
o: A 62-year-old with chronic constipation who strains during bowel movements
A 30-year-old whose mother and sister both have ulcerative colitis
A 58-year-old who eats a low-fiber diet and has hard stools
A 25-year-old who just finished a course of oral antibiotics
r: IBD LIVES UNDER THE AUTOIMMUNE UMBRELLA, SO FAMILY HISTORY IS THE STRONGEST RISK FACTOR FOR ULCERATIVE COLITIS. The immune system attacks the bowel instead of protecting it, and because it does not attack the same place in everyone, the umbrella holds both Crohn's and UC. Chronic constipation, straining, and a low-fiber diet describe the client who develops diverticular disease - pressure pushes the colon wall outward into pouches - and recent antibiotics point toward infectious diarrhea, not an autoimmune disease.

q: A client with suspected inflammatory bowel disease reports frequent diarrhea and fatigue. Which diagnostic tests should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
o: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
C-reactive protein (CRP)
Colonoscopy
Complete blood count (CBC)
Fecal occult blood test on a client with visibly bloody stools
Serum amylase and lipase
r: ESR AND CRP SHOW THAT INFLAMMATION IS PRESENT, THE COLONOSCOPY SHOWS WHERE IT IS, AND THE CBC SHOWS THE ANEMIA FROM CHRONIC BLOOD LOSS. ESR and CRP are the two the instructor said to remember specifically for IBD, because inflammation is the whole disease process. An FOBT looks for blood you cannot see - if the client already has visibly bloody stool, you do not need a test to prove blood is there. Amylase and lipase are pancreatic labs and have nothing to do with locating bowel inflammation.

q: A client with a long history of ulcerative colitis is admitted with a markedly distended abdomen, severe abdominal pain, a temperature of 102.4 F (39.1 C), and a heart rate of 128. The nurse recognizes these findings as indicating which condition?
o: An expected flare that will improve with a high-fiber diet
Toxic megacolon, a medical emergency
Colon cancer from years of chronic inflammation
Mild dehydration from bloody diarrhea
r: BIG SWOLLEN BELLY + SEVERE PAIN + FEVER + FAST HEART RATE = TOXIC MEGACOLON, AND IT IS A MEDICAL EMERGENCY. Think of blowing up a balloon: the colon gets bigger and bigger and then it pops, so treatment is NG decompression, NPO, IV fluids and electrolytes, corticosteroids to calm the inflammation, and surgery to actually fix it. This is not a routine flare and fiber would be dangerous here; colon cancer is the BAD LATER complication that shows up after years of irritation, and dehydration alone does not produce a rigid distended belly with fever. Remember the order UC complications kill in: BIG, BURST, BLEEDING, BAD LATER.

q: A client with ulcerative colitis has been having bloody diarrhea for several days. Which findings indicate that this bloody diarrhea has become an emergency? Select all that apply.
o: Blood pressure 86/48 mm Hg
Heart rate 126 beats/minute
Potassium 2.9 mEq/L
Hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL
Report of urgency with mucus in the stool
Temperature 98.6 F (37 C)
r: BLOODY DIARRHEA BECOMES AN EMERGENCY WHEN IT PRODUCES A LOW BLOOD PRESSURE, A FAST HEART RATE, A LOW POTASSIUM, AND ANEMIA - the client is now losing both blood and fluid faster than the body can compensate. That combination is the BLEEDING piece of big, burst, bleeding, bad later, and it needs fluids, electrolytes, and blood replacement. Urgency with blood and mucus is the everyday picture of an inflamed colon that cannot store stool, and a normal temperature is reassuring - neither one signals the crisis.

q: A client whose ulcerative colitis is in remission on mesalamine asks the nurse, "Why can't I just take prednisone all the time? It works so much better when I'm having an attack." Which response is best?
o: "Prednisone is the long-term medication, and mesalamine is only used during flares."
"Steroids are the big firefighters we save for a big fire - a severe flare - while mesalamine is the water we keep on the fire long term."
"Once you are in remission you no longer need either medication."
"Prednisone will cure your ulcerative colitis if you stay on it long enough."
r: PREDNISONE AND METHYLPREDNISOLONE ARE FOR SEVERE FLARES ONLY, NOT LONG-TERM USE, WHILE MESALAMINE AND SULFASALAZINE ARE THE LONG-TERM WATER-ON-THE-FIRE DRUGS. Option 0 simply reverses the two roles. The other IBD drugs fit the same analogy - azathioprine and methotrexate tell the immune system to chill, infliximab is the biologic that blocks the inflammatory chemicals, and loperamide or diphenoxylate-atropine are just the brakes for diarrhea. Option 3 is wrong for the most important reason of all: the goal of drug therapy is REMISSION, NOT CURE.

q: A client with severe ulcerative colitis has undergone a total colectomy with creation of an ileostomy. Which statements should the nurse include when reinforcing teaching and planning care? Select all that apply.
o: Removing the colon cures the ulcerative colitis
The client may have an ileostomy or a J-pouch
High ileostomy output is expected, especially at first
The client is at risk for dehydration and electrolyte loss
Oral fluids are started immediately after surgery
A purple or pale stoma is expected during the first 24 hours
r: NO COLON, NO COLITIS - because ulcerative colitis only ever involves the colon, taking the colon out cures the disease, and the stool then leaves through an ileostomy or a J-pouch. ILEOSTOMY = I LOSE WATER: high liquid output is expected and is exactly why this client is a big dehydration risk, which is why fluids, electrolytes, and I&O are the priority. Oral fluids are NOT started immediately - IV fluids are - and a stoma should be pink/beefy red and moist, so purple or pale means blood flow is gone and the provider must be notified.

q: A 22-year-old college student reports 6 months of cramping abdominal pain, frequent diarrhea without blood, a 20-pound unintentional weight loss, mouth sores that will not heal, fatigue, and diarrhea after eating. The client smokes a pack a day. Assessment shows a low BMI, mild right lower quadrant tenderness, and labs show a low albumin and low vitamin B12. The nurse suspects which condition?
o: Ulcerative colitis
Crohn's disease
Acute diverticulitis
Toxic megacolon
r: CROHN'S CRAWLS ANYWHERE FROM MOUTH TO ANUS AND GOES THROUGH ALL LAYERS, which is why this client has mouth sores at one end, right lower quadrant (terminal ileum) tenderness at the other, and NON-bloody diarrhea in between. The low albumin and low B12 are the giveaway - the small intestine is where nutrients are absorbed, so Crohn's starves the client; expect low sodium, potassium, and magnesium from diarrhea, high ESR, CRP, and WBC from inflammation, and a low hemoglobin from chronic disease. Ulcerative colitis would be colon-only with BLOODY diarrhea and left lower quadrant pain, diverticulitis is the older client with left-sided pain from years of straining, and toxic megacolon presents with a distended belly, fever, and tachycardia.

q: The nurse is planning care for the 22-year-old client newly diagnosed with Crohn's disease. Which complications should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
o: Bowel obstruction from strictures and narrowed bowel
Malnutrition with continued weight loss
Fistula formation
Dehydration with electrolyte loss
Cure of the disease once the diseased section of bowel is removed
Continuous inflammation limited to the rectum and colon
r: CROHN'S COMPLICATIONS ARE BLOCK, STARVE, TUNNEL, DRY OUT - obstruction, malnutrition, fistulas, and dehydration. Look at that swollen, narrowed bowel and ask whether stool can pass easily; it cannot, so it blocks. The damaged small intestine cannot absorb, so the client starves, the transmural inflammation tunnels into fistulas, and daily diarrhea dries the client out. Surgery repairs a fistula or a stricture but does NOT cure Crohn's, because it can come back anywhere from mouth to anus, and continuous rectal-to-colon inflammation is ulcerative colitis, not Crohn's skip lesions.

q: A 42-year-old client with a 20-year history of Crohn's disease comes to the clinic. Which findings should the nurse recognize as RED FLAGS for colorectal cancer that require provider follow-up? Select all that apply.
o: Long, thin, pencil-like stools
Blood in the stool
Ongoing unexplained weight loss
Fatigue caused by anemia
Greasy, floating stools after a fatty meal
One episode of constipation that resolved with a stool softener
r: LONG, THIN, PENCIL-LIKE STOOLS ARE THE CLASSIC RED FLAG because a growing tumor narrows the lumen and squeezes the stool down. A change in bowel habits, blood in the stool, ongoing unexplained weight loss, and fatigue from anemia round out the instructor's red-flag list. Greasy floating stools point to fat malabsorption, and a single episode of constipation that resolved is not the persistent CHANGE in bowel habits that signals cancer.

q: A 42-year-old client has had Crohn's disease for 20 years and says, "My symptoms are controlled, so why does my GI doctor still want a colonoscopy? Can't I just do the stool card at home?" What is the nurse's best response?
o: "The stool card is enough, because it detects cancer cells directly."
"Years of chronic inflammation raise your cancer risk, so the colonoscopy looks for cancer and removes polyps before they turn into cancer."
"The colonoscopy is done to confirm that you still have Crohn's disease."
"You do not need screening until you turn 45, so this can wait."
r: YEARS OF IRRITATION EQUAL CANCER RISK, which is why the I (inflammatory bowel disease) in PIFA - Polyps, IBD, Family history, Age 45 - makes this client a surveillance patient even when he feels well. FOBT FINDS BLOOD; COLONOSCOPY FINDS CANCER and can remove polyps before they become cancer, so the stool card cannot replace it. The scope is not being done to re-confirm Crohn's, and the age-45 rule is the START of screening for average-risk people, not a reason to delay a high-risk client.

q: A client with colon cancer returns from the operating room. The surgeon tells the family, "We removed the tumor and were able to reconnect the bowel." The nurse understands that the client had which procedure?
o: A permanent colostomy
An anastomosis
An ileostomy
A colostomy created because the bowel needs time to heal
r: A EQUALS ATTACH AGAIN - AN ANASTOMOSIS MEANS THE BOWEL WAS HOOKED BACK TOGETHER AND THERE IS NO STOMA. A colostomy is the other option, used when there is no way out and a new route is needed because the bowel needs time to heal, and that client WILL have a stoma. An ileostomy involves the ileum and follows removal of the colon, which is not what the surgeon described.

q: A 50-year-old male client returned to the med-surg unit at 10:30 from the PACU after removal of a colon tumor. At 10:45 the nurse documents: smokes half a pack per day; oriented to time and place; restless; incisional pain 9/10 with no pain medication given in the PACU; bowel sounds absent; has not voided; dressing intact with 2 cm of dried blood at midline; temp 98, pulse 80, respirations 24, BP 120/80, SpO2 93% on room air; D5 1000 mL infusing at 125 mL/hr. Which findings require immediate follow-up? Select all that apply.
o: Incisional pain of 9/10 with no pain medication given in the PACU
Restlessness
Absent bowel sounds
Has not voided since surgery
Dressing intact with 2 cm of dried blood at the midline incision
IV of D5 1000 mL infusing at 125 mL/hr
r: UNRELIEVED PAIN OF 9/10 PLUS RESTLESSNESS IS THE PROBLEM THAT NEEDS ACTION NOW - the restlessness is the evidence of the pain, and he never received anything in the PACU. ABSENT BOWEL SOUNDS ARE EXPECTED AFTER GI SURGERY because the bowel has to wake up slowly, and not voiding this soon after surgery is also expected, so neither is an immediate concern yet. A small area of DRIED blood on an intact dressing and a routine maintenance IV rate are normal post-op findings.

q: At 11:00 the same post-op client's SpO2 is still 93% on room air, respirations are 26, and pain is now 10/10. Which respiratory intervention should the nurse plan first?
o: Encourage deep breathing and coughing, and treat the pain so he is able to do it
Apply oxygen at 4 L/min by nasal cannula
Administer an albuterol nebulizer treatment
Request an NG tube for decompression
r: A SPO2 OF 93 PERCENT IS LOW-NORMAL, NOT HYPOXIA, AND IS EXPECTED TO IMPROVE WITH DEEP BREATHING AND COUGHING once the pain is controlled - a client splinting at 10/10 cannot expand his lungs. This client is most likely experiencing POST-OP PAIN as evidenced by RESTLESSNESS, not inadequate oxygenation or dehydration. Oxygen is a next step only if breathing exercises fail, albuterol is not indicated when breath sounds have not even been assessed, and an NG tube would have been placed in surgery if the surgeon had anticipated the need.

q: A client returns to the unit immediately after surgery with a new temporary colostomy. What is the nurse's priority action?
o: Tell the client he will never use his rectum again
Assess the stoma for color and blood flow
Change the ostomy pouch right away
Cover the stoma with dry gauze
r: THE POST-OP PRIORITY IS TO ASSESS THE STOMA FOR COLOR AND BLOOD FLOW: a healthy stoma is PINK OR BEEFY RED AND MOIST, while PURPLE OR PALE means blood flow is compromised and must be reported. Changing the pouch immediately is not the priority and disturbs a fresh surgical site, and covering a stoma with dry gauze does not protect it or tell you anything about perfusion. Telling him he will never use his rectum again is both untrue for a temporary colostomy and damaging to body image.

q: The nurse is planning care for a client on the first post-op day after colon resection with a new colostomy. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Assess the stoma, expecting it to be pink or beefy red and moist
Keep the client NPO until bowel sounds return, then start clear liquids and advance as tolerated
Medicate for pain so the client can walk, cough and deep breathe
Begin ostomy teaching and address body image, with the goal that the client feels confident caring for the ostomy himself
Document a dusky purple stoma as an expected post-op finding
Start a regular diet as soon as the client says he is hungry
r: PINK, POOP, PREPARE: PINK means the stoma is healthy and perfused, POOP means the bowel has started working (bowel sounds and output) BEFORE any feeding, and PREPARE means teach ostomy care and address BODY IMAGE before discharge. CLIENT CONFIDENCE IN SELF-CARE IS THE MOST IMPORTANT TEACHING OUTCOME - some clients will not even look at their stoma, so confidence matters even more than the steps of pouch care. A purple stoma is never expected and must be reported, and food is never advanced on hunger alone; no bowel sounds means no food.

q: A client with a Crohn's stricture has not passed stool or flatus for 24 hours, is vomiting, and his abdomen keeps getting larger. Which finding tells the nurse the obstruction has become severe?
o: High-pitched tinkling bowel sounds
No passage of flatus
Fecal-smelling vomit
Mild nausea
r: FECAL-SMELLING VOMIT MEANS THE STOOL IS BACKED UP SO FAR THAT IT IS COMING BACK UP, which indicates a severe obstruction. High-pitched tinkling bowel sounds are the EARLY finding as the bowel fights against the blockage; the emergency change is when those sounds go SILENT. No flatus and nausea are cardinal signs present in any obstruction, so they do not tell you the obstruction is worsening.

q: Which causes of intestinal obstruction should the nurse classify as MECHANICAL? Select all that apply.
o: A tumor in the colon
Adhesions from a previous abdominal surgery
A stricture from Crohn's disease
Volvulus (twisting of the bowel)
Paralytic ileus after abdominal surgery
A bowel that has simply stopped squeezing with nothing inside blocking it
r: M EQUALS MATERIAL BLOCKING THE BOWEL - tumors, Crohn's strictures, adhesions from prior surgery, hernias and volvulus are all physical blockages, and they are fixed by removing the blockage. NON-MECHANICAL obstruction is a paralytic ileus, which typically follows abdominal surgery: nothing is blocking the bowel, it just stopped squeezing. That distinction drives treatment - you wake up an ileus, but you must cut out or reduce a mechanical blockage.

q: The nurse is assigned two clients with intestinal obstruction. Which client should the nurse recognize as most likely to become critically ill first?
o: The client with early projectile vomiting, upper abdominal distension and severe dehydration
The client with lower abdominal distension, cramping and ribbon-like stools
The client with high-pitched bowel sounds and no flatus
The client reporting crampy pain that eases when he changes position
r: A SMALL BOWEL OBSTRUCTION BECOMES CRITICALLY ILL FASTER: the blockage is high, so the client vomits early, distends in the UPPER abdomen and dehydrates severely. A LARGE bowel obstruction is the slower picture - lower abdominal distension, RIBBON-LIKE stools and less vomiting - because the small intestine keeps emptying into the colon for a while. High-pitched bowel sounds and absent flatus occur in BOTH types, so they do not tell you which client is sicker.

q: A client is being treated for a paralytic ileus with NPO status, NG tube decompression and IV fluid replacement. Which finding best indicates that the bowel has "woken up" and the client is ready to begin oral intake?
o: The client says he feels hungry
Return of bowel sounds, passage of flatus, and a bowel movement
The abdomen is silent and soft to palpation
NG tube drainage has increased
r: THE BOWEL IS AWAKE ONLY WHEN BOWEL SOUNDS, FLATUS AND A BOWEL MOVEMENT ALL RETURN - until then, absolutely no food. Hunger is not evidence of returning peristalsis, and a silent abdomen means the bowel is still asleep. Increasing NG output means more is backing up, which is a reason to keep decompressing, not to feed.

q: A client with a known inguinal hernia reports that the bulge is now hard and severely painful, will not go back in, and he has a fever with a rigid, tender abdomen. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
o: Reducible hernia - teach him to push it back in while lying flat
Incarcerated hernia - schedule an outpatient repair in a few weeks
Strangulated hernia - a surgical emergency; notify the provider immediately
Any hernia can be managed with a truss until it becomes convenient to operate
r: STRANGULATED MEANS THE BLOOD SUPPLY IS GONE, leading to dead bowel, perforation, peritonitis and sepsis - a SURGICAL EMERGENCY, and the fever and rigid abdomen say it is already headed there. REDUCE EQUALS RETURN, so a reducible hernia is soft and goes back in; an incarcerated hernia is stuck and painful with trapped bowel and needs surgical evaluation, but it is not yet dead bowel and cannot wait weeks either. A truss is only for a client who is NOT having surgery, never a substitute for emergency repair.

q: A client is being discharged after inguinal hernia repair. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Increase fiber and fluids so you do not strain to have a bowel movement
Avoid heavy lifting, straining and forceful coughing
Apply ice to the area to decrease swelling
Report increasing redness or swelling at the surgical site
Return to all of your normal activities, including lifting, as soon as you get home
Wear a truss instead of following the activity restrictions
r: DON'T POP THE REPAIR - anything that raises abdominal pressure (straining, heavy lifting, forceful coughing) can reopen what the surgeon just fixed, which is why fiber and fluids to prevent constipation are teaching, not just comfort. Ice reduces post-op swelling, and new redness or swelling may signal infection and must be reported. Normal activity is NOT resumed immediately, and a truss is only used when surgery is not being done - it does not protect a fresh repair.

q: A young man reports a painful, swollen lump at the top of the gluteal cleft with redness, warmth and purulent, blood-tinged drainage. Which plan of care should the nurse anticipate?
o: Keep the area clean and dry, give antibiotics for infection, and prepare for incision and drainage if an abscess forms
Apply an occlusive moist dressing and a corticosteroid cream to soften the area
Teach sitz baths and a high-fiber diet, since this is a hemorrhoid
No treatment is needed because these lumps always resolve on their own
r: HAIR AND CHAIR EQUALS INFECTION - a pilonidal cyst comes from hair, friction and sweating at the top of the gluteal cleft, so care is to KEEP IT DRY AND CLEAN, add antibiotics if infected, do an I and D if an abscess forms, and remove it surgically if it keeps coming back. A moist occlusive dressing does the opposite of keeping it dry, and steroid cream does not treat an infection. This is an infected hair follicle in the skin, not a hemorrhoid, which is a swollen VEIN.

q: A client reports painless bright red bleeding with bowel movements and rectal itching, but denies pain with sitting and has no tender external lumps. Which problem does the nurse suspect, and what teaching is indicated?
o: External hemorrhoids; teach that pain with sitting is expected
Internal hemorrhoids; teach high fiber and fluids to stop straining, warm sitz baths, a donut cushion and analgesic ointment
A pilonidal cyst; teach to keep the area dry and expect purulent drainage
A strangulated hernia; prepare the client for emergency surgery
r: INTERNAL EQUALS INVISIBLE - PAINLESS BLEEDING AND ITCHING, while EXTERNAL EQUALS EXPOSED - pain with sitting, pain with bowel movements and tender lumps, which this client does not have. Hemorrhoids are swollen VEINS from too much pressure - a vascular problem, not a skin problem - so treatment targets the straining: high fiber and fluids, warm sitz baths, a donut cushion and analgesic ointments. A pilonidal cyst is an infected hair follicle at the top of the gluteal cleft, and a strangulated hernia involves trapped bowel with no blood supply.

q: A 78-year-old client is seen in the primary care clinic. Three months ago amlodipine was started for hypertension. The client then developed bilateral ankle swelling, and a second provider added furosemide. The client now reports dizziness on standing and has lost 4 lb. Which conclusion by the nurse is most appropriate?
o: The furosemide dose is too low and the edema is worsening
The ankle swelling confirms new-onset heart failure
This is a prescribing cascade; the edema is likely an amlodipine side effect
The dizziness is an expected finding in a client over age 75
r: Amlodipine causes dose-related peripheral edema, and a diuretic was added to treat that side effect instead of reassessing the original drug. That is the textbook PRESCRIBING CASCADE: A NEW DRUG ORDERED TO TREAT ANOTHER DRUG'S SIDE EFFECT. Heart failure edema is usually accompanied by weight gain, dyspnea, and crackles, not weight loss from over-diuresis, and dizziness on standing is never dismissed as normal aging.

q: An 80-year-old client arrives at the clinic for an annual visit. The nurse asked the client to bring in every medication from home. Which nursing action best completes an accurate medication reconciliation?
o: Copy the medication list from the last clinic note into the chart
Ask the client to name only the prescriptions taken daily
Verify the prescriptions and skip supplements, since they are not drugs
Open every bottle in the bag, including OTC and herbal products, and compare with the chart
r: The brown-bag review works only when the nurse physically inspects every container the client actually takes. OTC AND HERBAL PRODUCTS COUNT AS MEDICATIONS: ginkgo and high-dose fish oil raise bleeding risk with warfarin, and NSAIDs and antihistamines are bought without a prescription. Copying the old list or asking the client to recall from memory misses duplicate therapy and multiple prescribers.

q: An 82-year-old client on a med-surg unit tells the night nurse, "I always take a couple of Benadryl at home to fall asleep." The provider has written diphenhydramine 50 mg PO at bedtime PRN. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Give the diphenhydramine as ordered since it matches the home routine
Hold the dose and contact the provider about a safer sleep option
Give half the dose and reassess in one hour
Document that the client has a long-standing tolerance to the drug
r: Diphenhydramine is a first-generation antihistamine with strong ANTICHOLINERGIC effects and is on the Beers list for older adults. It causes confusion, urinary retention, dry mouth, blurred vision, and next-morning sedation, all of which drive FALLS AND DELIRIUM. Home use does not make it safe, and cutting the dose does not remove the anticholinergic risk; nonpharmacologic sleep measures are the standard first-line approach.

q: A 79-year-old client admitted for cellulitis becomes anxious and restless at 2200. A new order reads lorazepam 1 mg PO PRN anxiety. Which nursing intervention is the priority before administering the drug?
o: Raise all four side rails to keep the client in bed
Administer the dose and recheck the client in the morning
Screen for pain, hypoxia, full bladder, and unfamiliar surroundings
Ask the family to stay overnight so the dose can be doubled if needed
r: Restlessness in an older adult is a symptom, not a diagnosis, and pain, hypoxia, urinary retention, and sundowning are common reversible triggers. Benzodiazepines are Beers-list drugs that prolong sedation and directly increase FALL AND DELIRIUM RISK, so the nurse rules out treatable causes first. Four side rails are a physical restraint, and giving a benzodiazepine to sedate a confused client is a CHEMICAL RESTRAINT, not treatment.

q: A nurse reviews the home medication list of an 83-year-old client admitted after an unwitnessed fall at an assisted living facility. Which medications should the nurse flag for the provider as potentially inappropriate for an older adult? Select all that apply.
o: Glyburide 10 mg PO daily
Lisinopril 10 mg PO daily
Cyclobenzaprine 10 mg PO three times daily
Oxybutynin 5 mg PO twice daily
Acetaminophen 650 mg PO every 6 hours PRN
r: Glyburide is a LONG-ACTING SULFONYLUREA that causes prolonged hypoglycemia as GFR falls; cyclobenzaprine is a sedating muscle relaxant; oxybutynin is a potent anticholinergic. ALL THREE ARE BEERS-LIST DRUGS THAT CAUSE SEDATION, CONFUSION, AND FALLS. Lisinopril is an appropriate first-line antihypertensive, and acetaminophen is the preferred analgesic in older adults because it avoids NSAID GI and renal risk.

q: A 76-year-old client with osteoarthritis reports taking ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily for the past four months for knee pain. The nurse notes a creatinine of 1.6 mg/dL, a hemoglobin of 9.2 g/dL, and dark tarry stools. Which statement best explains these findings?
o: Ibuprofen commonly causes a harmless darkening of the stool
The anemia is an expected age-related change in bone marrow
The client needs a higher ibuprofen dose because the pain persists
Chronic NSAID use is causing GI bleeding and reduced renal perfusion
r: NSAIDs block prostaglandins, which strips the gastric mucosal barrier and constricts the renal afferent arteriole. In an older adult with an already reduced GFR, that produces the exact picture here: MELENA WITH ANEMIA PLUS A RISING CREATININE. Tarry stools are never a benign color change, and anemia is not normal aging; increasing the dose would worsen both organs.

q: An 85-year-old client in a long-term care facility takes digoxin 0.25 mg PO daily and metformin 1000 mg PO twice daily. The client reports nausea, anorexia, and "yellow-green halos" around lights. Which nursing action is the priority?
o: Encourage a high-potassium snack and continue the current doses
Reassure the client that visual changes are expected with cataracts
Hold the digoxin, check the apical pulse and digoxin level, and notify the provider
Administer an antiemetic and reassess in 4 hours
r: Nausea, anorexia, and yellow-green or halo vision are classic DIGOXIN TOXICITY signs, and digoxin is renally cleared with a narrow therapeutic window. AGING LOWERS GFR, SO RENALLY CLEARED DRUGS ACCUMULATE even when the dose never changed. Treating only the nausea or attributing halos to cataracts delays recognition of a life-threatening drug level, and metformin also requires renal monitoring for lactic acidosis risk.

q: A 77-year-old client is admitted with poor oral intake and a serum albumin of 2.4 g/dL. Home medications include warfarin and phenytoin. Which assessment finding should the nurse anticipate and monitor for most closely?
o: Reduced drug effect requiring higher doses of both medications
Delayed onset of action because absorption is slowed
No change in drug effect, since albumin does not affect these drugs
Increased bleeding and signs of phenytoin toxicity such as ataxia and nystagmus
r: Warfarin and phenytoin are highly protein bound, and only the unbound drug is pharmacologically active. LOW ALBUMIN MEANS MORE FREE DRUG, WHICH MEANS MORE EFFECT AND MORE TOXICITY at the same dose. Expect bruising, bleeding, and phenytoin toxicity signs such as ataxia and nystagmus; the drug is not less effective, and albumin affects distribution, not absorption speed.

q: A nursing student asks why a 74-year-old postoperative client stayed drowsy for nearly two days after a single dose of diazepam. Which response by the nurse demonstrates correct understanding of age-related pharmacokinetics?
o: Aging increases body fat and decreases total body water, so fat-soluble drugs are stored and released slowly
Aging increases stomach acid, so more of the drug is absorbed at once
Aging increases hepatic first-pass metabolism, so more active drug reaches the brain
Aging increases serum albumin, so more drug stays bound and active in the tissues
r: Older adults have proportionally MORE BODY FAT AND LESS TOTAL BODY WATER, so lipid-soluble drugs such as diazepam distribute into fat, build a reservoir, and have a markedly prolonged half-life. Hepatic first-pass metabolism DECREASES with age (which raises drug levels, it does not lower them), and albumin DECREASES rather than increases. This is exactly why the rule is START LOW, GO SLOW.

q: A 84-year-old client is admitted for a hip fracture repair. On postoperative day 1 the client is oriented in the morning but by evening is pulling at the IV and does not recognize family. The client received hydromorphone, promethazine, and prednisone in the past 12 hours. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Document the new baseline as early dementia and notify the family
Review the medication administration record and report the change to the provider
Apply soft wrist restraints to protect the IV site
Request an order for haloperidol to calm the client for the night
r: Sudden fluctuating confusion that is worse at night is DELIRIUM, and opioids, anticholinergic antiemetics such as promethazine, and steroids are all high-yield reversible causes. NEW-ONSET CONFUSION IN AN OLDER ADULT IS NEVER NORMAL AGING AND IS NEVER DEMENTIA UNTIL MEDS, INFECTION, AND HYPOXIA ARE RULED OUT. Restraints and antipsychotics worsen delirium and treat the nurse's alarm rather than the client's cause.

q: A home health nurse finds that an 81-year-old client who was alert last week is now confused and inattentive. Which actions should the nurse include in the assessment? Select all that apply.
o: Review all prescription, OTC, and herbal medications for recent additions
Obtain a urine specimen to screen for urinary tract infection
Reassure the family that confusion is an expected part of aging
Check oxygen saturation and assess hydration status
Request an order for a sedative to keep the client calm at home
r: A sudden change in attention and orientation is delirium, and the nurse hunts for the reversible cause: MEDS, INFECTION (ESPECIALLY UTI), HYPOXIA, AND DEHYDRATION. Anticholinergics, opioids, benzodiazepines, and steroids are the usual medication culprits, so the full list including OTC and herbals is reviewed. Calling confusion normal aging delays a workup, and a sedative is a chemical restraint that deepens the delirium.

q: A 88-year-old client with Alzheimer disease wanders the hallway of a long-term care unit in the late afternoon and becomes agitated. An unlicensed assistive personnel asks the nurse to "get something to knock her out." Which response by the nurse is best?
o: "I will call the provider for a standing order of quetiapine every evening."
"Let's put her in a reclining chair with a lap tray until she settles down."
"Let's toilet her, turn on the lights, and walk with her in the hallway."
"Agitation at this stage is untreatable, so we should just close her door."
r: Sundowning agitation in dementia is managed first with nonpharmacologic measures: toileting, pain relief, bright light, familiar routines, and safe supervised walking. ROUTINE SEDATIVES AND ANTIPSYCHOTICS IN DEMENTIA ARE CHEMICAL RESTRAINTS THAT INCREASE FALLS, DELIRIUM, AND MORTALITY. A lap tray the client cannot remove is a physical restraint, and isolating or ignoring the client abandons a safety need.

q: A 75-year-old client in a rehabilitation unit takes hydrochlorothiazide, metoprolol, and doxazosin. The client reports feeling lightheaded when getting out of bed in the morning. Which instruction should the nurse give?
o: "Stand up quickly so the dizziness passes faster."
"Skip your morning doses on days you feel lightheaded."
"Limit fluids in the morning to reduce trips to the bathroom."
"Sit on the edge of the bed for a full minute before you stand, and hold the rail."
r: Diuretics, beta blockers, and alpha blockers all blunt the baroreceptor response that is already slowed by stiffer vessels in aging, producing orthostatic hypotension. CHANGE POSITION SLOWLY: DANGLE, THEN STAND WITH SUPPORT, because this is a leading cause of falls and hip fractures. Standing fast worsens the drop, self-skipping doses is unsafe, and restricting fluids makes hypovolemia and dizziness worse.

q: A 79-year-old client living alone takes nine medications from three different prescribers. The client has arthritis in both hands, presbyopia, and a fixed income, and admits to "skipping the expensive one some weeks." Which nursing action best supports adherence?
o: Work with the provider and pharmacist to simplify the regimen, arrange a weekly pill organizer with large-print labels, and refer for prescription assistance
Give the client a printed 9-page drug information packet to review at home
Instruct the client to ask a neighbor to administer all the medications
Tell the client that missing doses is acceptable as long as it happens less than twice a week
r: Adherence barriers here are physical, sensory, cognitive, and financial all at once, so the plan must address each: fewer daily doses, an easy-open organizer, large-print labels, and cost assistance. FIX THE BARRIER, THEN CONFIRM UNDERSTANDING WITH TEACH-BACK, having the client explain the plan back in his or her own words. A dense printed packet ignores presbyopia and literacy, delegating to a neighbor is not a nursing plan, and no nurse endorses missed doses.

q: A 54-year-old man on a med-surg unit has a serum potassium of 2.8 mEq/L. A new order reads: Potassium chloride 20 mEq IV push now. What is the nurse's BEST action?
o: Give the dose slowly over 2 minutes while watching the cardiac monitor
Give the dose, then recheck the potassium level in 1 hour
Hold the dose and call the provider to clarify the route
Dilute the dose in 10 mL of normal saline and push it over 5 minutes
r: Hold the dose and clarify. NEVER IV PUSH POTASSIUM - it causes cardiac arrest. Pushing it slowly, or diluting it in a syringe first, is still an IV push and is still lethal. KCl must be premixed/diluted in a bag and infused on a pump.

q: A 71-year-old woman in the ICU is ordered potassium chloride 20 mEq in 100 mL NS IV over 2 hours for a potassium of 3.1 mEq/L. Which finding must the nurse verify FIRST before starting the infusion?
o: Urine output of at least 30 mL/hr
Serum calcium level
Presence of active bowel sounds
Capillary blood glucose
r: NO PEE, NO K. Potassium is excreted by the kidneys, so if urine output is under 30 mL/hr the dose stacks up and causes lethal hyperkalemia. Calcium, bowel sounds, and glucose are all assessed at some point, but none of them gate a KCl infusion.

q: A 60-year-old post-op patient is receiving potassium chloride 10 mEq in 100 mL NS IV peripherally. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Infuse the potassium on an electronic infusion pump
Increase the peripheral rate to 30 mEq/hr to correct the level faster
Maintain continuous cardiac monitoring during the infusion
Massage the site if the patient reports burning, to disperse the drug
Assess the IV site frequently for burning, redness, or swelling
r: Pump plus cardiac monitor plus frequent site checks is the potassium safety trio. PERIPHERAL MAX IS ABOUT 10 mEq/hr - higher concentrations require a central line. Never massage a burning site: burning signals phlebitis or infiltration, so STOP the infusion.

q: A 45-year-old woman is discharged on oral potassium chloride after treatment for hypokalemia. Which statement shows she understands the teaching?
o: I will take it first thing in the morning on an empty stomach.
I will lie down flat for 30 minutes after each dose.
I will crush the extended-release tablet if it is hard to swallow.
I will take it with a meal and a full glass of water.
r: ORAL KCl IS A GI IRRITANT - take it WITH FOOD AND A FULL GLASS OF WATER, sitting upright. An empty stomach causes nausea and ulceration, lying down lets the tablet burn the esophagus, and crushing an extended-release form dumps the entire dose at once.

q: A 68-year-old man with chronic kidney disease who takes lisinopril and spironolactone arrives in the ED with a potassium of 7.2 mEq/L. The monitor shows peaked T waves and a widening QRS. Which medication should the nurse anticipate giving FIRST?
o: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate PO
IV calcium gluconate
Regular insulin 10 units IV with dextrose 50%
Furosemide IV
r: CALCIUM GLUCONATE FIRST - it stabilizes the myocardium against lethal arrhythmias and buys time, but it does NOT lower the potassium. Insulin with D50 shifts K into cells within minutes, and sodium polystyrene or furosemide truly remove K but act far too slowly for a widening QRS. Note the cause: ACE INHIBITORS AND K-SPARING DIURETICS RAISE POTASSIUM.

q: A 59-year-old woman receives regular insulin 10 units IV with 50 mL of dextrose 50% for a potassium of 6.6 mEq/L. Which nursing action is the priority after administration?
o: Monitor for constipation and auscultate bowel sounds
Assess deep tendon reflexes every hour
Recheck the blood glucose within the next hour
Encourage an extra 500 mL of oral fluids
r: Insulin drives potassium INTO the cells, and it drives glucose in with it, so HYPOGLYCEMIA IS THE BIG RISK - recheck the blood sugar within the hour and keep monitoring. Constipation is a sodium polystyrene concern, and hourly deep tendon reflexes belong to magnesium therapy.

q: A 74-year-old man in the ICU has a potassium of 6.9 mEq/L. Which interventions actually REMOVE potassium from the body rather than shifting it? Select all that apply.
o: Nebulized albuterol
Sodium polystyrene sulfonate
IV calcium gluconate
Hemodialysis
Patiromer
r: Sort these three ways: REMOVE, SHIFT, or PROTECT. Sodium polystyrene sulfonate and patiromer bind potassium in the gut, and dialysis pulls it from the blood - true removal. Albuterol (like insulin with D50) only SHIFTS K into cells temporarily, and calcium gluconate only PROTECTS the heart.

q: Six hours after a total thyroidectomy, a 38-year-old woman reports tingling around her mouth and fingertips. Her calcium is 6.9 mg/dL and Chvostek sign is positive. Which medication should the nurse have ready?
o: Oral calcium carbonate
IV calcium gluconate
IV magnesium sulfate
IV potassium chloride
r: Symptomatic hypocalcemia after neck surgery (parathyroid injury) is an emergency - IV CALCIUM GLUCONATE is the treatment, with a cardiac monitor plus seizure and laryngospasm precautions at the bedside. Oral calcium is far too slow for tetany, and magnesium or potassium will not raise a calcium of 6.9.

q: A 29-year-old woman with preeclampsia is receiving an IV magnesium sulfate infusion. The nurse finds absent deep tendon reflexes, a respiratory rate of 9, and urine output of 15 mL/hr. After stopping the infusion, which drug should the nurse prepare?
o: Naloxone
Furosemide
Potassium chloride
Calcium gluconate
r: CALCIUM GLUCONATE IS THE ANTIDOTE FOR MAGNESIUM TOXICITY. Absent DTRs plus respiratory depression plus falling urine output is the classic triad - stop the magnesium first, then give the calcium. Naloxone reverses opioids, not magnesium, and potassium does nothing for this.

q: A 63-year-old man on long-term furosemide has received three doses of IV potassium chloride, but his potassium is still 3.0 mEq/L. Which laboratory value should the nurse check next?
o: Serum magnesium
Serum phosphorus
Serum albumin
Serum chloride
r: POTASSIUM WILL NOT CORRECT UNTIL MAGNESIUM IS CORRECTED - low Mg makes the kidneys keep dumping K no matter how much you replace. LOOP AND THIAZIDE DIURETICS WASTE BOTH K AND Mg, so suspect it in this patient. Phosphorus, albumin, and chloride do not block potassium repletion.

q: A 70-year-old woman with acute heart failure is ordered furosemide 80 mg IV. Which nursing action best prevents a serious adverse effect?
