o: Give the dose rapidly to speed up diuresis
Mix the dose in the same syringe as her potassium supplement
Administer the dose no faster than 20 mg per minute
Hold the dose if the patient reports increased urination
r: RAPID IV FUROSEMIDE CAUSES OTOTOXICITY - tinnitus and possible permanent hearing loss. Push it SLOWLY, about 20 mg/min or less. Increased urination is the expected therapeutic effect, not a reason to hold, and medications are never combined in one syringe like that.

q: A 66-year-old man is starting hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension. Which teaching point is MOST important for the nurse to include?
o: Limit foods such as bananas, potatoes, and orange juice.
Weigh yourself daily on the same scale at the same time, and rise slowly from lying to standing.
Take the dose at bedtime so you do not have to urinate during the day.
Your calcium level will drop on this drug, so avoid dairy products.
r: DAILY WEIGHT IS THE BEST INDICATOR OF FLUID STATUS (1 kg = about 1 L), and thiazides cause orthostatic hypotension, so change positions slowly. Thiazides WASTE potassium, so K-rich foods should be increased, not limited. Dose in the morning to protect sleep, and thiazides RAISE calcium rather than lowering it.

q: A 58-year-old woman with heart failure is being discharged on spironolactone. Which statement by the patient requires the nurse to intervene?
o: I bought a salt substitute so I can season my food without sodium.
I will call the clinic if I notice breast tenderness or enlargement.
I will weigh myself every morning before breakfast.
I will stand up slowly when I get out of bed.
r: SALT SUBSTITUTES ARE POTASSIUM CHLORIDE - paired with a K-SPARING diuretic they cause dangerous hyperkalemia, and K supplements are out for the same reason. Reporting gynecomastia, taking daily weights, and rising slowly are all correct spironolactone teaching.

q: A 47-year-old trauma patient in the ED requires fluid resuscitation and will also receive packed red blood cells. Which statements about IV fluids are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: 0.9% normal saline is the only IV fluid hung with blood products
Lactated Ringer's is isotonic and appropriate for resuscitation but is NOT run with blood
0.45% normal saline is the first choice for restoring intravascular volume in shock
0.45% normal saline shifts fluid into the cells and can cause cerebral edema
3% saline is isotonic and may be infused rapidly on any med-surg unit
r: ISOTONIC FLUIDS (0.9% NS, LR) STAY IN THE VESSELS for resuscitation, but LR contains calcium that clots with blood tubing - ONLY NS RUNS WITH BLOOD. Hypotonic 0.45% NS shifts water INTO cells, so it treats cellular dehydration and risks cerebral edema; it never restores volume in shock. 3% saline is HYPERTONIC, ICU only, and infused slowly.

q: A 76-year-old woman taking sertraline is admitted with SIADH, a sodium of 112 mEq/L, confusion, and a witnessed seizure. The provider orders 3% saline. Which nursing action is the priority during the infusion?
o: Infuse slowly on a pump with frequent neurologic checks and serial sodium levels
Infuse the first 500 mL rapidly to raise the sodium above 130 mEq/L within 2 hours
Encourage extra free water by mouth to prevent dehydration during the infusion
Piggyback the 3% saline into an existing 0.45% saline infusion
r: CORRECTING SODIUM TOO FAST CAUSES OSMOTIC DEMYELINATION - permanent, irreversible brain injury. Hypertonic saline goes SLOWLY on a pump in the ICU with frequent neuro checks and serial sodium draws. Free water worsens hyponatremia, and SSRIs like sertraline are a classic drug cause of SIADH.

q: A 52-year-old man receiving IV fluids reports pain at his IV site. The nurse finds the area cool, pale, and swollen, and the infusion has slowed. What should the nurse do FIRST?
o: Apply a warm compress and continue the infusion
Flush the catheter with 10 mL of normal saline to clear it
Increase the infusion rate to keep the vein open
Stop the infusion and remove the catheter
r: Cool, pale, swollen, and sluggish equals INFILTRATION. STOP THE INFUSION AND REMOVE THE IV FIRST, then elevate the extremity and restart in a new site. Flushing or increasing the rate forces more fluid into the tissue. Warm, red, streaking with a palpable cord is phlebitis, which also means stop and remove.

q: A 24-year-old client is taken to the OR for an emergency appendectomy. The nurse reviews the anesthesia plan. Which combination of agents places this client at the highest risk for malignant hyperthermia?
o: Propofol and fentanyl
Midazolam and IV lidocaine
Sevoflurane and succinylcholine
Bupivacaine spinal block and ondansetron
r: MALIGNANT HYPERTHERMIA IS TRIGGERED BY INHALED VOLATILE ANESTHETICS PLUS SUCCINYLCHOLINE. Sevoflurane is a volatile gas and succinylcholine is the classic depolarizing blocker, so that pair is the highest risk. Propofol, fentanyl, midazolam, and local or spinal anesthetics are non-triggering. MH is GENETIC, so always ask about family history of anesthesia problems before surgery.

q: A 16-year-old in the OR develops jaw rigidity, unexplained tachycardia, and a sharply rising end-tidal CO2 fifteen minutes into a general anesthetic. Which action does the nurse anticipate FIRST?
o: Apply a cooling blanket and ice packs to the groin and axillae
Stop the volatile anesthetic and prepare IV dantrolene
Draw a stat serum potassium and creatine kinase
Give IV acetaminophen to bring down the fever
r: DANTROLENE IS THE ANTIDOTE, AND STOPPING THE TRIGGER GOES WITH IT. Rising end-tidal CO2 is the earliest sign and masseter rigidity with tachycardia is the earliest reliable clinical sign, so treatment starts long before the temperature climbs. Cooling and labs follow, they do not come first. Antipyretics do nothing here because the heat comes from muscle hypermetabolism, not the hypothalamus.

q: A 30-year-old client in the PACU is being treated for malignant hyperthermia. Which interventions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Administer 100 percent oxygen at high flow
Reconstitute and give IV dantrolene sodium
Cover the client with forced-air warming blankets
Monitor the ECG and treat hyperkalemia and dysrhythmias
Restart succinylcholine to relax the rigid muscles
r: THE MH BUNDLE IS: STOP THE AGENT, 100 PERCENT OXYGEN, DANTROLENE, COOL THE CLIENT, TREAT HYPERKALEMIA AND DYSRHYTHMIAS. Hypermetabolism drives the CO2, potassium, and temperature up, so cooling is required and WARMING is exactly backward. Succinylcholine is a trigger, so giving more would worsen the crisis, not fix the rigidity.

q: A 68-year-old is scheduled for a total knee arthroplasty in 10 days. Which home medications should the nurse expect to be held before surgery? Select all that apply.
o: Warfarin
Metoprolol
Clopidogrel
Levothyroxine
Ginkgo biloba
r: BLEEDERS GET HELD, BETA BLOCKERS GET CONTINUED. Warfarin and clopidogrel are stopped on a surgeon-directed schedule, and bleeding herbals (garlic, ginkgo, ginseng, ginger, vitamin E, fish oil) stop roughly 1 to 2 weeks out. Metoprolol is continued to prevent rebound tachycardia and hypertension, and levothyroxine is taken with a sip of water. Metformin is the other classic hold around surgery and contrast.

q: A 72-year-old with hypertension asks the pre-op nurse whether to take his atenolol the morning of his hernia repair. What is the nurse's best response?
o: Hold it, because all cardiac drugs are stopped before anesthesia.
Hold it for 48 hours so you do not become bradycardic during surgery.
Take half a dose, but only if your blood pressure is over 140.
Take it with a small sip of water as ordered so your pressure does not rebound.
r: BETA BLOCKERS ARE USUALLY CONTINUED THROUGH SURGERY. Stopping them abruptly causes rebound tachycardia, hypertension, and myocardial ischemia. The hold options invent a risk that is smaller than the rebound risk, and clients never self-adjust doses. Contrast this with metformin and anticoagulants, which ARE held.

q: A 55-year-old just received IV midazolam in the pre-op holding area. Which nursing action is the priority?
o: Raise the side rails, lower the bed, and keep the client from getting up
Have the client sign the surgical consent now that he is calm and cooperative
Walk the client to the bathroom before transport to the OR
Offer sips of clear liquid to relieve his dry mouth
r: MIDAZOLAM CAUSES SEDATION AND AMNESIA, SO SAFETY FIRST: SIDE RAILS UP, BED LOW, NO AMBULATING. CONSENT MUST BE SIGNED BEFORE SEDATION, never after, because a sedated client cannot give informed consent. The client also stays NPO, so no fluids. Flumazenil is the reversal agent if he becomes oversedated.

q: A 45-year-old is scheduled for a colectomy at 0800 and the nurse has an order for IV cefazolin. When should the nurse plan to infuse it?
o: The night before surgery with the bowel prep
Immediately after the surgeon closes the incision
Within 60 minutes before the surgical incision
Only if the client spikes a fever in the PACU
r: PROPHYLACTIC ANTIBIOTICS GO IN WITHIN 60 MINUTES OF INCISION. That timing puts peak tissue levels right where the skin is opened, which is what actually lowers surgical site infection. Giving it the night before or after closure misses the window entirely, and waiting for a fever is treatment, not prophylaxis.

q: A 34-year-old woman receives a spinal anesthetic for a cesarean birth. Ten minutes later her BP is 82/44 and her heart rate is 48. Which does the nurse identify as the most likely cause?
o: Hemorrhage from the uterine incision
Sympathetic blockade from the spinal anesthetic
Anaphylaxis to the local anesthetic
Postdural puncture headache
r: SPINAL AND EPIDURAL BLOCKS CAUSE HYPOTENSION AND BRADYCARDIA FROM SYMPATHETIC BLOCKADE. Treat with IV fluids, positioning, and a vasopressor such as ephedrine or phenylephrine. Hemorrhage causes tachycardia, not bradycardia, and a postdural puncture headache shows up later as a positional headache. Also watch for a HIGH BLOCK causing respiratory compromise, and track return of sensation, motor function, and voiding.

q: A 61-year-old in the PACU is unarousable with a respiratory rate of 6 after receiving midazolam and rocuronium. Anesthesia reports the neuromuscular blockade was already fully reversed with sugammadex and no opioids were given. Which agent should the nurse anticipate?
o: Neostigmine
Naloxone
Acetylcysteine
Flumazenil
r: FLUMAZENIL REVERSES BENZODIAZEPINES; NALOXONE REVERSES OPIOIDS. No opioid was given, so naloxone has no target. Neostigmine and sugammadex reverse neuromuscular blockade, which is already reversed here, and acetylcysteine is the acetaminophen antidote. Both flumazenil and naloxone are SHORT-ACTING, so resedation is real and doses may need repeating.

q: While a provider infiltrates lidocaine for a laceration repair, a 27-year-old reports numbness around her lips, ringing in her ears, and a metallic taste. What is the nurse's first action?
o: Stop the injection immediately and alert the provider
Reassure her that these are expected effects of lidocaine
Offer ice chips to clear the metallic taste
Continue the injection at a slower rate
r: PERIORAL NUMBNESS, TINNITUS, AND A METALLIC TASTE ARE THE EARLY WARNING OF LOCAL ANESTHETIC SYSTEMIC TOXICITY. Untreated it marches on to seizures and cardiac arrest. Stop the drug, call for help, support the airway, and anticipate IV lipid emulsion. Reassuring her or slowing the rate lets a preventable emergency keep loading.

q: A 58-year-old has burning, shooting nerve pain that has persisted for four months after a shingles outbreak. Scheduled ibuprofen has not helped. Which medication does the nurse expect the provider to add?
o: Naproxen
Oxycodone with acetaminophen
Gabapentin
Senna
r: GABAPENTIN AND PREGABALIN ARE FIRST-LINE FOR NEUROPATHIC PAIN; DULOXETINE AND TRICYCLICS ALSO WORK. Postherpetic neuralgia responds poorly to NSAIDs, so adding naproxen just repeats a failed therapy. Opioids are not first-line for nerve pain, and senna is a stimulant laxative, not an analgesic. MULTIMODAL means combining classes that hit different pain pathways.

q: A 66-year-old taking oxycodone with acetaminophen after knee surgery tells the nurse he also takes over-the-counter acetaminophen 500 mg tablets for headaches. Which teaching is most important?
o: The over-the-counter product is a different drug, so it is safe to add.
Your prescription pain pill already contains acetaminophen; keep your total at or below about 4 grams a day.
You may take up to 8 grams daily as long as you space the doses out.
Acetaminophen only harms the kidneys, so just drink extra fluids.
r: ACETAMINOPHEN HIDES IN COMBINATION PRODUCTS AND THE CEILING IS ABOUT 4 G PER DAY, LESS WITH LIVER DISEASE OR ALCOHOL USE. Stacking a combination opioid on top of OTC acetaminophen is the classic accidental overdose. The toxicity is HEPATIC, not renal, and the antidote is acetylcysteine.

q: An 80-year-old with stage 3 chronic kidney disease and a history of GI bleeding asks the clinic nurse about taking ibuprofen every day for arthritis pain. Which response is best?
o: Daily ibuprofen is fine as long as you always take it with food.
Take it with an antacid and it will not bother your kidneys.
Double the dose on your bad days to stay ahead of the pain.
Daily ibuprofen is risky for you; let's ask your provider about scheduled acetaminophen instead.
r: NSAIDS CAUSE GI BLEEDING, KIDNEY INJURY, AND PLATELET INHIBITION, AND ARE AVOIDED IN OLDER ADULTS AND RENAL DISEASE. Food or an antacid may ease stomach upset but protects neither the kidneys nor against a bleed. Never coach a client to double a dose. Scheduled acetaminophen within the daily ceiling is the safer first step.

q: A 47-year-old received IV hydromorphone 30 minutes ago and is now difficult to arouse. Which assessment is the nurse's priority?
o: Respiratory rate and depth along with level of sedation
Bowel sounds and time of last bowel movement
Pain rating on the 0 to 10 scale
Urine output over the past shift
r: WITH OPIOIDS, ASSESS SEDATION LEVEL AND RESPIRATORY RATE FIRST, because respiratory depression is what kills and rising sedation shows up BEFORE the breathing slows. Constipation, pain score, and urinary retention all matter but none is the immediate threat to life. Naloxone reverses it but is short-acting, so watch for resedation and be ready to repeat.

q: A 52-year-old is starting morphine PCA after abdominal surgery. Which statements should the nurse include in teaching? Select all that apply.
o: A family member may press the button for you while you are sleeping.
You are the only person who should ever press the PCA button.
We will start a stimulant laxative such as senna to prevent constipation.
If you need a higher dose over time, it means you have become addicted.
We will check your sedation level and respiratory rate on a regular schedule.
r: PCA IS CLIENT-CONTROLLED ONLY; FAMILY MUST NEVER PUSH THE BUTTON, because the built-in safety is that an oversedated client cannot dose himself. Opioid constipation needs a STIMULANT laxative like senna or bisacodyl, not fiber alone. Needing more drug over time is TOLERANCE and withdrawal on stopping is physical DEPENDENCE; addiction is compulsive use despite harm. Sedation and respiratory rate are monitored every time.

q: A 70-year-old has rough scaly actinic keratoses on his scalp and forehead plus plaque psoriasis on his elbows. Which statement shows he understands his topical regimen?
o: The fluorouracil cream goes on my psoriasis plaques.
If my forehead gets red and crusted from the fluorouracil, I should stop it for good.
The fluorouracil treats the scaly spots on my scalp, and redness and crusting there means it is working.
Calcipotriene is an antibiotic, so I use it until the infection is gone.
r: 5-FLUOROURACIL AND IMIQUIMOD TREAT ACTINIC KERATOSIS, AND A RED, INFLAMED, CRUSTED RESPONSE IS THE EXPECTED SIGN IT IS WORKING. Psoriasis is treated with topical steroids, vitamin D analogs such as calcipotriene, phototherapy, and biologics, not 5-FU. Calcipotriene is a vitamin D analog, not an antibiotic. Sun protection and monthly skin checks go with all of it.

q: A 68-year-old comes to clinic with a painful unilateral vesicular rash along one dermatome that started yesterday. Which action is most important?
o: Apply a high-potency topical corticosteroid to the vesicles
Explain that antivirals only help once the lesions have crusted
Give the shingles vaccine today to treat the outbreak
Obtain an order for valacyclovir and start it now
r: ANTIVIRALS FOR HERPES ZOSTER MUST START WITHIN 72 HOURS OF RASH ONSET to shorten the course and cut the risk of postherpetic neuralgia. Acyclovir and valacyclovir are the drugs, and day 1 of the rash is squarely inside the window. Topical steroids do not touch the virus and vaccine is prevention, not treatment. She stays contagious to non-immune people until all lesions crust.

q: A 29-year-old with atopic dermatitis is discharged with triamcinolone cream. Which statement indicates she needs MORE teaching?
o: I will apply a thin layer only to the affected patches.
I will rub a thick layer on my face and under my breasts every day.
I will use a fragrance-free emollient regularly to keep my skin moisturized.
I will call if the treated skin gets thin, shiny, or bruises easily.
r: USE THE LOWEST POTENCY THAT WORKS, IN A THIN LAYER, AND AVOID THE FACE AND SKIN FOLDS. Those areas absorb far more drug and atrophy fast. Emollients are the backbone of eczema care, and thin, shiny, easily bruised skin is the atrophy sign to report. Oral or topical antihistamines can be added for the itch.

q: A 64-year-old woman is discharged from the medical unit with a new prescription for alendronate for osteoporosis. Which instruction should the nurse include?
o: Take the tablet at bedtime with a glass of milk.
Take the tablet with breakfast to prevent stomach upset.
Take the tablet first thing in the morning with a full glass of plain water and stay upright for at least 30 minutes.
Crush the tablet and mix it in applesauce if it is hard to swallow.
r: Bisphosphonates go down on an EMPTY STOMACH with PLAIN WATER, and the client stays UPRIGHT 30 MINUTES to prevent esophagitis and esophageal ulceration. Milk, food, juice, and calcium block absorption, so wait 30 minutes before anything else. Lying down lets the drug sit in the esophagus and burn it.

q: A 70-year-old man in the outpatient clinic has taken oral risedronate for 4 years and just received his first IV zoledronic acid infusion. Which findings should the nurse teach him to expect or report as drug related? Select all that apply.
o: New dull, aching pain in the thigh or groin
Improved appetite and steady weight gain
Jaw pain or a tooth socket that will not heal after an extraction
Bright red rectal bleeding within 1 hour of a dose
Fever, muscle aches, and joint pain for 1 to 3 days after the IV infusion
r: New THIGH OR GROIN PAIN can signal an ATYPICAL FEMUR FRACTURE, and jaw pain or a non-healing extraction site suggests OSTEONECROSIS OF THE JAW, which is why dental work is completed BEFORE starting therapy. IV zoledronic acid commonly causes transient FLU-LIKE SYMPTOMS. Weight gain is not a bisphosphonate effect, and the GI risk is esophageal irritation, not lower GI bleeding.

q: A 68-year-old woman with osteoporosis takes omeprazole daily for GERD. She reports taking all 1200 mg of her calcium carbonate in one dose at bedtime on an empty stomach. What is the nurse's best response?
o: Keep taking the calcium carbonate, just move the whole dose to the morning.
Stop the calcium and rely on vitamin D alone.
Continue taking the full 1200 mg on an empty stomach, since food blocks calcium.
Switch to calcium citrate and split it into two doses of about 600 mg taken hours apart.
r: CALCIUM CARBONATE NEEDS STOMACH ACID AND MUST BE TAKEN WITH FOOD, so a daily PPI blunts its absorption. CALCIUM CITRATE does not need acid and can be taken with or without food, making it the better choice on a PPI. The gut only absorbs about 500 to 600 mg at a time, so DOSES MUST BE SPLIT. Vitamin D helps absorption but does not replace the calcium itself.

q: A 59-year-old woman is admitted to the med-surg unit and the nurse reviews her home medications for osteoporosis risk. Which medications should the nurse flag as contributing to bone loss? Select all that apply.
o: Prednisone 10 mg daily for the past 3 years
Phenytoin for seizure control
Pantoprazole daily for the past 5 years
Metformin for type 2 diabetes
Subcutaneous heparin during a prolonged hospitalization
r: LONG-TERM CORTICOSTEROIDS ARE THE NUMBER ONE DRUG CAUSE OF OSTEOPOROSIS. Phenytoin speeds vitamin D breakdown, chronic PPIs cut calcium absorption, and prolonged heparin causes bone loss. Metformin does not harm bone. Any client on these drugs needs calcium, vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise, and DEXA screening.

q: A 63-year-old woman with osteoporosis and a history of DVT after a knee replacement is reviewing treatment options in clinic. Which new prescription should the nurse question?
o: Raloxifene daily
Denosumab subcutaneous injection every 6 months
Calcitonin nasal spray daily
Teriparatide daily subcutaneous injection
r: RALOXIFENE RAISES VTE RISK and is avoided with any history of DVT or PE. Denosumab, calcitonin, and teriparatide do not carry that clot risk. Any client started on raloxifene must report calf pain, unilateral leg swelling, or sudden shortness of breath.

q: A 72-year-old man is seen in clinic for knee osteoarthritis pain rated 4 out of 10. He has no liver disease and does not drink alcohol. Which medication does the nurse anticipate the provider will order first?
o: Oxycodone 5 mg every 6 hours as needed
Acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed
Prednisone 20 mg by mouth daily
Cyclobenzaprine 10 mg three times daily
r: ACETAMINOPHEN IS FIRST-LINE FOR OA, with a max of roughly 4 g per day and less if there is liver disease or alcohol use. NEVER START OA PAIN MANAGEMENT WITH OPIOIDS. Daily oral steroids are not standard OA therapy, and muscle relaxants sedate older adults and raise fall risk. Topical or oral NSAIDs and duloxetine come after acetaminophen.

q: A 78-year-old woman with osteoarthritis and hypertension is starting oral ibuprofen because acetaminophen no longer controls her hip pain. Which statement shows she understands the teaching?
o: I will take it on an empty stomach so it works faster.
If my blood pressure goes up, I should double the dose.
I will take the lowest dose that works, take it with food, and call if my stools turn black.
This drug protects my kidneys, so I do not need to worry about staying hydrated.
r: Oral NSAIDs cause GI BLEEDING, KIDNEY INJURY, AND HIGHER BLOOD PRESSURE, so use the LOWEST DOSE FOR THE SHORTEST TIME, take it WITH FOOD, and report black or tarry stools. A PPI may be added for GI protection. NSAIDs harm the kidneys, they do not protect them, and topical NSAIDs are a safer starting point for older adults.

q: A 44-year-old woman with newly diagnosed rheumatoid arthritis is being discharged on methotrexate. She says, So I take this pill every morning with the rest of my medicines. What is the nurse's best response?
o: Methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis is taken once a week on the same day, never daily.
That is correct, take it every morning with food.
Take it daily for the first month, then switch to once a week.
Take it every morning, but skip it on days your joints feel good.
r: METHOTREXATE IS WEEKLY, NEVER DAILY. Daily dosing is a classic fatal medication error that causes severe bone marrow suppression. Have her pick one day, circle it on a calendar, and confirm the day at every visit. DMARDs are also never skipped based on how the joints feel that morning.

q: A 38-year-old woman on weekly methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis returns to the clinic for follow-up. Which teaching points should the nurse reinforce? Select all that apply.
o: Take the prescribed folic acid to reduce side effects.
Report mouth sores, sore throat, or fever right away.
A drink or two with dinner is fine while on this medication.
Use reliable contraception; this drug must be stopped before pregnancy.
Once you feel better, routine blood counts and liver tests can be stopped.
r: FOLIC ACID reduces stomatitis and GI upset. STOMATITIS, FEVER, OR SORE THROAT signal bone marrow suppression or infection and must be reported immediately. Methotrexate is TERATOGENIC and contraindicated in pregnancy. ALCOHOL IS AVOIDED because both hit the liver, and CBC plus liver function tests are monitored for the entire course, not just at the start.

q: A 51-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis is due for his etanercept dose on the med-surg unit. Which finding requires the nurse to hold the drug and notify the provider?
o: Hemoglobin of 12.8 g/dL
Report of morning stiffness lasting about 90 minutes
Temperature of 101.4 F with a productive cough
Documentation of an eye exam completed last month
r: TNF INHIBITORS ARE HELD FOR FEVER OR ACTIVE INFECTION because they suppress immunity. Every biologic also requires TB SCREENING BEFORE THE FIRST DOSE, since they can reactivate latent TB. Prolonged morning stiffness is the RA itself, and the ANNUAL EYE EXAM belongs to hydroxychloroquine, which can damage the retina.

q: A 56-year-old man is admitted with osteomyelitis of the tibia and has a PICC line placed for a planned 6-week course of IV vancomycin. Which action is the nurse's priority before hanging the first dose?
o: Draw a vancomycin trough level now.
Infuse the dose over 20 minutes to reach a therapeutic level quickly.
Teach the client how to change the PICC dressing at home.
Confirm that blood and bone cultures have been obtained.
r: CULTURES ARE OBTAINED BEFORE THE FIRST ANTIBIOTIC DOSE or the organism may never be identified. Troughs are drawn just BEFORE the next scheduled dose, not before the first one. Vancomycin must run SLOWLY, at least 60 minutes, to avoid an infusion reaction, and it is NEPHROTOXIC AND OTOTOXIC, so watch creatinine, urine output, and hearing. Dressing teaching matters but is not the priority.

q: A 24-year-old man is 36 hours post femur fracture when he becomes confused and restless, with an SpO2 of 86 percent and petechiae across his chest and neck. Which new order should the nurse question?
o: Apply high-flow oxygen and prepare for possible BiPAP
Start a continuous heparin infusion
Maintain bed rest and keep the fracture immobilized
Begin IV fluid replacement
r: This is FAT EMBOLISM SYNDROME: hypoxemia, neuro changes, and a petechial rash 24 to 72 hours after a long-bone fracture. FES IS NOT A CLOT, SO ANTICOAGULANTS ARE NOT THE TREATMENT, unlike DVT or PE. Management is SUPPORTIVE OXYGENATION plus fluids, bed rest, and early fracture immobilization.

q: A 67-year-old woman is learning to self-administer enoxaparin at home after a total hip arthroplasty. Which statement indicates she needs more teaching?
o: I will pinch up a fold of skin on my abdomen and inject straight in.
I will push the air bubble out of the syringe before I inject.
I will alternate between the right and left sides of my abdomen.
I will not rub the site after I take the needle out.
r: DO NOT EXPEL THE AIR BUBBLE from a prefilled enoxaparin syringe; it seals the full dose into the tissue and reduces leakage and bruising. Do not aspirate and do not massage the site, and rotate sides with each dose. Monitor for bleeding and a FALLING PLATELET COUNT, which signals HIT.

q: An 81-year-old man is being discharged on warfarin after open reduction and internal fixation of a hip fracture. Which statement indicates correct understanding?
o: I will cut all green vegetables out of my diet.
If I miss a dose I will take two the next day.
Protamine sulfate is the antidote if I bleed too much.
I will keep my green vegetable intake about the same each week and go to all my INR appointments.
r: WARFARIN IS MONITORED WITH INR, and the goal is CONSISTENT vitamin K intake, not elimination, because swinging intake destabilizes the INR. The antidote for warfarin is VITAMIN K; PROTAMINE SULFATE REVERSES HEPARIN, which is monitored with aPTT. Never double up on a missed dose.

q: A 59-year-old man is 5 days post below-the-knee amputation and reports burning, shooting pain in the foot that was removed. What is the nurse's best action?
o: Reassure him the limb is gone, so the pain is not real and will fade.
Give the prescribed gabapentin and set up mirror therapy.
Withhold analgesia and reposition the residual limb on pillows.
Request an increase in his opioid dose as the only intervention.
r: PHANTOM LIMB PAIN IS REAL AND MUST BE TREATED, never dismissed. GABAPENTIN OR PREGABALIN, tricyclics, calcitonin, and mirror therapy target the neuropathic mechanism. OPIOIDS ALONE OFTEN DO NOT CONTROL IT. Muscle relaxants such as cyclobenzaprine are not the answer here and add sedation and fall risk.

q: A 19-year-old is 8 hours post casting for a closed tibial fracture and reports severe pain that got worse after IV morphine, plus intense pain when the toes are passively extended. What should the nurse do first?
o: Give the next morphine dose early and reassess in 30 minutes.
Elevate the leg above heart level and apply an ice pack.
Notify the provider immediately and prepare for cast bivalving.
Document the finding and reassess at the end of the shift.
r: PAIN UNRELIEVED BY OPIOIDS PLUS PAIN ON PASSIVE STRETCH IS THE EARLIEST RED FLAG FOR COMPARTMENT SYNDROME. MORE OPIOID IS ALWAYS THE WRONG ANSWER; notify the provider and prepare for bivalving or fasciotomy. DO NOT ELEVATE ABOVE THE HEART and DO NOT APPLY ICE, since both cut arterial flow. Keep the limb at heart level.

q: A 19-year-old client with asthma is admitted to the medical unit with wheezing and chest tightness. He is prescribed albuterol and fluticasone, both by metered-dose inhaler, at the same scheduled time. Which action by the nurse is correct?
o: Give the fluticasone first, then the albuterol right after it.
Give the albuterol first, wait 5 minutes, then give the fluticasone.
Give both inhalers back to back in any order, since timing does not matter.
Hold the albuterol because the client is already receiving an inhaled steroid.
r: Albuterol is a short-acting beta-2 agonist that opens the airways in minutes, so the steroid can then reach deeper lung tissue. Waiting about 5 minutes between puffs is the taught interval. Giving the steroid first wastes the dose in narrowed airways, and holding the rescue drug during active wheezing is unsafe. BRONCHODILATOR FIRST, WAIT 5 MINUTES, THEN THE STEROID.

q: A 34-year-old woman in the clinic has been using budesonide inhaler twice daily for 3 weeks. She reports white patches on her tongue and inner cheeks along with a sore mouth. Which statement by the client indicates the teaching she MISSED?
o: I use a spacer with my inhaler every time.
I take this inhaler every day even when I feel fine.
I do not rinse my mouth after I use my inhaler.
I shake the canister before each puff.
r: Steroid left in the mouth feeds Candida, which produces the white patches of oral thrush. Rinsing and spitting after every dose prevents it, and a spacer reduces oropharyngeal deposition. Using a spacer, daily dosing, and shaking the canister are all correct technique, not the cause. RINSE THE MOUTH AFTER A STEROID INHALER.

q: A 72-year-old man arrives in the emergency department with fever of 102.4 F, a productive cough, and crackles in the right base. The provider orders a sputum culture and sensitivity and IV ceftriaxone. Which action should the nurse take FIRST?
o: Collect the sputum specimen before the first antibiotic dose is given.
Start the ceftriaxone immediately and collect sputum after the infusion.
Wait for the chest x-ray result before doing either intervention.
Hold both orders until the white blood cell count returns.
r: Antibiotics kill organisms in the specimen and can produce a false negative culture, so the sputum must be obtained first. Once the specimen is collected, the antibiotic should be given promptly, because delayed antibiotics worsen pneumonia outcomes. Waiting on the x-ray or the WBC delays treatment for no benefit. CULTURE BEFORE THE FIRST ANTIBIOTIC DOSE, THEN GIVE IT FAST.

q: A 27-year-old client with persistent asthma tells the clinic nurse, I stopped carrying my albuterol because my salmeterol inhaler works longer, so I just use salmeterol when I start wheezing. Which response by the nurse is BEST?
o: That is fine as long as you do not use more than four doses a day.
Salmeterol works faster than albuterol, so that is a reasonable choice.
You can use either one, but salmeterol tends to cause fewer tremors.
Salmeterol takes too long to work for an attack, so keep carrying albuterol as your rescue inhaler.
r: Salmeterol is a long-acting beta agonist with a slow onset. It is a maintenance drug and will not reverse acute bronchospasm, so the client could deteriorate while waiting for it to work. It is also never used alone in asthma because of increased asthma-related death risk; it is paired with an inhaled corticosteroid. A LABA IS NEVER A RESCUE INHALER AND NEVER FLIES SOLO IN ASTHMA.

q: A 68-year-old man with COPD is starting tiotropium at home. While reviewing his history, which finding should the nurse report to the provider before the first dose?
o: A 40 pack-year smoking history
A diagnosis of narrow-angle glaucoma and benign prostatic hyperplasia
Use of a nasal cannula at 2 L per minute at night
A resting respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute
r: Tiotropium and ipratropium are anticholinergics, so they can raise intraocular pressure and worsen urinary retention. Glaucoma plus BPH is a real safety concern the provider needs to know about. A smoking history, low-flow oxygen, and a rate of 20 are all expected in COPD and do not block the drug. ANTICHOLINERGIC INHALERS: DRY MOUTH, URINARY RETENTION, CAUTION IN GLAUCOMA.

q: A 15-year-old girl has been taking montelukast nightly for 2 months. At the follow-up visit her mother says the teen has become withdrawn, is having nightmares, and made a comment about not wanting to be here anymore. What is the nurse's priority action?
o: Reassure the mother that mood swings are normal for this age group.
Tell the mother to give the dose in the morning instead of at bedtime.
Notify the provider immediately and screen the teen for suicidal ideation.
Instruct the mother to double the dose because symptoms are not controlled.
r: Montelukast carries a boxed warning for serious neuropsychiatric events including agitation, nightmares, depression, and suicidal thinking. A statement about not wanting to be here is a safety emergency that requires immediate screening and provider notification. Dismissing it as normal teen behavior, shifting the dose time, or doubling the dose all ignore the danger. MONTELUKAST: WATCH MOOD, BEHAVIOR, AND SUICIDAL THOUGHTS.

q: A 41-year-old man is starting rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for active pulmonary tuberculosis. Which statements should the nurse include in discharge teaching? Select all that apply.
o: Your urine, sweat, and tears may turn orange, and this is expected.
You can stop the medicines once your cough and night sweats go away.
Take the pyridoxine, vitamin B6, that was prescribed to protect your nerves.
Soft contact lenses will not be affected by any of these medicines.
Report any blurred vision or trouble telling red from green right away.
r: Rifampin harmlessly stains body fluids orange and permanently stains soft contacts, and it also makes oral contraceptives ineffective, so a backup method is needed. Isoniazid causes peripheral neuropathy, which pyridoxine prevents, and ethambutol causes optic neuritis, so color and vision changes are reported immediately. Treatment runs 6 to 9 months and is never stopped when symptoms improve, since that breeds resistant TB. R IS FOR ORANGE, I NEEDS B6 AND NO ALCOHOL, E IS FOR EYES.

q: A 70-year-old woman with severe COPD is admitted for an exacerbation on oxygen at 2 L per minute by nasal cannula with an ordered target saturation of 88 to 92 percent. She is also on IV methylprednisolone. Her saturation reads 89 percent and she is anxious, so a family member turns the oxygen up to 8 L per minute. Thirty minutes later she is drowsy and hard to arouse. What is the nurse's BEST action?
o: Increase the oxygen further and continue to monitor her.
Hold the methylprednisolone because steroids cause sedation.
Place her flat in bed and let her sleep undisturbed.
Return the oxygen to the ordered rate to keep saturation at 88 to 92 percent and notify the provider.
r: In severe COPD, very high-flow oxygen can blunt the hypoxic drive and worsen carbon dioxide retention, producing drowsiness and a decreasing level of consciousness. Titrating back to the ordered 88 to 92 percent target and notifying the provider addresses the cause. More oxygen makes it worse, letting her sleep misses impending respiratory failure, and steroids cause hyperglycemia and insomnia, not sedation. TITRATE COPD OXYGEN TO THE ORDERED TARGET, USUALLY 88 TO 92 PERCENT.

q: A 59-year-old man on oral theophylline calls the clinic reporting nausea, vomiting, a pounding heartbeat, and feeling jittery. He mentions he has been drinking several energy drinks daily to stay awake at work. His theophylline level drawn that morning is 26 mcg/mL. Which action does the nurse take FIRST?
o: Tell him this level is therapeutic and the symptoms are unrelated.
Instruct him to hold the next dose and come in immediately, and notify the provider.
Advise him to take the next dose with food to settle his stomach.
Suggest he add an extra dose since his symptoms suggest poor control.
r: Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic range of roughly 10 to 20 mcg/mL, so 26 is toxic. Nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, and restlessness are classic toxicity signs and seizures can follow, so the drug is held and the provider is notified now. Caffeine and energy drinks add to the stimulant effect and must be avoided, and taking the dose with food or adding a dose would only push the level higher. THEOPHYLLINE 10 TO 20; ABOVE THAT MEANS NAUSEA, TACHYCARDIA, SEIZURES.

q: A 55-year-old woman on the surgical unit develops sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and a heart rate of 122 after hip surgery. A pulmonary embolism is confirmed and a continuous IV heparin infusion is started with a plan to transition to warfarin. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Give a dose of intramuscular pain medication for the chest pain.
Monitor the aPTT and adjust the infusion per the ordered protocol.
Expect vitamin K to be the antidote if the heparin infusion causes bleeding.
Verify that protamine sulfate is available as the heparin reversal agent.
Monitor the INR once warfarin is started and teach a consistent vitamin K intake.
r: Heparin infusions are titrated to the aPTT, and protamine sulfate is the reversal agent. Warfarin is monitored by INR, and vitamin K is warfarin's antidote, not heparin's, which is why the vitamin K option is wrong. IM injections are avoided in anticoagulated clients because of hematoma risk. HEPARIN GOES WITH aPTT AND PROTAMINE; WARFARIN GOES WITH INR AND VITAMIN K.

q: A 61-year-old man with stable angina is being discharged with sublingual nitroglycerin. Which statement by the client shows he understands the teaching?
o: I will sit or lie down, put one tablet under my tongue, and call 911 if the pain is still there after that first dose.
I will take three tablets at once so the pain stops faster.
I will move the tablets into my weekly pill organizer so they are easy to find.
I will take a tablet only if the pain lasts longer than 30 minutes.
r: Current teaching is one tablet under the tongue, and if the pain is unrelieved after that first dose, call emergency services, then continue with a tablet every 5 minutes up to three total. Sitting or lying down prevents falls from the expected hypotension, and headache and burning are expected. Taking three at once causes severe hypotension, nitroglycerin must stay in its original dark container away from light and moisture, and waiting 30 minutes delays care for a possible MI. ONE TABLET, SIT DOWN, CALL 911 IF THE FIRST DOSE DOES NOT WORK.

q: A 58-year-old woman arrives at the emergency department with crushing substernal chest pain radiating to her jaw. The provider orders aspirin 324 mg now. How should the nurse administer this medication?
o: Give it whole with a full glass of water.
Crush it and mix it in applesauce.
Instruct her to chew the tablets before swallowing.
Hold it until the troponin result confirms an MI.
r: Chewing aspirin speeds absorption so the antiplatelet effect starts within minutes, which is the point during an evolving MI. Swallowing it whole or hiding it in applesauce slows absorption. Waiting on troponin wastes muscle, since troponin does not rise for 3 to 4 hours. CHEW THE ASPIRIN IN A SUSPECTED MI, DO NOT SWALLOW IT WHOLE.

q: A 64-year-old man was started on atorvastatin 6 weeks ago for hyperlipidemia. Which finding should he be taught to report to the provider immediately?
o: Mild constipation that improves with more fiber
A total cholesterol level that has dropped since starting the drug
Occasional soreness in the shoulders after mowing the lawn
Unexplained aching and weakness in both thighs with tea-colored urine
r: Diffuse unexplained muscle pain and weakness plus dark or tea-colored urine suggests rhabdomyolysis, which can destroy the kidneys and must be reported at once. Soreness clearly explained by exertion is not the same picture. Liver enzymes are also monitored, grapefruit juice is avoided because it raises drug levels, and a falling cholesterol is the goal, not a problem. STATIN PLUS MUSCLE PAIN PLUS DARK URINE EQUALS RHABDOMYOLYSIS.

q: A 66-year-old man in the emergency department reports chest pressure rated 7 out of 10. His blood pressure is 128/76 and heart rate 88. As the nurse prepares to give sublingual nitroglycerin, he mentions he took tadalafil last night. What is the nurse's priority action?
o: Give the nitroglycerin and recheck the blood pressure in 5 minutes.
Hold the nitroglycerin and notify the provider about the tadalafil.
Give half a tablet instead of a whole tablet to reduce the risk.
Have him lie flat and give the nitroglycerin with IV fluids running.
r: Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil and tadalafil combined with nitrates cause profound, potentially fatal hypotension. Nitroglycerin is withheld for roughly 24 hours after sildenafil and up to 48 hours after tadalafil, and the provider must be told so another therapy can be chosen. A half dose, fluids, or positioning does not make the combination safe. NEVER GIVE NITRATES WITHIN 24 TO 48 HOURS OF A PDE-5 INHIBITOR.

q: A 79-year-old woman with heart failure is due for her morning digoxin. She tells the nurse she has no appetite, feels nauseated, and that the lights in the room look like they have yellow-green halos around them. Her apical pulse is 54 and irregular. What should the nurse do FIRST?
o: Give the dose and encourage her to eat a light breakfast.
Give the dose and recheck the apical pulse in 1 hour.
Hold the dose, notify the provider, and request a digoxin level and potassium.
Give half the dose and document the visual changes.
r: Apical pulse under 60 counted for a full minute is a hold parameter, and anorexia, nausea, and yellow-green or halo vision are classic digoxin toxicity. Therapeutic level is roughly 0.5 to 2.0 ng/mL, and hypokalemia potentiates toxicity, so potassium matters too. Giving any amount of the dose worsens toxicity; severe cases are treated with digoxin immune Fab. APICAL PULSE UNDER 60 OR HALOS EQUALS HOLD THE DIGOXIN AND CALL.

q: A 52-year-old woman started lisinopril 3 weeks ago for hypertension. At her clinic visit she reports a dry hacking cough that keeps her awake at night. She has no fever and her lungs are clear. Which response by the nurse is BEST?
o: This sounds like a chest infection, so we will start an antibiotic today.
Take a cough suppressant at bedtime and continue the lisinopril as ordered.
Stop the lisinopril today and skip the follow-up since the cough will fade.
This is a known effect of this drug class, and the provider may switch you to a drug ending in sartan.
r: A dry, persistent cough is a hallmark ACE inhibitor effect from bradykinin buildup. It is not an infection, and it does not stop while the drug continues, so the usual fix is switching to an ARB such as losartan. Clients should never stop an antihypertensive on their own, and they must also watch for hyperkalemia, first-dose hypotension, and angioedema, which is an airway emergency. ACE COUGH MEANS SWITCH TO A SARTAN; FACIAL OR THROAT SWELLING IS AN EMERGENCY.

q: A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and a recent MI is discharged on metoprolol. Which statement by the client requires further teaching?
o: If I start feeling tired or my sugars run odd, I will just stop the metoprolol for a few days.
I will check my pulse before each dose and call if it is under 60.
I will check my blood sugar more often because this drug can hide my low sugar symptoms.
I will stand up slowly since this medicine can make me lightheaded.
r: Abruptly stopping a beta blocker causes rebound angina, tachycardia, hypertensive crisis, and can trigger another MI, so it must be tapered by the provider. Checking the pulse and holding for a rate under 60 or a low blood pressure is correct, as is rising slowly. Beta blockers blunt tachycardia and tremor, so diabetics lose their usual hypoglycemia warning signs and need more glucose checks. NEVER STOP A BETA BLOCKER ABRUPTLY.

q: A 68-year-old woman with heart failure is going home on furosemide, spironolactone, and hydrochlorothiazide-based blood pressure management. Which teaching points should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Weigh yourself every morning and call if you gain 2 to 3 pounds in a day or 5 pounds in a week.
Use a potassium-based salt substitute to keep your sodium intake low.
Take your diuretics in the morning so you are not up all night urinating.
Take your blood pressure medicine only on days when your reading is high.
Sit on the edge of the bed for a minute before standing to avoid dizziness.
r: Daily morning weights catch fluid retention early, and a gain of 2 to 3 pounds in a day or 5 pounds in a week gets reported; morning dosing prevents nighttime urination and rising slowly protects against orthostatic hypotension. Salt substitutes are potassium chloride and are dangerous with spironolactone, which is potassium sparing and already raises potassium. Antihypertensives are taken every day even when the client feels fine, because stopping causes rebound hypertension. DAILY WEIGHTS, MORNING DIURETICS, NO POTASSIUM SALT SUBSTITUTES.

q: A 45-year-old woman on a telemetry unit has a narrow-complex tachycardia at 190 beats per minute with a pulse and stable blood pressure. The provider orders adenosine 6 mg IV. Which action by the nurse is correct?
o: Infuse the dose slowly over 10 minutes through a distal hand IV.
Give it as a rapid IV push into a port closest to the heart, followed immediately by a rapid saline flush.
Dilute it in 250 mL of normal saline and hang it as a piggyback.
Hold the dose because a brief period of asystole after adenosine means it was given incorrectly.
r: Adenosine has a half-life of only a few seconds, so it must be pushed fast into the IV port nearest the heart and chased immediately with a rapid saline flush or it will never reach the AV node. A slow push, a distal site, or a piggyback wastes the drug. A few seconds of pause or asystole on the monitor is an expected effect, not an error, and the client should be warned about flushing and chest pressure. ADENOSINE: FAST PUSH, FAST FLUSH, CLOSEST PORT.

q: A 74-year-old man with atrial fibrillation is discharged on amiodarone and warfarin. Which teaching points and monitoring priorities should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Report a new cough or shortness of breath, since this drug can damage the lungs.
Expect periodic thyroid and liver function tests while you take this drug.
You can stop the warfarin once your heart rhythm feels regular again.
Wear sunscreen and protective clothing, because this drug causes severe sun sensitivity.
Skip your INR checks as long as you do not see any bruising.
r: Amiodarone is toxic to the lungs, thyroid, and liver, so new dyspnea or cough is reported immediately and thyroid and liver labs are drawn periodically. It also causes marked photosensitivity and blue-gray skin discoloration, so sun protection is required. Atrial fibrillation carries stroke risk whether or not the rhythm feels regular, so warfarin continues and INR is monitored on schedule, especially because amiodarone raises the INR. AMIODARONE HITS LUNGS, THYROID, LIVER, AND SKIN, AND IT PUSHES THE INR UP.

q: A client arrives on the unit after closed reduction and casting of a radial fracture. How often should the nurse perform neurovascular checks during the first 24 hours?
o: Every hour
Every 4 hours
Every 8 hours
Once per shift
r: Neurovascular assessment is done every hour for the first 24 hours, then every 1 to 4 hours. Swelling peaks in the first day, which is exactly when a cast or splint starts to compress the tissue underneath it.

q: A nurse is performing a neurovascular assessment on a casted leg. Which findings should the nurse report to the provider? Select all that apply.
o: Capillary refill of 5 seconds in the toes
Toes cool and pale compared with the other foot
Client reports numbness and tingling in the toes
Client can wiggle the toes on command
Pedal pulse palpable and equal to the other foot
Pain that increases when the toes are passively moved
r: Capillary refill should return within 3 seconds, the limb should be warm and normal in color, and sensation should be intact. Pain on PASSIVE movement is a hallmark of rising compartment pressure. Being able to move the toes and having an equal, palpable pulse are the expected findings.

q: A nurse cannot palpate the pedal pulse in a swollen, casted extremity. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Document the pulse as absent
Use a Doppler ultrasound to locate the pulse
Remove the cast to relieve the swelling
Elevate the leg above heart level and recheck in an hour
r: Edema commonly makes a pulse hard to palpate, so a Doppler is used before calling it absent. Documenting it as absent without verifying is inaccurate, nurses do not remove casts, and waiting an hour delays care if perfusion truly is compromised.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has an open tibial fracture with bone visible through the wound. Which action is the priority?
o: Irrigate the wound with sterile saline until it is clean
Push the protruding bone back beneath the skin
Cover the wound with a sterile dressing and immobilize the limb
Apply a tourniquet above the fracture site
r: Cover the open wound with a sterile dressing to reduce contamination and immobilize the limb as found. Never attempt to reposition protruding bone. A tourniquet is only for uncontrolled hemorrhage, and definitive irrigation and debridement happen in the operating room.

q: A nurse reviews an x-ray report that describes a fracture in which the bone is broken into several fragments. Which term describes this fracture?
o: Greenstick
Comminuted
Spiral
Impacted
r: Comminuted means the bone is fragmented into more than two pieces. Greenstick is an incomplete fracture in children, spiral winds around the bone from a twisting force, and impacted means one bone end is driven into the other.

q: An 80-year-old woman with osteoporosis reports sudden mid-back pain after lifting a laundry basket, and the nurse notes a loss of height and a rounded upper back. Which injury should the nurse suspect?
o: Muscle strain
Vertebral compression fracture
Spinal cord injury
Herniated lumbar disk
r: Osteoporotic bone collapses under ordinary load, producing vertebral compression fractures with height loss and kyphosis. A pathologic fracture is one that occurs through bone already weakened by disease.

q: A nurse is teaching a community class on fracture prevention. Which factors increase fracture risk? Select all that apply.
o: Osteoporosis
Low vitamin D levels
History of falls
Regular weight-bearing exercise
Long-term corticosteroid therapy
Advancing age
r: Osteoporosis, low vitamin D, falls, chronic corticosteroids and advancing age all raise fracture risk. Weight-bearing exercise is protective, because loading the bone stimulates bone formation.

q: A client's fracture has healed in a rotated position. Which term describes this outcome?
o: Nonunion
Malunion
Delayed union
Avascular necrosis
r: Malunion means the fracture healed but in the wrong alignment. Nonunion means it never healed, delayed union means healing is slower than expected, and avascular necrosis is bone death from interrupted blood supply.

q: A nurse is caring for a client whose plaster cast was applied 30 minutes ago. Which action is correct?
o: Support the cast with the palms of the hands
Grip the cast with the fingertips to test firmness
Cover the cast with a heavy blanket to speed drying
Rest the cast on the hard edge of the overbed table
r: Handle a wet plaster cast with the palms. Fingertips leave indentations, and every indentation becomes a pressure point against skin you cannot see. Let warm dry air circulate rather than covering it, and never rest a wet cast on a hard edge.

q: A client asks how long the new plaster cast will take to dry completely. Which response is accurate?
o: About 30 minutes
About 2 to 4 hours
24 to 72 hours
About 1 week
r: Plaster of Paris takes 24 to 72 hours to dry and is heavy and not water resistant. Synthetic fiberglass dries in roughly 30 minutes, is lighter and stronger, and is the more commonly used material now.

q: A nurse is teaching a client being discharged with a fiberglass arm cast. Which statements should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Blow cool air from a hair dryer into the cast if it itches
Slide a ruler under the cast to scratch hard-to-reach spots
Cover the cast with a plastic bag before showering
Report a hot area, new pain, drainage or an odor
Expect the cast to loosen once the swelling goes down
Keep the arm below heart level to reduce throbbing
r: Nothing goes inside a cast, ever, because unseen skin tears become infections. A hot spot, new pain, drainage or odor all suggest infection and are reported. The cast does loosen as swelling resolves and may need replacing. An arm cast is elevated ABOVE heart level for the first 24 to 48 hours.

q: A nurse assesses a newly applied leg cast. Which finding indicates the cast is an appropriate fit?
o: No space between the cast and the skin
One finger fits between the cast and the skin
Three fingers fit between the cast and the skin
The client reports the cast feels tight when the leg is dependent
r: Room for one finger between the skin and the cast means it is snug enough to immobilize but not so tight that it compresses circulation. No space at all risks neurovascular compromise; a very loose cast will not hold alignment.

q: A nurse notes a new area of drainage on a client's cast. Which action is most appropriate?
o: Circle the drainage and note the time to track the amount
Describe the color, amount and odor and report a sudden increase
Reinforce the cast with additional plaster over the area
Reassure the client that drainage is expected for the first week
r: Circling the drainage is not a reliable way to measure it and tends to frighten the client. Describe and document what is there and report any sudden increase, which may signal bleeding or infection.

q: A nurse finds that the weights on a client's skeletal traction are resting on the floor. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Remove the weights and notify the provider
Reposition the weights so they hang freely
Reduce the weight by half until the provider is reached
Raise the head of the bed to take tension off the ropes
r: Traction only works when the weights hang free. Reposition them, and if the problem cannot be corrected, notify the provider. Never remove or change the amount of weight, which is part of the prescription.

q: A client with a hip fracture is placed in Buck's traction while awaiting surgery. Which statement describes the purpose?
o: To realign the fractured bone ends
To decrease muscle spasm and immobilize the extremity before surgery
To allow the client to ambulate with partial weight bearing
To provide skeletal fixation through the femur
r: Buck's traction is a form of SKIN traction using light weights, 5 to 10 pounds, applied with a boot. Its purpose preoperatively is comfort and immobilization, not realignment. Realignment over time is what skeletal traction does with heavier weights.

q: A nurse is caring for a client in balanced suspension skeletal traction. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Assess neurovascular status every hour for the first 24 hours
Check the ropes and pulleys for fraying and knots every 8 to 12 hours
Remove the weights before repositioning the client in bed
Provide pin site care per facility protocol
Notify the provider for severe spasm pain unrelieved by medication or repositioning
Allow the weights to rest on the bed frame while the client sleeps
r: Weights hang free at all times and are never lifted or removed unless the prescription states traction may be removed. Neurovascular checks, rope and pulley inspection, pin care, and reporting unrelieved spasm pain are all correct.

q: Which weight range is expected for skin traction?
o: 1 to 4 pounds
5 to 10 pounds
15 to 30 pounds
30 to 45 pounds
r: Skin traction uses light weights, 5 to 10 pounds, because the pull is transmitted through the skin and more weight would damage it. Skeletal traction attaches to bone and can use 15 to 30 pounds.

q: A nurse is repositioning a client who has a halo fixation device. Which action is correct?
o: Grasp the halo rods to turn the client
Move the client as a unit without pressure on the rods
Loosen the vest straps before turning
Remove the anterior vest panel for skin care
r: Move the client as a unit and never pull, push or lift by the rods, which loosens the pins and causes pain. Keep the correct wrench with the client for emergencies, and never loosen or remove vest components without an order.

q: A nurse is providing pin site care for a client with an external fixator on four pins. Which action prevents cross-contamination?
o: Use one sterile swab and work from the cleanest to the dirtiest pin
Use a separate swab for each pin
Cleanse all pins with one saline-soaked gauze
Cleanse only the pins that show drainage
r: One swab per pin. A swab that touches more than one site carries organisms from pin to pin. Chlorhexidine is commonly used, but the specific protocol comes from the provider and the facility.

q: Which findings at a traction pin site should the nurse report? Select all that apply.
o: Purulent drainage with an odor
Redness spreading outward from the site
Skin tenting upward along the pin
A pin that moves slightly when touched
A thin, dry crust at the insertion point
r: Drainage, spreading redness, tenting of the skin and a loose pin are all reported. A nurse never tightens a loose pin. Crusting is managed per facility protocol rather than picked off on the nurse's own initiative.

q: For which client would the nurse expect external fixation to be used?
o: A child with a greenstick fracture of the wrist
An adult with a comminuted open fracture and extensive soft tissue damage
An older adult with a stable vertebral compression fracture
An athlete with a stress fracture of the metatarsal
r: External fixation holds a fracture with percutaneous pins attached to a rigid external frame. It is chosen for comminuted or nonunion fractures with extensive soft tissue damage, leg length discrepancies, and bone loss from tumors or osteomyelitis.

q: Which finding is the earliest indication of compartment syndrome?
o: Absent distal pulse
Numbness and tingling of the digits
Inability to move the fingers
Pale, cool skin
r: Paresthesia, numbness and tingling, is the first manifestation. The distal area then becomes pale and cool, and pulselessness and inability to move the digits come last. Waiting for a lost pulse means waiting too long.

q: A nurse suspects compartment syndrome in a client with a casted forearm. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Notify the provider immediately
Loosen the constricting dressing
Elevate the arm above the level of the heart
Apply an ice pack to the cast
Keep the extremity at heart level
Prepare the client for a possible fasciotomy
r: Both elevation above the heart and cold application further reduce arterial flow to a limb that is already ischemic. Relieve the constriction, keep the limb at heart level, notify the provider, and prepare for the fasciotomy that relieves the pressure and saves the limb.

q: A client is scheduled for a fasciotomy. Which explanation should the nurse give?
o: The bone will be realigned with pins and screws
The tissue will be surgically opened to relieve pressure and restore blood flow
The damaged muscle will be removed and replaced with a graft
The joint will be replaced with a prosthesis
r: A fasciotomy is a surgical incision through the fascia to release the pressure inside the compartment. It is done to restore perfusion before ischemia causes irreversible damage, and the wound is often left open initially.

q: A client is 24 hours post open reduction of a femur fracture. Which new finding most suggests fat embolism syndrome?
o: Serosanguineous drainage on the dressing
Petechiae across the chest and neck with dyspnea and confusion
Pain rated 7 out of 10 at the surgical site
Unilateral calf swelling and tenderness
r: Fat embolism appears 12 to 48 hours after a long bone or hip fracture or a total joint arthroplasty. Petechiae on the neck, chest, upper arms and abdomen is the finding that distinguishes it from a pulmonary embolism. Unilateral calf swelling suggests DVT instead.

q: A client is diagnosed with fat embolism syndrome. Which interventions should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
o: Administer oxygen
Administer corticosteroids
Massage the affected extremity to disperse the globules
Administer IV fluids and vasopressors for shock
Provide pain and antianxiety medication as needed
r: Treatment is oxygen for respiratory compromise, corticosteroids for cerebral edema, fluids and vasopressors for shock, and pain and anxiety management. Massaging the extremity can release more fat globules and is never done.

q: A client is being discharged after debridement for osteomyelitis of the tibia. Which statement should the nurse include?
o: Antibiotics will continue for at least 4 to 6 weeks
Stop the antibiotic once the pain resolves
Airborne precautions are required during dressing changes
Numbness below the wound is an expected finding
r: Bone infection requires a long course, at least 4 to 6 weeks of IV and then oral antibiotics, given on schedule to maintain a constant blood level. Pain relief does not mean the infection is gone. Standard precautions and clean technique are adequate for a wound left open to heal, and new numbness is always reported.

q: A nurse is assessing an 82-year-old for possible osteomyelitis. Which finding is the LEAST reliable indicator of infection in this client?
o: Elevated temperature
Localized erythema and edema
Elevated white blood cell count
Constant, pulsating bone pain that worsens with movement
r: Older adults often do not mount a fever with osteomyelitis. Rely on the local findings and the labs. Note also that many findings fade if the infection becomes chronic, which is why it gets missed.

q: Which client is at greatest risk for avascular necrosis following a fracture?
o: A client with a displaced femoral neck fracture on long-term prednisone
A client with a nondisplaced distal radius fracture
A client with a clavicle fracture
A client with a stress fracture of the tibia
r: Avascular necrosis follows circulatory compromise at the fracture site and is common with hip fractures and displaced fractures. Long-term corticosteroid use, radiation therapy, rheumatoid arthritis and sickle cell disease all add risk.

q: A client 8 weeks after a wrist fracture has burning pain far out of proportion to the injury, along with swelling, temperature and color changes, and hypersensitivity to light touch. Which complication should the nurse suspect?
o: Malunion
Complex regional pain syndrome
Osteomyelitis
Compartment syndrome
r: Complex regional pain syndrome combines pain out of proportion to the injury with autonomic changes in the limb: swelling, temperature and color change, sweating, and hypersensitivity, progressing to atrophy and stiffness. Early mobilization, multimodal pain control and pain specialist referral are the approach.

q: Which findings are characteristic of osteoarthritis rather than rheumatoid arthritis? Select all that apply.
o: Pain with activity that improves with rest
Symmetric involvement of the small joints of both hands
Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes
Fever, fatigue and weight loss
Client is usually overweight
Cartilage destruction with bone spur formation
r: Osteoarthritis is degenerative and non-systemic: activity-related pain that eases with rest, bony nodes at the finger joints, a usually overweight client, and cartilage loss with osteophytes. Symmetric small-joint disease and systemic symptoms belong to rheumatoid arthritis, where clients are often underweight.

q: A nurse notes bony enlargements at a client's distal interphalangeal joints. What are these called?
o: Bouchard's nodes
Heberden's nodes
Rheumatoid nodules
Tophi
r: Heberden's nodes are at the DISTAL interphalangeal joints; Bouchard's nodes are at the middle joints. Both are osteoarthritis findings. Rheumatoid nodules occur in RA, and tophi are urate deposits in gout.

q: A client with osteoarthritis takes acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours plus a combination analgesic containing 325 mg of acetaminophen twice daily. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Nothing, the total is within safe limits
Hold the combination product and notify the provider, because the total exceeds 3,000 mg in 24 hours
Increase the scheduled dose to 1,000 mg to improve relief
Give both and monitor for kidney injury
r: 650 mg times 4 doses is 2,600 mg, plus 650 mg from the combination product, totals 3,250 mg, over the 3,000 mg per 24 hour ceiling. Hidden acetaminophen in combination products is the classic source of unintended hepatotoxicity.

q: A nurse is teaching a client with knee osteoarthritis. Which statements should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Losing weight will reduce the load on your knees
Use heat for stiffness and cold for swelling
Wear well-fitted, supportive shoes
Morning stiffness lasting several hours is expected with this condition
Daily jogging will rebuild the cartilage in your knees
Tell your provider about any herbal supplements you take
r: Weight loss is the single most effective intervention for hip and knee OA. Heat helps stiffness, cold reduces inflammation, and supportive shoes reduce fall and strain risk. Prolonged morning stiffness is a rheumatoid arthritis pattern, and high-impact exercise worsens joint degeneration. Glucosamine, chondroitin, turmeric and ginger can interact with anticoagulants.

q: A nurse is teaching a client with acute low back pain. Which instruction is correct?
o: Remain on strict bed rest for one week
Apply heat for the first 3 days, then switch to ice
Bend at the knees and hold the load close to your body when lifting
Turn by twisting at the waist rather than moving your feet
r: Lift with the legs, back straight, load held close, and never twist while lifting. Avoid prolonged bed rest and start gentle stretching early. Use ice for the first 48 to 72 hours, then heat.

q: A client with chronic low back pain reports new urinary incontinence and numbness in the perineal area. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Reassure the client that this is common with chronic back pain
Notify the provider immediately
Encourage bed rest and reassess tomorrow
Apply a heating pad and administer the ordered muscle relaxant
r: New bowel or bladder changes with saddle numbness suggest cauda equina syndrome, a surgical emergency. Progressive leg weakness and fever with back pain are also red flags requiring immediate reporting.

q: A client's DEXA scan reports a T-score of negative 2.8. How should the nurse interpret this result?
o: Normal bone density
Osteopenia
Osteoporosis
The result cannot be interpreted without a Z-score
r: A T-score at or below negative 2.5 indicates osteoporosis. Negative 1.0 to negative 2.5 is osteopenia, and a score of negative 1.0 or higher is normal. The T-score compares her to a young healthy adult; the Z-score compares her to age-matched peers.

q: A nurse is preparing a client for a DEXA scan. Which instruction is appropriate?
o: You will need to fast for 8 hours before the scan
Remove any metal objects, but you may keep your clothing on
You will receive a contrast injection before the images are taken
You will need to hold your breath for 30 seconds at a time
r: A DEXA scan needs no fasting, no contrast and no breath holding. Clothing stays on, but metal objects come off because they interfere with the scan. The client lies still on the table while the selected area is scanned.

q: A nurse is teaching a client starting oral alendronate. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Take it first thing in the morning on an empty stomach
Take it with a full 8 ounce glass of water
Remain upright for at least 30 minutes afterward
Take it at bedtime with a light snack
Report indigestion, chest pain or trouble swallowing right away
Check with your provider before any dental procedure
r: Water, upright, wait. Early morning on an empty stomach with 8 ounces of water and 30 minutes upright is what prevents esophagitis and esophageal ulcers. Report esophageal symptoms immediately, and consult the provider before dental work because of the risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw.

q: A client who just received teriparatide reports dizziness on standing. Which response by the nurse is correct?
o: This is unrelated to your medication
Sit or lie down when this happens; it can occur for up to 4 hours after a dose
Stop the medication and call the clinic tomorrow
Take the next dose with food to prevent this
r: Orthostatic hypotension can occur for up to 4 hours after teriparatide. Teach safety rather than stopping the drug. Teriparatide is subcutaneous only, is limited to 2 years of use, and is avoided when there is a history of skeletal malignancy or radiation because of osteosarcoma risk.

q: Which client history would make the nurse question a new prescription for raloxifene?
o: Osteoporosis with a T-score of negative 2.7
Deep vein thrombosis after a knee replacement last year
A family history of breast cancer
Postmenopausal status for 6 years
r: Raloxifene is contraindicated with a history of DVT or pulmonary embolism because of thromboembolism risk. It should also be stopped 72 hours before prolonged bed rest, and clients report new calf pain or tenderness.

q: A nurse is teaching a client about calcium carbonate supplements. Which instruction is correct?
o: Take the entire daily dose at bedtime on an empty stomach
Take it with food, in divided doses, with 6 to 8 ounces of water
Take it at the same time as your alendronate for better absorption
Stop the supplement if you become constipated
r: Calcium is given with food in divided doses with 6 to 8 ounces of water, since a large single dose is poorly absorbed. Expect GI upset and monitor for constipation, which is managed with fluid and fiber rather than by stopping the supplement. Calcium must not be taken with a bisphosphonate, which needs an empty stomach.

q: A nurse is teaching a client after a total hip arthroplasty. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Use a raised toilet seat
Keep a pillow between your legs when you turn
Avoid bending your hip more than 90 degrees
Sit in low, soft chairs to reduce strain on the hip
Point your toes outward rather than inward
Cross your legs at the ankles only
r: Everything follows from abduction, neutral rotation and limited flexion. Low chairs force flexion past 90 degrees, and crossing the legs at the ankles or the knees adducts the hip. Long-handled shoehorns, dressing sticks and straight chairs with arms all help her stay within the limits.

q: Four hours after a total hip arthroplasty, a client reports sudden severe pain and says she felt a pop. The affected leg appears shorter and externally rotated. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Reposition the client onto the operative side
Perform gentle passive range of motion to the hip
Keep the client still, maintain leg alignment, and notify the provider
Administer the ordered analgesic and reassess in one hour
r: Sudden pain, a pop, and a shortened, rotated extremity mean prosthetic dislocation. Immobilize, maintain alignment, and notify the provider. Moving the joint or medicating and waiting risks nerve and vascular injury.

q: A nurse reviews the record of a client scheduled for a total knee arthroplasty. Which finding should the nurse report to the surgeon?
o: Age 58 years
Body mass index of 26
Urinary tract infection currently being treated
Knee arthroscopy 4 years ago
r: Any active infection, including a UTI, can seed the new joint and cause the prosthesis to fail, so surgery waits until it clears. Other risk raisers include a BMI over 40, smoking, age over 75, uncontrolled diabetes and malnutrition.

q: A nurse is caring for a client after a total knee arthroplasty. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Turn the continuous passive motion machine off during meals
Place a pillow under the lower calf and foot
Place a pillow directly behind the knee for comfort
Pad slightly above the ankle to keep the heels off the bed
Medicate for pain to support early ambulation
Increase the CPM flexion setting when the client tolerates it well
r: A pillow behind the knee causes a flexion contracture; put it under the calf and foot so the knee extends slightly, or let it rest flat. Turn the CPM off for meals, follow the prescribed settings without changing them, keep heels off the bed, and medicate so she can ambulate early.

q: Which instruction should the nurse include for a client discharged after a total knee arthroplasty?
o: Kneeling and deep knee bends are limited indefinitely
Avoid bending the knee more than 30 degrees for 6 weeks
Dislocation is common, so keep an abduction pillow in place at night
Discontinue physical therapy once the pain resolves
r: Dislocation is uncommon after a knee replacement, but kneeling and deep knee bends are limited indefinitely. Flexion is progressively increased, not restricted to 30 degrees, and therapy continues on schedule regardless of pain relief.

q: Which findings after joint arthroplasty should the nurse report immediately? Select all that apply.
o: Unilateral calf swelling, redness and pain
Sudden shortness of breath and chest pain
Temperature of 38.9 C (102 F) on postoperative day 3
Purulent drainage from the incision
Incisional pain rated 4 out of 10 that improves with the ordered analgesic
r: Calf findings suggest DVT, sudden dyspnea and chest pain suggest PE, and fever with purulent drainage suggests infection of the prosthesis. Incisional pain that responds to analgesia is expected.

q: A nurse is caring for a client 24 hours after a below-the-knee amputation. Which action is appropriate?
o: Continue elevating the residual limb on two pillows for one week
Discontinue elevation of the residual limb
Place a pillow directly under the residual limb while sleeping
Keep the knee flexed on a pillow for comfort
r: Elevation past 24 hours after a below-the-knee amputation promotes hip and knee flexion contractures, so it is stopped. A pillow under the stump also flexes the hip and knee and is avoided. Keep the knee extended, using a leg board in the wheelchair if needed.

q: Which position should the nurse encourage for a client with an above-the-knee amputation?
o: Prone, to maintain hip extension
High Fowler's, to promote lung expansion
Side-lying with the affected side down
Sitting in a wheelchair for most of the day
r: The prone position maintains hip extension and prevents a hip flexion contracture after an above-the-knee amputation. In side-lying, keep the unaffected side DOWN so the affected side is not abducted, keep the pelvis horizontal, and avoid prolonged sitting.

q: A client 3 weeks after an above-the-knee amputation reports burning, cramping pain in the missing foot. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
o: The foot is gone, so that pain cannot be real
This is phantom limb pain. It is real, and we treat it differently. Let's look at your options
This means your incision has become infected
Try to distract yourself and it will fade on its own
r: Phantom limb pain is real pain from severed nerve pathways, described as deep and burning, cramping, tingling, shooting or aching. It is treated differently from incisional pain: NSAIDs and acetaminophen, antidepressants such as amitriptyline or nortriptyline, and anticonvulsants such as gabapentin or pregabalin, plus TENS and mirror therapy.

q: A nurse is teaching residual limb care after a lower limb amputation. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Inspect all areas of the limb daily, using a mirror if needed
Wrap the limb with elastic bandages using a figure-eight pattern
Wrap in a circular pattern to apply even pressure
Wash with mild soap and water and dry thoroughly
Report any heat in the residual limb
Apply lotion inside the prosthetic socket each morning
r: A figure-eight wrap shapes and shrinks the limb without restricting blood flow the way a circular wrap does, and it is applied up to three times daily. Inspect daily, wash and dry thoroughly, and report heat, which suggests infection. Lotions and powders are not put in the socket unless prescribed.

q: Which item should the nurse keep at the bedside for a client immediately following a traumatic lower limb amputation?
o: A large tourniquet
An abduction pillow
A continuous passive motion machine
A wrench for the frame
r: Hemorrhage is the immediate postoperative danger, so a tourniquet stays at the bedside for a traumatic or emergent amputation. Monitor the dressing and drainage closely and compare limb perfusion with the other extremity.

q: What is the gold standard for confirming placement of a newly inserted NG or small-bore feeding tube?
o: Auscultating an air bolus over the stomach
Chest x-ray
Aspirate pH less than 5.5
Appearance of the aspirate
r: X-ray is the gold standard before first use. A pH under 5.5 and the look of the aspirate are supportive but not definitive alone, and the air-bolus auscultation method is not acceptable.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who is NPO and has an NG tube to suction. When the client reports nausea, which action should the nurse take?
o: Irrigate the tube with normal saline solution
Provide oral hygiene
Clamp the tube for 30 minutes
Increase the amount of suction
