r: Irrigate to check patency. If the tube is blocked, gastric pressure cannot be relieved, and that is what is causing the nausea. Oral care is comfort, not the fix. Clamping makes it worse, and increasing suction risks mucosal damage.

q: Which are legitimate uses for a single NG tube? Select all that apply.
o: Decompress the stomach — remove fluid and gas
Lavage — wash out the stomach after an overdose or GI bleed
Diagnostics — obtain gastric contents, check for blood, measure pH
Administer medications
Compress or cauterize a bleeding site
Provide long-term feeding for more than 6 months
r: One NG tube can decompress, lavage, sample, medicate, feed, and (with a specialty tube) compress a bleeding site. What it is NOT is a long-term device — NG tubes are temporary, roughly 4 to 6 weeks. Beyond that you move to a PEG, GJ or J tube.

q: Which client is an appropriate candidate for medication administration through an NG tube?
o: A client with a complete small bowel obstruction
A client with dysphagia after a stroke whose GI tract still works
A client with intestinal ischemia
A client with a prolonged paralytic ileus
r: The question is always: does the GI tract still work? A client who cannot swallow safely but has a working gut — dysphagia, obstructed esophagus, critically ill or unconscious — can use an NG tube. If the gut is not working, the tube has nowhere to deliver to.

q: Why is an NG tube commonly placed after an open abdominal surgery?
o: To provide immediate postoperative nutrition
To decompress the stomach and remove air introduced during surgery
To measure hourly urine output
To prevent wound dehiscence
r: Open surgery introduces air into the abdomen. The NG tube suctions it out and prevents distention. It is also used to treat a paralytic ileus after surgery.

q: How does gastric lavage through an NG tube work?
o: Continuous low suction removes secretions over several hours
Fluid is instilled into the stomach, then withdrawn to wash out contents
Air is injected to push contents into the duodenum
The tube is clamped so the stomach can absorb the toxin
r: Lavage = confirm placement, instill fluid, withdraw fluid. It flushes out toxins, blood or unwanted contents. It is used far less often now than it used to be.

q: Which procedure lets the provider see inside the esophagus, stomach and duodenum?
o: Colonoscopy
EGD (esophagogastroduodenoscopy)
Barium swallow
Abdominal ultrasound
r: The EGD, also called an upper endoscopy, passes a thin flexible scope with a camera through the mouth to view the esophagus, stomach and the first part of the small intestine. Minimally invasive.

q: What is the provider looking for during an EGD? Select all that apply.
o: Bleeding
Perforations
Blockages
Barrett's esophagus
GERD damage and ulcers
Diverticula in the sigmoid colon
r: An EGD assesses bleeding, perforation, blockage, cancer, Barrett's, GERD damage and ulcers. Sigmoid diverticula are lower GI — you need a colonoscopy for those.

q: What is the priority nursing assessment after an EGD, before allowing anything by mouth?
o: Bowel sounds in all four quadrants
Return of the gag reflex
Ability to ambulate independently
Absence of a sore throat
r: The throat was anesthetized and the client was sedated. Confirm the gag reflex has returned, then a swallow test, then PO intake. Giving fluids first risks aspiration. A sore throat is expected.

q: Which are key preparations before an EGD? Select all that apply.
o: Informed consent
NPO for 6 to 8 hours
IV access
Sedation readiness — airway equipment and reversal agents available
Prophylactic antibiotics
r: Consent, NPO 6 to 8 hours, IV access, and readiness for moderate sedation with airway equipment and reversal agents. Prophylactic antibiotics are not routine for a diagnostic EGD.

q: Which findings after an EGD should be reported immediately? Select all that apply.
o: Severe pain
Fever
Crepitus over the neck or chest
Hematemesis or melena with hemodynamic changes
A mildly sore throat
r: Severe pain, fever and crepitus suggest perforation. Blood with changing vital signs suggests bleeding. A mildly sore throat is expected after the scope.

q: What are the monitoring priorities during moderate sedation for an EGD? Select all that apply.
o: Airway patency
Oxygen saturation
Respiratory rate
Vital signs
Reversal agents immediately available
Hourly urine output
r: Airway, SpO2, respiratory rate, vital signs, and reversal agents at the bedside. Hourly urine output is not a sedation monitoring priority for a short procedure.

q: True or false: a colonoscopy can be used to visualize the small intestine.
o: True — the scope reaches the entire small bowel
False — neither an upper nor a lower scope sees past the entrance to the small bowel
True, but only the jejunum
False — a colonoscopy only sees the rectum
r: False. An EGD reaches the duodenum and a colonoscopy reaches the terminal ileum, but the bulk of the small intestine cannot be seen from either end.

q: How does a client prepare for a urea breath test for H. pylori?
o: Eat a high-protein meal 1 hour before
NPO, and hold PPIs, antibiotics and bismuth for 1 to 2 weeks
Take a double dose of the PPI the morning of the test
No preparation is needed
r: The client must be NPO and must hold PPIs, antibiotics and bismuth for 1 to 2 weeks — those drugs suppress the organism and cause false negatives.

q: Which test provides the definitive diagnosis of peptic ulcer disease?
o: Urea breath test
EGD
Stool antigen test
CBC
r: EGD is definitive — you see the ulcer. The urea breath test and the stool antigen test detect H. pylori, and the CBC checks H&H for bleeding, but only the scope confirms the ulcer.

q: When is total parenteral nutrition indicated instead of enteral nutrition?
o: When the client refuses to eat
When the gut is not working
When the client needs short-term supplementation
When the client has dysphagia
r: If the gut works, use the gut. TPN is for when the GI tract cannot absorb or cannot be used at all. Dysphagia with a working gut is an enteral feeding situation, not TPN.

q: What are advantages of enteral nutrition over TPN? Select all that apply.
o: Keeps the gut working and maintains gut integrity
Less expensive
Lower infection risk
More physiologic
Requires central venous access
r: Enteral feeding keeps the gut functioning, costs less, carries far less infection risk and is more physiologic. Central access is a TPN requirement, not an enteral one.

q: Which client is the best candidate for enteral nutrition?
o: A client with severe pancreatitis who cannot swallow safely after a stroke
A client with a complete small bowel obstruction, persistent vomiting and absent bowel sounds
A client in septic shock on high-dose vasopressors with intestinal ischemia
A client with a prolonged ileus after abdominal surgery
r: Ask one question: does the GI tract work? Client 1's gut works, she just cannot physically eat. Obstruction, intestinal ischemia and ileus all mean the gut is not working — those need TPN.

q: How do you decide between an NG tube and a J-tube?
o: NG for long-term feeding, J-tube for short-term
NG when the client cannot swallow but the stomach works; J-tube when the stomach cannot be used or there is a malabsorption problem
NG for children, J-tube for adults
They are interchangeable
r: NG tubes are temporary and non-surgical, through the nose to the stomach, typically up to 4 to 6 weeks. A jejunostomy tube is surgically placed through the abdomen into the jejunum for long-term feeding when the stomach cannot be used.

q: True or false: if the stomach is the client's problem, a gastrostomy tube is the right feeding route.
o: True — a G-tube bypasses the esophagus
False — a G-tube empties into the stomach and may worsen the problem; use a J-tube
True — as long as the head of bed is elevated
False — the client must use TPN instead
r: False. A G/PEG tube delivers straight into the stomach. If the stomach is the problem, or the client is at high aspiration risk or has gastric intolerance, go post-pyloric into the jejunum with a J/PEJ tube.

q: Which are correct nursing actions for enteral feeding? Select all that apply.
o: Verify tube placement before use
Elevate the head of the bed 30 to 45 degrees
Flush the tube with 30 mL of water before and after feeds and medications
Flush continuous feeds every 4 hours
Change tubing and delivery sets every 24 hours
Return a residual over 500 mL to the stomach
r: Before: verify placement. During: raise the head of the bed. After: monitor tolerance and flush. A residual over 500 mL is NOT returned — hold the feed and call the provider. Refrigerate open cans and discard them after 24 hours.

q: What is the biggest complication you are trying to prevent during enteral feeding?
o: Diarrhea
Aspiration
Constipation
Hyperkalemia
r: Aspiration. Head of bed 30 to 45 degrees, verify placement, use the correct formula, and flush to prevent clogging.

q: Why is the head of the bed elevated 30 to 45 degrees during and after enteral feeding?
o: To improve absorption of the formula
To prevent aspiration pneumonia
To reduce abdominal distention
To speed gastric emptying
r: Gravity keeps the formula down. Aspiration pneumonia is the top safety priority with tube feeding.

q: Which client should the nurse address first?
o: A clogged feeding tube
A blood glucose of 188 mg/dL
Redness around a PEG tube site
Coughing with dropping oxygen saturation
r: Coughing with falling saturation points to aspiration, which can progress to pneumonia. Airway and oxygenation beat a clogged tube, a mildly elevated glucose and a red site every time.

q: A client receiving enteral nutrition is hyperglycemic during the feeding. What should the nurse do?
o: Stop the feeding immediately and remove the tube
Monitor the blood glucose and give insulin if ordered; the rate or formula may need adjusting
Increase the feeding rate to dilute the glucose
Switch the client to TPN
r: Monitor glucose and treat per orders. The formula or the rate may need to change. You do not stop nutrition or jump to TPN over a manageable glucose.

q: What is the correct feeding tube flushing protocol?
o: 10 mL of normal saline once per shift
30 mL of water before and after medications and feeds
60 mL of juice after each medication
No flushing is needed with continuous feeds
r: 30 mL of water before and after medications and feeds, and every 4 hours with continuous feeds. Use liquid medications when possible. Water, not saline, and never juice.

q: What is the most common mechanical complication of enteral feeding?
o: Tube migration
Tube clogging or obstruction
Tube fracture
Nasal septum necrosis
r: Clogging is the most common. Prevent it with routine flushing; unclog with warm water or a pancreatic enzyme preparation per protocol.

q: Which are site complications of a PEG or J tube? Select all that apply.
o: Leakage
Cellulitis
Infection
Buried bumper
Refeeding syndrome
r: Leakage, cellulitis, infection and buried bumper are site problems — daily cleaning and assessment catch them. Refeeding syndrome is a metabolic complication, not a site one.

q: Which client is at highest risk for refeeding syndrome, and what does the nurse monitor?
o: An obese client; monitor sodium and chloride
A malnourished client with a history of alcohol use or anorexia; monitor potassium, magnesium, phosphorus and glucose
A client with GERD; monitor pH and bicarbonate
A postoperative client; monitor calcium and albumin
r: Malnourished clients, people with alcohol use disorder and clients with anorexia are at risk. Watch potassium, magnesium, phosphorus and glucose. Start slowly and give thiamine.

q: What is the benefit of cyclic enteral feeding?
o: It reduces the total calories needed
It allows daytime freedom and mobility while meeting needs overnight
It eliminates the risk of aspiration
It prevents tube clogging
r: Cyclic feeding runs overnight so the client can move, work and eat socially during the day. It does not remove the aspiration risk.

q: A client receiving TPN returns from physical therapy and the nurse notes the infusion pump is off. After restarting it, the nurse should monitor for which finding?
o: Hypertension
Excessive thirst
Fever
Diaphoresis
r: Sudden withdrawal of TPN causes rebound hypoglycemia. Diaphoresis, weakness, anxiety, confusion, tremors, tachycardia, headache, hunger and irritability are the signs. Hypertension suggests fluid overload, excessive thirst suggests hyperglycemia, and fever suggests infection — none is the priority right after an interruption.

q: Which access is required for total parenteral nutrition?
o: A 20-gauge peripheral IV in the forearm
A central line — PICC or CVC
A midline catheter
An intraosseous line
r: TPN is hypertonic and would destroy a peripheral vein. It must go through a central line. It also attracts bacteria, so sterile technique and glucose monitoring are essential.

q: When is a filter used on a TPN line?
o: Only when lipids are included
Always
Only for the first 24 hours
Only in clients with sepsis
r: Always — not just with lipids. The filter catches clots, clumps and air. Tubing is changed every 24 hours.

q: Does the TPN line need to be flushed before and after feedings?
o: Yes, with 30 mL of water
No — TPN runs continuously on a pump
Yes, with 10 mL of heparin
Only if lipids are running
r: TPN is a continuous pump infusion, so routine before-and-after flushing does not apply. Flushing is for NG tubes and intermittent feeds.

q: The next TPN bag is unavailable and the current bag has been hanging for 24 hours. What should the nurse do?
o: Keep the current bag running until the new one arrives
End the current bag and hang 10 to 20 percent dextrose in water to prevent hypoglycemia
Stop the infusion and leave the line capped
Slow the current bag to half the rate
r: TPN is a bacterial growth medium, so the bag comes down at 24 hours regardless. Hang dextrose 10 to 20 percent in water to prevent rebound hypoglycemia until the new bag arrives.

q: What happens if TPN infuses too fast or is stopped too abruptly?
o: Too fast causes hypoglycemia; too slow causes hyperglycemia
Too fast causes a hyperosmolar state; abrupt withdrawal causes rebound hypoglycemia
Neither has clinical effects
Both cause metabolic alkalosis
r: Too fast: hyperosmolar state — headache, nausea, fever, chills, malaise. Abrupt stop: rebound hypoglycemia — confusion, tremors, hypotension, tachycardia, cool clammy skin.

q: Which are correct monitoring parameters for a client on TPN? Select all that apply.
o: Daily weight, intake and output, glucose and temperature
Glucose every 4 hours initially
BUN, electrolytes, calcium and magnesium three times a week
CBC, platelets, prothrombin time, liver enzymes and albumin once a week
Tubing change every 72 hours
r: Daily weights, I&O, glucose and temperature; glucose q4h at first; chemistries three times a week; CBC, platelets, PT, LFTs and albumin weekly. Tubing is changed every 24 hours, not 72.

q: Which are complications of TPN? Select all that apply.
o: Hyperosmolar coma
Pneumothorax during line placement
Sepsis
Fluid volume overload
Air embolism
Tube clogging from crushed medications
r: Hyperosmolar coma, pneumothorax (confirm line placement by x-ray before use), sepsis, fluid overload and air embolism. Clogging from crushed medications is an enteral tube problem — nothing is given through the TPN line.

q: A client with a central venous access device is receiving parenteral nutrition. The nurse notes the infusion is running sluggishly despite attempts to increase the rate. What is the best action?
o: Ask the client to turn to the left side and perform the Valsalva maneuver
Stop the infusion and flush the IV catheter
Remove the central line and start a new catheter
Lower the head of the bed and administer oxygen by mask
r: Stop and flush to assess for occlusion. Removing the line is far too aggressive as a first step, and the left-side/Valsalva and lower-the-bed answers are air embolism interventions, which is not what is happening here.

q: Which clients may benefit from TPN? Select all that apply.
o: Severe Crohn's disease
Ulcerative colitis flare requiring bowel rest
Short bowel syndrome
A client with dysphagia and an intact gut
Severe adverse effects from oncology treatment
r: TPN spares the GI tract, so it fits severe IBD, short bowel syndrome, oncology treatment effects, pre-op optimization, alcohol use disorder, eating disorders and head and neck surgery. Dysphagia with a working gut is an enteral feeding situation.

q: Which describes the composition of TPN?
o: Dextrose and sterile water only
Amino acids, dextrose, carbohydrates, fat, electrolytes, vitamins, minerals and sterile water
Lipids only
Amino acids and electrolytes only
r: TPN is the complete formula. TNA is amino acids, lipids and dextrose. Lipids can also be given alone. Start around 50 mL/hr, increase to 100 to 125 mL/hr as tolerated, always on a pump, warmed to room temperature.

q: What is the most common cause of GERD?
o: Helicobacter pylori infection
An incompetent lower esophageal sphincter
Delayed gastric emptying
Excess pepsin secretion
r: An incompetent LES lets gastric contents move back up. That is the whole mechanism.

q: A nurse is developing a plan of care for a client with GERD. Which complication should the nurse monitor for?
o: Aspiration
Infection
Anemia
Weight loss
r: Aspiration is the serious complication. A failing LES lets acid and undigested food reflux, and those contents can be aspirated into the airway — especially lying down or asleep. Heartburn and indigestion are the most common symptoms, but aspiration is what can hurt the client.

q: A client reports heartburn after every meal, a chronic cough and a sour taste in the mouth. What condition is most likely?
o: Peptic ulcer disease
GERD
Gallstones
Gastroparesis
r: Heartburn, chronic cough and a sour taste is the classic GERD triad. GERD causes effortless regurgitation both upright and reclining.

q: Which GI condition commonly presents in a way that mimics a cardiac problem?
o: Appendicitis
GERD
Diverticulitis
Celiac disease
r: GERD can cause intermittent chest pain that looks cardiac. Rule out the heart first — you do not want to treat an MI with an antacid.

q: What is the purpose of esophageal pH monitoring in GERD?
o: It measures LES pressure
It is the most accurate diagnostic test and correlates symptoms with acid reflux episodes
It detects H. pylori
It measures gastric emptying time
r: pH monitoring is the most accurate diagnosis — it links what the client feels to actual acid reflux episodes.

q: Why is it important to treat GERD rather than manage symptoms alone?
o: To prevent H. pylori infection
To protect the esophageal lining — untreated reflux leads to Barrett's, dysplasia and esophageal cancer
To prevent gastric outlet obstruction
To avoid pernicious anemia
r: Chronic acid damage causes Barrett's esophagus — a metaplastic cell change — which can progress to dysplasia and then cancer.

q: True or false: Barrett's esophagus is curable.
o: True — PPIs reverse the cell changes
False — the cell change is done; you treat the GERD to prevent further damage and monitor with surveillance EGD
True — with a fundoplication
False — it always progresses to cancer
r: False. The metaplastic change is not reversed. Treat the GERD, avoid further damage, and do surveillance EGD based on the grade of dysplasia because of the cancer risk.

q: Which medication class neutralizes acid and gives fast, short-duration relief?
o: Antacids
H2 blockers
Proton pump inhibitors
Prokinetics
r: Antacids neutralize acid that is already there — fast on, fast off.

q: Which medication class reduces acid production and works well for mild or nighttime GERD symptoms?
o: Antacids
H2 blockers
Proton pump inhibitors
Sucralfate
r: H2 blockers such as famotidine reduce acid production. Good for mild or nocturnal symptoms.

q: Which medication class most strongly suppresses acid production and is the best long-term GERD treatment?
o: Antacids
H2 blockers
Proton pump inhibitors
Misoprostol
r: PPIs such as omeprazole and pantoprazole shut down the proton pump. Best long-term control.

q: What class of drug is ranitidine?
o: Proton pump inhibitor
H2 blocker
Antacid
Mucosal protectant
r: Ranitidine is an H2 blocker — reduces acid for GERD, ulcers and gastritis. Worth knowing: it was pulled from the US market in 2020 over NDMA contamination, so famotidine is the H2 blocker you will actually see on the unit.

q: Which are risk factors for a hiatal hernia? Select all that apply.
o: Age over 50
Obesity
Pregnancy
Smoking
Frequent heavy lifting
A history of GERD
r: All of them. A hiatal hernia is the stomach pushing up through the diaphragm, so anything that raises intra-abdominal pressure or weakens the hiatus counts.

q: Which are clinical manifestations of a hiatal hernia? Select all that apply.
o: May be completely asymptomatic
Pyrosis (heartburn)
Regurgitation
A feeling of fullness after eating
Abdominal bloating and belching
Bright red blood per rectum
r: Many are asymptomatic. When symptomatic: heartburn, regurgitation, fullness after eating, bloating and belching — often worse bending forward or lying down. Rectal bleeding is a lower GI finding.

q: Which type of hiatal hernia carries the highest risk of strangulation and often requires surgical repair?
o: Sliding (type I)
Paraesophageal (rolling)
Congenital diaphragmatic
Umbilical
r: The paraesophageal or rolling hernia can strangulate, so it frequently goes to surgery.

q: Which lifestyle points should the nurse teach a client with a hiatal hernia? Select all that apply.
o: Lose weight if overweight
Elevate the head of the bed 6 to 8 inches
Do not eat for 2 to 3 hours before bed
Avoid substances that relax the LES
Wear loose clothing
Lie down right after meals to rest the stomach
r: Weight loss, HOB elevation, no eating close to bedtime, avoid LES relaxers, loose clothing, and stop smoking. Lying down after eating is exactly what makes reflux worse.

q: A client with a hiatal hernia says: I eat dinner around 9 pm, I usually lie on the couch right afterward, I wear a tight belt because it helps my back, and I love coffee with every meal. Which statement is the highest priority for teaching?
o: Eating dinner at 9 pm
Lying on the couch immediately after eating
Wearing a tight belt
Drinking coffee with every meal
r: All four are problems, but lying down right after eating removes gravity entirely and has the greatest immediate impact on reflux from a hiatal hernia.

q: What is the nursing focus after a fundoplication?
o: Monitor for dysphagia and gas-bloat, progress the diet, reinforce lifestyle changes
Encourage carbonated beverages to test the repair
Keep the client flat for 24 hours
Restrict all oral intake for one week
r: Watch for dysphagia and gas-bloat syndrome, advance the diet as ordered, and keep reinforcing the lifestyle measures so reflux does not recur.

q: A client reports progressive difficulty swallowing solids, a 20-pound weight loss and has a history of Barrett's esophagus. What is the most likely condition?
o: GERD
Esophageal cancer
Hiatal hernia
Achalasia
r: Progressive dysphagia that starts with solids and moves to liquids, plus weight loss, on a background of Barrett's — that is esophageal cancer until proven otherwise. Five-year survival is roughly 25 percent because it is caught late.

q: What two functions are most impaired in a client with esophageal cancer?
o: Breathing and speaking
Swallowing and eating
Absorption and elimination
Chewing and tasting
r: They can breathe — they cannot get food and fluid in. Many end up with a PEG tube because nutrition is the immediate problem.

q: A client has severe dysphagia and unexplained weight loss. Which intervention is most appropriate?
o: NG tube for decompression
EGD
Enteral tube feeding
Endoscopic cauterization
r: You do not treat before you know. An EGD shows what is causing the obstruction — stricture, cancer, or something else.

q: A client with a recent stroke is alert but cannot swallow safely. Which intervention is most appropriate?
o: NG tube for decompression
EGD
Enteral tube feeding
Endoscopic cauterization
r: The GI tract still digests food — this is not a GI tract problem. Food just cannot safely get there, so enteral feeding is the answer.

q: A client has a bleeding gastric ulcer. Which intervention is most appropriate?
o: NG tube for decompression
EGD for diagnosis only
Enteral tube feeding
Endoscopic cauterization
r: Stop the bleeding. The EGD is used therapeutically here — cauterize the ulcer.

q: A 67-year-old client had an EGD one hour ago to evaluate difficulty swallowing. Which findings concern the nurse most? Select all that apply.
o: Sudden, severe chest pain
Difficulty swallowing
Shortness of breath
Heart rate 128/min
Blood pressure 88/52 mm Hg
r: High heart rate plus low blood pressure after an EGD means possible hemorrhage or esophageal perforation — food, blood and fluid leaking into the chest, which leads to sepsis and shock. Difficulty swallowing was the reason for the procedure, so it is not new.

q: Which are risk factors for esophageal perforation? Select all that apply.
o: Iatrogenic — caused by a medical procedure such as an EGD
Foreign body ingestion
Trauma
Malignancy
Chronic constipation
r: Procedures (especially EGD), swallowed foreign bodies, trauma and malignancy. Constipation is a lower GI issue.

q: What are the management priorities for esophageal perforation? Select all that apply.
o: NPO
IV fluids
Broad-spectrum antibiotics
Pain management
Surgical repair as soon as possible
Encourage clear liquids to keep the esophagus open
r: NPO, IV fluids for hypotension and hypovolemia, broad-spectrum antibiotics because contents leaked into the chest and abdomen, pain control and surgery ASAP. Nutrition comes later, and the gut still works so enteral or parenteral support is used.

q: What is the priority for a client with an esophageal foreign body obstruction?
o: Give IV glucagon immediately
Airway assessment and protection
Obtain a barium swallow
Encourage the client to drink water to push it down
r: Airway first — drooling is the sign that tells you it is a problem, and the client may need intubation. Then removal: IV glucagon to relax the smooth muscle, endoscopy with retrieval devices, or dilation. Watch for partial becoming complete.

q: What is the common agent in a chemical esophageal burn and the initial priority?
o: Acidic substances; give milk to neutralize
Alkaline substances; maintain the airway first
Alcohol; induce vomiting
Hot liquids; give ice chips
r: Alkaline substances cause the worst injury, and airway maintenance is the first priority. Never induce vomiting — it re-exposes the esophagus.

q: Which are manifestations of esophageal spasm? Select all that apply.
o: Dysphagia
Pyrosis (heartburn)
Regurgitation
Chest pain
Bloody diarrhea
r: Dysphagia, heartburn, regurgitation and chest pain. Bloody diarrhea belongs to lower GI disease.

q: How is esophageal spasm managed?
o: Antibiotics and bowel rest
Smooth muscle relaxants such as calcium channel blockers or nitroglycerin, plus PPIs and a soft diet
Immediate surgical repair
High-fiber diet and laxatives
r: Relax the smooth muscle with CCBs or nitroglycerin, add PPIs, use small frequent soft meals, and botulinum toxin is an option.

q: Which are disorders of the mouth and salivary structures? Select all that apply.
o: Parotitis — inflammation of the parotid gland
Sialadenitis — inflammation of the salivary glands
Sialolithiasis — salivary calculus (stone)
Neoplasms
Diverticulitis
r: Parotitis, sialadenitis, sialolithiasis and neoplasms (rare). Diverticulitis is a colon problem.

q: Inflammation of the parotid gland, inflammation of a salivary gland, and a salivary stone are called, in order:
o: Sialadenitis, parotitis, sialolithiasis
Parotitis, sialadenitis, sialolithiasis
Parotitis, sialolithiasis, sialadenitis
Sialolithiasis, parotitis, sialadenitis
r: Parotitis = parotid gland inflammation. Sialadenitis = salivary gland inflammation. Sialolithiasis = salivary calculus.

q: A client reports swelling below the jaw that gets worse every time they eat. What should the nurse suspect?
o: Parotitis
Sialolithiasis
Oral cancer
Temporomandibular joint disorder
r: A stone blocks the duct, so saliva backs up. Eating stimulates saliva production, which has nowhere to go — that is why it hurts most with meals.

q: Which treatments are used for sialadenitis and sialolithiasis?
o: Sialadenitis: warm compresses, hydration, antibiotics if bacterial. Sialolithiasis: massage, hydration, sour candy, surgical removal
Both are treated with corticosteroids only
Both require immediate surgery
Neither requires treatment
r: Sialadenitis causes pain, swelling and tenderness — warm compresses, hydration and antibiotics if bacterial. For a stone: massage, hydration, sour candy to stimulate flow, and surgical removal if it will not pass.

q: When is neck dissection surgery performed?
o: For chronic tonsillitis
For head and neck cancer — salivary tumor, oropharyngeal cancer or lymph node metastasis
For sleep apnea
For a thyroid nodule
r: Head and neck cancer: salivary tumor, oropharyngeal cancer, lymph node metastasis. The modified radical neck dissection is the most common version.

q: Which complications should the nurse expect after neck dissection surgery? Select all that apply.
o: Airway problems
Swelling
Infection
Difficulty swallowing and speaking
Limited shoulder and neck movement
Increased appetite
r: Airway is the one that kills — watch for increased respiratory rate, decreasing oxygen saturation, rising temperature and noisy respirations. Also stiffness, swelling, infection, swallowing and speech difficulty, and limited shoulder and neck motion.

q: Which are nursing interventions after neck dissection surgery? Select all that apply.
o: Monitor airway and respiratory status
Prevent aspiration
Manage pain
Care for the incision site
Provide effective communication strategies
Promote shoulder and neck motion
r: All of them. Airway first, then aspiration prevention, pain, incision care, a way to communicate when speech is impaired, and range of motion so the shoulder does not freeze.

q: What is the most common cause of peptic ulcer disease?
o: NSAID use
Helicobacter pylori infection
Stress
Spicy food
r: H. pylori is the most common cause. NSAIDs are the second big one. Stress and spicy food may aggravate symptoms but do not cause the ulcer.

q: What is the classic pain pattern of a duodenal ulcer?
o: Immediately with the first bite of food
1.5 to 3 hours after meals or at night, relieved by food or antacids
Only with an empty stomach in the morning, worsened by antacids
Constant, unrelated to eating
r: Duodenal ulcer pain comes 1.5 to 3 hours after a meal or wakes the client at night, and food or antacids relieve it. Eating helps.

q: How does gastric ulcer pain differ from duodenal ulcer pain?
o: Gastric pain occurs soon after eating and may not be relieved or may be worsened by food; it also carries a higher malignancy risk
Gastric pain is always relieved by food
Gastric pain occurs only at night
There is no difference
r: Gastric: pain soon after eating, food does not help and may make it worse, higher malignancy risk. Duodenal: pain 1.5 to 3 hours after eating, relieved by food.

q: A client reports burning epigastric pain relieved by eating crackers and has a positive H. pylori test. What is the likely condition?
o: Gastric ulcer
Duodenal ulcer
GERD
Gastroparesis
r: Relieved by eating = duodenal. In the small intestine, not the stomach.

q: A client reports burning epigastric pain after taking ibuprofen for the past week. What is the likely condition?
o: Duodenal ulcer
Early gastric ulcer or gastritis
Esophageal cancer
Appendicitis
r: A week of NSAIDs plus new burning epigastric pain points to early gastric ulcer or gastritis.

q: Which findings suggest perforation of a peptic ulcer? Select all that apply.
o: Sudden severe epigastric pain radiating to the shoulders
Rigid abdomen
Rebound tenderness
Absent bowel sounds
Signs of shock
Gradual improvement in pain over several days
r: Perforation is a surgical emergency: sudden severe pain radiating to the shoulders, a rigid board-like abdomen, rebound tenderness, absent bowel sounds and shock.

q: The nurse enters the room. Which finding requires immediate attention?
o: Vomiting undigested food after every meal
Black tarry stool and dizziness
Sudden severe abdominal pain with a rigid abdomen
Burning epigastric pain relieved by eating
r: A rigid abdomen with sudden severe pain means perforation — contents are leaking into the peritoneum and sepsis follows. Keep the client NPO and start IV fluids. Vomiting undigested food is pyloric stenosis, black stool with dizziness is a hemorrhage which is urgent but perforation takes priority, and burning pain relieved by eating is a duodenal ulcer.

q: A client has epigastric pain, nausea, relief of discomfort when eating, and black tarry stools. Which treatment regimen would the provider most likely initiate?
o: Omeprazole, clarithromycin and amoxicillin
Loperamide and a clear liquid diet
Lactulose and neomycin
Metoclopramide and a low-residue diet
r: This is a bleeding duodenal ulcer with H. pylori. Triple therapy: omeprazole to reduce acid, plus clarithromycin and amoxicillin — two antibiotics because H. pylori is often resistant to one.

q: What is triple therapy for peptic ulcer disease?
o: Three antibiotics
Two antibiotics plus either an H2 blocker or a PPI
An antacid, a laxative and an antiemetic
Three doses of a PPI daily
r: Two antibiotics plus acid suppression with an H2 blocker or a PPI.

q: Which are nursing interventions for peptic ulcer disease? Select all that apply.
o: Monitor for orthostatic changes in vital signs
Monitor H&H and other labs
Administer PPIs, H2 blockers, antacids, surface agents and H. pylori antibiotics
Teach the client to take sucralfate with a large meal
Educate on avoiding NSAIDs or using a PPI for prophylaxis
r: Orthostatics catch bleeding early, labs track the H&H, and the medication list covers PPIs (pantoprazole, omeprazole), H2 blockers (famotidine), antacids, surface agents (sucralfate, bismuth), antibiotics and misoprostol. Sucralfate goes on an EMPTY stomach, not with a meal.

q: Which findings suggest bleeding or chronic anemia from peptic ulcer disease? Select all that apply.
o: Hematemesis
Melena
Fatigue
Pallor
Orthostatic hypotension
Rising hemoglobin and hematocrit
r: Vomiting blood, black tarry stools, fatigue, pallor and orthostatic hypotension — with a DROPPING H&H, not a rising one.

q: What should the nurse teach a client with PUD about NSAIDs?
o: Take them with food and continue as needed
Avoid them, or use them with PPI prophylaxis; acetaminophen is the safer alternative
Double the dose to get faster relief
NSAIDs are safe if taken at bedtime
r: Avoid NSAIDs or cover with a PPI. Acetaminophen is safer for pain in a client with an ulcer.

q: A client vomits undigested food, has abdominal distention and weight loss. What is this called?
o: Dumping syndrome
Gastric outlet obstruction (pyloric stenosis)
Paralytic ileus
Achalasia
r: Food cannot leave the stomach, so it comes back up undigested, the abdomen distends and the client loses weight.

q: How should sucralfate be administered?
o: With meals for best coating
On an empty stomach — 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals, and separated from other medications by 2 hours
Only at bedtime with an antacid
Crushed in juice with other medications
r: Sucralfate needs an empty stomach to line the ulcer, and it binds other drugs — separate them by 2 hours.

q: What is the purpose of sucralfate?
o: It neutralizes stomach acid
It lines the stomach and forms a protective barrier so the ulcer can heal
It kills H. pylori
It speeds gastric emptying
r: Think band-aid. It coats the ulcer and inflamed tissue so healing can happen.

q: What is misoprostol used for, and what is the major contraindication?
o: Treating H. pylori; contraindicated in penicillin allergy
Preventing NSAID-induced ulcers by replacing prostaglandins; contraindicated in pregnancy
Reducing acid production; contraindicated in renal failure
Coating ulcers; contraindicated in liver disease
r: Misoprostol is a prostaglandin that thickens the mucus layer NSAIDs strip away. It is an abortifacient — absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy.

q: A client's gastritis is caused by long-term NSAID use. Which medication best addresses the underlying problem?
o: Misoprostol
Loperamide
Metoclopramide
Lactulose
r: Misoprostol replaces the prostaglandins the NSAIDs took away and rebuilds the stomach's shield.

q: What is bismuth subsalicylate used for?
o: A laxative
Antisecretory, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial and protective coating — works well against H. pylori
An opioid antidiarrheal
An antiemetic only
r: Pepto-Bismol. It reduces secretion, calms inflammation, has antimicrobial action against H. pylori and coats the lining.

q: What is lactulose used for?
o: Acid suppression
A laxative
Ulcer coating
Antibiotic therapy
r: Lactulose is a laxative — it is also used to lower ammonia in hepatic encephalopathy.

q: What is viscous lidocaine used for?
o: Numbing the mouth or esophagus — mouth ulcers, canker sores, tooth pain
Systemic pain control
Reducing gastric acid
Killing H. pylori
r: It is a topical oral numbing agent for the mouth and esophagus.

q: A large gastric ulcer is seen on EGD. Which medication categories would the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
o: A mucosal protectant such as sucralfate, given before food
A PPI such as omeprazole
An H2 blocker such as famotidine
A stimulant laxative
An opioid antidiarrheal
r: Protect the lining with sucralfate and cut acid production with a PPI or an H2 blocker. Laxatives and antidiarrheals have nothing to do with an ulcer.

q: What causes erosive gastritis?
o: H. pylori infection
NSAIDs, alcohol use and recent radiation
A gluten-containing diet
Bile reflux only
r: Erosive gastritis comes from NSAIDs, alcohol and radiation. Extensive mucosal damage causes ulcers and raises stomach cancer risk. Non-erosive gastritis is the H. pylori kind.

q: Which are clinical manifestations of gastritis? Select all that apply.
o: Dyspepsia and general abdominal discomfort
Upper abdominal pain or burning
Nausea, vomiting, reduced appetite and weight loss
Abdominal bloating and distention
Hematemesis and a stool positive for occult blood
Intolerance of spicy and fatty foods
r: All of them, plus headache, hiccuping that can last hours to days, anorexia and pernicious anemia in the chronic autoimmune form.

q: Chronic autoimmune gastritis is associated with which condition?
o: Iron deficiency anemia
Pernicious anemia
Sickle cell disease
Thalassemia
r: Antibodies against parietal cells and intrinsic factor mean B12 cannot be absorbed, which causes pernicious anemia.

q: Which medication promotes healing by coating the ulcerated and inflamed tissue in a client with H. pylori?
o: Sucralfate
Loperamide
Ondansetron
Docusate
r: Sucralfate coats the damaged surface so it can heal while the antibiotics clear the organism.

q: What is the rationale for small frequent meals in gastritis and PUD?
o: It increases total calorie intake
It reduces acid exposure and gastric distention and is better tolerated during a flare
It speeds gastric emptying
It prevents constipation
r: Less volume at once means less acid stimulation and less distention, and the client tolerates it better while the lining heals.

q: Which medication classes are used for both gastritis and PUD? Select all that apply.
o: PPIs
H2 receptor antagonists
Antacids
Sucralfate
H. pylori antibiotics
Osmotic laxatives
r: PPIs, H2 blockers, antacids, sucralfate, H. pylori antibiotics and sometimes misoprostol. Laxatives are not part of either regimen.

q: What lifelong treatment is required after a total gastrectomy?
o: Oral iron daily
Monthly IM vitamin B12 injections
Weekly folic acid
Daily potassium supplements
r: No stomach means no intrinsic factor, so B12 cannot be absorbed from the gut. Lifelong B12 injections.

q: What condition results from a deficiency of intrinsic factor normally secreted by the gastric mucosa?
o: Iron deficiency anemia
Pernicious anemia
Aplastic anemia
Sickle cell anemia
r: No intrinsic factor means impaired B12 absorption, which is pernicious anemia. After a gastrectomy this means lifelong B12 shots.

q: A client with a history of gastric bypass presents with a beefy red tongue. What is the likely cause?
o: Iron deficiency anemia
Pernicious anemia from loss of intrinsic factor
Folate deficiency
Vitamin C deficiency
r: Loss of parietal cells means no intrinsic factor, so B12 cannot be absorbed. A beefy red tongue plus NEUROLOGIC symptoms — paresthesias, balance problems — is what separates B12 deficiency from iron deficiency.

q: What is the timing and cause of early dumping syndrome?
o: Within 30 minutes; rapid gastric emptying causes a fluid shift and hypovolemia
1.5 to 3 hours; reactive hypoglycemia
6 to 8 hours; delayed absorption
24 hours; electrolyte loss
r: Within 30 minutes. Hypertonic contents dump into the small bowel, fluid shifts in, and the blood pressure falls while the heart rate rises.

q: What is the timing and cause of late dumping syndrome?
o: Within 30 minutes; fluid shift
1.5 to 3 hours; reactive hypoglycemia from an insulin surge
12 hours; bile reflux
Immediately; vagal response
r: 1.5 to 3 hours later. After the fluid shift the pancreas dumps a large amount of insulin, and the client becomes hypoglycemic.

q: Which are symptoms of dumping syndrome? Select all that apply.
o: Nausea and vomiting
Diaphoresis
Dizziness
Tachycardia
Palpitations
Constipation
r: Nausea, vomiting, diaphoresis, dizziness, tachycardia and palpitations. Constipation is not part of the picture — these clients usually have diarrhea or urgency.

q: Which dietary measures prevent dumping syndrome? Select all that apply.
o: Small frequent meals
High protein, low to moderate carbohydrate
No liquids with meals
Avoid simple sugars
Lie down after eating
Drink a large glass of juice with each meal
r: Small frequent high-protein meals, limit carbs, no fluids with meals, avoid simple sugars, and lie down after eating to slow gastric emptying. Juice with a meal is exactly what triggers an episode.

q: Which should be monitored or supplemented after a gastrectomy? Select all that apply.
o: Vitamin B12
Iron
Calcium and vitamin D
Folate
Signs of dumping syndrome
Increased NSAID use for pain
r: B12, iron, calcium, vitamin D and folate, with small frequent meals and monitoring for dumping and pernicious anemia. NSAIDs and aspirin-containing products are avoided.

q: Which four things should the nurse monitor in a client who just had stomach surgery or a gastrectomy? Select all that apply.
o: NG tube output — scant blood is expected for 12 to 24 hours
Return of bowel sounds
Bleeding
Infection
Encouraging a high-carbohydrate diet
r: NG output (a small amount of blood in the first 12 to 24 hours is expected), return of bowel sounds, bleeding and infection. Large amounts of carbohydrate trigger dumping, so that is avoided.

q: If part or all of the stomach is removed, which problems should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
o: Nutrient deficiency
Need for small frequent meals
Slower digestion from reduced acid
Dumping syndrome
Increased gastric acid production
r: Less stomach means nutrient deficiencies, smaller more frequent meals, slower digestion from less acid, and dumping. Acid production goes DOWN, not up.

q: What are the most common causes of mechanical versus non-mechanical bowel obstruction?
o: Mechanical: paralytic ileus. Non-mechanical: tumor
Mechanical: physical blockage from tumor, foreign object or stool. Non-mechanical: paralytic ileus from abdominal surgery or neuromuscular disorder
Both are caused by adhesions
Both are caused by infection
r: Mechanical means something is physically in the way. Non-mechanical means the bowel simply stopped moving — a paralytic ileus.

q: Which are risk factors for a non-mechanical intestinal obstruction? Select all that apply.
o: Abdominal surgery
Electrolyte imbalance
Abdominal infection
Decreased blood supply to the intestines
A swallowed foreign body
r: Surgery, electrolyte imbalance, infection and poor perfusion all stop peristalsis. A swallowed foreign body is a MECHANICAL cause.

q: Which are general signs and symptoms of intestinal obstruction? Select all that apply.
o: Abdominal distention
Abdominal pain
Constipation
Nausea and vomiting
Absent bowel sounds distal to the blockage
Increased appetite
r: Distention, pain, constipation, nausea and vomiting, and absent bowel sounds below the blockage.

q: What is the main symptomatic difference between a small and large bowel obstruction?
o: Small bowel causes more constipation; large bowel causes more vomiting
Small bowel causes profuse vomiting, severe fluid and electrolyte imbalance and colicky pain; large bowel causes less vomiting and less imbalance with longer-lasting pain spasms
There is no difference
Large bowel obstruction always causes fever
r: Small bowel is close to the beginning of the pipeline, so contents back up fast — profuse vomiting of food, severe fluid and electrolyte loss, colicky pain, and fever if it strangulates. Large bowel is further down, so there is less vomiting (and it may smell feculent), less imbalance, and no fever.

q: How does the pain of a small bowel obstruction differ from a large bowel obstruction?
o: SBO: crampy, intermittent, central and periumbilical. LBO: lower abdominal, crampy, progressing to constant
SBO: constant right upper quadrant. LBO: intermittent epigastric
Both are identical
SBO: painless. LBO: severe
r: SBO pain is crampy and intermittent around the umbilicus. LBO pain is lower abdominal, crampy, and becomes constant.

q: How do vomiting and distention differ between small and large bowel obstruction?
o: SBO: vomiting is late, distention is mild. LBO: vomiting is early, distention is severe

SBO: vomiting is early, frequent and may be feculent, which can cause metabolic alkalosis; distention is mild to moderate. LBO: vomiting is late or absent until severe; distention is prominent from stool and gas
Neither causes vomiting
Both cause identical patterns
r: SBO vomits early and often, and losing all that gastric acid causes metabolic ALKALOSIS. LBO vomits late if at all, but the abdomen distends dramatically because stool and gas accumulate.

q: How do bowel sounds differ between small and large bowel obstruction?
o: SBO: high-pitched, hyperactive tinkling early, absent late. LBO: hypoactive or absent later with less pronounced tinkling
SBO: always absent. LBO: always hyperactive
Both are normal throughout
Bowel sounds are not assessed in obstruction
r: Early SBO gives you high-pitched tinkling as the bowel fights the blockage, then goes silent. LBO sounds are hypoactive or absent later and the tinkling is less dramatic.

q: A client presents with high-pitched bowel sounds, distention, cramping pain and vomiting that smells like feces. What is the likely diagnosis?
o: Appendicitis
Intestinal obstruction
Diverticulitis
Cholecystitis
r: High-pitched sounds, distention, cramping and feculent vomiting are the early signs of intestinal obstruction.

q: What causes central abdominal pain, distension and vomiting?
o: Appendicitis
Bowel obstruction
Cholecystitis
Pancreatitis
r: Central pain plus distension plus vomiting is the obstruction picture.

q: What is the best way to diagnose an intestinal blockage?
o: Colonoscopy
Abdominal x-ray
Stool culture
Serum amylase
r: X-ray is the least invasive test that shows what and where the obstruction is.

q: What does an elevated lactate level indicate in a client with a small bowel obstruction?
o: Dehydration only
The bowel is becoming ischemic — losing its blood supply
An electrolyte imbalance
The obstruction is resolving
r: Lactic acid builds up when tissue is not getting oxygen. In an SBO, a rising lactate means the bowel is strangulating.

q: Which are common causes of small and large bowel obstruction? Select all that apply.
o: Small: adhesions after abdominal surgery
Small: incarcerated hernia
Small: Crohn's disease, intussusception, volvulus
Large: volvulus, neoplasm, diverticulitis
Large: appendicitis
r: Small bowel: adhesions, incarcerated hernia, Crohn's, intussusception (the intestine folds into itself) and volvulus. Large bowel: volvulus, neoplasm and diverticulitis.

q: What is a volvulus?
o: Inflammation of the appendix
Intestinal twisting that causes a mechanical blockage
An outpouching of the colon wall
A protrusion of bowel through the abdominal wall
r: The intestine twists on itself and blocks the lumen — a mechanical small or large bowel obstruction.

q: What causes ribbon-like stool?
o: Small bowel obstruction
Large intestinal blockage
Celiac disease
Ulcerative colitis
r: Only a thin stream can squeeze past the obstruction in the large intestine, so the stool comes out ribbon-like or loose.

q: What is the term for a client who cannot pass gas and has not passed stool for more than 8 hours despite feeling the urge to defecate?
o: Constipation
Obstipation
Tenesmus
Encopresis
r: Obstipation is complete — no gas, no stool, despite the urge. It signals obstruction.

q: What is the surgical procedure that reroutes part of the intestine through the abdominal wall?
o: Anastomosis
Ostomy — the opening is the stoma
Fundoplication
Herniorrhaphy
r: An ostomy ends in a stoma. An ileostomy is made from the ileum (small intestine); a colostomy from the large intestine.

q: What type of stool would you expect from an ileostomy compared with a colostomy?
o: Ileostomy: formed. Descending colostomy: liquid
Ileostomy: loose and watery. Ascending colostomy: liquid. Sigmoid or descending colostomy: more formed
All ostomies produce identical output
Ileostomy: no output at all
r: The colon's job is absorbing water. The earlier in the pipeline the stoma is, the more watery the output. Later means more formed.

q: What must be watched most closely in a client with a new ileostomy?
o: Constipation
Fluid volume deficit
Hyperkalemia
Weight gain
r: An ileostomy removes fluid that has not been absorbed yet. Watch heart rate, blood pressure and respiratory rate, replace fluids — especially if the client is NPO — and once bowel sounds return, start with ice chips and small sips.

q: What color is a healthy stoma?
o: Dark purple
Pink and moist
Pale and dry
Dusky gray
r: Pink and moist means it is perfused. Dark purple or blue, dusky or pale all mean compromised circulation — report it.

q: True or false: the opening of an ostomy pouch should be cut no more than 1/4 inch larger than the stoma.
o: True
False — no more than 1/8 inch larger
True, but only for ileostomies
False — it should be 1/2 inch larger
r: No more than 1/8 inch. Any larger and effluent leaks onto the skin; too small and you can cut off circulation to the stoma.

q: What should be taught to a client with a new ostomy? Select all that apply.
o: Chew food thoroughly
Avoid foods that cause gas
Avoid high-fiber foods for the first 6 to 8 weeks
Empty the pouch when it is one-half to one-third full
Change the pouch every 3 to 7 days
Irrigate every type of ostomy daily
r: Chew well, avoid gas producers, skip high fiber for the first 6 to 8 weeks, empty at one-half to one-third full and change every 3 to 7 days with a good skin barrier. Only SIGMOID colostomies are irrigated for regulation — not the others.

q: What is an anastomosis?
o: A surgical opening onto the abdominal wall
A surgical connection between two tubular structures — for example reconnecting the remaining colon after removing a cancerous section, so no colostomy is needed
The removal of the entire colon
A drainage tube placed in the bile duct
r: It reconnects the two ends after resection — bowel to bowel, vessel to vessel, ureter to ureter. That is how a client avoids a permanent colostomy.

q: What happens in appendicitis?
o: The appendix ruptures spontaneously without warning
The opening of the appendix becomes obstructed by fecalith, tumor or infection, causing inflammation and ischemia with bacterial overgrowth
The appendix twists on its blood supply
The appendix fills with bile
r: Obstruction leads to inflammation and ischemia, and bacteria overgrow behind the blockage.

q: Which are signs and symptoms of appendicitis? Select all that apply.
o: Right lower quadrant pain at McBurney's point
Rebound tenderness — minimal pain on pressing, sharp pain on release
Loss of appetite
Nausea and vomiting
Fever
Left lower quadrant pain
r: RLQ pain at McBurney's point plus rebound tenderness, anorexia, nausea and vomiting and fever. CT scan and an elevated WBC support it. LLQ pain points to diverticulitis instead.

q: Where is McBurney's point?
o: Right upper quadrant
Left upper quadrant
Right lower quadrant
Left lower quadrant
r: Right lower quadrant — between the umbilicus and the anterior superior iliac spine.

q: How is the obturator sign elicited and what does a positive result indicate?
o: Extend the right leg away from the body; pain indicates gallbladder disease
Rotate the flexed right leg inward at the hip; pain indicates an inflamed appendix
Press on the left lower quadrant; pain on the right indicates peritonitis
Tap the costovertebral angle; pain indicates kidney infection
r: Internal rotation of the flexed right hip stretches the obturator muscle. Pain means the inflamed appendix is sitting against it.

q: How is the psoas sign elicited?
o: Rotate the flexed hip inward
Extend the right leg outward and back from the body — using the abdominal muscles makes the inflamed appendix hurt
Press and release the right lower quadrant
Flex the neck and watch for hip flexion
r: The leg is extended away from the body. Moving the psoas muscle irritates the inflamed appendix and the client reports sharp pain.

q: Which are nursing interventions for appendicitis and appendectomy? Select all that apply.
o: Keep the client NPO
IV fluids
Antibiotics
Prepare for laparoscopic surgery unless the appendix has ruptured, which requires an open procedure
Apply heat to the right lower quadrant to relieve pain
Monitor for peritonitis and perforation
r: NPO, IV fluids, antibiotics and surgery. Never apply heat to a suspected appendicitis — it can hasten rupture. Watch for peritonitis and perforation.

q: A client with appendicitis reports that the severe right lower quadrant pain has suddenly gone away. What has likely occurred?
o: The appendicitis has resolved
The appendix has ruptured — a medical emergency
The pain medication is working
The obstruction has passed
r: Sudden relief means the pressure was released — the appendix ruptured. That is a red flag, not good news.

q: Which are causes or signs of peritonitis? Select all that apply.
o: Trauma or perforation of an organ
Rigid, board-like abdomen
Rebound tenderness
Nausea, vomiting and fever
Tachycardia
Hyperactive bowel sounds
r: Causes: trauma, infection, perforation of the appendix, a diverticulum or a peptic ulcer. Signs: rigid abdomen, pain, rebound tenderness, nausea and vomiting, fever and tachycardia. Bowel sounds go ABSENT, not hyperactive.

q: What happens to the bowels in peritonitis?
o: Peristalsis increases to clear the infection
The bowel shuts down, causing a paralytic ileus with absent bowel sounds
Nothing changes
Only the small bowel is affected
r: Fluid leaks into the peritoneal cavity, the bowel basically turns off, and you get a paralytic ileus with no bowel sounds. Sudden abdominal pain plus absent bowel sounds plus a rigid abdomen equals peritonitis.

q: A complication of abdominal perforation causing a tender, rigid abdomen with rebound tenderness is called what?
o: Ileus
Peritonitis
Volvulus
Intussusception
r: Peritonitis — and it is an emergency.

q: Which are interventions for peritonitis? Select all that apply.
o: NPO
NG tube to decompress
IV fluids
Antibiotics
Analgesics
Encourage a high-fiber diet
r: NPO, NG decompression, fluids, antibiotics and pain control. Diagnostics: abdominal x-ray, CT and ultrasound.

q: When is intra-abdominal lavage used?
o: For any case of constipation
When peritonitis is caused by a ruptured organ that has infected the cavity — the abdomen is opened and the entire peritoneal cavity is washed out
As a routine part of a laparoscopic appendectomy
To diagnose bowel obstruction
r: Open, wash out the whole cavity, then monitor closely for sepsis.

q: Which two conditions are the inflammatory bowel diseases?
o: IBS and celiac disease
Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis
Diverticulosis and diverticulitis
Gastritis and PUD
r: Crohn's and ulcerative colitis. Crohn's appears anywhere from mouth to anus and skips; UC is only the colon and rectum and is continuous.

q: Which statements correctly distinguish Crohn's disease from ulcerative colitis? Select all that apply.
o: Crohn's skips along the GI tract; UC progresses continuously
Crohn's occurs anywhere from mouth to anus; UC is only the large intestine
Crohn's inflammation extends through the entire lining; UC affects only the innermost layer
Crohn's typically presents in the lower right; UC in the lower left
Rectal bleeding is common in Crohn's and uncommon in UC
Crohn's has no cure; UC can be cured with a colectomy
r: The one that is backwards: bleeding is COMMON in UC and uncommon in Crohn's. Everything else is right. Crohn's shows cobblestoning; UC carries the higher colon cancer risk.

q: Are mouth sores a manifestation of Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis?
o: Ulcerative colitis
Crohn's disease — it can occur anywhere from mouth to anus
Both equally
Neither
r: Crohn's can appear anywhere along the GI tract, mouth to anus. UC is colon only.

q: Which are complications of Crohn's disease outside the digestive system? Select all that apply.
o: Skin lesions
Iritis
Mouth ulcers
Joint pain
Weight loss
Hearing loss
r: Skin lesions, iritis, mouth ulcers, joint pain and weight loss are all extraintestinal manifestations.

q: What is the most common complication of Crohn's disease?
o: Toxic megacolon
Bowel obstruction
Colon cancer
Peritonitis
r: Repeated inflammation causes strictures, and strictures obstruct.

q: How is anemia related to Crohn's disease?
o: It is unrelated
Malabsorption — particularly of folate and B12 — is common and leads to anemia
It is caused by the medications only
It occurs only after surgery
r: Crohn's damages the absorbing surface, so folate and B12 are not taken in. Chronic blood loss adds to it.

q: What labs would you expect in a client with chronic Crohn's during an active flare? Select all that apply.
o: Low H&H with anemia from chronic bleeding
Hypokalemia from diarrhea
Low albumin from malabsorption and protein loss
Elevated WBC, ESR and CRP from inflammation
Elevated serum calcium
r: Anemia, hypokalemia, low albumin and elevated inflammatory markers. Calcium is not characteristically elevated.

q: Which are clinical presentations of ulcerative colitis? Select all that apply.
o: Abdominal pain and cramping
Severe diarrhea that may be bloody or contain mucus or pus
Fever and chills
Anemia
Abdominal distention
Constipation with hard stools
r: UC lives in the large intestine, whose job is absorbing water — which is why fluid volume deficit is a key concern. Diagnostics: colonoscopy with biopsy, leukocytosis, anemia, decreased sodium, potassium, calcium and magnesium, and elevated ESR and CRP.

q: What is the term for the feeling of incomplete bowel emptying?
o: Obstipation
Tenesmus
Steatorrhea
Borborygmi
r: Tenesmus. It is typical of rectal inflammation and is classic for ulcerative colitis.

q: Which medications are used for Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis? Select all that apply.
o: 5-ASA agents such as sulfasalazine for maintenance
Corticosteroids for flare-ups
Infliximab — check a TB test first
Immunomodulators such as azathioprine or methotrexate
Antibiotics to prevent infection
Daily stimulant laxatives
r: 5-ASA for maintenance, not flares — it turns urine orange, requires folic acid and sunscreen, and is avoided with a sulfa allergy. Steroids for flares. Infliximab needs a TB test first and raises infection risk. Laxatives are not part of IBD management.

q: Which are treatment approaches for Crohn's and ulcerative colitis? Select all that apply.
o: Corticosteroids and 5-ASA agents such as mesalamine
Immunomodulators such as azathioprine
Biologics such as anti-TNF agents
TPN and bowel rest during severe flares
High-calorie, high-protein, low-residue diet
High-fiber diet during an acute flare
r: Steroids, 5-ASA, immunomodulators, biologics, bowel rest with TPN in a severe flare, and a high-calorie high-protein LOW-residue diet. Surgery: colectomy or ileostomy for UC, resection or strictureplasty for Crohn's. High fiber during a flare makes it worse.

q: Which are unique nursing interventions and education points for ulcerative colitis? Select all that apply.
o: Annual colonoscopy because of the high colon cancer risk
Emphasize not stopping medications
Monitor electrolytes, especially potassium
Focus on foods that move slowly through the GI tract, such as protein, and reduce fiber
Small frequent meals
Encourage a high-fiber, high-residue diet at all times
r: Annual scopes because of the cancer risk, medication adherence, potassium monitoring (a lot of fluid is leaving the client), slower-moving low-fiber foods, small frequent meals, and NPO with TPN to rest the bowel in a severe flare.

q: If a client with ulcerative colitis has a total colectomy, what will they need afterward?
o: Nothing — normal defecation resumes
A permanent ileostomy or a J-pouch
A temporary NG tube only
Lifelong TPN
r: A permanent ileostomy or a J-pouch — a diversion so waste leaves the body without a colon.

q: What is toxic megacolon?
o: A twisted segment of colon
Severe inflammation paralyzes the colon and it becomes massively dilated, with a high risk of perforation
An outpouching of the colon wall
Chronic constipation with impaction
r: Inflammation stops motility, gas and stool accumulate, the colon stretches, and then it perforates — peritonitis, sepsis. Ulcerative colitis can cause it.

q: A client with a history of ulcerative colitis presents with severe abdominal distention and pain, high fever, tachycardia, hypotension, rebound tenderness, absent bowel sounds, leukocytosis and altered mental status. What is the likely diagnosis?
o: Diverticulitis
Toxic megacolon
Appendicitis
Irritable bowel syndrome
r: Acute non-obstructive dilation of the colon — more than 6 cm in the transverse colon on x-ray — with systemic toxicity. It complicates IBD, most often UC, and infectious colitis such as C. difficile.

q: Which are nursing priorities for toxic megacolon? Select all that apply.
o: NPO
NG tube decompression
IV fluids and electrolytes
Vital signs every 15 to 30 minutes and serial abdominal girth
Antibiotics and preparation for surgery
Antidiarrheals and anticholinergics to slow the bowel
r: Do: NPO, decompress, fluids, frequent vitals and girth, antibiotics, prepare for surgery. AVOID antidiarrheals, opioids and anticholinergics — they worsen the dilation. Focus is preventing perforation; colectomy may be curative in UC.

q: What is the formation of bulging pouches in the GI wall that push the mucosal lining through the surrounding muscle called?
o: Diverticulitis
Diverticulosis
Polyposis
Volvulus
r: Diverticulosis is the pouches. When they become infected and inflamed it becomes diverticulitis, with pain and perforation risk. Most common in the sigmoid colon, and not everyone with diverticulosis develops diverticulitis.

q: Which are complications and findings of diverticulitis? Select all that apply.
o: Left lower quadrant pain
Bloating
Unrelenting cramps
Constipation
High temperature
Right lower quadrant rebound tenderness
r: Remember POUCH: Pain (LLQ, sigmoid), Observe bloating, Unrelenting cramps, Constipation, High temp. If it bursts, peritonitis. RLQ rebound tenderness is appendicitis.

q: Is frequent ambulation an appropriate nursing intervention for diverticulitis?
o: Yes — it promotes peristalsis and healing
No — it increases contraction and peristalsis when you want the bowel to rest
Yes — but only after antibiotics are finished
It makes no difference
r: You want bowel rest. Good interventions are a clear liquid diet, monitoring for peritonitis and giving the prescribed antibiotics.

q: What problem does a fistula from a diverticulum to the bladder or vagina create?
o: It relieves pressure in the colon
It creates a channel that lets intestinal contents flow into a normally sterile space
It has no clinical significance
It improves stool consistency
r: The bladder is sterile. Stool entering it means infection.

q: What can a person with celiac disease not digest?
o: Lactose
Gluten
Fructose
Fat
r: Gluten. Ingesting it activates the immune system and damages the intestinal lining, so fewer villi means malabsorption — including of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.

q: Which are signs, symptoms or treatments of celiac disease? Select all that apply.
o: Bloating and gas
Cramping and diarrhea
Steatorrhea
Avoid wheat, barley, rye, malt and brewer's yeast
Take a daily antibiotic
r: Bloating, gas, cramping, diarrhea and steatorrhea. The only treatment is strict gluten avoidance — bread, wheat-based oats, beer, sauces, wheat flour and brewer's yeast.

q: What happens to the villi in short bowel syndrome?
o: The villi grow larger to compensate
Removal of bowel means fewer villi overall, which causes malabsorption
The villi are unaffected
The villi become inflamed but functional
r: Less bowel means less absorptive surface. Signs: diarrhea, steatorrhea, dehydration and malnutrition.

q: What is the term for an inflammatory condition of the stomach and intestines commonly caused by viral infection?
o: Diverticulitis
Gastroenteritis
Celiac disease
Colitis
r: Gastroenteritis — from E. coli (bacterial) or viruses such as rotavirus and Norwalk, usually from contaminated food.

q: Why does gastroenteritis produce watery, non-bloody diarrhea?
o: The colon secretes extra mucus
The inflamed villi cannot absorb, so fluid passes straight through
Blood vessels constrict in the bowel wall
Bile is overproduced
r: Inflammation stops the villi from absorbing. It is a malabsorptive picture — and loss of villi or missing enzymes also causes steatorrhea, the greasy, oily, yellowish stool.

q: A condition presenting with abdominal pain, bloating and changes in the consistency of bowel movements is called what?
o: Inflammatory bowel disease
Irritable bowel syndrome
Celiac disease
Diverticulitis
r: IBS. Causes include stress, anxiety, depression, genetics and changes in gut flora.

q: What is the difference between melena and hematochezia?
o: Melena is fresh red blood; hematochezia is black tarry stool
Melena is black tarry stool with a strong foul odor from digested blood in an upper GI bleed; hematochezia is fresh maroon or red blood from a lower GI source
They are the same thing
Melena occurs only in children
r: Digested blood is black; undigested blood is red. Black means it came from high up and had time to be digested.

q: What distinguishes upper from lower GI bleeding?
o: Upper: esophagus, stomach or duodenum — black tarry stool, or coffee-ground or bright red emesis. Lower: colon — maroon stool; bright red usually means hemorrhoids
Upper bleeds are always painless
Lower bleeds always cause black stool
There is no way to distinguish them
r: Upper GI (esophagus, stomach, duodenum) gives melena or coffee-ground emesis. Lower GI (colon — ulcerative colitis, diverticulitis) gives maroon stool. Bright red on the paper is usually hemorrhoidal.

q: What test determines whether there is blood in the stool that could indicate GI bleeding?
o: Urea breath test
Fecal occult blood test
Stool osmolality
Serum amylase
r: Done at home, testing stool three times. Avoid anticoagulants for 7 days and avoid vitamin C, red meat and iron tablets because they cause false positives. Three positives means a likely GI bleed.

q: How often should stool testing for colorectal cancer screening be done?
o: Every year for guaiac-based or immunochemical testing; every 3 years for a stool DNA test
Once in a lifetime
Every 10 years for all stool tests
Only when symptoms appear
r: Annually for gFOBT or FIT, every 3 years for stool DNA.

q: At what age should a person of average risk have a first colonoscopy?
r: Age 45, then every 10 years unless high risk.

q: Which are significant risk factors for colorectal cancer? Select all that apply.
o: Regular tobacco use
A diet high in red meat
Family history of colorectal cancer
Frequent alcohol use
A diet high in fruits and vegetables
r: Tobacco, red meat (it stimulates bile secretion), family history and alcohol. Raw fruits and vegetables DECREASE the risk.

q: Colorectal cancer is which of the following?
o: The most common cancer and the leading cause of cancer death
The fourth most common cancer site in the US and the second leading cause of cancer death, with the liver as the primary site of metastasis
A rare cancer with excellent prognosis
Found only in older men
r: Fourth most common site, second leading cause of cancer death. It spreads to the liver first. Risks: adenomatous polyps, African American race, IBD, high-fat low-fiber diet, age over 50, smoking, inactivity, alcohol and family history.

q: Which are risk factors for colorectal adenocarcinoma? Select all that apply.
o: Age over 50
Family history, Lynch syndrome or FAP
Inflammatory bowel disease
High-fat, red meat diet
Smoking and obesity
High dietary fiber
r: It often arises from polyps. Fiber is protective, not a risk.

q: Which are treatments for colorectal cancer? Select all that apply.
o: Chemotherapy
Radiation
Surgery — open or laparoscopic, with anastomosis or colostomy
Lifelong antibiotics
r: Chemo, radiation and surgery. The colostomy may be temporary or permanent, or the surgeon may do an anastomosis and reconnect the bowel.

q: Which are risk factors for a hernia? Select all that apply.
o: Male sex
Older age
Chronic constipation
COPD with chronic coughing
Frequent heavy lifting
High fluid intake
r: Anything that raises intra-abdominal pressure: straining, coughing, lifting — plus male sex and age.

q: Why is a hernia damaging to the body?
o: It only causes cosmetic changes
It can strangulate the herniated portion, causing ischemia and necrosis
It causes malabsorption
It leads to gastric reflux
r: Strangulation cuts off perfusion and the tissue dies. It also alters the flow of food and fluid.

q: What is an irreducible hernia?
o: One that resolves on its own
One that cannot be pushed back with gentle palpation
One that occurs only in children
One found only in the groin
r: It will not go back in, which means risk of strangulation, loss of perfusion and dead tissue.

q: What is the most common type of hernia?
o: Umbilical
Inguinal
Incisional
Femoral
r: Inguinal — tissue, often bowel, pushes through a weak spot in the abdominal muscles in the groin. Indirect is more common (congenital weakness); direct is acquired from straining or aging. Signs: a groin bulge that may reduce when lying down, discomfort with straining, heaviness.

q: What is a truss pad used for?
o: To drain an abscess
A non-surgical option that holds a hernia in place and prevents protrusion during daily activities
To support an ostomy pouch
To measure abdominal girth
r: A truss with a hernia belt is a large elastic band that keeps the hernia where it belongs. It must be worn consistently. Definitive management is surgical repair, often with mesh.

q: What is an abnormal passageway connecting two parts of the body that should not be connected?
o: A stoma
A fistula
An anastomosis
A diverticulum
r: A fistula. Anal fistulas through the skin are common in Crohn's — an ulceration fills with bacteria from stool and creates a channel where stool exits where it does not belong. Surgery (fistulectomy) is the usual treatment because they do not heal on their own.

q: Which are nursing interventions for an anal fistula? Select all that apply.
o: Wound management — packed tightly so it heals from the inside out
Analgesics
Antibiotics
Sitz baths
Avoid constipation
Encourage prolonged sitting to promote drainage
r: Pack the wound so it heals from the inside out, manage pain and infection, sitz baths, and prevent constipation — the client may even get an ostomy to rest the colon and rectum.

q: What is a varicose vein of the anorectal area called?
o: A fistula
A hemorrhoid
A polyp
A fissure
r: A hemorrhoid — itchy, with bright red blood. Internal ones can be painless; external ones hurt and you can feel a lump.

q: A client has bright red rectal bleeding, rectal itchiness and pain. What could this be?
o: Colorectal cancer
Internal hemorrhoids
Diverticulitis
Crohn's disease
r: Internal hemorrhoids. With external ones you would also feel a lump.

q: A 22-year-old male cyclist presents with a painful red cyst near his tailbone at the top of the buttocks. What is the likely diagnosis?
o: Anal fistula
Pilonidal cyst
Hemorrhoid
Perirectal abscess
r: A pilonidal cyst fills with infected material and eventually needs incision and drainage. Teaching: keep it clean, remove hair in and around the site, avoid prolonged sitting, and finish the antibiotics.

q: Which are potential complications of frequent laxative use? Select all that apply.
o: Electrolyte imbalance
Dehydration
Increased risk of colon cancer
Bowel dependence
Impaired absorption of medications
r: Diarrhea causes electrolyte loss and dehydration, the bowel becomes dependent, and everything moves through too fast for medications to be absorbed. Laxatives do not increase colon cancer risk.

q: What is the correct order for teaching a client to use an incentive spirometer?
o: Sit upright, inhale into the device, exhale into the device, repeat
Sit upright, exhale, inhale slowly through the device, hold 3 to 5 seconds, exhale normally, repeat 10 times per hour while awake, then cough 2 to 3 times
Lie flat, breathe rapidly into the device 20 times
Cough first, then inhale into the device once per hour
r: Up, out, in, hold, out, repeat, cough. Sit upright, exhale first, inhale slowly through the device, hold for 3 to 5 seconds (10 is the goal), exhale normally — NOT into the device — repeat 10 times an hour while awake, then cough.

q: An 82-year-old client is started on a new medication. Which age-related change should the nurse consider when monitoring for adverse effects?
o: Increased gastric motility reduces drug absorption
Increased hepatic blood flow shortens drug half-life
Increased renal blood flow speeds drug clearance and lowers the risk of drug toxicity
Decreased glomerular filtration rate allows drugs to remain in the body longer
r: A normal age-related decline in GFR means drugs are excreted more slowly, so they accumulate and the risk of toxicity rises — dosage adjustment and monitoring of BUN, creatinine, and I&O are essential. Aging slows clearance rather than speeding it, so any option describing faster elimination is incorrect.

q: An older adult reports dizziness when getting out of bed each morning. Which age-related change best explains this finding?
o: Arterial stiffening with decreased cardiac output
Increased myocardial contractility
Decreased systolic blood pressure
Increased heart rate variability in response to physiologic stress
r: Aging brings arterial stiffness, decreased cardiac output, and reduced heart rate variability, so the body cannot adjust quickly to position change — the result is orthostatic hypotension. Contractility decreases rather than increases with age, and systolic pressure typically rises.

q: Which nursing actions help protect an older adult with orthostatic hypotension? Select all that apply.
o: Instruct the client to sit on the edge of the bed before standing
Assess blood pressure lying, sitting, and standing
Keep the call light and needed items within reach
Review the medication list for sedatives and antihypertensives
Encourage the client to rise quickly to strengthen the legs
r: Gradual position change, orthostatic vital signs, an accessible environment, and a medication review target the fall risk directly. Telling the client to rise quickly is exactly what triggers the drop in blood pressure and a fall.

q: Which age-related respiratory change places an older postoperative client at the greatest risk for pneumonia?
o: Increased chest wall compliance
Loss of lung elasticity with a weaker cough reflex
Increased tidal volume with more effective clearing of secretions
Decreased residual volume
r: Loss of lung elasticity, a stiffer chest wall, and a diminished cough reflex mean secretions are not cleared, which raises the risk of aspiration and pneumonia — this is why the incentive spirometer is emphasized after surgery. Chest wall compliance decreases with age and residual volume increases.

q: Which neurologic change is an expected part of aging that the nurse should monitor?
o: Loss of the ability to learn new information
Permanent decline in level of consciousness
Decreased nerve conduction velocity with slower reaction time
Gradual onset of dementia in all older adults after the age of 80
r: Slowed nerve conduction causes longer reaction times and reduced coordination, which is why fall precautions matter for every older adult. Dementia is never a normal age-related change — it is pathology and must be evaluated.

q: An older adult who was oriented yesterday is now confused and agitated with a new fever. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
o: This is normal sundowning and will resolve on its own
This confirms an irreversible cognitive decline
This is expected dementia progression and needs no workup
This is likely delirium from an underlying cause such as infection
r: Delirium has a rapid onset and always has an underlying cause — infection, dehydration, medications, sleep deprivation, or a UTI — and it is reversible when the cause is treated. Dementia is gradual, chronic, and irreversible, so a sudden change should never be dismissed as dementia.

q: The nurse knows that illness may present atypically in older adults. Which presentations support this principle? Select all that apply.
o: An infection presenting as new confusion rather than fever
Any abnormal laboratory value being expected with aging
A myocardial infarction presenting as fatigue rather than chest pain
Dementia developing as a normal consequence of aging
A urinary tract infection presenting with new agitation
r: Older adults frequently show confusion, fatigue, falls, or functional decline instead of classic symptoms, so a subtle behavior change deserves a full workup. Most laboratory values do not change with age and dementia is never normal aging — both are pathology that must be investigated.

q: An older adult reports constipation. Which age-related change best explains this?
o: Decreased GI motility with reduced nutrient absorption
Increased hepatic enzyme activity
Increased gastric acid production with faster emptying of the stomach
Increased GI motility
r: Slowed GI motility, decreased absorption, and reduced hepatic function make constipation a common age-related complaint, so fiber, fluids, and activity are the teaching priorities. Motility slows rather than speeds up with aging.

q: Which musculoskeletal changes should the nurse expect in an older adult? Select all that apply.
o: Decreased bone density, especially after menopause
Decreased muscle mass and tendon strength
Breakdown of articular cartilage
Gait and balance changes
Increased bone density from years of weight bearing
