PaO2 74 mmHg, PaCO2 44 mmHg, pH 7.38
r: Acute respiratory failure is defined by a PaO2 < 60, a PaCO2 > 50, and a pH < 7.35. A PaO2 of 74 is low-normal and the pH is still normal, so that client is compensating — not yet in failure.

q: A client's ABG shows PaO2 52 mmHg with a PaCO2 of 34 mmHg. Which type of respiratory failure does the nurse recognize?
o: Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
Chronic compensated respiratory acidosis
Type I (hypoxemic) respiratory failure
Type II (hypercapnic) respiratory failure
r: Type I failure is an oxygenation problem: PaO2 < 60 with a normal or low PaCO2 — classic for pneumonia, pulmonary edema, ARDS, COVID, and PE. Type II is the ventilation problem and requires a rising PaCO2 > 45, which this client does not have.

q: Which client is at greatest risk for developing type II (hypercapnic) respiratory failure?
o: A client with an opioid overdose and a respiratory rate of 6
A client with a small subsegmental pulmonary embolism
A client with early bacterial pneumonia
A client with acute pulmonary edema
r: Type II failure is a ventilation failure — CO2 is not being blown off. Drug overdose, COPD, neuromuscular disease, and severe asthma all cause it. Pneumonia and pulmonary edema classically cause type I hypoxemic failure, where the PaCO2 is normal or low.

q: Which conditions can precipitate acute respiratory failure? Select all that apply.
o: Flail chest
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Iron-deficiency anemia with a very low hemoglobin
Pulmonary embolism
Well-controlled hypothyroidism
Seasonal allergic rhinitis
r: ARF is not a disease itself — it is the consequence of another problem. COPD, PE, flail chest, pneumothorax, ARDS, asthma, pulmonary fibrosis, pneumonia, hypoventilation, hypovolemic shock, and low hemoglobin can all cause it. Rhinitis and controlled hypothyroidism do not impair gas exchange.

q: A postoperative client becomes restless and pulls at the bed linens. Vital signs show HR 112 and BP 156/88. What should the nurse suspect first?
o: An adverse reaction to the antibiotic
Postoperative delirium from anesthesia
Early hypoxia
Uncontrolled incisional pain
r: Restlessness is the first sign of hypoxia, and it is accompanied early by tachycardia and hypertension. Pain is a reasonable second thought, but assuming pain and medicating with an opioid before checking oxygenation could worsen hypoventilation — assess the airway and SpO2 first.

q: Which findings are EARLY manifestations of acute respiratory failure? Select all that apply.
o: Dyspnea
Headache
Tachycardia
Central cyanosis
Lethargy progressing to unresponsiveness
Restlessness
r: Early ARF shows restlessness, dyspnea, tachycardia, hypertension, fatigue, and headache. Central cyanosis and lethargy are late findings — by the time they appear the client is near respiratory arrest, so waiting for cyanosis to act is a fatal error.

q: Four clients are being monitored for respiratory failure. Which one should the nurse assess FIRST?
o: A client who has become lethargic and diaphoretic with central cyanosis
A client with a headache and a heart rate of 104
A client using accessory muscles who reports dyspnea
A client with orthopnea who sleeps on three pillows
r: Lethargy, diaphoresis, and central cyanosis are LATE signs of respiratory failure and immediately precede respiratory arrest. The others show early or chronic compensated findings; accessory muscle use is worrisome but the client is still alert and moving air.

q: A client with COPD is admitted in acute respiratory failure. Which trend most strongly indicates the need for intubation and mechanical ventilation?
o: SpO2 drifting from 92% to 89%
A progressively rising PaCO2 with a falling pH
An increase in productive cough
A hematocrit that has risen over several months
r: A climbing PaCO2 means the client can no longer ventilate; retained CO2 becomes acid and produces respiratory acidosis, then CO2 narcosis and loss of consciousness. A COPD client's SpO2 target is 88-92%, so 89% is acceptable and is not the trigger for intubation.

q: Which immediate interventions should the nurse anticipate for a client with COPD who is in acute respiratory failure? Select all that apply.
o: Administer oxygen as prescribed
Have the client perform deep-breathing exercises independently
Administer bronchodilators
Monitor serial ABGs
Administer a loop diuretic to dry the lungs
Prepare for mechanical ventilation
r: Oxygen, ventilatory support, serial ABGs, and bronchodilators are the immediate priorities, along with positioning in high-Fowler's. Diuretics are not indicated — this is not fluid overload — and the client is too compromised for deep-breathing exercises to be effective.

q: How often should the nurse minimally reassess vital signs, breathing pattern, and lung sounds in a client with acute respiratory failure?
o: Once per shift
Every 8 hours
Every 4 hours
At least every 2 hours
r: Clients in ARF deteriorate quickly, so assessment of VS, breathing pattern, and breath sounds is done at least every 2 hours. Every 4 hours may miss the window between early restlessness and late cyanosis.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes PaO2 from PaCO2?
o: PaCO2 reflects perfusion; normal is 60-80 mmHg
PaO2 reflects ventilation; normal is 35-45 mmHg
PaO2 reflects oxygenation; normal is 80-100 mmHg
PaCO2 reflects oxygenation; normal is 80-100 mmHg
r: O2 = oxygenation (PaO2 normal 80-100 mmHg) and CO2 = ventilation (PaCO2 normal 35-45 mmHg). Mixing these up is why students misclassify type I and type II failure — the PaCO2, not the PaO2, tells you whether the client is moving air.

q: A client has a respiratory rate of 32/min, SpO2 98% on 2 L/min nasal cannula, PaCO2 38 mmHg, and is alert and oriented. Which finding BEST indicates adequate ventilation?
o: The respiratory rate of 32/min
The SpO2 of 98%
Being alert and oriented
The PaCO2 of 38 mmHg
r: Ventilation is judged by CO2, and a PaCO2 of 38 is normal, meaning air is moving in and out effectively. SpO2 is tempting but it measures oxygenation, not ventilation — a client can have a perfect saturation while retaining CO2.

q: Which findings should the nurse associate with hypercapnia? Select all that apply.
o: Bright red hemoptysis
Nuchal rigidity
Persistent daytime sleepiness
Shortness of breath
Headache
New confusion and disorientation
r: Rising CO2 produces headache, dyspnea, daytime somnolence (CO2 narcosis), confusion, and eventually seizures. Hemoptysis and nuchal rigidity point elsewhere — toward PE/lung pathology and meningitis respectively, not CO2 retention.

q: What is the leading cause of acute respiratory distress syndrome?
o: Sepsis
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Left-sided heart failure
Obstructive sleep apnea
r: Sepsis is the number one cause — bloodstream bacteria reach the lungs and trigger a diffuse inflammatory process that scars the alveoli. Left-sided heart failure is the classic distractor, but ARDS is noncardiogenic pulmonary edema.

q: A client is receiving 100% oxygen by nonrebreather mask, yet the SpO2 remains 84% and the PaO2 is 51 mmHg. Which condition does this pattern most strongly suggest?
o: Chronic bronchitis
ARDS
Pleural effusion
Asthma exacerbation
r: The hallmark of ARDS is refractory hypoxemia — hypoxemia that does NOT improve with supplemental oxygen. That is the discriminator from every other cause of low saturation; asthma and bronchitis hypoxemia will usually respond to oxygen and bronchodilators.

q: A client with severe sepsis suddenly develops worsening respiratory distress, and the chest x-ray shows new bilateral infiltrates. What should the nurse suspect?
o: Pulmonary embolism
Aspiration of gastric contents
ARDS
Spontaneous pneumothorax
r: Rapid-onset severe dyspnea with bilateral infiltrates in a septic client is ARDS until proven otherwise; the inflammatory response causes diffuse alveolar damage and increased capillary permeability. A pneumothorax would give unilateral diminished breath sounds, not bilateral infiltrates.

q: Which statement best describes the pathophysiology of ARDS?
o: Air enters the pleural space and collapses the lung
Bronchial smooth muscle constricts, trapping air distally
Increased hydrostatic pressure from a failing left ventricle pushes fluid into the alveoli
Inflammation damages the alveolar-capillary membrane, so fluid leaks into the alveoli
r: ARDS is an inflammatory process: the alveolar-capillary membrane becomes leaky, so fluid enters the alveoli because of increased permeability, not because of cardiac backpressure. That is exactly why it is called noncardiogenic pulmonary edema.

q: During assessment of a client with ARDS, which physical finding is the nurse MOST likely to observe?
o: Bilateral crackles on auscultation
Hyperresonance on percussion
Diminished breath sounds in one lung
Unilateral wheezing
r: ARDS floods the alveoli bilaterally, producing bilateral crackles. Unilateral diminished sounds and hyperresonance point to a pneumothorax, which is a different emergency with a different fix.

q: The provider prescribes prone positioning for a client with ARDS. Which explanation should the nurse give the family?
o: It makes suctioning the airway easier
It redistributes blood flow through the lungs and helps collapsed alveoli re-expand
It decreases the amount of sedation the client will need
It prevents fluid from collecting in the pleural space
r: Prone positioning redistributes perfusion across the lungs and adds pressure to the anterior chest, which helps posterior alveoli re-expand and improves oxygenation. It does not reduce sedation needs — proned clients typically require more sedation.

q: Which interventions belong in the plan of care for a client with ARDS? Select all that apply.
o: Identify and treat the underlying cause
Position the client supine with the head of the bed flat
Place the client in the prone position as prescribed
Provide enteral nutrition support
Insert a chest tube to drain the alveolar fluid
Prepare for intubation and mechanical ventilation with PEEP
r: ARDS care is: treat the cause, intubate with PEEP, correct hypovolemia, prone the client, feed enterally, and sedate to reduce anxiety and oxygen demand. Supine is wrong, and a chest tube is useless because the fluid is inside the alveoli, not the pleural space.

q: Within what time frame after a precipitating event does ARDS typically develop?
o: Within 3 months
Within 2 to 4 weeks
Within 7 to 10 days
Within 72 hours
r: ARDS is defined by the rapid onset of severe dyspnea and V/Q mismatch, generally less than 72 hours after the triggering event. A slow decline over weeks suggests a different process such as fibrosis or worsening COPD.

q: Which clients are at increased risk for developing ARDS? Select all that apply.
o: A client who received multiple blood transfusions after trauma
A near-drowning victim
A client with a healed clavicle fracture
A client with well-controlled seasonal allergies
A client with gram-negative sepsis
A client who aspirated gastric contents
r: Sepsis, shock, DIC, aspiration, PE, pneumonia, near-drowning, trauma, multiple transfusions, smoke or toxic gas inhalation, opioid overdose, and COVID all trigger the inflammatory cascade of ARDS. Allergies and a healed fracture do not.

q: A client with ARDS has been prone for 12 hours. Which assessment is the nurse's priority during this therapy?
o: Peripheral pulses in the feet
Bowel sounds in all four quadrants
Skin integrity over pressure points and the face
Deep tendon reflexes
r: Prone positioning is effective but hard on the body — skin breakdown over the face, chest, knees, and other dependent surfaces plus client comfort are the key nursing concerns, along with securing the airway and lines. The other assessments are routine, not position-specific risks.

q: How is ARDS classified in terms of severity?
o: By the peak expiratory flow rate
By the size of the pleural effusion on x-ray
By the level of the serum D-dimer
By the degree of hypoxemia that does not respond to supplemental oxygen
r: ARDS severity is graded by the degree of hypoxemia that fails to respond to oxygen therapy, supported by chest x-rays showing diffuse infiltrates from fluid backed up by inflammation. D-dimer relates to clot burden and is used for PE, not ARDS staging.

q: What is the primary purpose of adding PEEP for a client with ARDS?
o: To keep alveoli open at the end of expiration so gas exchange can occur
To remove carbon dioxide more quickly
To reduce the amount of oral secretions
To decrease the client's respiratory rate
r: Positive end-expiratory pressure holds alveoli open at end-expiration, improving surface area for gas exchange and preventing atelectasis. It is an oxygenation tool; CO2 removal depends mostly on rate and tidal volume.

q: Which findings in a client with ARDS require the nurse to notify the provider immediately? Select all that apply.
o: SpO2 of 86% despite a nonrebreather at 15 L/min
Sudden absence of breath sounds on the right with tracheal deviation
A temperature of 100.2 degrees Fahrenheit
New confusion with worsening hypoxia
Bilateral crackles that were documented on admission
r: Refractory hypoxemia despite oxygen, new confusion with hypoxia, and absent breath sounds with tracheal deviation (tension pneumothorax) are all red flags demanding immediate action. Crackles already documented and a low-grade fever are expected in ARDS and do not change the plan by themselves.

q: The high-pressure alarm sounds on a client's ventilator. Which cause should the nurse suspect?
o: A disconnected circuit at the ventilator
Secretions obstructing the endotracheal tube
A leak around the endotracheal tube cuff
A loose humidifier connection
r: High pressure = obstruction or increased resistance: secretions, kinked tubing, the client biting the tube, bronchospasm, or a pneumothorax. Disconnections, cuff leaks, and loose connections all cause the pressure to fall, so they set off the low-pressure alarm.

q: The low-pressure alarm sounds on a ventilator. What does this alarm most likely indicate?
o: The client is biting the endotracheal tube
The client has thick secretions in the airway
There is a leak or disconnection in the system
The client has developed bronchospasm
r: Low pressure = a leak or disconnection — the circuit came apart, the cuff is underinflated, or the tube is displaced. Biting, secretions, and bronchospasm all increase resistance and trigger the high-pressure alarm instead.

q: A ventilator alarm is sounding and the nurse cannot immediately identify or correct the cause. What should the nurse do FIRST?
o: Increase the ventilator's set tidal volume
Suction the client for 30 seconds
Silence the alarm and call respiratory therapy
Manually ventilate the client with a bag-valve device on 100% oxygen
r: If the problem cannot be fixed at once, disconnect the client and manually ventilate with a bag-valve device on 100% oxygen while help is summoned — oxygenation cannot wait for troubleshooting. Silencing the alarm to make a phone call leaves the client without ventilation, and suctioning for 30 seconds worsens hypoxia.

q: Which situations would cause a high-pressure ventilator alarm? Select all that apply.
o: The client biting on the endotracheal tube
Kinked ventilator tubing
Accumulated secretions in the airway
The ventilator circuit disconnected from the endotracheal tube
Bronchospasm
An underinflated endotracheal tube cuff
r: Anything that raises resistance in the circuit — secretions, kinks, biting, bronchospasm, or a new pneumothorax — triggers the high-pressure alarm. A disconnection or an underinflated cuff lowers circuit pressure and sets off the low-pressure alarm instead.

q: The apnea alarm sounds on a client who is being weaned from the ventilator. What is the nurse's first action?
o: Assess the client
Call the provider for new orders
Document the event and continue the weaning trial
Reset the ventilator to the previous settings
r: The apnea alarm is the most important alarm because it means the client who is supposed to be initiating breaths has stopped breathing. Always assess the client first, then the machine — changing settings before laying eyes on the client can delay recognition of a displaced tube or arrest.

q: A nurse uses the DOPE mnemonic to troubleshoot a deteriorating intubated client. What does DOPE stand for?
o: Dehydration, Oxygenation, Pressure, Edema
Displacement, Obstruction, Pneumothorax, Equipment failure
Delirium, Overdose, Pain, Exhaustion
Drainage, Occlusion, Perfusion, Elevation
r: Displacement of the tube, Obstruction, Pneumothorax, and Equipment failure are the four fixable causes of sudden decompensation on a ventilator. Working this list is what turns an alarm into a diagnosis rather than a guess.

q: Which interventions are part of the ventilator-associated pneumonia prevention bundle? Select all that apply.
o: Provide oral care with chlorhexidine
Suction the client on a set schedule every 2 hours
Provide DVT and peptic ulcer prophylaxis
Perform daily sedation interruption with a weaning readiness assessment
Change the ventilator circuit every 24 hours routinely
Elevate the head of the bed 30 to 45 degrees
r: The VAP bundle is HOB 30-45 degrees, daily sedation interruption with a weaning assessment, oral care with chlorhexidine, and DVT plus peptic ulcer prophylaxis. Suctioning is done PRN only — scheduled suctioning traumatizes the airway and increases infection risk.

q: A 70-year-old client is on mechanical ventilation after surgery. Which action best prevents ventilator-associated pneumonia?
o: Administer sedatives to keep the client calm and still
Limit oral care to once a day so the client is not disturbed
Elevate the head of the bed 30 to 45 degrees
Reposition the client every 4 hours
r: Elevating the HOB 30-45 degrees reduces aspiration of gastric and oral secretions, the main route to VAP. Deep continuous sedation actually increases VAP risk and ventilator days, which is why daily sedation interruption is in the bundle.

q: Which agent is used for the oral care component of the ventilator bundle?
o: Lemon-glycerin swabs
Normal saline only
Hydrogen peroxide
Chlorhexidine
r: Chlorhexidine reduces oral bacterial colonization, which is the reservoir for VAP. Lemon-glycerin swabs dry the mucosa and hydrogen peroxide is irritating; neither reduces pneumonia risk.

q: Which are recognized complications of mechanical ventilation? Select all that apply.
o: Airway trauma
Improved gastric motility
Pressure injuries
Infection
Increased surfactant production
Nutritional deficits
r: Remember PANIC: Pressure injury, Airway trauma, Nutritional problems, Infection (the most important), and Clots. Ventilated clients typically have slowed GI motility and no increase in surfactant, so those options are distractors.

q: A ventilated client suddenly becomes agitated, the high-pressure alarm sounds, breath sounds are absent on the left, and the trachea is deviated to the right. What is the nurse's priority action?
o: Notify the provider immediately and prepare for needle decompression
Increase the PEEP setting to re-expand the lung
Obtain a routine morning chest x-ray
Suction the endotracheal tube and reassess
r: Absent breath sounds with tracheal deviation in a ventilated client is a tension pneumothorax from barotrauma — too much pressure popped alveoli. This is a medical emergency requiring immediate needle decompression; increasing PEEP would add pressure and kill the client faster.

q: How can mechanical ventilation cause a pneumothorax?
o: The tube irritates the pleural lining until it tears
Excessive pressure overdistends and ruptures alveoli
The humidifier introduces fluid into the pleural space
Suctioning pulls air across the chest wall
r: Barotrauma occurs when ventilator pressure overdistends alveoli until they rupture, letting air into the pleural space. This is why low tidal volumes and careful PEEP titration are used in ARDS — the lungs are already stiff and fragile.

q: What is the correct endotracheal tube cuff pressure range?
o: 5 to 10 cm H2O
20 to 30 cm H2O
40 to 50 cm H2O
60 to 70 cm H2O
r: Cuff pressure is maintained at 20-30 cm H2O. Too low allows aspiration around the cuff (VAP risk); too high compresses tracheal mucosa and causes ischemia, necrosis, and later tracheal stenosis.

q: A client has been orally intubated for 18 days. Which outcome should the nurse anticipate discussing with the team?
o: Switching to a nasopharyngeal airway
Extending intubation to 6 weeks to avoid surgery
Placement of a tracheostomy if the airway is still needed
Removing the cuff to reduce pressure on the vocal cords
r: Endotracheal tubes should stay in no longer than 14-21 days; beyond that the risk of vocal cord damage and tracheal injury rises, so a tracheostomy is created. Leaving the tube for 6 weeks can permanently paralyze the vocal cords.

q: Which methods are used to verify endotracheal tube placement? Select all that apply.
o: Chest x-ray
Measuring the client's peak expiratory flow
Observation of symmetrical chest rise
Checking the pulse oximeter reading alone
End-tidal CO2 detection
Auscultation for bilateral breath sounds
r: Placement is confirmed with end-tidal CO2, a chest x-ray, bilateral breath sounds, and symmetrical chest rise. SpO2 alone is unreliable because it lags by minutes — an esophageal intubation can look acceptable on the pulse oximeter at first.

q: Which medication sequence is correct when preparing a client for endotracheal intubation?
o: Give the paralytic alone; sedation is unnecessary
Give an anticoagulant before both
Give the paralytic first, then the sedative
Give the sedative before the paralytic
r: Sedate before paralyzing. A paralyzed but awake client is fully aware and terrified while unable to move or breathe. Once paralysis is given the airway must be established immediately, so equipment and personnel are ready before the drug is pushed.

q: The nurse is manually ventilating a client with a bag-valve device. What is the general pacing rule?
o: One breath every 1 to 2 seconds
One breath every 5 to 6 seconds
One breath every 15 seconds
As fast as the nurse can squeeze the bag
r: Deliver about one breath every 5-6 seconds to avoid overinflation. Bagging too fast causes gastric insufflation, air trapping, and decreased venous return — it makes the client worse, not better.

q: Which ventilator mode delivers a preset tidal volume with every breath, whether the breath is initiated by the client or by the machine?
o: Assist-control (AC)
Synchronized intermittent mandatory ventilation (SIMV)
Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP)
Pressure support ventilation (PSV)
r: Assist-control gives a full preset tidal volume for every breath, so it does the most work for the client — useful in acute failure, but it can cause respiratory alkalosis if the client is tachypneic. SIMV only supports the set breaths and lets spontaneous breaths be whatever volume the client generates, which is why it is often used in weaning.

q: Which ventilator setting is adjusted primarily to improve a client's oxygenation rather than ventilation?
o: Respiratory rate
PEEP and FiO2
Tidal volume
Inspiratory trigger sensitivity
r: FiO2 and PEEP drive oxygenation (the PaO2). Rate and tidal volume drive minute ventilation and therefore the PaCO2 — if the client is retaining CO2, raising the FiO2 will not fix it.

q: Which findings suggest a client is ready to begin weaning from mechanical ventilation? Select all that apply.
o: The client requires increasing amounts of FiO2
The client is hemodynamically stable
The underlying cause of respiratory failure has resolved or improved
The client has a new fever with purulent secretions
The client can initiate spontaneous breaths
ABGs are acceptable on low ventilator support
r: Weaning starts once the underlying cause is treated, the client is stable, is triggering breaths, and has acceptable ABGs on minimal support. Escalating FiO2 or a new infection means the client is going the wrong direction and weaning would fail.

q: During a weaning trial, a client's respiratory rate rises to 36/min, the SpO2 falls to 87%, and the client becomes agitated and diaphoretic. What should the nurse do first?
o: Increase the nasal cannula flow rate and continue
Encourage the client to relax and continue the trial
Return the client to full ventilator support and notify the provider
Administer a sedative and restart the trial in 10 minutes
r: Tachypnea, desaturation, agitation, and diaphoresis are signs of a failed weaning trial; the client is fatiguing and must be placed back on full support before arrest occurs. Sedating and pushing on masks deterioration rather than treating it.

q: Which nursing actions are appropriate for a client receiving mechanical ventilation? Select all that apply.
o: Deflate the cuff each shift to rest the trachea
Assess bilateral breath sounds and symmetrical chest movement
Monitor ABGs to guide ventilator setting changes
Keep the head of the bed flat to prevent hypotension
Provide range-of-motion, mouth care, and skin care
Reposition and turn the client frequently
r: Assessment of breath sounds and chest movement, frequent ABGs, turning, and hygiene measures prevent the PANIC complications. Flat positioning invites aspiration and VAP, and routinely deflating the cuff allows secretions to pour into the lungs.

q: The nurse is caring for four ventilated clients. Which client should the nurse assess FIRST?
o: A client due for scheduled oral care
A client whose family is asking about the weaning plan
A client whose high-pressure alarm sounded once and self-resolved after coughing
A client whose low-pressure alarm is sounding continuously and whose SpO2 is 83%
r: A continuous low-pressure alarm with desaturation means a disconnection or displaced tube — the client is not being ventilated at all. A transient high-pressure alarm that resolved with coughing was secretions clearing and is not the immediate threat.

q: A client on a ventilator is fighting the breaths and the alarms are cycling repeatedly. What should the nurse assess for first?
o: Patient-ventilator dyssynchrony and its causes, such as pain, hypoxia, or secretions
Whether the room temperature is comfortable
The client's most recent hemoglobin A1C
Whether the family is visiting too often
r: Fighting the vent signals dyssynchrony, and the causes are clinical: hypoxia, pain, anxiety, secretions, or a displaced tube. Reaching for more sedation without assessing can mask a tube problem or worsening hypoxia.

q: Which finding in an intubated client requires the most immediate nursing intervention?
o: A cuff pressure of 24 cm H2O
Breath sounds heard only on the right side after repositioning
Blood-tinged secretions on suctioning once
The client mouthing words to the family
r: Breath sounds on one side only suggest the tube has migrated into the right mainstem bronchus — the left lung is not being ventilated and will collapse. A cuff of 24 cm H2O is normal, and a single episode of blood-tinged secretions is expected after suctioning.

q: A nursing student asks what a V/Q mismatch means. What is the nurse's best explanation?
o: It is an infection of the pleural space
It is a problem with the heart's ability to pump
It is a problem with gas exchange from a mismatch between ventilation and perfusion
It is a problem with the chest wall's ability to expand
r: V/Q means ventilation over perfusion: a V problem means air cannot get in, and a Q problem means blood cannot get through. Either way the result is impaired gas exchange, which is why both look like hypoxemia at the bedside.

q: Which statement correctly describes shunting?
o: Ventilation is present but no blood arrives at the alveoli
Both ventilation and perfusion are completely absent
The airways are dilated and gas exchange is increased
Perfusion is present but the alveoli are not ventilated, so blood passes by without picking up oxygen
r: Shunt is wasted perfusion — the blood is there but the air is not, so no diffusion occurs. The classic mix-up is calling shunt a blood flow issue; it is a ventilation issue with intact blood flow, seen in pneumonia, atelectasis, and ARDS.

q: Which statement correctly describes dead space ventilation?
o: Alveoli are ventilated but blood cannot get through, so diffusion cannot occur
The alveoli are filled with inflammatory fluid
The pleural space fills with air
Air cannot reach the alveoli because of mucus plugging
r: Dead space is wasted ventilation: the alveoli are ready and full of air, but there is no blood to accept the oxygen. That is a perfusion problem — the textbook example is a pulmonary embolism.

q: A client with a confirmed pulmonary embolism asks why breathing normally does not fix the low oxygen level. What is the nurse's best response?
o: The clot blocks air from entering the lungs
The clot blocks blood flow, so oxygen in the alveoli has no blood to enter
The clot causes the airways to narrow and trap air
The clot fills the alveoli with fluid
r: PE is a perfusion problem, not a ventilation problem. The alveoli may be perfectly ventilated, but no blood reaches them, so gas exchange cannot occur in that region — the definition of dead space.

q: Which conditions primarily cause a ventilation (V) problem? Select all that apply.
o: Pneumonia
COPD
Asthma
Airway obstruction by a foreign body
Hypovolemic shock
Massive pulmonary embolism
r: Ventilation problems are the ones where air cannot get in or out: asthma, COPD, pneumonia, and airway obstruction. PE and shock are perfusion problems — the air arrives fine but the blood does not.

q: A client's hypoxemia does not improve despite increasing FiO2 to 100%. Which type of V/Q abnormality best explains this?
o: Hyperventilation
Dead space ventilation
Intrapulmonary shunting
Increased anatomic dead space from rapid shallow breathing
r: In a shunt, blood bypasses alveoli that are collapsed or fluid-filled, so added oxygen never reaches that blood — the hallmark refractory hypoxemia of ARDS. Dead space chiefly impairs CO2 clearance and usually responds better to supplemental oxygen.

q: Which result of a pulmonary embolism should the nurse anticipate?
o: Left ventricular hypertrophy within hours
Increased surfactant production
Improved gas exchange in the affected lung region
V/Q mismatch with right heart strain
r: A PE impairs gas exchange, creates a V/Q mismatch, and forces the right ventricle to pump against a blocked pulmonary circuit, producing right heart strain. Left-sided hypertrophy is a chronic systemic hypertension finding, not an acute PE effect.

q: Where does a pulmonary embolism most commonly originate?
o: A deep vein thrombosis in the leg
A clot forming in the left atrium
A carotid artery plaque
A thrombus in the pulmonary vein
r: Most PEs are DVTs that break loose, travel up the venous system and through the right side of the heart, and lodge in the pulmonary arteries. A thrombus is stationary; once it travels it is an embolus.

q: Virchow's triad describes the risk factors for which condition?
o: Asthma exacerbation
Pulmonary embolism
Pneumothorax
Atelectasis
r: Virchow's triad — venous stasis, hypercoagulability, and vessel injury — explains clot formation and therefore PE risk. It has nothing to do with airway or pleural disorders.

q: Which clients are at increased risk for a pulmonary embolism? Select all that apply.
o: A 45-year-old woman using hormone replacement therapy
A client with atrial fibrillation and obesity
A client with a fractured clavicle who remains fully ambulatory
A client who is 3 days post total hip arthroplasty
A client with a BMI of 20
A client who just completed a long overseas flight
r: Estrogen therapy, immobility, orthopedic surgery, obesity, and atrial fibrillation are all recognized PE risks. A BMI of 20 is normal-to-low and confers no added risk, and the clavicle is not a long bone and does not limit mobility, so that client's risk is not increased.

q: A 65-year-old client who had hip surgery 2 weeks ago arrives in the ED with sudden dyspnea, chest pain that worsens with deep breathing, blood-streaked sputum, and a rapid irregular heartbeat. Which diagnosis should the nurse suspect?
o: Community-acquired pneumonia
Acute exacerbation of asthma
Pulmonary embolism
Pericarditis
r: Sudden dyspnea with pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, and hemoptysis after recent surgery and immobility is PE until proven otherwise. Pneumonia has a more gradual onset with fever and productive cough, and does not typically start abruptly.

q: Which manifestations are consistent with an acute pulmonary embolism? Select all that apply.
o: Tachycardia and tachypnea
Bradycardia with a bounding pulse
Gradual onset of a productive green cough over 5 days
Pleuritic chest pain
Sudden onset dyspnea
A feeling of impending doom
r: PE presents suddenly: dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, tachypnea, anxiety with a sense of impending doom, cough, hemoptysis, diaphoresis, and a falling SpO2. A slowly worsening purulent cough points to infection, and bradycardia is not the expected compensatory response.

q: Which diagnostic test is most commonly used to confirm a pulmonary embolism?
o: Peak expiratory flow measurement
Sputum culture
Chest x-ray
CT pulmonary angiography
r: CT angiography is the most common confirmatory test. Before it, assess for iodine or shellfish allergy and hold metformin per protocol because of the contrast dye; a plain chest x-ray is often normal in PE and cannot rule it out.

q: A client with a low pretest probability of PE has a negative D-dimer. How should the nurse interpret this result?
o: It helps rule out a pulmonary embolism in this low-risk client
It confirms the client has a DVT
It indicates the client needs immediate thrombolytics
It confirms the client has a pulmonary embolism
r: D-dimer is a non-specific test: it rises with any clot breakdown, so a positive result cannot confirm PE. A negative D-dimer in a low-risk client is useful because it helps rule out PE.

q: Which ABG pattern is most typical early in an acute pulmonary embolism?
o: Hypercapnia with metabolic acidosis
Hypoxemia with respiratory alkalosis
Hypoxemia with respiratory acidosis
Normal PaO2 with metabolic alkalosis
r: The client hyperventilates from hypoxia and anxiety, blowing off CO2, so early ABGs show hypoxemia with respiratory alkalosis. Respiratory acidosis is the pattern of a client who cannot ventilate, such as COPD with pneumonia — it is a late or different picture.

q: A client suddenly develops dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, and a PE is suspected. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Apply oxygen and notify the provider or rapid response
Massage the client's calf to improve circulation
Establish or maintain IV access
Place the client in high-Fowler's position
Stay with the client
Have the client ambulate in the hallway to improve oxygenation
r: Stay with the client, sit them up, oxygenate, escalate, and secure IV access for anticoagulation. Never massage the legs when a DVT is suspected — it can dislodge more clot — and ambulating an acutely hypoxic client is unsafe.

q: A client with a new PE is started on heparin. The spouse asks if the medicine will dissolve the clot. What is the nurse's best response?
o: No, heparin is given only to treat the chest pain
Yes, heparin dissolves the clot within hours
No, heparin prevents the clot from getting larger while the body breaks it down
Yes, but only if it is given by mouth
r: Anticoagulants (heparin, enoxaparin, warfarin) prevent clot growth and new clots — they do not dissolve clots. Only thrombolytics such as alteplase actually dissolve an existing clot, and those are reserved for severe or life-threatening PE.

q: Alteplase is prescribed for a client with a massive pulmonary embolism. What is the purpose of this drug?
o: To reverse the effects of heparin
To reduce airway inflammation
To prevent existing clots from enlarging
To dissolve the existing clot
r: Alteplase is a thrombolytic that dissolves clot and is reserved for severe or life-threatening PE. Heparin and enoxaparin only prevent extension; confusing the two leads students to expect the wrong bleeding risk profile.

q: A client is being discharged on warfarin after a pulmonary embolism. Which laboratory value does the nurse teach the client will be monitored?
o: PT and INR, with a target INR of about 2 to 3
Serum creatinine only
Hemoglobin A1C
Serum potassium
r: Warfarin is monitored with PT/INR, therapeutic around 2-3 for VTE. Clients should also keep vitamin K intake consistent rather than eliminating greens, since erratic intake is what destabilizes the INR.

q: Which teaching points should the nurse include for a client starting an anticoagulant? Select all that apply.
o: Stop the medication as soon as the chest pain resolves
Take an extra dose if a dose is missed by more than an hour
Use a soft toothbrush and an electric razor
Report a sudden severe headache
Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs unless prescribed
Report black stools or coffee-ground emesis
r: Bleeding precautions and reporting signs of occult or intracranial bleeding are the core teaching; aspirin and NSAIDs add bleeding risk. Doubling doses and self-discontinuing are both dangerous — symptom relief does not mean the clot risk is gone.

q: Which measures help prevent pulmonary embolism? Select all that apply.
o: Crossing the legs while seated to support circulation
Moving the legs periodically during long travel
Use of sequential compression devices
Adequate hydration
Early ambulation after surgery
Remaining on bed rest for several days after surgery
r: Prevention targets venous stasis: ambulate early, use compression devices, hydrate, avoid crossing the legs, stop smoking, take anticoagulants as prescribed, and move the legs during travel. Prolonged bed rest and leg crossing both promote stasis and clot formation.

q: Which client finding is a contraindication to starting anticoagulant therapy?
o: A history of well-controlled hypertension
Active gastrointestinal bleeding
A body mass index of 31
A history of atrial fibrillation
r: Active bleeding, peptic ulcer disease, and recent major trauma or surgery are contraindications to anticoagulation. Obesity and atrial fibrillation are actually indications or risk factors that make anticoagulation more likely, not less.

q: The nurse is assigned four clients. Which client should be seen FIRST?
o: A client with asthma requesting a refill teaching session on a spacer
A client 2 days post-op reporting incisional pain rated 5 of 10
A client who suddenly reports sharp chest pain with deep breathing, dyspnea, and a heart rate of 124 after 3 days of bed rest
A client with COPD whose SpO2 is 90% on 2 L nasal cannula
r: Sudden pleuritic chest pain with dyspnea and tachycardia after immobility is a PE until proven otherwise and is immediately life-threatening. The COPD client's SpO2 of 90% is acceptable for that population (target 88-92%), and pain and teaching can wait.

q: A client with a suspected DVT reports calf tenderness. Which action should the nurse avoid?
o: Measuring and comparing calf circumference
Notifying the provider of the finding
Elevating the extremity as prescribed
Massaging the calf to relieve the discomfort
r: Never massage a suspected DVT — it can dislodge the clot and send it to the lungs as a PE. Elevation, measurement, and notification are all safe and appropriate.

q: The high-pressure alarm is sounding on a ventilated client. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Disconnect the ventilator and leave the client on room air
Check the tubing for kinks or accumulated water
Silence the alarm and document that it occurred
Suction the airway if secretions are present
Assess the client's airway, chest rise, and color
Insert a bite block if the client is biting the tube
r: A high-pressure alarm means resistance, so the nurse assesses the client first and then works the fixable causes: secretions, kinks or water in the tubing, biting, and bronchospasm. Silencing the alarm without assessing and disconnecting the client from support are both unsafe.

q: Which tests are used in the evaluation of a client with a suspected pulmonary embolism? Select all that apply.
o: CT pulmonary angiography
Arterial blood gas analysis
Sputum culture and sensitivity
Venous ultrasound of the legs
Mantoux tuberculin skin test
D-dimer
r: PE workup includes CT angiography (the most common confirmatory test), D-dimer, ABGs, a V/Q scan, and a leg ultrasound to find the DVT source. A PPD screens for TB exposure and a sputum culture identifies pneumonia — neither detects a clot.

q: Which interventions would the nurse expect to improve oxygenation in a client with ARDS? Select all that apply.
o: Increasing the FiO2 as prescribed
Decreasing the tidal volume to allow the PaCO2 to rise
Increasing the PEEP as prescribed
Administering a diuretic to drain fluid from the pleural space
Placing the client in the prone position
Increasing the set respiratory rate
r: FiO2 and PEEP are the oxygenation controls, and prone positioning redistributes perfusion so collapsed alveoli can re-expand. Rate and tidal volume changes affect CO2 removal, not oxygenation, and there is no pleural fluid to diurese — the fluid in ARDS is inside the alveoli.

q: Which statement best describes the underlying problem in asthma?
o: Chronic airway inflammation with reversible bronchoconstriction and mucus production
Permanent destruction of alveolar walls with loss of elastic recoil
Fibrotic scarring of lung tissue from inhaled dust particles
Blockage of a pulmonary artery branch by a traveling clot
r: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disorder producing reversible obstruction from bronchoconstriction, inflammation, and mucus. Alveolar wall destruction with loss of elastic recoil describes emphysema, which is progressive and not fully reversible.

q: A nurse is teaching a client newly diagnosed with asthma about trigger avoidance. Which of the following should the nurse include as common asthma triggers? Select all that apply.
o: Increased dietary fiber intake
Cold air and exercise
Aspirin and NSAIDs
Second-hand cigarette smoke
Gastroesophageal reflux and postnasal drip
r: Cold air, exercise, smoke, GERD/postnasal drip, and aspirin/NSAIDs (as well as beta blockers, allergens, strong odors, and stress) are documented asthma triggers. Dietary fiber has no relationship to airway hyperresponsiveness — students often assume any diet change matters, but the trigger list is about inhaled irritants, allergens, and drugs.

q: A client in severe respiratory distress from asthma had loud bilateral wheezing 10 minutes ago. The nurse now auscultates almost no breath sounds. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Document that the wheezing has resolved and recheck in 30 minutes
Call the rapid response team and prepare for intubation
Lower the head of the bed so the client can rest
Encourage the client to use the incentive spirometer
r: A silent chest after wheezing means airflow has become so limited that no sound is generated — this is impending respiratory failure, not improvement. Documenting resolved wheezing is the classic trap: absence of wheezing in a severe attack is worse than wheezing.

q: A client is having an acute asthma attack. Which prescribed inhaler should the nurse administer first?
o: Beclomethasone
Salmeterol
Albuterol
Montelukast
r: Albuterol is a short-acting beta2 agonist — the rescue inhaler that reverses bronchospasm in minutes. Salmeterol is a LABA: it is a long-acting maintenance drug and takes far too long to work in an acute attack.

q: A client is prescribed an inhaled corticosteroid for asthma control. Which instruction is most important for the nurse to give?
o: Use this inhaler at the first sign of wheezing
Stop the inhaler once symptoms disappear
Swallow the rinse water to coat the throat
Rinse the mouth with water and spit after each use
r: Inhaled corticosteroids deposit drug in the oropharynx and cause oral candidiasis (thrush), so the client rinses and spits — swallowing the water defeats the purpose. Using it at the first sign of wheezing is wrong: it is a controller, not a rescue inhaler.

q: Which of the following should the nurse include when teaching a client about self-management of asthma? Select all that apply.
o: Rinse the mouth after using an inhaled corticosteroid
Seek help if the rescue inhaler is not relieving symptoms
Know which inhaler is the rescue inhaler and which is the controller
Discontinue the controller inhaler on days without symptoms
Use a spacer with the metered-dose inhaler if one is prescribed
r: Spacer use, distinguishing rescue vs controller, rinsing after steroids, and seeking help when the rescue inhaler fails are all core teaching. Stopping the controller on good days is the dangerous distractor — controllers work only when taken daily, and stopping them raises exacerbation risk.

q: A client with asthma reports a peak expiratory flow reading of 65% of personal best. The nurse should tell the client this falls into which zone?
o: Yellow zone
Green zone
Red zone
Blue zone
r: Yellow is 50-79% of personal best and signals caution — the client should use the rescue inhaler and follow the action plan. Green is 80-100% (good control); 65% is clearly below that threshold.

q: A client with asthma calls the clinic reporting a peak flow of 45% of personal best. What should the nurse instruct the client to do?
o: Continue the usual controller inhaler and recheck in the morning
Use the rescue inhaler and seek emergency care now
Double the dose of the inhaled corticosteroid
Rest quietly and repeat the peak flow in four hours
r: Below 50% is the red zone — a medical alert requiring the rescue inhaler and immediate care. Waiting to recheck delays treatment while airflow is already severely limited, and doubling the steroid does nothing acutely because it is not a bronchodilator.

q: A client is admitted in status asthmaticus. Which of the following interventions should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
o: Prepare for possible emergency intubation
Administer systemic corticosteroids
Administer oxygen
Administer a nebulized short-acting bronchodilator
Withhold IV fluids to prevent pulmonary edema
r: Status asthmaticus is asthma unresponsive to usual treatment and progressing toward respiratory failure, so oxygen, bronchodilators, systemic steroids, epinephrine, and readiness to intubate are all expected. IV fluids are given, not withheld — hydration helps thin the thick mucus plugging the airways.

q: Which statement by a client taking salmeterol indicates correct understanding?
o: I will use this inhaler whenever I feel my chest getting tight
I should stop my other inhalers now that I have this one
I take this every day to prevent attacks, not to stop one
I only need this inhaler before I exercise
r: Salmeterol is a LABA used for long-term maintenance, typically combined with an inhaled corticosteroid. Using it for sudden chest tightness is the dangerous misunderstanding — it has a slow onset and cannot rescue a client in bronchospasm.

q: A nurse assesses a client during an asthma attack. Which of the following findings would the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
o: Tachypnea
Use of accessory muscles
Bilateral wheezing
Bradycardia with a fever of 102°F
Cough
r: Wheezing, tachypnea, accessory muscle use, cough, anxiety, and tachycardia are expected in an acute attack. Bradycardia with fever is not — asthma is not an infectious process, and bradycardia in a struggling asthmatic is an ominous late sign of exhaustion, not an expected finding.

q: A nurse observes a client using a metered-dose inhaler. Which of the following actions indicate correct technique? Select all that apply.
o: Exhaling fully before inhaling the dose
Pressing the canister down while breathing in
Inhaling as fast and forcefully as possible
Holding the breath for several seconds after the puff
Shaking the inhaler before use
r: Shake, exhale fully, actuate while inhaling, then hold the breath so the drug deposits in the airways rather than being exhaled. Fast forceful inhalation is wrong — it drives the aerosol onto the back of the throat instead of into the lower airways, which is exactly why a spacer is added for clients who struggle with timing.

q: A client asks why a spacer was added to the metered-dose inhaler. Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?
o: It doubles the amount of drug in each puff
It allows the inhaler to be used without shaking it first
It eliminates the need to rinse the mouth after steroid inhalers
It holds the mist so more medication reaches the lungs instead of the mouth
r: A spacer suspends the aerosol so the client can inhale it slowly, improving lung deposition and reducing oropharyngeal drug. It does not change the dose delivered, and while it reduces oral deposition, the client still rinses after inhaled corticosteroids.

q: A thin client with COPD sits in a tripod position, uses pursed-lip breathing, and has an increased anteroposterior chest diameter. Which type of COPD do these findings most reflect?
o: Emphysema, the pink puffer
Chronic bronchitis, the blue bloater
Asthma with reversible obstruction
Bronchiectasis with copious purulent sputum
r: Emphysema = the pink puffer: alveolar wall destruction, air trapping, barrel chest, thin body habitus, pursed-lip breathing. The blue bloater of chronic bronchitis is cyanotic and edematous with a heavy productive cough, not primarily thin and dyspneic.

q: A nurse notes a barrel chest in a client with emphysema. What causes this finding?
o: Fluid accumulating in the pleural space
Chronic air trapping and hyperinflation of the lungs
Collapse of alveoli from retained secretions
Right ventricular hypertrophy pushing the sternum outward
r: Loss of elastic recoil means air cannot be fully exhaled, so the lungs stay hyperinflated and the anteroposterior diameter increases over time. Alveolar collapse (atelectasis) causes the opposite — loss of lung volume and diminished breath sounds, not chest expansion.

q: A client with COPD is receiving oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula with an SpO2 of 90%. A new graduate nurse suggests increasing the flow rate to bring the saturation above 95%. What is the best response?
o: Yes, all clients should be maintained above 95%
Increase it to 6 L/min and recheck in an hour
The target for this client is 88-92%; too much oxygen can suppress the drive to breathe
Switch to a nonrebreather mask to reach the goal faster
r: In COPD the target SpO2 is 88-92% because chronic CO2 retention shifts the stimulus to breathe toward hypoxic drive; over-oxygenating can blunt that drive and worsen CO2 retention. Applying the general >95% goal is the trap — that target belongs to clients without chronic hypercapnia.

q: A nurse teaches pursed-lip breathing to a client with COPD. Which explanation of its purpose is correct?
o: It increases the respiratory rate to blow off more carbon dioxide
It prevents the client from needing supplemental oxygen
It strengthens the accessory muscles of the neck and shoulders
It prolongs exhalation and keeps airways open so trapped air can escape
r: Pursed-lip breathing creates back pressure that splints airways open during a slow, prolonged exhalation, relieving air trapping and dyspnea. Increasing the rate is counterproductive — a faster rate shortens exhalation and makes trapping worse.

q: Which of the following should the nurse include in discharge teaching for a client with COPD? Select all that apply.
o: Space activities with planned rest periods
Lie flat during periods of shortness of breath
Use pursed-lip breathing during activity
Stop smoking and avoid respiratory irritants
Receive the influenza and pneumococcal vaccines
r: Smoking cessation, vaccination, pursed-lip breathing, and energy conservation are the core COPD self-management points. Lying flat is wrong — the supine position pushes abdominal contents against the diaphragm and worsens dyspnea, so these clients are kept upright in high-Fowler's or tripod.

q: A client with COPD has lost 12 pounds and reports being too tired to finish meals. Which dietary plan should the nurse recommend?
o: Small, frequent high-calorie, high-protein meals
Three large high-fiber meals daily
A low-protein diet to reduce metabolic demand
Clear liquids only until the appetite improves
r: The work of breathing burns calories while a hyperinflated chest and full stomach worsen dyspnea, so small, frequent, calorie- and protein-dense meals are best. Large meals are the tempting choice for weight gain but they distend the abdomen, press on the diaphragm, and leave the client too breathless to eat.

q: A client with a COPD exacerbation is dyspneic with an SpO2 of 86%. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Obtain a sputum specimen for culture
Place the client in high-Fowler's position and apply prescribed oxygen
Start an IV for antibiotic administration
Teach diaphragmatic breathing exercises
r: Positioning for maximal chest expansion and applying prescribed oxygen addresses breathing immediately. Sputum cultures and IV antibiotics matter, but they treat the cause over hours — they do not relieve hypoxemia in the next 60 seconds.

q: A nurse reviews the CBC of a client with long-standing COPD and finds an elevated hematocrit. How should the nurse interpret this result?
o: It indicates an acute infection is developing
It suggests the client is fluid overloaded
It is a compensatory response to chronic hypoxemia
It is an unexpected finding that should be reported as a lab error
r: Chronic hypoxemia stimulates erythropoietin, so the body makes more red cells — secondary polycythemia, which raises the hematocrit. Students often expect a low hematocrit; in COPD the value is elevated, and it reflects long-term low oxygen, not infection.

q: A client with severe COPD develops jugular vein distention, dependent edema, and hepatomegaly. The nurse recognizes these findings as which complication?
o: Atelectasis
Pneumothorax
Pulmonary embolism
Cor pulmonale
r: Cor pulmonale is right-sided heart failure caused by chronic lung disease, and right-sided failure backs blood up into the systemic circulation — JVD, peripheral edema, and liver congestion. A pneumothorax presents acutely with unilateral absent breath sounds, not gradual systemic fluid overload.

q: A client is started on prednisone for a COPD exacerbation. Which laboratory value should the nurse monitor most closely?
o: Serum potassium
Serum sodium
Serum calcium
Serum magnesium
r: Systemic corticosteroids cause hypokalemia, which can trigger dysrhythmias with flattened or inverted T waves. Sodium is affected too, but steroids cause sodium and fluid retention with edema — the value that becomes dangerously low and arrhythmogenic is potassium.

q: A client is beginning a course of prednisone for COPD. Which of the following adverse effects should the nurse teach the client to report or monitor? Select all that apply.
o: Elevated blood glucose
Difficulty sleeping
Slow heart rate with weight loss
Swelling of the ankles and feet
Delayed wound healing
r: Corticosteroids delay wound healing and cause fluid retention with peripheral edema, insomnia, hyperglycemia, hypokalemia, and tachycardia. Bradycardia with weight loss is the opposite pattern — steroids classically produce weight gain and a faster heart rate.

q: A client on beclomethasone/formoterol for COPD maintenance says, "After each dose I rinse my mouth and swallow the water." What is the nurse's best response?
o: That is correct and helps the medication work longer
Rinse and then spit the water out to help prevent thrush
You should not rinse at all after using this inhaler
Use this inhaler only when you feel short of breath
r: The client must rinse and spit — swallowing the rinse water reintroduces the corticosteroid and does not protect against oral candidiasis. This is also a maintenance combination inhaler, so using it only for shortness of breath is a second error.

q: Which client with COPD should the nurse assess first?
o: A client with a chronic productive cough and an SpO2 of 90%
A client using pursed-lip breathing after walking to the bathroom
A client who is newly confused with an SpO2 of 84%
A client asking about the pneumococcal vaccine
r: New confusion with hypoxemia signals cerebral hypoxia and possible CO2 narcosis — a change in mental status is the red flag that demands immediate assessment. A chronic productive cough with an SpO2 of 90% is expected baseline for COPD, and pursed-lip breathing after exertion is a correctly performed technique.

q: A client is admitted with suspected active pulmonary tuberculosis. Which precaution should the nurse initiate?
o: Contact precautions with gown and gloves
Droplet precautions with a surgical mask
Standard precautions only until cultures return
Airborne precautions in a negative-pressure room
r: TB spreads by tiny droplet nuclei that remain suspended in air, so it requires airborne precautions in a negative-pressure room with an N95 for staff. Droplet precautions with a surgical mask are adequate for larger droplets such as influenza — they do not filter airborne particles.

q: A nurse is preparing to give a bed bath to an immobile client with active tuberculosis. Which of the following actions are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Wear gloves and a gown
Have the client wear an N95 respirator during transport off the unit
Wear an N95 particulate respirator
Remove the N95 after leaving the room
Place the client in a negative-pressure room
r: Staff wear an N95, gown, and gloves, the client stays in a negative-pressure room, and the respirator is removed after exiting so contaminated air is never inhaled inside the doorway. The client wears a surgical mask when leaving the room, not an N95 — the goal is to contain the client's droplets, not filter what the client breathes in.

q: A client received a Mantoux tuberculin skin test. How should the nurse read the result?
o: Measure the induration 48 to 72 hours after injection
Measure the area of redness immediately after injection
Measure the redness at 24 hours after injection
Ask the client to report any itching at the site
r: The Mantoux is read at 48-72 hours by measuring the induration — the palpable, raised, hardened area. Measuring erythema is the classic error; redness alone is not counted and would falsely inflate the result.

q: A client who is HIV positive has a Mantoux test with 6 mm of induration. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
o: Negative, because induration must be at least 10 mm
Positive, because the cutoff for high-risk clients is 5 mm
Negative, because induration must be at least 15 mm
Inconclusive; the test must be repeated in one week
r: For high-risk clients — HIV, immunosuppression, recent TB contact, or an abnormal chest x-ray — induration of 5 mm or more is positive. Applying the 10 mm or 15 mm cutoff to an immunosuppressed client would miss the diagnosis, because a weakened immune system mounts a smaller reaction.

q: A healthy 30-year-old office worker with no known risk factors has 12 mm of induration on a Mantoux test. How should the nurse interpret this?
o: Positive, and the client has active tuberculosis
Positive, because any induration over 10 mm is positive for everyone
Negative, because low-risk clients require 15 mm or more
Negative, because only erythema is measured
r: For clients with no risk factors, the cutoff is 15 mm, so 12 mm is negative. The 10 mm threshold applies to moderate-risk groups such as recent immigrants from high-prevalence countries, health care workers, injection drug users, and children under 5.

q: A client who received the BCG vaccine as a child needs TB screening. Which test is preferred?
o: A repeat Mantoux test in the opposite arm
A single sputum specimen for culture
A chest x-ray alone
An interferon-gamma release assay such as QuantiFERON
r: IGRA blood tests such as QuantiFERON and T-SPOT are preferred after BCG because prior vaccination causes a false-positive skin test. Repeating the Mantoux does not solve the problem — the vaccine-induced immune response will still produce induration.

q: A client's Mantoux test is read as positive. Which statement by the nurse is most accurate?
o: This means you have been exposed to TB; further testing is needed to see if the disease is active
This confirms that you have active tuberculosis right now
This means you are immune to tuberculosis
This means you are contagious and must stay isolated at home
r: A positive PPD shows an immune response to exposure — it is a screening test only and cannot distinguish latent from active disease. Confirming active TB requires a chest x-ray and sputum AFB testing, which is why telling the client they have active TB is wrong.

q: Which of the following findings would the nurse expect in a client with active pulmonary tuberculosis? Select all that apply.
o: Hemoptysis
Persistent cough lasting more than 3 weeks
Unintentional weight loss
Drenching night sweats
Sudden high fever of 104°F with rigors
r: Active TB produces a chronic picture: cough over 3 weeks, hemoptysis, night sweats, weight loss, fatigue, and a low-grade fever. A sudden spiking fever with rigors points toward acute bacterial pneumonia — TB is insidious and develops over weeks to months.

q: A client hospitalized with active TB has been on RIPE therapy for several weeks. Which finding indicates the client is no longer considered infectious?
o: The client reports feeling well and has gained weight
Three consecutive negative sputum acid-fast bacillus cultures
A repeat Mantoux test that is now negative
A normal white blood cell count
r: Infectiousness is determined by three consecutive negative sputum AFB cultures, not by how the client feels. The PPD will remain positive for life once a client has been sensitized, so it can never be used to show the infection has cleared.

q: A client starting rifampin for tuberculosis should be taught which of the following?
o: Your oral contraceptive will still be fully effective
Take an antacid with each dose to prevent nausea
Your urine, sweat, and tears may turn orange, and this is expected
Stop the drug if your skin looks yellow and restart when it clears
r: Rifampin turns body fluids orange — a harmless but alarming effect that also stains contact lenses. The contraceptive statement is false and clinically important: rifampin reduces the effectiveness of oral contraceptives, so an additional method is needed.

q: A client taking isoniazid reports nausea, right upper quadrant discomfort, and dark urine. What should the nurse do first?
o: Reassure the client that these are expected effects of the drug
Administer an antiemetic and continue the medication
Instruct the client to take the drug with a large meal
Hold the dose and notify the provider to evaluate liver function
r: These are signs of hepatotoxicity, isoniazid's most serious adverse effect, so the nurse holds the dose and notifies the provider for liver function testing. Calling them expected effects would allow ongoing liver injury — and this is why baseline LFTs are drawn before RIPE therapy begins.

q: A client on isoniazid is prescribed pyridoxine. The nurse explains that this vitamin is given to prevent which adverse effect?
o: Peripheral neuropathy
Optic neuritis
Orange body fluids
Elevated uric acid
r: Isoniazid interferes with pyridoxine metabolism, causing peripheral neuropathy — numbness and tingling in the hands and feet — which vitamin B6 prevents. Optic neuritis is the hallmark of ethambutol and is not prevented by B6, so pairing the two is the common mix-up.

q: A client taking ethambutol reports that colors look washed out and vision is blurry. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Reassure the client that this resolves with continued therapy
Notify the provider immediately; these findings suggest optic neuritis
Instruct the client to take the drug at bedtime instead
Administer an artificial tear solution
r: Ethambutol causes optic neuritis with decreased visual acuity and loss of red-green color discrimination, which must be reported at once because it can become permanent if the drug is continued. Reassuring the client that it will resolve is exactly wrong — the change is not expected and requires prompt evaluation.

q: A client on pyrazinamide reports a painful, swollen, red great toe. Which laboratory value should the nurse expect to be elevated?
o: Serum sodium
Serum potassium
Serum uric acid
Serum amylase
r: Pyrazinamide raises uric acid and can precipitate gout, which classically presents as an acutely painful, swollen great toe. It is also hepatotoxic, but that shows up as jaundice and elevated liver enzymes — not joint pain.

q: A nurse is reviewing RIPE therapy with a client newly diagnosed with active TB. Which of the following statements by the client indicate correct understanding? Select all that apply.
o: I will have blood drawn to check my liver during treatment
I will take vitamin B6 with my isoniazid
I will report any changes in my vision right away
I will take all four medications for at least six months
I can stop taking the medications once my cough goes away
r: RIPE runs 6-12 months with serial liver function monitoring, prompt reporting of vision changes (ethambutol), and B6 alongside isoniazid. Stopping when symptoms resolve is the classic adherence failure — symptoms improve long before the organism is eradicated, and stopping early breeds resistance.

q: A client with active TB has repeatedly missed clinic appointments and doses. Which intervention best promotes adherence?
o: Provide a written medication schedule and call weekly
Shorten the treatment course to three months
Reduce the number of drugs to make the regimen simpler
Arrange directly observed therapy
r: Directly observed therapy (DOT) has a health care worker watch the client swallow each dose, which is the proven strategy for nonadherent clients. Written schedules and phone calls help motivated clients but do not verify ingestion, and no nurse may shorten a regimen or drop drugs.

q: Before starting RIPE therapy, which baseline study is most important for the nurse to ensure has been obtained?
o: Liver function tests
Serum creatinine
Coagulation studies
Serum calcium
r: Multiple RIPE drugs — especially isoniazid, rifampin, and pyrazinamide — are hepatotoxic, so baseline LFTs are drawn and monitored throughout therapy. Renal function matters for many drugs, but hepatic injury is the specific and predictable risk of this regimen.

q: A tall, thin 19-year-old man suddenly develops sharp right-sided chest pain and dyspnea while sitting at his desk. Breath sounds are absent on the right. The nurse suspects which condition?
o: Hemothorax from blunt trauma
Spontaneous pneumothorax
Pleural effusion
Atelectasis
r: A spontaneous (simple) pneumothorax occurs without injury, classically in tall, thin young men, and produces sudden pleuritic pain with absent breath sounds on the affected side. A hemothorax follows trauma and adds signs of blood loss such as hypotension.

q: A client with blunt chest trauma has absent breath sounds on the left, severe dyspnea, hypotension, and the trachea deviated toward the right. What should the nurse do first?
o: Obtain a stat chest x-ray
Place the client in Trendelenburg position
Call for immediate assistance and prepare for needle decompression
Encourage slow deep breathing and reassess in 10 minutes
r: Tracheal deviation away from the affected side with hypotension is a tension pneumothorax — trapped air compresses the mediastinum and obstructs venous return, so needle decompression cannot wait. Waiting for the chest x-ray is the fatal delay: this is a clinical diagnosis treated before imaging.

q: Which of the following findings would the nurse expect in a client with a tension pneumothorax? Select all that apply.
o: Tracheal deviation toward the unaffected side
Hypotension
Severe dyspnea and tachycardia
Absent breath sounds on the affected side
Bilateral coarse crackles with pink frothy sputum
r: Rising pressure in the pleural space collapses the lung, shifts the mediastinum away from the affected side, and compresses the great vessels, producing hypotension, dyspnea, and tachycardia. Bilateral crackles with pink frothy sputum is pulmonary edema — a fluid problem in the alveoli, not trapped air in the pleural space.

q: A provider performs needle decompression for a tension pneumothorax. What should the nurse expect to occur?
o: The needle is left in place and sutured to the chest wall
The needle is withdrawn completely and the site is sealed airtight
The needle is used to instill sterile saline into the pleural space
The needle is removed and the catheter remains so trapped air can escape
r: After puncture, the needle is removed and the catheter stays, giving trapped air a route out and relieving mediastinal compression until a chest tube is placed. Sealing the site airtight would re-trap air and allow the tension to rebuild.

q: A client involved in a motor vehicle crash has dyspnea, rapid shallow breathing, tachycardia, hypotension, and diminished breath sounds on the right. Which condition should the nurse suspect?
o: Hemothorax
Simple pneumothorax
Asthma exacerbation
Atelectasis
r: A hemothorax is blood collecting in the pleural space, so the client shows both respiratory compromise and signs of blood loss — hypotension and tachycardia. A simple pneumothorax also causes diminished breath sounds, but it does not cause hypovolemia from bleeding.

q: A client has an open chest wound with air audibly moving in and out. What is the nurse's priority action?
o: Apply a sterile dressing sealed on all four sides
Apply a sterile occlusive dressing taped on three sides
Pack the wound with sterile gauze
Leave the wound open to air and notify the provider
r: Taping the occlusive dressing on three sides creates a flutter valve: air escapes on exhalation but cannot be sucked in on inhalation. Sealing all four sides traps air inside and can convert the injury into a tension pneumothorax.

q: A nurse palpates the chest wall around a client's chest tube insertion site and feels a crackling, popping sensation under the skin. How should the nurse document this finding?
o: Pleural friction rub
Pitting edema
Crepitus from subcutaneous emphysema
Tactile fremitus
r: Crepitus, or subcutaneous emphysema, is air leaking into the subcutaneous tissue and feels like crackling under the fingertips. A pleural friction rub is a sound heard with the stethoscope, not something felt on palpation — the discriminator is that crepitus is a tactile finding.

q: A nurse is teaching a nursing student about chest tubes. Which statement best describes their purpose?
o: To deliver medication directly into the lung tissue
To provide a route for supplemental oxygen
To measure the pressure inside the pulmonary artery
To restore negative intrapleural pressure by removing air, blood, fluid, or pus
r: A chest tube drains air (pneumothorax), blood (hemothorax), fluid (effusion), or pus (empyema) so the lung can re-expand under restored negative intrapleural pressure. It is a drainage device, not a medication or monitoring route.

q: A nurse observes gentle continuous bubbling in the suction control chamber of a wet chest drainage system. What action should the nurse take?
o: Nothing; this is the expected finding for that chamber
Clamp the tube and notify the provider
Turn off the wall suction immediately
Replace the entire drainage system
r: Gentle bubbling in the suction control chamber is normal and shows the prescribed suction level is being maintained. The chamber where continuous bubbling is abnormal is the water seal — students who confuse the two chambers create unnecessary alarm.

q: A nurse notes that the fluid in the water-seal chamber rises and falls with the client's respirations. How should the nurse interpret this?
o: An air leak is present in the system
This is tidaling, an expected finding
The lung has fully re-expanded
The tubing is obstructed
r: Tidaling is the normal fluctuation of the water-seal fluid with the pressure changes of breathing and confirms the system is patent. An air leak is signaled by continuous bubbling instead, and cessation of tidaling suggests either full lung re-expansion or an obstruction.

q: A client's chest tube system shows continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Clamp the chest tube near the insertion site
Increase the wall suction
Assess the tubing and connections from the client toward the drainage unit
Milk the tubing to clear an obstruction
r: Continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber means an air leak, and the most common cause is a loose connection, so the nurse assesses from the client toward the unit first. Clamping is the trap answer — it traps air in the pleural space and risks a tension pneumothorax.

q: A nurse finds no tidaling and no bubbling in the water-seal chamber of a client whose dyspnea is worsening. What is the priority action?
o: Document the finding as evidence the lung has re-expanded
Clamp the tube and transport the client to radiology
Disconnect the tube and flush it with sterile saline
Check the tubing for kinks, dependent loops, or obstruction
r: Loss of tidaling with worsening symptoms points to an obstruction, so the nurse checks for kinks, dependent loops, or clots and keeps tubing coiled flat on the bed. Documenting re-expansion is only reasonable when the client is improving; here the clinical picture contradicts it.

q: A chest tube is accidentally pulled out of a client's chest during repositioning. What should the nurse do first?
o: Cover the site with a sterile occlusive dressing taped on three sides
Reinsert the tube using sterile technique
Place the client in Trendelenburg position
Apply firm pressure over the site with a bare gloved hand
r: Cover the opening immediately with a sterile occlusive dressing taped on three sides so air can escape but cannot be drawn in, then notify the provider. Reinserting a chest tube is outside RN scope, and it wastes the seconds that matter.

q: A client's chest tube becomes disconnected from the drainage system. What should the nurse do?
o: Clamp the chest tube until a new system arrives
Submerge the end of the tube in sterile water while obtaining a new system
Reconnect the contaminated tubing and continue
Remove the chest tube and cover the site
r: Placing the tube end in sterile water re-establishes the water seal, letting air out while preventing it from entering the pleural space. Clamping is contraindicated — it seals air inside and can cause a tension pneumothorax.

q: A nursing student asks why chest tubes are almost never clamped. What is the nurse's best response?
o: Clamping increases the risk of infection at the insertion site
Clamping causes the drainage to become bloody
Clamping can trap air in the pleural space and cause a tension pneumothorax
Clamping makes tidaling impossible to assess accurately
r: With the tube clamped, air entering the pleural space has no way out, so pressure builds toward a tension pneumothorax. Brief clamping is permitted only for changing the drainage system or locating an air leak — never routinely, and never during transport.

q: Which of the following are appropriate nursing actions for a client with a chest tube? Select all that apply.
o: Keep the drainage system below the level of the client's chest
Coil the tubing flat on the bed to prevent dependent loops
Strip and milk the tubing every shift to maintain patency
Monitor the insertion site for redness and drainage
Tape all connections securely
r: Keeping the unit below chest level uses gravity to drain and prevents backflow; coiling tubing, taping connections, and monitoring the site are all standard. Stripping or milking is never routine — it generates extreme negative pressure that can damage lung tissue.

q: Which of the following chest tube findings should the nurse report to the provider immediately? Select all that apply.
o: Sudden bright red drainage
Continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber
Drainage greater than 100 mL per hour
Tidaling in the water-seal chamber with respirations
No drainage accompanied by worsening dyspnea
r: A sudden increase in output, bright red blood, an abrupt stop in drainage with worsening symptoms, and continuous water-seal bubbling all signal hemorrhage, obstruction, or an air leak. Tidaling is the one normal finding in this list — it confirms the system is working.

q: Which of the following are risk factors for lung cancer? Select all that apply.
o: Chronic exposure to industrial chemical fumes
Regular aerobic exercise
Asbestos and occupational dust exposure
Cigarette smoking
Second-hand smoke exposure
r: More than 85% of lung cancers are caused by cigarette smoke, with second-hand smoke and inhaled occupational agents such as asbestos, coal dust, and chemical fumes adding risk. Exercise is not a risk factor, and smoking cessation remains the single best prevention for both lung cancer and COPD progression.

q: A 62-year-old smoker reports a cough that has changed in character over 2 months, blood-streaked sputum, and hoarseness. Which action is most appropriate?
o: Reassure the client that this is typical smoker's cough
Recommend an over-the-counter cough suppressant
Advise the client to return if weight loss develops
Facilitate prompt evaluation with chest imaging, since these suggest possible lung cancer
r: A changing chronic cough, hemoptysis, and hoarseness in a smoker are early lung cancer signs requiring prompt workup with chest x-ray or CT. Waiting for weight loss is dangerous — lung cancer is usually diagnosed late, often after metastasis, which is why early signs must be pursued.

q: Which of the following findings in a client with known lung cancer suggest advanced or metastatic disease? Select all that apply.
o: New bone pain
Enlarged liver and lymph nodes
Neurologic changes such as confusion or seizures
Facial and upper extremity swelling with distended neck veins
A dry cough of two weeks' duration
r: Bone pain, neurologic changes, hepatomegaly with lymphadenopathy, and superior vena cava syndrome all indicate spread beyond the lung and shift the client to a higher stage. A recent dry cough is an early, local symptom and does not by itself imply metastasis.

q: Which statement about lung cancer types is accurate?
o: Small cell lung cancer is aggressive, strongly linked to smoking, and metastasizes early
Small cell lung cancer is the most common type and rarely spreads
Non-small cell lung cancer includes only squamous cell carcinoma
Non-small cell lung cancer is unrelated to tobacco exposure
r: Small cell lung cancer is aggressive, tightly tied to smoking, and spreads early, which is why it is usually treated systemically. Non-small cell is the more common group and includes adenocarcinoma, squamous cell, and large cell — not squamous cell alone.

q: A client returns to the unit after a right pneumonectomy. Which position is appropriate?
o: Left side-lying with the right lung up
On the right side or supine
Prone with the head turned to the left
Trendelenburg with both lungs dependent
r: After a pneumonectomy the client is positioned on the operative side or supine, which keeps the remaining lung free to expand and limits fluid shifting into it. Turning onto the unaffected side puts the good lung down and compresses the client's only functioning lung — the exact position to avoid.

q: Which of the following are nursing priorities for a client after a lobectomy? Select all that apply.
o: Keep the client on strict bed rest without repositioning for 48 hours
