r: A transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt reroutes blood around the diseased liver, lowering portal hypertension so ascites and varices improve. It does not remove scarring or cure cirrhosis, and shunting ammonia-rich blood past the liver can actually worsen encephalopathy.

q: Which precautions should the nurse implement for a client with cirrhosis and an INR of 2.4? Select all that apply.
o: Use a soft-bristled toothbrush
Apply prolonged pressure after venipuncture
Use an electric razor
Avoid IM injections when possible
Encourage vigorous flossing after every meal
Administer aspirin for comfort
r: The damaged liver makes fewer clotting factors, so PT and INR are prolonged and the client bleeds easily; soft brush, electric razor, prolonged pressure, and avoiding IM sticks all reduce that risk. Aspirin impairs platelets further and vigorous flossing causes gum bleeding.

q: Which finding in a client with cirrhosis is caused by portal hypertension?
o: Fetor hepaticus
Jaundice
Caput medusae
Palmar erythema
r: Caput medusae, the cluster of distended veins around the umbilicus, results directly from portal hypertension forcing blood into collateral vessels. Jaundice comes from elevated bilirubin and fetor hepaticus from unmetabolized compounds, not from portal pressure.

q: Which over-the-counter medication should the nurse teach a client with liver disease to avoid?
o: Docusate sodium
Loratadine
Calcium carbonate
Acetaminophen
r: Acetaminophen is metabolized by the liver and is directly hepatotoxic in liver disease, so it is avoided. This is the mirror image of kidney teaching, where the drug to avoid is the NSAID — keeping the two straight is the point of this question.

q: Which types of hepatitis are transmitted by the fecal-oral route?
o: A and E
B and C
C and D
B and D
r: Hepatitis A and E are spread fecal-oral through contaminated food, water, shellfish, or stool contact. B, C, and D are bloodborne, spread by blood and body fluids, which changes both the precautions and the teaching.

q: Which types of hepatitis are transmitted through blood and body fluids? Select all that apply.
o: Hepatitis B
Hepatitis C
Hepatitis D
Hepatitis A
Hepatitis E
r: B, C, and D are bloodborne, spread by needles, transfusions, sexual contact, and perinatally. A and E are fecal-oral, so hand hygiene and food and water safety are the prevention for those two.

q: A client is diagnosed with hepatitis D. Which additional infection must the nurse recognize the client also has?
o: Hepatitis A
Hepatitis B
Hepatitis C
Hepatitis E
r: Hepatitis D can only exist with hepatitis B, so preventing or vaccinating against B also prevents D. Hepatitis C is bloodborne as well, but it does not require a coexisting infection.

q: Which statement about hepatitis C should the nurse include in teaching?
o: It never becomes chronic
A vaccine is available and a three-dose series should be started before discharge
There is no vaccine, but it is often curable with direct-acting antivirals
It is spread mainly by contaminated water
r: There is no hepatitis C vaccine, yet the infection is frequently cured with direct-acting antivirals. Hep C is bloodborne, often becomes chronic, and carries the highest association with cirrhosis and liver cancer, which is why treatment matters.

q: Which statement by a client recovering from acute hepatitis A indicates effective infection-control teaching?
o: I can share utensils once I feel better
I can donate blood in 3 months
I will avoid alcohol for 2 weeks
My partner should receive the hepatitis A vaccine
r: Hepatitis A is fecal-oral, so vaccinating close contacts plus strict hand hygiene is the key prevention step. Alcohol should be avoided for 3 to 6 months, not 2 weeks, and the client cannot donate blood until testing is negative.

q: How should the nurse distinguish chronic from acute hepatitis?
o: Chronic hepatitis lasts longer than 6 months
Chronic hepatitis lasts less than 6 weeks
Chronic hepatitis never causes jaundice
Chronic hepatitis only occurs with hepatitis A
r: Hepatitis lasting more than 6 months is chronic and can progress to cirrhosis and liver cancer; acute hepatitis is sudden in onset and under 6 months. Hepatitis A is the one that essentially never becomes chronic.

q: A nurse is admitting a client who has hepatitis B with ascites. Which action should the nurse include in the plan of care?
o: Measure abdominal girth at the base of the ribcage
Provide a high-calorie, high-carbohydrate diet
Weigh the client weekly
Initiate contact precautions
r: A high-calorie, high-carbohydrate diet with moderate protein and fat rests the liver and supports regeneration. Girth is measured at the largest part of the abdomen and weights are taken daily, and hepatitis B requires standard precautions, not contact precautions.

q: A nurse reviews new orders for a client with severe acute hepatitis B and an INR of 2.0. Which orders require clarification? Select all that apply.
o: Vitamin K 10 mg IV
Acetaminophen 1 g PO every 6 hours
Lactulose 25 mL PO three times daily
Low-protein diet at 40 g per day
Neomycin 1 g PO every 6 hours
Entecavir 0.5 mg PO daily
r: Acetaminophen is hepatotoxic and must be questioned, and a low-protein diet is used only during acute encephalopathy — otherwise protein should be moderate to support healing. Vitamin K corrects the prolonged INR, and lactulose, neomycin, and entecavir are all appropriate for this client.

q: Which nursing actions reduce transmission of hepatitis C in a hemodialysis unit? Select all that apply.
o: Use dedicated dialyzers for HCV-positive clients
Perform meticulous environmental disinfection between treatments
Dispose of sharps immediately in a puncture-resistant container
Wear double gloves for all vascular access
Place HCV-positive clients in airborne isolation
r: Hepatitis C is bloodborne, so dedicated equipment, thorough disinfection between treatments, and immediate sharps disposal are what break transmission. Double gloving adds no protection, and airborne isolation is wrong because the virus is not transmitted through the air.

q: Which laboratory value is the most liver-specific indicator of hepatocellular injury?
o: Amylase
AST
ALT
Alkaline phosphatase
r: ALT is found primarily in hepatocytes, so an elevation points directly to liver cell injury. AST also rises with liver damage but is present in muscle and heart as well, which makes it less specific.

q: A client has an elevated alkaline phosphatase. Which condition should the nurse suspect?
o: Kidney failure
Pancreatic islet cell failure
Muscle injury
Biliary obstruction
r: ALP rises with bile duct obstruction such as gallstones or cholecystitis — a useful memory hook is that ALPs have stones and blocked passages. Muscle injury raises AST and CK, not alkaline phosphatase.

q: Which lab is often the first to rise with a biliary duct obstruction and is also useful for monitoring alcohol use and drug toxicity?
o: GGT
Albumin
Ammonia
Hemoglobin
r: GGT is specific to the hepatobiliary system and typically elevates earliest in duct obstruction, and it rises with alcohol and hepatotoxic drugs. Albumin reflects the liver's synthetic function over time and falls slowly rather than rising early.

q: A client with cirrhosis has an albumin of 2.1 g/dL. Which finding should the nurse expect?
o: Increased urine output
Ascites and peripheral edema
Hypertension and bounding pulses
Hyperglycemia
r: Albumin holds fluid inside the vessels, so when the damaged liver stops making it, fluid shifts into the tissues and peritoneum causing edema and ascites. This is why a low albumin, not a high one, predicts third spacing.

q: A client with hepatic dysfunction has a prolonged PT and elevated INR. Which nursing action is indicated?
o: Prepare to administer heparin
Encourage a high-fat diet
Implement bleeding precautions
Restrict fluids
r: The liver makes vitamin K-dependent clotting factors, so hepatic damage prolongs the PT and raises the INR, putting the client at risk for bleeding. Adding an anticoagulant such as heparin would compound an already dangerous bleeding risk.

q: A client is jaundiced. Which laboratory elevation explains this finding?
o: Alkaline phosphatase
Albumin
Ammonia
Bilirubin
r: Jaundice is caused by elevated bilirubin, which the damaged or obstructed liver cannot excrete. Elevated ammonia also indicates liver failure, but it causes encephalopathy and mental status change, not yellow skin.

q: Which substances are normally metabolized by the liver? Select all that apply.
o: Alcohol
Ammonia
Medications
Hormones
Carbon dioxide
r: The liver detoxifies alcohol, medications, and hormones and converts ammonia to urea. Carbon dioxide is a respiratory waste eliminated by the lungs, not the liver.

q: Which effects occur when bile production is impaired? Select all that apply.
o: Fat malabsorption
Steatorrhea
Vitamin K deficiency
Increased INR
Hypoglycemia
r: Bile emulsifies fat, so without it fat is malabsorbed, stools become fatty and greasy (steatorrhea), and the fat-soluble vitamins including K are not absorbed — raising the INR. Hypoglycemia is not a direct result of impaired bile flow.

q: Which findings suggest fat-soluble vitamin deficiency in a client with chronic liver disease? Select all that apply.
o: Easy bruising
Night blindness
Osteoporosis
Prolonged bleeding time
Glossitis
r: The fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E, and K: night blindness reflects low A, osteoporosis low D, and bruising with prolonged bleeding low K. Glossitis points to B-vitamin deficiency, which is water-soluble and not caused by fat malabsorption.

q: Which action should the nurse take immediately after a liver biopsy?
o: Position the client on the right side to apply pressure to the site
Ambulate the client in the hallway every hour to prevent respiratory complications
Encourage a high-fat meal
Position the client on the left side
r: Lying on the right side compresses the biopsy site against the chest wall and helps prevent hemorrhage, the main complication, and the INR is checked before and after. Ambulating immediately increases bleeding risk in a client who already has impaired clotting.

q: Which findings should the nurse recognize as the later, more liver-specific signs of hepatitis? Select all that apply.
o: Jaundice
Dark urine
Pruritus
Easy bruising and bleeding
Vague malaise and fatigue
Rhinorrhea and sore throat
r: Jaundice, dark urine, pruritus, and bleeding tendencies appear later and reflect true hepatocellular dysfunction and loss of clotting factors. Malaise, fatigue, and GI upset are the early, nonspecific signs that look like any viral illness, and upper respiratory symptoms are not part of hepatitis at all.

q: Which findings indicate that a client's cirrhosis has become decompensated? Select all that apply.
o: Jaundice
Ascites
Hepatic encephalopathy
Bleeding esophageal varices
Mild fatigue with a normal appetite
Mild right upper quadrant discomfort only
r: Decompensated cirrhosis is defined by the complications: jaundice, portal hypertension with ascites and varices, encephalopathy, and hepatorenal syndrome. Compensated cirrhosis looks deceptively mild — fatigue, poor appetite, and slight RUQ discomfort — which is why those two options do not belong.

q: Which dietary instructions should the nurse give a client with cirrhosis who is not currently encephalopathic? Select all that apply.
o: Eat a high-calorie, high-carbohydrate diet
Eat small, frequent meals
Limit sodium intake
Avoid all alcohol
Eat as much protein as you like at every meal
Follow a low-calorie diet to reduce liver workload
r: Resting the liver means high-calorie, high-carbohydrate nourishment in small frequent meals, with sodium restriction for ascites and complete alcohol avoidance. Protein stays moderate rather than unlimited, and a low-calorie diet starves a client who is already catabolic.

q: Which assessment is most important when a client is started on total parenteral nutrition?
o: Blood glucose
Bowel sounds
Skin turgor
Capillary refill
r: TPN is a highly concentrated dextrose solution, so blood glucose is checked every 4 hours and electrolytes at least daily; hyperglycemia is the most common complication of improper delivery. Bowel sounds matter for enteral feeding, but TPN bypasses the GI tract entirely.

q: A client's TPN bag is nearly empty and the next bag has not arrived from pharmacy. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Stop the infusion and flush the line with normal saline
Allow the bag to run dry and restart when the new bag arrives
Hang dextrose 10% in water as prescribed and notify pharmacy
Slow the infusion to a keep-vein-open rate of 5 mL/hr
r: TPN is never stopped abruptly or allowed to run out — the pancreas is still releasing insulin for a high-dextrose load, so a sudden stop causes rebound hypoglycemia. Hanging D10W as prescribed maintains the glucose supply until the next bag arrives; a backup bag should always be available.

q: How often should the TPN bag and tubing be changed?
o: Every 12 hours
Every 24 hours
Every 48 hours
Every 72 hours
r: The bag is changed — with the tubing — every 24 hours because the high-dextrose, high-protein solution is an excellent medium for bacterial growth. Hanging a bag longer to avoid waste is exactly how a central line infection starts.

q: Which statement describes correct administration of total parenteral nutrition?
o: It is infused by gravity through a peripheral IV
It may be given through a large-bore nasogastric tube
The rate may be increased to catch up if the infusion falls behind
It is infused through a central venous catheter using an infusion pump
r: TPN is hypertonic and would destroy a peripheral vein, so it requires a central venous catheter and must be delivered by infusion pump for an exact rate. Speeding up to catch up causes hyperglycemia and fluid overload — the rate is verified, never increased to make up lost volume.

q: Which actions are part of safe TPN administration? Select all that apply.
o: Check blood glucose every 4 hours
Monitor serum electrolytes at least daily
Keep a backup bag available so the solution never runs out
Abruptly discontinue the infusion if the client reports nausea
Administer the solution using an infusion pump
r: Safe TPN means glucose every 4 hours, daily electrolytes, a pump-controlled rate, and never letting the bag run dry. Abruptly stopping the infusion is the dangerous option — it produces rebound hypoglycemia; nausea is assessed and reported while the infusion continues as ordered.

q: A client has a functioning GI tract but cannot take food orally. Which form of nutrition support should the nurse anticipate?
o: Total parenteral nutrition through a central line
Peripheral parenteral nutrition
Enteral tube feeding
Intravenous fluids with dextrose only
r: If the gut works, use it — enteral feeding preserves gut integrity, costs less, and avoids central line and metabolic complications. Parenteral nutrition is reserved for clients who cannot use the GI tract, such as those with sepsis, major burns, or a nonfunctioning bowel.

q: A client receiving continuous nasogastric feedings is found lying flat in bed. What is the nurse's priority action?
o: Assess bowel sounds
Raise the head of the bed to at least 30 degrees
Stop the feeding and notify the provider
Check the gastric residual volume
r: A flat position with a running feed is an active aspiration risk, so the immediate correction is to elevate the head of the bed to 30–45 degrees. Checking residual is part of routine monitoring but does nothing about the formula currently pooling near the airway.

q: Before administering an intermittent enteral feeding, the nurse must first:
o: Flush the tube with 50 mL of air
Warm the formula in the microwave
Verify tube placement and check gastric residual volume
Position the client flat in bed to reduce the chance of reflux
r: Verifying placement and checking residual are the two safety checks that prevent instilling formula into the lung and detect delayed emptying. Placement is confirmed by x-ray initially and by aspirate pH (1–4) at the bedside; an air bolus is no longer considered a reliable check.

q: A client receiving enteral feedings reports nausea and abdominal cramping. What is the nurse's priority action?
o: Administer an antiemetic
Increase the feeding rate to finish sooner
Reposition the client onto the left side and continue the feeding
Pause the feeding and check the gastric residual volume
r: Nausea and cramping suggest intolerance or delayed gastric emptying, so the nurse pauses the feeding and measures residual volume before anything else — continued infusion into a full stomach risks aspiration. Medicating first treats the symptom while the underlying volume problem keeps building.

q: An older adult with dysphagia begins to choke while being fed thin liquids. What is the priority nursing intervention?
o: Suction the mouth and throat
Turn the client onto the left side
Stop feeding the client immediately
Apply oxygen at 2 L/min by nasal cannula
r: The first action is to stop the feeding and remove any remaining food, because continuing to deliver liquid into an unprotected airway makes aspiration worse. Suction and oxygen come after the source is stopped — you remove the threat to the airway before treating its effects.

q: Which macronutrient is the most calorie dense?
o: Carbohydrates
Proteins
Fats
Fiber
r: Fats supply 9 kcal/g, more than double the 4 kcal/g in carbohydrates and protein, and they also carry the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K. Carbohydrates are the primary energy source, which is a different concept from calorie density.

q: Which laboratory value best reflects a client's long-term protein status?
o: Hemoglobin
Albumin
Potassium
Sodium
r: Albumin is a protein made by the liver with a long half-life, so a low level reflects sustained protein malnutrition. Hemoglobin reflects oxygen-carrying capacity, and electrolytes shift with fluid status — none of these track protein stores over time.

q: Which nursing responsibilities apply to a client receiving enteral feedings? Select all that apply.
o: Verify tube placement before feeding
Keep the head of the bed elevated at least 30 degrees
Flush the tube to prevent clogging
Keep the client flat during and after the feeding
Provide routine oral and skin care
r: Enteral care centers on preventing aspiration and maintaining tube patency: verify placement, keep the head of bed at or above 30 degrees, flush routinely, and give oral care since the client is not eating. Lying flat is the one action that directly causes the complication these interventions exist to prevent.

q: Which interventions are appropriate for a client with dysphagia? Select all that apply.
o: Position the client in high Fowler's for meals
Teach the chin-tuck technique
Offer thin liquids to ease swallowing
Provide small bites
Minimize distractions during meals
r: Dysphagia care means upright positioning, chin tuck, small bites, and a quiet environment so the client can concentrate on swallowing. Thin liquids are the highest aspiration risk because they move fast and are hard to control — thickened liquids are used instead.

q: For which clients would the nurse anticipate enteral tube feeding? Select all that apply.
o: A client in a coma with a functioning GI tract
A client with head and neck trauma
A client with severe dysphagia after a stroke
A client with a paralytic ileus and a nonfunctioning GI tract
A client with an esophageal tumor
r: Enteral feeding is used when the GI tract works but oral intake is not possible — coma, head or neck trauma or tumors, severe dysphagia, and advanced dementia. A client with a nonfunctioning gut cannot absorb formula and needs parenteral nutrition instead; that distinction is the whole point of the question.

q: A client has a BMI of 42. How should the nurse classify this result?
o: Healthy weight
Class 1 obesity
Class 2 obesity
Class 3, or severe, obesity
r: A BMI greater than 40 is class 3 (severe) obesity, the range at which bariatric surgery is most often considered. Class 1 is 30–35 and class 2 is 35–40, while a healthy BMI is 18.5–24.9.

q: A client asks about the most common bariatric procedure, in which part of the stomach is removed. Which procedure is the nurse describing?
o: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass
Duodenal switch with ileal transposition
Adjustable gastric banding
Sleeve gastrectomy
r: Sleeve gastrectomy is the most common procedure; it is purely restrictive and removes the portion of stomach that secretes ghrelin, the hunger hormone, without creating malabsorption. Gastric bypass is both restrictive and malabsorptive, which is a different mechanism.

q: Which teaching is essential for a client who has had a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass?
o: Vitamin and mineral supplementation will be needed for life
Supplements can be stopped once weight loss stabilizes
No dietary restrictions are needed after 6 weeks
Fluids should be taken with every meal to aid digestion
r: Gastric bypass is restrictive and malabsorptive — bypassing the duodenum and part of the jejunum means iron, calcium, B12, and fat-soluble vitamins are poorly absorbed, so supplementation is lifelong. Drinking with meals is specifically discouraged because it accelerates gastric emptying and triggers dumping.

q: Which complications should the nurse monitor for after bariatric surgery? Select all that apply.
o: Hemorrhage
Venous thromboembolism
Bile reflux
Dumping syndrome
Chronic constipation from increased stomach capacity
r: Hemorrhage, VTE, bile reflux, dumping syndrome, and dysphagia are the expected postoperative complications, and anastomotic leak is the most feared. Stomach capacity is reduced, not increased, so the stated rationale for constipation is wrong.

q: On postoperative day 2 after a sleeve gastrectomy, a client has a heart rate of 128/min with mild abdominal pain and a temperature of 100.2 F. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Document the findings as expected postoperative changes
Notify the provider immediately about the unexplained tachycardia
Administer the prescribed as-needed analgesic and reassess in an hour
Encourage ambulation to relieve gas pain
r: Unexplained tachycardia after bariatric surgery is an anastomotic leak until proven otherwise and is a surgical emergency, so the provider is notified at once for a CT scan. Incisional pain, low-grade fever, and decreased bowel sounds alone are expected — it is the tachycardia that changes this picture.

q: Gastric contents have leaked into the peritoneal cavity of a postoperative bariatric client. Which findings should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
o: Fever
Severe abdominal pain
Tachycardia
Elevated white blood cell count
Increased bowel sounds with hunger
r: Leakage causes peritonitis — fever, abdominal pain, tachycardia, leukocytosis, and progression to sepsis — diagnosed by CT and treated with immediate surgery. Peritonitis produces diminished or absent bowel sounds, not hyperactive ones with an appetite.

q: A client asks why dumping syndrome happens after bariatric surgery. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
o: The stomach empties too slowly, so food ferments in the gastric pouch before moving on
The stomach produces too much acid after surgery
Food moves too rapidly from the small stomach into the intestine, pulling fluid with it
The intestine absorbs sugar too slowly, causing bloating
r: With little holding capacity, a hyperosmolar bolus dumps into the small intestine and draws fluid out of the vascular system, producing cramping, diarrhea, dizziness, and tachycardia. Delayed emptying is the opposite mechanism and does not explain the vasomotor symptoms.

q: Which findings should the nurse expect in a client experiencing dumping syndrome? Select all that apply.
o: Bradycardia with hypertension
Abdominal cramping
Diarrhea
Constipation relieved by eating
Dizziness after eating
r: The fluid shift into the bowel produces cramping, diarrhea, dizziness, diaphoresis, and tachycardia, usually 10–30 minutes after eating. Blood pressure falls and heart rate rises as intravascular volume drops, so bradycardia with hypertension is inconsistent.

q: A client reports weakness, sweating, and palpitations about 2 hours after eating. How should the nurse classify this?
o: An anastomotic leak
Bile reflux
Early dumping syndrome
Late dumping syndrome
r: Early dumping occurs 10–30 minutes after eating; late dumping occurs 1–3 hours after eating, when a reactive insulin surge drops the blood glucose. A leak presents with unexplained tachycardia, fever, and abdominal pain rather than symptoms tied to meal timing.

q: Which instructions should the nurse include to help a client prevent dumping syndrome? Select all that apply.
o: Eat small, frequent, dry meals
Drink fluids between meals rather than with meals
Choose higher-protein, lower-carbohydrate foods
Lie down or recline for 20 to 30 minutes after eating
Drink a large glass of juice with each meal
r: Small dry meals, fluids between rather than with meals, more protein with fewer simple carbohydrates, added fiber, and reclining after eating all slow gastric emptying and blunt the fluid shift. Juice with a meal is a concentrated carbohydrate load with fluid — the exact combination that triggers an episode.

q: A client 6 weeks after sleeve gastrectomy asks how large meals should be. Which response by the nurse is best?
o: Meals should be no larger than about 1 cup
Meals should be about 2 to 3 cups to prevent weight loss
Meal size does not matter as long as the food is soft
Three large meals daily are preferred over frequent small ones
r: The remaining stomach holds very little, so meals of about 1 cup or less prevent distension, vomiting, and dumping. Larger meals overfill the sleeve and are the most common cause of postoperative vomiting and pain.

q: Which finding in a client on the first postoperative day after gastric bypass requires the nurse to notify the provider?
o: Temperature of 100.0 F
Heart rate of 130/min with restlessness
Pain at the incision rated 4 out of 10
Decreased bowel sounds
r: Sustained, unexplained tachycardia with restlessness is the earliest sign of an anastomotic leak or hemorrhage and must be reported immediately. Incisional pain, diminished bowel sounds, and a low-grade temperature are all expected on the first postoperative day.

q: A nurse assesses a stoma created two days ago. Which finding requires immediate intervention?
o: Moist, reddish-pink stoma
A small amount of bleeding when the stoma is cleaned
Slight protrusion of the stoma above the skin
Dusky, bluish-colored stoma
r: A dusky, purple, or black stoma indicates ischemia — the blood supply is compromised and the provider must be notified immediately. Mild edema, slight protrusion, and a little bleeding with cleaning are expected in a new stoma because stomal tissue is highly vascular.

q: Which description characterizes a healthy stoma?
o: Pale pink and dry
Moist and pink to red
Dry and dark red-brown
Moist and grayish-purple
r: A healthy stoma is moist and pink to beefy red, reflecting good perfusion of vascular mucosal tissue. A dry, pale, dusky, or purple stoma signals impaired blood flow or dehydration of the tissue and must be reported.

q: Which stoma findings require the nurse to notify the provider? Select all that apply.
o: Black discoloration of the stoma
Stoma retracting below skin level
Beefy red, moist stoma
No output from an ileostomy for several hours with abdominal cramping
A small amount of serosanguineous drainage at the stoma edge
r: Black or dusky color signals necrosis, retraction below skin level threatens the seal and the bowel, and absent ileostomy output with cramping suggests obstruction — all require prompt reporting. A beefy red moist stoma and minor serosanguineous drainage are normal findings.

q: A client with a new ileostomy asks why the stool is liquid. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
o: "The colon absorbs most nutrients, so output stays thin."
"Water is absorbed in the colon, and an ileostomy bypasses the colon."
"Your stomach is not fully digesting your food yet."
"This means a postoperative complication has developed."
r: The large intestine reabsorbs water; an ileostomy exits from the small intestine and bypasses the colon entirely, so output is liquid and continuous. The colon does not absorb most nutrients — the small intestine does — and liquid output is expected, not a complication.

q: Which stool consistency should the nurse expect from a descending colostomy?
o: Liquid
Semi-liquid
Formed
Mucus only
r: The farther along the colon the stoma is, the more water has already been reabsorbed, so a descending colostomy produces formed stool. An ascending colostomy produces liquid output and a transverse colostomy produces soft, paste-like stool — location of the stoma is what determines consistency.

q: What is the most important ongoing assessment for a client with a new ileostomy?
o: Monitoring for dehydration and electrolyte imbalance
Monitoring for constipation
Assessing for absent bowel sounds in all four quadrants once each shift
Checking for excessive flatus
r: Ileostomy output is liquid and continuous, so the client loses large volumes of water and electrolytes and is at high risk for dehydration. Constipation is not a concern when the colon is bypassed, which is why that distractor can be eliminated on anatomy alone.

q: Which foods should the nurse teach a client with a new ileostomy to limit or avoid? Select all that apply.
o: Popcorn
Nuts and seeds
Raw carrots
White rice
Applesauce
r: High-insoluble-fiber foods such as popcorn, nuts, seeds, and raw carrots can form a food bolus obstruction at the narrow stoma outlet. White rice and applesauce are low-residue foods that are well tolerated; the teaching also includes limiting gas-forming and odor-producing foods.

q: A nurse notes liquid effluent leaking from beneath the ostomy wafer. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
o: This is an expected finding with a new stoma
No intervention is needed as long as the pouch is still attached to the wafer
Follow-up is required because the leaking effluent will damage the skin
The finding should be documented only
r: Leaking effluent is corrosive to peristomal skin, and skin breakdown is the primary complication of ostomy care — the wafer must be removed, the skin assessed, and a properly sized appliance applied. Documenting without acting allows a preventable wound to develop.

q: An ostomy pouch should be emptied when it is:
o: Completely full
Three-quarters full
Emptied once daily on a set schedule
One-third to one-half full
r: The pouch is emptied at one-third to one-half full; a heavier pouch pulls on the wafer and causes leakage and seal failure. Fixed daily schedules ignore how much output the client is actually producing, which varies with stoma location and diet.

q: Which technique does the nurse use when providing routine colostomy care?
o: Sterile technique with sterile gloves
Clean technique with clean gloves
Surgical asepsis with a sterile field
Sterile technique only during the first week
r: A stoma opens onto the colonized GI tract, so routine ostomy care uses clean technique, with soap and water and clean gloves. Sterile technique is reserved for entering sterile cavities such as the bladder or the lower airway.

q: During ostomy teaching, a client says, "I cannot look at it. This is too much for me right now." What is the nurse's best response?
o: Stop the session, acknowledge the client's feelings, and plan to revisit teaching later
Continue the teaching session as planned so that the client will be ready for discharge tomorrow
Ask a family member to learn the care instead
Leave written instructions and end the interaction
r: A client who is emotionally overwhelmed cannot absorb new information, so the nurse stops, acknowledges the feelings, and returns when the client is ready. Pushing on or handing the task to family bypasses the client's own adaptation and undermines eventual self-care.

q: In which position should the nurse place a client to administer a cleansing enema?
o: Supine
Right Sims'
Prone
Left Sims'
r: Left Sims' follows the natural anatomy of the descending and sigmoid colon, letting fluid flow in by gravity and be retained. Right-side or supine positioning works against the curve of the colon and causes the client to expel the solution early.

q: Before administering an enema to a client with a cardiac history, which assessment is essential?
o: Blood glucose
Deep tendon reflexes
Oxygen saturation
Pulse rate and rhythm
r: Rectal distention and straining stimulate the vagus nerve, which can cause bradycardia and is dangerous for a client with cardiac disease — a baseline pulse lets the nurse recognize the drop. Enemas are also never given with the client sitting on the toilet, because that angle risks rectal wall injury.

q: Which factors increase a client's risk for constipation? Select all that apply.
o: Low fiber intake
Opioid use
Immobility
Increased fluid intake
Habitually ignoring the urge to defecate
r: Constipation results from slowed peristalsis or dry stool — low fiber, opioids, immobility, and ignoring the urge all contribute. Opioids are the one to memorize: they slow GI motility rather than increase it. Adequate fluid intake prevents constipation.

q: Which findings suggest a fecal impaction? Select all that apply.
o: Oozing liquid stool
Abdominal distention
Nausea
Rectal fullness
Large formed stools passed daily
r: With impaction, only liquid stool seeps around the hardened mass, so the client also reports rectal fullness, distention, and nausea. The trap is charting the oozing liquid as diarrhea and giving an antidiarrheal, which worsens the impaction.

q: Untreated constipation can progress to which complication?
o: Chronic diarrhea
Electrolyte imbalance
Intestinal obstruction
Gastroesophageal reflux
r: Stool that continues to harden and accumulate can become an impaction and ultimately an intestinal obstruction, a surgical emergency. Electrolyte imbalance is the classic complication of diarrhea, where fluid and electrolytes are rapidly lost.

q: A post-operative client has a distended abdomen with no bowel sounds in any quadrant. What should the nurse suspect?
o: Gastroenteritis
Peritonitis
Irritable bowel syndrome
Paralytic ileus
r: Paralytic ileus — a temporary halt in peristalsis after anesthesia and abdominal surgery — presents with absent bowel sounds, distention, and no passage of stool or flatus. Gastroenteritis would produce hyperactive sounds and diarrhea, the opposite picture.

q: A client with a suspected paralytic ileus has been reported to the provider. Which intervention can the nurse perform without an order?
o: Insert a nasogastric tube to intermittent suction
Administer intravenous fluids
Encourage ambulation, maintain NPO status, and monitor intake and output
Encourage at least 3000 mL of oral fluids daily
r: Ambulation stimulates peristalsis, and maintaining NPO status with strict intake and output are independent nursing actions. NG insertion and IV fluids are invasive and require an order, and pushing oral fluids into a client who must stay NPO risks vomiting and aspiration.

q: Which diet is appropriate for a client during acute diarrhea?
o: High-fiber
Unrestricted regular diet
High-fat
Low-residue
r: A low-residue diet reduces stool bulk and slows transit, giving the irritated bowel time to recover. High-fiber diets are the treatment for constipation; adding fiber during acute diarrhea increases stool volume and worsens fluid and electrolyte loss.

q: Which factors influence a client's bowel elimination pattern? Select all that apply.
o: Fiber and fluid intake
Level of physical activity
Opioid and antibiotic use
Psychological stress
Eye color
r: Elimination is shaped by diet, fluids, activity, medications, stress, age, positioning, pregnancy, and surgery — stress commonly produces diarrhea while depression and immobility slow motility. These are the modifiable factors the nurse can actually target in a plan of care.

q: Which actions are correct when collecting a stool specimen? Select all that apply.
o: Have the client void before collecting the specimen
Place the labeled specimen in a biohazard bag
Avoid collecting stool that has fallen into the toilet water
Fill the specimen container to the top
Hold the specimen until the end of the shift before sending it
r: The client voids first so urine does not contaminate the sample, the specimen is transported in a labeled biohazard bag as potentially infectious, and toilet water contaminates and dilutes it. Overfilling the container and delaying transport both compromise results.

q: A nurse is performing an abdominal assessment. Which technique must be performed before palpation and percussion?
o: Auscultation
Deep palpation
Light percussion
Rectal examination
r: Auscultation is done before palpation and percussion because manipulating the abdomen stimulates the bowel and produces falsely altered bowel sounds. Inspection comes first overall, but the key sequencing rule to remember is listen before you touch.

q: A patient's BP is 182/118 mmHg with confusion, severe headache, and blurred vision. Which type of hypertensive emergency is this?
o: Hypertensive urgency — diastolic only elevated
Hypertensive urgency — no organ damage
Hypertensive emergency — acute target organ damage is occurring
Stage 2 hypertension — requires lifestyle change only
r: Hypertensive EMERGENCY = severely elevated BP WITH acute target organ damage (neuro, cardiac, renal). This patient has neurological symptoms (confusion) = emergency. Requires IV vasodilators, NOT oral meds.

q: The nurse is educating a client about their new lisinopril prescription. Which side effect is SPECIFIC to ACE inhibitors and should be reported?
o: Peripheral edema
Persistent dry cough
Reflex tachycardia
Hypokalemia
r: A persistent, dry, non-productive cough is the hallmark adverse effect of ACE inhibitors (-PRIL). It is caused by the accumulation of bradykinin. If intolerable, an ARB (-SARTAN) can be substituted — ARBs do NOT cause cough.

q: A client on metoprolol for hypertension has Type 2 diabetes. Which concern should the nurse prioritize regarding this combination?
o: Metoprolol causes hyperkalemia in diabetics
Beta blockers can mask signs of hypoglycemia
Beta blockers worsen diabetic neuropathy
Metoprolol is contraindicated in all diabetics
r: Beta blockers (especially non-selective) can MASK the signs of hypoglycemia (tachycardia, tremor) that diabetics rely on to detect low blood sugar. The nurse should teach the client to monitor glucose more frequently and watch for diaphoresis, which beta blockers do NOT suppress.

q: What is the PRIORITY goal when treating a hypertensive emergency with IV nitroprusside?
o: Normalize BP to less than 120/80 within 30 minutes
Reduce BP by 20–25% within the first hour, then gradually
Achieve a diastolic of less than 80 within 2 hours
Reduce systolic below 140 immediately
r: The goal in hypertensive emergency is to reduce MAP (mean arterial pressure) by 20–25% in the FIRST HOUR — NOT to normalize. Rapid reduction can cause ischemic stroke, MI, or acute renal failure due to hypoperfusion.

q: Which classification does a BP reading of 138/88 mmHg fall under?
o: Normal
Elevated
Stage 1 Hypertension
Stage 2 Hypertension
r: Stage 1 HTN = Systolic 130–139 OR Diastolic 80–89. This reading (138/88) fits Stage 1. Management includes lifestyle modifications and possibly medication depending on CV risk.

q: The nurse is caring for a client who is experiencing heart palpitations. Which interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care?
o: Have the client bear down as if for a bowel movement (Valsalva)
Ask the client to cough forcefully
Administer IV lidocaine immediately
Place client in Trendelenburg position
Obtain 12-lead ECG
r: Bearing down (Valsalva maneuver) and forceful coughing stimulate the vagus nerve, increasing parasympathetic tone and slowing the heart rate. A 12-lead ECG identifies the rhythm. Lidocaine is not first-line for palpitations without diagnosis; Trendelenburg is not recommended.

q: A client on hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) for hypertension reports muscle cramps and weakness. Which electrolyte should the nurse prioritize assessing?
o: Sodium
Potassium
Calcium
Magnesium
r: Thiazide and loop diuretics cause potassium WASTING (hypokalemia). Hypokalemia causes muscle weakness, cramping, and cardiac dysrhythmias. The nurse must check serum potassium and assess ECG.

q: Which antihypertensive medication should NEVER be stopped abruptly because of risk of severe rebound hypertension?
o: Amlodipine (CCB)
Clonidine (central alpha-2 agonist)
Lisinopril (ACEi)
Furosemide (loop diuretic)
r: Clonidine (and beta blockers) MUST NEVER be stopped abruptly — this causes severe rebound hypertension crisis. The dose should be tapered gradually. Same applies to beta blockers.

q: A client has chest pain that occurs during exercise and is relieved by rest and one sublingual nitroglycerin. The troponin is negative. What type of angina is this?
o: Unstable angina
Variant (Prinzmetal) angina
Stable (exertional) angina
NSTEMI
r: Stable angina is predictable, occurs with exertion, and is RELIEVED by rest or nitroglycerin within 15 minutes. Troponin is NORMAL. This is NOT an MI and does not indicate myocardial death.

q: Which statement by a client indicates understanding of CAD prevention teaching?
o: I will stop taking my statin when my cholesterol normalizes
I will follow a moderate exercise regimen
I only need to take aspirin when I have chest pain
High HDL levels increase my risk for CAD
r: Regular moderate exercise is a key modifiable risk factor for CAD prevention. Statins should not be stopped without provider guidance; aspirin for CAD prevention is daily; HIGH HDL is protective (good cholesterol), not a risk.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has CAD progressed to STEMI. Which procedure should the nurse anticipate?
o: Emergency CABG only
Heart catheterization and percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI)
Thrombolytics are always preferred over PCI
Synchronized cardioversion
r: For STEMI, the priority is PCI (cardiac catheterization with balloon angioplasty and stent) within 90 minutes of arrival ("door-to-balloon"). If PCI not available within 90 min, thrombolytics may be used.

q: A nurse is reinforcing teaching about modifiable risk factors for CAD. Which should be included?
o: High levels of stress
Diabetes mellitus
Family history of CAD
Hypertension
Hyperlipidemia
Age over 65
r: Stress, diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia are all MODIFIABLE risk factors for CAD. Family history and age are NON-modifiable (cannot be changed). Focus teaching on modifiable factors.

q: Which lipid panel result is most concerning for increased CAD risk?
o: Total cholesterol 185, HDL 62, LDL 95, TG 130
Total cholesterol 240, HDL 38, LDL 155, TG 200
Total cholesterol 195, HDL 58, LDL 110, TG 140
Total cholesterol 175, HDL 72, LDL 85, TG 100
r: Option B is most concerning: Total cholesterol 240 (should be <200), HDL 38 (should be >60 — low HDL is a risk), LDL 155 (should be <130 — elevated LDL = bad), TG 200 (should be <150). ALL values are unfavorable.

q: What is the primary nursing action when a client with stable angina reports chest pain during ambulation in the hallway?
o: Administer oxygen 2L NC immediately
Stop activity; have client sit down; check vital signs; obtain ECG
Call rapid response team immediately
Administer nitroglycerin SL right away before any assessment
r: Priority: STOP activity to reduce myocardial O2 demand. Have client sit/lie down. Assess pain (PQRSTU), obtain VS, then ECG. THEN administer NTG if ordered AND BP is adequate (>90 systolic). Do not give NTG first without assessment.

q: A stress test is performed for a client with stable CAD. The test is STOPPED early. What is the most appropriate reason?
o: Client reached 85% of target heart rate
Client reports chest pain during the test
Client becomes fatigued and wants to stop
The protocol only runs for 10 minutes
r: Chest pain (angina) during stress testing = POSITIVE test = indicates ischemia. The test must be STOPPED immediately. Other stopping criteria include: severe dyspnea, ST elevation, significant drop in BP, syncope, or dangerous arrhythmias.

q: A 62-year-old male has chest pain radiating to the left arm, diaphoresis, and nausea. VS: BP 156/92, HR 102, RR 22, SpO2 94%. ECG shows ST elevation. Which initial medication should the nurse administer?
o: Heparin 5000 units IV bolus
Metoprolol 20 mg PO
Aspirin 325 mg PO (chewed)
Furosemide 40 mg IV
r: ASPIRIN is the first-line INITIAL medication for suspected ACS/STEMI — it inhibits platelet aggregation and reduces thrombus formation immediately. It should be chewed for fastest absorption. Heparin, metoprolol, and furosemide may follow but are NOT the INITIAL first drug. Dose note: the accepted initial dose is 162 to 325 mg of non-enteric-coated aspirin, CHEWED so it is absorbed within minutes. Different sources print 160, 162, 300 or 325 mg; the tested points are aspirin first and chewed, not the exact number.

q: A client post-STEMI has troponin levels drawn every 6 hours. The nurse knows troponin remains elevated for how long after an MI?
o: 6–12 hours
24–48 hours
7–14 days
2–3 days
r: Troponin I and T remain elevated for 7–14 days after MI. This is why troponin is the GOLD STANDARD — it stays elevated longest. Initial rise: 3–6 hours; peaks: 12–24 hours; returns to normal: 7–14 days.

q: Which ECG finding is MOST specific for a STEMI?
o: T-wave inversion in 2 leads
ST depression in 2 contiguous leads
ST elevation in 2 or more contiguous leads
Prolonged QRS duration
r: ST ELEVATION in 2 or more contiguous leads is the hallmark of STEMI (full-thickness MI). ST depression or T-wave inversion indicates ischemia/NSTEMI. Wide QRS suggests bundle branch block or ventricular origin.

q: Nitroglycerin is CONTRAINDICATED in which MI patient?
o: Patient with anterior wall MI and BP of 130/80
Patient who took sildenafil (Viagra) 12 hours ago
Patient with hypertension and HR of 88
Patient with stable chest pain and SpO2 of 96%
r: Nitroglycerin is ABSOLUTELY contraindicated within 24–48 hours of PDE-5 inhibitor use (sildenafil/Viagra, tadalafil/Cialis, etc.) — the combination causes severe, potentially fatal hypotension. Also contraindicated if systolic BP <90 or right ventricular MI.

q: The nurse is monitoring a client after CABG surgery. Which chest tube drainage finding should be reported IMMEDIATELY to the provider?
o: 30 mL/hr over 2 hours
50 mL/hr, serosanguinous
150 mL/hr
180 mL/hr
r: Chest tube output >150 mL/hr after CABG is excessive and should be reported IMMEDIATELY. This may indicate hemorrhage from the graft or pericardium. The nurse should also monitor for cardiac tamponade (Beck's triad: JVD, hypotension, muffled heart sounds).

q: A nurse is collecting data from a client with CAD. Which manifestations require IMMEDIATE intervention?
o: Angina
Shortness of breath
Diaphoresis
Nausea
Stable blood pressure of 128/78
Mild ankle edema
r: Angina, dyspnea, diaphoresis, and nausea in a CAD patient are classic signs of ACS/impending MI and require IMMEDIATE intervention (ECG, aspirin, troponin, notify provider). Stable BP and mild ankle edema do not require immediate action in this context.

q: A nurse is interpreting an ECG strip and identifies: HR 75 bpm, regular rhythm, P wave before every QRS, PR interval 0.16 sec, QRS 0.08 sec. This rhythm is:
o: Sinus tachycardia
Normal sinus rhythm (NSR)
Sinus bradycardia
1st degree AV block
r: Normal Sinus Rhythm (NSR) criteria: HR 60–100 (75 ), regular (), P before every QRS (), PR 0.12–0.20 (0.16 ), QRS <0.12 (0.08 ). ALL criteria met = NSR. Perfect.

q: An ECG shows: HR 145 bpm, regular rhythm, P waves NOT identifiable, QRS 0.06 sec. What is this rhythm?
o: Ventricular tachycardia
Normal sinus rhythm
Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT)
Atrial fibrillation
r: SVT: regular, rapid rate (100–280), P waves hidden in preceding T wave or absent, NARROW QRS (supraventricular = above ventricles). VTach would have WIDE QRS. AFib would be IRREGULAR.

q: What does the P wave on an ECG represent?
o: Ventricular depolarization (contraction)
Ventricular repolarization (relaxation)
Atrial depolarization (contraction)
AV node delay
r: P wave = atrial depolarization = atria contracting. QRS = ventricular depolarization (contraction). T wave = ventricular repolarization. U wave (when visible) = after-depolarization.

q: What is the correct sequence for ECG rhythm interpretation?
o: P wave -> Rate -> Rhythm -> PR interval -> QRS
Rate -> Rhythm regularity -> P wave -> PR interval -> QRS -> T wave
QRS -> P wave -> Rate -> PR interval -> T wave
Rate -> QRS -> P wave -> T wave -> PR interval
r: The ATI/NCLEX standard sequence: 1-Rate, 2-Rhythm regularity, 3-P wave assessment, 4-PR interval, 5-QRS duration, 6-T wave/ST segment changes. Following this sequence prevents missing key findings.

q: A 6-second telemetry strip shows 9 QRS complexes. What is the heart rate?
o: 54 BPM
90 BPM
63 BPM
100 BPM
r: Count QRS complexes in 6-second strip × 10 = heart rate. 9 QRS × 10 = 90 BPM. This is within normal range (60–100 BPM).

q: The PR interval on a normal ECG represents:
o: Time for the SA node to fire
Ventricular depolarization through the myocardium
The delay in the AV node and atrial depolarization
Repolarization of the ventricles
r: The PR interval (0.12–0.20 sec) represents atrial depolarization + the delay at the AV node (allows atria to contract and fill ventricles before ventricular depolarization). Prolonged PR >0.20 = 1st degree AV block.

q: One large box on ECG paper represents how many seconds?
o: 0.04 sec
0.08 sec
0.12 sec
0.20 sec
r: One large box = 5 small boxes × 0.04 sec each = 0.20 sec. One small box = 0.04 sec. 30 large boxes = 6 seconds. 300 large boxes = 1 minute. These are essential for calculating rates and intervals.

q: A client has sinus bradycardia with HR 38 bpm, BP 80/50, and altered mental status. What is the FIRST pharmacological treatment?
o: Synchronized cardioversion
Amiodarone 300 mg IV
Atropine 0.5–1 mg IV
Epinephrine 1 mg IV
r: Symptomatic bradycardia (low BP, AMS = signs of decreased cardiac output) is treated FIRST with IV Atropine (0.5–1 mg, repeat q3–5 min, max 3 mg). If atropine fails -> Transcutaneous pacing -> Permanent pacemaker. Amiodarone is for tachyarrhythmias. Cardioversion is for tachyarrhythmias.

q: Which is the HALLMARK characteristic of atrial fibrillation on a rhythm strip?
o: Regular rhythm with tall peaked P waves
Sawtooth F waves at 240–360 per minute
Irregularly irregular rhythm with no discernible P waves
Wide bizarre QRS at rate >100
r: AFib hallmark: IRREGULARLY IRREGULAR rhythm + ABSENT P waves (replaced by chaotic fibrillatory baseline). The ventricular response is irregular. Sawtooth = Atrial flutter. Wide bizarre QRS = VTach. Regular with peaked P = some SVTs.

q: A client in AFib asks why they need to take warfarin. The best nurse response is:
o: Warfarin will convert your heart back to normal rhythm
Warfarin prevents blood clots that can cause stroke because the atria are not contracting effectively
Warfarin strengthens the heart muscle
Warfarin controls your heart rate during atrial fibrillation
r: In AFib, the atria quiver rather than contracting effectively. Blood pools in the atria -> clots form -> clot can travel to brain = STROKE. Anticoagulants (warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban) prevent this. Warfarin does NOT control rate or rhythm.

q: The nurse is preparing for synchronized cardioversion for a client in AFib. Which assessment is MOST important BEFORE the procedure?
o: Check sodium level
Verify anticoagulation status (has patient been on anticoagulants?)
Assess for peripheral edema
Measure CVP
r: Before elective cardioversion for AFib, the client MUST be anticoagulated for at least 3 weeks (or TEE performed to rule out atrial clot). If cardioversion is performed without anticoagulation, the clot in the atrium can be thrown -> STROKE. This is a life-or-death assessment.

q: A client on a telemetry unit suddenly becomes unresponsive, has no pulse, and the monitor shows a chaotic waveform. What is the IMMEDIATE nursing action?
o: Call the provider and await orders
Initiate synchronized cardioversion at 100 joules
Begin CPR and call for defibrillator (VFib protocol)
Administer IV atropine and prepare pacing
r: Chaotic waveform + pulseless = VENTRICULAR FIBRILLATION. This is cardiac arrest. IMMEDIATE CPR + defibrillation (unsynchronized) is the ONLY treatment. Do NOT waste time calling provider first — initiate code blue and DEFIB immediately.

q: Which dysrhythmia is treated with DEFIBRILLATION (NOT cardioversion)?
o: AFib with rapid ventricular rate (stable)
SVT not responding to adenosine
Ventricular fibrillation (VFib)
Atrial flutter with 2:1 block
r: Defibrillation (unsynchronized) is for PULSELESS rhythms: VFib and pulseless VTach. Cardioversion (synchronized) is for rhythms WITH a pulse: AFib, VTach with pulse, SVT, atrial flutter. Remember: VFib = chaotic = no QRS to sync to = must defibrillate.

q: Atropine is contraindicated in which dysrhythmia?
o: Symptomatic sinus bradycardia
3rd degree AV block in a symptomatic patient
Ventricular fibrillation
1st degree AV block with HR 50 and hypotension
r: VFib requires DEFIBRILLATION — there is no cardiac conduction to accelerate with atropine. Atropine is used for bradycardias. Asystole is also treated with epinephrine (not just atropine). Atropine works by blocking vagal tone.

q: A client has a pacemaker set at 70 BPM. The telemetry shows: pacing spike, then a wide QRS, HR 70, regular. What does this indicate?
o: Pacemaker failure to sense
Pacemaker capture — device is working correctly
VTach with pacemaker artifact
Malfunction requiring immediate intervention
r: Pacemaker CAPTURE = the pacing stimulus (spike) successfully generates a cardiac depolarization (followed by a QRS complex). This is what we want to see — it means the pacemaker is working correctly. Wide QRS after ventricular pacing spike is expected.

q: A patient with an ICD reports feeling a "blow to the chest" once while walking to the kitchen. What is the most appropriate nursing action?
o: Reassure patient — occasional shocks mean the device is working perfectly and require no follow-up
Notify the provider because the ICD delivered a shock, indicating a dangerous rhythm occurred
Prepare for immediate defibrillation — the ICD malfunctioned
Assume it was muscle spasm and document normally
r: Any ICD shock means the device detected a life-threatening rhythm (VFib or VTach) and fired to terminate it. This must be REPORTED to the provider IMMEDIATELY and the patient assessed. The cause of the event must be investigated. Multiple shocks in a short period = emergency.

q: A client with a permanent pacemaker begins hiccupping continuously every second. What does the nurse SUSPECT?
o: Normal post-operative finding — reassure patient
Client needs a respiratory treatment
The pacemaker generator may be stimulating the diaphragm — lead displacement
This is a side effect of anesthesia — will resolve on its own
r: Continuous hiccups after pacemaker insertion indicate the lead may have migrated and is now pacing the DIAPHRAGM instead of the heart. This must be reported to the provider immediately and confirmed with chest X-ray and ECG.

q: Which is the CORRECT description of asystole on a rhythm strip?
o: Chaotic, irregular waves with no identifiable complexes
Wide QRS complexes at rate >100 with no P waves
Absence of all electrical activity — flat line confirmed in 2 leads
Sawtooth baseline at 300 per minute
r: Asystole = no cardiac electrical activity = flat line. It must be confirmed in 2 leads to rule out fine VFib. Treatment: CPR + Epinephrine. NO defibrillation (nothing to shock). Chaotic = VFib; Wide rapid = VTach; Sawtooth = Atrial flutter.

q: A nurse is reinforcing discharge teaching for a client with AFib about preventing complications. Which should be included?
o: Avoid over-the-counter decongestants
Stop anticoagulants if you feel okay
Report any unusual bruising or bleeding while on anticoagulants
Monitor for signs of stroke (facial droop, arm weakness, speech difficulty)
Decongestants and stimulants can trigger AFib
r: OTC decongestants (pseudoephedrine) and stimulants can trigger AFib episodes. Clients must monitor for stroke signs (face, arms, speech). Report bleeding on anticoagulants. NEVER stop anticoagulants without provider guidance — high stroke risk.

q: Which ECG finding differentiates 1st degree AV block from normal sinus rhythm?
o: Irregular R-to-R interval
PR interval greater than 0.20 seconds
Presence of wide QRS complex
Absent P waves before QRS
r: 1st degree AV block = all criteria of NSR EXCEPT the PR interval is PROLONGED >0.20 sec (>5 small boxes). All P waves still conduct (1:1 ratio). Rate and QRS are normal. No treatment needed — just monitor.

q: Which is the most DANGEROUS type of second-degree AV block that can rapidly progress to complete heart block?
o: Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach)
1st degree AV block
Mobitz Type II
Junctional rhythm
r: Mobitz Type II (2nd degree type II) is DANGEROUS — it can suddenly progress to complete (3rd degree) heart block or asystole without warning. Requires PACEMAKER. Wenckebach (Mobitz I) rarely progresses and often resolves on its own.

q: A nurse is assessing post-op nursing care for a client with a newly inserted permanent pacemaker. Which actions are appropriate?
o: Obtain chest X-ray to assess lead placement and rule out pneumothorax
Continue monitoring for hiccups that may indicate diaphragm pacing
Allow full range of motion on the affected arm immediately
Assess incision site for bleeding or hematoma
Monitor cardiac rhythm continuously
r: Chest X-ray confirms lead placement and rules out pneumothorax. Hiccups may indicate lead displacement and diaphragm pacing. Incision monitoring for complications is routine. Continuous cardiac monitoring ensures pacemaker function. Arm should be LIMITED in motion (~2 weeks) to prevent lead displacement — NOT full ROM immediately.

q: The nurse is reviewing a client's cardiac history. Which client has the HIGHEST priority for ICD placement?
o: Client with controlled HTN and stable angina
Client who survived out-of-hospital VFib cardiac arrest
Client with 1st degree AV block on beta blockers
Client with occasional PACs (premature atrial contractions)
r: Survivors of VFib (or hemodynamically significant VTach) are at extremely HIGH risk for sudden cardiac death recurrence. ICD is indicated. The ICD will detect and terminate future lethal arrhythmias automatically. This is a life-saving intervention.

q: A client with heart failure has BNP of 850 pg/mL. What does this indicate?
o: Normal finding — no concern
Significant cardiac stress; heart chambers are stretched; likely worsening heart failure
Indicates MI has occurred
Elevated BNP means the kidneys are failing
r: BNP (B-type natriuretic peptide) is released by heart chambers when they are STRETCHED (volume overload). Normal <100 pg/mL. BNP 850 indicates significant cardiac stress and is consistent with worsening heart failure. Used to diagnose and monitor treatment effectiveness.

q: A nurse reviewing a client's ECG notes the PR interval progressively lengthens with each beat until a QRS is dropped, then the pattern repeats. This rhythm is:
o: 3rd degree (complete) heart block
2nd degree Mobitz Type II
2nd degree Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach)
1st degree AV block
r: Wenckebach (2nd degree Type I): PR interval progressively lengthens beat by beat UNTIL a QRS is dropped (P wave with no QRS), then resets and the pattern repeats. This is a cyclic pattern. Treat underlying cause; rarely progresses to complete block.

q: What does "Levine's sign" (clutching chest with fist) during assessment suggest?
o: Anxiety attack
Classic presentation of myocardial ischemia or infarction
Musculoskeletal chest pain
Esophageal spasm
r: Levine's sign (clutching chest with clenched fist) is a classic nonverbal sign associated with myocardial ischemia/infarction. It suggests the substernal, crushing, pressure-like quality of cardiac chest pain. Treat as suspected MI until proven otherwise.

q: An ABI (ankle-brachial index) of 0.7 indicates:
o: Normal arterial circulation
Mild peripheral arterial disease
Significant peripheral arterial disease requiring intervention
Venous insufficiency
r: ABI interpretation: ≥1.0 = Normal; 0.9–0.99 = borderline; 0.7–0.89 = Mild PAD; 0.4–0.69 = Moderate PAD (requires workup); <0.4 = Severe PAD (limb-threatening). ABI 0.7 = mild/moderate PAD. Cause is atherosclerosis in peripheral arteries.

q: A nurse is caring for a client newly diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy. Which teaching should be included?
o: Weigh yourself daily at the same time in similar clothing
Restrict fluid intake to approximately 2L/day
Report weight gain of 2 lbs in a day or 5 lbs in a week
Continue normal alcohol consumption — it does not affect the heart
Take medications only when symptoms appear
Monitor for increased shortness of breath
r: Daily weight monitoring, fluid restriction, reporting rapid weight gain (fluid accumulation), and monitoring dyspnea are all correct teaching points for dilated cardiomyopathy/heart failure. Alcohol worsens cardiomyopathy (is often a cause). Medications must be taken regularly (chronic condition), NOT just when symptomatic.

q: Which client is at HIGHEST risk for developing infective endocarditis?
o: 60-year-old with controlled HTN
35-year-old IV drug user with a history of tricuspid valve repair
45-year-old with type 2 diabetes well-controlled
55-year-old with chronic venous insufficiency
r: IV drug users are at HIGHEST risk for infective endocarditis because bacteria enter the venous system directly and settle on heart valves, particularly the tricuspid valve (right-sided endocarditis). Prior valve damage also significantly increases risk.

q: Beck's Triad is the classic presentation of which cardiac emergency?
o: Myocardial infarction
Cardiac tamponade
Tension pneumothorax
Hypertensive crisis
r: Beck's Triad = Cardiac TAMPONADE: JVD (elevated venous pressure) + Muffled heart sounds (fluid around heart) + Hypotension (decreased cardiac output). Treatment: pericardiocentesis (needle aspiration of pericardial fluid). This is a life-threatening emergency.

q: A nurse is caring for a client with dilated cardiomyopathy. Which interventions are appropriate?
o: Prepare client for insertion of left ventricular assistive device (LVAD)
Increase O2 to 4L/min via nasal cannula
Administer furosemide 80 mg IV push
Encourage vigorous exercise to strengthen the heart
Restrict sodium and fluid intake
r: LVAD may be needed for severe ventricular dysfunction. Oxygen for hypoxia is appropriate. IV furosemide treats fluid overload/pulmonary congestion. Sodium/fluid restriction reduces cardiac workload. Vigorous exercise is contraindicated in dilated cardiomyopathy — it increases myocardial oxygen demand.

q: A client with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) asks what caused their condition. The best nurse response is:
o: Your condition was caused by viral infection of the heart muscle
Your heart condition is caused by thickening of the ventricular walls and septum
Your condition is caused by alcohol use and will improve if you stop drinking
Your heart muscle stretched and thinned due to heart failure
r: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) = thickening (hypertrophy) of the ventricular walls and interventricular septum — usually hereditary (autosomal dominant). This is the #1 cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes. The thickening obstructs blood outflow and prevents proper filling.

q: A nurse is reviewing history for a client with heart failure. Which conditions contribute to heart failure?
o: Thyrotoxicosis (hyperthyroidism)
Anemia
Hypertension
Thiamine deficiency
Controlled Type 2 diabetes with normal A1C
r: Thyrotoxicosis (increased metabolic demand), anemia (decreased O2 delivery = compensatory increased HR), hypertension (increased afterload), and thiamine deficiency (B1 deficiency = wet beriberi heart failure) all cause or contribute to heart failure. Well-controlled diabetes alone does not directly cause HF, though uncontrolled DM can.

q: A client is taking digoxin for heart failure and AFib. Which finding should the nurse hold the digoxin and notify the provider?
o: HR 68 bpm, regular
Potassium 3.8 mEq/L
HR 52 bpm, with nausea and visual changes
BP 118/74 mmHg
r: Digoxin toxicity signs: bradycardia (<60), nausea/vomiting, visual changes (yellow-green halos), dysrhythmias. HR 52 + GI symptoms + visual changes = HOLD digoxin, notify provider, check digoxin level and potassium. Hypokalemia increases digoxin toxicity risk.

q: A client with AFib is on warfarin. Which lab value monitors therapeutic warfarin levels?
o: aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time)
INR (International Normalized Ratio)
Platelet count
Hemoglobin and hematocrit
r: INR (International Normalized Ratio) monitors WARFARIN therapy. Therapeutic INR for AFib = 2.0–3.0. aPTT monitors HEPARIN therapy. Platelet count monitors for thrombocytopenia (HIT with heparin). Both INR and INR are related to prothrombin time (PT).

q: A client on heparin drip has an aPTT result of 120 seconds. The normal aPTT is 25–35 seconds. What should the nurse do FIRST?
o: Increase heparin rate — aPTT needs to be higher
Administer protamine sulfate immediately without assessment
Assess the client for signs of bleeding, then notify provider
Continue infusion — 120 seconds is within the target range for therapeutic anticoagulation
r: Supratherapeutic aPTT indicates over-anticoagulation -> bleeding risk. Therapeutic aPTT for heparin = 60–100 seconds (1.5–2.5× normal). aPTT 120 = too high. FIRST: assess for bleeding (urine, stools, gums, neuro). Then notify provider — may need to decrease or hold heparin. Protamine sulfate = antidote for heparin overdose, but requires order.

q: Which statement about the difference between metoprolol and carvedilol is accurate?
o: Both are selective beta-1 blockers
Metoprolol is cardioselective (beta-1); carvedilol blocks both beta-1, beta-2, AND alpha-1
Carvedilol is used for tachycardia only; metoprolol is for HTN only
Both are first-line for asthma patients with HTN
r: Metoprolol = SELECTIVE beta-1 blocker (heart only — "1 heart"). Carvedilol = non-selective beta blocker (beta-1, beta-2) + alpha-1 blocker = more complete heart failure treatment. Non-selective beta blockers should be AVOIDED in asthma/COPD (block beta-2 = bronchospasm).

q: A client on clopidogrel (Plavix) after stent placement asks if they can stop taking it because they feel fine. What is the MOST important teaching?
o: Yes, if you feel fine for 3 months you can stop taking it
You may stop after 6 months as the stent should be stable by then
Never stop antiplatelet therapy without cardiology approval — risk of sudden stent thrombosis (heart attack)
Stopping and restarting is fine as needed
r: Drug-eluting stents REQUIRE dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel) for at least 12 months after placement to prevent in-stent thrombosis. STOPPING abruptly can cause ACUTE STENT THROMBOSIS — a life-threatening event. This is a critical safety teaching.

q: A nurse is preparing to administer medications to a client with peripheral artery disease (PAD). Which medications should the nurse anticipate?
o: Cilostazol (Pletal)
Pentoxifylline
Metoprolol
Warfarin for routine PAD
Aspirin
r: Cilostazol and pentoxifylline improve blood flow and reduce claudication in PAD. Aspirin is used as antiplatelet therapy to prevent arterial clotting. Metoprolol (beta blocker) can be used but must be used carefully in PAD (can reduce peripheral circulation). Warfarin is not typically used for routine PAD (venous anticoagulant).

q: CASE: A 49-year-old male presents to ED with BP 198/102, HR 106, severe headache, blurred vision, nausea, and not taking prescribed HTN medications. What is the PRIORITY nursing action?
o: Provide education about medication compliance immediately
Insert IV access and prepare for IV antihypertensive therapy
Administer oral antihypertensive and monitor for 2 hours
Obtain a 12-lead ECG only
r: This is a hypertensive EMERGENCY (BP 198/102 + neurological symptoms). PRIORITY = IV access for IV vasodilator therapy. Then: continuous BP monitoring q5 min, cardiac monitoring, neuro assessment, labs. Education after stabilization. A 12-lead ECG is part of workup but IV access is first priority.

q: CASE: A client with atrial fibrillation arrives with HR 145, BP 115/75, crackles bilaterally, SpO2 95%, irregular rhythm. A pulse deficit is noted. What should the nurse prioritize FIRST?
o: Synchronized cardioversion immediately without any other assessment
Place on cardiac monitor, administer O2 if SpO2 drops, establish IV access, and notify provider
Administer digoxin to slow the rate immediately without order
Defibrillate at 200 joules for rapid AFib
r: First priority: Monitoring, oxygenation, IV access, and provider notification. Cardioversion may be needed but requires provider order, anticoagulation assessment, and sedation preparation. Defibrillation is WRONG for AFib with a pulse (AFib needs SYNCHRONIZED cardioversion). Digoxin requires an order.

q: CASE: After synchronized cardioversion for AFib, the client converts to NSR. Which assessment is MOST critical in the next 30 minutes?
o: Temperature and urinalysis
Neurological status — watch for signs of stroke
Check for peripheral edema
Measure CVP
r: After cardioversion, a clot from the atrium may be dislodged -> stroke. Neurological assessment is CRITICAL in the immediate post-cardioversion period. Signs of stroke: facial droop, arm weakness, speech changes (FAST). Also monitor rhythm, BP, and oxygen saturation.

q: A nurse is reinforcing discharge teaching for a client with a newly implanted ICD. Which statement by the client indicates understanding?
o: I should feel an occasional mild shock — this means the device is functioning correctly
I will need weekly clinic visits for the first month after implant
I will attend scheduled follow-ups and the device can be monitored remotely
If I feel nothing from the device, it means it is working fine
r: ICDs are monitored via remote monitoring (Medtronic CareLink, etc.) and scheduled clinic visits. A shock = dangerous rhythm was detected (NOT normal function). Feeling no shock is expected during normal sinus rhythm — the ICD only fires when detecting VF/VT.

q: A client asks why they feel a "tingling" when they touch a friend who has an ICD and the device fires. What is the correct explanation?
o: The friend's ICD is malfunctioning
The shock energy from an ICD can be felt by bystanders as a small tingle — not harmful
The bystander is having a cardiac event
Direct contact with ICD patients during firing is dangerous and should be avoided
r: Anyone touching an ICD patient when the device fires may feel a small electrical impulse (tingling). This is NOT harmful to the bystander. The ICD can fire while being touched — bystanders do NOT need to step away. This is important client and family teaching.

q: A nurse is evaluating outcomes after ICD implantation. Which assessment finding indicates the ICD is successfully controlling the dysrhythmia?
o: Sustained VTach on the monitor for 45 seconds before converting
Continuous sinus rhythm with no shocks delivered
Patient reports frequent "kicking" in the chest from shocks
aPTT is supratherapeutic
r: Successful ICD function = prevention of sustained lethal arrhythmias. Continuous sinus rhythm without shocks = optimal outcome. Frequent shocks = ICD is firing repeatedly to terminate recurring dangerous rhythms — provider must investigate the cause.

q: Which statement correctly explains the mechanism of a stress test?
o: The test measures intracardiac pressures directly via catheter
The test evaluates how well the heart functions under increased oxygen demand to identify ischemia
The test is used only for clients who have already had an MI
Nuclear tracers in stress tests are radioactive and require radiation isolation for 1 week
r: Stress testing evaluates how well the heart responds to INCREASED metabolic demand (exercise or pharmacologic stress). Ischemia or reduced blood flow becomes apparent under stress. Normal resting ECG may mask CAD that only becomes apparent with increased demand. Nuclear tracers used are low-dose and do not require isolation.

q: A nurse cares for a client with pericarditis. Which lab tests will have ABNORMAL results?
o: C-reactive protein (CRP)
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
White blood cell count (WBC)
Fasting glucose
Lipid panel
r: Pericarditis = inflammation of the pericardium. CRP and ESR are inflammatory markers — ELEVATED. WBC elevated = infection/inflammation. Glucose and lipid panel are unrelated to acute pericarditis.

q: Discharge teaching for cardiomyopathy should include which instructions?
o: Restrict fluids to approximately 2L per day
Limit dietary sodium intake
Check weight every morning
Report ankle edema
Take medications only when you have symptoms
r: Cardiomyopathy/HF: fluid restriction (~2L/day), low-Na diet, daily AM weights (detect early fluid gain), report ankle edema (early fluid overload sign). Medications MUST be taken daily on schedule — NOT only when symptomatic.

q: A client with valvular dysfunction says "I get short of breath when I make my bed." What does this indicate to the nurse?
o: Normal aging process — no concern
Valvular dysfunction is affecting ADLs
Anxiety about their diagnosis
Respiratory infection unrelated to cardiac issue
r: Dyspnea with minimal ADL exertion (making a bed) = valvular dysfunction significantly impacting function. The heart cannot meet even low-level oxygen demand. This is a priority clinical finding requiring documentation and provider notification.

q: A client with chronic venous disease asks why their legs swell and feel heavy. The BEST nurse response:
o: "Your arteries are blocked, reducing blood to your legs"
"Your heart is too weak to pump effectively"
"Damaged veins cause blood to pool in your legs instead of returning to the heart"
"Your kidneys are not filtering excess fluid"
r: Chronic venous disease = damaged venous valves -> blood pools (venous stasis) in legs instead of returning to heart against gravity -> swelling, heaviness. This is a VENOUS RETURN problem, not arterial delivery or heart pump failure.

q: Which is the priority home safety teaching for a client discharged with oxygen therapy for heart failure?
o: Change the nasal cannula weekly
Maintain at least 6 feet between oxygen equipment and any open flame
Extension cords are acceptable for the concentrator
Smoking outdoors while connected to oxygen tubing is safe
r: Oxygen dramatically accelerates combustion. Safety: maintain 6 FEET from open flames (candles, gas stoves, cigarettes). Smoking while on oxygen has caused fatal fires. This is the #1 home safety priority for oxygen users.

q: A client with acute pericarditis will likely exhibit which manifestations?
o: Sharp chest pain — worse lying flat, better sitting forward
Hiccups
Difficulty swallowing (dysphagia)
Bilateral pitting ankle edema
Unilateral leg warmth and redness
r: Pericarditis: 1) Sharp pleuritic chest pain WORSE supine, BETTER leaning forward (pathognomonic); 2) Hiccups = phrenic nerve irritation from inflamed pericardium; 3) Dysphagia = esophageal compression. Ankle edema = tamponade/HF, not simple pericarditis.

q: Which medication is given IV during a pharmacologic stress test for clients who cannot walk on a treadmill?
o: Adenosine to briefly stop the heart
Dobutamine to increase heart rate and contractility
Nitroglycerin to dilate coronary arteries
Digoxin to improve cardiac contractility
r: Dobutamine (beta-1 agonist) mimics exercise by increasing HR and contractility pharmacologically. Used when patients cannot physically exercise. Allows detection of stress-induced ischemia without treadmill walking.

q: A client with aortic regurgitation says: "The valve is not closing completely and blood is backing up." This indicates:
o: Misunderstanding — correct them
Correct understanding of valvular regurgitation pathophysiology
They are confusing regurgitation with stenosis
Anxiety about their diagnosis
r: Valvular REGURGITATION = valve fails to close completely -> blood leaks BACKWARD. In aortic regurgitation: blood flows back from aorta into LV during diastole. The client accurately describes the mechanism. Stenosis = valve fails to OPEN (different mechanism entirely).

q: For AFib complication prevention, which discharge teaching is most important?
o: Avoid all exercise indefinitely
Avoid over-the-counter decongestants
Take anticoagulants only when palpitations occur
Unlimited caffeine is fine
r: OTC decongestants (pseudoephedrine/phenylephrine) are sympathomimetics that increase HR and BP -> can trigger AFib episodes or make rate control harder. AFib patients must avoid OTC stimulants and decongestants. All medications must be taken as scheduled — not only with symptoms.

q: The PRIMARY occupational risk factor for developing chronic venous disease is:
o: Lifting heavy objects
Sedentary desk work
Standing for prolonged periods of time
Exposure to workplace chemicals
r: Prolonged standing = #1 occupational risk for venous disease. Gravity causes continuous blood pooling in leg veins without muscle pump assistance -> valve incompetence over time. High-risk occupations: nurses, teachers, chefs, factory workers. Compression stockings are recommended.

q: The underlying cause of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is:
o: Viral infection of the myocardium
Thickening of the ventricular walls and septum — usually genetic (autosomal dominant)
Excessive alcohol use dilating the heart
Coronary artery blockages
r: HCM = genetic mutation (autosomal dominant) -> hypertrophy of ventricular walls and septum -> obstructs outflow, reduces filling. #1 cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes. Identified on echocardiogram. Family history screening important.

q: Premature atrial beats (PACs) typically require which treatment?
o: Immediate cardioversion
Long-term anticoagulation
Usually no treatment — reduce alcohol, caffeine, stress, smoking; beta blocker if needed
Emergency pacemaker insertion
r: PACs are common, usually benign ectopic atrial beats. Treatment is typically not required. Lifestyle teaching: reduce alcohol, caffeine, tobacco, stress. MD may prescribe beta blocker for symptomatic or frequent PACs. NOT life-threatening — no cardioversion or anticoagulation needed.

q: Which structural cardiac change causes hypertension to lead to heart failure?
o: HTN reduces blood flow to kidneys causing fluid overload only
HTN forces LV to pump against increased resistance -> LV hypertrophy -> stiffening -> pump failure
HTN directly destroys heart valve leaflets
HTN decreases heart rate reducing cardiac output
r: HTN -> chronic pressure overload on LV -> compensatory LV hypertrophy -> myocardial stiffening -> diastolic dysfunction -> eventually systolic pump failure -> heart failure. HTN is the LEADING cause of HF due to these structural changes. This is why BP control is critical.

q: A patient is admitted with a BP of 194/126 mmHg. The provider orders IV antihypertensives. Which goal is CORRECT for the first hour of treatment?
o: Reduce BP to 120/80 mmHg within 60 minutes
Reduce BP by 20–25% within 60 minutes
Reduce BP to 140/90 mmHg as quickly as possible
Hold all antihypertensives until a CT head is completed
