r: THE THIRD CHECK OF THE LABEL AGAINST THE MAR IS PERFORMED AT THE BEDSIDE IMMEDIATELY BEFORE ADMINISTRATION, AFTER IDENTIFYING THE CLIENT WITH TWO IDENTIFIERS. Checking after documentation would be too late to prevent an error, and documentation is always done AFTER the medication is given, never before. Pharmacy delivery is not one of the nurse's three checks.

q: A nurse is reviewing a newly written medication prescription. Which of the following components must be present for the prescription to be complete? (Select all that apply.)
o: The client's full name
The name of the medication
The dosage and route
The frequency or time of administration
The client's admitting diagnosis
The client's insurance information
r: A COMPLETE MEDICATION PRESCRIPTION CONTAINS THE CLIENT'S FULL NAME, THE DATE AND TIME IT WAS WRITTEN, THE DRUG NAME, DOSAGE, ROUTE, FREQUENCY, AND THE PRESCRIBER'S SIGNATURE. The admitting diagnosis and insurance data belong to the medical record but are not required elements of a prescription. IF ANY REQUIRED ELEMENT IS MISSING OR ILLEGIBLE, THE NURSE MUST CLARIFY WITH THE PRESCRIBER BEFORE ADMINISTERING.

q: A nurse is transcribing four new prescriptions. Which prescription should the nurse clarify with the provider before transcribing it?
o: Furosemide 40 mg PO daily
Digoxin 0.125 mg PO daily
Insulin glargine 10 U subcutaneously at bedtime
Morphine 2 mg IV every 4 hr PRN for pain
r: THE ABBREVIATION 'U' FOR UNITS IS ON THE OFFICIAL DO-NOT-USE LIST BECAUSE IT IS EASILY MISREAD AS A ZERO OR A FOUR AND HAS CAUSED TENFOLD INSULIN OVERDOSES; 'UNITS' MUST BE WRITTEN OUT. Digoxin 0.125 mg is written correctly, because a LEADING zero is required while a TRAILING zero (such as 1.0 mg) is prohibited. Spelling out 'morphine' rather than using 'MS' and writing 'daily' rather than 'QD' are also correct.

q: A nurse discovers that a client received 10 times the prescribed dose of an anticoagulant 20 min ago. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Complete an incident report
Assess the client for bleeding and obtain vital signs
Notify the provider of the error
Notify the charge nurse and the pharmacy
r: WHEN A MEDICATION ERROR OCCURS, THE NURSE'S FIRST ACTION IS ALWAYS TO ASSESS THE CLIENT FOR ADVERSE EFFECTS, THEN NOTIFY THE PROVIDER, THEN COMPLETE AN INCIDENT REPORT. Notifying the provider is essential but comes second, because the provider needs assessment data to decide on treatment such as an antidote. The incident report is an internal quality-improvement document, is completed last, and is never filed in the medical record.

q: A client who has heart failure tells the nurse, 'I am not taking that water pill today.' Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Document that the client refused the medication
Ask the client the reason for refusing the medication
Explain the consequences of not taking the diuretic
Notify the provider that the dose was refused
r: THE NURSE MUST FIRST ASSESS THE REASON FOR THE REFUSAL, BECAUSE THE REASON DIRECTS THE INTERVENTION; A CLIENT AVOIDING FREQUENT BATHROOM TRIPS NEEDS A DIFFERENT RESPONSE THAN ONE WHO FEELS DIZZY. Explaining consequences is premature before the concern is identified and may feel coercive. Documentation and provider notification are both required, but they follow assessment, and a competent client always retains the right to refuse.

q: A client asks why the oral dose of a medication is much larger than the IV dose of the same medication. Which response by the nurse is appropriate?
o: 'Oral medications get diluted by the fluids you drink with them.'
'Part of an oral medication is broken down by your liver before it ever reaches your bloodstream.'
'Oral medications are removed by the kidneys faster than IV medications are.'
'Stomach acid destroys most of any medication, so the dose is always doubled.'
r: THE FIRST-PASS EFFECT MEANS ORAL DRUGS ARE ABSORBED FROM THE GI TRACT AND CARRIED THROUGH THE PORTAL CIRCULATION TO THE LIVER, WHERE A PORTION IS METABOLIZED BEFORE REACHING SYSTEMIC CIRCULATION, SO A LARGER ORAL DOSE IS NEEDED. IV medications bypass absorption and the first pass entirely and have 100% bioavailability. Excretion rate is not what accounts for the dose difference.

q: A nurse is caring for a client receiving IV vancomycin every 12 hr. The provider prescribes a trough level. When should the nurse plan to obtain the blood sample?
o: 30 min after the infusion is complete
Immediately before the next scheduled dose
Halfway between two scheduled doses
At the same time each morning regardless of the dosing schedule
r: A TROUGH LEVEL IS THE LOWEST SERUM CONCENTRATION AND IS DRAWN IMMEDIATELY BEFORE (WITHIN 30 MIN OF) THE NEXT SCHEDULED DOSE TO CONFIRM THE DRUG REMAINS IN THE THERAPEUTIC RANGE. A sample drawn shortly after the infusion reflects the PEAK, the highest concentration, which is used to evaluate for toxicity. A level drawn at a random time cannot be meaningfully interpreted.

q: A nurse is reviewing the medication regimen of an 82-year-old client who takes seven medications. Which of the following age-related changes increase this client's risk for medication toxicity? (Select all that apply.)
o: Decreased glomerular filtration rate
Decreased hepatic blood flow and enzyme activity
Decreased serum albumin
Increased proportion of body fat
Increased total body water
Increased gastric acid production
r: AGING REDUCES RENAL EXCRETION AND HEPATIC METABOLISM, SO DRUGS AND THEIR METABOLITES ACCUMULATE AND OLDER ADULTS GENERALLY REQUIRE LOWER DOSES. Lower serum albumin leaves more free (active) drug circulating, and a higher fat-to-water ratio prolongs the action of fat-soluble drugs. Total body water DECREASES rather than increases with aging, and gastric acid production decreases, so those two options are incorrect.

q: A nurse enters the room of a client receiving oxygen by nasal cannula and finds the pulse oximeter alarming with a reading of 84%. The client is sitting upright and can speak only in short phrases. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Replace the pulse oximetry probe with a new one
Assess the client's respiratory effort and auscultate lung sounds
Silence the alarm and recheck the reading in 5 min
Document the oxygen saturation reading
r: ASSESS THE CLIENT BEFORE THE EQUIPMENT; SPEAKING IN SHORT PHRASES CORROBORATES TRUE HYPOXEMIA RATHER THAN A FAULTY PROBE. Changing the probe first assumes the device is wrong and delays recognition of respiratory compromise. Silencing an alarm without evaluating the client is never appropriate, and documentation always follows assessment and intervention.

q: A nurse is preparing to administer morning medications to a client who has dysphagia and a gastrostomy tube. Which prescribed medication should the nurse withhold and clarify with the provider?
o: Acetaminophen 650 mg tablet
Metoprolol succinate extended-release 50 mg tablet
Lisinopril 10 mg tablet
Levothyroxine 50 mcg tablet
r: EXTENDED-RELEASE AND ENTERIC-COATED PRODUCTS MUST NEVER BE CRUSHED, BECAUSE CRUSHING DESTROYS THE RELEASE MECHANISM AND DELIVERS THE ENTIRE DOSE AT ONCE, RISKING TOXICITY. The nurse should contact the provider for an immediate-release or liquid form. Acetaminophen, lisinopril, and levothyroxine are plain immediate-release tablets that may be crushed and dissolved in water for tube administration.

q: A nurse is administering three medications through a client's nasogastric tube. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)
o: Verify tube placement before administering the medications
Elevate the head of the bed to at least 30 degrees
Dissolve and administer each medication separately
Flush with 15 to 30 mL of water before, between, and after the medications
Mix all three medications together in one syringe to save time
Add the crushed medications directly to the enteral formula bag
r: PLACEMENT IS VERIFIED FIRST, AND EACH MEDICATION IS GIVEN SEPARATELY WITH A 15 TO 30 mL WATER FLUSH BEFORE, BETWEEN, AND AFTER DOSES TO PREVENT TUBE OCCLUSION AND DRUG INTERACTIONS. Combining drugs in one syringe or adding them to the formula bag can cause precipitation, clogging, and unpredictable absorption. Keeping the head of the bed elevated during and after administration reduces aspiration risk.

q: A nurse is teaching a client who has a new prescription for sublingual nitroglycerin. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
o: 'I will place the tablet under my tongue and let it dissolve.'
'I will swallow the tablet with a full glass of water.'
'I will sit or lie down before I take the tablet.'
'If my chest pain is not relieved 5 minutes after the first tablet, I will call 911.'
r: SUBLINGUAL TABLETS DISSOLVE AGAINST THE HIGHLY VASCULAR MUCOSA UNDER THE TONGUE AND MUST NOT BE CHEWED, SWALLOWED, OR TAKEN WITH WATER, BECAUSE SWALLOWING SUBJECTS THE DRUG TO THE FIRST-PASS EFFECT AND DESTROYS ITS RAPID ONSET. Sitting or lying down is correct, because nitroglycerin causes vasodilation, hypotension, and dizziness. Current teaching is to call 911 if pain is unrelieved 5 min after the first dose.

q: A nurse is applying a transdermal analgesic patch to a client. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)
o: Wear gloves while handling the patch
Remove the previous patch and cleanse that area of skin
Apply the new patch to a clean, dry, hairless area and date and initial it
Rotate the application site with each new patch
Apply a heating pad over the patch to improve absorption
Place the new patch over the same site to maintain a steady blood level
r: GLOVES PREVENT THE NURSE FROM ABSORBING THE MEDICATION, AND THE OLD PATCH MUST ALWAYS BE REMOVED AND THE SKIN CLEANSED BEFORE A NEW PATCH IS APPLIED, BECAUSE A RETAINED PATCH CAUSES AN ACCIDENTAL OVERDOSE. Sites are rotated to prevent irritation, and the patch is dated and initialed so it is not overlooked. HEAT INCREASES ABSORPTION AND CAN CAUSE TOXICITY, so heating pads, electric blankets, and hot baths must be avoided over the patch.

q: A nurse is observing a nursing student instill eye drops for a client. Which action by the student requires the nurse to intervene?
o: The student asks the client to look up toward the ceiling
The student drops the medication directly onto the client's cornea
The student pulls down the lower lid to expose the conjunctival sac
The student applies gentle pressure over the nasolacrimal duct after instilling the drop
r: OPHTHALMIC MEDICATION IS INSTILLED INTO THE LOWER CONJUNCTIVAL SAC, NEVER DIRECTLY ONTO THE CORNEA, WHICH IS EXQUISITELY SENSITIVE AND EASILY INJURED. Asking the client to look up and pulling down the lower lid correctly expose the sac and reduce blinking. Applying pressure to the nasolacrimal duct for 30 to 60 sec limits systemic absorption and is appropriate technique.

q: A nurse is preparing to instill otic drops in a 2-year-old child. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Pull the pinna up and back
Pull the pinna down and back
Insert the dropper tip into the ear canal to create a seal
Instill the drops directly from the refrigerator to soothe the ear
r: FOR A CHILD YOUNGER THAN 3 YEARS, THE PINNA IS PULLED DOWN AND BACK TO STRAIGHTEN THE SHORTER, MORE HORIZONTAL CANAL; UP AND BACK IS USED FOR CLIENTS 3 YEARS AND OLDER. The dropper must never touch or occlude the canal, because that contaminates the solution and can injure the ear. Cold drops can cause vertigo, nausea, and pain, so solutions are warmed to room temperature.

q: A nurse is teaching a client who has asthma about newly prescribed albuterol and fluticasone inhalers. Which statement by the client indicates the teaching was effective?
o: 'I will use the fluticasone first so it has more time to work.'
'I will use the albuterol first, wait about a minute, then take the fluticasone and rinse my mouth.'
'I will use both inhalers only when I start to feel short of breath.'
'I will rinse my mouth right after the albuterol and before the fluticasone.'
r: THE BRONCHODILATOR IS ALWAYS USED FIRST TO OPEN THE AIRWAYS SO THE CORTICOSTEROID CAN REACH THE LOWER AIRWAYS, AND THE MOUTH IS RINSED AFTER THE STEROID TO PREVENT ORAL CANDIDIASIS AND HOARSENESS. Taking fluticasone first reduces steroid deposition in the lungs. Fluticasone is a maintenance medication taken on a fixed schedule, not a rescue inhaler, so using it only for symptoms is unsafe.

q: A nurse administers a tuberculin skin test intradermally on the client's inner forearm and notes that no wheal forms at the site. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Massage the site to distribute the solution evenly
Document the finding and read the site in 48 to 72 hr
Repeat the injection at a site at least 5 cm (2 in) from the original site
Apply a warm compress and reassess the site in 30 min
r: ABSENCE OF A BLEB OR WHEAL MEANS THE SOLUTION WAS DEPOSITED TOO DEEPLY (SUBCUTANEOUSLY), THE TEST IS INVALID, AND IT MUST BE REPEATED AT ANOTHER SITE AT LEAST 5 cm AWAY, WITH BOTH ATTEMPTS DOCUMENTED. Intradermal injections use a 26 to 27 gauge needle inserted 5 to 15 degrees with the bevel up. Massaging would disperse the solution and further invalidate the result rather than fix it.

q: A nurse is observing a newly hired nurse administer subcutaneous heparin. Which action by the newly hired nurse requires intervention?
o: Selecting a site on the abdomen at least 5 cm (2 in) away from the umbilicus
Inserting the needle at a 90-degree angle
Massaging the site after withdrawing the needle
Holding a skin fold between the thumb and forefinger during the injection
r: THE SITE IS NEVER MASSAGED AFTER SUBCUTANEOUS HEPARIN, BECAUSE MASSAGE INCREASES TISSUE TRAUMA AND CAUSES BRUISING AND HEMATOMA FORMATION; THE NURSE ALSO DOES NOT ASPIRATE BEFORE INJECTING HEPARIN. The abdomen at least 5 cm from the umbilicus is the preferred site, and a 90-degree angle with a bunched skin fold is correct when using a short subcutaneous needle.

q: A nurse is preparing to administer a 2 mL IM injection to an adult client. Which site should the nurse select as the safest option?
o: Dorsogluteal
Ventrogluteal
Deltoid
Rectus femoris
r: THE VENTROGLUTEAL SITE IS THE SAFEST IM SITE FOR ADULTS BECAUSE IT IS FREE OF LARGE NERVES AND BLOOD VESSELS, HAS DENSE MUSCLE MASS, AND ACCOMMODATES UP TO 3 mL. The dorsogluteal site is no longer recommended because of the risk of sciatic nerve injury. The deltoid holds only about 1 mL and is reserved for small-volume injections such as vaccines.

q: A nurse is administering an IM injection of an irritating medication using the Z-track technique. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)
o: Pull the skin and subcutaneous tissue 2.5 to 3.5 cm (1 to 1.5 in) laterally before inserting the needle
Insert the needle at a 90-degree angle
Wait about 10 seconds after injecting before withdrawing the needle
Release the displaced tissue after the needle is withdrawn
Massage the site vigorously after the injection
Select the deltoid site for a 3 mL volume
r: THE Z-TRACK METHOD SEALS MEDICATION IN THE MUSCLE: DISPLACE THE SKIN LATERALLY, INJECT AT 90 DEGREES, WAIT 10 SEC, WITHDRAW, THEN RELEASE THE TISSUE SO THE TRACK ZIGZAGS SHUT. Massaging would force the irritating drug back into subcutaneous tissue, causing pain and staining. The deltoid tolerates only about 1 mL, so a 3 mL dose requires the ventrogluteal site.

q: A nurse is preparing to administer 10 units of NPH insulin and 6 units of regular insulin from two vials in one syringe. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Inject 6 units of air into the regular insulin vial
Inject 10 units of air into the NPH vial
Withdraw 6 units of regular insulin
Withdraw 10 units of NPH insulin
r: AIR IS INJECTED INTO THE CLOUDY (NPH) VIAL FIRST WITHOUT THE NEEDLE TOUCHING THE SOLUTION, THEN INTO THE CLEAR (REGULAR) VIAL, AND THE CLEAR INSULIN IS DRAWN UP BEFORE THE CLOUDY: 'CLEAR BEFORE CLOUDY.' Withdrawing NPH first would contaminate the regular insulin vial with intermediate-acting insulin and alter its onset. Regular insulin is drawn only after air has been placed in both vials.

q: A nurse is teaching a client who has type 1 diabetes mellitus about insulin administration. Which of the following statements by the client indicate an understanding of the teaching? (Select all that apply.)
o: 'I will not mix my insulin glargine with any other insulin.'
'I will rotate my injection sites within my abdomen.'
'I will shake the NPH vial hard to mix it well.'
'I will keep a fast-acting carbohydrate with me at all times.'
'I can keep the vial I am currently using at room temperature for up to 28 days.'
'I will draw up the cloudy insulin before the clear insulin.'
r: INSULIN GLARGINE IS NEVER MIXED WITH ANOTHER INSULIN AND IS NEVER GIVEN IV, AND SITES ARE ROTATED WITHIN ONE ANATOMIC AREA (USUALLY THE ABDOMEN) TO KEEP ABSORPTION PREDICTABLE AND PREVENT LIPOHYPERTROPHY. Cloudy insulin is gently rolled between the palms rather than shaken, because shaking creates bubbles and can damage the suspension. Clear is always drawn before cloudy, so the last statement indicates a need for further teaching.

q: A nurse is observing a newly hired nurse administer injections on the unit. Which action requires the nurse to intervene?
o: Activating the safety shield immediately after withdrawing the needle
Recapping a used needle with two hands before disposal
Placing the used syringe in the sharps container inside the client's room
Using a needleless connector to administer an IV medication
r: USED NEEDLES ARE NEVER RECAPPED; IF RECAPPING IS UNAVOIDABLE, ONLY THE ONE-HANDED SCOOP TECHNIQUE IS ACCEPTABLE, BECAUSE TWO-HANDED RECAPPING IS A LEADING CAUSE OF NEEDLESTICK INJURIES. Engaging the safety device immediately, using needleless systems, and disposing of sharps at the point of use in a puncture-resistant container are all correct practices.

q: A nurse prepares hydromorphone 1 mg IV for a client from a 2 mg prefilled syringe. Which action should the nurse take with the remaining medication?
o: Discard the remaining medication alone in the sharps container after administration
Waste the remaining medication in the presence of a second nurse and have both nurses document it
Return the partially used syringe to the automated dispensing cabinet
Label the syringe and save the remaining dose for the client's next scheduled dose
r: PARTIAL DOSES OF CONTROLLED SUBSTANCES MUST BE WASTED IN THE PRESENCE OF A SECOND NURSE, WITH BOTH NURSES DOCUMENTING THE WASTE IMMEDIATELY, AS REQUIRED BY FEDERAL LAW AND FACILITY POLICY. Discarding it alone leaves the count unverified and is a policy violation even though the drug is destroyed. Saving a partial dose or returning it to the cabinet creates a risk for diversion and contamination.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has a draining wound infected with Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Which nursing action best interrupts the mode-of-transmission link in the chain of infection?
o: Administering the prescribed IV antibiotic on time
Performing hand hygiene before and after all client contact
Encouraging the client to eat a high-protein, high-calorie diet
Obtaining a wound culture as prescribed
r: HAND HYGIENE INTERRUPTS THE MODE OF TRANSMISSION AND IS THE SINGLE MOST EFFECTIVE ACTION FOR PREVENTING THE SPREAD OF INFECTION. Antibiotics act on the infectious agent, and improving nutrition strengthens the susceptible host, so those break different links. Obtaining a culture is a diagnostic action and does not break any link in the chain.

q: A client who was exposed to influenza 2 days ago reports fatigue, mild headache, and 'just not feeling right,' with a temperature of 37.4 C (99.3 F). The nurse should recognize that the client is in which stage of infection, and what is the most important implication?
o: Incubation stage; the client has no organisms present yet
Prodromal stage; the client is highly contagious to others
Illness stage; specific symptoms confirm the diagnosis
Convalescent stage; symptoms are beginning to resolve
r: THE PRODROMAL STAGE PRODUCES VAGUE, NONSPECIFIC SYMPTOMS SUCH AS MALAISE, FATIGUE, AND LOW-GRADE FEVER, AND IT IS THE STAGE IN WHICH THE CLIENT IS MOST CONTAGIOUS. During incubation the organism is replicating but the client has NO symptoms, so that option does not match this presentation. Distinct, characteristic symptoms such as high fever, cough, and myalgia define the illness stage.

q: A nurse is assessing a client who has a surgical wound infection. Which of the following findings indicate that the infection has become systemic and require the nurse to notify the provider? (Select all that apply.)
o: Temperature 38.9 C (102 F)
Heart rate 118/min
WBC count 18,000/mm3
Purulent drainage at the incision
Malaise and generalized muscle aches
Redness and warmth limited to the incision edges
r: SYSTEMIC INFECTION AFFECTS THE WHOLE BODY AND PRODUCES FEVER, TACHYCARDIA, LEUKOCYTOSIS, MALAISE, AND ANOREXIA, AND MAY SIGNAL PROGRESSION TOWARD SEPSIS. Purulent drainage, redness, and warmth confined to the incision are signs of a LOCALIZED infection only and are expected findings in a wound infection. The systemic findings are the ones that require prompt provider notification.

q: A nurse is teaching a group of nursing students about the acute inflammatory response. Which of the following statements should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)
o: Vasodilation increases blood flow to the area, causing redness and warmth
Chemical mediators such as histamine increase capillary permeability
Fluid shifting into the interstitial tissue produces edema
White blood cells migrate to the site and increase in number there
Vasoconstriction at the site lowers the local tissue temperature
Inflammation always indicates that an infection is present
r: IN ACUTE INFLAMMATION, CHEMICAL MEDIATORS CAUSE VASODILATION AND INCREASE CAPILLARY PERMEABILITY, PRODUCING THE CLASSIC REDNESS, WARMTH, SWELLING, PAIN, AND LOSS OF FUNCTION, WHILE WBCs MIGRATE TO AND INCREASE AT THE SITE. Local temperature RISES because blood flow increases, so the vasoconstriction option is incorrect. Inflammation is a protective response to any injury, such as a sprain or burn, and does not always mean infection.

q: A nurse has finished providing care for a client who has Clostridioides difficile infection and has removed the gown and gloves. Which hand hygiene action should the nurse take?
o: Apply alcohol-based hand rub to all surfaces of the hands
Wash the hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds
Apply alcohol-based hand rub followed by moisturizing lotion
Omit hand hygiene because gloves were worn during care
r: ALCOHOL-BASED HAND RUB DOES NOT KILL C. DIFFICILE SPORES; SOAP AND WATER ARE REQUIRED BECAUSE FRICTION AND RINSING PHYSICALLY REMOVE THE SPORES FROM THE HANDS. The same rule applies to norovirus and whenever hands are visibly soiled. Hand hygiene is always performed after glove removal, because gloves can have microscopic defects and hands become contaminated during removal.

q: A nurse is reviewing hand hygiene practices with staff. In which of the following situations must soap and water be used rather than an alcohol-based hand rub? (Select all that apply.)
o: The nurse's hands are visibly soiled with blood
After caring for a client who has C. difficile
After caring for a client who has norovirus gastroenteritis
After the nurse uses the restroom
Before entering the room of a client on protective precautions
After removing gloves when the hands are not visibly soiled
r: SOAP AND WATER ARE REQUIRED WHENEVER THE HANDS ARE VISIBLY SOILED, AFTER CONTACT WITH SPORE-FORMING ORGANISMS SUCH AS C. DIFFICILE, AFTER CARE OF A CLIENT WITH NOROVIRUS, AND AFTER USING THE RESTROOM. Alcohol-based rub is acceptable and even preferred for routine decontamination, including before entering a protective-precautions room and after glove removal when hands are clean. Alcohol is ineffective against spores.

q: A nurse is admitting a client who has a wound infected with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Which personal protective equipment should the nurse plan to wear when providing wound care?
o: Gloves only
Gown and gloves
Surgical mask and gloves
N95 respirator, gown, and gloves
r: MRSA REQUIRES CONTACT PRECAUTIONS, WHICH CALL FOR A GOWN AND GLOVES FOR ALL CLIENT AND ENVIRONMENTAL CONTACT, PLUS A PRIVATE ROOM AND DEDICATED EQUIPMENT. Gloves alone are insufficient because clothing contacts the client and bed linens. An N95 is reserved for airborne organisms such as TB, measles, and varicella, and a mask is added only if splashing is anticipated.

q: A nurse is caring for a client admitted with suspected meningococcal meningitis. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Place the client in a negative-pressure room and wear an N95 respirator
Place the client in a private room and wear a surgical mask when within 1 m (3 ft) of the client
Place the client in a private room and wear a gown and gloves for all contact
Place the client in a semiprivate room and wear a face shield only during procedures
r: MENINGOCOCCAL MENINGITIS REQUIRES DROPLET PRECAUTIONS: A PRIVATE ROOM AND A SURGICAL MASK WHEN WORKING WITHIN ABOUT 1 m (3 ft) OF THE CLIENT. Droplets are large and fall quickly, so a negative-pressure room and N95 respirator are unnecessary and are reserved for airborne organisms. Other droplet examples include influenza, pertussis, mumps, and rubella.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has active pulmonary tuberculosis. Which action by an assistive personnel requires the nurse to intervene?
o: The AP dons a fit-tested N95 respirator before entering the room
The AP props the door of the client's room open to hear the client more easily
The AP places a surgical mask on the client before transport to radiology
The AP performs hand hygiene before leaving the room
r: THE DOOR OF AN AIRBORNE INFECTION ISOLATION ROOM MUST REMAIN CLOSED AT ALL TIMES TO MAINTAIN NEGATIVE PRESSURE; PROPPING IT OPEN ALLOWS CONTAMINATED AIR TO ESCAPE INTO THE CORRIDOR. Staff wear a fit-tested N95 or higher respirator, while the CLIENT wears a surgical mask during necessary transport, so those actions are correct. Hand hygiene is always appropriate.

q: A nurse has finished providing care for a client on contact and droplet precautions while wearing a gown, mask, goggles, and gloves. In which order should the nurse remove the personal protective equipment before leaving the room?
o: Gloves, goggles, gown, mask
Gown, gloves, goggles, mask
Mask, goggles, gloves, gown
Gloves, gown, mask, goggles
r: PPE IS REMOVED FROM MOST TO LEAST CONTAMINATED: GLOVES FIRST, THEN GOGGLES OR FACE SHIELD, THEN GOWN, THEN MASK OR RESPIRATOR, FOLLOWED BY HAND HYGIENE. The mask is removed last (and outside the room for airborne precautions), because taking it off earlier with contaminated hands would expose the nurse's mucous membranes. Donning follows essentially the reverse order: gown, mask, goggles, gloves.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has severe neutropenia following chemotherapy. Which of the following actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? (Select all that apply.)
o: Place the client in a private room with positive-pressure airflow
Do not allow fresh flowers or potted plants in the room
Screen visitors and staff for signs and symptoms of infection
Avoid invasive procedures such as indwelling urinary catheters when possible
Place the client in a negative-pressure room
Provide fresh raw fruits and vegetables to increase vitamin intake
r: PROTECTIVE (NEUTROPENIC) PRECAUTIONS PROTECT THE CLIENT FROM THE ENVIRONMENT AND REQUIRE A PRIVATE ROOM WITH POSITIVE-PRESSURE AIRFLOW AND HIGH-EFFICIENCY FILTRATION, NO FRESH FLOWERS OR PLANTS, AND NO RAW FRUITS OR VEGETABLES, ALL OF WHICH HARBOR ORGANISMS. A negative-pressure room protects OTHERS from the client and is used for airborne precautions, making it the opposite of what this client needs. Limiting invasive devices removes portals of entry.

q: A nurse is setting up a sterile field for a complex dressing change. Which action by the nurse contaminates the field and requires the nurse to start over?
o: Holding sterile items above waist level and in front of the body
Placing a sterile gauze package 1 cm (0.5 in) from the edge of the field
Opening the outermost flap of a sterile package away from the body first
Keeping the sterile field within the nurse's line of vision at all times
r: THE OUTER 2.5 cm (1 in) BORDER OF A STERILE FIELD IS CONSIDERED CONTAMINATED, SO AN ITEM PLACED 1 cm FROM THE EDGE CONTAMINATES THE FIELD AND IT MUST BE SET UP AGAIN. Sterile items are kept above the waist and within the line of vision, and the first flap of a package is opened away from the body, so those actions are correct. Surgical asepsis eliminates all microorganisms, whereas medical asepsis only reduces their number.

q: A nurse is identifying clients who are at increased risk for a health care-associated infection. Which of the following clients should the nurse identify as being at greatest risk? (Select all that apply.)
o: An 84-year-old client who has an indwelling urinary catheter
A client receiving chemotherapy who has a WBC count of 1,800/mm3
A client who has poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and a foot ulcer
A 4-week-old infant admitted with respiratory syncytial virus
A 30-year-old client admitted for an elective outpatient knee arthroscopy
r: OLDER ADULTS, IMMUNOCOMPROMISED CLIENTS, CLIENTS WHO HAVE CHRONIC DISEASE SUCH AS DIABETES, AND INFANTS WITH IMMATURE IMMUNE SYSTEMS ARE AT HIGHEST RISK, AND INDWELLING DEVICES ARE THE LEADING CAUSE OF HEALTH CARE-ASSOCIATED INFECTIONS. The healthy young adult having a brief outpatient procedure has intact defenses and minimal exposure. Removing invasive devices as early as possible is a key preventive measure.

q: A nurse is providing postmortem care for a client who died 15 min ago. The family is expected to arrive within the hour to view the body. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Insert the client's dentures and close the mouth
Lower the head of the bed completely flat
Leave the client's eyes open so the family can see them
Delay washing away drainage and soiling until after the family has viewed the body
r: DENTURES ARE INSERTED AND THE MOUTH CLOSED AS SOON AS POSSIBLE, BECAUSE RIGOR MORTIS BEGINS WITHIN 2 TO 4 HR AND MAKES PLACEMENT IMPOSSIBLE, DISTORTING FACIAL APPEARANCE. The head of the bed is ELEVATED SLIGHTLY, about 30 degrees, to keep blood from pooling in the face and causing discoloration, so lying the client flat is incorrect. The eyelids are gently closed, and the body is cleaned and re-dressed before the family views it.

q: A client who was admitted after a motor-vehicle crash dies, and the death is referred to the medical examiner. Which action should the nurse take when preparing the body?
o: Remove the endotracheal tube and IV catheters before the family arrives
Leave all tubes, lines, and drains in place and clamp or cap them
Remove the tubes but place them in a labeled bag at the bedside
Remove only the invasive lines that were inserted in the emergency department
r: WHEN A DEATH IS A CORONER OR MEDICAL EXAMINER CASE OR AN AUTOPSY IS PLANNED, ALL TUBES, LINES, DRAINS, AND DEVICES ARE LEFT IN PLACE AND CLAMPED OR CAPPED, BECAUSE THEIR POSITION IS PART OF THE EVIDENCE. Removing them, even if they are bagged and saved, destroys evidence of placement and exceeds the nurse's authority. In a routine expected death without autopsy, the nurse may remove tubes according to facility policy.

q: A client who has been hospitalized for 4 days tells the nurse, "I am in bed 9 hours a night, but I wake up feeling like my body never rested. The aides come in every couple of hours." The nurse understands that the client is most likely being deprived of which stage of sleep?
o: Stage N1 (light transitional sleep)
Stage N2 (onset of true sleep)
Stage N3 (slow-wave/deep sleep)
REM sleep
r: N3 IS THE DEEP SLOW-WAVE STAGE WHERE PHYSICAL RESTORATION, TISSUE REPAIR, AND GROWTH HORMONE RELEASE OCCUR, so a client deprived of N3 wakes physically unrefreshed. N3 occurs mostly in the first third of the night and is the stage most easily lost to frequent awakenings. REM is tempting, but REM loss produces irritability, poor concentration, and impaired memory consolidation rather than the physical fatigue described.

q: A client is receiving scheduled morphine following abdominal surgery. The client reports, "I sleep, but I have not had a single dream since surgery." Which explanation should the nurse provide?
o: "Opioids suppress REM sleep, which is the stage when most dreaming occurs."
"Opioids increase deep sleep, so dreams are simply forgotten."
"Loss of dreaming means you are developing a tolerance to the morphine."
"Dreaming only occurs in the first sleep cycle of the night."
r: OPIOIDS SUPPRESS REM SLEEP, and REM IS THE STAGE OF VIVID DREAMING AND MEMORY CONSOLIDATION. This is an expected, reversible medication effect rather than a sign of tolerance, which is defined by needing more drug for the same analgesic effect. Dreaming is not limited to the first cycle; REM periods actually lengthen with each successive 90-minute cycle across the night.

q: A nurse is planning nighttime care for a client on a busy medical unit. To allow the client to complete at least one full sleep cycle without interruption, the nurse should cluster care to provide an uninterrupted block of approximately how long?
o: 30 minutes
60 minutes
90 minutes
4 hours
r: ONE COMPLETE SLEEP CYCLE THROUGH NREM AND REM LASTS ABOUT 90 MINUTES, so clustering assessments, medications, and vital signs to protect 90-minute blocks allows the client to reach restorative N3 and REM sleep. Blocks of 30 to 60 minutes usually allow only N1 and N2, so the client never reaches deep sleep. Requiring a 4-hour block is unrealistic on most acute care units and is not necessary to complete a cycle.

q: An 78-year-old client says, "Something is wrong with me. I fall asleep by 8:30 p.m., wake up three or four times at night, and I am wide awake at 5 a.m." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
o: "That pattern suggests a sleep disorder, and you should be evaluated for insomnia."
"Earlier bedtimes and more nighttime awakenings are expected changes with aging; let's review what your daytime routine looks like."
"You should stay in bed until at least 7 a.m. so your body relearns a normal schedule."
"Taking a sleep aid every night is the safest way to correct this pattern."
r: NORMAL AGE-RELATED SLEEP CHANGES INCLUDE EARLIER BEDTIME AND WAKE TIME, MORE FREQUENT AWAKENINGS, LESS N3 DEEP SLEEP, AND MORE DAYTIME NAPPING; total sleep need remains about 7 to 9 hours. Validating the change while assessing daytime habits, including naps, is therapeutic and gathers data. Routinely recommending nightly sleep aids is unsafe in older adults because sedative-hypnotics increase confusion and fall risk.

q: A nurse is teaching a group of caregivers about sleep in older adults. Which statements by the nurse are accurate? (Select all that apply.)
o: "Older adults spend less time in deep, slow-wave sleep."
"Older adults typically need only 4 to 5 hours of sleep each night."
"Older adults often go to bed earlier and wake earlier."
"Frequent nighttime awakenings become more common with age."
"Daytime napping tends to increase, which can shorten nighttime sleep."
"REM sleep disappears entirely after age 70."
r: AGING REDUCES N3 DEEP SLEEP AND INCREASES NIGHTTIME AWAKENINGS, WITH A PHASE ADVANCE TOWARD EARLIER SLEEP AND WAKE TIMES AND MORE DAYTIME NAPPING. The total sleep requirement does NOT drop to 4 to 5 hours; older adults still need roughly 7 to 9 hours, and the 4 to 5 hour claim is a common misconception that leads caregivers to normalize sleep deprivation. REM sleep decreases modestly but never disappears.

q: A nurse is reviewing the medication administration record and intake history of a client who reports difficulty sleeping. Which findings should the nurse identify as likely contributors to the client's sleep disturbance? (Select all that apply.)
o: Furosemide scheduled at 2000
A glass of wine at bedtime to help fall asleep
Metoprolol prescribed daily
Prednisone taken in the morning with breakfast
Two cups of decaffeinated tea in the afternoon
A cigarette smoked shortly before bedtime
r: DIURETICS GIVEN LATE IN THE EVENING CAUSE NOCTURIA AND SHOULD BE SCHEDULED EARLY IN THE DAY, and ALCOHOL SHORTENS SLEEP ONSET BUT FRAGMENTS SLEEP AND SUPPRESSES REM IN THE SECOND HALF OF THE NIGHT. Beta blockers such as metoprolol are associated with insomnia and nightmares, and nicotine is a stimulant that delays sleep onset. Prednisone does disturb sleep, but morning dosing is the correct timing that minimizes that effect, and decaffeinated tea has negligible caffeine.

q: A nurse is evaluating teaching about sleep hygiene for a client with chronic insomnia. Which client statement indicates the teaching was effective?
o: "If I am still awake after about 20 minutes, I will get up and do something quiet until I feel sleepy."
"I will stay in bed and keep trying to fall asleep no matter how long it takes."
"I will watch television in bed until I doze off."
"I will sleep in on weekends to catch up on the hours I lost during the week."
r: A CORE SLEEP HYGIENE RULE IS TO GET OUT OF BED IF SLEEP DOES NOT COME WITHIN ABOUT 20 MINUTES, because lying awake conditions the brain to associate the bed with frustration and wakefulness. THE BED SHOULD BE USED ONLY FOR SLEEP AND SEX, so watching television in bed reinforces the wrong association, and screens emit light that suppresses melatonin. Sleeping in on weekends is wrong because a consistent wake time every day, including days off, is what stabilizes the circadian rhythm.

q: A nurse is discharging a client who has insomnia. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?
o: "I will keep my bedroom dark, quiet, and slightly cool."
"I will do my aerobic workout right before bed so I am tired enough to sleep."
"I will get up at the same time every morning, even on weekends."
"I will stop drinking coffee after lunchtime."
r: EXERCISE PROMOTES SLEEP ONLY WHEN COMPLETED AT LEAST 2 TO 3 HOURS BEFORE BEDTIME; vigorous activity close to bedtime raises core body temperature, heart rate, and catecholamines and DELAYS sleep onset. A dark, quiet, cool room and a fixed wake time are correct sleep hygiene measures. Stopping caffeine by early afternoon is also correct because caffeine has a half-life of roughly 5 to 6 hours.

q: A nurse is teaching sleep hygiene to a client who works rotating shifts. Which instructions should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)
o: Keep the sleep environment dark, quiet, and cool
Limit daytime naps to about 20 to 30 minutes and avoid napping late in the day
Eat a large, heavy meal shortly before going to sleep to prevent hunger awakenings
Reserve the bed for sleep rather than reading, eating, or working
Have an alcoholic nightcap to fall asleep faster after a night shift
Use the smartphone in bed until sleepy
r: A DARK, QUIET, COOL ROOM; SHORT EARLY NAPS; AND USING THE BED ONLY FOR SLEEP ARE STANDARD SLEEP HYGIENE MEASURES. ALCOHOL IS THE MOST COMMONLY MISUSED SLEEP AID: IT SHORTENS SLEEP ONSET BUT FRAGMENTS SLEEP AND SUPPRESSES REM LATER IN THE SLEEP PERIOD, so it is avoided. Heavy meals near bedtime cause reflux and arousals, and screen use in bed suppresses melatonin while reinforcing wakefulness in the bed.

q: A nurse is caring for four clients on a postoperative unit. Which finding requires immediate follow-up?
o: A client who has obstructive sleep apnea and is receiving IV hydromorphone, with a respiratory rate of 9/min and loud snoring
A client who has obstructive sleep apnea reporting daytime sleepiness and morning headache
A client who has restless legs syndrome pacing the hallway at 2300
A client who has narcolepsy who fell asleep briefly during a conversation
r: A CLIENT WITH OBSTRUCTIVE SLEEP APNEA WHO RECEIVES OPIOIDS IS AT HIGH RISK FOR AIRWAY OBSTRUCTION AND RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, AND A RESPIRATORY RATE BELOW 12/MIN REQUIRES THE NURSE TO STIMULATE THE CLIENT, WITHHOLD FURTHER OPIOID, AND NOTIFY THE PROVIDER. Daytime sleepiness and morning headache are classic but expected findings of untreated sleep apnea and are not emergencies. Pacing with restless legs and a brief sleep attack with narcolepsy are characteristic of those disorders and do not threaten airway or breathing.

q: A client newly prescribed CPAP for obstructive sleep apnea tells the nurse, "The mask bothers me, so I only wear it for the first hour or two until I fall asleep." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
o: "That is reasonable, since the airway collapses mainly at the beginning of the night."
"CPAP must be worn the entire time you are asleep, including naps, to keep your airway open; let's work on mask fit and comfort."
"You can stop the CPAP once your snoring improves."
"Try holding your breath when the pressure feels uncomfortable."
r: CPAP MUST BE WORN THROUGHOUT EVERY SLEEP PERIOD, INCLUDING NAPS, BECAUSE IT WORKS ONLY WHILE IT IS ON, SPLINTING THE AIRWAY OPEN WITH POSITIVE PRESSURE. Apneic events actually cluster during REM sleep, which predominates in the LATER part of the night, so removing the device after an hour leaves the highest-risk period untreated. The correct nursing intervention for intolerance is troubleshooting fit, humidification, and desensitization rather than reducing wear time.

q: A client reports an irresistible urge to move the legs that begins in the evening, worsens at rest, and is temporarily relieved by walking. Which additional assessment is the priority for the nurse to obtain?
o: Serum iron and ferritin levels
Apnea-hypopnea index from a sleep study
History of cataplexy with strong emotion
Number of vivid dreams per week
r: THE DESCRIPTION IS CLASSIC RESTLESS LEGS SYNDROME, AND IRON DEFICIENCY IS THE MOST COMMON REVERSIBLE CAUSE, so serum iron and ferritin are the priority laboratory data. An apnea-hypopnea index evaluates obstructive sleep apnea, which presents with snoring and witnessed apnea rather than an urge to move. Cataplexy is specific to narcolepsy, in which sudden loss of muscle tone occurs with strong emotion.

q: A nurse is planning interventions to promote rest for a client on a busy telemetry unit. Which actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)
o: Cluster assessments, medications, and treatments to protect uninterrupted blocks of sleep
Dim hallway and room lighting during nighttime hours
Set nonessential monitor alarms to appropriate limits and respond promptly to reduce alarm noise
Keep the room temperature comfortable and control strong odors
Perform routine linen changes and bathing at 0200 to avoid interfering with daytime therapies
Leave the television on all night so environmental noise masks hallway sounds
r: CLUSTERING CARE TO PROTECT UNINTERRUPTED SLEEP BLOCKS IS THE SINGLE MOST EFFECTIVE NURSING ACTION FOR PROMOTING REST IN THE HOSPITAL, and it is supported by dimming lights, controlling alarm and conversation noise, and managing temperature, odor, and privacy. Routine hygiene and linen changes at 0200 are nonessential tasks that fragment sleep and should be rescheduled. Leaving the television on adds light and unpredictable sound, both of which promote arousals.

q: A nurse is assessing a client who has been in the ICU for 6 days with frequent interruptions and continuous lighting. Which findings should the nurse attribute to sleep deprivation? (Select all that apply.)
o: Irritability and emotional lability
Impaired short-term memory and difficulty concentrating
Increased sensitivity to pain
Slowed reaction time and poor decision making
Increased deep tendon reflexes on the right side only
Sustained fever of 39.4 C (103 F)
r: SLEEP DEPRIVATION PRODUCES IRRITABILITY, IMPAIRED MEMORY AND CONCENTRATION, SLOWED REACTION TIME, AND A LOWERED PAIN THRESHOLD, WHICH MEANS SLEEP LOSS AND PAIN WORSEN EACH OTHER IN A CYCLE. Unilateral hyperreflexia is a focal neurologic finding suggesting a lesion and requires separate evaluation, not attribution to poor sleep. A sustained high fever indicates infection and must be investigated rather than explained by sleep loss.

q: A nurse enters the room of a client who is 1 day postoperative and finds the client laughing with visitors. When asked, the client rates the incisional pain as 8 on a 0 to 10 scale and requests the prescribed analgesic. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Administer the prescribed analgesic after checking the vital signs and sedation level
Document that the client's behavior is inconsistent with the reported pain rating
Ask the client to re-rate the pain after the visitors leave
Explain that a rating of 8 usually indicates severe distress and reassess in 1 hour
r: PAIN IS WHATEVER THE CLIENT SAYS IT IS, EXISTING WHENEVER THE CLIENT SAYS IT DOES, AND SELF-REPORT IS THE GOLD STANDARD FOR ASSESSMENT. Distraction such as laughing and socializing is a recognized coping behavior and does NOT invalidate the report, so the nurse acts on the report after verifying respiratory rate and sedation level before an opioid. Delaying treatment to re-rate later or documenting inconsistency reflects nurse bias and is a leading cause of undertreated pain.

q: A nurse is caring for an adult client who is intubated, mechanically ventilated, and unable to communicate. Which tool should the nurse use to assess this client's pain?
o: Numeric rating scale of 0 to 10
Wong-Baker FACES scale
Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool (CPOT)
PAINAD scale
r: THE CPOT (OR THE BEHAVIORAL PAIN SCALE) IS THE VALIDATED CHOICE FOR INTUBATED OR NONVERBAL CRITICALLY ILL ADULTS, scoring facial expression, body movements, muscle tension, and ventilator compliance. A numeric scale requires a client who can self-report, and Wong-Baker FACES also requires the client to look at faces and point, which an intubated sedated client cannot reliably do. PAINAD is validated specifically for advanced dementia, not for ventilated critical care clients.

q: A nurse is performing a complete pain assessment using the OLDCARTS framework for a client reporting abdominal pain. Which data should the nurse collect? (Select all that apply.)
o: When the pain started and whether it began suddenly or gradually
Where the pain is located and whether it radiates
What the pain feels like, such as burning, cramping, or aching
What makes the pain better or worse and what the client's acceptable pain goal is
The client's insurance coverage for analgesics
The nurse's own judgment of how much pain this diagnosis should cause
r: A COMPLETE PAIN ASSESSMENT COVERS ONSET, LOCATION AND RADIATION, DURATION, CHARACTER OR QUALITY, AGGRAVATING AND ALLEVIATING FACTORS, TIMING, SEVERITY, AND THE CLIENT'S FUNCTIONAL GOAL FOR PAIN CONTROL. Quality descriptors matter clinically because burning, shooting, or tingling pain suggests NEUROPATHIC pain requiring adjuvant agents rather than an opioid alone. Insurance coverage is a discharge planning concern, and substituting the nurse's judgment for the client's report is a leading cause of undertreated pain because SELF-REPORT IS THE GOLD STANDARD.

q: A client who has diabetes reports constant burning, shooting, and tingling pain in both feet that is worse at night and is not relieved by oxycodone. The nurse should anticipate a prescription for which medication?
o: Gabapentin
Additional oxycodone
Ibuprofen
Naloxone
r: BURNING, SHOOTING, AND TINGLING PAIN IS NEUROPATHIC, AND NEUROPATHIC PAIN RESPONDS BEST TO ADJUVANT ANALGESICS SUCH AS ANTICONVULSANTS (GABAPENTIN, PREGABALIN) AND CERTAIN ANTIDEPRESSANTS (DULOXETINE, AMITRIPTYLINE) RATHER THAN TO OPIOIDS ALONE. Escalating the opioid is the tempting answer, but poor opioid response is exactly what characterizes neuropathic pain and simply adds sedation and constipation risk. NSAIDs target inflammatory nociceptive pain, and naloxone is an opioid reversal agent.

q: A client reports an acute ankle injury sustained 2 hours ago with swelling and throbbing pain. Which nursing intervention is most appropriate?
o: Apply an ice pack for 15 to 20 minutes with a cloth barrier and elevate the extremity
Apply a heating pad directly to the skin for 1 hour
Apply moist heat and encourage weight bearing
Massage the swollen area vigorously to disperse the fluid
r: COLD IS INDICATED FOR ACUTE INJURY IN THE FIRST 24 TO 48 HOURS BECAUSE VASOCONSTRICTION LIMITS EDEMA, BLEEDING, AND INFLAMMATION, WHILE HEAT IS USED LATER FOR STIFFNESS, MUSCLE SPASM, AND CHRONIC PAIN. Applications are limited to 15 to 20 minutes with a barrier between the device and skin to prevent tissue injury, and a heating pad placed directly on skin for an hour risks burns. Vigorous massage over an acutely swollen, possibly fractured joint can worsen tissue damage.

q: A nurse is planning nonpharmacologic and complementary interventions for a client with chronic low back pain. Which interventions are appropriate for the nurse to include? (Select all that apply.)
o: Guided imagery and progressive relaxation with slow deep breathing
Music therapy or another distraction technique during painful procedures
Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) as prescribed
Asking the client about the use of herbal supplements and dietary products
Instructing the client to stop all prescribed analgesics once complementary therapies begin
Advising the client to avoid all physical activity until the pain resolves completely
r: NONPHARMACOLOGIC AND COMPLEMENTARY MEASURES SUCH AS IMAGERY, RELAXATION, DISTRACTION, MUSIC, MASSAGE, REPOSITIONING, ACUPRESSURE, AND TENS ARE USED WITH, NOT INSTEAD OF, PRESCRIBED ANALGESICS AS PART OF MULTIMODAL ANALGESIA. THE NURSE MUST ALWAYS ASK ABOUT HERBAL AND DIETARY SUPPLEMENTS BECAUSE OF INTERACTIONS, for example ginkgo, garlic, ginger, and fish oil increasing bleeding risk with NSAIDs or anticoagulants, and St. John's wort altering the metabolism of many drugs. Stopping prescribed analgesics is outside the nurse's scope, and prolonged inactivity worsens chronic low back pain rather than relieving it.

q: A client with osteoarthritis takes acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours and reports also taking two tablets of an over-the-counter cold remedy containing acetaminophen 325 mg per tablet three times daily. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Calculate the client's total daily acetaminophen intake and notify the provider
Document the medications and reassess in 1 week
Instruct the client to take the acetaminophen with food
Encourage the client to increase fluid intake to protect the kidneys
r: THE MAXIMUM ACETAMINOPHEN DOSE FOR A HEALTHY ADULT IS 4 g (4,000 mg) IN 24 HOURS, AND EXCEEDING IT CAUSES HEPATOTOXICITY. This client takes 650 x 4 = 2,600 mg plus 650 x 3 = 1,950 mg, a total of 4,550 mg/day, which is above the limit, so the nurse must calculate the total and report it. Taking it with food and increasing fluids do not address the hepatotoxic dose, and waiting a week allows ongoing liver injury.

q: A nurse is teaching a client who has a new prescription for ibuprofen for chronic knee pain. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?
o: "I will take it with food or a full glass of milk."
"I will call my provider if my stools look black and tarry."
"I can take my daily aspirin and add naproxen when the ibuprofen is not enough."
"I should tell my provider if my ankles start to swell or I make less urine."
r: COMBINING MULTIPLE NSAIDS, INCLUDING ASPIRIN PLUS IBUPROFEN PLUS NAPROXEN, MULTIPLIES THE RISK OF GI BLEEDING AND RENAL INJURY WITHOUT IMPROVING ANALGESIA. NSAIDs should be taken with food or milk to limit gastric irritation, and black tarry stools signal GI bleeding that must be reported immediately. Edema and decreased urine output are early signs of NSAID-related renal impairment and are correctly reported.

q: A nurse is preparing to administer the scheduled dose of IV morphine to a postoperative client. On assessment the client is difficult to arouse, and the respiratory rate is 9/min with shallow effort. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Administer the morphine and monitor closely
Withhold the morphine, stimulate the client, and assess oxygenation
Administer naloxone immediately
Document the findings and reassess in 30 minutes
r: THE NURSE MUST HOLD THE OPIOID AND REASSESS WHEN THE RESPIRATORY RATE IS BELOW 12/min, THEN STIMULATE THE CLIENT, POSITION FOR AIRWAY PATENCY, APPLY OXYGEN AND PULSE OXIMETRY, AND NOTIFY THE PROVIDER. Giving the dose would deepen respiratory depression. Naloxone is the antidote and may be needed, but it requires a prescription or protocol and is not the FIRST action when simple stimulation and airway support may restore adequate ventilation; naloxone also reverses analgesia and can precipitate withdrawal.

q: A nurse is monitoring several clients receiving opioid analgesia. Which finding is the earliest warning of impending opioid-induced respiratory depression?
o: Respiratory rate of 10/min
Oxygen saturation of 90% on room air
A rising sedation score, with the client drifting off to sleep during conversation
Report of nausea and pruritus
r: SEDATION ALWAYS PRECEDES RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, SO AN INCREASING SEDATION LEVEL IS THE EARLIEST AND MOST SENSITIVE WARNING SIGN AND IS WHY SEDATION SCALES ARE ASSESSED WITH EVERY OPIOID DOSE. A respiratory rate of 10/min and a falling oxygen saturation are late findings that appear after sedation has already deepened, and pulse oximetry is especially delayed in clients receiving supplemental oxygen. Nausea and pruritus are common opioid side effects unrelated to respiratory risk.

q: A nurse is caring for a client starting long-term opioid therapy for cancer pain. Which interventions and teaching points should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)
o: Start a bowel regimen with a stimulant laxative and stool softener at the same time the opioid begins
Assess respiratory rate and sedation level before and after each dose
Teach that nausea and sedation usually improve within several days as tolerance develops
Teach that constipation will resolve on its own once tolerance develops
Instruct the client to change positions slowly because of orthostatic hypotension
Reassure the client that needing a higher dose over time always means addiction
r: CONSTIPATION IS THE ONE OPIOID SIDE EFFECT TO WHICH TOLERANCE DOES NOT DEVELOP, SO A BOWEL REGIMEN IS STARTED WITH THE FIRST DOSE AND CONTINUED FOR THE DURATION OF THERAPY. Respiratory rate and sedation are assessed before and after dosing, and sedation, nausea, and orthostatic effects typically diminish as tolerance develops. TOLERANCE (needing more drug for the same effect) AND PHYSICAL DEPENDENCE (withdrawal on abrupt discontinuation) ARE EXPECTED PHYSIOLOGIC RESPONSES AND ARE NOT ADDICTION, which is compulsive use despite harm.

q: A nurse is teaching a client and family about a newly started morphine PCA pump. Which statements should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)
o: "Only you may press the button; family members must never press it for you."
"Press the button when you first begin to feel pain rather than waiting until it is severe."
"The pump has a lockout interval, so extra presses during that time will not deliver more medication."
"If you fall asleep, your spouse should press the button so you stay ahead of the pain."
"Tell the nurse if the pain is not controlled so the settings can be reevaluated."
"You may remove the pulse oximeter once you feel comfortable."
r: ONLY THE CLIENT MAY PRESS THE PCA BUTTON; PCA BY PROXY, MEANING A FAMILY MEMBER OR STAFF PRESSING IT, DEFEATS THE BUILT-IN SAFETY MECHANISM AND HAS CAUSED FATAL RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION. The safety design depends on the sedated client being unable to press the button, so pressing it during sleep is exactly the dangerous action. Early dosing and a lockout interval are correct teaching, and continuous respiratory and sedation monitoring must remain in place.

q: A nurse administers IV hydromorphone to a client reporting pain rated 8 out of 10. At what point should the nurse reassess the client's pain to evaluate the effectiveness of the intervention?
o: In 5 minutes
In 15 to 30 minutes
In 60 minutes
At the next scheduled assessment in 4 hours
r: EVALUATION IS COMPLETED BY REASSESSING PAIN AT THE MEDICATION'S PEAK EFFECT: ABOUT 15 TO 30 MINUTES AFTER AN IV ANALGESIC AND ABOUT 60 MINUTES AFTER AN ORAL ANALGESIC. Reassessing at 5 minutes is too early because peak effect has not occurred and may lead to unnecessary redosing and stacking. Waiting 60 minutes or until the next routine assessment delays recognition of inadequate relief or oversedation.

q: A client with metastatic cancer has continuous pain rated 7 out of 10 and takes an immediate-release opioid PRN, requesting it every 3 to 4 hours around the clock. Which recommendation should the nurse discuss with the provider?
o: Change to scheduled around-the-clock long-acting opioid dosing with PRN doses available for breakthrough pain
Continue PRN dosing only, to reduce the risk of addiction
Space the PRN doses to every 6 hours to prevent tolerance
Replace the opioid with acetaminophen and relaxation techniques
r: FOR CONTINUOUS CHRONIC OR TERMINAL PAIN, AROUND-THE-CLOCK SCHEDULED DOSING WITH A LONG-ACTING AGENT PLUS PRN BREAKTHROUGH DOSES MAINTAINS STEADY BLOOD LEVELS AND PREVENTS THE PEAKS AND VALLEYS OF PRN-ONLY DOSING. Withholding or spacing doses out of fear of addiction is a classic barrier to effective pain management and leads to undertreatment; physical dependence and tolerance are expected and are not addiction. Acetaminophen and relaxation alone cannot control severe cancer pain, though they may be added as part of multimodal therapy.

q: A nurse is reviewing risk for undertreated pain on a medical-surgical unit. Which clients should the nurse identify as being at increased risk for having their pain undertreated? (Select all that apply.)
o: An 86-year-old client with advanced dementia who moans and grimaces during repositioning
A client who is intubated and sedated in the ICU
A client with a history of opioid use disorder reporting postoperative pain of 9 out of 10
A client with limited English proficiency and no interpreter present
An alert adult client who uses a numeric rating scale and asks for medication when needed
A postoperative client who uses a PCA pump and reports pain of 3 out of 10
r: CLIENTS WHO CANNOT SELF-REPORT (ADVANCED DEMENTIA, INTUBATION, LANGUAGE BARRIERS) AND CLIENTS STIGMATIZED BY A SUBSTANCE USE HISTORY ARE AT THE HIGHEST RISK FOR UNDERTREATED PAIN. Behavioral tools such as PAINAD, CPOT, and FLACC and the use of a qualified interpreter with a Wong-Baker FACES scale close that gap. A client with opioid use disorder often needs HIGHER, not lower, doses because of tolerance, and withholding analgesia is not a treatment for addiction.

q: A nurse is assessing pain in a client with advanced dementia who cannot report pain verbally. Which observations support the presence of pain? (Select all that apply.)
o: Grimacing and furrowed brow
Noisy, labored breathing and repeated groaning
New restlessness, rigidity, and resistance to care
Consolable by voice and touch within seconds and returning to calm sleep
Guarding a hip and refusing to bear weight
Relaxed body posture with normal breathing during a full bath
r: THE PAINAD SCALE SCORES BREATHING, NEGATIVE VOCALIZATION, FACIAL EXPRESSION, BODY LANGUAGE, AND CONSOLABILITY, SO GRIMACING, GROANING, LABORED BREATHING, RIGIDITY, AND GUARDING ARE VALID PAIN INDICATORS IN NONVERBAL CLIENTS. Behavioral change and agitation in dementia should be evaluated as possible pain before being treated as a behavioral problem. Being easily consoled and returning to calm sleep scores as no distress and does not support pain.

q: A nurse is teaching a client to take 2 tsp of an oral solution at home. The client will use a calibrated oral syringe marked in milliliters. How many mL should the nurse instruct the client to draw up? (Round to the nearest whole number.)
o: 5 mL
10 mL
15 mL
30 mL
r: FORMULA: desired amount x conversion factor. 1 tsp = 5 mL, SO 2 tsp x 5 mL/tsp = 10 mL. Key equivalents to memorize: 1 tsp = 5 mL, 1 TBSP = 15 mL = 3 tsp, 1 oz = 30 mL, 1 cup = 240 mL. A common wrong answer is 5 mL, which comes from converting only 1 tsp instead of 2; another is 15 mL, which comes from confusing tsp with Tbsp.

q: A nurse is preparing to administer 45 mL of magnesium hydroxide to a client who will continue the medication at home using a household tablespoon. How many tablespoons equal the prescribed dose?
o: 1.5 Tbsp
3 Tbsp
4.5 Tbsp
9 Tbsp
r: FORMULA: total mL divided by mL per household unit. 1 TBSP = 15 mL, SO 45 mL divided by 15 mL/Tbsp = 3 Tbsp. A common wrong answer is 9, which is the number of TEASPOONS (45 divided by 5), a mix-up of tsp and Tbsp. Another error is 1.5, obtained by dividing 45 by 30 after confusing the tablespoon with the ounce.

q: A nurse is admitting an infant who weighs 15 lb 8 oz. What is the infant's weight in kilograms? (Round to the nearest hundredth.)
r: STEP 1, convert ounces to pounds: 16 oz = 1 lb, so 8 oz divided by 16 = 0.5 lb, giving 15.5 lb. STEP 2, convert to kilograms: 1 kg = 2.2 lb, SO 15.5 lb divided by 2.2 = 7.045, WHICH ROUNDS TO 7.05 kg. A common wrong answer is 7.50, from writing 15 lb 8 oz as 15.8 lb; another is 6.82, from dropping the 8 oz entirely (15 divided by 2.2). Choosing 34.10 means the student MULTIPLIED by 2.2 instead of dividing, which is the error to watch for since pounds are always the larger number.

q: A provider prescribes levothyroxine 0.088 mg PO daily. The pharmacy supplies levothyroxine 44 mcg tablets. How many tablets should the nurse administer per dose?
o: 0.5 tablet
1 tablet
2 tablets
4 tablets
r: STEP 1, make units match: 1 mg = 1,000 mcg, SO 0.088 mg x 1,000 = 88 mcg (move the decimal 3 places RIGHT when going from mg to mcg). STEP 2, apply DESIRED divided by HAVE x QUANTITY: 88 mcg divided by 44 mcg x 1 tablet = 2 tablets. A common wrong answer is 0.5 tablet, which happens when the student moves the decimal the wrong direction and treats 0.088 mg as smaller than the tablet strength. Always convert before calculating, never compare mg to mcg directly.

q: A nurse is preparing acetaminophen 240 mg PO for a child. The bottle is labeled acetaminophen 160 mg/5 mL. How many mL should the nurse administer? (Round to the nearest tenth.)
o: 3.3 mL
5 mL
7.5 mL
10 mL
r: FORMULA: DESIRED divided by HAVE x QUANTITY = 240 mg divided by 160 mg x 5 mL = 1.5 x 5 = 7.5 mL. A common wrong answer is 3.3 mL, which results from INVERTING the ratio (160 divided by 240 x 5). Another is 10 mL, from rounding 240 up to 320 mg, which is two full 5 mL doses.

q: A provider prescribes an antibiotic 45 mg/kg/day PO divided into equal doses every 8 hr for a child who weighs 66 lb. How many mg should the nurse administer per dose?
o: 450 mg
675 mg
990 mg
r: STEP 1, convert weight: 66 lb divided by 2.2 = 30 kg. STEP 2, total daily dose: 30 kg x 45 mg/kg/day = 1,350 mg/day. STEP 3, DIVIDE BY THE NUMBER OF DOSES: every 8 hr means 24 divided by 8 = 3 DOSES PER DAY, so 1,350 divided by 3 = 450 mg per dose. THE SINGLE MOST COMMON ERROR IS ANSWERING 1,350 mg, WHICH IS THE TOTAL DAILY DOSE GIVEN AS ONE DOSE; another is 675 mg, from dividing by 2 doses instead of 3. Choosing 990 mg means the student used pounds instead of kilograms (66 x 45 divided by 3).

q: The safe dose range for a medication is 15 to 40 mg/kg/day PO divided every 6 hr. A child weighs 22 lb. What is the maximum safe amount the nurse may give in a single dose?
o: 40 mg
100 mg
200 mg
400 mg
r: STEP 1, convert weight: 22 lb divided by 2.2 = 10 kg. STEP 2, maximum daily dose: 10 kg x 40 mg/kg/day = 400 mg/day. STEP 3, DIVIDE BY DOSES PER DAY: every 6 hr = 4 DOSES, so 400 divided by 4 = 100 mg MAXIMUM PER DOSE. Answering 400 mg is the classic error of reporting the daily maximum as a single dose, which would give the child four times the safe amount in 24 hr. Answering 40 mg comes from multiplying 40 mg/kg by 1 kg instead of 10 kg.

q: A nurse reconstitutes a 500 mg vial of powdered medication with 2 mL of diluent as directed, yielding a concentration of 250 mg/mL. The prescription reads 375 mg IM now. How many mL should the nurse withdraw? (Round to the nearest tenth.)
o: 0.8 mL
1.5 mL
2 mL
3 mL
r: FORMULA: DESIRED divided by HAVE x QUANTITY, USING THE CONCENTRATION PRINTED AFTER RECONSTITUTION, NOT THE POWDER STRENGTH ON THE VIAL. 375 mg divided by 250 mg x 1 mL = 1.5 mL. A common wrong answer is 0.8 mL, from using the 500 mg powder strength (375 divided by 500 x 1). Answering 2 mL means the student gave the entire reconstituted volume, which would deliver 500 mg, a 33% overdose.

q: A provider prescribes 1,000 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride IV to infuse over 8 hr. The nurse is using an electronic infusion pump. Which rate in mL/hr should the nurse program?
o: 80 mL/hr
125 mL/hr
133 mL/hr
150 mL/hr
r: FORMULA: total volume in mL divided by total time in hr = 1,000 mL divided by 8 hr = 125 mL/hr. A common wrong answer is 133 mL/hr, from dividing by 7.5 hr or from a transposed digit; another is 80 mL/hr, from inverting the fraction (8 divided by 1,000 x 100). PUMP RATES ARE ALWAYS EXPRESSED IN mL/hr AND ARE NOT AFFECTED BY THE TUBING DROP FACTOR.

q: A nurse is to infuse an IV antibiotic in 250 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride over 90 min using an infusion pump. Which rate in mL/hr should the nurse program? (Round to the nearest whole number.)
o: 100 mL/hr
150 mL/hr
167 mL/hr
278 mL/hr
r: STEP 1, convert minutes to hours: 90 min divided by 60 min/hr = 1.5 hr. STEP 2, FORMULA: volume divided by time = 250 mL divided by 1.5 hr = 166.67, WHICH ROUNDS TO 167 mL/hr. A common wrong answer is 278 mL/hr, which comes from dividing 250 by 0.9 after mistakenly treating 90 min as 0.9 hr. Answering 150 mL/hr comes from setting the rate to the volume infused in the first hour without accounting for the remaining 100 mL.

q: A nurse is administering 1,000 mL of lactated Ringer's IV over 10 hr by gravity using tubing with a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL. What flow rate in gtt/min should the nurse set? (Round to the nearest whole number.)
o: 17 gtt/min
25 gtt/min
50 gtt/min
100 gtt/min
r: STEP 1, find mL/hr: 1,000 mL divided by 10 hr = 100 mL/hr. STEP 2, FORMULA: (mL/hr x DROP FACTOR) divided by 60 min = (100 x 15) divided by 60 = 1,500 divided by 60 = 25 gtt/min. A common wrong answer is 17 gtt/min, from using a 10 gtt/mL drop factor instead of the 15 gtt/mL printed on the package. Answering 100 gtt/min means the student stopped at mL/hr and never applied the drop factor.

q: A nurse is infusing 250 mL of IV fluid over 2 hr by gravity with tubing that has a drop factor of 20 gtt/mL. What flow rate in gtt/min should the nurse set? (Round to the nearest whole number.)
o: 21 gtt/min
42 gtt/min
83 gtt/min
125 gtt/min
r: STEP 1, find mL/hr: 250 mL divided by 2 hr = 125 mL/hr. STEP 2, FORMULA: (mL/hr x DROP FACTOR) divided by 60 = (125 x 20) divided by 60 = 2,500 divided by 60 = 41.67, WHICH ROUNDS TO 42 gtt/min. DROPS ARE ALWAYS ROUNDED TO A WHOLE NUMBER because a partial drop cannot be delivered. A common wrong answer is 21 gtt/min, from dividing the volume by 2 hr twice; 125 gtt/min is the mL/hr rate reported without applying the drop factor.

q: At 1000 a nurse notes that 800 mL remains in a client's IV bag infusing at 150 mL/hr. Approximately how much longer will the infusion take?
o: 5 hr 3 min
5 hr 20 min
5 hr 33 min
6 hr
r: FORMULA: volume remaining divided by rate = 800 mL divided by 150 mL/hr = 5.33 hr. TO CONVERT THE DECIMAL PORTION TO MINUTES, MULTIPLY BY 60, NOT BY 100: 0.33 x 60 = 20 min, so the answer is 5 hr 20 min (the bag empties at about 1520). The classic wrong answer is 5 hr 33 min, from reading the decimal .33 directly as 33 minutes. Answering 6 hr comes from rounding the hours up instead of converting the remainder.

q: A nurse is calculating a client's 8-hr oral intake. The client consumed 6 oz of coffee, 4 oz of apple juice, 1 cup of broth, 4 Tbsp of gelatin, and 2 tsp of a liquid supplement. What is the client's total intake in mL?
o: 460 mL
600 mL
610 mL
670 mL
r: CONVERT EACH ITEM USING 1 oz = 30 mL, 1 CUP = 240 mL, 1 TBSP = 15 mL, 1 tsp = 5 mL, THEN ADD. Coffee 6 x 30 = 180; juice 4 x 30 = 120; broth = 240; gelatin 4 x 15 = 60; supplement 2 x 5 = 10. Total = 180 + 120 + 240 + 60 + 10 = 610 mL. A common wrong answer is 600 mL, from omitting the small 10 mL supplement; 460 mL results from using 1 oz = 15 mL, and 670 mL results from using 1 Tbsp = 30 mL.

q: A provider prescribes enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously every 12 hr for a client who weighs 154 lb. The available prefilled syringe is labeled 100 mg/mL. How many mL should the nurse administer per dose? (Round to the nearest tenth.)
o: 0.7 mL
1.4 mL
1.5 mL
r: STEP 1, convert weight: 154 lb divided by 2.2 = 70 kg. STEP 2, calculate the dose: 70 kg x 1 mg/kg = 70 mg per dose. STEP 3, DESIRED divided by HAVE x QUANTITY: 70 mg divided by 100 mg x 1 mL = 0.7 mL. A common wrong answer is 1.5 mL, from using pounds instead of kilograms (154 mg divided by 100). Answering 0.35 mL comes from incorrectly halving the dose because the drug is given twice daily, but 1 mg/kg IS ALREADY THE PER-DOSE AMOUNT, NOT THE DAILY TOTAL.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has been on bed rest for 5 days following a pelvic fracture. Which of the following assessment findings requires immediate follow-up?
o: The client reports a decreased appetite at the last two meals
Bowel sounds are absent in all four quadrants
The client's last stool was formed and passed 2 days ago
The client reports feeling bored and asks for a television
r: ABSENT BOWEL SOUNDS IN ALL FOUR QUADRANTS SUGGEST PARALYTIC ILEUS, a complication of immobility that requires immediate provider notification. Anorexia and constipation are expected metabolic and GI effects of immobility and are managed with fiber, fluids, and increased activity rather than urgent intervention. Boredom reflects the psychosocial effects of immobility and is important, but it is not the priority finding.

q: A nurse is planning care for a client who will be immobile for an extended period following a spinal cord injury. Which of the following complications should the nurse anticipate? (Select all that apply.)
o: Atelectasis
Orthostatic hypotension
Increased bone density
Renal calculi
Joint contractures
Increased peristalsis
r: Immobility causes pooled secretions and shallow breathing (atelectasis and pneumonia), loss of plasma volume with blunted baroreceptor response (orthostatic hypotension), urinary stasis with hypercalcemia (RENAL CALCULI), and shortening of muscle fibers and connective tissue (CONTRACTURES). Immobility produces DISUSE OSTEOPOROSIS, so bone density DECREASES rather than increases. Peristalsis SLOWS with immobility, causing constipation, not increased motility.

q: A nurse is teaching a nursing student about performing passive range-of-motion exercises for a client who is unconscious. Which statement by the student indicates an understanding of the teaching?
o: 'These exercises will rebuild the client's muscle strength.'
'The main goal of these exercises is to prevent contractures.'
'I should move each joint until the client reports discomfort.'
'I should perform these exercises only once a day, at bath time.'
r: THE PRIMARY GOAL OF PASSIVE ROM IS TO PREVENT CONTRACTURES and maintain joint flexibility. Passive ROM does not build strength because the client is not contracting the muscle; ACTIVE ROM is required for strengthening. An unconscious client cannot report discomfort, so the nurse moves each joint only to the point of resistance, and ROM is performed at least 2 to 3 times daily rather than once.

q: A nurse is teaching a client who has left-sided weakness following a stroke how to use a single-point cane. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
o: 'I will hold the cane in my right hand.'
'I will hold the cane on my left side since that leg is weak.'
'I will move the cane forward first, then my left leg, then my right leg.'
'The top of the cane should line up with the crease of my wrist.'
r: THE CANE IS ALWAYS HELD ON THE CLIENT'S STRONG (UNAFFECTED) SIDE, so a client with left-sided weakness holds the cane in the RIGHT hand; the statement about holding it on the left requires correction. Advancing the cane, then the weak leg, then the strong leg, and sizing the cane so the handle is level with the wrist crease with 15 to 30 degrees of elbow flexion are all correct.

q: A nurse is teaching a client who has a right leg injury how to use crutches on stairs. Which of the following instructions should the nurse include?
o: 'Lead with your right leg going up the stairs and with your left leg going down.'
'Lead with your left leg going up the stairs and with your right leg going down.'
'Lead with both crutches going up and with your left leg going down.'
'Keep both legs together and hop up each step.'
r: The rule is UP WITH THE GOOD LEG, DOWN WITH THE BAD. The unaffected left leg steps up first, and going down the affected right leg moves with the crutches. Leading up with the injured leg forces the weak limb to bear full body weight against gravity and greatly increases the risk of a fall.

q: A nurse is reviewing fall risk factors for an older adult client admitted to a medical unit. Which of the following are EXTRINSIC fall risk factors? (Select all that apply.)
o: A cluttered pathway between the bed and the bathroom
The client takes furosemide and lorazepam
The call light is placed on a table out of the client's reach
The client has a history of two falls in the past year
The client ambulates in loose slippers with smooth soles
r: EXTRINSIC RISK FACTORS ARE IN THE ENVIRONMENT: clutter, an out-of-reach call light, improper footwear, wet floors, poor lighting, cords, and a bed left in a high position. INTRINSIC factors belong to the client, including advanced age, a history of falls, weakness, confusion, sensory deficits, incontinence, orthostatic hypotension, and medications such as diuretics, sedatives, and antihypertensives. Therefore the furosemide and lorazepam use and the fall history are intrinsic, not extrinsic.

q: A nurse enters a client's room and finds the client lying on the floor beside the bed. Which action should the nurse take FIRST?
o: Notify the provider
Assess the client for injury and obtain vital signs
Complete an incident report
Assist the client back into bed
r: ASSESS THE CLIENT FIRST, including level of consciousness, airway, obvious injury, and vital signs, before moving the client or contacting anyone. Moving a client who has an undetected fracture or head injury can cause further harm. Provider notification follows the assessment, and the incident report is completed last.

q: A client sustained an unwitnessed fall on the unit. After assessing the client and notifying the provider, which action should the nurse take?
o: Document in the medical record that an incident report was completed
Chart the objective findings in the medical record and complete the incident report separately
Place a copy of the incident report in the client's chart
Ask the client's family to sign the incident report
r: The nurse charts OBJECTIVE, FACTUAL FINDINGS in the medical record (how and where the client was found, assessment data, interventions, and who was notified) and completes the incident report as a separate risk-management document. AN INCIDENT REPORT IS NEVER CHARTED, REFERENCED, OR FILED IN THE MEDICAL RECORD, because it is an internal quality-improvement tool and referencing it makes it discoverable in litigation.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who is confused and repeatedly pulling at an IV line. Which action should the nurse take FIRST?
o: Apply soft wrist restraints to both wrists
Obtain a PRN restraint order from the provider
Attempt less restrictive alternatives, such as family presence and camouflaging the IV site
Raise all four side rails and move the client to a room near the nurses' station
r: LESS RESTRICTIVE ALTERNATIVES MUST BE ATTEMPTED AND DOCUMENTED BEFORE RESTRAINTS ARE USED, including diversion, family presence, covering or camouflaging the IV site, frequent toileting, and reorientation. PRN RESTRAINT ORDERS ARE NEVER PERMITTED, and raising all four side rails is itself considered a restraint.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has bilateral soft wrist restraints. Which of the following tasks may the nurse delegate to an assistive personnel? (Select all that apply.)
o: Repositioning the client every 2 hr
Offering fluids and assisting with meals
Performing range-of-motion exercises to the restrained extremities
Assessing skin integrity and circulation beneath the restraint
Determining whether the restraint is still needed
Assisting the client to the bathroom during a scheduled restraint release
r: Assistive personnel may perform standardized, predictable tasks such as repositioning, ROM, offering food and fluids, and toileting during scheduled restraint releases. ASSESSMENT OF CIRCULATION AND SKIN INTEGRITY AND THE DECISION ABOUT CONTINUED NEED FOR RESTRAINT CANNOT BE DELEGATED, because both require nursing judgment and remain the RN's responsibility.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has bilateral soft wrist restraints applied. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)
o: Secure the restraint straps to the bed frame using a quick-release knot
Verify that two fingers can slide between the restraint and the client's skin
Tie the straps to the side rails so the restraint moves with the rail
Assess neurovascular status and skin under the restraint at least every 2 hr
Obtain a renewal of the time-limited restraint order according to facility policy
Request a PRN restraint order so the restraints can be reapplied as needed
r: RESTRAINTS ARE SECURED WITH A QUICK-RELEASE KNOT TO THE BED FRAME, NEVER TO A SIDE RAIL, because raising or lowering the rail would jerk or tighten the restraint and injure the client. Two fingers should slide easily underneath, circulation and skin are assessed at least every 2 hr with release, ROM, toileting, and fluids, and orders are TIME-LIMITED and must be renewed. PRN RESTRAINT ORDERS ARE NEVER ACCEPTABLE.

q: A nurse is preparing to reposition a client who weighs 250 lb (113 kg) and is unable to assist. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)
o: Raise the bed to the level of the nurse's waist before repositioning
Obtain additional staff and use a friction-reducing sheet or a mechanical lift
Pivot the entire body rather than twisting at the waist
Lift using the back muscles while keeping the knees straight
Hold the client's weight as far from the nurse's center of gravity as possible
r: Safe patient handling means RAISING THE BED TO THE CAREGIVER'S WAIST HEIGHT DURING THE TASK, getting help, using lift sheets or mechanical lifts, keeping a wide base of support, and pivoting the whole body because TWISTING AT THE WAIST IS THE MOST COMMON CAUSE OF CAREGIVER BACK INJURY. The nurse lifts with the leg muscles by bending the knees, not the back, and keeps the load close to the center of gravity. The bed is returned to the LOWEST position after the task, for the client's fall safety.

q: A nurse observes a client seated in a chair begin to have a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Which action should the nurse take FIRST?
o: Insert an oral airway to protect the tongue
Ease the client to the floor and turn the client onto the side
Restrain the client's extremities to prevent injury
Obtain vital signs and a blood glucose level
