r: CLEAN-CATCH MIDSTREAM MEANS: cleanse front to back FIRST, start the stream INTO THE TOILET to flush out perineal flora, then catch the MIDDLE portion in the container. Starting in the container collects contaminants and gives a falsely positive culture. Cleansing after starting to void defeats the purpose entirely.

q: The healthcare provider prescribes morphine 0.5 mg/kg IM. The client weighs 20 lb. How many mg will the nurse administer? (Round to the nearest tenth.)
o: 4.5 mg
9.1 mg
10 mg
22 mg
r: Convert first: 20 lb ÷ 2.2 = 9.09 kg. Then multiply: 9.09 × 0.5 mg/kg = 4.5 MG. THE CLASSIC ERROR IS SKIPPING THE POUND-TO-KILOGRAM CONVERSION and calculating 20 × 0.5 = 10 mg, which more than doubles the dose. Getting 9.1 means you stopped at the kilogram conversion and forgot to apply the mg/kg.

q: A nurse is caring for an older adult client who is incontinent. Which effects of aging might contribute to urinary alterations? Select all that apply.
o: Decreased bladder contractility may lead to urine retention and stasis
Increased bladder motility decreases the incidence of urinary tract infections
Diminished ability of the kidneys to concentrate urine may result in nocturia
Decreased bladder muscle tone may reduce the capacity of the bladder to hold urine
Neuromuscular problems may interfere with voluntary control of urination
r: AGING REDUCES BLADDER CONTRACTILITY, MUSCLE TONE AND RENAL CONCENTRATING ABILITY, and neuromuscular changes impair voluntary control — all four raise the risk of retention, stasis, nocturia and incontinence. The false option is reversed: aging does NOT increase bladder motility, and urinary stasis actually INCREASES UTI risk in older adults. Watch for distractors that claim aging IMPROVES something.

q: The nurse is caring for a group of clients on the acute care unit. Which client(s) will benefit from urinary catheterization? Select all that apply.
o: A client with an enlarged prostate that is unable to void
A client that is unable to mobilize to the bathroom following abdominal surgery
A client that developed a urinary tract infection
A confused client that requires a sterile urine specimen to be obtained
r: A CATHETER REQUIRES A MEDICAL INDICATION, NOT CONVENIENCE. Acute retention from an enlarged prostate is a true indication, and a straight cath is appropriate to obtain a sterile specimen from a confused client who cannot cooperate with a clean catch. BEING UNABLE TO WALK TO THE BATHROOM IS NOT AN INDICATION — that is exactly the convenience catheter that drives CAUTI rates, and a bedpan or toileting assistance is the answer. Having a UTI is a reason to AVOID a catheter, not place one.

q: A nurse is assessing the freshly voided urine of a client. Which two characteristics would indicate a urinary system problem? Select all that apply.
o: The urine is amber colored
The urine pH is 6.0
The urine is translucent
The urine is cloudy
There is pus in the urine
r: CLOUDINESS AND PYURIA (PUS) ARE BOTH ABNORMAL and suggest infection. Normal urine is amber or straw-colored, CLEAR/TRANSLUCENT, and has a pH around 4.6–8.0 — so amber, translucent and a pH of 6.0 are all expected findings. The trap is that three of the five options are deliberately NORMAL.

q: A nurse is explaining the vascular response of inflammation to a client receiving anti-inflammatory drugs. Which statement should be included in the teaching?
o: Vasodilation increases blood delivery to the injury site
Decreased blood flow limits the spread of infection
Chemical mediators reduce vascular permeability
White blood cell count decreases at the injury site
r: VASODILATION WIDENS THE VESSELS AND INCREASES BLOOD FLOW, delivering oxygen, nutrients and immune cells — which is exactly why you see redness, warmth and swelling. All three distractors are the physiology REVERSED: blood flow increases (not decreases), chemical mediators INCREASE vascular permeability, and WBCs INCREASE at the site.

q: A nurse is explaining the prodromal stage of infection to the parent of a child diagnosed with strep throat. Which statement by the parent indicates a NEED FOR FURTHER TEACHING?
o: “In this stage, my child cannot easily spread strep throat.”
“My child is most contagious during this stage.”
“My child should stay home from school right now.”
“The symptoms right now are vague and nonspecific.”
r: THE PRODROMAL STAGE IS WHEN THE CLIENT IS MOST CONTAGIOUS, even though symptoms are still vague — so saying the child can't easily spread it is exactly wrong and needs correcting. The other three are all accurate. Know the four stages: INCUBATION (exposed, no symptoms) → PRODROMAL (vague symptoms, MOST contagious) → ILLNESS (specific symptoms) → CONVALESCENCE (recovery).

q: A client reports fatigue, mild sore throat, and low-grade fever, stating, “I feel like I'm coming down with something.” The nurse identifies the client as being in which stage of infection?
o: Incubation
Prodromal
Illness
Convalescence
r: VAGUE, NONSPECIFIC SYMPTOMS PLUS “COMING DOWN WITH SOMETHING” IS THE PRODROMAL STAGE — and this is when the client is MOST CONTAGIOUS. In incubation there are no symptoms at all; the illness stage brings specific symptoms like a high fever and severe sore throat; convalescence is recovery.

q: A nurse is preparing to administer a scheduled oral medication. The client states, “I do not want to take the medication.” Which action should the nurse take FIRST?
o: Ask the client to explain the reason for refusing the medication
Explain the purpose and benefits of the medication
Document the refusal in the medical record
Notify the health care provider of the refusal
r: ASSESSMENT ALWAYS COMES FIRST — find out WHY before you teach, document or notify. The reason drives everything that follows: nausea, a side effect, a misunderstanding, or a values-based refusal each require a different response. Clients have the right to refuse; after assessing you educate, then document, then notify the provider.

q: A provider explains to a client that they have an idiosyncratic reaction in which they are UNDER-reacting to a medication. After the provider leaves, the client asks the nurse, “What did the doctor mean by an idiosyncratic reaction?” What is the nurse's BEST response?
o: “Your reaction is an unexpected underreaction to the medication.”
“Your immune system is attacking the medication.”
“You are having a toxic buildup of the medication.”
“You should ask the provider to explain that.”
r: AN IDIOSYNCRATIC REACTION IS AN UNPREDICTABLE, OFTEN GENETICALLY BASED OVER- OR UNDER-RESPONSE to a normal dose — explaining it in plain language is within the nurse's scope. An immune attack describes an ALLERGIC reaction and toxic buildup describes TOXICITY, so both are the wrong mechanism. Deflecting back to the provider abandons a client asking a reasonable question you can answer.

q: A provider prescribes a pediatric client 10 mL of liquid acetaminophen every 6 hours at home. The nurse should teach the parent to give how many teaspoons per dose?
o: 1 teaspoon
2 teaspoons
3 teaspoons
5 teaspoons
r: 1 TSP = 5 mL, so 10 ÷ 5 = 2 TEASPOONS. Always teach caregivers to use the ORAL SYRINGE or dosing cup that comes with the medication rather than a kitchen spoon, which varies widely in volume and causes real dosing errors in children.

q: A nurse educator is teaching strategies to break the chain of infection. Which should be included? Select all that apply.
o: Proper hand hygiene
Use of surgical asepsis
Effective vaccine programs
Proper food storage
Reusing single-use equipment between clients
r: EACH INTERVENTION BREAKS A DIFFERENT LINK: hand hygiene interrupts the MODE OF TRANSMISSION, surgical asepsis blocks the PORTAL OF ENTRY, vaccines protect the SUSCEPTIBLE HOST, and proper food storage eliminates the RESERVOIR. Reusing single-use equipment does the opposite — it creates a reservoir and a transmission route. Hand hygiene remains the single most effective measure.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who reports fatigue and has a fever and swollen lymph nodes. The nurse suspects which type of infection?
o: Localized infection
Systemic infection
Colonization without infection
An allergic response
r: FEVER, FATIGUE AND SWOLLEN LYMPH NODES ARE WHOLE-BODY FINDINGS, so this is a SYSTEMIC infection. A LOCALIZED infection stays confined to one site and shows redness, warmth, swelling, pain and possibly drainage AT THAT SITE only. Colonization means organisms are present without causing signs of illness at all.

q: A charge nurse is making assignments. One client is highly infectious and cannot be placed with clients at risk for infection. Which client is MOST easily infected?
o: A client with a chronic disease
A client admitted for an elective procedure
A client with a healed surgical incision
A client being discharged in the morning
r: CHRONIC DISEASE COMPROMISES IMMUNITY, making that client the most susceptible host. Think about who else lands in this category on an exam: the immunocompromised, clients on steroids or chemotherapy, older adults, infants, and the malnourished. A healed incision means the skin barrier is intact again, and neither an elective admission nor a pending discharge suggests impaired defenses.

q: A nurse is preparing to admit a client with C. difficile. Before the client arrives, which measures should the nurse ensure are in place? Select all that apply.
o: Gloves and gown for everyone entering the room, including visitors
Dedicated equipment kept in the room
Soap and water available for hand hygiene
Alcohol-based hand sanitizer at the bedside as the primary hand hygiene method
An N95 respirator for all staff entering
r: C. DIFF REQUIRES CONTACT PRECAUTIONS: gown and gloves for ALL who enter, dedicated equipment (or disinfect between clients), and SOAP AND WATER FOR HAND HYGIENE. ALCOHOL SANITIZER DOES NOT KILL C. DIFF SPORES — you need the mechanical friction of handwashing to physically remove them. An N95 is for AIRBORNE precautions such as TB, measles or varicella, not for C. diff.

q: A nurse observes an assistive personnel using alcohol-based hand sanitizer after assisting a client who has C. difficile. What should the nurse do?
o: Intervene and instruct them to wash with soap and water
Take no action; alcohol-based sanitizer is acceptable after glove removal
Document the observation and report it at the end of the shift
Remind them to use sanitizer for a full 30 seconds
r: INTERVENE IMMEDIATELY — ALCOHOL-BASED SANITIZER DOES NOT KILL C. DIFF SPORES, so soap and water is required. Waiting to document and report at end of shift leaves the spores on their hands right now, and extending the sanitizer contact time doesn't fix a product that is ineffective against spores. Remember the exceptions to sanitizer: C. DIFF, NOROVIRUS, and VISIBLY SOILED HANDS.

q: A nurse is caring for a hospice client who has died after a prolonged illness. Which action should the nurse take during post-mortem care?
o: Place the client's dentures in the mouth before rigor mortis sets in
Remove all tubes and lines immediately regardless of circumstances
Lay the body completely flat with the head lowered
Delay closing the eyelids until the family has left
r: INSERT DENTURES BEFORE RIGOR MORTIS — once rigor sets in (about 2–4 hours) the mouth cannot be opened, and dentures maintain facial appearance for the family's viewing. ELEVATE the head of the bed slightly to prevent discoloration of the face, close the eyelids gently, and DO NOT REMOVE TUBES OR LINES if an autopsy is planned or it is a coroner's case.

q: After realizing that the wrong medication was administered to a client, what is the FIRST action the nurse should take?
o: Assess the client for adverse reactions
Complete an incident report
Notify the health care provider
Notify the charge nurse and pharmacy
r: CLIENT SAFETY COMES BEFORE PAPERWORK — ASSESS FIRST for any adverse reaction, then notify the provider, then complete the incident report. This is the same pattern as a fall: assess → notify → document. And remember the incident report is an internal quality document that is NEVER referenced in the medical record.

q: A nurse is preparing to administer morning medications to a client with dysphagia. Which action should the nurse take FIRST?
o: Verify whether any medications are available in liquid form or may be crushed
Crush all of the tablets and mix them in applesauce
Hold the medications and notify the provider
Have the client take the pills with a large glass of water
r: CHECK THE FORMULATION FIRST — a liquid form may exist, and NOT EVERY TABLET CAN BE CRUSHED (never crush enteric-coated or extended-release, which would dump the entire dose at once). Crushing everything is therefore unsafe, a large glass of water increases aspiration risk in dysphagia, and holding all the medications is premature before you've explored a safe route.

q: A nurse is caring for a client in palliative care. Which statement is APPROPRIATE documentation for a client receiving end-of-life care?
o: “Client reports pain as 4 out of 10 after morphine administration.”
“Client appears comfortable and is doing much better today.”
“Family seems to be in denial about the client's condition.”
“Client did not seem to want the pain medication offered.”
r: GOOD DOCUMENTATION IS FACTUAL, OBJECTIVE AND MEASURABLE — a numeric pain rating tied to an intervention is exactly that. “Appears,” “seems” and “doing much better” are subjective interpretations, and labeling the family as “in denial” is a judgment, not an observation. Chart what the client SAID and what you OBSERVED and DID.

q: A nurse assesses a wound with full-thickness skin loss in which adipose (fat) tissue is visible, but no muscle, tendon or bone is exposed. How should the nurse stage this pressure injury?
o: Stage 1
Stage 2
Stage 3
Stage 4
r: ADIPOSE VISIBLE = STAGE 3 (full thickness, fat exposed, no muscle/tendon/bone). Stage 4 is when you can see MUSCLE, TENDON, FASCIA OR BONE. Stage 2 is PARTIAL thickness with exposed dermis, and Stage 1 is INTACT skin with non-blanchable erythema. If slough or eschar hides the base, it is UNSTAGEABLE.

q: A nurse assesses an area of partial-thickness skin loss with exposed dermis and a pink-red, moist wound bed that resembles a ruptured blister. This is which stage?
o: Stage 1
Stage 2
Stage 3
Unstageable
r: PARTIAL THICKNESS WITH EXPOSED DERMIS = STAGE 2, and the ruptured-blister appearance is the classic description. Stage 1 skin is still INTACT (non-blanchable erythema only), Stage 3 exposes ADIPOSE tissue, and a wound is UNSTAGEABLE only when slough or eschar obscures the base so you cannot see how deep it goes.

q: Mr. Thompson's Braden Scale score is 9. How should the nurse interpret this result?
o: No risk for pressure injury
Mild risk for pressure injury
Moderate risk for pressure injury
Very high risk for pressure injury
r: ON THE BRADEN SCALE, A LOWER SCORE MEANS HIGHER RISK, and ≤9 IS VERY HIGH RISK (19–23 no risk, 15–18 mild, 13–14 moderate, 10–12 high). The Braden PREDICTS RISK — it does NOT stage an existing wound. Its six subscales are sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition, and friction/shear.

q: Which client is at GREATEST risk for developing a pressure injury?
o: A 54-year-old who is obese and has been bed-bound for 2 weeks
A 30-year-old who is ambulatory after an appendectomy
A 68-year-old who uses a walker and is continent
A 45-year-old admitted for observation after a migraine
r: IMMOBILITY IS THE STRONGEST SINGLE PREDICTOR, and two weeks bed-bound plus obesity (moisture in skin folds, difficulty repositioning, poorer tissue perfusion) stacks the risk. The other clients are all mobile — and mobility is protective. Other risk factors worth knowing: incontinence, poor nutrition and hydration, diabetes, advanced age, edema, and sensory deficits.

q: A client sustained a deep laceration from a rusty object. The wound was left open for 10 days while the infection was treated, then surgically closed. This describes which type of wound healing?
o: Primary intention
Secondary intention
Tertiary intention
Regeneration
r: TERTIARY INTENTION (DELAYED PRIMARY CLOSURE) IS EXACTLY THIS: left open 5–10 days so contamination or infection can be treated, THEN surgically closed. Primary intention is a clean wound closed right away with minimal scarring, and secondary intention is left open to granulate in from the bottom up with significant scarring.

q: A nurse assessing a surgical wound notes thick, yellow-green drainage with a foul odor. What should the nurse do?
o: Report it — this suggests infection
Document it as expected serosanguineous drainage
Reinforce the dressing and reassess in 8 hours
Irrigate the wound with hydrogen peroxide and continue routine care
r: PURULENT DRAINAGE — THICK, YELLOW/GREEN AND FOUL-SMELLING — MEANS INFECTION AND MUST BE REPORTED. Know all four: SEROUS is clear and watery (normal), SEROSANGUINEOUS is pink (normal post-op), SANGUINEOUS is bright red (active bleeding, report), and PURULENT is infection. Waiting 8 hours delays treatment of an active infection.

q: A nurse suspects a client has developed a DVT in the right calf. Which action must the nurse AVOID?
o: Massaging the calf to improve circulation
Measuring the circumference of both calves
Elevating the extremity and notifying the provider
Stopping ambulation until the client is evaluated
r: NEVER MASSAGE A CALF WITH A SUSPECTED DVT — you can dislodge the clot and cause a PULMONARY EMBOLISM. The correct actions are to stop activity, elevate the leg, measure and compare calf circumferences, notify the provider, and prepare for ultrasound and anticoagulation. Watch for PE afterward: sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachypnea, tachycardia, and a sense of impending doom.

q: A nurse is beginning a complete bed bath. Which area should the nurse wash FIRST?
o: The face
The chest
The perineal area
The feet
r: WASH FACE FIRST AND THE PERINEAL AREA LAST — the principle is CLEAN TO DIRTY, so you never carry organisms from a contaminated area to a clean one. The order is face → neck → chest → arms → abdomen → legs and feet → back → perineum. Use warm, not hot, water and keep the client covered for warmth and privacy.

q: A nurse is providing perineal care to an uncircumcised male client. Which action is essential?
o: Replace the foreskin over the glans after cleaning
Leave the foreskin retracted so the area can air dry
Clean from the base of the shaft toward the meatus
Use hot water and vigorous friction to remove smegma
r: ALWAYS REPLACE THE FORESKIN AFTER CLEANING — leaving it retracted causes constriction, swelling and impaired circulation (paraphimosis), which is a genuine emergency. Clean in a circular motion FROM THE MEATUS OUTWARD, not toward it, so you move away from the cleanest area. For female clients, the rule is always FRONT TO BACK.

q: A client has limited hand dexterity from arthritis and is struggling to brush effectively. Which recommendation is BEST?
o: An electric toothbrush
A firm-bristled manual toothbrush
Rinsing with mouthwash instead of brushing
Having the family brush the client's teeth daily
r: AN ELECTRIC TOOTHBRUSH HAS A WIDER, EASIER-TO-GRIP HANDLE AND DOES THE SCRUBBING MOTION FOR THE CLIENT, which PROMOTES INDEPENDENCE — always the preferred goal. A firm-bristled brush damages gums and still requires the dexterity they lack. Mouthwash alone doesn't remove plaque, and having the family take over removes independence the client can still keep.

q: Which statement by a client with diabetes indicates the foot-care teaching was EFFECTIVE?
o: “I will dry carefully between my toes and skip the lotion there.”
“I will soak my feet in warm water every night to soften the skin.”
“I will cut my toenails in a rounded curve to match my toe.”
“I will go barefoot around the house so my feet can breathe.”
r: DRY BETWEEN THE TOES AND PUT NO LOTION THERE — trapped moisture breeds fungal infection and skin breakdown. DO NOT SOAK the feet (it macerates skin and neuropathy means they may not feel the water temperature), cut nails STRAIGHT ACROSS to prevent ingrown nails, and NEVER GO BAREFOOT because a neuropathic client won't feel an injury.

q: Which is the BEST fall-prevention teaching point for a community-dwelling older adult?
o: Promote regular exercise to maintain strength and balance
Limit walking to reduce the chance of falling
Use throw rugs to mark changes in flooring
Keep the home dimly lit at night to promote sleep
r: REGULAR EXERCISE MAINTAINS STRENGTH, BALANCE AND GAIT — it is the most effective long-term fall-prevention strategy. Limiting walking causes deconditioning and actually INCREASES fall risk. THROW RUGS ARE A CLASSIC TRIPPING HAZARD and should be removed, and dim lighting increases risk — use night lights along the path to the bathroom.

q: A nurse is caring for a client with a new disability. Which client statement is MOST concerning and requires immediate follow-up?
o: “I feel like a burden to my family.”
“I'm frustrated that this is taking so long.”
“I'm not sure I'll ever get back to my old hobbies.”
“Some days are harder than others.”
r: “I FEEL LIKE A BURDEN” IS A HOPELESSNESS AND WORTHLESSNESS STATEMENT and is a recognized warning sign for self-harm — it demands immediate follow-up and further assessment. Frustration, uncertainty about hobbies and acknowledging hard days are normal, expected adjustment responses to a new disability. Always pick the statement suggesting the client sees no value in their own life.

q: A nurse is working at a community health fair and is administering influenza vaccines to adults who have no symptoms of illness. Which level of prevention is the nurse practicing?
o: Primary prevention
Secondary prevention
Tertiary prevention
Quaternary prevention
r: PRIMARY PREVENTION KEEPS THE DISEASE FROM EVER OCCURRING, and immunization is the classic example along with seat belts, helmets, exercise, and health education. Secondary prevention is wrong here because secondary involves screening an asymptomatic person for a disease that may already be present, such as a mammogram or a blood pressure screening. No disease process exists yet in the client receiving a vaccine, so the action is primary.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who had a myocardial infarction 3 weeks ago and is now attending a supervised cardiac rehabilitation program. The nurse should identify this program as which level of prevention?
o: Primary prevention
Secondary prevention
Tertiary prevention
Health maintenance
r: TERTIARY PREVENTION LIMITS DISABILITY AND RESTORES FUNCTION AFTER A DISEASE IS ALREADY ESTABLISHED, which is exactly what cardiac rehab, post-stroke physical therapy, and diabetic support groups do. Secondary prevention is incorrect because the disease has already been diagnosed and is symptomatic; secondary applies to detection in an asymptomatic client. The presence of an established diagnosis is the clue that shifts the answer from secondary to tertiary.

q: A nurse is reviewing the community clinic schedule and must identify which services are examples of secondary prevention. Which of the following should the nurse identify as secondary prevention? (Select all that apply.)
o: Screening mammogram for a 52-year-old woman with no breast symptoms
Tuberculin skin test (PPD) for a newly hired hospital employee
Blood pressure screening booth at a shopping center
Teaching parents about proper car seat installation
Physical therapy for a client recovering from a stroke
Fecal occult blood testing for an asymptomatic 50-year-old
r: SECONDARY PREVENTION IS EARLY DETECTION AND SCREENING IN AN ASYMPTOMATIC PERSON, so mammograms, PPD testing, blood pressure screening, Pap smears, colonoscopy, and fecal occult blood testing all qualify. Car seat teaching is primary prevention because it prevents injury from ever happening. Post-stroke physical therapy is tertiary because the disease has already occurred and the goal is restoring function.

q: A nurse is planning a program for a community that has a high incidence of type 2 diabetes mellitus. Which activity should the nurse include as a primary prevention strategy?
o: Offering fasting blood glucose screening to adults at the senior center
Teaching a nutrition and physical activity class to adults who do not have diabetes
Leading a support group for clients newly diagnosed with diabetes
Providing foot care instruction to clients who have diabetic neuropathy
r: PRIMARY PREVENTION TARGETS PEOPLE WITHOUT THE DISEASE AND REMOVES RISK FACTORS SO THE DISEASE NEVER DEVELOPS, and nutrition plus exercise education for a healthy population does exactly that. Fasting glucose screening is tempting but it is secondary prevention because it detects disease early in an asymptomatic person. The support group and neuropathy foot care are tertiary because those clients already have diabetes.

q: A nurse is teaching a group of nursing students about levels of prevention. Which statement by a student indicates an understanding of tertiary prevention?
o: "I would classify a colonoscopy for a 50-year-old with no symptoms as tertiary prevention."
"I would classify teaching bicycle helmet use to children as tertiary prevention."
"I would classify a speech therapy program for a client after a stroke as tertiary prevention."
"I would classify a hepatitis B vaccine series as tertiary prevention."
r: TERTIARY PREVENTION BEGINS AFTER THE DISEASE IS ESTABLISHED AND FOCUSES ON REHABILITATION AND PREVENTING FURTHER DISABILITY, so speech therapy after a stroke is correct. The colonoscopy is secondary prevention because it screens an asymptomatic client. Helmet teaching and the hepatitis B vaccine are both primary prevention because they stop injury or disease before it starts.

q: A nurse is counseling a healthy 25-year-old client whose blood pressure today is 114/72 mm Hg. The client asks how often the blood pressure should be checked. Which response should the nurse make?
o: "Because your reading is normal, you should have it rechecked at least every 2 years."
"You do not need it checked again until you turn 40."
"You should have it checked every month at home."
"Blood pressure screening is only recommended if you have symptoms."
r: AN ADULT WITH A NORMAL BLOOD PRESSURE (LESS THAN 120/80 MM HG) SHOULD BE RESCREENED AT LEAST EVERY 2 YEARS BEGINNING AT AGE 20. Waiting until age 40 is incorrect because hypertension is asymptomatic and screening is the only way to detect it early. Saying screening is only needed with symptoms is wrong for the same reason and defeats the purpose of secondary prevention.

q: A nurse is assessing a 48-year-old client for cardiovascular risk. Which of the following are MODIFIABLE risk factors the nurse should address in the teaching plan? (Select all that apply.)
o: Cigarette smoking
Family history of myocardial infarction before age 55
Sedentary lifestyle
Body mass index of 34
Male gender
Untreated hypertension
r: MODIFIABLE RISK FACTORS ARE THOSE THE CLIENT CAN CHANGE THROUGH BEHAVIOR OR TREATMENT, including smoking, inactivity, obesity, diet, and uncontrolled hypertension. Family history and gender are nonmodifiable and cannot be altered by teaching, although they do raise overall risk and justify closer screening. Nursing interventions for health promotion focus on the modifiable factors.

q: A nurse manager is aligning a clinic's outreach program with the national Healthy People initiative. Which program goal best reflects the overarching aims of Healthy People?
o: Increasing the number of hospital beds available in the county
Attaining longer lives free of preventable disease and eliminating health disparities
Reducing the cost of prescription medications for the clinic
Increasing the number of specialists who accept clinic referrals
r: THE HEALTHY PEOPLE INITIATIVE SETS NATIONAL OBJECTIVES TO INCREASE QUALITY AND YEARS OF HEALTHY LIFE AND TO ELIMINATE HEALTH DISPARITIES AMONG POPULATION GROUPS. Increasing hospital beds and specialist access addresses treatment capacity rather than population-level health promotion and disease prevention. Healthy People is a prevention framework, not a facility or reimbursement plan.

q: A nurse is planning to teach a client who has newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus how to self-administer insulin. Which teaching strategy is most appropriate for this learning domain?
o: Providing a pamphlet describing the action of insulin
Discussing the client's feelings about lifelong injections
Demonstrating the injection technique and having the client perform a return demonstration
Asking the client to list the signs of hypoglycemia
r: SELF-INJECTION IS A PSYCHOMOTOR SKILL, AND PSYCHOMOTOR LEARNING IS TAUGHT BY DEMONSTRATION AND EVALUATED BY RETURN DEMONSTRATION. The pamphlet and the list of hypoglycemia signs address the cognitive domain, which is knowledge and understanding, not skill performance. Discussing feelings addresses the affective domain, which involves attitudes and values.

q: A nurse enters the room to teach a postoperative client about incentive spirometry. The client is grimacing and reports incisional pain rated 8 on a scale of 0 to 10. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Begin the teaching and keep the session brief
Administer the prescribed analgesic and return when the pain is controlled
Provide written instructions for the client to read later
Ask a family member to learn the technique instead
r: UNRELIEVED PAIN IS A MAJOR BARRIER TO LEARNING BECAUSE IT PREVENTS THE CLIENT FROM FOCUSING, SO THE NURSE MUST TREAT THE PAIN BEFORE TEACHING. Beginning a brief session is incorrect because retention will be poor no matter how short the session is. Handing over written material or shifting the teaching to a family member does not meet the client's own learning need and skips the fixable barrier.

q: A nurse is assessing an older adult client's readiness to learn about a new anticoagulant. Which of the following findings should the nurse identify as barriers to learning? (Select all that apply.)
o: The client reports being unable to hear the nurse's voice clearly
The client states, "I am too tired to talk right now."
The client asks what foods should be avoided with this medication
The client's primary language differs from the nurse's and no interpreter is present
The client reads at a fourth-grade level and the handout is written at a twelfth-grade level
r: SENSORY DEFICITS, FATIGUE, LANGUAGE DIFFERENCES, AND LOW HEALTH LITERACY ARE ALL BARRIERS THAT MUST BE ADDRESSED BEFORE EFFECTIVE TEACHING CAN OCCUR. Asking what foods to avoid is not a barrier; it is a sign of motivation and readiness to learn, which is the ideal time to teach. The nurse should obtain an interpreter and use materials written at approximately a fifth-grade reading level.

q: A nurse has finished teaching a client how to change a wound dressing at home. Which action best evaluates whether learning has occurred?
o: Asking the client, "Do you understand how to change your dressing?"
Asking the client to explain and demonstrate the dressing change in his own words and actions
Giving the client a printed handout to take home
Documenting that the client nodded during the teaching session
r: THE TEACH-BACK METHOD AND RETURN DEMONSTRATION ARE THE ONLY RELIABLE WAYS TO EVALUATE LEARNING, because the client must reproduce the information or skill. Asking "Do you understand?" is a closed question that invites a yes answer even when the client is confused, so it is never an acceptable evaluation method. Handouts and nodding document exposure to information, not comprehension.

q: A nurse is writing outcomes for a client who has a new colostomy. Which outcome addresses the AFFECTIVE domain of learning?
o: The client will state three signs of stoma complications before discharge
The client will empty and change the ostomy pouch independently
The client will look at the stoma and verbalize acceptance of the body change
The client will list foods that increase gas production
r: THE AFFECTIVE DOMAIN INVOLVES FEELINGS, ATTITUDES, VALUES, AND ACCEPTANCE, so looking at the stoma and verbalizing acceptance is affective. Stating complications and listing foods are cognitive outcomes because they measure knowledge recall. Emptying and changing the pouch is psychomotor because it measures a physical skill.

q: A nurse is developing a teaching plan for a 55-year-old client who has heart failure. Which of the following principles of adult learning should the nurse apply? (Select all that apply.)
o: Relate new information to the client's previous life and work experiences
Focus on information the client can apply immediately to daily life
Present all discharge content in one long session on the day of discharge
Involve the client in setting the goals of the teaching session
Emphasize that the provider expects the client to comply with the plan
r: ADULT LEARNERS ARE SELF-DIRECTED, PROBLEM-CENTERED, AND MOTIVATED BY INFORMATION THEY CAN USE IMMEDIATELY, so building on prior experience, keeping content relevant, and sharing goal-setting all increase learning. Cramming everything into one session on discharge day overwhelms the client and reduces retention; teaching should begin at admission and be given in short segments. Emphasizing provider expectations is an authoritarian approach that undermines the self-direction adult learners need.

q: A nurse is teaching the parents of a 2-month-old infant about safe sleep. Which statement by a parent indicates a need for further teaching?
o: "I will place my baby on her back for every sleep."
"I will put a soft quilt and bumper pads in the crib to keep her comfortable."
"I will keep stuffed animals and pillows out of the crib."
"I will use a firm mattress that fits snugly in the crib."
r: INFANTS MUST BE PLACED SUPINE ON A FIRM SURFACE WITH NO SOFT BEDDING, PILLOWS, BUMPER PADS, OR STUFFED TOYS, because soft objects increase the risk of sudden infant death syndrome and suffocation. The quilt and bumper pad statement is the incorrect one and therefore requires further teaching. The other three statements all reflect correct safe sleep practice.

q: A nurse is examining a 14-month-old toddler and notes that the anterior fontanel is still slightly open. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Notify the provider immediately about increased intracranial pressure
Document the finding as an expected assessment for this age
Prepare the child for an emergency head CT scan
Teach the parents to restrict the child's fluid intake
r: THE ANTERIOR FONTANEL NORMALLY CLOSES BETWEEN 12 AND 18 MONTHS, so an open anterior fontanel at 14 months is an expected finding to document. The posterior fontanel closes much earlier, by 2 to 3 months. A bulging or tense fontanel would suggest increased intracranial pressure and require reporting, but a simply open fontanel at this age does not. Other expected infant growth markers are birth weight doubling by 6 months and tripling by 12 months.

q: A nurse is teaching a parenting class about injury prevention for toddlers. Which of the following should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)
o: Store all cleaning products and medications in locked cabinets
Never leave the toddler unattended near a bathtub, bucket, or pool
Cut hot dogs and grapes lengthwise into small pieces
Allow the toddler to sit in the front passenger seat if properly buckled
Place gates at the top and bottom of stairways
r: POISONING, DROWNING, CHOKING, AND FALLS ARE THE LEADING INJURY RISKS FOR TODDLERS BECAUSE THEY ARE MOBILE, CURIOUS, AND PUT OBJECTS IN THEIR MOUTHS. Locking chemicals, constant supervision around any water, cutting round foods, and using stair gates all address these risks. Placing a toddler in the front seat is unsafe; children should ride in the back seat, and a car seat is used until the child meets height and weight requirements for the next restraint.

q: A nurse observes a 2-year-old playing beside another 2-year-old in the clinic waiting area. Each child plays with his own truck and neither interacts with the other. Which statement should the nurse make to the parent?
o: "This is parallel play and it is expected at this age."
"Your child may have a developmental delay in social skills."
"Children this age should be sharing toys and playing cooperatively."
"You should separate the children to avoid conflict."
r: TODDLERS ENGAGE IN PARALLEL PLAY, PLAYING ALONGSIDE BUT NOT WITH OTHER CHILDREN, WHICH IS A NORMAL EXPECTED FINDING. Cooperative play with shared goals and rules does not appear until the school-age years, so expecting it at age 2 is developmentally inappropriate. Associative play, where children play together loosely without organized rules, emerges in the preschool years.

q: A nurse is caring for a hospitalized 9-year-old. Which of the following interventions support the developmental stage of industry versus inferiority? (Select all that apply.)
o: Allow the child to keep up with schoolwork while hospitalized
Encourage the child to participate in his own care, such as recording intake
Provide board games and craft projects the child can complete
Restrict visits from classmates to promote rest
Discourage questions about the illness to avoid worry
r: THE SCHOOL-AGE CHILD IS IN ERIKSON'S INDUSTRY VERSUS INFERIORITY STAGE AND NEEDS OPPORTUNITIES TO ACHIEVE, PRODUCE, AND MASTER TASKS. Schoolwork, participating in care, and finishing projects all build a sense of accomplishment. Restricting peers and discouraging questions promote feelings of inferiority and isolation; peers are increasingly important at this age and the child is capable of concrete logical explanation.

q: A nurse is planning a health promotion program for a high school. Which topic should the nurse prioritize based on the leading cause of death in this age group?
o: Skin cancer prevention and sunscreen use
Motor vehicle safety, including seat belt use and not driving under the influence
Calcium intake and bone density
Prevention of type 2 diabetes mellitus
r: UNINTENTIONAL INJURY, PRIMARILY MOTOR VEHICLE CRASHES, IS THE LEADING CAUSE OF DEATH IN ADOLESCENTS, so motor vehicle safety is the priority topic. Risk-taking behavior, peer influence, and a sense of invincibility make this age group especially vulnerable. Sun protection, calcium, and diabetes prevention are all valuable but do not address the leading cause of mortality for adolescents.

q: A nurse is assessing a 78-year-old client during a routine visit. Which of the following findings should the nurse identify as EXPECTED age-related changes? (Select all that apply.)
o: Decreased skin elasticity and thinner skin
New onset of confusion over the past 2 days
Decreased near vision requiring reading glasses
Slowed reaction time and gait speed
Urinary incontinence
Decreased ability to hear high-frequency sounds
r: EXPECTED AGING CHANGES INCLUDE THINNER LESS ELASTIC SKIN, PRESBYOPIA, PRESBYCUSIS WITH LOSS OF HIGH-FREQUENCY HEARING, AND SLOWED REACTION TIME. CONFUSION IS NEVER A NORMAL PART OF AGING and new onset confusion must be investigated for causes such as infection, hypoxia, dehydration, or medication effects. Urinary incontinence is also not a normal aging change and requires assessment rather than acceptance.

q: A nurse is caring for an 82-year-old client who was admitted for dehydration. The client was alert and oriented yesterday but today is disoriented to place and time and is pulling at the IV line. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Apply wrist restraints to protect the IV site
Document the finding as expected confusion related to aging
Assess the client for hypoxia, infection, and medication effects and notify the provider
Reorient the client and continue the current plan of care
r: AN ACUTE CHANGE IN MENTAL STATUS IN AN OLDER ADULT IS DELIRIUM UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE AND IS NEVER ATTRIBUTED TO NORMAL AGING; common causes include urinary tract infection, hypoxia, dehydration, and polypharmacy. The nurse must assess for a physiologic cause and report the change. Restraints are not a first action and require a provider prescription, and simply reorienting fails to address the underlying cause.

q: A 52-year-old client tells the nurse, "My children have moved out and I feel like I have nothing left to offer anyone." Using Erikson's theory, which nursing response best supports this client's developmental task?
o: "Tell me about ways you might mentor others or contribute to your community."
"Most people your age feel this way; it will pass."
"You should focus on reviewing your life and accepting the past."
"This is a sign that you should consider retiring early."
r: THE MIDDLE ADULT TASK IS GENERATIVITY VERSUS STAGNATION, WHICH IS MET BY GUIDING THE NEXT GENERATION THROUGH MENTORING, VOLUNTEERING, OR COMMUNITY INVOLVEMENT. Encouraging the client to explore these roles directly addresses the risk of stagnation. Life review and acceptance of the past belong to integrity versus despair in the older adult, so that option targets the wrong stage.

q: A nurse is preparing a 5-year-old for surgery. Based on the child's cognitive stage, which teaching approach is most appropriate?
o: Provide a written booklet describing the surgical procedure step by step
Use a doll and simple equipment to show what will happen, using concrete words
Explain the long-term risks and benefits so the child can weigh options
Discuss how the anesthesia medication works at the cellular level
r: A 5-YEAR-OLD IS IN PIAGET'S PREOPERATIONAL STAGE, WHICH IS CONCRETE, EGOCENTRIC, AND DOMINATED BY MAGICAL THINKING, SO PLAY WITH DOLLS AND ACTUAL EQUIPMENT IS THE BEST TEACHING METHOD. Written booklets and abstract discussions of risk, benefit, and cellular action require formal operational thinking, which does not develop until about age 11 or older. Concrete demonstration also reduces the preschooler's fear of bodily harm.

q: A nurse is preparing to perform an abdominal assessment on a client. Which sequence should the nurse use?
o: Inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation
Inspection, auscultation, percussion, palpation
Auscultation, inspection, palpation, percussion
Palpation, inspection, auscultation, percussion
r: THE ABDOMEN IS THE EXCEPTION TO THE USUAL ORDER: INSPECT, THEN AUSCULTATE BEFORE PERCUSSING AND PALPATING, because touching the abdomen first can alter bowel sounds and produce false findings. The standard order for every other body system is inspection, palpation, percussion, then auscultation. Selecting the standard order for the abdomen is the most common error on this item type.

q: A nurse obtains a blood pressure of 168/96 mm Hg using a cuff that is too narrow for the client's arm. Which statement about this reading is accurate?
o: The reading is falsely low and should be repeated with a smaller cuff
The reading is falsely high and should be repeated with a correctly sized cuff
The cuff size does not affect accuracy as long as the stethoscope is placed correctly
The reading is accurate and should be reported to the provider
r: A CUFF THAT IS TOO SMALL OR TOO NARROW PRODUCES A FALSELY HIGH READING, WHILE A CUFF THAT IS TOO LARGE PRODUCES A FALSELY LOW READING. The bladder width should be about 40 percent of the arm circumference and the bladder should encircle about 80 percent of the arm. Reporting the value before correcting the technique could lead to unnecessary antihypertensive treatment.

q: A nurse is reviewing sources of error in blood pressure measurement with a newly licensed nurse. Which of the following techniques would produce a FALSELY HIGH reading? (Select all that apply.)
o: Positioning the client's arm below the level of the heart
Using a cuff that is too wide for the client's arm
Taking the blood pressure immediately after the client walked to the room
Deflating the cuff too slowly, causing venous congestion
Wrapping the cuff loosely around the arm
r: THE ARM BELOW HEART LEVEL, RECENT ACTIVITY, SLOW DEFLATION CAUSING VENOUS CONGESTION, AND A LOOSELY WRAPPED CUFF ALL RAISE THE READING FALSELY. A cuff that is too wide is the one option that lowers the reading. The client should rest quietly for at least 5 minutes with the arm supported at heart level before measurement.

q: A nurse is preparing to count a client's respirations. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Tell the client that respirations are being counted so the client remains still
Count respirations while keeping fingers on the radial pulse site after taking the pulse
Count for 15 seconds and multiply by 4 for all clients
Ask the client to take deep breaths during the count
r: RESPIRATIONS SHOULD BE COUNTED WITHOUT THE CLIENT'S AWARENESS, BECAUSE KNOWING THEY ARE BEING WATCHED CAUSES THE CLIENT TO ALTER THE RATE AND DEPTH. Keeping the fingers on the radial pulse while observing chest rise accomplishes this. Counting for a full minute is required when the pattern is irregular, and asking for deep breaths destroys the accuracy of the measurement entirely.

q: A nurse is measuring orthostatic vital signs. Supine readings are BP 128/78 mm Hg and pulse 76/min. After the client stands for 2 minutes, the readings are BP 104/64 mm Hg and pulse 98/min. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Document the findings as within expected limits
Assist the client to lie down and notify the provider of orthostatic hypotension
Repeat the measurement immediately in the standing position
Encourage the client to ambulate in the hallway to improve circulation
r: ORTHOSTATIC HYPOTENSION IS A DROP IN SYSTOLIC PRESSURE OF AT LEAST 20 MM HG OR DIASTOLIC OF AT LEAST 10 MM HG WITHIN 3 MINUTES OF STANDING, OFTEN WITH A COMPENSATORY RISE IN HEART RATE. This client dropped 24 mm Hg systolic and 14 mm Hg diastolic, so the finding is positive and the client is at high risk for falls and syncope. Ambulating the client is unsafe, and documenting the values as normal misses a significant safety risk.

q: A nurse and another nurse simultaneously measure a client's apical pulse as 96/min and radial pulse as 78/min. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Document a pulse deficit of 18 and report the finding to the provider
Record the radial pulse as the client's official heart rate
Recount only the radial pulse for a full minute
Document that the pulses are within expected limits
r: A PULSE DEFICIT IS THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE APICAL AND RADIAL RATES AND INDICATES THAT SOME VENTRICULAR CONTRACTIONS ARE TOO WEAK TO PERFUSE THE PERIPHERY, WHICH OCCURS WITH DYSRHYTHMIAS SUCH AS ATRIAL FIBRILLATION. A deficit of 18 is significant and must be reported. Recording only the radial rate would underestimate the actual ventricular rate and hide the abnormality.

q: A nurse is preparing to obtain an oral temperature on a client who just finished drinking a cup of hot coffee. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Obtain the oral temperature now and subtract 0.5 degrees C
Wait 15 to 30 minutes before obtaining the oral temperature
Obtain the temperature now and document that coffee was consumed
Obtain a temperature from the axilla instead without waiting
r: HOT OR COLD ORAL INTAKE, SMOKING, AND CHEWING GUM ALTER ORAL TEMPERATURE READINGS, SO THE NURSE MUST WAIT 15 TO 30 MINUTES BEFORE MEASURING. Subtracting an arbitrary amount is not an accepted practice and produces an unreliable value. Switching to the axilla is inaccurate as an automatic substitution because axillary readings run lower and are the least accurate route.

q: A nurse is reviewing the vital signs of four adult clients. Which of the following findings require follow-up? (Select all that apply.)
o: Temperature 38.9 degrees C (102.0 degrees F)
Heart rate 52/min in a client reporting dizziness
Respiratory rate 16/min
Oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air
Blood pressure 116/74 mm Hg
r: EXPECTED ADULT RANGES ARE TEMPERATURE 36 TO 38 DEGREES C, PULSE 60 TO 100/MIN, RESPIRATIONS 12 TO 20/MIN, BP LESS THAN 120/80 MM HG, AND SPO2 95 TO 100 PERCENT. The fever, the symptomatic bradycardia, and the saturation of 88 percent all fall outside these ranges and require follow-up, with the low oxygen saturation being the most urgent. A respiratory rate of 16/min and a BP of 116/74 mm Hg are both within expected limits.

q: A nurse is assessing pain in an alert adult client 2 hours after abdominal surgery. Which assessment finding is the most reliable indicator of the client's pain?
o: The client's heart rate and blood pressure
The client's self-report of pain rated 7 on a 0 to 10 scale
The nurse's observation that the client is watching television
The amount of analgesic the client received in the operating room
r: PAIN IS THE FIFTH VITAL SIGN, AND THE CLIENT'S SELF-REPORT IS ALWAYS THE MOST RELIABLE INDICATOR OF PAIN. Vital sign changes are unreliable because they normalize with ongoing pain even when pain persists. Behaviors such as watching television or sleeping are distraction and coping mechanisms and must never be used to discount a client's reported pain.

q: A nurse auscultates fine crackles in the bilateral lung bases of a client who has a history of heart failure and reports increasing shortness of breath. Which condition do these findings most likely indicate?
o: Narrowed bronchioles from bronchospasm
Fluid in the alveoli and small airways
Secretions in the large airways that will clear with coughing
Inflamed pleural surfaces rubbing together
r: CRACKLES ARE PRODUCED BY AIR PASSING THROUGH FLUID IN THE ALVEOLI AND SMALL AIRWAYS AND ARE CLASSIC FOR HEART FAILURE, PULMONARY EDEMA, AND PNEUMONIA. Wheezes, not crackles, result from narrowed bronchioles as in asthma. Rhonchi are the coarse low-pitched sounds caused by secretions in large airways that often clear after coughing, and a pleural friction rub is the grating sound of inflamed pleura.

q: A nurse is assessing four clients. Which finding requires immediate intervention?
o: Expiratory wheezes in a client who has asthma and is using a bronchodilator
High-pitched inspiratory stridor in a client 2 hours after a thyroidectomy
Rhonchi that clear after a client coughs productively
Bronchial breath sounds heard over the trachea
r: STRIDOR IS A HIGH-PITCHED CROWING SOUND THAT SIGNALS UPPER AIRWAY OBSTRUCTION AND IS A MEDICAL EMERGENCY, especially after thyroidectomy where swelling or hematoma can compress the trachea. Wheezes in an asthmatic client being treated are expected and concerning only if they worsen or disappear with poor air movement. Rhonchi that clear with coughing and bronchial sounds over the trachea are both normal or resolving findings.

q: A nurse is auscultating the abdomen of a client on the first postoperative day after abdominal surgery. Which of the following statements about this assessment are accurate? (Select all that apply.)
o: The diaphragm of the stethoscope is used to auscultate bowel sounds
Bowel sounds must be absent for a full 5 minutes of listening in a quadrant before being documented as absent
Normal bowel sounds occur about 5 to 30 times per minute
Hypoactive bowel sounds after abdominal surgery are an expected finding
Auscultation is performed after deep palpation of all four quadrants
r: BOWEL SOUNDS ARE HIGH PITCHED AND ARE HEARD BEST WITH THE DIAPHRAGM, OCCUR 5 TO 30 TIMES PER MINUTE, AND CANNOT BE CALLED ABSENT UNTIL THE NURSE HAS LISTENED FOR A FULL 5 MINUTES IN THAT QUADRANT. Hypoactive sounds are expected after abdominal surgery and with anesthesia or opioids. Auscultation must come BEFORE palpation in the abdomen because palpating first alters bowel sounds.

q: A nurse assesses an older adult client and finds that the skin over the forearm remains tented for several seconds after being pinched. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Document decreased turgor as a reliable sign of dehydration in this client
Assess skin turgor over the sternum or forehead and evaluate other fluid status indicators
Immediately administer an IV fluid bolus
Document the finding as an expected age-related change requiring no follow-up
r: SKIN TURGOR OVER THE FOREARM IS UNRELIABLE IN OLDER ADULTS BECAUSE DECREASED ELASTICITY FROM AGING MIMICS DEHYDRATION; THE STERNUM OR FOREHEAD IS THE PREFERRED SITE. The nurse should also evaluate mucous membranes, urine output, and daily weight rather than relying on turgor alone. Administering fluids requires a prescription and should not be based on a single unreliable finding.

q: A nurse is performing a neurovascular check on a client who has a newly applied long leg cast. Which finding requires immediate follow-up?
o: Capillary refill of the toes in 2 seconds
Client reports tingling and numbness in the toes and pain unrelieved by analgesics
Pedal pulse graded 2+
Toes warm and pink bilaterally
r: PARESTHESIA AND PAIN UNRELIEVED BY ANALGESICS ARE AMONG THE EARLIEST OF THE 6 P'S OF IMPAIRED ARTERIAL CIRCULATION AND SUGGEST COMPARTMENT SYNDROME, WHICH REQUIRES IMMEDIATE REPORTING. The 6 P's are pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, and poikilothermia. Capillary refill under 3 seconds, a 2+ pulse, and warm pink toes are all normal and reassuring findings.

q: A nurse is assessing a client who had a head injury. The client opens his eyes to painful stimuli, makes incomprehensible sounds, and withdraws from pain. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Document the findings and reassess in 4 hours
Report the decline in level of consciousness to the provider immediately
Ask the client to state his name and the date
Encourage the family to talk to the client to stimulate a response
r: A DECLINING LEVEL OF CONSCIOUSNESS IS THE EARLIEST AND MOST SENSITIVE INDICATOR OF NEUROLOGIC DETERIORATION AND MUST BE REPORTED IMMEDIATELY. These findings correspond to a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 8 (eye opening 2, verbal 2, motor 4), and a GCS of 8 or less indicates coma with an unprotected airway. Waiting 4 hours to reassess delays potentially lifesaving intervention, and a client making only incomprehensible sounds cannot answer orientation questions.

q: A nurse is performing a neurologic assessment. Which of the following findings should the nurse document as EXPECTED? (Select all that apply.)
o: Pupils equal, round, 3 mm, and briskly reactive to light with accommodation
Muscle strength graded 5/5 in all extremities
Client is oriented to person, place, time, and situation
One pupil 6 mm and nonreactive while the other is 3 mm and reactive
Steady, coordinated gait with arms swinging in opposition
r: PERRLA, SYMMETRIC 5/5 MUSCLE STRENGTH, FULL ORIENTATION TO PERSON PLACE TIME AND SITUATION, AND A STEADY COORDINATED GAIT ARE ALL EXPECTED NEUROLOGIC FINDINGS. A UNILATERALLY DILATED NONREACTIVE PUPIL IS AN EMERGENCY suggesting increased intracranial pressure with cranial nerve III compression and must be reported immediately. Muscle strength is graded 0 to 5, with 5 representing full strength against gravity and full resistance.

q: A nurse is preparing a 34-year-old client for a lumbar puncture in an outpatient clinic. Which of the following positions should the nurse help the client assume during the procedure?
o: Prone with the head turned to one side
Supine with the head of the bed elevated to 45 degrees
Side lying with the knees drawn up to the abdomen and the chin tucked toward the chest
Sitting upright with both legs extended straight out on the bed
r: The LATERAL RECUMBENT C-SHAPE (side lying, knees to chest, chin tucked) widens the spaces between the vertebrae so the needle can pass. Prone and supine positions close those intervertebral spaces and block access. Sitting is used only when the client leans forward over a bedside table, not with the legs extended.

q: A nurse is caring for a client 6 hr after a lumbar puncture who reports a throbbing headache that worsens when sitting up and eases when lying flat. Which of the following actions should the nurse take first?
o: Keep the client flat in bed and encourage oral fluids
Ambulate the client in the hallway to promote circulation
Apply a warm compress over the puncture site
Withhold all oral fluids until the headache resolves
r: A positional headache after a lumbar puncture comes from a CSF LEAK at the puncture site. Lying FLAT plus increased FLUIDS (and caffeine) restores CSF volume and pressure; a blood patch is used if that fails. Ambulating makes the headache worse, withholding fluids is the opposite of what is needed, and a warm compress does nothing to replace lost CSF.

q: A nurse is preparing a 58-year-old client for a lumbar puncture on a medical unit. Which of the following actions should the nurse take before the procedure? (Select all that apply.)
o: Verify that the client's coagulation studies are on the chart
Ask the client to empty the bladder
Maintain the client NPO for 12 hr before the procedure
Confirm that prescribed anticoagulants were held as ordered
Shave the client's entire back from the shoulders to the sacrum
r: BLEEDING RISK is the reason to check coagulation studies and confirm anticoagulants were held; an epidural or spinal hematoma can compress the cord. An EMPTY BLADDER keeps the client comfortable while curled in the flexed position for a prolonged time. A 12 hr NPO order is not standard because there is no general anesthesia, and shaving the entire back is unnecessary; only the site is prepped.

q: A nurse is caring for a client 18 hr after a lumbar puncture. Which of the following findings should the nurse report to the provider immediately?
o: The client reports mild tenderness at the puncture site
The client has taken in 2,000 mL of oral fluid since the procedure
Temperature of 38.8 C (101.8 F) with nuchal rigidity and photophobia
The client remained flat in bed for the first 4 hr after the procedure
r: Fever with NUCHAL RIGIDITY and photophobia points to MENINGITIS, an infectious complication of the puncture. Mild site tenderness, generous fluid intake, and lying flat afterward are all expected findings. Also report CLOUDY CSF (a sign of infection) and any new numbness or weakness in the legs, which suggests a spinal hematoma.

q: A nurse is preparing to insert a peripheral IV catheter in an 82-year-old client who has thin, fragile, tortuous veins. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
o: Apply a tourniquet tightly and leave it in place for 3 min
Slap the vein briskly several times to promote dilation
Use a blood pressure cuff inflated below the client's diastolic pressure in place of a tourniquet
Select the largest gauge catheter available for the infusion
r: A BP cuff at LOW PRESSURE distends the vein without the shearing force a tight tourniquet puts on FRAGILE VEINS that have lost subcutaneous support. A tight or prolonged tourniquet and slapping the vein both cause bruising, hematoma, and vein rupture in older adults. Use the SMALLEST gauge that will deliver the prescribed therapy, never the largest.

q: A nurse is monitoring an 88-year-old client who is receiving 0.9% sodium chloride IV at 125 mL/hr. Which of the following findings should the nurse report as a sign of fluid volume overload?
o: Dry mucous membranes and poor skin turgor
Urine specific gravity of 1.035
Flat neck veins while the client is supine
Crackles in the lung bases with new shortness of breath
r: Reduced CARDIAC and RENAL RESERVE puts older adults at high risk for FLUID VOLUME OVERLOAD; crackles, dyspnea, distended neck veins, and dependent edema are the warning signs. Dry membranes, concentrated urine, and flat neck veins all point to fluid DEFICIT instead. Slow the infusion, raise the head of the bed, and notify the provider.

q: A nurse is securing a newly inserted IV catheter for a 79-year-old client whose skin is thin and tears with minimal friction. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
o: Wrap the extremity circumferentially with elastic tape to hold the catheter in place
Apply a skin barrier protectant, then secure the site with a transparent semipermeable dressing and minimal tape
Layer several strips of wide cloth tape over the hub for extra stability
Leave the site open to air without any dressing so it can be observed
r: THIN SKIN tears when adhesive is removed, so use a skin BARRIER, a transparent dressing, and MINIMAL TAPE; the clear dressing still allows the site to be inspected every hour. Circumferential wraps act like a tourniquet and hide infiltration until it is severe. Wide cloth tape multiplies adhesive injury, and no dressing at all leaves the insertion site open to infection.

q: A nurse is choosing a site to start an IV infusion for a 76-year-old client who is right-handed and lives alone. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)
o: Choose a vein in the left forearm
Avoid veins that lie directly over a joint or area of flexion
Use the antecubital fossa as the first choice for this routine infusion
Stabilize the vein by applying skin traction just below the insertion site
Select a vein on the back of the right hand so the left arm stays free
r: Use the NONDOMINANT arm and a FOREARM vein; the forearm has more supporting tissue than the back of the hand, which has fragile, mobile veins and little subcutaneous cushion in older adults. Joints and areas of flexion kink the catheter and cause dislodgement and infiltration. TRACTION BELOW the site anchors rolling veins. The antecubital fossa is saved for emergencies or specific therapies, not routine infusions.

q: A nurse is assessing a 67-year-old client who has a tracheostomy. Which of the following findings indicates that the client needs to be suctioned?
o: Respiratory rate of 16/min and even chest excursion
Coarse gurgling sounds auscultated over the trachea
SpO2 of 97% on 2 L/min by tracheostomy collar
Clear breath sounds throughout all lung fields
r: COARSE GURGLING over the trachea means SECRETIONS are pooling in the airway, which is a direct indication to suction. A normal respiratory rate, a good SpO2, and clear breath sounds all show a patent airway with no need to suction. Other true indications include restlessness, a falling SpO2, visible secretions, an ineffective cough, tachypnea, and rising peak airway pressures on a ventilator.

q: A newly hired nurse tells the charge nurse that she suctions every client who has a tracheostomy once every 2 hr to keep the airway clear. Which of the following responses by the charge nurse is appropriate?
o: That is correct, because scheduled suctioning prevents mucus plugs.
Increase it to every hour if the client is receiving mechanical ventilation.
Suctioning is done PRN based on your assessment findings, not on a set schedule.
Only suction when the provider writes an order for a specific time.
r: Suctioning is PRN NOT SCHEDULED. Routine q2h suctioning traumatizes the mucosa, causes hypoxemia and bradycardia, and raises infection risk with no proven benefit. Increasing the frequency to hourly makes the harm worse. The nurse does not need a timed provider order; assessment findings such as gurgling, restlessness, or a dropping SpO2 drive the decision.

q: A nurse is preparing to perform open endotracheal suctioning for an adult client in the ICU. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
o: Apply continuous suction while advancing the catheter into the airway
Suction for 30 seconds during each pass to clear the maximum amount of secretions
Hyperoxygenate the client before suctioning and limit each pass to 10 to 15 seconds
Repeat suctioning passes back to back until no further secretions return
r: HYPEROXYGENATE first and hold each pass to 10 TO 15 SECONDS to prevent HYPOXEMIA. Suction is applied only on WITHDRAWAL; suctioning while advancing strips and traumatizes the mucosa. Thirty second passes and back-to-back repeats drop the SpO2 sharply; limit to 2 or 3 passes with reoxygenation and rest between each one.

q: A nurse is suctioning a client's endotracheal tube when the cardiac monitor shows the heart rate falling from 88/min to 48/min. Which of the following actions should the nurse take first?
o: Continue suctioning quickly so the pass can be finished
Stop suctioning and administer oxygen to the client
Document the finding and reassess the client in 15 min
Increase the suction pressure to clear the secretions faster
r: Bradycardia during suctioning is VAGAL STIMULATION from catheter contact plus hypoxemia, so STOP and OXYGENATE immediately. Finishing the pass or raising the suction pressure deepens the hypoxia and worsens the vagal response. Documenting first delays treatment; stabilize the client, then document and notify the provider.

q: A nurse is pouring a liquid medication into a calibrated medication cup for a client on a medical unit. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
o: Hold the cup up at eye level with one hand while pouring the dose
Set the cup on a flat surface and read the dose at the base of the meniscus at eye level
Read the dose at the top edge of the curved surface of the liquid
Measure the dose using a household teaspoon from the client's tray
r: Set the cup on a FLAT SURFACE and read the BASE OF THE MENISCUS at EYE LEVEL; holding the cup in the air tilts it and distorts the reading. Reading the top of the curve overestimates the dose. Household teaspoons are not calibrated and vary widely in volume, so use a calibrated cup or an oral syringe instead.

q: A nurse pours 15 mL of a liquid antacid from a multidose bottle, but the prescribed dose is 10 mL. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
o: Pour the extra 5 mL back into the stock bottle
Administer the full 15 mL because the difference is small
Save the extra 5 mL in a labeled cup for the client's next dose
Discard the excess 5 mL and administer the prescribed 10 mL
r: DISCARD THE EXCESS. Returning poured medication to the stock bottle contaminates the entire supply. Giving 15 mL is a medication ERROR because it is not the prescribed dose, and saving poured liquid for later risks contamination and mislabeling. Pour with the LABEL PALMED so drips never obscure it.

q: A nurse is administering single-dose (unit-dose) oral liquid medications to clients on a medical unit. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)
o: Open the unit-dose package at the bedside after identifying the client
Shake a suspension thoroughly before measuring the dose
Draw a 3 mL oral dose into a Luer lock parenteral syringe
Hold the bottle with the medication label facing the palm of the hand
Open and pour all of the unit-dose packages in the medication room before entering client rooms
r: Unit-dose packages stay SEALED until the BEDSIDE, after two client identifiers are checked, so the drug stays identifiable and an unused dose can be returned. SHAKE suspensions or the client gets an uneven concentration of drug. PALM THE LABEL so drips do not destroy it. Never use a parenteral or Luer syringe for an oral dose because it can be connected to IV tubing by mistake, and pre-pouring in the med room defeats bedside identification.

q: A nurse is administering 5 mL of an oral liquid medication to an 84-year-old client who has dysphagia following a stroke. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
o: Mix the medication into a full glass of water and have the client drink it through a straw
Use an oral syringe to place small amounts along the side of the mouth toward the cheek
Instruct the client to tip the head back and swallow the dose quickly
Pour the dose into a medication cup and have the client drink it in one swallow
r: An ORAL SYRINGE lets the nurse deliver SMALL AMOUNTS along the SIDE of the mouth toward the cheek so the client controls each swallow, which lowers ASPIRATION risk. Tipping the head BACK opens the airway and promotes aspiration; the chin should be tucked down instead. Diluting in a full glass or gulping the dose delivers far too much volume at once for a client with dysphagia.

q: A 71-year-old client is admitted to the medical unit from the emergency department, and later that day is transferred to the telemetry unit. Two days later the provider writes discharge orders. Which of the following statements by the new graduate nurse indicates a correct understanding of when medication reconciliation must be performed?
o: Medication reconciliation is completed only one time, at the point of admission.
Medication reconciliation is required only when a client is discharged to home with new prescriptions.
Medication reconciliation is performed at admission, at each transfer between units or levels of care, and at discharge.
Medication reconciliation is performed only if the client reports taking more than five medications at home.
r: Medication reconciliation happens at EVERY TRANSITION OF CARE: admission, transfer, and discharge. Each handoff is a point where meds get dropped, duplicated, or wrongly dosed, which is why it is a NATIONAL PATIENT SAFETY GOAL. Admission-only and discharge-only are wrong because they leave the transfer handoff unprotected, and the number of medications does not determine whether reconciliation is required.

q: A nurse is completing the admission medication reconciliation for a 64-year-old client admitted for cellulitis. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)
o: Ask the client's daughter to bring in the actual medication bottles from home.
Document only the prescription medications, since OTC products are not clinically significant.
Record the name, dose, route, frequency, and time of the last dose taken for each medication.
Write the new inpatient prescriptions for any home medication that appears to have been omitted.
Ask specifically about herbals, vitamins, eye drops, inhalers, and transdermal patches.
r: A COMPLETE HOME LIST means everything the client puts in or on the body, so OTCs, herbals, vitamins, eye drops, inhalers, and patches all count; bringing in the actual bottles is the most accurate way to verify. Name, dose, route, frequency, and LAST DOSE TAKEN are the required data elements. Documenting prescriptions only is wrong because herbals and OTCs cause real interactions, and the nurse gathers and verifies but the PROVIDER reconciles and prescribes.

q: During admission medication reconciliation, a 58-year-old client says, "I just take my blood pressure pill and my water pill." The nurse notes the client's fingers are stained yellow-brown and the client mentions drinking an herbal tea nightly for sleep. Which of the following actions should the nurse take first?
o: Document the two medications the client reported and notify the provider that the list is complete.
Instruct the client that herbal products do not need to be reported because they are natural.
Hold all newly ordered medications until the client can name every product taken at home.
Ask the client open-ended questions about herbals, vitamins, and any other over-the-counter products used.
r: Clients routinely UNDER-REPORT OTC AND HERBAL PRODUCTS because they do not think of them as medicine, so the nurse probes with open-ended questions to build an accurate list. Documenting only two drugs propagates an incomplete list, telling the client herbals do not count is false since many interact with anticoagulants and sedatives, and blanket-holding all ordered medications is not the nurse's independent call and could harm the client.

q: A nurse is discharging an 80-year-old client who had two home medications discontinued and three new medications added during the hospital stay. Which of the following findings best indicates that discharge medication reconciliation and teaching were effective?
o: The client's updated written medication list was placed in the electronic health record and faxed to the pharmacy.
The client uses the updated written list to explain which two medications to stop and when to take each new medication.
The client states, "I will keep taking everything the same way I did before I came in."
The client's family member signs the discharge instruction sheet acknowledging receipt.
r: TEACH-BACK USING THE UPDATED WRITTEN LIST is the evaluation step; the client demonstrating what to stop and what to start proves comprehension, not just exposure. Filing or faxing the list and obtaining a signature document the process but prove nothing about client understanding, and continuing everything as before means the discontinued drugs will be DUPLICATED with the new ones.

q: A 77-year-old client on home hospice with end-stage COPD reports severe air hunger. The oxygen saturation is 95 percent on room air and the respiratory rate is 30/min. Which of the following interventions should the nurse anticipate as first-line for the sensation of dyspnea?
o: Apply a nonrebreather mask at 12 L/min.
Administer low-dose oral morphine as prescribed.
Perform deep nasotracheal suctioning.
Encourage the client to lie flat to conserve energy.
r: LOW-DOSE MORPHINE IS FIRST-LINE for the SENSATION of dyspnea at end of life; it blunts the central respiratory drive, reduces air hunger, and lowers preload. High-flow oxygen does not relieve dyspnea in a client who is NOT HYPOXEMIC at 95 percent, deep suctioning is traumatic and does not treat air hunger, and lying flat worsens the work of breathing.
topic: Comfort Measures for Dyspnea at End of Life

q: A nurse is caring for a 68-year-old client with terminal lung cancer who feels short of breath despite an oxygen saturation of 97 percent. Which of the following nonpharmacologic measures should the nurse use to relieve the sensation of breathlessness?
o: Raise the room temperature and add extra blankets.
Have the client lie supine with the head of bed flat.
Direct a small fan toward the client's face and position the client upright leaning over an overbed table.
Restrict visitors and leave the client alone in a darkened room.
r: MOVING COOL AIR ACROSS THE FACE stimulates TRIGEMINAL RECEPTORS and is an evidence-based way to reduce the sensation of breathlessness; upright or tripod positioning over an overbed table maximizes chest expansion. A warm room with extra blankets and lying supine both worsen air hunger, and leaving a breathless client alone increases anxiety, which intensifies dyspnea.
topic: Comfort Measures for Dyspnea at End of Life

q: A 74-year-old client is actively dying and has loud, wet, rattling respirations. The client is unresponsive and does not appear distressed. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
o: Administer prescribed glycopyrrolate and reposition the client onto the side.
Perform deep oropharyngeal suctioning every hour.
Increase the IV fluid rate to thin the secretions.
Administer a prescribed dose of naloxone.
r: The DEATH RATTLE is pooled upper airway secretions the dying client can no longer clear; ANTICHOLINERGICS such as glycopyrrolate, scopolamine, or atropine drops dry secretions, and side-lying positioning lets them drain. Deep suctioning is traumatic and only stimulates more secretions, extra IV fluid increases them, and naloxone would reverse comfort-directed opioids and cause needless suffering.
topic: Comfort Measures for Dyspnea at End of Life

q: The daughter of a dying client with severe dyspnea says, "I do not want her to have any more morphine. I am afraid it will stop her breathing and kill her." Which of the following responses should the nurse make?
o: "You are right that morphine is risky; I will ask the provider to switch to oxygen only."
"Try not to worry about it. The provider has already decided this is what she needs."
"If you refuse the morphine, we will have to document that you declined comfort care."
"That is a common worry. Low doses titrated to her comfort relieve the feeling of air hunger without hastening her death; may I tell you what to watch for?"
r: Fear that opioids HASTEN DEATH is a common misconception, and the nurse should address it directly with accurate information plus an invitation to keep talking. LOW DOSES TITRATED TO SYMPTOM RELIEF treat air hunger without shortening life. Agreeing that morphine is dangerous reinforces the myth, dismissing the worry blocks communication, and threatening documentation is coercive and nontherapeutic.
topic: Comfort Measures for Dyspnea at End of Life

q: A nurse is preparing to administer a continuous enteral feeding through a gastrostomy tube for a 62-year-old client who has had three loose stools in the past 8 hours. The nurse takes the formula bag directly from the refrigerator. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
o: Warm the formula in the microwave for 30 seconds before hanging it.
Hang the chilled formula and increase the rate to finish the feeding sooner.
Allow the formula to reach room temperature before hanging it.
Dilute the chilled formula with equal parts sterile water.
r: COLD FORMULA CAUSES CRAMPING AND DIARRHEA; enteral formula should be given at ROOM TEMPERATURE. Microwaving heats unevenly and can burn the gastric mucosa, increasing the rate makes diarrhea worse, and diluting is not done without a prescription and changes the delivered calories.
topic: Causes of Diarrhea with Enteral (G-Tube) Feedings

q: A 70-year-old client receiving enteral feedings through a gastrostomy tube develops frequent watery stools. Which of the following factors should the nurse identify as possible contributing causes? (Select all that apply.)
o: The formula is being delivered by rapid bolus rather than continuous infusion.
The client is receiving a liquid medication that contains sorbitol.
The formula bag was changed 6 hours ago using clean technique.
The client completed a course of broad-spectrum antibiotics last week.
The head of the bed is elevated to 35 degrees during the feeding.
r: RAPID BOLUS delivery triggers a dumping-type response, SORBITOL in liquid medications is an osmotic laxative, and recent BROAD-SPECTRUM ANTIBIOTICS cause antibiotic-associated diarrhea and C. DIFFICILE. Changing the bag at 6 hours is within the usual 4 to 8 hour open-system hang time and is correct practice, and elevating the head of bed prevents ASPIRATION rather than causing diarrhea.
topic: Causes of Diarrhea with Enteral (G-Tube) Feedings

q: A nurse notices that an open-system enteral formula bag for a 55-year-old client has been hanging at the bedside for 14 hours, and the client has begun having foul-smelling diarrhea and a low-grade fever. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
o: Add fresh formula to the existing bag to dilute the older formula.
Discard the formula, change the bag and tubing, and hang fresh formula labeled with the date and time.
Place the current bag on ice and continue the infusion at the same rate.
Stop all enteral nutrition indefinitely and request a prescription for total parenteral nutrition.
r: BACTERIAL CONTAMINATION from excessive HANG TIME is a classic cause of diarrhea; open-system formula is limited to about 4 to 8 hours, and bag and tubing are changed every 24 hours with clean technique and clear date and time labeling. Topping off an old bag spreads contamination, icing does not kill bacteria and cold formula worsens diarrhea, and jumping to TPN is far beyond the problem.
topic: Causes of Diarrhea with Enteral (G-Tube) Feedings

q: A client receiving continuous gastrostomy tube feedings reports abdominal cramping and has had several loose stools. Which of the following actions should the nurse take first?
o: Stop the tube feeding and notify the provider that the client cannot tolerate enteral nutrition.
Administer a prescribed antidiarrheal and continue the feeding at the current rate.
Increase the rate so the prescribed volume is completed before the next shift.
Assess the client, check gastric residual, and review the medication list for sorbitol-containing or magnesium-containing liquids.
