r: ASSESS BEFORE ACTING: the nurse checks the client and residual and screens the MED LIST for SORBITOL or MAGNESIUM liquids, which are the most commonly missed cause of tube-feeding diarrhea. Do NOT automatically stop the feeding without assessing, antidiarrheals mask the cause and are not first, and increasing the rate directly worsens diarrhea.
topic: Causes of Diarrhea with Enteral (G-Tube) Feedings

q: A nurse is teaching a 66-year-old client who has a new prescription for furosemide twice daily for heart failure. Which of the following statements by the client indicates correct understanding of the timing of the doses?
o: "I will take one dose at bedtime and one when I wake up during the night."
"I will take the first dose in the morning and the second no later than late afternoon."
"I will take both doses together with my evening meal."
"I will take it only on days when my ankles look swollen."
r: Furosemide is dosed in the MORNING with any second dose by LATE AFTERNOON to prevent NOCTURIA and the fall risk of nighttime bathroom trips. Bedtime and evening dosing guarantee the client is up all night, and taking it only when swelling appears means the client is self-adjusting a prescribed medication for heart failure.

q: A 59-year-old client taking furosemide reports leg cramps, unusual muscle weakness, and a heartbeat that "skips around." Which of the following instructions should the nurse give the client?
o: "Limit foods such as bananas and potatoes while you are on this medication."
"These are expected effects of the medication and do not need to be reported."
"Report these findings to your provider, and include potassium-rich foods such as bananas, potatoes, spinach, oranges, and tomatoes in your diet."
"Increase your intake of milk and cheese to correct these symptoms."
r: A LOOP DIURETIC WASTES POTASSIUM, and cramps, weakness, fatigue, and an irregular pulse are classic HYPOKALEMIA findings that must be reported. Potassium-rich foods such as bananas, potatoes, spinach, oranges, and tomatoes are the teaching point; restricting them worsens the deficit, dismissing an irregular pulse is unsafe, and dairy supplies CALCIUM, not potassium.

q: A nurse is administering IV furosemide to a 73-year-old client who is also receiving gentamicin. Which of the following findings should the nurse instruct the client to report immediately?
o: Ringing in the ears or a change in hearing.
A metallic taste in the mouth after eating.
Increased urine output during the first 2 hours after the dose.
Mild thirst in the afternoon.
r: Furosemide is OTOTOXIC, and the risk climbs with RAPID IV PUSH and with AMINOGLYCOSIDES such as gentamicin, so tinnitus or any hearing change must be reported immediately because damage can become permanent. Increased urine output is the expected therapeutic effect, and metallic taste and mild thirst are not the priority ototoxicity warning signs.

q: A nurse is providing discharge teaching to a 68-year-old client who has heart failure and new prescriptions for furosemide and digoxin. Which of the following instructions should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)
o: "Furosemide is potassium-sparing, so avoid potassium-rich foods."
"Weigh yourself daily at the same time in the same clothing and report a gain of 2 pounds in a day or 5 pounds in a week."
"Rise slowly from sitting or lying down, because this medication can make you dizzy."
"Stop the furosemide on any day you feel your heart racing or see visual halos."
"Wear sunscreen and protective clothing, because this medication can make your skin burn more easily."
r: DAILY WEIGHTS at the same time in the same clothing catch fluid retention early; 1 kg (2 lb) in a day or 2.3 kg (5 lb) in a week gets reported. ORTHOSTATIC HYPOTENSION means changing positions slowly, and PHOTOSENSITIVITY means sunscreen. Furosemide is NOT POTASSIUM-SPARING (that is spironolactone); it WASTES potassium, and low potassium raises the risk of DIGOXIN TOXICITY, so halos and palpitations are reported to the provider rather than treated by the client stopping a prescribed drug.

q: A nurse is performing a well-child assessment on a 4-month-old infant at a pediatric clinic. Which of the following findings should the nurse identify as a developmental deviation requiring further evaluation?
o: The infant does not yet babble consonant sounds such as ba-ba
The infant has not rolled from the back to the abdomen
The infant's head lags behind the body when pulled to a sitting position
The infant does not sit steadily without support
r: HEAD CONTROL BY 4 MONTHS IS THE BENCHMARK; persistent head lag at 4 months signals a neuromuscular or motor delay and needs referral. Babbling (6 to 9 months), rolling back to abdomen (about 6 months), and sitting unsupported (about 8 to 9 months) are all skills not yet due at 4 months, so they are expected, not deviations. Remember the earlier red flag too: no social smile by 2 to 3 months is abnormal.

q: A nurse is assessing a 12-month-old at a well-child visit. Which of the following findings should the nurse report to the provider?
o: The child picks up a small cracker using the thumb and index finger
The child's arms abduct and extend symmetrically when startled by a loud noise
The child cruises along the furniture but does not yet walk alone
The child says mama, dada, and one other meaningful word
r: A PERSISTENT MORO REFLEX PAST 6 MONTHS IS ABNORMAL and suggests a central nervous system problem, so it is reported. A pincer grasp should be present by 12 months, cruising is normal with independent walking expected by 15 months (a red flag only if absent at 18 months), and 3 to 5 words at 12 months is on target. Primitive reflexes that stick around are always the red flag.

q: A nurse is interviewing the parent of a 24-month-old during a routine visit. Which of the following findings should the nurse identify as requiring further developmental evaluation? Select all that apply.
o: The parent reports the child no longer says several words she used clearly at 15 months
The child plays beside another toddler with a separate set of blocks and does not share
The child does not yet combine two words into a phrase such as more juice
The child says no frequently and resists being dressed by the parent
The parent reports the child has reached for everything with only the left hand since 11 months of age
r: REGRESSION IS ALWAYS A RED FLAG AT ANY AGE, so loss of previously acquired words is reported immediately. No two-word phrases by 24 months signals expressive language delay, and hand dominance before 18 months suggests weakness on the opposite side. Parallel play at 2 years and negativism during autonomy versus shame and doubt are EXPECTED toddler behavior, not deviations.

q: A nurse is caring for a hospitalized 5-year-old who has started wetting the bed and asking to be fed by a parent, behaviors the child had outgrown at home. Which of the following responses by the nurse is appropriate?
o: Perform all of the child's morning care to reduce the child's stress
Tell the parent this behavior indicates a developmental disorder requiring referral
Restrict fluids and remind the child that big kids stay dry at night
Reassure the parent this is a temporary stress response and let the child choose the order of care tasks
r: REGRESSION DURING HOSPITALIZATION IS AN EXPECTED, TEMPORARY STRESS RESPONSE, not a true developmental deviation like regression that occurs at home without a stressor. A preschooler is in INITIATIVE VERSUS GUILT, so offering choices and letting the child help preserves initiative. Doing everything for the child fosters guilt, shaming increases regression, and referral is not needed for stress-related regression.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has Clostridioides difficile associated diarrhea. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
o: Use alcohol-based hand rub after removing gloves and leaving the room
Return the stethoscope to the shared supply cart after the assessment
Store extra dressing supplies in the cabinet under the room sink
Wash hands with soap and running water after providing client care
r: C. DIFFICILE FORMS SPORES THAT ALCOHOL DOES NOT KILL, so soap and water with friction is required to physically remove them. Soap and water is also required for norovirus and any time hands are visibly soiled. Contact precautions require DEDICATED single-client equipment, and supplies are never stored under a sink because of drain splash and leak contamination.

q: A nurse is teaching a group of nursing students about the chain of infection. Which of the following actions should the nurse identify as breaking the chain at the SUSCEPTIBLE HOST link?
o: Placing a client who has active tuberculosis in a negative pressure airborne isolation room
Teaching a client to cover the mouth with a tissue when coughing
Ensuring an older adult receives adequate protein and the recommended immunizations
Disinfecting the shared glucometer with a wipe before returning it to the cart
r: STRENGTHENING THE HOST breaks the chain at the susceptible host link; nutrition, immunization, glycemic control, and sleep make the host less likely to develop infection. Negative pressure isolation blocks the MODE OF TRANSMISSION, covering a cough blocks the PORTAL OF EXIT, and disinfecting shared equipment eliminates a RESERVOIR. Same goal, different links.

q: A charge nurse is making rounds on a medical unit to identify environmental reservoirs for microorganisms. Which of the following observations require corrective action? Select all that apply.
o: A vase of fresh flowers with standing water sits at the bedside of a client who is neutropenic
A box of sterile gauze is stored in the cabinet directly under the room sink
A stethoscope dedicated to one client on contact precautions hangs on the wall inside that client's room
A nebulizer cup sits uncovered and wet on the overbed table between scheduled treatments
A covered linen hamper with a foot-operated lid is positioned just inside the room doorway
r: STANDING WATER IS A RESERVOIR FOR GRAM-NEGATIVE ORGANISMS such as Pseudomonas; flower water and wet nebulizer or humidifier equipment must go, and respiratory equipment is rinsed, dried, and covered between uses. Supplies stored under a sink are exposed to drain leaks and splash. A dedicated in-room stethoscope and a covered foot-pedal hamper are CORRECT practice and need no action.

q: A charge nurse is observing a newly hired nurse provide care on a medical-surgical unit. Which of the following actions by the new nurse requires intervention?
o: Wiping the blood pressure cuff with a disinfectant wipe before taking it to the next client's room
Applying alcohol-based hand rub after removing gloves when the hands have visible wound drainage on them
Changing the continuous IV administration set at the interval specified by facility policy
Placing a package of clean linens on the overbed table rather than on the floor
r: ALCOHOL RUB DOES NOT WORK ON VISIBLY SOILED HANDS because organic material blocks it; soap and water is required, so this action needs intervention. Disinfecting shared equipment between clients removes a reservoir, IV tubing changed on schedule prevents intraluminal contamination, and clean items are never set on the FLOOR, which is always considered contaminated.

q: A nurse is caring for a client on postoperative day 5 following a colectomy. The client coughs, reports a sudden giving way sensation in the abdomen, and the nurse observes a loop of bowel protruding through the separated incision. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
o: Gently replace the bowel into the abdomen and apply an abdominal binder
Position the client in high Fowler's position with the legs extended
Cover the wound with sterile gauze moistened with sterile normal saline
Offer the client sips of clear liquids while awaiting the surgeon
r: EVISCERATION IS A SURGICAL EMERGENCY; cover the organs with STERILE SALINE-MOISTENED dressings to keep tissue from drying and necrosing, place the client in low Fowler's with knees FLEXED to reduce abdominal tension, keep NPO, and notify the surgeon. NEVER push organs back in, since that introduces infection and can injure bowel. High Fowler with legs straight increases tension on the wound, and fluids are withheld because the client is going to the operating room.

q: A nurse is assessing a client 12 hours after an exploratory laparotomy. Which of the following findings should the nurse report to the surgeon FIRST?
o: Heart rate 124/min, blood pressure 106/88 mm Hg, restlessness, and cool clammy skin
Oral temperature 37.8 C (100 F) with diminished breath sounds in the bases
Absence of flatus and hypoactive bowel sounds in all four quadrants
Incisional pain rated 6 on a scale of 0 to 10 that is relieved by the ordered analgesic
r: TACHYCARDIA WITH A NARROWING PULSE PRESSURE AND RESTLESSNESS IS EARLY INTERNAL HEMORRHAGE; compensation keeps the systolic up, so hypotension is a LATE sign and the nurse cannot wait for it. A low-grade fever with diminished bases in the first 48 hours suggests atelectasis, treated with incentive spirometry, splinted coughing, and ambulation. Hypoactive sounds and no flatus this early are expected, and controlled incisional pain is expected.

q: A nurse is assessing a client on the first postoperative day after an open cholecystectomy. Which of the following findings should the nurse identify as EXPECTED?
o: Thick yellow-green purulent drainage seeping from the incision
A small amount of serosanguineous drainage on the dressing
A rigid, board-like abdomen with rebound tenderness
Oral temperature of 39.2 C (102.6 F) with chills
r: A SMALL AMOUNT OF SEROSANGUINEOUS DRAINAGE IS EXPECTED in the first 24 to 48 hours as the wound seals. Purulent drainage plus fever typically appears on postoperative day 3 to 5 and signals WOUND INFECTION; a rigid board-like abdomen suggests hemorrhage or peritonitis; and a temperature above 38 C with chills is never expected. Watch for a sudden INCREASE in serosanguineous drainage on day 4 or 5, which warns of impending dehiscence.

q: A nurse is caring for a client on postoperative day 3 following an abdominal hysterectomy. The client has a distended abdomen, absent bowel sounds, no passage of flatus, and has vomited 300 mL of green fluid. Which of the following actions should the nurse take first?
o: Encourage the client to drink a carbonated beverage to stimulate peristalsis
Administer the scheduled opioid analgesic before ambulating the client
Apply a warm compress to the abdomen and reassess in 1 hour
Withhold oral intake and notify the surgeon of the findings
r: THIS IS PARALYTIC ILEUS; absent bowel sounds beyond 24 to 48 hours with distention, no flatus, and vomiting means the gut is not moving, so the client is kept NPO and the surgeon is notified for possible NG decompression. Giving oral fluids to a client who is vomiting with an obstructed gut risks ASPIRATION. Opioids further slow peristalsis and worsen ileus, and a warm compress delays needed treatment. Early ambulation prevents ileus but does not treat established ileus with vomiting.

q: A nurse on a medical unit receives report on four clients. Which of the following clients should the nurse assess FIRST?
o: An 80-year-old who has a Braden Scale score of 13 and is due to be repositioned
A 74-year-old who received lorazepam 30 min ago and is asking for help to the bathroom
A 62-year-old with left-sided weakness after a stroke who has not had a swallow screen and whose family has started feeding the client breakfast
A 55-year-old who has an indwelling urinary catheter and an oral temperature of 38 C (100.4 F)
r: AIRWAY BEATS EVERYTHING; a client with post-stroke dysphagia risk who is eating before a swallow screen can ASPIRATE right now, so the nurse intervenes immediately. The sedated client is a real fall risk and is next, but the client is asking for help rather than already moving. A Braden of 13 needs repositioning and the catheter client needs a fever workup, but neither is an immediate airway threat.

q: A nurse is identifying clients at risk for falls on a medical unit. Which of the following clients should the nurse identify as being at GREATEST risk?
o: A 78-year-old admitted overnight with a urinary tract infection who is intermittently confused and receiving furosemide
A 65-year-old who ambulates independently with a steady gait and has no history of falls
A 30-year-old on postoperative day 2 who uses a walker correctly and calls for assistance
A 52-year-old on bed rest who is alert, oriented, and has a bedside commode within reach
r: RISK FACTORS STACK: age over 65, altered mental status, a diuretic causing urinary urgency, and an unfamiliar environment overnight add up to the highest fall risk. The other clients have one factor at most and are alert, cooperative, and using devices correctly. Morse-style scoring rewards this thinking: mental status, history of falling, medications, gait, and IV or device use.

q: A nurse is reviewing Braden Scale results for four clients on a long-term care unit. Which of the following clients should the nurse identify as being at greatest risk for a pressure injury?
o: A client with a score of 20 who ambulates in the hall three times daily
A client with a score of 18 who reports occasional moisture from perspiration
A client with a score of 11 who is bedfast, incontinent of urine, and eats less than half of each meal
A client with a score of 16 who uses a walker and requires minimal assistance with meals
r: ON THE BRADEN SCALE, A LOWER SCORE MEANS HIGHER RISK; a score of 11 falls in the high risk range. This client also fails multiple subscales at once: activity (bedfast), mobility, moisture (incontinence), and nutrition. Scores of 16 to 20 indicate mild or no risk, and single mild deficits do not carry the same danger as several low subscales combined with friction and shear.

q: A nurse is identifying clients at increased risk for a health care associated infection. Which of the following clients should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: A 60-year-old receiving chemotherapy who has an absolute neutrophil count of 400/mm3
A 72-year-old who has had an indwelling urinary catheter in place for 6 days
A 24-year-old who had an appendectomy 3 years ago and has a well-healed scar
An 84-year-old who has a serum albumin of 2.1 g/dL and a stage 3 pressure injury
A 35-year-old who has well-controlled asthma managed with a daily inhaled corticosteroid
r: IMMUNOSUPPRESSION, INDWELLING DEVICES, MALNUTRITION, AND BREAKS IN SKIN INTEGRITY are the core infection risk factors, along with advanced age and poorly controlled diabetes. Neutropenia removes the first line of defense, every catheter day raises CAUTI risk, and low albumin with an open wound means poor healing plus a portal of entry. A healed old surgical scar and controlled asthma on a low-dose inhaled steroid do not create meaningful risk.

q: A nurse on a medical unit is assessing a 68-year-old client who has a peripheral IV in the left forearm infusing 0.9% sodium chloride. The skin around the site is cool, pale, and puffy, the skin feels taut, and the pump keeps alarming for occlusion. Which of the following actions should the nurse take first?
o: Flush the catheter briskly with 10 mL of sodium chloride to clear the occlusion
Apply a warm compress and continue the infusion at a slower rate
Stop the infusion, remove the catheter, and elevate the extremity
Milk the tubing above the site to restore the flow rate
r: COOL AND PALE AND SWOLLEN AND TAUT = INFILTRATION, so fluid is leaking into tissue and the catheter must come out; elevating the arm helps reabsorption and the new site goes in the OTHER arm. Flushing or milking pushes more fluid into the tissue and worsens injury. Continuing the infusion at any rate keeps damaging tissue, and a compress is only useful AFTER the catheter is removed.

q: A nurse is administering a vesicant chemotherapy agent through a peripheral IV to a 54-year-old client in an infusion clinic. The client reports sudden burning pain at the site, and the nurse notes early blistering of the skin. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
o: Remove the catheter immediately and apply firm pressure to the site
Stop the infusion, leave the catheter in place, and aspirate residual drug
Increase the rate of the primary fluid to dilute the medication in the tissue
Apply a tourniquet above the site and elevate the arm above heart level
r: BURNING PLUS BLISTERING WITH A VESICANT = EXTRAVASATION, and the catheter is the only route to aspirate residual drug and instill an antidote, so it STAYS IN until the provider directs removal. Pulling the catheter first destroys that access. Increasing the rate drives more vesicant into tissue, and a tourniquet traps the drug and worsens necrosis.

q: A nurse is assessing a 42-year-old client who has had a peripheral IV in the right hand for 3 days. The site is red and warm, is tender to touch, and the nurse palpates a firm cord along the path of the vein. There is no drainage and the client is afebrile. Which of the following interpretations and actions is correct?
o: Infiltration; slow the infusion and apply a cool compress
Catheter-related bacteremia; obtain blood cultures before removing the catheter
Venous spasm; apply a warm compress and continue infusing at the ordered rate
Phlebitis; discontinue the IV, apply warm moist compresses, and restart in another site
r: RED, WARM, TENDER, PALPABLE CORD = PHLEBITIS, so the line comes out, warm moist heat goes on, a new site is started elsewhere, and the nurse grades the phlebitis per policy. Infiltration is COOL and PALE, not red and warm. No fever, no purulent drainage means this is not bacteremia, and venous spasm causes cramping pain with slowed flow, not a cord with redness.

q: A nurse is caring for an 80-year-old client who has heart failure and is receiving IV fluids at 150 mL/hr. The client now reports shortness of breath. The nurse notes crackles in the bases, distended neck veins, a bounding pulse, blood pressure 172/94 mm Hg, and a 2 kg weight gain since yesterday. Which of the following actions should the nurse take first?
o: Place the client in the left lateral Trendelenburg position
Slow the infusion to a keep-vein-open rate and raise the head of the bed
Discontinue the IV catheter and restart it in the opposite arm
Obtain a blood culture from the IV site and notify the provider
r: CRACKLES PLUS DISTENDED NECK VEINS PLUS BOUNDING PULSE PLUS WEIGHT GAIN = CIRCULATORY OVERLOAD, so the nurse cuts the volume to KVO and sits the client up to ease breathing, then notifies the provider and anticipates a diuretic and oxygen. Left lateral Trendelenburg is the AIR EMBOLISM position. Restarting the IV elsewhere does not reduce the fluid load, and cultures address infection, which this client does not show.

q: A nurse is changing the tubing on a central venous catheter for a 60-year-old client when the client suddenly becomes dyspneic and reports chest pain. The client is hypotensive and anxious, and the nurse auscultates a churning murmur over the precordium. Which of the following actions should the nurse take first?
o: Lower the head of the bed and place the client flat and supine
Administer a prescribed IV diuretic and reassess the lung sounds
Clamp the catheter and position the client in left lateral Trendelenburg
Remove the central catheter and hold pressure over the insertion site
r: SUDDEN DYSPNEA PLUS CHEST PAIN PLUS CHURNING MURMUR DURING TUBING CHANGE = AIR EMBOLISM, so clamp the line to stop more air entry and turn the client LEFT LATERAL TRENDELENBURG to trap air in the right atrium, then give 100% oxygen and notify the provider. Flat supine does not trap the air. A diuretic treats overload, not air, and yanking the catheter can allow even more air to enter.

q: A nurse is precepting a newly licensed nurse about preventing peripheral IV complications on a busy surgical unit. Which of the following actions by the newly licensed nurse indicate an understanding of prevention? (Select all that apply.)
o: Secures the catheter with a stabilization device so the hub does not move
Milks the tubing when the pump alarms to restore the flow rate
Uses an electronic infusion pump for high-alert medications such as potassium
Selects the smallest available vein over an area of flexion for a large-volume infusion
Assesses the insertion site at least every shift and more often per facility policy
r: PREVENTION = STABILIZE, PUMP, AND ASSESS. Securing the catheter prevents mechanical phlebitis and dislodgement, pumps control high-alert drugs like potassium to prevent speed shock and extravasation, and routine site checks catch problems early. MILKING the tubing forces fluid into tissue and can dislodge a clot or catheter fragment, and a tiny vein over a joint raises infiltration and phlebitis risk; choose an appropriate gauge in a straight, non-flexion vein.

q: A nurse is assessing a 71-year-old client who has a tracheostomy on a medical-surgical unit. Which of the following findings indicate that the client needs suctioning? (Select all that apply.)
o: Lung sounds clear to auscultation in all fields after a productive cough
Coarse gurgling crackles auscultated over the trachea
New restlessness with SpO2 falling from 96% to 88%
The client states the last suctioning was 2 hours ago and asks to be suctioned on schedule
Visible secretions bubbling in the tracheostomy tube with a weak, ineffective cough
r: SUCTION FOR FINDINGS, NOT FOR THE CLOCK. Gurgling or coarse crackles over the trachea, restlessness with a dropping SpO2, and visible secretions the client cannot cough out are all ASSESSMENT-BASED indicators of retained secretions. Clear lung sounds after an effective productive cough mean the client is clearing the airway independently, and routine scheduled suctioning is not indicated because it causes needless hypoxemia and mucosal trauma.
topic: Recognizing the Need for Suctioning and Airway Clearance

q: A nurse is performing endotracheal suctioning for an adult client in the intensive care unit. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
o: Apply continuous suction while advancing the catheter into the airway
Apply suction only while withdrawing and rotating the catheter, for 10 to 15 seconds
Perform at least 5 consecutive passes to fully clear the airway
Set the wall suction regulator to 250 mm Hg to remove thick secretions
r: SUCTION ON THE WAY OUT ONLY, 10 TO 15 SECONDS PER PASS. Suctioning while advancing strips oxygen and shears the mucosa. Limit to 2 to 3 passes with rest and hyperoxygenation between them, because more passes cause hypoxemia. Adult wall suction should be about 100 to 150 mm Hg; 250 mm Hg causes mucosal trauma and bloody secretions.
topic: Recognizing the Need for Suctioning and Airway Clearance

q: A nurse is suctioning a 65-year-old client who has an endotracheal tube. Midway through the second pass, the cardiac monitor shows the heart rate dropping from 82/min to 44/min and the client becomes dusky. Which of the following actions should the nurse take first?
o: Complete the pass quickly, then reassess the heart rate
Increase the suction pressure to shorten the time the catheter is in the airway
Instill 5 mL of sterile saline into the tube to loosen secretions
Stop suctioning immediately, withdraw the catheter, and hyperoxygenate the client
r: NEW BRADYCARDIA DURING SUCTIONING = VAGAL STIMULATION PLUS HYPOXEMIA, so STOP, pull the catheter, and give 100% oxygen right away. Finishing the pass prolongs the vagal stimulus and the hypoxia. Raising the pressure worsens both trauma and oxygen loss, and saline instillation is not recommended because it drops SpO2 and pushes organisms deeper.
topic: Recognizing the Need for Suctioning and Airway Clearance

q: A nurse is preparing to suction a client who has a new tracheostomy. Which of the following actions should the nurse take to reduce the risk of suctioning-related hypoxemia?
o: Withhold supplemental oxygen until all passes are finished so secretions mobilize
Suction on a strict every-2-hour schedule regardless of assessment findings
Hyperoxygenate with 100% oxygen before suctioning and between each pass
Use the largest catheter that will fit inside the tracheostomy tube lumen
r: HYPEROXYGENATE BEFORE AND BETWEEN PASSES builds an oxygen reserve, which is the single best defense against suctioning hypoxemia. Withholding oxygen guarantees desaturation. Clock-based suctioning adds unnecessary hypoxic episodes and mucosal injury, and an oversized catheter occludes the airway and pulls out more oxygen than secretions; the catheter should occupy no more than about half the lumen.
topic: Recognizing the Need for Suctioning and Airway Clearance

q: A nurse is teaching an assistive personnel about airway clearance techniques on a rehabilitation unit. Which of the following statements by the nurse is correct?
o: Tracheostomy and endotracheal suctioning require sterile technique, while oropharyngeal suctioning uses clean technique
Oropharyngeal suctioning requires sterile gloves and a sterile field at the bedside
The same catheter may be reused for the trachea and then the mouth during one session
Clean technique is acceptable for tracheostomy suctioning as long as the client is at home on hospice
r: STERILE BELOW THE VOCAL CORDS, CLEAN ABOVE THEM. The lower airway is normally sterile, so tracheostomy and ET suctioning use sterile technique; the mouth is already colonized, so oral suctioning is clean. Sterile setup for oral suctioning is unnecessary. NEVER go from trachea to mouth with the same catheter; that direction moves oral flora toward the lungs, and the mouth is always suctioned last with a separate device.
topic: Recognizing the Need for Suctioning and Airway Clearance

q: A nurse is caring for four clients. Which of the following clients should the nurse suction first?
o: A 58-year-old with a tracheostomy who has clear breath sounds and coughs thick sputum into a tissue without help
A 34-year-old postoperative client with an oral airway who has a strong cough and SpO2 of 97%
A 47-year-old with a chest tube who reports mild pleuritic pain and has diminished sounds at the base on the operative side
A 72-year-old on a ventilator with rising peak inspiratory pressures, coarse gurgling over the trachea, and increasing agitation
r: RISING PEAK INSPIRATORY PRESSURE PLUS GURGLING PLUS AGITATION = SECRETIONS OBSTRUCTING THE AIRWAY, the only client with an airway that is actively failing to clear. The tracheostomy client with clear sounds and an effective cough is clearing secretions on his own, and the postoperative client with a strong cough and SpO2 of 97% needs coughing and deep breathing, not a catheter. Diminished sounds at a chest tube site with pleuritic pain point to splinting and pain control, not suctioning.
topic: Recognizing the Need for Suctioning and Airway Clearance

q: A charge nurse is planning care for a stable client on bed rest who needs a complete bath. Which approach is appropriate?
o: The nurse must give the bath personally because skin assessment cannot be delegated
Assistive personnel may give the bath, and the nurse remains accountable for assessing the skin
Assistive personnel may give the bath and chart the skin assessment findings
The bath should be delayed until the nurse has time to do it
r: Bathing a stable client is a standard, predictable task that assistive personnel may perform, but the nurse still owns the assessment and the documentation of skin findings. Choosing the first option confuses delegating the task with delegating the assessment; the nurse can get skin data at another point in the shift or ask the aide to report what was seen.

q: A nurse is preparing to give a bed bath. Which water temperature should the nurse use?
o: About 32 C (90 F)
About 38 C (100 F)
About 43 C (110 F)
About 52 C (125 F)
r: Roughly 43 C (110 F) is warm enough to clean and relax the client without burning fragile skin. Water near 52 C (125 F) can scald an older adult in seconds, and lukewarm water chills the client and cleans poorly.

q: A nurse is washing a client's arm during a bed bath. Which technique should the nurse use?
o: Short circular strokes moving from the shoulder toward the hand
Long strokes moving from the hip toward the ankle
Firm scrubbing over bony areas to stimulate circulation
Long, firm strokes moving from the hand toward the shoulder
r: Washing from distal to proximal, meaning from the hand toward the shoulder, supports venous return toward the heart. Stroking away from the heart or scrubbing bony prominences does nothing for circulation and can injure thin skin.

q: A nurse is bathing a client who has a history of deep vein thrombosis in the left leg. Which modification should the nurse make?
o: Omit washing the legs during the bath
Use light strokes over the lower legs instead of firm pressure
Massage the calf firmly to improve venous return
Apply a hot pack to the calf before washing it
r: Firm pressure or massage over a leg with a clot history risks dislodging a thrombus and causing a pulmonary embolus, so the nurse cleans gently with light strokes. Massaging the calf feels helpful but is the specific action that creates the embolic risk; skipping the legs entirely is unnecessary and leaves skin unassessed.

q: An 84-year-old client reports dry, itchy skin and states that they shower daily using hot water and a deodorant soap. Which teaching should the nurse provide?
o: Continue daily showers but raise the water temperature
Apply an alcohol-based rub to the skin after each shower
Shower less often, use warm rather than hot water, and apply moisturizer afterward
Scrub with a stiff brush to remove the flaking skin
r: Aging skin is thinner, drier, and produces less oil, so frequent hot soapy baths strip what little moisture remains. Turning the water up or using alcohol products dries the skin further and increases the risk of cracks that become entry points for infection.

q: A nurse is removing dentures for a client who cannot do so independently. Which action should the nurse take to remove the upper denture?
o: Grasp the front of the upper denture with a gauze square and move it down and out
Grasp the front of the upper denture and lift it up and out
Ask the client to bite down while pulling the denture straight back
Use bare fingers so the grip does not slip
r: The upper plate breaks its seal when it is eased down and out, and gauze over a gloved hand gives a secure hold on a slippery, fragile device. Lifting up and out is the motion for the lower denture, and bare hands expose the nurse to oral secretions.

q: A client removes their dentures at bedtime. How should the nurse store them?
o: Wrapped in a tissue on the bedside table
Left dry in an open emesis basin
Soaking in hot water to sanitize them
In a labeled denture cup with enough water to cover them
r: Dentures stay moist so they do not warp and so they slide back in comfortably, and the labeled cup prevents the very common loss that happens when dentures are wrapped in tissue or set on a tray. Hot water can distort the acrylic, which is why tepid water is used for rinsing and storage.

q: A nurse is about to provide oral care for a client who is unresponsive after a head injury. Which position should the nurse use?
o: Supine with the bed flat
Side-lying with the head turned toward the mattress and suction within reach
High Fowler with the neck extended
Prone with a towel under the chin
r: Turning the client to the side with the head angled toward the mattress lets secretions and rinse pool in the lower cheek and drain out rather than into the airway, and suction must be ready before care starts. Lying flat or with the neck extended sends fluid straight toward the trachea in a client who cannot protect the airway.

q: Assistive personnel tell the nurse they plan to soak and trim the toenails of a client who has peripheral vascular disease. Which response should the nurse make?
o: That is fine as long as the water is not too hot
Go ahead and trim them, but do not soak the feet first
Please do not trim the nails; this client's foot care is done by a qualified professional, and I will check for an order
Only trim the nails on the foot with the stronger pulse
r: Impaired circulation means a small nick can become a nonhealing ulcer, so nail care for clients with peripheral vascular disease, diabetes, or immunosuppression is not routine delegated care and requires a qualified professional and a provider order. Adjusting the water temperature does not remove the risk created by cutting the nails themselves.

q: A nurse is observing a newly licensed nurse provide hygiene care. Which action requires the observing nurse to intervene?
o: Clipping the toenails of a client who has diabetes mellitus without checking for a provider order
Smoothing a rough fingernail edge with an emery board for a client who has no vascular disease
Inspecting the skin between the toes while giving a bed bath
Drying carefully between the toes after washing the feet
r: Nails are generally not cut for a client with diabetes without a provider order because neuropathy and poor perfusion turn a tiny cut into an infected wound. Filing a nail edge for a client with intact circulation is low risk, and inspecting and drying between the toes are exactly the assessments that prevent breakdown.

q: A nurse is providing perineal care for a female client who has an indwelling urinary catheter. In which direction should the nurse cleanse?
o: From the rectum toward the pubic area
Back and forth across the perineum
Starting at the anus and moving outward in circles
From the pubic area back toward the rectum, using a clean section of the cloth for each stroke
r: Cleansing front to back carries organisms away from the urethral meatus and lowers the risk of a catheter-associated urinary tract infection. Any back-and-forth or back-to-front motion drags fecal flora toward the meatus, which is the exact mechanism the technique exists to prevent.

q: A nurse is observing perineal care being provided to an uncircumcised male client. Which action requires follow-up?
o: Cleaning the tip of the penis in a circular motion outward from the meatus
Leaving the foreskin retracted after cleaning and drying the area
Retracting the foreskin before washing the glans
Using a clean section of the washcloth for each stroke
r: The foreskin must be returned to its usual position after care, because leaving it retracted constricts the glans and can cause swelling and impaired blood flow. Retracting it to clean and wiping outward from the meatus are both correct steps, which is why the omission at the end is easy to miss.

q: A nurse is changing linens on an occupied bed and has turned the client onto one side. Which action should the nurse take next?
o: Lower both side rails so the client can move freely
Place the soiled linens on the floor next to the bed
Raise the side rail on the side the client is facing before moving to the opposite side
Lower the bed to its lowest position to protect the nurse's back
r: Raising the rail the client is turned toward keeps the client from rolling out of a raised bed while the nurse works on the far side. Lowering the bed at this point actually strains the nurse's back and does nothing to prevent a fall, and soiled linens go in a hamper, never on the floor or against the uniform.

q: A nurse is preparing to comb the hair of a client who has tightly curled hair. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Use a wide-toothed comb or pick and ask the client how they usually care for their hair
Use a fine-toothed comb and pull briskly through the tangles
Braid the hair tightly so it stays neat between shampoos
Shampoo the hair daily with the facility supply
r: A wide-toothed comb or pick moves through tightly curled hair without breaking it, and hair care is strongly tied to culture and identity, so the client's own routine guides the plan. A fine-toothed comb pulled through curls snaps hair and hurts, and daily shampooing dries many hair types.

q: A client on strict bed rest asks to have their hair washed. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Explain that shampooing must wait until activity is advanced
Transfer the client to a shower chair for a quick wash
Brush the hair and apply powder to absorb the oil instead
Use a shampoo trough at the bedside or a no-rinse shampoo cap
r: A plastic trough or a no-rinse cap lets the nurse honor the request without violating activity limits, and clean hair strongly supports self-image during a long stay. Transferring the client to a shower chair breaks the bed rest order, and powder masks odor rather than cleaning the scalp.

q: A client who is receiving warfarin asks the nurse for help shaving. Which item should the nurse provide?
o: A single-blade safety razor with generous shaving cream
An electric razor
A straight razor used after a warm compress
A disposable razor moved against the direction of hair growth
r: An electric razor does not break the skin, which matters for any client on anticoagulants or with a low platelet count because a small shaving nick can bleed for a long time. Shaving cream and warm compresses make a blade shave more comfortable but do nothing to prevent the cut itself.

q: A nurse is shaving a client's face with a blade razor. Which technique should the nurse use?
o: Move the razor against the direction of hair growth for a closer result
Keep the skin loose so the blade glides over it
Hold the skin taut and stroke in the direction of hair growth, using short strokes near the chin and lips
Shave dry so the skin is not softened
r: Taut skin and strokes that follow hair growth reduce nicks and irritation, and short strokes give control over the curved areas around the chin and lips. Shaving against the grain gives a closer shave but raises the risk of cuts and ingrown hairs, and dry skin drags on the blade.

q: A client declines a morning shower, explaining that they bathe in the evening and do not wash their hair on certain days for religious reasons. Which response should the nurse make?
o: Adjust the plan of care to match the client's routine and record the preferences
Explain that facility routine requires bathing in the morning
Ask a family member to persuade the client to shower now
Document that the client refused hygiene care
r: Hygiene practices are shaped by culture and personal habit, and honoring them costs nothing clinically while preserving trust and dignity. Charting a refusal misrepresents what happened, since the client is not declining hygiene, only the timing and one specific element.

q: A client who requires assistance with bathing tells the nurse they feel humiliated at needing help. Which action best supports the client's dignity?
o: Complete the bath as quickly as possible to shorten the exposure
Reassure the client that staff see this every day so there is no reason to feel embarrassed
Bring in a second staff member so the bath finishes faster
Let the client wash whatever areas they can and ask how they prefer the care to be done
r: Loss of control is the source of the distress, so returning choices and letting the client do any part of the care directly addresses it. Telling the client not to feel embarrassed dismisses the feeling rather than resolving it, and adding staff increases exposure instead of reducing it.

q: An older adult who takes a diuretic and an antidepressant reports a constantly dry mouth. Which explanation should the nurse give?
o: Dry mouth is not related to medications
Saliva production decreases with age, and both of these medications reduce it further
This finding means dehydration is present and IV fluids are needed
This is an early sign of gum disease
r: Reduced saliva is an expected aging change that is amplified by diuretics, antidepressants, antihypertensives, and anti-inflammatory drugs. Dry mouth alone does not establish dehydration, though it does raise the risk of caries and gum disease, which is why oral care becomes more important rather than less.

q: A client remains unresponsive and requires oral care every 2 hr. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Turn the client onto one side so the face angles down toward the mattress
Insert a gloved finger between the molars to hold the mouth open
Have suction equipment set up and within reach
Pour a large volume of rinse toward the back of the mouth to flush debris
Use a small amount of solution on a soft brush or swab
Place the client flat on the back with the bed lowered
r: Side-lying positioning, ready suction, and minimal fluid all serve one goal: keeping rinse out of the airway in a client with no gag reflex. Flooding the mouth or laying the client flat causes aspiration, and placing fingers between the teeth risks a bite injury since an unconscious client can still clamp down.

q: A nurse is teaching a client who has type 2 diabetes mellitus how to care for the feet at home. Which of the following instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Look at your feet every day, including the skin between the toes
Dry your feet completely after washing them in lukewarm water
Rub lotion generously between the toes to prevent cracking
Cut the toenails straight across and smooth the edges with an emery board
Use an over-the-counter pad to dissolve any corns or calluses
Feel inside your shoes for rough seams or objects before putting them on
r: Daily inspection, thorough drying, straight nail trimming, and checking shoes all prevent the unnoticed injury that starts a diabetic foot ulcer. Moisturizer between the toes traps moisture and encourages fungal breakdown, and over-the-counter corn removers contain harsh chemicals that burn insensate skin.

q: A nurse is identifying clients who need especially thorough oral hygiene. Which of the following clients should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: A client who is unconscious following a head injury
A client who is receiving nothing by mouth and is dehydrated
A client who ambulates independently and eats a regular diet
A resident of a long-term care facility who has dementia
A client who is alert and completes all self-care without help
r: Clients who are unconscious, dehydrated, cognitively impaired, or seriously ill cannot clear their own mouths, and the resulting bacterial load is a direct route to aspiration pneumonia. Independent clients still need oral care, but they can perform it themselves, so nursing time goes to those who cannot.

q: A nurse is assigning hygiene tasks on a medical unit. Which of the following may be delegated to assistive personnel? Select all that apply.
o: Giving a complete bed bath to a stable client on bed rest
Trimming the toenails of a client who has peripheral vascular disease
Helping a client with routine denture care
Teaching a client with diabetes how to inspect the feet
Shampooing a client's hair with a no-rinse cap
Deciding whether a reddened area over the sacrum blanches
r: Bathing, denture care, and shampooing are standard predictable tasks on a stable client and fall within the role of assistive personnel. Nail care for a client with vascular disease, client teaching, and evaluating a pressure area are nursing judgment or high-risk skills and stay with the nurse.

q: A nurse is providing perineal care for a client who can do very little to help with the procedure. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Cleanse from the pubic area back toward the rectum
Use the same section of the washcloth for each stroke
Retract the foreskin to clean the tip of the penis, then return it to its usual position
Pat the area completely dry before covering the client
Leave the area uncovered so it can air dry
r: Front-to-back cleansing, replacing the foreskin, and drying thoroughly protect skin integrity and reduce urinary infection risk. Reusing the same cloth surface simply spreads organisms, and leaving the client exposed to air dry sacrifices privacy and warmth for no benefit.

q: A nurse is teaching a family member about expected age-related changes in an older adult. Which of the following should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: The skin becomes thinner and drier
Fingernails and toenails grow more slowly
Sweating increases noticeably
Hair growth increases in the nose, ears, and eyebrows
Saliva production rises, so dry mouth is unlikely
The tissue supporting the teeth weakens, raising the risk of gum disease
r: Thinner drier skin, slower nail growth, coarser hair in the ears and nose, and a weakening periodontal membrane are all expected with aging and shape how often hygiene care is given. Perspiration and saliva both decrease rather than increase, which is why over-bathing dries the skin and why dry mouth is so common.

q: A nurse is giving a complete bed bath. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Raise the bed to a height that protects the nurse's back
Offer the client a bedpan or a trip to the toilet before starting
Wash the legs and feet before washing the face
Keep a bath blanket over the areas that are not being washed
Continue using the same basin of water through perineal care
Change the water once it becomes cool
r: Adjusting the bed height, toileting first, draping, and refreshing cooled water make the bath safe and comfortable and prevent interruption partway through. The face is washed before the lower body, and perineal care always uses fresh water because reusing the basin moves organisms to the urethral area.

q: A nurse is changing the linens on an occupied bed. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Turn the client to one side and roll the used linens toward the client's back
Raise the side rail on the far side before turning the client toward it
Hold the soiled linens against the uniform to keep them off the floor
Smooth the clean bottom sheet so no wrinkles remain under the client
Shake the clean sheets open over the bed to unfold them quickly
r: Rolling the used linen under the client, guarding the turning side with a rail, and eliminating wrinkles keep the client safe and protect skin from pressure and shear. Soiled linen held against the uniform contaminates the nurse's clothing, and shaking linens sends organisms into the air.

q: A nurse is cleaning the dentures of a client who cannot manage them independently. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Apply clean gloves and use a gauze square for a secure grip
Remove the lower denture by lifting its front edge upward and outward
Rinse the dentures under hot running water
Store the dentures in a labeled cup with enough water to cover them
Set the dentures on the meal tray while the client eats
r: Clean gloves with gauze give a safe grip on a slippery device, the lower plate releases with an up-and-out motion, and a labeled water-filled cup keeps dentures moist and identifiable. Hot water can warp the acrylic, and dentures left on a meal tray are among the most commonly lost items in a facility.

q: An older adult tells the nurse they now hold the newspaper at arm's length to read it. Which age-related change explains this finding?
o: The lens has become cloudy and blocks light
The lens has lost elasticity and no longer focuses on near objects
Pressure inside the eye has increased
The center of the retina has deteriorated
r: Presbyopia is the expected stiffening of the lens with age, which makes close focus difficult while distance vision stays useful. A cloudy lens describes cataracts, which blur vision at all distances rather than only up close.

q: A client newly diagnosed with cataracts asks the nurse what is happening to their eye. Which response should the nurse make?
o: The fluid pressure inside your eye is too high
The blood vessels in the back of your eye are leaking
The lens of your eye has become cloudy, so less light reaches the back of the eye
A growth is pressing on the nerve that carries images to your brain
r: A cataract is clouding of the lens, so light entering the eye is scattered and vision becomes hazy and dim. Elevated internal pressure describes glaucoma and leaking retinal vessels describe diabetic retinopathy; both are different problems with different treatments.

q: A nurse reviews tonometry results showing an intraocular pressure of 28 mm Hg. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Report the result, because it is above the expected range and suggests glaucoma
Document the result as expected for the client's age
Recheck the client's near vision with a Rosenbaum chart
Reassure the client that pressure always rises after eye drops
r: Expected intraocular pressure is about 10 to 21 mm Hg, so 28 mm Hg is elevated and needs provider follow-up before optic nerve damage progresses to permanent vision loss. Documenting it as normal for age misses the point, since elevated pressure is never an expected aging change even though glaucoma becomes more common with age.

q: A nurse is walking a client who has severe vision loss to the bathroom. Which technique should the nurse use?
o: Hold the client by the upper arm and steer from behind
Walk beside the client with a hand on the client's back for direction
Ask the client to hold the nurse's shoulders and follow directly behind
Offer an arm, let the client take hold of it, and walk about a half step ahead
r: The client holds the nurse's arm and walks slightly behind, which lets the nurse's body movement signal turns, steps, and stops while the client stays in control of their own pace. Pushing or steering from behind removes that feedback and feels frightening, and it is the most common way this skill is done wrong.

q: A nurse enters the room of a client who is blind. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Touch the client's hand so they know someone has come in
Say the client's name and identify yourself before approaching the bed
Speak in a louder voice than usual
Wait quietly for the client to speak first
r: Announcing yourself by name before you come close prevents the startle that unexpected touch causes and orients the client to who is in the room. Touching first is the intuitive choice but it arrives without warning; explanation always precedes contact with a client who cannot see it coming.

q: A nurse delivers a meal tray to a client who has significant vision loss but eats independently. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Cut all the food and feed the client
Set down the tray and let the client explore it
Describe the position of each food and drink using clock positions before leaving
Ask a family member to come in for every meal
r: Describing the tray by clock position gives the client the information needed to eat without help, which protects independence and dignity. Feeding a client who can feed themselves creates unnecessary dependence, and leaving the tray undescribed invites spills and missed food.

q: A nurse is giving discharge instructions to a client who has a moderate hearing deficit and does not wear a hearing aid. Which approach should the nurse use?
o: Face the client in a well-lit room and speak at a normal rate in a slightly lower pitch
Raise the voice to a shout directed at the better ear
Exaggerate lip movements so the words are easier to read
Give the information while charting so the client hears it more than once
r: Facing the client in good light supports lip reading and facial cues, and lowering pitch helps because age-related loss affects high frequencies first. Shouting distorts words and raises pitch, and exaggerated mouth movements actually make speech harder to read.

q: A client's hearing aid begins making a whistling sound. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Replace the battery
Send the device out for repair
Clean the ear mold with rubbing alcohol
Reseat the ear mold in the ear and turn the volume down
r: Whistling is feedback, which almost always means the mold is not seated correctly or the volume is set too high, so repositioning and lowering the volume fixes it at the bedside. A dead battery produces no sound at all rather than a whistle, and alcohol damages the mold.

q: A nurse is teaching a client how to clean a new hearing aid. Which instruction should the nurse give?
o: Soak the whole device in warm soapy water once a week
Wash the ear mold with mild soap and water while keeping the rest of the device dry
Wipe the mold with rubbing alcohol every day
Clean inside the device with a swab moistened with hydrogen peroxide
r: Only the ear mold gets washed, with mild soap and water, while the electronic portion stays dry and away from extreme temperatures. Alcohol and soaking both damage the device, and alcohol additionally dries and cracks the mold so it seats poorly and whistles.

q: A client asks how to care for a hearing aid with a disposable battery when it will not be worn for several days. Which instruction should the nurse give?
o: Leave the aid switched on so it is ready when needed
Store the aid in the bathroom near the sink
Turn the aid off and remove the battery
Wrap the aid in a damp cloth so the mold stays flexible
r: Turning the device off and removing the disposable battery preserves battery life and prevents corrosion of the contacts. Moisture is the other main enemy of a hearing aid, so bathroom storage and damp cloths cause exactly the damage the client is trying to avoid.

q: A client with new hearing aids says, Now that I have these, I will be able to follow conversations in a crowded restaurant again. Which response should the nurse make?
o: Hearing aids make sounds louder, but they also amplify background noise, so busy places can still be difficult
Hearing aids filter out background noise, so restaurants will be easier now
Turning the volume all the way up in a restaurant will solve the problem
Hearing aids restore hearing to what it was before the loss
r: Amplification raises the volume of everything, including clatter and other conversations, and it does not help the brain interpret what it hears. Turning the volume up in a loud room increases the distortion and often causes feedback, so it worsens the very problem the client described.

q: A client who had a left-hemisphere stroke follows directions accurately but produces only single words with visible effort. How should the nurse describe this finding?
o: Receptive aphasia, because the client cannot understand what is said
Global aphasia, because both understanding and speech are lost
Dysarthria, because speech is slurred although sentences stay complete
Expressive aphasia, because the client understands but cannot produce speech
r: Expressive or Broca aphasia leaves comprehension intact while the ability to form words is impaired, which is why the client can follow directions but cannot answer in sentences. Receptive aphasia is the mirror image, and dysarthria is a muscle weakness problem in which language is intact but articulation is slurred.

q: A client speaks in long, smooth strings of words that do not make sense and cannot follow simple one-step commands. Which approach should the nurse use?
o: Ask open-ended questions and allow extra time for a complete answer
Combine short, simple statements with gestures and demonstration
Speak louder, since the client is not registering the request
Provide a writing board so the client can write out full sentences
r: This is receptive or Wernicke aphasia, in which speech is fluent but comprehension is impaired, so gestures and demonstration carry meaning that words cannot. A writing board helps the client who understands but cannot speak, which is the opposite deficit, and volume does not fix a comprehension problem.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has aphasia following a stroke. Which action promotes communication?
o: Speak rapidly to cover more material in the time available
Have a family member answer for the client
Ask questions that can be answered yes or no and allow time to respond
Correct each incorrect word so the client relearns it
r: Simple yes or no questions plus generous response time let the client participate successfully instead of failing repeatedly. Answering for the client is faster but it removes their voice from their own care and deepens withdrawal.

q: A client in the intensive care unit is restless, reports racing scattered thoughts, and has not slept. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Cluster care and reduce lights, alarms, and noise in the room
Request a prescription for a sedative
Turn on the television for distraction
Move the client to a room closer to the nurses station
r: These findings point to sensory overload, so the first step is removing the excess input by clustering care and quieting the environment. Medication treats the symptom while the cause continues, and a television or a busier location adds stimulation rather than reducing it.

q: A client has been in protective isolation for two weeks and is now withdrawn, bored, and unsure what day it is. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Limit conversation so the client can rest
Keep the shades closed during the day to promote sleep
Explain that these feelings are part of being ill and no action is needed
Place a clock and calendar in view and stop in to talk at set times each shift
r: Orientation cues plus scheduled meaningful contact treat sensory deprivation directly by restoring input the isolation removed. Reducing conversation and daylight seems restful but it deepens the deprivation and worsens the confusion and withdrawal.

q: A nurse is teaching the family of an older adult about expected sensory changes with aging. Which information should the nurse include?
o: Complete loss of taste is expected
High-pitched sounds become harder to hear and near vision blurs
Total hearing loss in one ear is common
Sudden loss of central vision is a normal change
r: Losing high-frequency hearing and the ability to focus up close are the classic expected changes, which is why lowering vocal pitch and offering large print help. Sudden central vision loss suggests macular degeneration and abrupt one-sided deafness is never expected; both need evaluation rather than reassurance.

q: A nurse is reviewing home safety with a client who has peripheral neuropathy of the feet. Which statement by the client requires follow-up?
o: I check the bottoms of my feet with a mirror every night
I am going to label the faucets so I know which one is hot
I put a heating pad on my feet at night because they feel cold
I set my water heater no higher than 120 F
r: A client who cannot feel temperature can sustain a serious burn from a heating pad without ever noticing it, so this statement needs correction. Mirror inspection, labeled faucets, and a water heater capped near 120 F are all correct protections for skin that has lost sensation.

q: A Weber test lateralizes to a client's right ear, and the Rinne test on the right shows bone conduction lasting longer than air conduction. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
o: Conductive hearing loss in the right ear
Sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear
Sensorineural hearing loss in the left ear
Both ears are within expected findings
r: In conductive loss the sound lateralizes to the affected ear and bone conduction exceeds air conduction, because something is blocking sound from reaching the inner ear while bone transmission still works. In sensorineural loss the tone shifts to the better ear and air conduction still exceeds bone conduction, just for a shorter time.

q: A client receiving furosemide and gentamicin reports new ringing in both ears. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Document the finding as an expected effect of therapy
Instruct the client to take the medications with food
Irrigate the ear canals to remove cerumen
Report the tinnitus to the provider promptly, since it may indicate ototoxicity
r: Loop diuretics and aminoglycosides are both ototoxic, and new tinnitus is an early warning that inner ear damage is developing and may become permanent. Treating it as expected delays the medication change that could preserve the client's hearing.

q: A nurse makes a home visit to a client who has macular degeneration. Which finding requires intervention?
o: A handrail on both sides of the staircase
A small area rug at the top of the stairs
A magnifying glass on the reading table
An additional lamp installed in the hallway
r: A loose rug at the top of stairs is a tripping hazard for a client who cannot see the edge, and it is the single most dangerous item on this list. Handrails, added lighting, and magnifiers are all appropriate adaptations that support safety and independence.

q: A nurse is teaching a client with reduced vision about home safety. Which of the following should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Remove throw rugs and keep walkways clear
Add lighting to stairways and check that the handrails are secure
Rearrange the furniture frequently to keep the client alert
Mark the edge of each step with a strongly contrasting color
Keep frequently used items in the same familiar place
Keep the rooms dim to reduce glare and eye strain
r: Clear paths, good lighting, high-contrast step edges, and predictable placement of belongings all let a client with low vision move safely using memory and contrast. Rearranging furniture destroys the mental map the client relies on, and dim lighting reduces the little usable vision that remains.

q: A nurse is preparing to teach a client who has a hearing deficit. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Get the client's attention before beginning to speak
Raise the voice to a shout so the words carry
Sit facing the client in a well-lit room
Turn off the television and close the door to reduce background noise
Continue talking while turning to gather supplies
r: Gaining attention first, facing the client in good light, and eliminating competing noise give the client access to both the words and the visual cues that fill in gaps. Shouting raises pitch and distorts speech, and talking while turned away removes lip and facial cues entirely.

q: A client has aphasia 3 days after a stroke. Which of the following nursing actions support communication with this client? Select all that apply.
o: Greet the client by name at the start of each interaction
Have only one person speak at a time
Finish the client's sentences to spare them the effort
Ask questions that can be answered with yes or no
Speak louder than usual because comprehension is reduced
Use a picture board set up by speech therapy
r: Using the client's name, keeping one speaker at a time, simplifying questions, and using tools from speech therapy all reduce the processing load and let the client succeed. Finishing sentences feels kind but takes the client's voice away, and volume does not help a language deficit because hearing is not the problem.

q: A nurse is planning care for a client at risk for sensory deprivation. Which of the following interventions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Provide large-print reading material or audio books
Limit visitors to one brief visit each day
Offer back rubs and hand holding if the client welcomes touch
Encourage crossword puzzles or other mentally engaging activities
Keep the lights low and the shades drawn during the day
r: Deprivation is treated by adding meaningful input across the senses, so reading material, appropriate touch, and mental engagement all fit. Restricting visitors and darkening the room are interventions for sensory overload and would worsen deprivation, which is the discrimination this question tests.

q: A nurse is caring for a client experiencing sensory overload in a critical care unit. Which of the following interventions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Move the client to a private room if one is available
Cluster care so the client has uninterrupted rest periods
Leave the television on continuously for company
Offer earplugs and dark glasses
Manage pain promptly so discomfort does not add to the stimulation
Bring in several family members at once to reorient the client
r: Overload improves when total input drops, so a private room, clustered care, earplugs and dark glasses, and good pain control all help. Continuous television and a roomful of visitors add stimulation, which is the opposite of what this client needs even though both feel comforting.

q: A client has been fitted with hearing aids for the first time and is being taught how to care for them. Which of the following client statements indicate an understanding of the teaching? Select all that apply.
o: I will wash the ear mold with mild soap and water and keep the rest of the device dry
I will wipe the ear molds with rubbing alcohol every morning
I will turn the aid off and take the battery out when I put it away for the night
I will keep the volume just high enough to hear without any squealing
I will spray my hair while the aids are in so I do not have to remove them
r: Mild soap on the mold only, removing the battery during extended storage, and using the lowest setting that avoids feedback are the core points of hearing aid care. Alcohol and hairspray both damage the device, and hairspray residue in particular clogs the microphone opening.

q: A nurse is assessing a client for reduced visual acuity. Which of the following findings support this problem? Select all that apply.
o: Frequent headaches
Reports of seeing two of one object
Improved ability to judge distance
Squinting or closing one eye to look at something
Sharper color perception at night
r: Headaches from eye strain, diplopia, and favoring one eye are all common signs that visual acuity is declining. Depth perception and night vision get worse rather than better with reduced acuity, which is why driving safety becomes a concern.

q: A nurse is orienting a new graduate to the factors that contribute to sensory alterations. Which of the following should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Long-term exposure to loud noise at work
Cerumen packed against the tympanic membrane
A course of gentamicin
Drinking three cups of coffee daily
Peripheral neuropathy related to diabetes mellitus
Wearing corrective lenses for nearsightedness
r: Noise exposure and aminoglycosides damage the inner ear, impacted cerumen blocks sound conduction, and neuropathy blunts touch and position sense, so all four alter sensory perception. Corrective lenses represent a deficit that has already been managed, and routine caffeine intake is unrelated.

q: A nurse is planning care for a client who is deaf and communicates using sign language. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Arrange a professional sign language interpreter for the consent discussion
Ask the client's teenage son to interpret the surgical explanation
Provide written materials and visual teaching aids
Set up closed captioning on the television in the room
Look at the interpreter rather than the client while explaining the procedure
r: Facilities must provide a professional interpreter, and written material plus captioning give the client full access to information. Using a family member, especially a minor, risks inaccuracy and violates privacy, and the nurse should speak to and look at the client, not the interpreter.

q: A nurse plans to teach a client how to use an incentive spirometer 2 hr after abdominal surgery. The client rates incisional pain as 8 on a scale of 0 to 10 and is grimacing. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Shorten the teaching session to 5 min
Administer the prescribed analgesic and teach once the pain is controlled
Give the client a written handout to read later
Ask the client's spouse to learn the technique instead
r: Readiness to learn must be established before teaching begins, and severe pain makes attention and retention impossible, so relieving the pain comes first. Handing over a handout or shortening the session still delivers teaching into a brain that cannot process it, and delegating the learning to the spouse leaves the client unable to perform the skill.

q: A nurse is preparing to teach four clients about newly prescribed therapies. Which client demonstrates the greatest readiness to learn?
o: A client who asks what supplies will be needed at home to change the dressing
A client who says, 'I do not want to hear about that diagnosis right now.'
A client who is pacing and states they cannot stop thinking about the biopsy results
A client who received an opioid 15 min ago and is drowsy
r: Asking practical questions about the upcoming task signals motivation and engagement, the clearest evidence of readiness. Denial, high anxiety, and sedation all block learning, and anxiety in particular is easy to misread as attentiveness when the client is actually unable to absorb information.

q: A nurse is assessing factors that could interfere with a client's ability to learn discharge instructions. Which findings should the nurse identify as barriers? (Select all that apply.)
o: The client reports uncontrolled pain
The client reads at a fourth-grade level and the handout is written at a college level
The client asks the nurse to repeat the demonstration
The client's roommate has a loud television and frequent visitors
The client left their eyeglasses and hearing aids at home
The client identifies a specific goal of returning to work
r: Pain, a mismatch between reading level and materials, environmental noise, and uncorrected sensory deficits all interfere with taking in and storing new information. Asking for a repeat demonstration and naming a personal goal are signs of engagement and motivation, not barriers.

q: A nurse is teaching a client about the purpose and adverse effects of a new antihypertensive medication. Which teaching method best fits this learning domain?
o: Having the client practice the skill on a model
Arranging a support group discussion about feelings
Using discussion and written material, then asking the client to explain the information back
Role-playing a conversation with a family member
r: Knowledge and understanding of facts belong to the cognitive domain, which is best served by explanation, printed material, and verbal recall. Practicing on a model addresses psychomotor learning, and group discussion of feelings targets the affective domain, so neither matches this objective.

q: A nurse is teaching a client who has newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes mellitus how to self-administer insulin. Which teaching strategy should the nurse use?
o: Provide an illustrated pamphlet about insulin action
Show a video about living with diabetes mellitus
Lead a discussion about the client's feelings regarding injections
Demonstrate the injection, then have the client perform a return demonstration
r: Injection technique is a psychomotor skill, and skills are learned through demonstration followed by supervised practice with feedback. Written material and videos build cognitive knowledge but never prove the client can physically perform the task.

q: A client who has a new colostomy turns away during pouch changes and states, 'I cannot look at it. It is not me anymore.' Which learning domain should the nurse address first?
o: Affective
Psychomotor
Cognitive
Kinesthetic
r: The client's difficulty is with feelings, values, and acceptance of an altered body image, which is the affective domain, and unaddressed emotion will block skill learning. Jumping to psychomotor teaching about pouch technique is the tempting error, because the client cannot practice a skill on a stoma they will not look at.

q: A nurse is writing learning objectives for a client who has heart failure. Which objectives belong to the cognitive domain? (Select all that apply.)
o: The client will state three symptoms that should be reported to the provider
The client will correctly weigh themselves using the home scale
The client will identify high-sodium foods from a sample menu
The client will describe the reason for taking the diuretic in the morning
The client will express feelings about limiting fluids at family gatherings
r: Stating, identifying, and describing are all knowledge-based verbs that place an objective in the cognitive domain. Performing the weight measurement is psychomotor and expressing feelings about a lifestyle change is affective, which is why the verb chosen for an objective matters.

q: A nurse has finished teaching a client how to care for a new incision at home. Which action best evaluates whether learning occurred?
o: Ask the client, 'Do you understand everything I explained?'
Ask the client to explain the dressing change in their own words and demonstrate it
Give the client a printed instruction sheet to take home
Document that the client was alert and nodded during the teaching
r: Teach-back and return demonstration are the only methods that show what the client actually retained and can do. A yes or no question about understanding invites a polite yes, and nodding is a social cue that frequently masks confusion or low health literacy.

q: A nurse taught a client with a new colostomy how to empty and change the pouch yesterday. Which finding indicates that learning occurred?
o: The client states that the teaching was very clear
The client watched the entire instructional video
The client empties and changes the pouch correctly without prompting
The client's spouse reports that the client read all of the handouts
r: Evaluation of a psychomotor objective requires observing the client perform the skill independently and correctly. Verbal appreciation, video viewing, and reading are all exposure to information rather than evidence that the client can do the task.

q: A nurse is developing written discharge materials for a general medical unit. Which actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)
o: Write the material at approximately a fifth-grade reading level
Use a large, easy-to-read font size such as 14 point
Include as much medical terminology as possible so the material is precise
Focus on what the client needs to do rather than background theory
Provide the material in the client's preferred language
Use long paragraphs to keep the document short
r: Effective materials are accurate, accessible, and actionable: plain language at about a fifth-grade level, readable type, action-focused content, and the client's own language. Dense paragraphs and technical vocabulary raise the reading burden and are a main reason clients leave with instructions they cannot use.

q: A nurse gives a client a consent form and medication instructions. The client smiles, nods, says, 'I forgot my glasses, I will read it later,' and hands the papers to their adult child. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
o: The client is refusing the treatment
The client has a vision problem that requires an ophthalmology referral
The client prefers that the family manage all care decisions
The client may have limited health literacy and needs the information explained verbally and verified with teach-back
r: Smiling, nodding, deferring paperwork to a relative, and the forgotten-glasses explanation are classic ways adults conceal difficulty with reading, so the nurse should shift to plain verbal teaching and confirm understanding. Reading nodding as agreement or as a simple vision issue is exactly the misinterpretation that sends clients home unable to follow instructions.
