q: A nurse observes a newly hired nurse teaching an older adult client who has presbycusis. Which action by the new nurse requires intervention?
o: The new nurse shouts the instructions in a high-pitched voice from the doorway
The new nurse faces the client in a well-lit room
The new nurse breaks the teaching into two short sessions
The new nurse provides a handout in large print
r: Shouting from a distance in a high pitch is the least effective approach, because age-related hearing loss affects high frequencies first and the client also loses the visual cues of the speaker's face. Facing the client, using short sessions, and providing large print are all appropriate adaptations for aging vision, hearing, and attention.

q: A nurse is planning a teaching session for an 80-year-old client about a new medication schedule. Which strategies should the nurse use? (Select all that apply.)
o: Speak in a normal tone at a slightly lower pitch and face the client
Schedule several brief sessions rather than one long one
Allow extra time for the client to respond to questions
Assume the client cannot learn new skills because of age
Relate the new information to the client's existing routine
Teach in the hallway lounge during the shift change
r: Older adults learn well when sensory changes are accommodated, sessions are short, pacing is unhurried, and new content is anchored to what they already do. Aging alone does not prevent learning, and a busy, noisy setting adds distraction that shortens attention and retention.

q: A nurse is preparing to teach a 4-year-old child about an upcoming dressing change. Which approach should the nurse use?
o: Explain the procedure in detail the day before so the child can prepare
Use simple words and let the child handle the supplies and practice on a doll
Give the child a written booklet describing each step
Direct all teaching to the parents while the child plays
r: Preschoolers learn through play and hands-on exploration, and simple concrete language with a doll lets the child rehearse what will happen. Long lead time before a procedure increases fear at this age, and teaching only the parents leaves the child unprepared for what they will experience.

q: A nurse is teaching a 16-year-old client who has newly diagnosed asthma about inhaler use. Which approach should the nurse use?
o: Provide the teaching only when a parent is present to supervise
Emphasize the long-term risk of lung damage in 30 years
Include the client in setting goals and discuss how to manage the inhaler at school and with friends
Tell the client the parents will be responsible for all medication administration
r: Adolescents respond to autonomy, participation in goal setting, and content that fits their immediate social world, such as using an inhaler at school. Distant consequences and parent-controlled plans undercut the independence that drives adherence in this age group.

q: A client who speaks limited English is being admitted. The client's 12-year-old daughter offers to interpret, and an adult son says he can help as well. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Allow the daughter to interpret because the client is comfortable with her
Ask the adult son to interpret and have the daughter leave the room
Use gestures and simple English to avoid involving the family
Obtain a facility-approved medical interpreter
r: Only a trained, facility-approved medical interpreter should be used, because family members may filter, edit, or lack the vocabulary for medical content, and privacy is compromised. Using a child is never acceptable, and an adult relative is not an acceptable substitute either even though it feels more reasonable.

q: A nurse is preparing to interview a client through a medical interpreter. Which actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)
o: Brief the interpreter beforehand about the purpose and type of questions
Speak directly to the client and maintain eye contact with the client
Ask one question at a time and pause for the interpretation
Use familiar idioms and metaphors to make the explanation friendlier
Speak slowly and clearly at a normal volume
Interrupt the interpreter to move the interview along when time is short
r: Preparing the interpreter, addressing the client rather than the interpreter, using short single questions, and speaking clearly at normal volume keep the client at the center of the exchange. Idioms and metaphors rarely translate, and interrupting distorts the message and signals disrespect.

q: A nurse observes a colleague using an interpreter. The colleague faces the interpreter and says, 'Tell her that she needs to take this pill every morning.' Which action should the nurse take?
o: Remind the colleague to look at and speak directly to the client
Take no action, since the message is being conveyed accurately
Suggest the colleague speak more loudly so the client can hear
Recommend that the colleague ask a family member to confirm the message
r: The nurse speaks to the client in the first person and watches the client's face and body language; the interpreter is a conduit, not the person receiving care. Accurate word-for-word translation is not the whole task, because addressing the interpreter excludes the client from their own conversation and prevents the nurse from reading nonverbal responses.

q: A client scheduled for surgery in the morning says, 'I keep thinking about everything that could go wrong tomorrow.' Which response by the nurse is therapeutic?
o: 'Your surgeon has done this operation hundreds of times.'
'Tell me more about what is on your mind.'
'Why are you focusing on the negative?'
'Everything is going to be fine, so try to get some sleep.'
r: An open-ended invitation encourages the client to explore the fear and gives the nurse the information needed to help. Citing the surgeon's experience sounds reassuring but is false reassurance that ends the conversation without addressing what the client is actually afraid of.

q: A nurse is reviewing recorded responses made to a client who stated, 'I do not think I can handle this diagnosis.' Which responses are nontherapeutic? (Select all that apply.)
o: 'Do not worry, everyone feels that way at first and it passes.'
'Why would you say something like that?'
'This must feel overwhelming right now.'
'You should focus on being grateful that it was caught early.'
'Tell me what worries you the most about it.'
r: False reassurance, why questions that demand justification, and advice that dismisses the emotion all shut the client down. Naming the feeling and asking an open-ended question keep the conversation open and communicate that the nurse is willing to hear the answer.

q: A client who has not been taking a prescribed antihypertensive tells the nurse, 'I just stopped taking it.' Which response should the nurse avoid?
o: 'Help me understand what led to stopping the medication.'
'What was happening for you when you decided to stop?'
'Why did you stop taking a medication your provider prescribed?'
'Tell me about any problems you had while taking it.'
r: A direct why question implies criticism, puts the client on the defensive, and usually produces an excuse rather than the real reason. The other options seek exactly the same information with wording that invites an honest answer, such as an unaffordable copay or an adverse effect.

q: A client whose partner died 4 months ago and who now has a new diagnosis of diabetes mellitus states tearfully, 'How could you possibly understand what I am going through?' Which response should the nurse make?
o: 'I do understand. I lost my own mother last year.'
'Let us focus on your blood glucose readings for now.'
'You are right, I cannot understand.'
'I have not lived through what you have, but I would like to hear what this has been like for you.'
r: Empathy acknowledges the limits of the nurse's experience while conveying genuine willingness to understand the client's, which keeps the focus on the client. Sharing the nurse's own loss is sympathy that shifts attention to the nurse, and changing the subject to laboratory values abandons the client's distress.

q: A nurse wants to convey attentiveness and openness while talking with an anxious client. Which nonverbal behaviors should the nurse use? (Select all that apply.)
o: Sit down at the client's eye level
Keep arms and legs uncrossed
Stand near the door with a hand on the doorknob
Maintain eye contact as appropriate for the client's culture
Chart on the computer with the back turned to the client while listening
Use a relaxed posture and an unhurried pace
r: Sitting at eye level, an open posture, culturally appropriate eye contact, and unhurried pacing tell the client there is time and interest. Standing in the doorway or facing a screen signals that the nurse is leaving or divided, and clients read that message more strongly than anything the nurse says.

q: A client who is tearful and clenching the bed rail tells the nurse, 'I am fine, really.' Which response should the nurse make?
o: 'You say you are fine, but you seem upset. I have time to listen.'
'I am glad to hear you are doing well today.'
'You need to be honest with me if you want me to help you.'
'I will come back later when you are ready to talk.'
r: Naming the mismatch between the words and the nonverbal message gently gives the client permission to say what is really happening. Accepting the words at face value ignores the stronger nonverbal message, and telling the client to be honest sounds accusatory and increases defensiveness.

q: A nurse has completed discharge teaching about a new anticoagulant. Which elements should the nurse include in the documentation? (Select all that apply.)
o: The specific content that was taught
The teaching method and materials provided
The nurse's opinion that the client seemed unmotivated
Who was present during the teaching
How understanding was evaluated, the client's response, and any further teaching needed
A word-for-word transcript of the entire conversation
r: Documentation should show what was taught, how, to whom, how learning was verified, and what remains to be done, because unrecorded teaching is legally treated as teaching that never happened. Subjective judgments about motivation are not objective data and do not belong in the record.

q: Which documentation entry best demonstrates that a client learned to self-administer enoxaparin?
o: Teaching completed. Client verbalized understanding.
Client independently selected the site, expelled no air from the syringe, and injected the medication correctly using proper technique. Written instructions given.
Reviewed injection technique with client and family. Handout provided.
Client educated on anticoagulant therapy. No questions.
r: The entry describing the observed return demonstration records objective evidence that the client can perform the skill. The phrase verbalized understanding is the most commonly charted and the weakest, because it documents a statement rather than a demonstrated ability.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who is scheduled for discharge and is working with assistive personnel. Which task should the nurse delegate?
o: Teaching the client how to use a walker for the first time
Evaluating whether the client can name their new medications
Assisting the stable client to ambulate to the bathroom with the walker
Explaining the signs of infection the client should report at home
r: Assistive personnel perform standard, predictable tasks for stable clients, such as assisting with ambulation using a device the client has already been taught to use. Teaching and evaluation of learning are RN responsibilities and cannot be delegated, no matter how routine the content seems.

q: A nurse is writing a learning objective for a client who is starting warfarin. Which objective is written correctly?
o: The client will know about warfarin therapy.
The nurse will teach the client about foods high in vitamin K.
The client will understand the importance of laboratory monitoring.
The client will identify three foods high in vitamin K before discharge.
r: A usable objective is client-centered, measurable, and has a time frame, so identify three foods before discharge can actually be evaluated. Know and understand describe internal states that cannot be observed, and an objective that starts with the nurse describes the nurse's activity rather than the client's learning.

q: A nurse is beginning the teaching-learning process with a client who has a new diagnosis of hypertension. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Assess what the client already knows, wants to know, and is ready to learn
Select the printed materials and videos to be used
Write measurable learning objectives for the session
Schedule a return demonstration for blood pressure monitoring
r: The teaching-learning process mirrors the nursing process, so assessment of learning needs, readiness, and current knowledge comes before planning, implementation, and evaluation. Choosing materials or writing objectives first designs the session around assumptions instead of around the client.

q: A nurse is preparing the environment for a teaching session about wound care. Which actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)
o: Ensure the client has voided and is comfortably positioned
Adjust the lighting and reduce background noise
Confirm the client is wearing glasses and hearing aids if used
Conduct the session immediately after a painful procedure
Include the family caregiver who will help at home, with the client's permission
r: Physical comfort, a quiet well-lit setting, working sensory aids, and involvement of the person who will help at home all support retention. Teaching right after a painful procedure guarantees that discomfort and fatigue compete with the content.

q: A nurse is communicating with a client who has expressive aphasia after a stroke. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Speak loudly and finish the client's sentences to save effort
Ask questions that can be answered with yes or no and offer a picture board, allowing extra time to respond
Direct all questions to the family member at the bedside
Limit interaction until speech therapy has been completed
r: Expressive aphasia affects the production of speech, not comprehension or intelligence, so simple response formats, communication aids, and unhurried time let the client participate. Finishing sentences or routing questions to the family is faster but removes the client's voice and increases frustration.

q: A client who has a new diagnosis of type 2 diabetes mellitus states, 'My blood sugar does not bother me, so I do not see why I need to change anything.' Which action should the nurse take?
o: Provide a detailed handout on long-term complications and end the session
Document that the client refused teaching
Explore what the client values and connect glucose control to a goal that matters to the client
Tell the client that untreated diabetes leads to amputation and blindness
r: A client who does not perceive the condition as a threat is not yet motivated, and linking the plan to something the client already cares about creates the personal relevance that drives behavior change. Frightening the client with worst-case outcomes may raise anxiety to a level that blocks learning rather than promoting it.

q: A client who was told 2 days ago about a terminal diagnosis says, 'The lab must have mixed up my results.' The client needs teaching about a new pain medication. Which approach should the nurse use?
o: Postpone all teaching until the client accepts the diagnosis
Repeat the details of the prognosis before teaching about the medication
Ask the family to learn the information and pass it along later
Teach only what the client needs right now, focusing on the immediate use of the medication
r: A client in denial can still learn concrete, present-focused information, so teaching is limited to what is needed today rather than long-range planning. Restating the prognosis or waiting for acceptance leaves the client without pain control while they work through a stage that may last days or weeks.

q: A nurse is assessing whether a client is ready for teaching about a new tube feeding regimen. Which findings indicate readiness to learn? (Select all that apply.)
o: The client asks how the pump alarm works
The client rates their pain as 2 on a scale of 0 to 10 and is resting comfortably
The client states, 'I will figure it out when I get home. Just leave the papers.'
The client has arranged for the caregiver to be present during the session
The client repeatedly changes the subject to when the discharge papers will be signed
r: Asking task-specific questions, being physically comfortable, and arranging for the caregiver to attend all show motivation and the capacity to attend to new information. Deferring the content and steering the conversation away from it signal avoidance or anxiety, and teaching delivered at that point is unlikely to be retained.

q: A client who has just been diagnosed with stage III lung cancer is scheduled to begin chemotherapy. The provider has also requested a palliative care consult, and the client asks the nurse, 'Does this mean they have given up on me?' Which response should the nurse make?
o: 'Palliative care is offered only after all treatment options have been tried.'
'You will need to choose between the chemotherapy and the palliative care team.'
'Palliative care can start now and work alongside your chemotherapy to keep you comfortable.'
'Palliative care begins once your provider expects you to live 6 months or less.'
r: Palliative care may begin at the time of diagnosis and is provided at the same time as treatment aimed at cure or disease control; its focus is relief of physical, emotional, and spiritual suffering. The tempting distractor confuses palliative care with hospice, which is the service tied to a limited prognosis and a shift away from curative treatment.

q: A nurse is reviewing four clients on a medical unit. Which client is the most appropriate candidate for a hospice referral?
o: A client who has newly diagnosed heart failure and is starting a new medication regimen
A client who has end-stage liver disease, a prognosis of less than 6 months, and has declined further disease-directed treatment
A client who has severe osteoarthritis pain that is poorly controlled on oral analgesics
A client who is 2 days postoperative following a bowel resection for a curable tumor
r: Hospice is designed for clients whose life expectancy is generally about 6 months or less and who have chosen comfort over treatment intended to cure the disease. The client with uncontrolled arthritis pain needs aggressive symptom management and possibly a palliative consult, but pain alone does not meet hospice criteria.

q: A nurse is teaching a family about hospice services. Which statements should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)
o: Care is provided to both the client and the family as the unit of care
The client must be admitted to an inpatient hospice facility to receive services
Services can be delivered in the client's home, a long-term care facility, or a hospital
All medications are discontinued once hospice begins
Bereavement support for the family continues after the client dies
The client must give up the right to change their mind about hospice
r: Hospice treats the client and family together, is delivered wherever the client lives, and includes bereavement follow-up for survivors. Medications are not stopped; drugs that provide comfort, such as opioids and antiemetics, are continued or added, and a client may revoke hospice at any time to resume disease-directed treatment.

q: A client asks the nurse to explain what a living will does. Which response should the nurse make?
o: 'It is a written record of the treatments you would want or refuse if you could no longer speak for yourself.'
'It names a specific person who will make all of your health care decisions for you.'
'It divides your property and money among your family after your death.'
'It is a provider order that keeps the staff from performing CPR.'
r: A living will documents the client's own treatment preferences, such as ventilator support or artificial nutrition, for a time when the client cannot communicate. Naming a decision maker is the function of the health care proxy or durable power of attorney for health care, and a DNR is a provider order, not an advance directive written by the client.

q: A client who has early dementia wants to be sure someone they trust can speak for them when they can no longer make their own decisions. Which document should the nurse discuss with the client?
o: A do-not-resuscitate order
An organ donor registration
A living will
A durable power of attorney for health care
r: A durable power of attorney for health care, also called a health care proxy, appoints a specific person to make medical decisions once the client loses decision-making capacity. A living will is a close distractor, but it records treatment choices rather than designating a person to interpret new situations as they arise.

q: A nurse is teaching a group of older adults about advance directives. Which statements should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)
o: An advance directive can be changed or revoked by the client at any time while they still have capacity
Having an advance directive is required before a client can be admitted to a hospital
A copy should be given to the health care facility and to the person named as the decision maker
The directive takes effect only when the client is no longer able to make or communicate decisions
Once signed, the document cannot be altered without a court order
r: Clients retain the right to revise or cancel a directive as long as they have capacity, the document should be on the chart and shared with the proxy, and it guides care only when the client can no longer speak for themselves. Facilities must ask about and offer information on directives, but no client can be required to have one as a condition of care.

q: A client who has metastatic cancer has a do-not-resuscitate order. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? (Select all that apply.)
o: Administer prescribed opioids to keep the client's pain controlled
Provide oral care and reposition the client for comfort
Withhold oxygen even if the client reports shortness of breath
Continue to assess the client and respond to changes in condition
Offer emotional and spiritual support to the client and family
Stop answering the call light for nonurgent requests
r: A DNR order limits only the use of CPR and related resuscitation measures; every other element of nursing care, including analgesia, hygiene, oxygen for dyspnea, assessment, and psychosocial support, continues unchanged. The distractors reflect the common and dangerous misreading of DNR as 'do not treat.'

q: The adult child of a client who has a new do-not-resuscitate order tells the nurse, 'So now you are just going to let him suffer and stop taking care of him.' Which response should the nurse make?
o: 'That decision was made by the provider, so you will need to discuss it with them.'
'The order only means we will not attempt CPR. We will keep treating his pain and caring for him the same way.'
'We can cancel the order if you would rather we do everything.'
'Try not to think about it. He is comfortable right now.'
r: Correcting the misconception directly relieves the family's fear and is accurate: comfort measures, pain medication, and nursing care are not withheld under a DNR. Deflecting to the provider abandons the family in the moment and does not address the false belief that care will be withdrawn.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who is expected to die within the next 24 hr. Which finding should the nurse expect?
o: Blood pressure rising above the client's baseline
Pupils that constrict briskly to light
Cool, mottled skin over the knees and feet
An increase in urine output with pale, dilute urine
r: Mottling and coolness of the extremities reflect the failing peripheral circulation typical of the final hours. As death approaches the blood pressure falls, pupils become sluggish or fixed, and urine output decreases and darkens, so the other options describe the opposite of expected findings.

q: The family of a client who is actively dying asks the nurse what changes to expect. Which manifestations should the nurse describe? (Select all that apply.)
o: A gradual decrease in level of consciousness
Irregular breathing with periods of apnea
Loss of bowel and bladder control
A strong, bounding radial pulse
Noisy, gurgling respirations from pooled secretions
Increased muscle tone with a rigid jaw
r: Decreasing consciousness, Cheyne-Stokes respirations, incontinence, and audible airway secretions are all expected as body systems shut down. The pulse becomes weak and thready rather than bounding, and muscle tone is lost, which is why the face relaxes and the jaw often falls open.

q: The partner of a dying client anxiously tells the nurse, 'He stops breathing for almost half a minute and then breathes fast and deep again. Is he suffocating?' Which response should the nurse make?
o: 'I will request an order for oxygen by nonrebreather mask right away.'
'This pattern of pauses and deep breaths is expected near the end of life, and it does not mean he is struggling or in distress.'
'You should step out of the room until his breathing settles.'
'I will suction his airway to open it up.'
r: Cheyne-Stokes breathing is a normal neurologic change at the end of life and is not experienced as suffocation by an unresponsive client, so explanation and presence are what the family needs. Applying a high-flow mask or suctioning treats the family's anxiety with an intervention the client does not need and can add distress.

q: A nurse hears loud, wet, gurgling respirations in a client who is unresponsive and within hours of death. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Perform deep nasotracheal suctioning
Increase the rate of the intravenous fluids
Encourage the client to cough and deep breathe
Reposition the client onto their side with the head of the bed elevated
r: Repositioning to a side-lying position with the head elevated lets pooled oral secretions drain by gravity and is the first, least invasive measure for the terminal secretions known as the death rattle. Deep suctioning is the tempting choice but stimulates the gag reflex, causes distress, and often increases secretions without improving the sound.

q: A nurse is teaching family members who are keeping vigil at the bedside of an unresponsive client who is near death. Which instruction should the nurse include?
o: 'Keep speaking to him and telling him you are here, because hearing is believed to be the last sense lost.'
'There is no reason to talk to him now, since he cannot perceive anything.'
'Discuss the funeral arrangements at the bedside so he can hear your plans.'
'Avoid touching him, because his skin is too sensitive to tolerate contact.'
r: Hearing is thought to persist longer than the other senses, so families are encouraged to speak and to be careful about what is said in the room. Touch is also retained as pressure sensation and is comforting, so avoiding contact deprives the client of an important connection.

q: A client who has end-stage COPD and is receiving hospice care has a respiratory rate of 32/min and reports severe air hunger. Morphine is prescribed for dyspnea. The client's daughter says, 'That will slow his breathing down and kill him faster.' Which action should the nurse take?
o: Hold the morphine and request a nonopioid alternative
Give a lower dose than prescribed to be safe
Explain that the dose is titrated to relieve the sensation of breathlessness, then administer the morphine as prescribed
Wait until the client loses consciousness before giving the medication
r: Low-dose opioids are the standard treatment for terminal dyspnea; the goal is relief of suffering, and adequate dosing is ethically appropriate even if it may shorten life, because the intent is comfort rather than death. Withholding or reducing the dose leaves the client in air hunger and is a failure of comfort care, not a safety measure.

q: A client who has terminal pancreatic cancer is receiving around-the-clock extended-release morphine. The client's spouse tells the nurse, 'I do not want him getting hooked on that drug.' Which response should the nurse make?
o: 'I will ask the provider to switch him to as-needed dosing only.'
'Scheduled dosing keeps the pain from returning, and addiction is not a concern in this situation.'
'He can have the medication only when the pain becomes severe again.'
'You are right to be worried; opioids are very addictive.'
r: Fear of addiction is a leading cause of undertreated pain at the end of life, and scheduled dosing maintains steady blood levels so pain does not have to return before it is treated. Switching to as-needed dosing sounds responsive to the family but produces cycles of breakthrough pain that are harder to control.

q: A nurse is planning care for a client in the final days of life. Which interventions should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)
o: Provide oral care with moist swabs every 2 to 4 hr
Apply lubricating drops to the eyes if the client cannot close them
Restrict family visits to scheduled hours to allow rest
Reposition the client at least every 2 hr and use pressure-relieving surfaces
Change soiled linens and clothing promptly to keep the client clean and odor free
Place an incontinence brief over the client's indwelling urinary catheter
r: Frequent oral and eye care, repositioning, and prompt cleansing preserve comfort, skin integrity, and dignity. Limiting family presence increases the fear of dying alone, and a brief placed over an indwelling catheter traps moisture and hides drainage problems, so it is never appropriate.

q: A client near the end of life is mouth breathing and reports a very dry mouth. Which intervention should the nurse use?
o: Swab the mouth with lemon-glycerin sponges every hour
Offer full glasses of ice water on a set schedule
Rinse the mouth with an alcohol-based mouthwash
Moisten the mouth with water or a saline-soaked swab and apply lip balm
r: Water or saline swabs plus a lip moisturizer relieve dryness without irritating fragile tissue. Lemon-glycerin swabs and alcohol-containing rinses are the classic wrong answers because they dry and erode the mucosa further, and large volumes of fluid risk aspiration in a client with a weakening gag reflex.

q: A client who has been calm during hospice care becomes restless, plucks at the bed linens, and tries to climb out of bed. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Assess the client for pain, a distended bladder, and low oxygen saturation
Apply a soft wrist restraint to prevent a fall
Administer the prescribed as-needed sedative
Dim the lights and leave the client alone to rest
r: Terminal restlessness often has a reversible trigger such as untreated pain, urinary retention, constipation, or hypoxia, so assessment comes before medication. Sedating first is tempting because it looks like symptom control, but it masks a cause the nurse could correct in minutes.

q: A client dies unexpectedly, and the death has been referred to the medical examiner. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Remove the endotracheal tube and all intravenous lines before the family enters
Bathe the body thoroughly and dress it in a clean gown
Leave all tubes, lines, and drains in place
Discard the intravenous tubing and dressings in the room trash
r: When a death is a medical examiner or coroner case, or when organ donation is being considered, all invasive devices stay in place because they are part of the evidence and record of care. Removing tubes is correct routine postmortem practice but is exactly what must not be done in a reportable death.

q: A nurse is providing postmortem care for a client whose death does not require an autopsy. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Position the body flat with the head lower than the trunk
Elevate the head of the bed slightly and insert the client's dentures
Tightly bind the wrists and ankles together with gauze
Delay closing the eyes until the family has left the unit
r: Raising the head reduces pooling of blood in the face that would cause discoloration, and dentures are replaced early before rigor mortis makes the jaw impossible to manage. Lying the body flat or head down worsens facial discoloration, and eyes and mouth are closed promptly for the same reason.

q: A nurse is performing postmortem care after a client's expected death on a medical unit. Which actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)
o: Confirm that the death has been pronounced and documented before beginning care
Wear gloves and follow standard precautions throughout
Wash the body, remove soiled dressings, and apply clean ones as needed
Remove the client's wedding ring and place it in the trash with other belongings
Attach identification tags to the body and to the shroud according to policy
Ask the family to leave immediately so the body can be transported
r: Care begins after the death is certified, uses standard precautions because body fluids remain infectious, includes cleansing and identification, and follows facility policy for tagging. Valuables are inventoried and released to the family with documentation, and families are offered time with the body, which supports the start of healthy grieving.

q: A client is declared brain dead and may be a candidate for organ donation. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Ask the family to sign the donation consent form
Tell the family that donation is what the client would have wanted
Wait for the family to raise the subject of donation
Notify the organ procurement organization so a trained requestor can approach the family
r: Federal requirements direct facilities to report potential donors to the organ procurement organization, and specially trained requestors, not the bedside nurse, discuss donation with the family. Obtaining the signature or advocating for donation personally blurs the nurse's role and can be perceived as pressure during acute grief.

q: A client who died carries a signed donor card, but the family tells the nurse they are opposed to donation. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Notify the organ procurement organization and provide emotional support while trained staff meet with the family
Tell the family the donor card is legally binding and proceed with organ recovery
Document the family's refusal and take no further action
Ask the family to reconsider because several people are waiting for transplants
r: The nurse's role is to report the potential donor and support the family while the procurement specialists handle the conversation and any legal questions about the documented wishes. Arguing the point or pressing the family exceeds the nurse's role and damages trust at the most vulnerable moment.

q: After a client's death, family members ask to wash the body themselves and request that only women be present. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Explain that only staff are permitted to handle the body
Arrange privacy and time for the family to perform the ritual with female staff assisting as needed
Complete the postmortem care quickly first, then invite the family in
Ask the family to submit the request to the ethics committee
r: Death rituals vary widely among cultures and faiths, and accommodating them supports grieving and shows respect. Finishing the care first seems efficient but takes away the very ritual the family asked to perform.

q: A client who is near death asks the nurse to arrange for a visit from a member of the clergy of their faith. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Explain that the facility chaplain covers all faiths and cannot make outside referrals
Ask the family whether the visit is really necessary
Contact the requested spiritual advisor or the pastoral care department promptly
Offer to pray with the client instead
r: Facilitating the client's own spiritual practice is a core end-of-life nursing responsibility and should be acted on without delay. Substituting the nurse's prayer, however well meant, replaces the client's stated preference with the nurse's own and may not fit the client's tradition.

q: A nurse is caring for a dying client whose cultural and religious practices differ from the nurse's own. Which actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)
o: Ask the client and family which practices and rituals are important to them
Assume the client shares the beliefs common to their ethnic group
Identify who in the family the client wants involved in decision making
Discourage traditional healing practices that are unfamiliar
Accommodate requests about diet, dress, and care of the body when possible
r: Asking rather than assuming, identifying the family decision maker, and accommodating preferences are the foundations of culturally responsive care. Assuming beliefs from group membership stereotypes the client, and dismissing traditional practices that are not harmful shuts down communication and trust.

q: The spouse of a client who has advanced ALS tells the nurse, 'I have already cried for him. Some days it feels like I lost him months ago, and he is still right here.' Which type of grief should the nurse identify?
o: Disenfranchised grief
Prolonged grief disorder
Complicated grief
Anticipatory grief
r: Anticipatory grief is mourning that begins before the death, which is common in long, progressive illnesses and can help the family prepare. Prolonged grief disorder is the tempting distractor, but it describes grief that stays disabling long after a death has already occurred.

q: Which client is most likely to be experiencing disenfranchised grief?
o: A client whose grief follows an early pregnancy loss that friends and coworkers do not acknowledge
A client whose parent died 3 weeks ago and who cries daily
A client who is sad about retiring from a long career
A client whose spouse died 2 years ago and who has resumed usual activities
r: Disenfranchised grief is loss that society does not openly recognize or support, such as miscarriage, the death of a pet, a death by suicide, or the death of an incarcerated person, so the person grieves without social permission. Crying daily 3 weeks after a parent's death is ordinary uncomplicated grief and is generally well supported by others.

q: A nurse is following up with a client 14 months after the death of their spouse. Which finding requires further evaluation?
o: The client visits the cemetery on the anniversary of the death
The client became tearful while describing the spouse's last week of life
The client has stopped working, rarely leaves the house, and says life has no purpose without the spouse
The client has begun attending a bereavement support group
r: Grief that still causes marked impairment in daily functioning more than a year after an adult's loss suggests prolonged grief disorder and warrants referral for evaluation, including screening for suicidal ideation. Anniversary visits and tearful reminiscing are normal expressions of grief even years later and do not indicate a disorder.

q: A nurse is assessing a client 5 months after the death of their parent. Which findings are consistent with normal, uncomplicated grief? (Select all that apply.)
o: The client describes waves of sadness that are becoming less frequent
The client reports occasional trouble falling asleep and low appetite
The client states they deserve to die because they did not visit more often
The client has returned to work and is starting to talk about future plans
The client has kept the parent's room locked and unchanged and refuses to enter it
r: Uncomplicated grief includes fluctuating sadness and somatic complaints such as fatigue, sleep changes, and appetite loss, with some movement toward acceptance by about 6 months. Statements of self-blame with a wish to die and refusal to acknowledge the death by preserving the space untouched point toward complicated grief and need follow-up.

q: A client who has terminal cancer tells the nurse, 'If I can just make it to my daughter's wedding in June, I will do whatever the doctors say.' Which stage of grief does this statement reflect?
o: Denial
Anger
Depression
Bargaining
r: Bargaining is the attempt to negotiate for more time or a better outcome, often framed as a trade with a provider or a higher power. Denial is the close distractor, but this client clearly accepts the prognosis and is negotiating within it rather than rejecting it.

q: A nurse is supporting the family of a client who is dying in the hospital. Which actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)
o: Allow family members to stay at the bedside overnight
Explain the physical changes that are occurring and what to expect next
Reassure the family that the client is in a better place
Offer information about bereavement groups and community resources
Encourage the family to avoid crying in front of the client
r: Presence, honest anticipatory explanation, and referral to bereavement resources address what families actually need during the vigil. Cliches such as a better place and instructions to hide emotion shut down expression of grief and impose the nurse's values on the family.

q: The daughter of a client who just died says to the nurse, 'I should have made him see a doctor months ago. This is my fault.' Which response should the nurse make?
o: 'There was nothing anyone could have done.'
'You should not blame yourself for this.'
'You are wondering whether something you did differently would have changed this.'
'Do you want me to call someone to sit with you?'
r: Reflecting the feeling invites the daughter to keep talking about the guilt, which is a normal and common part of early grief. Telling her not to blame herself sounds kind but closes the topic and denies the emotion she just voiced.

q: A client who is receiving end-of-life care in the hospital tells the nurse, 'I am afraid of dying alone.' Which actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)
o: Check on the client frequently rather than only when called
Consider moving the client to a room near the nurses' station
Limit conversation so the client can rest undisturbed
Let the client know when procedures and assessments will occur
Close the client's door and keep visitors out of the room
r: Frequent contact, proximity to staff, and keeping the client informed all reduce the fear of abandonment that dying clients commonly describe. Limiting conversation and restricting visitors increase isolation, which is exactly the fear the client expressed.

q: A nurse is teaching a community wellness class about normal sleep. The nurse should explain that REM sleep makes up about what portion of total sleep time in a healthy adult?
o: About 5 percent
About 20 to 25 percent
About 45 percent
About 75 percent
r: REM accounts for roughly one fifth to one quarter of adult sleep time, and the three NREM stages account for the rest. The 75 percent option is tempting because that figure belongs to NREM sleep as a whole, not to REM.

q: A client is very difficult to arouse, has steadily decreasing vital signs, and is getting the deepest physical rest of the night. The nurse should document that the client is in which stage of sleep?
o: Stage 1 NREM
Stage 2 NREM
Stage 3 NREM
REM
r: Stage 3 NREM is slow wave or delta sleep, when vital signs steadily fall, sympathetic activity drops, and physical restoration occurs. REM is the tempting choice because arousal is also difficult in REM, but REM brings fluctuating vital signs, vivid dreaming, and cognitive rather than physical restoration.

q: A client asks the nurse when dreaming usually begins after falling asleep. Which response is accurate?
o: About 10 minutes after you fall asleep
About 30 minutes after you fall asleep
About 90 minutes after you fall asleep
About 4 hours after you fall asleep
r: The first REM period generally begins roughly 90 minutes after sleep onset and then recurs about every 90 minutes, lengthening with each cycle. Answers of 10 or 30 minutes describe the light NREM stages that come first, not the onset of vivid dreaming.

q: A nurse is reviewing the characteristics of REM sleep with a nursing student. Which characteristics should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Vivid dreaming occurs
Skeletal muscle tone is lost
REM periods lengthen with each cycle across the night
The sleeper is easily awakened by a light touch
Vital signs are at their lowest and steadiest point
Cognitive restoration and memory consolidation occur
r: REM brings vivid dreaming, loss of skeletal muscle tone, lengthening REM periods through the night, and cognitive restoration. Being easily roused describes stage 1 NREM, and low steady vital signs describe stage 3 NREM, whereas vital signs in REM fluctuate.

q: A nurse observes a client doze off during a conversation, rouse instantly when spoken to, and describe feeling relaxed and drowsy. This finding is consistent with which stage of sleep?
o: Stage 1 NREM
Stage 2 NREM
Stage 3 NREM
REM
r: Stage 1 NREM is very light sleep lasting only a few minutes, with muscle relaxation, drowsiness, and easy arousal. Stage 2 requires somewhat more stimulation to wake the client, and stage 3 and REM are both difficult to interrupt.

q: The parent of a 15-year-old asks the nurse how much sleep a teenager actually needs. Which response is accurate?
o: About 4 to 5 hours a night
About 6 hours a night
About 9 to 10 hours a night
About 14 to 16 hours a night
r: Adolescents average about 9 to 10 hours of sleep a day, more than the 7 to 8 hours adults need. The 14 to 16 hour range applies to infants, whose total daily sleep including naps ranges from about 9 to 15 hours or more.

q: The family of an 80-year-old client tells the nurse that the client must be ill because he wakes several times each night and dozes briefly during the day. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
o: Waking at night at this age usually means there is a hidden illness
Older adults spend more time in deep sleep than younger adults do
Older adults require about 10 hours of sleep each night
Sleep normally becomes lighter with age, with more awakenings and less deep sleep
r: Aging reduces time spent in stage 3 NREM and increases nighttime arousals, so lighter and more fragmented sleep is expected while total sleep need stays near 7 to 8 hours. The option about more deep sleep is the reverse of what happens, and assuming illness without any other findings skips assessment.

q: A nurse is documenting a client's sleep history. Which description meets the definition of chronic insomnia?
o: Two consecutive nights of restless sleep
Poor sleep for a few days following a stressful event
Poor sleep on the nights before an early work shift
Difficulty sleeping that has continued for a month or longer
r: Chronic insomnia persists for a month or more, while acute insomnia lasts only a few days and is usually tied to a specific stressor. Recognizing the difference matters because chronic insomnia calls for a broader workup rather than short-term measures alone.

q: A nurse is collecting data from a client who reports trouble falling asleep. Which findings should the nurse identify as likely contributors? Select all that apply.
o: Drinks two cups of coffee after dinner every night
Eats a large meal within 30 minutes of bedtime
Finishes a vigorous workout at 2100 and goes to bed at 2200
Takes a 20-minute walk after breakfast each morning
Reports constant worry about an upcoming biopsy
Keeps the bedroom cool and dark
r: Caffeine late in the day, a heavy meal at bedtime, exercise finished too close to bedtime, and anxiety all delay sleep onset. A morning walk actually promotes sleep because exercise helps when it is completed at least 3 hours before bed, and a cool dark room supports sleep rather than disturbing it.

q: A nurse notes that a client who had abdominal surgery yesterday has been awake and restless since 0200. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Bring the client a cup of warm milk
Determine whether the client has unrelieved incisional pain
Administer the PRN sedative-hypnotic
Turn on the television so the client can relax
r: Assessment precedes intervention, and unrelieved pain is one of the most common reasons a postoperative client cannot sleep. Giving a sedative is tempting because it addresses the sleeplessness, but it masks pain, adds fall risk, and leaves the real cause untreated.

q: A nurse is teaching about obstructive sleep apnea. Which description should the nurse use?
o: Sudden uncontrollable episodes of falling asleep during the day
Relaxation of tongue and throat structures that blocks the upper airway during sleep
Failure of the brain respiratory center to signal the muscles to breathe
Repeated leg jerking that fragments sleep
r: In obstructive apnea the soft tissues of the mouth and throat relax and occlude the upper airway, producing repeated pauses in airflow with falling oxygen saturation. The option about the brain failing to signal breathing describes central sleep apnea, and sudden daytime sleep attacks describe narcolepsy.

q: A nurse is collecting data from a client being evaluated for obstructive sleep apnea. Which findings support this diagnosis? Select all that apply.
o: Loud snoring interrupted by gasping
Breathing pauses witnessed by the bed partner
Excessive daytime sleepiness
Morning headache
Awakening after 8 hours feeling completely refreshed
Oxygen saturation that rises during apneic periods
r: Apnea produces snoring with gasping, witnessed pauses longer than 10 seconds, daytime sleepiness from fragmented sleep, and morning headache from overnight carbon dioxide retention. Feeling fully refreshed argues against apnea, and saturation falls rather than rises during apneic episodes.

q: A client has a new prescription for CPAP for obstructive sleep apnea. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
o: I will clean the mask and tubing the way the instructions describe
I will wear the device any time I sleep, including naps
I will call the clinic if the mask leaves sores on my nose
I will use the machine only on nights when I feel very tired
r: CPAP works only while it is worn, so it must be used during every sleep period, including naps, regardless of how the client feels that day. Reporting skin breakdown is correct because pressure injury from the mask is a real complication that a different mask or padding can solve.

q: A nurse is caring for a postoperative client who has obstructive sleep apnea and is receiving opioid analgesia. Which finding requires immediate action?
o: Reports pain of 4 on a 0 to 10 scale
Snoring audible from the doorway
Asks to have the head of the bed raised
Respiratory rate of 8/min with oxygen saturation of 86 percent
r: A respiratory rate of 8/min with a saturation of 86 percent is respiratory depression layered on top of an already compromised airway, and breathing problems outrank every other finding. Snoring is expected in this client and warrants monitoring and positioning, but it is not the emergency that hypoventilation with desaturation is.

q: A client has newly diagnosed narcolepsy. Which instruction is the priority for the nurse to include?
o: Do not drive or operate machinery until the sleep attacks are controlled
Avoid caffeine with every meal
Limit nighttime sleep to no more than 6 hours
Stop the prescribed stimulant once you feel alert
r: Narcolepsy causes sudden uncontrollable sleep attacks, so the highest priority is preventing injury to the client and others during driving or machine operation. Stopping the stimulant when feeling alert is unsafe because the medication is what is producing the alertness.

q: A nurse is teaching a client who has narcolepsy about daily management. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Keep the same sleep and wake times every day
Take short planned naps during the day
Take the prescribed stimulant on schedule
Tell your employer so hazardous tasks can be reassigned
Drive only on familiar routes close to home
Have an alcoholic drink in the evening to deepen night sleep
r: A fixed schedule, scheduled short naps, prescribed stimulants, and workplace accommodation all reduce sleep attacks and injury risk. Driving on a familiar route is still driving and does not prevent an attack, and alcohol fragments sleep and worsens daytime sleepiness.

q: At 0300 a nurse finds a hospitalized client who has a history of sleepwalking standing in the hallway and appearing unaware of the surroundings. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Shake the client firmly to wake them fully
Quietly guide the client back to bed
Ask the client why they left the room
Apply a soft wrist restraint for safety
r: Calmly redirecting the client back to bed protects them from falls and injury without triggering the confusion and agitation that abrupt awakening causes. Restraints require a prescription, are never a first response, and would increase agitation and injury risk in a client who is not fully awake.

q: A nurse is teaching the family of an adult who sleepwalks about home safety. Which measures should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Keep floors clear of clutter and cords
Lock exterior doors and windows at night
Arrange for the client to sleep in a ground floor bedroom when possible
Place an alarm or chime on the bedroom door
Wake the client abruptly whenever an episode begins
Leave the stairway gate open so the client can move freely
r: Clearing hazards, securing exits, sleeping on one level, and alerting the family to movement all reduce the chance of injury during an episode. Waking the client abruptly causes disorientation and agitation, and an open stairway is exactly the hazard the family is trying to remove.

q: The parent of a 4-year-old reports that the child screams and thrashes about an hour after falling asleep, cannot be consoled, and has no memory of it the next morning. Which response by the nurse is appropriate?
o: These are nightmares, so ask the child to describe the dream in the morning
Wake the child completely each time so the episode does not repeat
Stay nearby, keep the child from injury, and let the episode pass without fully waking the child
This finding needs an urgent neurology referral
r: Sleep terrors arise out of deep NREM sleep early in the night, the child is not truly awake, and there is no recall, so the parent should protect the child and wait for the episode to end. Nightmares are the tempting alternative, but those occur during REM later in the night and the child remembers them and can be comforted.

q: A client has slept poorly for several nights in the hospital. Which findings should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
o: Irritability and mood changes
Decreased concentration and slowed reaction time
Increased sensitivity to pain
Daytime drowsiness
Improved short-term memory
Increased physical endurance
r: Loss of NREM and REM sleep produces irritability, poor concentration, slowed responses, heightened pain sensitivity, and daytime sleepiness. Memory consolidation and physical restoration both depend on adequate sleep, so those functions decline rather than improve.

q: A nurse is identifying factors that are interfering with a hospitalized client's sleep. Which factors should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Alarms and staff conversation in the hallway
Overhead lights turned on for an 0400 blood draw
Vital signs and assessments repeated through the night
Unrelieved surgical pain
A back rub offered at bedtime
A bedtime routine that matches the client's routine at home
r: Noise, bright light at night, repeated interruptions, and untreated pain are the leading causes of fragmented hospital sleep. A back rub and a familiar bedtime routine are comfort measures that promote sleep rather than interfere with it.

q: Which nursing action best promotes restorative sleep for a hospitalized client?
o: Group nighttime care so the client has uninterrupted 90-minute blocks
Offer a PRN sleep medication at 2100 every night
Encourage the client to nap for 2 hours each afternoon
Leave the television on low all night for background noise
r: Clustering care to protect blocks of about 90 minutes lets the client complete a full cycle and reach deep NREM and REM sleep. Routine sedatives are tempting but reduce sleep quality, and long afternoon naps and constant television noise both make nighttime sleep worse.

q: At 0200 the nurse observes assistive personnel on the unit. Which action requires the nurse to intervene?
o: Dimming the hallway lights near client rooms
Answering a call light promptly and quietly
Bringing a warm blanket to a client who is awake
Holding a loud conversation about weekend plans outside a client's door
r: Loud conversation outside client rooms at night is a preventable noise source that fragments sleep, so the nurse should intervene and redirect the staff. Dimming lights, answering call lights quietly, and providing a warm blanket all support the therapeutic environment.

q: A client on prolonged bed rest tells the nurse that day and night feel the same. Which action should the nurse take to support the client's circadian rhythm?
o: Open the blinds for daylight during the day and dim the room at night
Keep the room dim day and night so the client can rest whenever possible
Offer caffeine in the late afternoon to keep the client awake
Allow the client to sleep at any hour, day or night
r: Daylight exposure during waking hours and darkness at night are the strongest cues for resetting the sleep-wake cycle. Letting the client sleep at random hours seems client centered but deepens the day-night reversal, and late caffeine interferes with sleep onset that night.

q: Which nighttime task is appropriate for the nurse to delegate to assistive personnel caring for a stable client?
o: Teaching the client about sleep hygiene for home
Assessing the client's usual sleep history
Giving the client a back rub at bedtime
Evaluating whether the sleep plan improved the client's rest
r: A back rub for a stable client is a standard comfort measure well within the assistive personnel role. Assessment, teaching, and evaluation of outcomes stay with the nurse and cannot be delegated even when the client is stable.

q: A nurse is teaching a client about sleep hygiene at home. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Finish exercise at least 3 hours before bedtime
Limit caffeine, nicotine, and alcohol for at least 4 hours before bedtime
Limit fluids 2 to 4 hours before bedtime
Follow the same bedtime routine each night
Take two 30-minute naps every afternoon
Stay in bed watching television until sleep comes
r: Exercise completed several hours before bed, limiting stimulants and alcohol, limiting evening fluids to reduce nocturia, and a consistent routine all support sleep onset and continuity. Regular daytime naps reduce nighttime sleep drive, and using the bed for television weakens the association between the bed and sleeping.

q: Which statement by a client indicates an understanding of teaching about insomnia?
o: I will stay in bed until I fall asleep, no matter how long it takes
I will have a nightcap to help me drift off
I will sleep late on weekends to make up the difference
If I am still awake after about 20 minutes, I will get up and do something quiet
r: Getting out of bed after about 20 minutes of wakefulness and returning when sleepy keeps the bed linked with sleep rather than with frustration. Lying awake in bed for hours strengthens that negative association, and sleeping in on weekends shifts the body clock and makes the next week worse.

q: Which statement by a client requires further teaching about substances and sleep?
o: A glass of wine at bedtime keeps me asleep all night
Caffeine can stay in my system for hours
Smoking before bed can make it harder to fall asleep
A heavy late meal can disturb my sleep
r: Alcohol may shorten the time to fall asleep but it fragments the second half of the night and suppresses restorative sleep, so the client wakes unrefreshed. The other statements are accurate, since caffeine has a long duration of action and nicotine is a stimulant.

q: A client reports new difficulty sleeping. Which prescribed medications should the nurse identify as possible contributors? Select all that apply.
o: Theophylline, a bronchodilator
An antihypertensive
Prednisone
A diuretic scheduled at 2100
Docusate sodium
A daily multivitamin
r: Bronchodilators and corticosteroids are stimulating, several antihypertensives disturb sleep and dreaming, and an evening diuretic causes nocturia that repeatedly interrupts the night. A stool softener and a multivitamin have no such effect, so they are not the source of the problem.

q: A client asks the nurse whether taking a sleep medication every night is a good long-term plan. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
o: Sleep medications increase the amount of deep and REM sleep you get
Sleep medications can help for a short time, but they reduce the quality of restorative sleep and can cause next-day drowsiness
Sleep medications are safest when taken every night indefinitely
Sleep medications work best when taken with an evening alcoholic drink
r: Hypnotics can shorten sleep onset briefly but they suppress deep and REM sleep, cause carryover sedation, and may lead to rebound insomnia when stopped. Combining them with alcohol is dangerous because both depress the central nervous system.

q: The nurse administers a sedative-hypnotic at 2200 to an older adult client. Which action is the priority?
o: Encourage the client to drink extra fluids
Document the time of administration
Leave the overhead light on all night
Lower the bed, ensure the call light is within reach, and remind the client to call before getting up
r: Sedatives cause confusion and unsteady gait in older adults, so fall prevention is the priority right after administration. Extra fluids are actively harmful here because they send a sedated client to the bathroom repeatedly during the night.

q: A client asks the nurse which herbal product is commonly used to promote sleep and reduce anxiety. Which product should the nurse identify?
o: Ginkgo biloba
Echinacea
Valerian
Ginger
r: Valerian is used to promote sleep and reduce anxiety, and the nurse should still tell the client to report its use because many herbal products are not regulated like prescription drugs and can interact with them. Ginkgo is taken for memory, echinacea for immune support, and ginger for nausea.

q: A client who had surgery yesterday is laughing with visitors when the nurse arrives. When asked, the client rates the pain as 8 on a 0 to 10 scale and requests the prescribed analgesic. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Ask the client to rate the pain again after the visitors leave
Administer the prescribed analgesic based on the client's report
Document that the behavior does not match the report and hold the dose
Explain that pain of that intensity would make laughing impossible
r: Pain is whatever the client says it is, existing whenever the client says it does, so the report drives the intervention even when the client is smiling or distracted. Visiting and laughing are coping and distraction behaviors, and treating them as evidence against pain is a classic cause of undertreatment.

q: A nurse is teaching a group of students about pain assessment. Which source of information should the nurse identify as the single most reliable indicator of a client's pain?
o: The client's own report of the pain
The client's vital signs
The nurse's observation of the client's behavior
The amount of tissue damage seen on imaging
r: Self-report is the most reliable indicator of pain because pain is a subjective experience that no measurement can verify from the outside. Vital signs and behavior are supporting data that are especially useful when the client cannot self-report, but they never override or replace what the client says.

q: A newly licensed nurse is caring for a client with chronic low back pain who rates the pain as 9 while his heart rate is 74 and his blood pressure is 122/70. Which statement by the newly licensed nurse requires follow-up by the charge nurse?
o: Chronic pain can persist long after the tissue has healed
I will ask the client what pain level would be acceptable to him
His vital signs are normal, so a rating of 9 must be exaggerated
Scheduled dosing may control his pain better than waiting for PRN requests
r: In chronic pain the body adapts and vital signs return to baseline, so normal pulse and blood pressure never rule out severe pain and cannot be used to discount a client's rating. The other statements reflect correct principles, since chronic pain outlasts healing and around-the-clock dosing keeps persistent pain at a tolerable level.

q: A nurse is reviewing assignments with a student. Which client should the student identify as having chronic pain?
o: A client 12 hours after an appendectomy
A client reporting chest pain during a myocardial infarction
A client with a fractured femur reporting hip pain
A client with episodic low back pain since a fall 2 years ago
r: Chronic pain is ongoing or recurrent, lasts longer than about 6 months, and continues beyond the expected time for tissue healing, which fits the back pain persisting 2 years after the injury. The postoperative, cardiac, and fracture clients all have acute pain that is protective and expected to resolve as the tissue heals.

q: A nurse is caring for a client with acute pain following a traumatic injury. Which findings should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
o: Tachycardia
Elevated blood pressure
Diaphoresis
Guarding of the injured area
Bradycardia and hypotension as the earliest response
No change in facial expression
r: Acute pain triggers a sympathetic fight-or-flight response with a rising pulse and blood pressure and sweating, along with behaviors such as guarding, grimacing, and moaning. Bradycardia and hypotension are not the expected early response to acute pain, and an unchanged facial expression is more typical of long-standing chronic pain.

q: A client with diabetes describes constant burning and shooting pain with a pins and needles quality in both feet. Which prescription should the nurse anticipate as most likely to relieve this pain?
o: An NSAID alone
Gabapentin, an antiseizure adjuvant
A topical antibiotic ointment
An antacid before meals
r: Burning, shooting, pins and needles pain from damaged nerves is neuropathic and responds best to adjuvant medications such as antiseizure agents, antidepressants, and topical analgesics. NSAIDs are tempting because they treat pain, but they work on inflamed tissue and do little for pain generated by the nerve itself.

q: A client reports deep, cramping, poorly localized abdominal pain that is also felt in the right shoulder. How should the nurse classify this pain?
o: Somatic nociceptive pain
Neuropathic pain
Visceral nociceptive pain
Phantom pain
r: Visceral pain arises from internal organs, is deep and hard to pinpoint, and frequently refers to a site away from the source, such as the shoulder. Somatic pain comes from bone, joint, muscle, or skin and is sharper and easier to localize.

q: A client with gallbladder disease reports pain in the right shoulder. The nurse should document this finding as which type of pain?
o: Referred pain
Phantom pain
Breakthrough pain
Allodynia
r: Referred pain is felt in an area away from the actual source because nerves from different regions share the same spinal pathways, and gallbladder pain classically refers to the right shoulder. Breakthrough pain is a flare of pain in a client on a stable analgesic regimen, and allodynia is pain from a normally harmless stimulus such as clothing or a breeze.

q: A client who had a below-the-knee amputation 2 weeks ago reports burning pain in the foot that is no longer there. Which response by the nurse is appropriate?
o: That pain cannot be real because the limb has been removed
Try not to think about the limb and the sensation will fade
Phantom sensations always stop within a few days
The pain is real and comes from the nerves that supplied the limb, and we can treat it
r: Phantom limb pain is genuine neuropathic pain generated by the nerves and central pathways that once served the limb, and it responds to adjuvant medications and nonpharmacologic measures. Telling the client the pain is imaginary or will simply pass dismisses a real problem and damages trust.

q: A nurse is reviewing types of pain with a student. Which examples are neuropathic in origin? Select all that apply.
o: Phantom limb pain
Diabetic peripheral neuropathy
Pain below the level of a spinal cord injury
Postherpetic neuralgia
Pain at a surgical incision
Pain from a fractured rib
r: Neuropathic pain comes from atypical or damaged nerves, which is the mechanism in phantom limb pain, diabetic neuropathy, pain below a cord injury, and the nerve pain that lingers after shingles. Incisional and fracture pain are nociceptive because intact nerves are reporting real tissue damage.

q: A nurse is choosing pain scales for a group of clients. Standardized numeric self-report scales are generally appropriate beginning at about what age?
o: 3 years
5 years
7 years
12 years
r: Self-report with a standardized numeric scale is reliable for most clients from about age 7 upward, because that is when children reliably grasp ranking and numbers. Younger children are better served by a picture-based scale, and waiting until age 12 would needlessly deny school-age children the chance to rate their own pain.

q: A nurse is assessing pain in an alert 5-year-old who is 1 day postoperative and can point to pictures. Which pain assessment tool is most appropriate?
o: Numeric rating scale of 0 to 10
FACES scale
FLACC scale
PAINAD scale
r: A picture-based FACES scale lets a preschooler who can point give an actual self-report, which is always preferred when the child can participate. The FLACC is a behavioral tool for children too young or too impaired to self-report, so using it here would discard information the child can provide.

q: A nurse needs to assess pain in an 18-month-old toddler after surgery. Which tool should the nurse use?
o: FLACC scale
Numeric rating scale
PAINAD scale
Visual analog scale
r: FLACC scores face, legs, activity, cry, and consolability, making it the right observational tool for infants and young children who cannot report pain in words or numbers. PAINAD is also observational but was developed for adults with advanced dementia, not for toddlers.

q: A nurse is caring for an 84-year-old client with advanced dementia who cannot answer questions about pain but grimaces and resists care. Which assessment tool should the nurse use?
o: Numeric rating scale
FACES scale
PAINAD scale
Visual analog scale
r: PAINAD scores breathing, vocalization, facial expression, body language, and consolability, and it is designed for adults with advanced dementia who can no longer self-report. FACES still requires the client to interpret pictures and choose, which a client at this stage of dementia usually cannot do reliably.

q: A nurse is planning pain assessments on a busy unit. For which clients should the nurse plan to use an observational behavioral pain scale rather than self-report? Select all that apply.
o: A 9-month-old infant on the first postoperative day
A client with advanced dementia who cannot answer questions
A client who is intubated and sedated
An alert 30-year-old with a fractured wrist
A client with early dementia who states the pain is a 6
An 8-year-old who can count and rank numbers
r: Behavioral tools are used only when self-report is impossible, which is the case for infants, clients with advanced dementia who cannot answer, and clients who are intubated and sedated. Any client who can give a number, including the client with early dementia and the school-age child, should be allowed to self-report.

q: A nurse suspects pain in a client with advanced dementia who cannot self-report. Which behaviors support that conclusion? Select all that apply.
o: Grimacing with a furrowed brow
New agitation and restlessness
Moaning during repositioning
Guarding a body area when it is touched
Sleeping soundly through repositioning
Eating an entire meal without difficulty
r: Facial expression, new agitation, vocalization with movement, and guarding are the behavioral cues that stand in for self-report in a nonverbal client. Sleeping through care and eating a full meal are not indicators of pain and would not prompt analgesia.

q: A client with metastatic cancer rates the pain as 8 on a 0 to 10 scale. The heart rate is 72 and the blood pressure is 118/70. An opioid is prescribed for moderate to severe pain. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Administer the prescribed opioid
Recheck the vital signs in 30 minutes before deciding
Explain that the vital signs show the pain is mild
Document that the client may be seeking medication
r: Vital signs stabilize when pain persists over time, so a client with long-standing cancer pain can have a normal pulse and blood pressure while in severe pain, and the self-report governs the decision. Delaying the dose to recheck vital signs uses an unreliable measure to override a reliable one and leaves the client in pain.

q: A nurse is reviewing populations at risk for having their pain undertreated. Which clients should the nurse identify as being at increased risk? Select all that apply.
o: An infant who cannot verbalize pain
An older adult with cognitive impairment
A client with a history of opioid use disorder
A preschool-age child
An alert adult who rates pain on a 0 to 10 scale
A client whose analgesic is already scheduled around the clock
r: Infants, young children, older adults, and clients with substance use disorder are undertreated most often because they cannot report pain clearly or because staff attitudes and fear of addiction discount their reports. Clients who can rate their pain and clients on scheduled dosing are far less likely to be missed.

q: A client rates postoperative incisional pain as 2 on a 0 to 10 scale. Prescriptions include acetaminophen for mild pain, oxycodone for moderate pain, and IV hydromorphone for severe pain. Which medication should the nurse administer?
o: Request a morphine PCA from the provider
The prescribed acetaminophen
The oral oxycodone
The IV hydromorphone
r: The analgesic ladder begins with a nonopioid for mild pain and moves up only as the pain intensity requires, so acetaminophen matches a rating of 2. Choosing an opioid for mild pain exposes the client to sedation, respiratory depression, and constipation with no added benefit.

q: A client with advanced cancer rates pain as 9 on a 0 to 10 scale despite taking a scheduled nonopioid plus a weak opioid. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Continue the current regimen and reassess in 24 hours
Recommend distraction as the main treatment
Hold all analgesics until the provider rounds
Contact the provider about a strong opioid scheduled around the clock with a dose available for breakthrough pain
r: When pain persists at the second step of the ladder, the next step is a strong opioid given around the clock with a breakthrough dose available, and there is no ceiling dose that limits titration for cancer pain. Continuing an ineffective regimen or holding analgesics entirely leaves severe pain untreated, and nonpharmacologic measures are added to analgesia rather than substituted for it.

q: A client who had a knee replacement has physical therapy scheduled at 1000 and has a PRN oral opioid available every 4 hours, last given at 0600. Which action by the nurse is best?
o: Wait until the client reports pain during the therapy session
Ask the therapist to shorten the session instead
Hold the opioid so the client can participate fully
Give the dose about 30 to 45 minutes before the session
r: It takes less medication to prevent pain than to chase it, so dosing before a predictably painful activity allows the client to participate and improves the outcome of therapy. Waiting for the client to hurt during therapy means the peak effect arrives after the session is over.

q: A nurse is monitoring a client who is receiving an opioid analgesic. Which adverse effects should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
o: Constipation
Sedation
Urinary retention
Diarrhea
An increase in respiratory rate
Hypertension
r: Opioids slow gut motility, depress the central nervous system, and can impair bladder emptying, producing constipation, sedation, and urinary retention along with nausea and orthostatic hypotension. Opioids slow the respiratory rate rather than raise it and lower blood pressure rather than raise it, and they cause constipation rather than diarrhea.

q: A nurse is teaching new graduates about opioid adverse effects. Which effect should the nurse identify as the most dangerous?
o: Constipation
Nausea
Respiratory depression
Pruritus
r: Respiratory depression is the adverse effect that kills, so it outranks every other opioid effect and drives the monitoring plan. Constipation is the most persistent effect and nausea is the most common early complaint, but neither threatens the airway and breathing.

q: A client is prescribed morphine 4 mg IV every 4 hours PRN, with instructions to hold the dose if the respiratory rate is below 12/min. The client reports pain of 7 and is drowsy but arousable, with a respiratory rate of 10/min. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Administer the dose because the client reports pain of 7
Hold the dose, stay with the client, and reassess the respiratory status
Administer naloxone immediately
Document the finding and reassess in 4 hours
r: A respiratory rate below the parameter means the nurse holds the dose, remains with the client, stimulates and monitors breathing, and notifies the provider before any further opioid is given. Naloxone is reserved for severe depression such as a rate below 8/min with an unarousable client, because it reverses analgesia abruptly and can precipitate severe pain and withdrawal.

q: A client received an opioid 30 minutes ago. Which finding is the earliest warning that respiratory depression may be developing?
o: The client is increasingly difficult to keep awake during conversation
The respiratory rate is 12/min
The client reports generalized itching
The blood pressure is 110/64
r: Sedation always precedes opioid-induced respiratory depression, so a rising level of sedation is the earliest actionable cue and calls for stimulation, monitoring, and holding further doses. A rate of 12/min is still within acceptable limits, and itching, while uncomfortable, does not threaten breathing.

q: A client received naloxone for opioid-induced respiratory depression and is now awake with a respiratory rate of 16/min. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Stop monitoring now that the respiratory rate is normal
Expect the client to remain comfortable for several hours
Give the next scheduled opioid dose right away
Continue close respiratory monitoring, because naloxone wears off before the opioid does
