r: Naloxone has a shorter duration of action than most opioids, so sedation and respiratory depression can return and repeat doses may be needed. The client is also likely to have abrupt severe pain, so comfort must be reassessed and managed carefully rather than assumed.

q: A client has been taking an opioid for chronic cancer pain for several months. Which adverse effect should the nurse expect to persist for as long as the client takes the medication?
o: Sedation
Nausea
Constipation
Orthostatic hypotension
r: Tolerance develops to sedation, nausea, and orthostatic hypotension within days to weeks, but it does not develop to constipation, which continues for the entire course of therapy. That is why a bowel regimen is maintained rather than stopped once the client seems settled on the medication.

q: A client is starting scheduled oxycodone for chronic pain. Which action should the nurse take regarding bowel function?
o: Begin a stool softener and stimulant laxative at the same time the opioid is started
Wait until the client has gone 3 days without a stool
Encourage a low-fiber diet to rest the bowel
Give a bulk-forming laxative only if the client asks for one
r: Because constipation is predictable and does not resolve with tolerance, the bowel regimen starts with the first opioid dose rather than after the problem appears. Waiting for 3 days without a stool allows impaction to develop, and a low-fiber diet and bulk laxatives without adequate fluid make opioid constipation worse.

q: A nurse is teaching a client who takes long-term opioids about preventing constipation. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Take the prescribed stimulant laxative on a schedule, not only when constipated
Increase fluid intake unless the provider has restricted fluids
Add fiber to the diet as tolerated
Stay as physically active as your condition allows
Wait until constipation develops before taking anything for it
Take a bulk-forming laxative without increasing fluids
r: Scheduled stimulant laxatives, fluids, fiber, and activity together keep stool moving against the slowed motility opioids cause. Waiting for constipation to appear invites impaction, and a bulk-forming product taken without enough fluid can worsen the obstruction rather than relieve it.

q: A client takes a hydrocodone and acetaminophen combination tablet at home for chronic pain. Which statement by the client requires follow-up?
o: I take my combination tablet only as it is prescribed
I read labels to check for acetaminophen in cold remedies
When the pain is bad I add two extra acetaminophen tablets to my prescribed pill
I keep my total acetaminophen under 4 g in a day
r: Adding extra acetaminophen to a combination product that already contains it can push the daily total past the 4 g limit for a client with a healthy liver and cause hepatotoxicity. Checking labels on over-the-counter remedies and tracking the daily total are exactly the behaviors that prevent unintentional overdose.

q: A nurse enters the room of a client using a morphine PCA and the client's daughter says she presses the button whenever her mother falls asleep so the pain does not return. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Thank the daughter for helping keep the pain controlled
Suggest that the daughter press the button only at night
Ask the daughter to leave the room during the infusion
Explain that only the client may press the button, and teach the daughter why
r: The PCA is safe because a sedated client cannot press the button, so the built-in protection against overdose disappears the moment anyone else presses it. Teaching the family this rule is a nursing priority, and simply limiting when the daughter presses it or removing her from the room fails to correct the dangerous misunderstanding.

q: A nurse finds a client using a morphine PCA difficult to arouse, with a respiratory rate of 7/min and shallow breathing. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Document the findings and continue to monitor
Stop the PCA infusion and stimulate the client while assessing the breathing
Ask a family member to watch the client
Lower the head of the bed
r: Stopping further opioid delivery and rousing the client to support breathing addresses the airway and breathing threat immediately, and oxygen, provider notification, and naloxone follow per protocol. Continuing to monitor without stopping the pump lets more drug infuse, and lowering the head of the bed worsens ventilation in a sedated client.

q: A client has an acutely sprained ankle with swelling that occurred 1 hour ago. Which intervention should the nurse plan?
o: Apply a cold pack to the ankle
Apply moist heat for 30 minutes
Massage the ankle firmly
Alternate heat and cold every 5 minutes
r: Cold constricts vessels and limits swelling and inflammation, which is what a fresh injury needs, and it also dulls transmission of the pain signal. Heat increases blood flow and is useful later for stiffness and muscle relaxation, but applying it to a new injury increases edema.

q: A nurse is planning nonpharmacologic comfort measures for a client with pain. Which measures are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Music through earphones
Guided imagery
Repositioning with gentle massage of tense muscles
A quiet, dimly lit room with reduced stimulation
Requiring the client to stop using analgesics
Vigorous massage over a leg with a suspected clot
r: Distraction, imagery, gentle touch, and reducing environmental stimuli all lower perceived pain and are used alongside analgesics. Nonpharmacologic measures never replace prescribed analgesia against the client's wishes, and massaging a limb with a suspected thrombus can dislodge the clot.

q: A client receives acupuncture at a clinic while continuing the prescribed analgesic regimen. How should the nurse describe this approach?
o: Alternative therapy
Complementary therapy
Allopathic therapy
Placebo therapy
r: A complementary therapy is used along with conventional treatment, while an alternative therapy replaces conventional care entirely. Since the client is continuing the prescribed analgesics, the acupuncture is complementary, and together they represent integrative care.

q: A nurse is discussing complementary therapies that nurses can provide without specialized licensing or certification. Which therapies should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Guided imagery
Breath work
Humor
Playing music at the bedside
Chiropractic spinal manipulation
Acupuncture
r: Guided imagery, breath work, humor, music, simple touch, and meditation are within nursing practice and need no separate credential. Chiropractic manipulation and acupuncture require a licensed or certified practitioner, so the nurse arranges a referral rather than performing them.

q: A client scheduled for surgery next week reports taking ginkgo biloba and garlic supplements daily. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Reassure the client that herbal products are safe because they are natural
Advise the client to double the dose to promote healing
Report the use to the provider, because these products can increase bleeding risk
Explain that these products are tested by the FDA in the same way as prescription drugs
r: Garlic inhibits platelet aggregation and ginkgo also increases bleeding tendency, so the surgical team must know about them before the procedure. Many herbal products are not regulated like prescription medications, so being natural does not make them free of adverse effects or drug interactions.

q: A nurse is reviewing expected vital sign ranges with a group of nursing students. Which set of values should the nurse identify as within normal limits for a healthy adult at rest?
o: Temperature 35.0 C, pulse 52, respirations 10, blood pressure 88/54
Temperature 36.8 C, pulse 78, respirations 16, blood pressure 118/76
Temperature 38.4 C, pulse 108, respirations 24, blood pressure 148/92
Temperature 37.0 C, pulse 44, respirations 28, blood pressure 92/48
r: A resting adult should have a temperature near 36.5 to 37.5 C, a pulse of 60 to 100 per minute, respirations of 12 to 20 per minute, and a blood pressure under 120/80. The third set is tempting because each value looks only mildly off, but a pulse over 100, respirations over 20, and a systolic over 130 together describe a client in distress, not a normal baseline.

q: A nurse is caring for an 84-year-old client on a medical unit. Which of the following statements about vital signs in older adults should guide the nurse's assessment? Select all that apply.
o: Baseline body temperature is often lower, so a smaller rise can still mean infection
Systolic pressure tends to rise because arteries become less elastic
Older adults are at higher risk for orthostatic drops with position change
A fever always accompanies infection in this age group
Respiratory rate ranges are typically much lower than adult ranges, around 6 to 10 per minute
r: Aging lowers baseline temperature and blunts the febrile response, stiffens arteries so systolic pressure climbs, and impairs the baroreceptor reflex that protects blood pressure on standing. The idea that infection always produces fever is the dangerous misconception here, because an older adult may present only with confusion, weakness, or a slightly elevated temperature.

q: A nurse is comparing vital signs in infants and young children with adult values. Which of the following statements should the nurse identify as accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Heart rate is normally faster in infants than in adults
Respiratory rate is normally faster in infants than in adults
Blood pressure is normally lower in infants and rises with age
Bradycardia in an infant is a reassuring sign of good conditioning
The apical site is preferred for counting the pulse in an infant
r: Infants have faster heart and respiratory rates and lower blood pressures than adults, and their rates are counted apically because peripheral pulses are difficult to palpate accurately. Bradycardia in an infant is never reassuring; it usually reflects hypoxia and demands immediate attention, which is the opposite of the conditioned-athlete reasoning that applies to some adults.

q: A nurse needs the most accurate reflection of core temperature for a client whose temperature readings have been inconsistent. Which route should the nurse select, assuming no contraindications?
o: Axillary
Oral
Temporal artery
Rectal
r: Of the routine noninvasive routes, rectal measurement most closely reflects core temperature. Axillary is the tempting choice for a squirming or confused client because it is easy and safe, but it is the least accurate route and lags behind true core temperature.

q: A nurse is choosing a temperature route for several clients. For which of the following clients should the nurse avoid the rectal route? Select all that apply.
o: A client who has neutropenia following chemotherapy
A client who had rectal surgery 2 days ago
A client who has diarrhea
A client who is receiving oxygen by nasal cannula
A client who has a history of hypertension controlled with medication
r: Rectal measurement is avoided when the mucosa is fragile or the route is unusable, which includes neutropenia because of infection and bleeding risk, recent rectal surgery, and active diarrhea. Oxygen by nasal cannula does not affect the rectal route and in fact does not rule out an oral reading either, since it is a mask or mouth breathing that makes the oral route unreliable.

q: A client finishes a cup of hot coffee just as the nurse arrives to take an oral temperature. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Take the oral reading now and subtract 0.5 C from the result
Document that the temperature could not be obtained
Place the probe under the tongue for twice the usual time
Wait 15 to 30 minutes before taking the oral reading
r: Hot or cold liquids, smoking, and chewing gum alter mouth temperature, so the nurse waits 15 to 30 minutes before an oral reading. Subtracting an estimated amount invents data, and no correction factor is reliable enough to base clinical decisions on.

q: A nurse is obtaining a tympanic temperature on an adult client. Which action should the nurse take to ensure an accurate reading?
o: Pull the pinna up and back before inserting the probe
Pull the pinna down and back before inserting the probe
Insert the probe until resistance is met
Use the ear the client has been lying on
r: Straightening the adult ear canal by pulling the pinna up and back aims the probe at the tympanic membrane and its shared blood supply with the hypothalamus. Down and back is the technique for a child under 3 years, and lying on an ear warms it and produces a falsely elevated reading.

q: A nurse discovers an unresponsive adult client and must check for a pulse. Which site should the nurse use?
o: Radial
Carotid
Dorsalis pedis
Brachial
r: The carotid is the central pulse the nurse checks in an unresponsive adult, because it remains palpable when peripheral perfusion has failed. The radial pulse is the routine site for a stable client, but it can be absent during shock even when the heart is still beating.

q: A nurse is preparing to auscultate an apical pulse. Where should the nurse place the stethoscope?
o: Second intercostal space at the right sternal border
Second intercostal space at the left sternal border
Fourth intercostal space at the left sternal border
Fifth intercostal space at the left midclavicular line
r: The apex of the heart sits at the fifth intercostal space at the left midclavicular line, which is where the apical rate is counted. The second intercostal space landmarks are the aortic and pulmonic areas used for evaluating valve sounds, not for counting the apical rate.

q: A nurse is preparing to administer digoxin to a client. Which action should the nurse take before giving the dose?
o: Count the radial pulse for 30 seconds and double it
Measure the blood pressure in both arms
Check the client's temperature
Count the apical pulse for 1 full minute
r: Digoxin slows conduction, so the apical rate must be counted for a full minute and the dose withheld and the provider notified if it is below 60 per minute in an adult. A radial count is not acceptable here because digoxin can produce beats that do not perfuse to the wrist, which would make the rate look higher than the heart is actually contracting.

q: A nurse palpates a radial pulse that is irregular. Which action should the nurse take next?
o: Document the pulse as irregular and continue with care
Count the radial pulse for 15 seconds and multiply by four
Auscultate the apical pulse for 1 full minute
Apply a pulse oximeter and record the displayed heart rate
r: An irregular rhythm makes any partial count inaccurate, so the nurse listens at the apex for a full minute to get a true rate. Reading the number off a pulse oximeter is tempting because it is fast, but the device can miss weak beats and does not evaluate rhythm.

q: A nurse determines that a client's apical rate is 96 per minute and the radial rate is 78 per minute. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
o: The client has a pulse deficit of 18, indicating some beats are not perfusing peripherally
The client has a bounding peripheral pulse that reflects an increase in stroke volume
The radial artery is occluded and requires immediate surgery
The measurement is invalid and should be discarded
r: A pulse deficit is the apical rate minus the radial rate and means some ventricular contractions are too weak to generate a palpable peripheral pulse, a pattern often seen with atrial fibrillation. It does not by itself indicate arterial occlusion, which would affect one limb rather than producing a difference between central and peripheral rates.

q: A nurse plans to measure a client's pulse deficit. Which technique should the nurse use?
o: Count the apical rate for 1 minute, then count the radial rate for the next minute
Have a second nurse count the radial rate while the first nurse counts the apical rate for the same full minute
Compare the radial pulse in the right arm with the radial pulse in the left arm
Compare the apical rate with the rate shown on the cardiac monitor
r: The two rates must be counted simultaneously by two people over the same full minute, because the heart rate can change from one minute to the next and a sequential count would produce a meaningless difference. Comparing right and left radial pulses evaluates arterial flow to each arm, which is a different assessment entirely.

q: A nurse observes that a client's breathing alternates between periods of increasingly deep breaths and periods of apnea in a repeating cycle. How should the nurse document this pattern?
o: Kussmaul respirations
Cheyne-Stokes respirations
Biot respirations
Bradypnea
r: A regular crescendo and decrescendo pattern punctuated by apnea is Cheyne-Stokes breathing, seen with heart failure, drug effects, and end of life. Kussmaul respirations are the tempting alternative but are consistently deep and rapid without the waxing and waning cycle, and they signal metabolic acidosis such as diabetic ketoacidosis.

q: A nurse is assessing respirations on four clients. Which of the following findings should the nurse report to the provider? Select all that apply.
o: Respiratory rate of 8 per minute in an adult receiving opioid analgesia
Deep, rapid, sighing respirations in a client who has hyperglycemia
Respiratory rate of 16 per minute with an even, unlabored pattern
Use of accessory neck muscles and nasal flaring
Audible high-pitched crowing on inspiration
r: A rate of 8 with opioids signals respiratory depression, Kussmaul breathing signals metabolic acidosis, accessory muscle use signals increased work of breathing, and inspiratory stridor signals upper airway narrowing, which is the most urgent of these. A rate of 16 that is even and effortless is normal and needs no report, and choosing it reflects confusing a documented number with an abnormal one.

q: A nurse is selecting a blood pressure cuff for an adult client who has a large upper arm. Which principle should guide the choice?
o: The bladder width should be about 40 percent of the arm circumference and the bladder length about 80 percent of the way around the arm
Any cuff will work as long as it is inflated 30 mm Hg above the expected systolic pressure and deflated slowly enough to hear each sound clearly
The bladder should encircle the arm completely and overlap
A thigh cuff should be used on the forearm instead
r: Correct sizing means a bladder roughly 40 percent as wide as the arm circumference and long enough to wrap about 80 percent around the arm, which distributes pressure evenly over the artery. Believing that inflation technique can compensate for a poorly fitted cuff is the common error, because cuff size changes the reading no matter how carefully it is inflated.

q: A nurse uses a standard adult cuff on a client whose upper arm is too large for it. How will this affect the reading?
o: The reading will be falsely low
The reading will be accurate but harder to hear
Only the diastolic reading will be affected
The reading will be falsely high
r: A cuff that is too narrow or too small for the arm requires extra pressure to compress the artery, so the recorded pressure is falsely high. The mirror image is just as important to remember: a cuff that is too wide or too large gives a falsely low reading, and mixing up the two directions is the most common mistake on this concept.

q: A nurse has only a large adult cuff available and applies it to a thin adult client with a small upper arm. Which reading should the nurse anticipate?
o: A falsely high systolic and diastolic reading
An accurate reading, since larger cuffs are more comfortable
A falsely low systolic and diastolic reading
A widened pulse pressure with an accurate mean
r: A cuff that is too wide or too large for the limb compresses the artery with less pressure than is actually needed, producing a falsely low reading. Comfort has nothing to do with accuracy, and using an oversized cuff can mask hypertension by making the pressure look acceptable.

q: A nurse is reviewing blood pressure technique with a newly hired nurse. Which of the following actions would produce a falsely high reading? Select all that apply.
o: Placing the client's arm below heart level
Measuring while the client's legs are crossed
Applying the cuff over a thick sweater sleeve
Supporting the arm at heart level on a table
Allowing the client to rest quietly for 5 minutes first
r: An arm below heart level adds hydrostatic pressure, crossed legs raise systolic pressure, and a cuff over bulky clothing prevents even compression, so all three inflate the number. Supporting the arm at heart level and letting the client rest first are correct technique, and selecting them confuses proper steps with sources of error. An arm held above heart level produces the opposite problem, a falsely low reading.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has an arteriovenous fistula in the left arm and an IV infusing in the right forearm. Where should the nurse measure the blood pressure?
o: Left upper arm
Right upper arm above the IV site, with the infusion paused during the measurement
Either thigh using an appropriately sized cuff
Left forearm
r: The extremity with a fistula must never be used because cuff pressure can damage or clot the access, and inflating above an infusing IV risks infiltration and interrupts the infusion. A thigh or popliteal measurement with a correctly sized cuff is the appropriate alternative when both arms are unavailable.

q: A nurse wants to avoid missing an auscultatory gap when measuring a client's blood pressure. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Palpate the radial pulse while inflating, then inflate 30 mm Hg beyond the point the pulse disappears
Inflate the cuff to 200 mm Hg on every client
Deflate the cuff at 5 to 10 mm Hg per second so the measurement is completed quickly
Use the bell of the stethoscope over the brachial artery
r: Estimating systolic pressure by palpation and then inflating 30 mm Hg above that point ensures the cuff starts above any silent gap, so the true systolic is not missed. Routinely inflating to 200 is unnecessarily painful and still does not confirm the starting point relative to that client's actual pressure, and deflating faster than 2 to 3 mm Hg per second causes its own errors.

q: A nurse measures a client's blood pressure as 124/76 mm Hg with a pulse of 72 while supine. After the client stands for 2 minutes, the pressure is 100/64 mm Hg with a pulse of 96. How should the nurse interpret these findings?
o: The findings are expected with position change
The client has orthostatic hypotension and is at risk for falls
The client has hypertension that requires treatment
The client is developing a cardiac dysrhythmia
r: A systolic drop of about 20 mm Hg or a diastolic drop of about 10 mm Hg on standing, especially with a compensatory rise in heart rate, defines orthostatic hypotension and predicts dizziness and falls. A small transient change is normal, but this systolic fall of 24 with a heart rate increase of 24 is well beyond expected variation.

q: A nurse is measuring orthostatic vital signs. Which of the following actions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Have the client lie supine for about 5 minutes before the first measurement
Measure blood pressure and pulse in the supine, sitting, and standing positions
Take the readings within 1 to 3 minutes after each position change
Return the client to a lying position if dizziness or lightheadedness occurs
Use a different arm for each position to save time
r: Accurate orthostatic readings require a supine rest period, sequential measurements in three positions with the pulse taken each time, prompt readings after each change, and immediate return to lying if symptoms appear. Switching arms introduces a new variable, since normal arm-to-arm differences would be misread as a positional drop.

q: A client who has been on bed rest reports dizziness and appears pale when helped to stand for the first time. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Assist the client back to a sitting or lying position
Obtain a blood pressure reading while the client is standing
Notify the provider
Offer the client a glass of water
r: Client safety comes before data collection, so the nurse returns the client to a safe position to prevent a fall and syncope. Getting the standing pressure would document the problem but leaves the symptomatic client upright and at immediate risk of injury.

q: A nurse obtains an SpO2 reading of 84 percent on a client who appears comfortable, is speaking in full sentences, and has pink mucous membranes. Which of the following factors could explain an inaccurate reading? Select all that apply.
o: Cold fingers with poor peripheral perfusion
Dark nail polish on the finger with the probe
The probe placed on the same arm as an inflating blood pressure cuff
Client movement during the measurement
The client having eaten a meal 20 minutes earlier
r: Pulse oximetry depends on pulsatile arterial flow and clear light transmission, so cold or poorly perfused extremities, nail polish, an inflating cuff proximal to the probe, and motion all corrupt the signal. Recent food intake affects oral temperature, not oxygen saturation, and confusing those two assessments is the error being tested.

q: A nurse is caring for a client rescued from a house fire who has carbon monoxide poisoning. The pulse oximeter reads 99 percent. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
o: The client is well oxygenated and does not need supplemental oxygen
The oximeter probe is malfunctioning and should be replaced
The reading confirms that the airway is patent
The reading is unreliable because the oximeter cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin
r: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin tightly and the oximeter reads that bound hemoglobin as saturated, so the number can look normal or high while tissues are severely hypoxic. Trusting the display and withholding oxygen is the fatal error here; these clients need high-flow oxygen and arterial blood gas or carboxyhemoglobin measurement.

q: A nurse notes that a client's SpO2 has fallen from 96 percent to 88 percent and the client is now restless and using accessory muscles. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Document the finding and recheck in 30 minutes
Reposition the probe to a different finger
Raise the head of the bed and apply oxygen as prescribed
Call the provider to request an arterial blood gas
r: The client has objective signs of increased work of breathing along with the low reading, so this is real hypoxemia and breathing takes priority over further investigation. Repositioning the probe is the right first move only when the number is low but the client looks and sounds fine, which is not the case here.

q: A nurse completes rounds on a medical unit. Which of the following vital sign findings in adult clients require prompt notification of the provider? Select all that apply.
o: Apical pulse of 48 per minute in a client prescribed digoxin
SpO2 of 87 percent on room air with increased work of breathing
Systolic blood pressure of 86 mm Hg with cool, clammy skin
Oral temperature of 36.9 C
Respiratory rate of 8 per minute after IV morphine
r: Bradycardia below 60 in a client on digoxin, hypoxemia with respiratory effort, hypotension with poor perfusion, and opioid-related respiratory depression all demand immediate action. A temperature of 36.9 C is normal, and flagging it reflects reporting a number simply because it was measured rather than because it falls outside the expected range.

q: A nurse is delegating tasks to assistive personnel (AP) on a medical unit. Which of the following vital sign tasks are appropriate to delegate? Select all that apply.
o: Measuring routine vital signs on a stable client awaiting discharge
Reporting a measured blood pressure of 88/50 mm Hg to the nurse
Taking an axillary temperature on a stable client on contact precautions
Deciding whether a client's heart rate of 54 per minute means digoxin should be held
Teaching a client how to use a home blood pressure monitor
Assessing a client who becomes short of breath during vital signs
r: An AP may obtain and report vital signs on stable, predictable clients, since collecting the number is a standard task. Interpreting a value to make a medication decision, teaching, and assessing a client whose condition is changing all require nursing judgment and cannot be delegated even though the client contact looks similar.

q: An assistive personnel reports that a client's blood pressure is 158/94 mm Hg. The client just returned from physical therapy and reports pain rated 8 out of 10. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Notify the provider of the elevated reading
Address the client's pain and allow rest, then recheck the pressure
Withhold the client's next dose of antihypertensive medication
Document the reading as the client's new baseline
r: Pain, exertion, and anxiety all raise blood pressure, so the nurse treats the reversible cause and rechecks before treating the number as a true reading. Reporting or acting on a single reading taken under these conditions can lead to unnecessary medication changes based on data that does not reflect the client's baseline.

q: A nurse receives report on four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
o: A client with a temperature of 37.8 C who is receiving antibiotics
A client with a blood pressure of 138/86 mm Hg who reports a headache
A client with a respiratory rate of 30 per minute and an SpO2 of 88 percent
A client with a pulse of 58 per minute who exercises daily
r: Airway and breathing come first, and tachypnea with a saturation below 90 percent identifies the client whose oxygenation is failing right now. A resting pulse of 58 in a conditioned client is often normal, and a mildly elevated temperature on antibiotics is expected, so neither outranks active hypoxemia.

q: A nurse is teaching a client how to measure blood pressure at home. Which of the following client statements indicate an understanding of the teaching? Select all that apply.
o: I will sit quietly with my feet flat on the floor for about 5 minutes first
I will rest my arm on a table so the cuff is level with my heart
I will put the cuff on my bare upper arm rather than over my sleeve
I will take my reading right after my morning coffee and cigarette
I will keep my legs crossed so I stay comfortable during the reading
r: Resting quietly with feet flat, supporting the arm at heart level, and applying the cuff to a bare arm all remove the common sources of error. Caffeine and nicotine temporarily raise pressure and crossed legs raise systolic pressure, so both of those habits would make the home readings falsely high.

q: A nurse is choosing a site for a pulse oximeter probe on a client who has peripheral vascular disease and cool hands. Which site should the nurse select?
o: Earlobe
Index finger of the hand with the IV
Toe of the affected extremity
Finger with acrylic nails
r: When peripheral perfusion is poor, a more central site such as the earlobe, bridge of the nose, or forehead gives a more reliable signal. A toe on an extremity with vascular disease has the least reliable flow of all the choices, and artificial nails block light transmission just as polish does.

q: A nurse is preparing to examine a client's thorax. In which order should the nurse use the assessment techniques?
o: Inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation
Palpation, inspection, auscultation, percussion
Auscultation, inspection, palpation, percussion
Inspection, auscultation, palpation, percussion
r: The standard sequence for every body system except the abdomen is inspection, palpation, percussion, and auscultation, moving from least to most intrusive. The fourth option is the abdominal sequence, and applying it to the chest is the most common mix-up because the abdominal exception gets memorized without its boundary.

q: A nurse is performing an abdominal assessment. In which order should the nurse proceed?
o: Inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation
Auscultation, inspection, percussion, palpation
Inspection, auscultation, percussion, palpation
Palpation, percussion, auscultation, inspection
r: The abdomen is the one exception to the usual order: the nurse inspects, then auscultates, then percusses, and palpates last. Beginning with inspection is still correct, so the trap is finishing the sequence the usual way with palpation second instead of last.

q: A nursing student asks why the abdomen is auscultated before it is palpated. Which response by the nurse is correct?
o: Palpation is uncomfortable and the client may refuse the rest of the exam
Touching and pressing on the abdomen alters bowel motility and changes the sounds heard
Auscultation must always precede palpation in every body system
Palpation warms the skin and muffles the stethoscope
r: Pressing on the abdomen stimulates or suppresses peristalsis, so sounds heard afterward no longer reflect the client's true baseline. Client comfort is a real consideration, but it is not the reason for the reordering, and the sequence change applies only to the abdomen rather than to every system.

q: A client reports tenderness in the right lower quadrant. Which action should the nurse take during palpation?
o: Palpate the tender area first so the client does not anticipate it
Use deep palpation over the tender area to identify the exact source
Avoid palpating the abdomen entirely
Palpate the nontender quadrants first and the tender area last
r: Palpating tender areas last prevents guarding and pain from distorting the findings in the rest of the abdomen. Starting with the painful area or moving straight to deep palpation causes the client to tense the abdominal wall, which makes every subsequent finding unreliable.

q: A nurse is preparing to palpate a client's abdomen. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Warm the hands before touching the client
Ask the client to bend the knees slightly to relax the abdominal muscles
Begin with light palpation before deep palpation
Deeply palpate a pulsating mass to determine its size
Watch the client's face for signs of discomfort during palpation
r: Warm hands, a relaxed position, light palpation before deep, and watching the client's expression all produce accurate findings without causing harm. A pulsating midline mass may be an aneurysm, and deep palpation of it can cause rupture, so this is the one action that must never be taken.

q: A nurse percusses over a healthy adult client's lung fields. Which sound should the nurse expect?
o: Flatness
Resonance
Dullness
Tympany
r: Normal air-filled lung tissue produces resonance, a low-pitched hollow sound. Dullness in a lung field suggests fluid or consolidation such as pneumonia or a pleural effusion, which is why hearing it over the lungs is a finding to report rather than a normal variation.

q: A nurse is reviewing percussion tones with a nursing student. Which of the following pairings are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Resonance is heard over normal lung tissue
Dullness is heard over the liver
Tympany is heard over the intestines
Flatness is heard over muscle and bone
Hyperresonance is an expected finding over the lungs of a healthy young adult
r: Percussion tones move from flat over dense tissue, to dull over solid organs, to resonant over normal lung, to tympanic over air-filled hollow organs. Hyperresonance in an adult signals excess air trapping, as in emphysema or a pneumothorax, so calling it normal would mean missing a significant finding.

q: A nurse plans to auscultate a client's bowel sounds and normal breath sounds. Which part of the stethoscope should the nurse use?
o: The bell, held lightly against the skin
The bell, pressed firmly against the skin
The diaphragm, pressed firmly against the skin
Either side, as long as the tubing is longer than 45 cm
r: The diaphragm transmits high-pitched sounds such as breath sounds, bowel sounds, and normal heart sounds and is pressed firmly to seal against the skin. The bell is held lightly and is reserved for low-pitched sounds such as murmurs and bruits, and pressing the bell firmly turns it into a diaphragm and filters out the very sounds it was chosen for.

q: A nurse is beginning a head-to-toe assessment on a newly admitted client. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Auscultate the lungs posteriorly in all fields, comparing side to side
Palpate the pedal pulses
Assess the abdomen
Observe the client's general appearance and level of consciousness
r: The general survey, including appearance, behavior, and level of consciousness, begins the moment the nurse enters the room and frames everything that follows. Jumping to a specific system such as the lungs or feet skips the overview that tells the nurse how sick the client is and which system needs attention first.

q: A nurse auscultates fine, high-pitched popping sounds at the bases of both lungs at the end of inspiration in a client who has heart failure. How should the nurse document this finding?
o: Crackles
Wheezes
Vesicular breath sounds
Pleural friction rub
r: Crackles are discontinuous popping sounds produced when air moves through fluid in small airways and alveoli, a common finding when fluid backs up in heart failure. Wheezes are the tempting alternative but are continuous musical sounds caused by narrowed airways, as in asthma, rather than by fluid.

q: A nurse is auscultating lung sounds. Which of the following findings should the nurse report to the provider? Select all that apply.
o: Absent breath sounds over the right lower lobe
Coarse crackles that do not clear with coughing
A grating sound heard on both inspiration and expiration over the lateral chest
Soft, low-pitched breath sounds heard over the peripheral lung fields
Bronchovesicular sounds heard between the scapulae
r: Absent sounds suggest collapse, consolidation, or pneumothorax, crackles that persist after coughing suggest fluid rather than mobile secretions, and a grating rub suggests inflamed pleura. Vesicular sounds in the periphery and bronchovesicular sounds between the scapulae are normal for those locations, and reporting them reflects not matching the sound to where it was heard.

q: A nurse auscultates an extra low-pitched sound just after S2 in a client who has fluid volume excess. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
o: It is a normal splitting of S2 heard during inspiration
It is a pericardial friction rub
It is an S3, which can indicate fluid overload or heart failure
It is a murmur caused by a narrowed valve
r: An S3 follows S2 and reflects rapid ventricular filling against a volume-overloaded or failing ventricle, so in an adult with fluid excess it is a significant finding. A murmur is the tempting choice but is a swishing sound from turbulent flow across a valve rather than a distinct extra beat, and the two are distinguished by quality and timing.

q: A nurse is auscultating the mitral area to evaluate S1. Where should the nurse place the stethoscope?
o: Second intercostal space at the right sternal border
Second intercostal space at the left sternal border
Fourth intercostal space at the left lower sternal border
Fifth intercostal space at the left midclavicular line
r: The mitral or apical area lies at the fifth intercostal space at the left midclavicular line, where S1 is loudest and where the apical pulse is counted. The second intercostal space sites are the aortic and pulmonic areas, where S2 is loudest, which is why the landmark chosen changes which sound is best heard.

q: A nurse listens over a client's right lower quadrant and hears no bowel sounds after 30 seconds. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Listen in each quadrant for up to 5 minutes before documenting absent bowel sounds
Document that bowel sounds are absent and notify the provider immediately
Palpate the abdomen deeply to stimulate peristalsis, then listen again
Percuss the abdomen and record the findings instead
r: Bowel sounds are irregular, so absence can only be documented after listening for up to 5 minutes in a quadrant. Palpating to stimulate sounds is doubly wrong here because it changes the very motility being assessed and produces a finding that is not the client's baseline.

q: A nurse is assessing a client 6 hours after abdominal surgery and hears hypoactive bowel sounds in all four quadrants. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
o: It is an unexpected finding that requires immediate provider notification
It is an expected finding related to anesthesia and surgical handling of the bowel
It indicates the client is ready to begin a regular diet
It confirms a bowel obstruction has developed
r: Anesthesia and manipulation of the intestines temporarily slow peristalsis, so hypoactive sounds in the early postoperative period are expected and are the reason bowel sounds are checked before advancing a diet. Sounds that remain absent for a prolonged period with distention and vomiting would suggest paralytic ileus, but a single hypoactive assessment this soon after surgery does not.

q: A nurse assesses a client who awakens only with vigorous shaking, gives brief mumbled responses, and immediately falls back asleep. How should the nurse document this level of consciousness?
o: Alert
Lethargic
Stuporous
Comatose
r: Stupor describes a client who requires vigorous or painful stimulation to arouse and returns immediately to an unresponsive state. A lethargic client is drowsy but awakens easily to voice and can maintain a conversation, which is the distinction being tested; a comatose client does not arouse at all.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who had a head injury. Which finding should the nurse recognize as the earliest indication of increasing intracranial pressure?
o: A widening pulse pressure
Vomiting without nausea
A fixed and dilated pupil
A change in level of consciousness
r: A change in level of consciousness, such as new restlessness, confusion, or increasing drowsiness, is the earliest and most sensitive indicator of rising intracranial pressure. Widening pulse pressure and a fixed dilated pupil are real signs, but they are late findings, and waiting for them means the deterioration was missed hours earlier.

q: A nurse asks a client their name, where they are, the current month, and what brought them to the hospital. Which aspect of the assessment is the nurse performing?
o: Orientation to person, place, time, and situation
Cranial nerve function, specifically the nerves controlling eye movement
Cerebellar function
Sensory perception
r: These four questions establish orientation, which is documented as the client being oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Cranial nerve testing evaluates specific functions such as eye movement and facial sensation, and confusing the two leads to documenting a neurologic exam that was never performed.

q: A nurse assessing a client 2 hours after a fall notes that the left pupil is 6 mm and does not react to light while the right pupil is 3 mm and brisk. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Notify the provider immediately
Recheck the pupils in 4 hours
Document the finding as an expected variation
Dim the lights and repeat the assessment in the morning
r: A newly unequal, dilated, nonreactive pupil suggests pressure on the oculomotor nerve from rising intracranial pressure and requires immediate notification. Delaying the recheck is the dangerous choice, because this change can progress to herniation within a short time, and a small number of people do have naturally unequal pupils but that variation is longstanding and both pupils still react.

q: A nurse finds that a client receiving IV opioid analgesia has bilateral pinpoint pupils and a respiratory rate of 8 per minute. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Document the pupil size and reaction and continue routine monitoring on the current schedule
Stimulate the client and support the airway while preparing to give naloxone as prescribed
Increase the IV fluid rate
Reassess the pupils in 15 minutes
r: Constricted pupils with a depressed respiratory rate point to opioid toxicity, and breathing takes priority, so the nurse arouses the client, supports ventilation, and anticipates naloxone. Continued monitoring alone is the trap, because respiratory depression from opioids worsens while the nurse waits.

q: A nurse is documenting the results of a pupillary assessment. Which of the following components should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Size of each pupil in millimeters
Equality of the two pupils
Speed of the reaction to light
Presence of accommodation
The client's visual acuity measured with a Snellen chart
r: A pupil assessment documents size, equality, reactivity to light, and accommodation, the elements summarized as PERRLA. Visual acuity is a separate vision screening and is not part of pupillary assessment, so including it substitutes a different test for the one being documented.

q: A nurse presses the nail bed of a client's finger and observes that color returns after 5 seconds. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
o: Normal capillary refill
A sign of adequate arterial circulation to the fingers and hand
Delayed capillary refill suggesting impaired perfusion
An expected finding in all older adults
r: Color should return within about 2 to 3 seconds, so a 5-second refill indicates reduced peripheral perfusion. Cool environments and aging can slow refill somewhat, but treating a markedly delayed refill as simply age-related risks missing shock or an arterial problem in the limb.

q: A nurse is assessing circulation in the leg of a client who has a newly applied cast. Which of the following findings indicate impaired peripheral perfusion? Select all that apply.
o: Toes that are cool and pale compared with the other foot
Capillary refill of 6 seconds in the toes
A dorsalis pedis pulse that is weaker than on the unaffected side
Numbness and tingling in the toes
Toes that are warm with brisk capillary refill
r: Coolness, pallor, delayed refill, a diminished distal pulse, and paresthesia are the classic signs that blood flow past the cast is compromised and must be reported before tissue damage occurs. Warm toes with brisk refill describe intact circulation and are the comparison finding the nurse is hoping to see.

q: A nurse presses over a client's tibia and notes an indentation of about 6 mm that takes 30 seconds to disappear. How should the nurse document this finding?
o: 1 plus pitting edema
2 plus pitting edema
Nonpitting edema
3 plus pitting edema
r: Pitting edema is graded from 1 plus, a barely detectable 2 mm indentation that rebounds immediately, up to 4 plus, a deep 8 mm indentation lasting several minutes; a 6 mm pit that lingers is 3 plus. Documenting this as 1 plus or 2 plus is the common error and understates a finding that signals significant fluid retention.

q: A nurse is assessing a client who has heart failure for edema. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Press over a bony prominence such as the tibia for several seconds
Check the sacrum in a client who has been on bed rest
Compare one extremity with the other
Weigh the client daily at the same time on the same scale
Assess only the ankles, since edema is always dependent
r: Edema is assessed by pressing over bone, checking dependent areas including the sacrum in a client who is lying down, comparing sides, and tracking daily weights, which detect fluid retention before edema is visible. Limiting the assessment to the ankles misses sacral and periorbital edema entirely, which is exactly what happens in a client who stays in bed.

q: A nurse is completing a general survey on a client entering the clinic. Which of the following observations belong in the general survey? Select all that apply.
o: Posture and gait
Hygiene and grooming
Speech pattern and affect
Signs of acute distress such as labored breathing
The results of the client's most recent chest x-ray
r: The general survey is what the nurse observes overall, including posture, gait, hygiene, body build, speech, affect, and any obvious distress. Diagnostic test results are part of the chart review rather than direct observation, and treating them as survey data means documenting something the nurse did not actually see.

q: A nurse walks into the room and finds a client sitting upright, leaning forward on the overbed table, and speaking in three-word phrases. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Assess the client's respiratory status and oxygen saturation
Ask the client to lie flat for the assessment
Continue with the scheduled head-to-toe assessment in the usual order
Document that the client prefers to sit upright
r: The tripod position and short phrases are visible signs of respiratory distress, so the general survey redirects the nurse straight to breathing rather than to a routine sequence. Asking the client to lie flat would worsen the work of breathing, which is why position changes for convenience are unsafe when the survey shows distress.

q: A nurse is using inspection during a physical assessment. Which of the following actions support accurate inspection? Select all that apply.
o: Provide adequate lighting
Expose only the body part being examined and keep the client draped
Compare the finding with the same area on the opposite side
Look and observe before touching the client
Rely on the client's report rather than direct observation when the client is reliable
r: Good lighting, appropriate exposure with draping, side-to-side comparison, and observing before touching are what make inspection produce usable objective data. Substituting the client's report for observation converts objective data into subjective data, and the two are documented differently for a reason.

q: A nurse is assessing a client's carotid arteries. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Palpate both carotid arteries at the same time to compare them
Palpate one carotid artery at a time
Percuss over the carotid artery before auscultating
Press firmly over the carotid sinus to check for a response
r: Only one carotid is palpated at a time, because compressing both can reduce blood flow to the brain and stimulating the carotid sinus can cause a sharp drop in heart rate. Comparing the two sides simultaneously seems efficient, but it is exactly the action that creates the risk.

q: A nurse is delegating care for a stable client to assistive personnel (AP). Which of the following tasks are appropriate to delegate? Select all that apply.
o: Measuring the client's height and weight
Reporting that the client's foot feels cool to touch
Assisting the client to ambulate to the bathroom
Auscultating the client's bowel sounds before the diet is advanced
Determining whether the client's edema has worsened since yesterday
r: Obtaining measurements, reporting an observation, and assisting a stable client with ambulation are standard, predictable tasks within the AP role. Auscultating bowel sounds and judging whether a finding has changed are assessment and evaluation, which stay with the nurse no matter how experienced the AP is.

q: A nurse is teaching a community group about levels of prevention. Which activity should the nurse describe as primary prevention?
o: Screening adults over age 45 for colorectal cancer
Leading a car seat installation class for expectant parents
Supervising a cardiac rehabilitation exercise session
Teaching a client who has a spinal cord injury to shift weight hourly
r: Primary prevention happens before any disease or injury occurs and protects healthy people, so car seat education fits. Colorectal screening is tempting, but screening finds disease that is already present without symptoms, which makes it secondary prevention.

q: A nurse at a health department is planning heart disease programs. Which activity should the nurse include as primary prevention?
o: Offering cholesterol screening at a community center
Referring clients who have had a myocardial infarction to cardiac rehabilitation
Teaching a class on heart-healthy eating and daily physical activity to healthy adults
Checking blood pressure weekly for clients who already have hypertension
r: Nutrition and activity teaching for people who do not yet have heart disease lowers their risk before disease develops, which is primary prevention. Cholesterol screening looks like prevention, but it detects an existing problem early, so it belongs to secondary prevention.

q: Which nursing action is an example of secondary prevention?
o: Administering influenza vaccine at a workplace clinic for employees
Teaching helmet safety to members of a community bicycle club
Arranging outpatient physical therapy for a client after a stroke
Checking blood pressure at a screening event for adults with no symptoms
r: Secondary prevention finds a condition early in people who have no symptoms yet, which is exactly what a blood pressure screening does. Physical therapy after a stroke is tertiary, because the disease is already established and the goal is limiting disability.

q: Which client situation should the nurse identify as tertiary prevention?
o: A healthy adult receives the herpes zoster vaccine at a clinic
A client who has emphysema attends pulmonary rehabilitation
A client who has no symptoms has a screening colonoscopy
A middle adult attends a class on lowering dietary sodium
r: Tertiary prevention begins after illness or injury is established and aims to limit disability and restore function, which describes pulmonary rehabilitation. The screening colonoscopy is tempting, but the client has no known disease, so that is secondary prevention.

q: A nurse is identifying primary prevention activities for a community project. Which of the following activities are primary prevention? Select all that apply.
o: Providing immunizations at a school-based clinic
Performing screening mammography on clients who have no symptoms
Teaching families to install and test smoke detectors
Supervising range-of-motion exercises after a hip replacement
Leading a prenatal nutrition class for pregnant clients
Fitting a hearing aid for a client who has diagnosed hearing loss
r: Immunization, injury prevention teaching, and prenatal nutrition education all act before disease or injury occurs, so they are primary prevention. Mammography detects existing disease early and is secondary, while rehabilitation exercises and hearing aid fitting limit disability after a condition exists, which is tertiary.

q: Which of the following are examples of secondary prevention? Select all that apply.
o: Teaching adolescents about the risks of vaping
Blood glucose screening at a community health fair
Contact tracing after a client is diagnosed with tuberculosis
Vision screening before a child enters kindergarten
Home modification to prevent pressure injuries after a spinal cord injury
r: Screening and case finding identify disease early in people who feel well, so glucose screening, contact tracing, and prekindergarten vision screening are secondary prevention. Vaping education comes before disease and is primary, while pressure injury prevention after a spinal cord injury limits complications of an existing condition and is tertiary.

q: Which of the following nursing activities are examples of tertiary prevention? Select all that apply.
o: Scheduling a routine Papanicolaou test for a 30-year-old client
Referring a client who has a new colostomy to a support group
Administering hepatitis B vaccine to a newborn
Teaching pressure injury prevention to a client who has a spinal cord injury
Arranging speech therapy for a client after a traumatic brain injury
Offering a bone density scan to a client who has no symptoms
r: Tertiary prevention supports optimal functioning and prevents long-term consequences after illness or injury, so support group referral, pressure injury teaching, and speech therapy all qualify. The Pap test and the bone density scan are screenings in clients without symptoms, which makes them secondary, and the newborn vaccine is primary.

q: A school nurse performs annual scoliosis screening on students who have no complaints. How should the nurse classify this activity?
o: Primary prevention, because the students are healthy at the time of the screening
Tertiary prevention, because early treatment limits disability later in the student's life
Primary prevention, because the nurse also teaches the students about posture and back care
Secondary prevention, because it detects a spinal curve in students who have no symptoms
r: Screening an asymptomatic population for an existing condition is secondary prevention, regardless of how healthy the group appears. The tertiary option is tempting because treatment does reduce disability later, but tertiary prevention starts only after the condition is diagnosed.

q: A nurse is reviewing risk factors for coronary artery disease with a client. Which risk factor should the nurse identify as modifiable?
o: Smoking one pack of cigarettes daily
Having a father who had a myocardial infarction at age 45
Being 68 years of age
Assigned sex at birth
r: Modifiable risk factors are behaviors the client can change, and tobacco use is the strongest modifiable cardiac risk factor. Family history feels changeable because the nurse discusses it during counseling, but genetics cannot be altered, so it is nonmodifiable.

q: A nurse is collecting data about an adult client's risk for chronic disease. Which of the following should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Family history of diabetes mellitus and cardiovascular disease
Tobacco, alcohol, and other substance use
The client's height at age 18
Usual eating patterns and level of physical activity
Occupational and environmental exposures
r: Risk assessment combines nonmodifiable factors such as family history with modifiable ones such as substance use, diet, activity, and workplace exposures. Height at age 18 is historical data that does not change the client's current risk profile or the counseling plan.

q: A 50-year-old client who has no increased risk for colorectal cancer asks about screening. Which client statement indicates understanding?
o: I can have a colonoscopy every 10 years, or a stool test for hidden blood every year
I will need to have a colonoscopy done every single year from now until I turn 75
I do not need any kind of screening for colon cancer until I am at least 60 years old
A yearly chest x-ray will show my provider whether I have developed colon cancer
r: For average-risk adults, acceptable options include colonoscopy about every 10 years, flexible sigmoidoscopy about every 5 years, or annual high-sensitivity stool testing for occult blood, generally from age 45 to 75. Yearly colonoscopy is tempting because more often sounds safer, but that interval is reserved for clients at increased risk.

q: A 42-year-old female client with no risk factors asks how often she should have a mammogram. Which response by the nurse is correct?
o: Every 2 years
Every 6 months
Only if you feel a lump in your breast
Once every 10 years
r: Mammography every 2 years is recommended for clients ages 40 to 74 who have no added risk. Waiting for a lump defeats the purpose of screening, which is to find disease before any symptom appears.

q: A 32-year-old female client had a normal Papanicolaou test performed together with human papillomavirus testing. Which information should the nurse provide about the next screening?
o: You should repeat the Papanicolaou test again in about 6 months
Screening can be repeated in 5 years because HPV testing was done with the Pap test
No further cervical screening is needed for you once you have passed age 30
The Papanicolaou test must be repeated every single year until you reach age 65
r: From ages 21 to 65 the Pap test is generally done every 3 years, and starting at age 30 the interval can extend to 5 years when HPV co-testing is performed and results are normal. The yearly option is tempting because that was the older practice, but current guidelines lengthened the interval.

q: A nurse is reviewing screenings that apply to a specific sex rather than to all adults. Which of the following are sex-specific screenings? Select all that apply.
o: Papanicolaou test
Body mass index measurement
Mammography
Blood pressure measurement
Prostate-specific antigen test
r: Cervical cytology, mammography, and prostate-specific antigen testing target organs present in one sex. Blood pressure and body mass index are measured at routine visits for every adult regardless of sex.

q: A healthy 24-year-old client asks when cholesterol screening should start. Which response by the nurse is correct?
o: At age 35, and then yearly
At age 50, and then every 10 years
At age 20, at least every 5 years
At age 65, and then every 2 years
r: Blood cholesterol screening begins at about age 20 and is repeated a minimum of every 5 years for adults without added risk. Waiting until midlife is tempting because heart disease is more common then, but early results establish a baseline and identify risk that can be treated for decades.

q: A 38-year-old client who has obesity and no symptoms asks about screening for diabetes mellitus. Which response by the nurse is appropriate?
o: Screening is not recommended until you turn 50
You should be screened now, and about every 3 years if the results are normal
You only need screening if you develop increased thirst and urination
Your blood glucose should be checked every month
r: Blood glucose screening is recommended starting at about age 35 to 40 for clients who are overweight or have obesity, with repeat testing roughly every 3 years when results are normal. Waiting for symptoms is tempting but misses years of untreated hyperglycemia, which is the point of screening.

q: A nurse is reviewing routine health maintenance with a 41-year-old client. Which client statement indicates understanding of the teaching?
o: I will schedule a physical examination every year now that I am past 40
I only need an eye examination if my vision starts to change
A physical examination every 5 years is enough at my age
I should see a dentist only when a tooth hurts
r: Routine physical examinations shift from about every other year in the 20s and 30s to yearly after age 40, and a complete eye examination is recommended at age 40. The eye statement is tempting because vision often feels normal, but conditions such as glaucoma progress silently, and dental assessment is recommended at least yearly regardless of pain.

q: A 70-year-old client asks how often hearing should be checked. Which response by the nurse is correct?
o: Every month
Only after you notice that you cannot hear
Every 1 to 3 years
About every 10 years
r: Hearing screening is offered about every 1 to 3 years for adults 65 and older, and more often if loss is noted. Waiting until the client notices a problem delays detection, because age-related loss develops gradually and is often first noticed by family.

q: A nurse is planning a health promotion session for a group of middle adults. Which of the following should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Bone density scanning to screen for osteoporosis
Annual tuberculosis skin testing for everyone in the group
Screening for depression and anxiety
Eye examination for glaucoma every 2 to 3 years
Blood pressure measurement at every health care visit
Human papillomavirus vaccine series for all attendees
r: Middle adults benefit from bone density scanning, mental health screening, periodic eye examinations, and blood pressure checks at each visit. Tuberculosis testing is reserved for people with known exposure or added risk rather than the general population, so routine annual testing is not indicated.

q: During which period should the nurse expect routine screening for idiopathic scoliosis to be emphasized?
o: Middle adulthood, when age-related bone loss usually begins
Infancy, before the child begins to sit up and walk
Toddlerhood, during the period of rapid weight gain
School age and adolescence, before and during growth spurts
r: Lateral spinal curvature typically appears and progresses during the rapid growth of the school-age and adolescent years, so screening is timed around growth spurts. Middle adulthood is tempting because bone changes occur then, but osteoporosis screening, not scoliosis screening, is the concern at that age.

q: A nurse is reviewing the immunization schedule with parents of a newborn. Which of the following vaccines are recommended during the first 12 months of life? Select all that apply.
o: Hepatitis B
Human papillomavirus
Rotavirus
Diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis (DTaP)
Herpes zoster
Haemophilus influenzae type b
r: Hepatitis B starts at birth, and rotavirus, DTaP, and Hib begin at 2 months along with inactivated poliovirus and pneumococcal vaccine. HPV is given around ages 11 to 12 and herpes zoster is an adult vaccine, so neither belongs in infancy.

q: A nurse is reviewing immunizations with the guardian of an 11-year-old child. Which vaccines should the nurse expect to be recommended at this age?
o: Rotavirus and the hepatitis B series
Human papillomavirus and meningococcal ACWY
Herpes zoster and pneumococcal vaccine
The first dose of measles, mumps, and rubella
r: HPV vaccine and the first meningococcal ACWY dose are recommended at ages 11 to 12, with a second meningococcal dose at 16. Rotavirus and the first MMR dose belong to infancy and early childhood, and zoster and pneumococcal vaccines are for older adults or high-risk clients.

q: A nurse is planning a presentation for adults over 65 years of age. Which of the following immunizations should the nurse include as routinely recommended? Select all that apply.
o: Human papillomavirus vaccine
Pneumococcal vaccine
Annual seasonal influenza vaccine
Herpes zoster vaccine
Tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis booster
Rotavirus vaccine
r: Pneumococcal, annual influenza, herpes zoster, and tetanus and diphtheria with pertussis are routine for healthy older adults. HPV vaccine is aimed at adolescents and young adults, and rotavirus is given only to infants.

q: A nurse is teaching a 24-year-old client about immunizations. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?
o: I need a tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis booster even as an adult
I completed my childhood shots, so I do not need any more vaccines
I should get an influenza vaccine every year
I should ask my provider whether I still need the HPV series
r: Childhood immunization does not end the need for vaccines, because adults need annual influenza vaccine, tetanus and diphtheria boosters, and sometimes catch-up doses. The HPV statement sounds uncertain but is correct, since young adults may still complete that series.

q: A client asks the nurse what Healthy People 2030 is. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
o: It is a federal insurance program for families who have a low income
It is the national agency that accredits hospitals and clinics
It is the organization that issues nursing licenses in each state
It is a set of national health objectives that is updated about every 10 years
r: Healthy People sets measurable national health objectives that are revised roughly every decade and carried out through collaboration among governments, organizations, businesses, and individuals. It does not pay for care, accredit facilities, or license nurses.

q: Which of the following statements about the Healthy People initiative are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: The objectives can be measured at local, state, and national levels
The objectives apply only to acute care hospitals
The objectives are revised about every 10 years
Implementation depends on collaboration among governments, organizations, businesses, and individuals
One aim is identifying health disparities that need further research and data collection
r: The initiative sets measurable goals at every level of government, is updated each decade, relies on broad collaboration, and targets health disparities through research and data. Limiting it to hospitals misses the point, since most objectives address community and population health.

q: A client who smokes one pack of cigarettes daily tells the nurse he has no interest in quitting. Which response by the nurse is best?
o: If you do not quit now, you will end up with lung cancer
I will get you the quit line number so you can call today
What would need to change for you to consider quitting?
Most people are able to quit on their own if they really want to
r: An open-ended question explores the client's own reasons and keeps the door open without arguing, which is what supports a client who is not yet ready to change. Handing over a quit line number is tempting because it is concrete help, but offering a plan before the client is ready usually ends the conversation.

q: A client is starting a smoking cessation plan. Which client statement indicates understanding of the teaching?
o: Switching to a pipe instead of cigarettes will protect my lungs
I will pick a quit date and clear the cigarettes, lighters, and ashtrays out of my house
I will keep one pack on hand in case I have a stressful day
I should only use nicotine replacement after I have been smoke free for 6 months
r: Setting a quit date and removing smoking cues from the environment are core steps of an effective cessation plan. Keeping a pack for stressful days is tempting because it feels like a safety net, but easy access is one of the strongest predictors of relapse.

q: A healthy adult client asks the nurse how much exercise is recommended each week. Which response is correct?
o: At least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity each week, plus strengthening twice
Thirty minutes of vigorous aerobic activity one time each week is enough
Ten minutes of gentle stretching each day is enough for most healthy adults
Sixty minutes of aerobic activity every single day with no rest days at all
r: The general adult recommendation is about 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity weekly with muscle strengthening twice a week, and it can be divided into sessions that fit the client's schedule. Stretching alone is tempting because it feels like exercise, but it does not provide the cardiovascular or metabolic benefit of aerobic activity.

q: An older adult client who lives alone has lost weight over the past 6 months and reports constipation. Which instruction should the nurse include?
o: Limit your fluid intake so you do not have accidents on the way to the bathroom
Choose foods high in refined sugar to add extra calories quickly
Skip breakfast so you will have more appetite at lunch
Increase fluids and fiber, and eat with other people when you can
r: More fluid and fiber address constipation, and eating with others improves intake because isolation at mealtime is a common cause of poor nutrition in older adults. Restricting fluids to control incontinence is a frequent client habit, but it worsens both constipation and dehydration risk.

q: A nurse is reviewing a client's record. Which finding should the nurse identify as a social determinant of health?
o: The client's hemoglobin A1c result today is 8.2 percent
The client lives where there is no grocery store and has no transportation
The client has a strong family history of hypertension and stroke
The client's blood pressure at this visit is 148 over 92
r: Social determinants are conditions in the environment where people live and work, such as food access, transportation, housing, income, and education. Family history influences risk as well, but it is a biologic factor rather than a social condition.

q: A client who has diabetes mellitus reports being unable to afford insulin and having no reliable transportation to appointments. Which of the following nursing actions address social determinants of health? Select all that apply.
o: Refer the client to a social worker for medication assistance programs
Document that the client is noncompliant with the treatment plan
Provide a list of clinics that are on public transportation routes
Ask about the client's access to food when planning the meal pattern
Tell the client that insulin must come before other household expenses
Request a home health referral for follow-up between visits
r: Connecting the client with financial assistance, reachable clinics, realistic food planning, and home follow-up removes the actual barriers to care. Labeling the client noncompliant and instructing them to prioritize insulin over rent or food blames the client for conditions they do not control and does not change the outcome.

q: An ostomy nurse is providing preoperative education to a client scheduled for a sigmoid colostomy. Which client statement indicates readiness to learn?
o: I would rather not look at anything to do with the stoma right now
Can you show me how the pouch is changed before my surgery?
My daughter will take care of all of this for me when I get home
I am too worn out to talk about any of this today
r: Asking to see the skill signals motivation and willingness to participate, which are the markers of readiness to learn. Naming a caregiver sounds cooperative, but it shifts responsibility away from the client and does not show that the client is ready to engage.

q: A nurse is preparing to teach a newly diagnosed client about self-administration of insulin. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Gather printed materials and a demonstration kit
Set a mutual goal for the teaching session
Determine what the client already knows and wants to learn
Schedule a time for the client's return demonstration
r: Assessment precedes planning and implementation in teaching just as it does in any nursing process step, so the nurse first identifies existing knowledge, learning style, and barriers. Setting a mutual goal is essential, but goals cannot be set realistically until the nurse knows the client's starting point.

q: A nurse is identifying barriers to learning for a hospitalized client. Which of the following are barriers? Select all that apply.
o: Uncontrolled incisional pain
Fear and anxiety about the new diagnosis
Prior experience caring for a relative who had the same condition
Frequent interruptions and noise on the unit
The client's belief that the information will help them
Fatigue after a night with almost no sleep
r: Pain, fear, environmental distraction, and fatigue all reduce attention and retention, so the nurse addresses them before teaching. Prior caregiving experience and perceived benefit are enhancers, because adults learn by building on what they already know and are motivated when they see value.

q: Which of the following factors enhance client learning? Select all that apply.
o: The client perceives a personal benefit from the information
The nurse teaches during shift change so more staff are nearby
The client actively participates in the session
The nurse uses precise nursing terminology such as administer and monitor
Materials match the client's age and education level
r: Perceived benefit, active participation, and age- and education-appropriate materials all improve learning. Nursing jargon is tempting because it sounds accurate, but unfamiliar terms create a comprehension barrier, and shift change adds noise and interruptions.

q: A client who rates incisional pain as 8 on a 0 to 10 scale is scheduled for teaching about dressing changes. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Teach the client quickly now, before the pain becomes any worse
Give the prescribed analgesic and teach once the client is comfortable
Ask a family member to learn the dressing change procedure instead
Document that the client refused the scheduled teaching session
r: Physical discomfort blocks concentration and retention, so relieving pain first makes the session effective rather than wasted. Teaching a family member is tempting and may be appropriate later, but it does not meet the client's own learning need and skips the fixable barrier.

q: Which approach by the nurse best reflects the principles of adult learning?
o: Set goals together with the client and connect new content to past experiences
Direct the teaching to the family, since adults absorb information passively
Present all the information in one long session to save the client time
Use a standard handout without asking what the client already knows
r: Adults identify what they need to learn, build on prior experience, and engage more when goals are mutual, so collaborative goal setting is the strongest approach. A single long session is tempting because it seems efficient, but it exceeds attention span and does not allow for feedback or practice.

q: Which of the following statements about adult learners are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Adults can often identify what they need to learn
Adults learn best when the nurse sets the goals for them
Adults build new learning on prior information and life experience
Adults rarely benefit from written materials
Concerns such as employment or finances can interfere with readiness to learn
r: Adult learners bring experience, help define their own needs, and are distracted by unresolved life concerns that the nurse may need to help address first. Nurse-set goals reduce engagement, and written materials remain useful when they are written at an appropriate reading level.

q: A nurse is writing learning objectives for a client who has diabetes mellitus. Which objective is written correctly?
o: The client will understand diabetes mellitus and its complications
The nurse will teach the client about daily foot care before discharge
The client will know the reasons that insulin therapy is necessary
The client will draw up the correct insulin dose without cues before discharge
r: A usable objective is client centered, measurable, and time limited, so an observable action such as drawing up the correct dose can actually be evaluated. Understand and know are tempting because they describe the real goal, but the nurse cannot measure them directly, and an objective describing what the nurse will do measures the nurse, not the learner.

q: A client newly diagnosed with heart failure has many learning needs and will be discharged tomorrow. Which content should the nurse teach first?
o: Recipes that fit a long-term low sodium eating pattern
How to take the new medications and which symptoms to report
The pathophysiology of how heart failure develops
Local support groups the client could join
r: With limited time, survival information comes first, meaning medications and the warning signs that require a call to the provider. Sodium recipes matter for long-term control but can be reinforced at follow-up, and disease pathophysiology does not change what the client must do tonight.

q: A client lists the signs of hypoglycemia and states when to call the provider. Which domain of learning does this demonstrate?
o: Cognitive
Affective
Psychomotor
Kinesthetic
r: Recalling information and applying it to decide when to act are intellectual behaviors, which define the cognitive domain. Psychomotor is tempting because managing diabetes involves skills, but this client is thinking and verbalizing rather than performing a task.

q: Which teaching strategy best supports learning in the affective domain?
o: A step-by-step demonstration of proper insulin injection technique
A written quiz about counting carbohydrates in common foods
