A discussion group in which clients share their feelings about the diagnosis
A lecture explaining how insulin works in the body to lower glucose
r: The affective domain involves feelings, beliefs, and values, so discussion and shared reflection are the methods that reach it. A lecture delivers facts efficiently, which serves the cognitive domain but does little to change how a client feels about living with the illness.

q: A nurse is teaching a client to change a wound dressing at home. Which teaching method is most appropriate?
o: Give the client a pamphlet with step-by-step photographs of each step
Explain each step of the dressing change during morning rounds
Show a video of the procedure and then answer the client's questions
Demonstrate the dressing change and have the client return the demonstration
r: Psychomotor skills require guided practice, so demonstration followed by return demonstration both teaches and evaluates the skill. Video and printed photographs are useful supports, but watching never confirms that the client's hands can do the task safely.

q: Which of the following strategies are appropriate when the learning need is in the psychomotor domain? Select all that apply.
o: Guided practice with the actual equipment
A group discussion about personal values
Having the client perform a return demonstration
A written test of definitions
Breaking the skill into simple steps that build toward the whole task
r: Skill learning depends on perception, guided response, and practice, so hands-on work, return demonstration, and simple-to-complex sequencing are the right tools. A written test measures cognitive recall, and values discussion belongs to the affective domain.

q: At approximately what reading level should the nurse prepare written materials for clients?
o: Fifth to sixth grade
Eighth to ninth grade
Twelfth grade
Whatever level the nurse finds clearest
r: Written and spoken client materials should be at or below a fifth- to sixth-grade reading level so that clients across a wide range of literacy can use them. Writing at a high school level is tempting because most adults finished high school, but health literacy is usually several grades below general reading ability, especially under stress.

q: A nurse is developing a printed instruction sheet for clients. Which of the following should the nurse do? Select all that apply.
o: Write in the second person, such as your leg rather than the leg
Print the key points in all capital letters for emphasis
Use active voice, such as take the medication with food
Avoid terms such as administer, monitor, and implement
Use a small type size so the information fits on one page
Leave white space and include simple pictures
r: Second person, active voice, everyday words, generous white space, and simple images all make instructions easier to follow. All capital letters and small crowded type are tempting because they seem emphatic and efficient, but both reduce readability, especially for clients with low literacy or poor vision.

q: A nurse learns that a client reads at about a third-grade level. Which teaching approach is most appropriate?
o: Provide a detailed booklet for the client to study at home later
Ask the client to read the instructions out loud to prove understanding
Use simple words and pictures, then ask the client to teach the steps back
Ask a family member to explain all of the information to the client later
r: Plain spoken language, visual aids, and teach-back allow a client with low literacy to learn and lets the nurse verify comprehension without relying on reading. Asking the client to read aloud is embarrassing and tests reading rather than understanding, which usually ends honest participation.

q: A client who speaks only Haitian Creole needs teaching about a new medication. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Request a trained medical interpreter
Ask the client's adult son to interpret for the session
Ask a bilingual employee from another department to help
Use short English sentences with gestures and pictures
r: A trained medical interpreter has the vocabulary and neutrality needed for accurate health teaching and protects confidentiality. Using a family member is tempting because he is present and willing, but relatives filter information, may lack medical vocabulary, and can create privacy problems.

q: A nurse is teaching a client through a medical interpreter. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Speak directly to the client rather than to the interpreter
Ask the interpreter to summarize rather than translate everything
Use short sentences and pause frequently
Use medical terminology so the interpreter can be exact
Allow extra time for the teaching session
r: Addressing the client, speaking in short segments, and allowing extra time keep the client at the center of the interaction and support accuracy. Asking for a summary lets someone else decide what matters, and jargon increases the chance of mistranslation rather than reducing it.

q: Which method best evaluates whether a client understood teaching about a new oral medication?
o: Ask the client whether they have any questions about the medication
Ask the client to explain in their own words when and how to take it
Give the client a printed handout about the drug to review at home
Have the client sign the medication teaching record before discharge
r: Teach-back requires the client to state the information back, which reveals gaps that a yes or no question hides. Asking whether the client has questions is tempting because it sounds inviting, but clients frequently say no even when they understood very little.

q: A nurse set an objective that a client would ambulate safely with crutches. Which finding indicates the objective was met?
o: The client states that the crutches feel comfortable
The client names three safety rules for crutch use
The family reports the client practiced with the crutches last night
The client walks the length of the hallway using the correct gait without cues
r: A psychomotor objective is evaluated by observing the client perform the skill correctly and independently. Naming safety rules demonstrates cognitive learning only, and a client can recite the rules perfectly while still walking unsafely.

q: A nurse is preparing discharge teaching for a client going home after surgery. Which of the following must the teaching include? Select all that apply.
o: Names, doses, and timing of the discharge medications
A copy of the nurse's shift documentation
Signs and symptoms that require a call to the provider
Date, time, and location of follow-up appointments
The facility billing codes for the hospital stay
Activity restrictions, wound care, and diet instructions
r: Discharge teaching must cover the medication plan, warning signs and who to call, follow-up appointments, and activity, wound, and diet instructions, because these determine whether the client stays safe at home. Shift notes and billing codes are records, not instructions, and do not help the client manage recovery.

q: When should the nurse begin discharge teaching for a hospitalized client?
o: On the morning of discharge
As soon as the provider writes the discharge order
At the time of admission
At the first follow-up appointment
r: Discharge planning and teaching start at admission so content can be delivered in small pieces, reinforced, and evaluated before the client leaves. Waiting for the discharge order is common practice but leaves no time for practice, questions, or return demonstration.

q: A nurse is preparing to teach a client about wound care before discharge. Which task may the nurse delegate to assistive personnel?
o: Explaining the schedule for the new anticoagulant
Evaluating whether the client performs the dressing change correctly
Determining the client's readiness to learn
Gathering the printed materials and supplies for the teaching session
r: Assistive personnel may perform standard supportive tasks such as collecting supplies and handouts for a stable client. Teaching, assessment, and evaluation of learning all require nursing judgment and cannot be delegated, no matter how routine the content seems.

q: A nurse has finished teaching a client to use a metered dose inhaler. What should the nurse document?
o: That the teaching about the inhaler was completed before discharge
The nurse's opinion about how motivated the client appeared to be
Only the title of the handout that was given to the client
The content taught, who was present, the method, and the client's response
r: Documentation of teaching must be factual and specific, recording what was taught, how, who received it, and objective evidence of the client's understanding. Teaching completed is tempting because it is quick, but it gives the next nurse no information about what still needs reinforcement.

q: Which of the following should the nurse include when documenting a client education session? Select all that apply.
o: The specific content that was taught
The client's insurance authorization number
The method used, such as demonstration or video
The client's response and the evidence that learning occurred
The nurse's judgment that the client is not a motivated learner
r: Teaching records should state the content, the method, and objective evidence of the client's response so care can be continued by others. Labeling the client unmotivated is a subjective opinion rather than a fact, and insurance data belongs in the financial record.

q: A nurse is planning a group teaching session. Which statement about group teaching is accurate?
o: Groups larger than 20 clients tend to increase learner satisfaction
Groups of six or fewer let clients learn from one another and raise satisfaction
Group teaching is equally effective for every client on the unit
Group teaching removes the need to assess individual learning needs
r: Small groups let the nurse use several strategies at once and let learners benefit from each other's questions and experiences. Group teaching does not suit every client, because physical limitations, emotional distress, or privacy concerns can make an individual session necessary.

q: A nurse is teaching an older adult client who has mild hearing and vision changes. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Use large, high-contrast print materials
Speak in a high-pitched, loud voice
Keep sessions short and repeat the key points
Reduce background noise in the room
Face the client and speak clearly at a normal pace
Schedule the session right after giving an opioid analgesic
r: Large print, brief repeated sessions, a quiet room, and clear face-to-face speech compensate for common age-related sensory changes. Raising pitch actually makes speech harder to hear because high tones are lost first, and teaching immediately after an opioid dose competes with sedation.

q: Which principle should guide the order in which a nurse presents teaching content?
o: Begin with the most complex skill so everything afterward feels easier
Follow the order the topics appear in the facility handout
Move from simple to complex and from familiar to unfamiliar
Cover all content in a single session so nothing is forgotten
r: Learning activities should build from simple to complex and connect new material to what the client already knows, which supports retention and confidence. Starting with the hardest task is tempting as a shortcut, but early failure discourages the learner and slows the whole process.

q: A client who was just told they have cancer says the laboratory must have mixed up the results when the nurse begins teaching about chemotherapy. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Continue with the planned teaching because treatment starts soon
Tell the client the diagnosis is certain and the teaching must be finished
Acknowledge the client's feelings and postpone detailed teaching for now
Ask a family member to sign the teaching record for the client instead
r: Denial and acute emotional distress block learning, so the nurse addresses feelings first and returns to detailed content when the client can absorb it. Pushing forward because of the schedule is tempting, but information given during denial is rarely retained and damages trust.

q: A nurse is evaluating teaching for a client who is starting warfarin. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?
o: I will use a soft toothbrush and an electric razor
I will keep my intake of green vegetables about the same each week
I will report black or tarry stools to my provider
I will take aspirin whenever I get a headache
r: Aspirin adds antiplatelet effect on top of anticoagulation and significantly raises bleeding risk, so this statement shows the teaching did not take hold. The vegetable statement sounds wrong to many clients who think they must avoid greens entirely, but keeping vitamin K intake consistent is exactly what is recommended.

q: A nurse is preparing a client for an invasive diagnostic procedure. Which statement describes the nurse's role in informed consent?
o: The nurse explains the risks, benefits, and alternatives of the procedure
The nurse decides whether the client is legally competent to give consent
The nurse may sign the consent form for a client who is too anxious
The nurse witnesses the signature and verifies that the client understands
r: The provider obtains consent by explaining the purpose, description, risks, alternatives, and the right to refuse, while the nurse witnesses the signature and verifies that the client understood. Explaining the procedure is tempting because nurses teach constantly, but describing the procedure itself is the provider's legal responsibility.

q: A client who has signed a consent form asks the nurse, what exactly are they going to take out during this procedure? Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Explain the procedure using the facility teaching booklet
Reassure the client that the surgeon performs this procedure often
Stop the preparation and notify the provider to clarify the information
Have the client sign a second consent form
r: If the client cannot describe what is planned, the consent is not informed, so the nurse halts the process and notifies the provider, who is responsible for clarifying. Teaching from a booklet is tempting because the information is accurate, but the nurse explaining the procedure does not satisfy the legal requirement that the provider inform the client.

q: A charge nurse is reviewing informed consent with newly licensed nurses. Which of the following statements should the charge nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: The provider explains the purpose, risks, benefits, and alternatives of the procedure
The nurse may describe the surgical technique in detail if the provider is unavailable
The client must give consent voluntarily and without coercion
The nurse verifies understanding and witnesses the client's signature
A family member may sign for a competent adult who feels nervous
The nurse documents unanswered questions and notification of the provider
r: Consent requires the provider to inform, the client to agree freely, and the nurse to verify understanding, witness the signature, and document any questions and provider notification. A competent adult must sign personally, and a nurse who explains the procedure in the provider's place is acting outside the consent process.

q: Which of the following individuals may legally give consent on behalf of another person? Select all that apply.
o: The parent of a minor child
The adult neighbor who drove the client to the hospital
A legal guardian
A person who holds durable power of attorney for health care
The nurse assigned to care for the client
A court-appointed representative
r: Parents of minors, legal guardians, health care power of attorney holders, and court-appointed representatives have legal authority to consent for someone else. A neighbor or the assigned nurse has no legal standing, no matter how involved or well informed they are.

q: A client who is deaf and communicates by sign language is scheduled for a bronchoscopy. Which action best supports valid informed consent?
o: Arrange a qualified medical interpreter for the provider's explanation
Ask the client's spouse to sign the consent form for the procedure
Write a brief explanation on paper and have the client sign the form
Ask the provider to speak slowly so the client is able to read lips
r: When a hearing impairment or language difference prevents communication, a trained medical interpreter must be used so the client actually receives and understands the information. A written note is tempting because it is fast, but it does not confirm comprehension and may not match the client's preferred language or literacy level.

q: Just before transport to the procedure area, a client who signed the consent form states, I have changed my mind, I do not want this done. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Explain that the procedure room is already scheduled and continue with transport
Hold the transport and notify the provider of the client's decision
Ask the family to persuade the client to go through with it
Document the refusal and send the client to the procedure area
r: Consent can be withdrawn at any time, so the nurse stops the process and informs the provider, then documents the client's statement. Enlisting the family to change the client's mind is coercion, which invalidates any consent that follows.

q: A nurse is preparing a client for an invasive diagnostic procedure. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Verify that the signed consent form is on the chart
Remove the client's identification band so it does not interfere with the sterile field
Confirm allergies, including iodine, contrast, and shellfish
Obtain and record baseline vital signs
Provide a full breakfast so the client does not feel weak
Verify how long the client has been NPO if fasting was prescribed
r: Consent verification, allergy history, baseline vital signs, and NPO status are standard preprocedure safety checks that protect the client during and after the procedure. The identification band stays on for the client identification process, and feeding a client who is NPO risks aspiration under sedation.

q: A nurse is monitoring a client who received moderate sedation for a diagnostic procedure. Which finding requires immediate action?
o: Respiratory rate of 8 per minute with shallow chest movement
Blood pressure of 118 over 72
The client is drowsy but awakens when spoken to
A small amount of dried blood at the puncture site
r: Sedation depresses respiration, and a rate of 8 with shallow breathing threatens oxygenation, so airway and breathing come first. Drowsiness that resolves with voice is expected after sedation and does not require intervention by itself.

q: A nurse is assisting with a lumbar puncture. Which position should the nurse help the client assume for the procedure?
o: Prone with both arms resting at the sides of the body
Supine with the head of the bed elevated to 30 degrees
Side lying with the knees drawn up and the chin tucked down
Sitting upright and leaning backward against the pillows
r: Curling into a C shape on the side widens the spaces between the vertebrae so the needle can be placed. Sitting is sometimes used with the client leaning forward over a table, but leaning backward closes the interspaces and makes access harder.

q: Which instruction should the nurse give a client immediately after a lumbar puncture?
o: Sit upright for 4 hours so that no spinal fluid leaks out
Limit the fluids you drink for the next 24 hours
Walk in the hallway right away to prevent blood clots
Stay lying flat for the prescribed time and drink extra fluids
r: Lying flat and increasing fluid intake help replace cerebrospinal fluid and reduce the risk of a spinal headache after the procedure. Sitting upright and restricting fluids both increase headache risk, which is the opposite of the goal.

q: Three hours after a lumbar puncture, a client reports a throbbing headache that worsens when sitting up. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Assist the client to lie flat and encourage oral fluid intake
Prepare the client for an emergency computed tomography scan
Notify the provider that the client is showing signs of meningitis
Have the client sit up straight and take slow deep breaths
r: A postural headache after a lumbar puncture is a common spinal headache from cerebrospinal fluid loss, and it is treated first with flat positioning and fluids. Meningitis is tempting because headache is a symptom, but meningitis presents with fever and nuchal rigidity rather than a headache that improves when lying down.

q: Which finding after a lumbar puncture should the nurse report to the provider immediately?
o: Mild soreness at the insertion site
New numbness and weakness in both legs
Headache that is relieved by lying flat
Urine output of 60 mL per hour
r: New numbness, tingling, or weakness in the lower extremities suggests nerve irritation or compression such as a hematoma and requires immediate provider notification. A headache relieved by lying flat is the expected spinal headache and is managed with positioning and fluids rather than an urgent call.

q: Which of the following actions should the nurse include in the care of a client after a lumbar puncture? Select all that apply.
o: Keep the client flat for the prescribed period
Withhold all analgesics for 24 hours
Encourage increased oral fluid intake
Inspect the puncture site for drainage or swelling
Ambulate the client in the hallway every hour
Check movement and sensation in the lower extremities
r: Flat positioning, extra fluids, site inspection, and neurologic checks of the legs address the two main risks after the procedure, which are spinal headache and nerve or bleeding complications. Hourly ambulation defeats the purpose of flat positioning, and there is no reason to withhold ordered analgesics.

q: A nurse is preparing a client for a paracentesis. Which action should the nurse take immediately before the procedure?
o: Place the client in the side lying position
Ask the client to empty the bladder
Administer a cleansing enema
Restrict oral fluids for 12 hours
r: An empty bladder sits below the needle insertion site and greatly reduces the risk of accidental bladder puncture. Side lying is tempting because it is used for many procedures, but paracentesis is performed with the client upright so fluid pools in the lower abdomen.

q: Which position should the nurse help a client assume for a paracentesis?
o: Prone with a small pillow placed under the abdomen
Trendelenburg position with the legs elevated on pillows
Upright, sitting on the edge of the bed or in high Fowler
Left side lying with the knees flexed toward the chest
r: Sitting upright lets gravity collect the ascitic fluid in the lower abdomen away from the bowel and diaphragm, which makes drainage safer and easier. Trendelenburg would shift fluid and abdominal contents toward the diaphragm and worsen the client's breathing.

q: A client has had 5 L of ascitic fluid removed during a paracentesis. Which finding requires immediate follow-up?
o: Blood pressure that falls from 124 over 78 to 86 over 50 with tachycardia
A decrease in abdominal girth measured after the procedure
The client reports that breathing feels easier than before
A dressing over the puncture site that is dry and intact
r: Rapid removal of a large volume shifts fluid out of the vascular space, and hypotension with tachycardia signals hypovolemia that needs immediate attention. A smaller girth and easier breathing are the expected benefits of the procedure, not complications.

q: Which of the following nursing actions are appropriate for a client having a paracentesis? Select all that apply.
o: Measure weight and abdominal girth before and after the procedure
Position the client prone during the procedure
Have the client void just before the procedure begins
Monitor vital signs for hypotension after fluid removal
Encourage the client to cough forcefully as the needle is inserted
Record the amount, color, and character of the fluid removed
r: Weight and girth measurements document the fluid removed, voiding protects the bladder, vital sign monitoring detects hypovolemia, and describing the drainage provides diagnostic information. Prone positioning and forceful coughing during needle insertion both increase the risk of organ injury.

q: Which instruction should the nurse give the client just before the needle is inserted for a thoracentesis?
o: Breathe deeply and continuously throughout the entire procedure
Cough firmly whenever you feel pressure or fullness in your chest
Hold still and avoid coughing or deep breathing during needle placement
Turn from side to side to help the fluid move toward the needle
r: Movement, coughing, and deep breathing shift the lung toward the needle and raise the risk of puncturing it, so the client stays still and is told to report any urge to cough. Deep breathing feels helpful because it is encouraged after most procedures, but during needle placement it is dangerous.

q: Thirty minutes after a thoracentesis, which finding should the nurse report immediately?
o: Sudden shortness of breath with absent breath sounds on the affected side
Oxygen saturation of 95 percent on room air
A small amount of serosanguineous drainage on the site dressing
The client reports mild soreness at the puncture site
r: New dyspnea with absent breath sounds suggests pneumothorax, a breathing emergency that requires immediate provider notification and a chest x-ray. Slight drainage and mild soreness at the site are expected and are monitored rather than reported urgently.

q: A client has just had a bone marrow aspiration and biopsy from the posterior iliac crest. Which action should the nurse take immediately after the procedure?
o: Ambulate the client to prevent stiffness
Apply firm pressure over the site and observe for bleeding
Place the client in Trendelenburg position
Offer the client a full meal since fasting is now over
r: Direct pressure followed by a pressure dressing controls bleeding, which is the main complication, especially when platelet counts are low. Early ambulation is tempting because the client feels fine, but resting on the site for the prescribed time helps hemostasis.

q: Which of the following nursing actions are appropriate for a client scheduled for a bone marrow biopsy? Select all that apply.
o: Verify that the signed consent form is on the chart
Withhold all analgesia after the procedure
Position the client prone or side lying for a posterior iliac crest site
Tell the client to expect brief sharp pain or pressure when the marrow is withdrawn
Keep the client NPO for 24 hours after the procedure
Monitor the site for bleeding, particularly if the platelet count is low
r: Consent verification, correct positioning, honest preparation for the brief pain of aspiration, and bleeding surveillance are the core nursing responsibilities for this procedure. Withholding analgesia and prolonged NPO status serve no purpose, since the client may eat once fully awake and site pain is expected to need treatment.

q: A client has returned from an upper endoscopy performed with a topical throat anesthetic and moderate sedation. Which action should the nurse take before offering oral fluids?
o: Offer small sips of cold water to soothe the throat
Check that the client's gag reflex has returned
Ask the client whether the throat is sore
Raise the head of the bed and provide the meal tray
r: The throat spray suppresses the gag reflex, so anything by mouth before it returns creates a high risk of aspiration. Offering sips of water is tempting because clients are thirsty and the fluid seems harmless, but even water can be aspirated when the reflex is absent.

q: A nurse is teaching a client scheduled for a colonoscopy. Which of the following should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Follow the prescribed bowel cleansing regimen the day before the test
Eat a high-fiber meal the evening before to keep the bowel moving
Drink only clear liquids as directed before the procedure
Arrange for someone else to drive you home afterward
Plan to drive yourself home once you feel awake
You will likely receive moderate sedation during the test
r: Bowel cleansing, clear liquids, a ride home, and information about sedation are all part of standard colonoscopy preparation teaching. A high-fiber meal leaves residue that blocks visualization, and no client may drive after receiving sedation regardless of how alert they feel.

q: Four hours after a colonoscopy, which finding should the nurse follow up on immediately?
o: The client passes a small amount of flatus
The client reports mild cramping that is gradually easing
The client is drowsy but is becoming more alert over time
The client has severe abdominal pain with a rigid, distended abdomen
r: Severe pain with abdominal rigidity and distention suggests bowel perforation and hemorrhage, which is an emergency. Passing flatus is actually a good sign after air is instilled during the procedure, and mild cramping that is resolving is expected.

q: A client is scheduled for an intravenous pyelogram with contrast media. Which information is most important for the nurse to obtain before the procedure?
o: The client's usual bowel elimination pattern and last bowel movement
History of iodine, contrast, or shellfish allergy and kidney function results
The position the client prefers to be in during the examination
Whether the client has ever had this examination in the past
r: Iodine-based contrast can trigger an allergic reaction and is nephrotoxic, so allergy history along with BUN and creatinine results must be reviewed and reported before the dye is given. A shellfish allergy alone does not automatically rule out contrast, but it does require further assessment and provider notification.

q: A client who takes metformin daily is scheduled for a computed tomography scan with contrast media. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Give the metformin with a small sip of water before the scan
Double the metformin dose to prevent hyperglycemia during fasting
Take no action, because metformin does not interact with contrast
Notify the provider, since metformin is usually held around contrast studies
r: Contrast media can impair kidney function, and continuing metformin in that setting raises the risk of lactic acidosis, so the medication is typically held around the procedure per provider prescription. Giving the dose as usual is tempting because clients are told never to skip diabetes medications, but this is a specific and well established exception.

q: Which of the following should the nurse assess before a client receives iodinated contrast media? Select all that apply.
o: Allergy to iodine, contrast dye, or shellfish
Whether the client prefers a private room after the scan
Recent BUN and serum creatinine results
Whether the client takes metformin
Whether the client could be pregnant
The client's favorite fluids to drink afterward
r: Allergy history, kidney function, metformin use, and possible pregnancy all change whether and how the contrast study proceeds. Room preference and beverage choice are comfort details that have no bearing on the safety of contrast administration.

q: Which instruction should the nurse give a client after a study using intravenous contrast media?
o: Limit the amount of fluid you drink for the next 24 hours
Expect your urine to look bloody for about the next 2 days
Drink extra fluids to help clear the dye unless fluids are restricted
Avoid all physical activity for a full week after the scan
r: Increasing fluids promotes renal excretion of the contrast and helps protect kidney function, so long as the client has no fluid restriction from heart or kidney disease. Restricting fluids would concentrate the dye in the kidneys and increase the risk of contrast-induced injury.

q: A nurse is collecting specimens for diagnostic testing. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Label the container with the client's identifying information at the bedside
Allow toilet water to rinse the stool sample into the container
Use a sterile container for a urine culture and sensitivity specimen
Send specimens to the laboratory promptly after collection
Store sputum specimens at the bedside until the end of the shift
Collect stool for occult blood testing from three separate bowel movements
r: Bedside labeling prevents misidentification, sterile containers preserve culture accuracy, prompt transport protects specimen integrity, and serial guaiac testing uses three separate stools. Water and urine contaminate stool samples, and specimens left sitting at the bedside can grow organisms or degrade before analysis.

q: A nurse is describing mental health to a group of clients. Which statement best reflects mental health as a concept?
o: The permanent absence of any psychiatric diagnosis
The ability to cope with stress, maintain relationships, and adapt to change
A fixed trait a person either has or lacks for life
Complete freedom from sadness, worry, or conflict
r: Mental health is a dynamic capacity to cope, relate, and adapt along a continuum. It is not simply the absence of a diagnosis, is not fixed, and does not require the absence of all negative emotion.

q: A nurse plans a primary prevention program for a community. Which activity fits primary prevention?
o: Screening adolescents for early depression
Teaching stress-management skills to healthy workers
Leading a relapse-prevention group for clients with schizophrenia
Providing crisis intervention after a suicide attempt
r: Primary prevention aims to prevent illness before it occurs (health teaching, stress management). Screening is secondary (early detection); relapse prevention is tertiary; crisis intervention is secondary.

q: Which nurse is historically credited with defining the therapeutic nurse-client relationship as the foundation of psychiatric nursing?
o: Florence Nightingale
Hildegard Peplau
Virginia Henderson
Dorothea Dix
r: Hildegard Peplau described the nurse-client relationship as the central therapeutic tool of psychiatric nursing. The others contributed to nursing but not this specific framework.

q: A nurse completes a psychiatric admission assessment. Which components should be included? Select all that apply.
o: Mental status examination
Suicide and violence risk assessment
Biopsychosocial history
The nurse's personal opinion of the client's character
Current coping and support systems
r: A thorough psych assessment includes the mental status exam, risk assessment, biopsychosocial history, and coping/support review. A judgmental personal opinion is subjective and inappropriate.

q: A client is admitted involuntarily. Which statement about the client's rights is accurate?
o: The client automatically loses the right to refuse all medications
The client may still refuse specific treatments unless legally declared incompetent
The client forfeits confidentiality upon admission
The client cannot participate in treatment planning
r: Involuntary commitment addresses where the client receives care, not blanket loss of rights. Unless separately adjudicated incompetent, the client retains the right to refuse specific treatments and other rights.

q: A nurse threatens to give an injection to a competent client who is refusing it, stating the client will be held down. Before touching the client, this action constitutes which tort?
o: Battery
Assault
Negligence
Defamation
r: Assault is a threat that creates fear of imminent harmful contact. Battery is the actual unwanted contact. Negligence is unintentional; defamation harms reputation.

q: A client makes a serious, specific threat to kill a named coworker. Which nursing action reflects the duty to warn (Tarasoff)?
o: Maintain full confidentiality regardless of the threat
Warn and protect the identified potential victim and notify the team
Discharge the client to avoid liability
Document the threat but take no further action
r: When a client voices a serious, specific threat against an identifiable person, the duty to warn overrides confidentiality; the team must warn and protect the intended victim.

q: Which situations are examples of intentional torts in psychiatric nursing? Select all that apply.
o: Restraining a competent, non-dangerous client for staff convenience (false imprisonment)
Touching a client without consent (battery)
Failing to institute ordered suicide precautions (negligence)
Telling visitors false, damaging information about a client (defamation)
Threatening a client with seclusion to force compliance (assault)
r: False imprisonment, battery, defamation, and assault are intentional torts. Failure to act reasonably (missed suicide precautions) is unintentional negligence/malpractice.

q: A nurse ensures a client is cared for in the setting that allows the most freedom while still meeting safety needs. This reflects which right?
o: The right to refuse treatment
The right to the least restrictive environment
The right to privacy
The right to informed consent
r: The least restrictive environment principle requires using the option that maximizes autonomy while still ensuring adequate, safe care.

q: A client says, 'I feel like nothing will ever get better.' Which nurse response is most therapeutic?
o: 'Don't worry, everything will be fine.'
'You sound hopeless. Tell me more about what you're feeling.'
'Why do you feel that way?'
'You have so much to live for.'
r: Reflecting the feeling and inviting elaboration keeps exploration open. False reassurance, 'why' questions, and dismissing feelings are nontherapeutic and block communication.

q: When a client's spoken words conflict with their body language, the nurse should recognize that:
o: The verbal message is always more accurate
The nonverbal message usually reflects the true emotion
Both should be ignored until the client calms down
The nurse should confront the client about lying
r: Nonverbal cues (tone, posture, facial expression) carry most of the emotional message; when verbal and nonverbal conflict, the nonverbal is generally the more reliable indicator.

q: Which techniques are therapeutic communication? Select all that apply.
o: Using silence to allow the client time
Offering false reassurance
Asking open-ended questions
Reflecting the client's feelings
Giving personal advice about what to do
r: Silence, open-ended questions, and reflection are therapeutic. False reassurance and giving advice are nontherapeutic because they block feelings and remove client autonomy.

q: Which nurse statements are nontherapeutic and should be avoided? Select all that apply.
o: 'Everything happens for a reason.'
'I'll sit here with you for a while.'
'Why didn't you take your medication?'
'You shouldn't feel that way.'
'Tell me more about what happened.'
r: Clichés, accusatory 'why' questions, and dismissing feelings are nontherapeutic. Offering self and inviting elaboration are therapeutic.

q: A nurse uses SOLER to strengthen active listening. Which behavior is consistent with SOLER?
o: Crossing the arms to appear relaxed
Leaning slightly toward the client with open posture
Avoiding eye contact to reduce pressure
Standing over the client while speaking
r: SOLER = Sit squarely, Open posture, Lean in, Eye contact, Relax. Leaning in with an open posture conveys attentiveness. Crossed arms and avoiding eye contact are closed cues.

q: According to Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome, which stage is characterized by the fight-or-flight sympathetic surge?
o: Resistance
Alarm
Exhaustion
Recovery
r: The alarm stage triggers the sympathetic fight-or-flight response. Resistance is adaptation/coping, and exhaustion occurs when reserves are depleted.

q: A client in panic-level anxiety is pacing and cannot follow directions. What is the nurse's priority?
o: Teach relaxation breathing techniques in detail
Ensure client and environmental safety and stay with the client
Explore the underlying cause of the anxiety
Encourage the client to journal about feelings
r: Panic-level anxiety is disorganizing and unsafe; the priority is safety and staying with the client. Teaching and insight-oriented work are ineffective until anxiety decreases.

q: A client who drinks heavily states, 'I can quit anytime; I just enjoy it.' Which defense mechanism is the client using?
o: Projection
Denial
Sublimation
Displacement
r: Denial refuses to accept a painful reality (the drinking problem). Projection attributes feelings to others, sublimation channels urges constructively, and displacement redirects emotion to a safer target.

q: After being reprimanded by a manager, a client goes home and yells at their spouse. This best illustrates:
o: Displacement
Reaction formation
Regression
Rationalization
r: Displacement redirects an emotion from a threatening source (manager) to a safer target (spouse). Reaction formation acts opposite to true feelings; regression reverts to earlier behavior; rationalization uses excuses.

q: Which defense mechanisms are generally considered more adaptive/mature ways of channeling anxiety? Select all that apply.
o: Sublimation
Suppression
Denial
Altruism
Projection
r: Sublimation, conscious suppression, and altruism are relatively mature. Denial and projection distort reality and are more primitive.

q: A nurse describes milieu therapy to a new staff member. Which statement is accurate?
o: It relies solely on group psychotherapy sessions
It uses the entire treatment environment as a therapeutic tool
It is limited to medication management
It applies only to outpatient settings
r: Milieu therapy deliberately structures the whole environment — people, structure, and daily activities — to be therapeutic. It is broader than any single intervention.

q: Which action is the nurse's highest priority when maintaining a therapeutic milieu on an inpatient unit?
o: Scheduling recreational activities
Conducting environmental safety rounds to remove hazards
Decorating the unit to feel homelike
Posting the daily menu
r: Safety is the top milieu priority. Removing sharps, cords, belts, and other hazards and knowing client locations protects clients. Comfort and activities are important but secondary to safety.

q: Which principles support a safe, therapeutic milieu? Select all that apply.
o: Consistent limit-setting by all staff
Predictable structure and routines
Using restraints routinely to prevent problems
Involving clients in community decisions
Continuous attention to environmental safety
r: Consistency, structure, client involvement, and safety build a therapeutic milieu. Restraints are a last resort, never routine or preventive.

q: A client whispers, 'I'm planning to hurt myself, but promise you won't tell anyone.' What is the nurse's best response?
o: 'I promise to keep your secret.'
'I care about your safety, so I cannot keep that secret and must share it with the team.'
'Let's talk about something more positive.'
'You don't really mean that.'
r: Safety overrides confidentiality when a client is at risk. The nurse cannot promise secrecy, must notify the team, and should institute appropriate precautions. Minimizing or changing the subject is unsafe.

q: A client is escalating and becoming verbally aggressive. Which de-escalation approach should the nurse use first?
o: Immediately apply physical restraints
Use a calm voice, allow personal space, and offer choices
Confront the client firmly about the behavior
Move closer and maintain steady physical contact
r: De-escalation begins with the least restrictive measures: calm tone, respecting personal space, and offering choices. Restraint is a last resort after less-restrictive measures fail.

q: A client with acute suicidal ideation and a plan requires which level of care?
o: Intensive outpatient program
Inpatient acute psychiatric hospitalization
Community support group
Telephone follow-up only
r: Imminent danger to self requires the most protective setting — inpatient acute care with close monitoring — until the client is stabilized and safe.

q: A client attends a structured day program at the hospital but returns home each evening. This describes which setting?
o: Assertive community treatment
Partial hospitalization program
Inpatient unit
Residential treatment
r: A partial hospitalization program (PHP) provides intensive structured treatment during the day while the client lives at home, bridging inpatient and outpatient care.

q: Which settings are part of the community-based end of the mental health care continuum? Select all that apply.
o: Community mental health centers
Intensive outpatient programs
Locked acute inpatient units
Assertive community treatment teams
Home-based psychiatric care
r: Community mental health centers, IOP, ACT teams, and home care are community-based, less restrictive options. A locked acute inpatient unit is the most restrictive end of the continuum.

q: Which statement about deinstitutionalization is accurate?
o: It increased long-term hospital stays
It shifted care toward community settings, increasing the need for case management
It eliminated the need for outpatient services
It removed all client rights protections
r: Deinstitutionalization moved care from long-stay hospitals into the community, promoting autonomy but increasing the need for coordinated case management to prevent gaps in follow-up.

q: A nurse is caring for an 8-year-old client and applies Erikson's developmental theory. Which psychosocial task is the priority focus for this age group?
o: Trust versus mistrust
Industry versus inferiority
Identity versus role confusion
Intimacy versus isolation
r: School-age children (6-12 yr) work on Industry vs Inferiority, mastering skills and competence. Trust vs mistrust is infancy, identity vs role confusion is adolescence, and intimacy vs isolation is young adulthood.

q: A nurse is planning cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) interventions. Which actions reflect the principles of CBT? Select all that apply.
o: Help the client identify distorted automatic thoughts
Use free association to uncover unconscious childhood conflicts
Guide the client to reframe catastrophizing into balanced thinking
Set specific, present-focused, time-limited goals
Focus primarily on interpreting the client's dreams
r: CBT is present-focused and goal-directed: it identifies and restructures cognitive distortions and reframes them. Free association and dream interpretation belong to psychoanalysis, not CBT.

q: A nurse notices a client is reacting to the nurse as though the nurse were the client's critical mother. The nurse should document this as which phenomenon?
o: Countertransference
Resistance
Transference
Regression
r: Transference is when the client unconsciously redirects feelings about a significant figure onto the nurse. Countertransference is the reverse (nurse to client). Recognizing transference helps maintain therapeutic boundaries.

q: A newly formed therapy group is meeting for the first time. Which action is the priority for the nurse leader during this orientation phase?
o: Confront members who avoid discussing feelings
Establish trust, group rules, and shared goals
Summarize progress and evaluate outcomes
Encourage members to give one another feedback on conflict
r: The orientation (forming) phase focuses on establishing trust, setting ground rules, and defining goals. Confrontation and peer feedback belong to the working phase; summarizing and evaluating occur at termination.

q: A member repeatedly dominates group discussion and interrupts others. Which nursing responses appropriately manage this behavior? Select all that apply.
o: Tactfully redirect the conversation to include other members
Ignore the behavior so the member does not feel singled out
Acknowledge the member's input, then invite others to share
Immediately remove the member from the group
Set and reinforce the group norm of shared participation
r: A monopolizing member fills a self-serving individual role that disrupts group process. The nurse redirects, acknowledges then broadens, and reinforces participation norms. Ignoring it allows harm; abrupt removal is not the first-line response.

q: A client states, 'I thought I was the only one who felt this way until I heard others in group.' This therapeutic benefit is best described as which of Yalom's factors?
o: Catharsis
Altruism
Universality
Instillation of hope
r: Universality is the realization that one's problems and feelings are shared by others, reducing isolation. Catharsis is emotional release, altruism is helping others, and instillation of hope is optimism from seeing others improve.

q: A client is experiencing acute anxiety in the clinic with rapid breathing and muscle tension. Which stress-management intervention should the nurse implement first?
o: Teach a long-term progressive muscle relaxation program
Guide the client in slow diaphragmatic deep breathing
Refer the client for biofeedback training
Provide written material on cognitive reframing
r: For acute anxiety, slow diaphragmatic breathing is the priority: it is immediate, requires no equipment, and activates the parasympathetic 'rest' response. The other options are valuable but not the first bedside action.

q: A nurse is teaching relaxation and coping techniques for stress management. Which strategies are appropriate to include? Select all that apply.
o: Progressive muscle relaxation
Guided imagery
Avoiding all physical activity to conserve energy
Mindfulness meditation
Assertiveness and 'I' statements
r: PMR, guided imagery, mindfulness, and assertiveness all reduce stress. Regular physical activity relieves stress, so avoiding all exercise is not therapeutic.

q: A client returns to the unit after electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) and is drowsy and disoriented. Which nursing action is the priority?
o: Position the client side-lying and monitor the airway
Provide detailed discharge teaching about follow-up
Encourage the client to ambulate to prevent stiffness
Document that the treatment was ineffective
r: After ECT the airway is the priority because the client received an anesthetic and muscle relaxant. Side-lying (recovery) positioning prevents aspiration. Post-ECT confusion is expected and temporary, so teaching is deferred and ambulation is unsafe until fully oriented.

q: A nurse is preparing a client for a first ECT treatment. Which pre-procedure actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Verify that informed consent has been signed
Confirm the client has been NPO after midnight
Have the client void before the procedure
Give the client a full breakfast for energy
Remove dentures and take baseline vital signs
r: Pre-ECT care includes verified consent, NPO status (aspiration prevention under anesthesia), voiding, removing dentures/jewelry, and baseline vitals. Feeding the client violates NPO and creates aspiration risk.

q: A nurse is reviewing the history of a client scheduled for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). Which finding is the priority to report to the provider?
o: The client reports mild seasonal headaches
The client has a metal aneurysm clip in the head
The client drinks two cups of coffee daily
The client feels nervous about the first session
r: Ferromagnetic metal or implants in or near the head are a contraindication to TMS because the magnetic field can dislodge or heat them. This safety finding must be reported before treatment. The other findings are not contraindications.

q: A nurse is monitoring a client during the recovery period immediately after ECT. Which findings require nursing intervention? Select all that apply.
o: Oxygen saturation dropping to 86%
Mild disorientation to time
Increasing difficulty breathing with noisy respirations
A brief complaint of headache
Client unable to maintain a patent airway
r: Airway and oxygenation problems (falling SpO2, respiratory distress, inability to maintain the airway) are urgent and require immediate intervention. Mild transient disorientation and headache are expected post-ECT effects.

q: A client is having a panic attack in the hallway. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Stay with the client and remain calm
Teach the client deep-breathing exercises
Explore possible triggers for the attack
Leave to give the client privacy and quiet
r: During panic the perceptual field is distorted and the client can behave unsafely, so the priority is to stay with the client and provide a calm presence; teaching and exploring triggers wait until anxiety drops to mild or moderate.

q: Which findings support a level of severe anxiety? Select all that apply.
o: Greatly reduced perceptual field
Focus on scattered specific details
Impaired problem-solving
Sharpened, alert learning ability
Feeling of impending doom
r: Severe anxiety narrows perception dramatically, fixes attention on fragmented details, impairs problem-solving, and often brings a sense of dread. Sharpened alert learning is a feature of mild anxiety, not severe.

q: A client with generalized anxiety disorder states, 'I only take my buspirone when I feel really nervous.' Which response is best?
o: That is the correct way to use this medication
Buspirone works only when taken every day as prescribed
You should switch to taking it every other day
Add an extra dose whenever panic starts
r: Buspirone must be taken consistently every day to build a therapeutic effect; it does not provide immediate relief, so PRN use indicates the client needs re-teaching.

q: Which points should the nurse include when teaching a client about lorazepam for short-term anxiety relief? Select all that apply.
o: Avoid alcohol while taking this drug
Do not stop the medication abruptly
This drug is safe for long-term daily use
Drowsiness and sedation can occur
Physical dependence can develop
r: Benzodiazepines potentiate CNS depression with alcohol, must be tapered to avoid withdrawal, commonly cause sedation, and carry dependence and tolerance risk, so they are indicated only for short-term use.

q: The nurse knows that learning and problem-solving are BEST at which level of anxiety?
o: Mild
Severe
Panic
Moderate
r: Mild anxiety sharpens the perceptual field and heightens alertness and motivation, making it the optimal state for learning; higher levels progressively impair cognition.

q: A client reports flashbacks, nightmares, and hypervigilance that began 6 weeks ago after an assault. Which disorder is most consistent with these findings?
o: Acute stress disorder
Post-traumatic stress disorder
Adjustment disorder
Generalized anxiety disorder
r: PTSD is diagnosed when trauma-related intrusion, avoidance, negative mood, and arousal symptoms persist longer than 1 month; symptoms lasting 3 days to 1 month would be acute stress disorder.

q: Which manifestations would the nurse expect in a client with PTSD? Select all that apply.
o: Intrusive flashbacks
Avoidance of reminders of the trauma
Exaggerated startle response
Persistent euphoric mood
Emotional numbing and detachment
r: PTSD clusters include intrusion, avoidance, hyperarousal such as an exaggerated startle, and negative mood or numbing; a persistently euphoric mood is not a feature.

q: A provider prescribes prazosin for a veteran with PTSD. The nurse explains this medication is primarily used to:
o: Reduce trauma-related nightmares
Prevent daytime flashbacks entirely
Provide immediate sedation during panic
Cure the underlying disorder
r: Prazosin, an alpha-adrenergic blocker, is used to decrease the frequency and intensity of trauma-related nightmares; the nurse should monitor for orthostatic hypotension.

q: A client with PTSD becomes tearful and stops talking while describing the trauma. Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?
o: We can pause; you can share at your own pace
You need to finish telling me what happened
That was a long time ago, try to move past it
Let's talk about something more pleasant instead
r: Allowing the client to control the pace of disclosure conveys respect and safety; pushing the client, minimizing the trauma, or abruptly changing the subject are nontherapeutic.

q: Which are priority safety issues to screen for in a client with a trauma-related disorder? Select all that apply.
o: Suicidal ideation
Self-harm behaviors
Substance use
Preferred learning style
Aggression toward others
r: Trauma disorders carry elevated risk of suicide, self-harm, substance use, and aggression, so these are priority screens; learning style, while useful for teaching, is not a safety priority.

q: A client is admitted with major depressive disorder. Which nursing assessment takes priority?
o: Determining the client's sleep pattern
Assessing suicidal ideation and plan
Evaluating recent appetite changes
Reviewing the client's family history
r: Safety is always the priority in depression; the nurse must directly assess for suicidal ideation, a plan, and available means before addressing sleep, appetite, or history.

q: Which findings are consistent with major depressive disorder? Select all that apply.
o: Anhedonia
Feelings of worthlessness or guilt
Decreased ability to concentrate
Flight of ideas
Psychomotor retardation
r: The SIG-E-CAPS features of MDD include loss of interest, guilt or worthlessness, poor concentration, and psychomotor changes; flight of ideas is a manic finding, not depressive.

q: A severely depressed client who was withdrawn suddenly appears calm, brighter, and energetic. Which action is the priority?
o: Reduce the frequency of observation
Increase suicide precautions and observation
Praise the client for rapid improvement
Discharge planning can now begin
r: A sudden lift in mood may mean the client now has the energy to carry out a suicide plan; suicide risk can rise as energy returns, so observation should be increased, not decreased.

q: Which statements reflect therapeutic communication with a depressed client? Select all that apply.
o: Sitting in silence with the client
Offering self by spending time with the client
Using open-ended prompts
Telling the client to cheer up
Asking why the client feels so sad
r: Silence, offering self, and open-ended prompts build trust; false reassurance such as cheer up and why questions that demand justification are nontherapeutic.

q: A client taking phenelzine asks which food is safe. Which response is correct?
o: Aged cheddar cheese
Pepperoni pizza
Fresh grilled chicken
Draft beer
r: Fresh, unaged foods such as freshly cooked chicken are safe; aged cheese, cured or fermented meats, and tap or draft beer are high in tyramine and can precipitate a hypertensive crisis with an MAOI.

q: The nurse reviews a maintenance lithium level for a client with bipolar I disorder. Which result is within the expected therapeutic range?
o: 0.9 mEq/L
1.8 mEq/L
2.4 mEq/L
0.2 mEq/L
r: The therapeutic maintenance range for lithium is about 0.6 to 1.2 mEq/L; 0.9 is therapeutic, while 1.8 and 2.4 indicate toxicity and 0.2 is subtherapeutic.

q: Which findings would the nurse expect during an acute manic episode? Select all that apply.
o: Pressured speech
Grandiosity
Decreased need for sleep
Psychomotor retardation
Impulsive spending
r: Mania features pressured speech, grandiosity, reduced need for sleep, and impulsive high-risk behavior; psychomotor retardation is a depressive finding.

q: A client in acute mania will not sit down to eat and has lost weight. Which intervention is the priority?
o: Insist the client sit at the table for full meals
Provide high-calorie finger foods the client can carry
Restrict fluids to encourage structured mealtimes
Serve meals only in the group dining room
r: A manic client is too hyperactive to sit for meals and is at risk for exhaustion and dehydration, so offering high-calorie portable finger foods meets nutritional needs while working with the client's activity level.

q: Which findings indicate lithium toxicity and should be reported? Select all that apply.
o: Coarse hand tremor
Confusion and ataxia
Persistent vomiting
Fine tremor present since starting therapy
Seizures
r: Coarse tremor, confusion, ataxia, ongoing vomiting, and seizures signal rising toxicity; a mild fine tremor is a common expected early side effect rather than toxicity.

q: A client starting lamotrigine reports a new skin rash. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Reassure the client that rash is harmless
Hold the medication and notify the provider
Increase the dose to build tolerance
Apply lotion and continue the drug
r: A rash with lamotrigine can signal the life-threatening Stevens-Johnson syndrome, so the nurse should hold the drug and notify the provider immediately rather than dismissing or continuing it.

q: A client with schizophrenia says the voices are telling him to hurt himself. Which action is the priority?
o: Document the statement in the chart
Ask directly what the voices are telling him to do
Encourage the client to ignore the voices
Leave the client alone to reduce stimulation
r: Command hallucinations are a safety emergency; the nurse must directly assess the content of the voices to determine the risk of harm to self or others and implement safety measures.

q: Which are negative symptoms of schizophrenia? Select all that apply.
o: Flat affect
Alogia
Avolition
Auditory hallucinations
Anhedonia
r: Negative symptoms are losses of normal function, remembered as the 5 A's: flat affect, alogia, avolition, anhedonia, and asociality; hallucinations are a positive symptom.

q: A client states that spiders are crawling on the wall. Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?
o: There are no spiders; you are imagining that
I don't see any spiders, but you seem frightened
Let me help you brush the spiders off the wall
I will call someone to remove the spiders now
r: The nurse should neither argue with nor reinforce the hallucination; presenting reality while acknowledging the client's feeling validates the emotion without confirming the false perception.

q: Which are positive symptoms of schizophrenia? Select all that apply.
o: Delusions
Auditory hallucinations
Disorganized speech
Social withdrawal
Bizarre behavior
r: Positive symptoms are additions to normal function: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, and bizarre behavior; social withdrawal is a negative symptom.

q: A client on haloperidol develops a temperature of 40 C, muscle rigidity, and altered consciousness. Which condition should the nurse suspect?
o: Tardive dyskinesia
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Akathisia
Serotonin syndrome
r: High fever, lead-pipe rigidity, and altered mental status with an antipsychotic indicate neuroleptic malignant syndrome, a medical emergency requiring the drug to be stopped and immediate treatment.

q: A client with borderline personality disorder tells the nurse, "You're the only one here who understands me; the other nurses are terrible." Which defense mechanism is the client using?
o: Splitting
Sublimation
Reaction formation
Projection
r: Viewing staff as all-good or all-bad and flipping between those views is splitting, the hallmark defense in borderline personality disorder.

q: Which nursing approach best counters manipulation and splitting on an inpatient unit?
o: Assign a different nurse each shift to avoid attachment
Grant occasional exceptions to build rapport
Maintain consistent limits and communicate the plan among all staff
Debate the client's complaints until they see reason
r: Consistency and team communication prevent the client from playing staff against one another; exceptions and arguing reinforce the behavior.

q: A client with antisocial personality disorder is admitted. Which findings does the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
o: Lack of remorse for harming others
Deep, stable long-term relationships
Deceit and manipulation for personal gain
Impulsivity and reckless disregard for safety
Intense fear of being alone
r: Antisocial PD features a disregard for others' rights: no remorse, deceit, manipulation, and impulsivity. Stable relationships and fear of abandonment are not characteristic (fear of abandonment fits borderline PD).

q: The nurse observes a client with borderline personality disorder cutting the forearm with a paper clip. What is the priority nursing action?
o: Ignore the behavior so it is not reinforced
Assess the injury and ensure the client's safety
Immediately place the client in seclusion
Tell the client they will lose privileges
r: Every self-harm behavior requires assessment and safety first. Self-injury in BPD often relieves tension but must always be taken seriously; ignoring or purely punitive responses are unsafe.

q: A client with a personality disorder repeatedly tests unit rules. Which nurse statement reflects appropriate limit-setting?
o: "If you keep this up, none of us will help you."
"Quiet hours are at 10 PM; the television will be turned off then, as it is for everyone."
"I'll let it slide tonight since you've had a hard day."
"Why do you always have to cause problems?"
r: Effective limit-setting is calm, matter-of-fact, applied equally to all, and states the expectation and consequence without anger, threats, or exceptions.

q: An 80-year-old develops acute confusion and inattention over 8 hours. Vital signs show a low-grade fever. What should the nurse suspect first?
o: Alzheimer's dementia
Delirium from an underlying cause such as infection
Normal aging
Major depressive disorder
r: A sudden change in mentation in an older adult is delirium until proven otherwise; a common reversible cause is infection such as a UTI. Dementia has a gradual onset.

q: Which features are characteristic of delirium rather than dementia? Select all that apply.
o: Sudden onset over hours to days
Fluctuating level of consciousness
Often reversible when the cause is treated
Gradual, irreversible memory decline
Markedly impaired attention
r: Delirium is acute, fluctuating, attention-impairing, and reversible. Gradual irreversible decline describes dementia.

q: A client with Alzheimer's becomes increasingly agitated and confused each evening. This pattern is known as:
o: Confabulation
Sundowning
La belle indifference
Splitting
r: Sundowning is worsening confusion and agitation in the late afternoon/evening. Interventions include increasing light and reducing stimulation.

q: Which intervention is most appropriate for a client with moderate Alzheimer's disease who cannot recall recent events?
o: Frequently quiz the client to strengthen memory
Provide a consistent routine and simple one-step directions
Correct every inaccurate statement to keep the client oriented
Rearrange the room often to provide stimulation
r: Consistency, simple directions, and a familiar environment reduce anxiety. Quizzing, repeated correction, and frequent change increase distress.

q: A nurse cares for a client with delirium. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Identify and treat the underlying cause
Provide a calm, well-lit, low-stimulation environment
Reorient the client frequently
Ensure glasses and hearing aids are used
Withhold family visits to reduce stimulation
r: Treating the cause, a calm environment, reorientation, and sensory aids all help. Familiar family presence is reassuring and should be encouraged, not withheld.

q: Which medication class is used to prevent seizures and delirium tremens during alcohol withdrawal?
o: Opioids
Benzodiazepines
Stimulants
Antipsychotics
r: Benzodiazepines (e.g., lorazepam, chlordiazepoxide) are first-line to prevent alcohol-withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens, often dosed by CIWA-Ar score.

q: A client is brought to the ED with respiratory depression and pinpoint pupils after suspected drug use. Which antidote does the nurse anticipate?
o: Flumazenil
Naloxone
Disulfiram
Thiamine
r: Respiratory depression with pinpoint (constricted) pupils indicates opioid overdose; naloxone reverses it. Because naloxone is short-acting, monitor for recurrent respiratory depression.

q: Which findings would the nurse expect during alcohol withdrawal? Select all that apply.
o: Tremors
Tachycardia and hypertension
Constricted pupils and slowed respirations
Anxiety and insomnia
Risk of seizures
r: Alcohol withdrawal causes autonomic hyperactivity: tremors, tachycardia, hypertension, anxiety, insomnia, and seizure risk. Constricted pupils and slowed respirations describe opioid intoxication.

q: A client who chronically uses cocaine stops abruptly. Which withdrawal finding is expected?
o: Life-threatening seizures and delirium tremens
Severe fatigue, hypersomnia, depression, and cravings
Dilated pupils, hypertension, and fever
Rhinorrhea, yawning, and diarrhea
r: Stimulant withdrawal is a 'crash': fatigue, hypersomnia, increased appetite, depression, and intense cravings with suicide risk. Fever/hypertension occur in intoxication, not withdrawal.

q: Why must flumazenil be used with extreme caution in a benzodiazepine-dependent client?
o: It can precipitate refractory seizures and acute withdrawal
It causes immediate respiratory depression
It has no effect on benzodiazepines
It reverses opioid overdose too aggressively
r: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine sedation but can trigger severe, refractory seizures and acute withdrawal in dependent clients, so it is used cautiously.

q: A client is started on disulfiram. Which teaching points should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Avoid alcohol in all forms, including mouthwash and sauces
Drinking alcohol may cause flushing, nausea, and vomiting
Aftershave and cologne can trigger a reaction
The medication produces a pleasant euphoria with alcohol
Effects can occur even from hidden sources of alcohol
r: Disulfiram causes an unpleasant (not euphoric) reaction with any alcohol exposure, including hidden sources, supporting abstinence.

q: Which finding is most characteristic of anorexia nervosa rather than bulimia nervosa?
o: Body weight within or above the normal range
Significantly low body weight with amenorrhea and lanugo
Eroded dental enamel from vomiting
Russell's sign on the knuckles
r: Anorexia features significantly low weight, amenorrhea, lanugo, and bradycardia. Normal weight, enamel erosion, and Russell's sign are associated with bulimia's binge-purge cycle.

q: A nurse reviews labs for a client who purges by self-induced vomiting. Which findings are expected? Select all that apply.
o: Hypokalemia
Metabolic alkalosis
Risk of cardiac dysrhythmias
Hyperkalemia
Eroded tooth enamel
r: Vomiting causes loss of potassium and acid, producing hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis, dysrhythmia risk, and dental erosion. Potassium is low, not high.

q: A severely malnourished client with anorexia begins nutritional rehabilitation. The nurse monitors most closely for which complication?
o: Refeeding syndrome
Hypertensive crisis
Serotonin syndrome
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
r: Reintroducing nutrition triggers an insulin surge that shifts phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells, causing refeeding syndrome with cardiac and respiratory risk.

q: Which nursing intervention is appropriate during meals for a hospitalized client with bulimia nervosa?
o: Allow the client privacy immediately after eating
Observe the client during and for about one hour after meals
Praise the client for gaining weight
Permit the client to weigh and record their own intake
r: Observation during and after meals prevents purging and hiding food. Post-meal privacy enables purging, and praising weight or appearance can be distressing.

q: Which interventions are appropriate for a client with an eating disorder? Select all that apply.
o: Stabilize cardiac status and electrolytes as a priority
Weigh the client at the same time daily using the same scale
Establish a structured, consistent mealtime routine
Engage in bargaining about how much food must be eaten
Address distorted body image and perfectionism
r: Medical stabilization, consistent weighing and meal structure, and addressing body image are appropriate. Bargaining over food creates power struggles and should be avoided.

q: A client is preoccupied with fear of having a serious illness despite repeated negative tests and few actual symptoms. This best describes:
o: Somatic symptom disorder
Illness anxiety disorder
Conversion disorder
Malingering
r: Illness anxiety disorder is preoccupation with having or acquiring a serious illness with minimal or no somatic symptoms. Somatic symptom disorder involves distressing actual symptoms.

q: A soldier develops sudden arm paralysis before deployment, but shows little concern about it and has no neurologic cause. This presentation suggests:
o: Factitious disorder
Malingering
Conversion disorder
Illness anxiety disorder
r: Conversion disorder is an unconscious neurologic deficit (here, paralysis) linked to a psychological conflict, sometimes with la belle indifference (indifference to the deficit).

q: Which nurse statement is most therapeutic for a client with somatic symptom disorder?
o: "These symptoms are all in your head."
"I can see these symptoms are distressing for you; let's talk about what's been stressful."
"There is nothing physically wrong, so there is no reason to worry."
"You are faking these symptoms for attention."
r: Acknowledging the client's distress as real while redirecting to stressors and coping is therapeutic. Dismissing or accusing the client damages rapport and increases symptom focus.

q: Which nursing interventions are appropriate for a client with a somatic symptom disorder? Select all that apply.
o: Rule out true medical causes before assuming a psychological origin
Schedule brief, regular visits not tied to new symptoms
Acknowledge the client's distress as real
Confront the client angrily about faking symptoms
Redirect the client toward coping and stress management
r: Ruling out medical causes, regular scheduled visits, validating distress, and teaching coping are appropriate. Angry confrontation is nontherapeutic and harmful to the relationship.

q: A client reports back pain and requests opioids, but findings are inconsistent and the client wants documentation to avoid returning to work. This is most consistent with:
o: Conversion disorder
Malingering
Somatic symptom disorder
Illness anxiety disorder
r: Deliberately faking symptoms for an external incentive (drugs, avoiding work) is malingering, which is not classified as a mental disorder.

q: A nurse is teaching a client who is starting fluoxetine for depression. Which statement indicates the client understands the therapy?
o: I should feel completely better within 3 days.
I will take this only on days I feel anxious.
It may take several weeks before I notice the full benefit.
I can stop the medication as soon as my mood improves.
r: SSRIs require about 4 to 6 weeks for full therapeutic effect, must be taken on a regular schedule, and should be tapered rather than stopped abruptly.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who takes phenelzine, an MAOI. Which food should the client be taught to avoid?
o: Fresh grilled chicken
Aged cheddar cheese
White rice
Steamed carrots
r: Aged cheese is high in tyramine; with an MAOI, tyramine can trigger a hypertensive crisis. Fresh, unaged foods are safe.

q: A client's lithium level is 2.3 mEq/L. Which finding does the nurse expect?
o: No symptoms; this is a therapeutic level
Mild fine hand tremor only
Coarse tremor, confusion, and ataxia
Complete resolution of manic symptoms
r: Therapeutic lithium is 0.6 to 1.2 mEq/L. A level of 2.3 indicates moderate to severe toxicity, producing coarse tremor, confusion, ataxia, and slurred speech.

q: A nurse is monitoring a client who started an SSRI and was also given a serotonergic drug. Which set of findings suggests serotonin syndrome?
o: Bradycardia, hypothermia, and constipation
Agitation, hyperreflexia, fever, and diaphoresis
Lead-pipe rigidity developing over two weeks
Dry mouth, urinary retention, and blurred vision
r: Serotonin syndrome has a rapid onset with agitation, confusion, hyperreflexia/myoclonus, fever, diaphoresis, and autonomic instability. Slow-onset lead-pipe rigidity describes NMS.

q: A nurse is teaching a client prescribed buspirone for generalized anxiety disorder. Which point is most important to include?
o: Take an extra dose whenever you feel a panic attack coming.
Full anti-anxiety effects may take 1 to 4 weeks.
This medication commonly causes physical dependence.
Expect significant drowsiness and sedation.
r: Buspirone has a delayed onset of 1 to 4 weeks, must be taken regularly (not PRN), does not cause dependence, and is non-sedating.

q: A nurse is caring for a client taking lithium. Which actions help prevent lithium toxicity? Select all that apply.
o: Maintain a consistent daily sodium intake
Encourage 2 to 3 L of fluid per day
Start a new thiazide diuretic without notifying the provider
Advise avoiding dehydration during hot weather or illness
Take NSAIDs freely for any aches
r: Lithium and sodium are handled together by the kidney, so steady sodium and hydration prevent toxicity. Thiazide diuretics and NSAIDs raise lithium levels and require provider guidance.

q: A nurse is teaching about benzodiazepines such as lorazepam. Which statements are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking this medication
These are intended for long-term daily use for years
Do not stop the medication abruptly
Avoid driving until you know how it affects you
Flumazenil can reverse a benzodiazepine overdose
r: Benzodiazepines are for short-term use; they cause CNS depression (avoid alcohol/driving), must be tapered to avoid withdrawal seizures, and are reversed by flumazenil.

q: A nurse reviews the record of a client starting carbamazepine. Which findings should the nurse monitor for as potential complications? Select all that apply.
o: Signs of infection or sore throat (blood dyscrasias)
Low serum sodium (SIADH)
A spreading rash (Stevens-Johnson syndrome)
Improved seizure control
Unusual bruising or bleeding
r: Carbamazepine can cause agranulocytosis/aplastic anemia, hyponatremia/SIADH, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and thrombocytopenia. Improved seizure control is a therapeutic effect, not a complication.

q: A nurse assesses a client taking amitriptyline, a tricyclic antidepressant. Which anticholinergic effects should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
o: Dry mouth
Constipation
Urinary retention
Diarrhea
Blurred vision
r: TCAs block cholinergic receptors, causing dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, and blurred vision. Diarrhea is not an anticholinergic effect.

q: A client taking haloperidol develops sudden spasms of the neck and tongue with an upward-fixed gaze a few hours after a dose increase. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Hold all future doses and reassure the client it will pass
Administer the prescribed IM anticholinergic such as benztropine
Draw a stat creatine kinase level
Encourage the client to walk to relieve the restlessness
r: These are signs of acute dystonia, an early extrapyramidal reaction that can threaten the airway. The priority treatment is a fast-acting anticholinergic (benztropine or diphenhydramine), typically IM/IV.

q: Which finding best distinguishes neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) from ordinary extrapyramidal symptoms?
o: Motor restlessness and pacing
Fine tremor and shuffling gait
High fever with lead-pipe rigidity and elevated creatine kinase
Involuntary lip-smacking and tongue movements
