r: NMS is a life-threatening emergency marked by hyperthermia, severe 'lead-pipe' muscle rigidity, autonomic instability, altered mental status, and a sharply elevated CK. The other options describe akathisia, parkinsonism, and tardive dyskinesia.

q: A client on clozapine calls to report a fever and sore throat. What is the nurse's priority concern?
o: Tardive dyskinesia
Agranulocytosis
Metabolic syndrome
Acute dystonia
r: Clozapine can cause agranulocytosis, a dangerous fall in neutrophils. Fever and sore throat may signal infection from neutropenia, so the ANC must be checked before assuming a minor illness.

q: Which class of antipsychotic is most strongly associated with metabolic syndrome (weight gain, hyperglycemia, and dyslipidemia)?
o: First-generation high-potency agents
Second-generation (atypical) agents
Anticholinergic antiparkinson agents
Depot first-generation agents
r: Second-generation antipsychotics such as olanzapine and quetiapine are most linked to metabolic syndrome, so weight, waist circumference, fasting glucose/A1c, and lipids are monitored.

q: Before starting oral naltrexone for alcohol use disorder in a client with a history of opioid use, the nurse should confirm that the client has been opioid-free for approximately how long?
o: 12 to 24 hours
2 to 3 days
7 to 10 days
4 to 6 weeks
r: Naltrexone is an opioid antagonist and will precipitate acute withdrawal if opioids are still present. A drug-free interval of about 7 to 10 days is needed before the first dose.

q: A nurse is teaching a client who will begin disulfiram. Which points should be included? Select all that apply.
o: Avoid alcohol in all forms, including mouthwash and cough syrup
Aftershave and colognes can trigger a reaction
The reaction can occur up to 2 weeks after the last dose
A small amount of wine with dinner is acceptable
Report flushing, throbbing headache, nausea, and palpitations
r: Disulfiram causes acetaldehyde buildup with any alcohol exposure, so all sources must be avoided, including hidden ones; the reaction can occur up to about 2 weeks after stopping. No amount of alcohol is safe, making the wine statement incorrect.

q: Which teaching points are appropriate for a school-age child starting methylphenidate for ADHD? Select all that apply.
o: Give the last dose by mid-afternoon to limit insomnia
Monitor height and weight over time
Store the medication in a locked, secure place
Give doses on an empty stomach for best absorption
The medication is a controlled substance and should never be shared
r: Stimulants cause insomnia, appetite suppression with growth effects, and have abuse potential (Schedule II). Doses should be given with or after meals to reduce appetite loss, so the empty-stomach instruction is incorrect.

q: Which are recognized extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) associated with antipsychotic therapy? Select all that apply.
o: Acute dystonia
Akathisia
Parkinsonism
Tardive dyskinesia
Agranulocytosis
r: Acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, and tardive dyskinesia are the four EPS types. Agranulocytosis is a hematologic complication (notably with clozapine), not an EPS.

q: A nurse is monitoring a child taking atomoxetine for ADHD. Which finding requires immediate follow-up?
o: Mild decrease in appetite
Report of new or worsening suicidal thoughts
Gradual improvement in focus over two weeks
Occasional stomach upset with dosing
r: Atomoxetine carries a boxed warning for increased suicidal ideation in children and adolescents. New or worsening suicidal thoughts require immediate follow-up; the other findings are expected or minor.

q: A client in alcohol withdrawal is at risk for seizures and delirium tremens. Which medication class is the mainstay of treatment?
o: Benzodiazepines
First-generation antipsychotics
CNS stimulants
Opioid antagonists
r: Benzodiazepines (such as chlordiazepoxide, diazepam, or lorazepam) are the standard treatment for alcohol withdrawal because they prevent withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens and are then tapered.

q: A nurse caring for a client actively dying and no longer responsive should keep which principle in mind when providing care?
o: Vision is the last sense to be lost, so keep the lights dim
Hearing is thought to be the last sense to be lost, so continue speaking calmly to the client
The client can no longer perceive anything, so conversation is unnecessary
Touch should be avoided because it may startle an unresponsive client
r: Hearing is believed to be the last sense a dying person loses. The nurse should continue to speak to the client, explain care, and encourage the family to talk, assuming the client may still hear.

q: A client whose spouse died six years ago is unable to work, keeps the spouse's belongings untouched, and reports daily intense yearning that prevents normal functioning. This best reflects which type of grief?
o: Anticipatory grief
Normal (uncomplicated) grief
Complicated grief
Disenfranchised grief
r: Complicated grief is prolonged, intense, and impairs daily functioning well beyond the expected time frame, raising the risk for major depression. Normal grief eases over time and allows a return to function.

q: Which statement by a terminally ill client indicates the bargaining stage described by Kubler-Ross?
o: There must be a mistake in my lab results.
Why is this happening to me? It isn't fair.
If I can just live to see my son graduate, I will be at peace.
I feel ready now and I am at peace with what is coming.
r: Bargaining involves making deals, often with a higher power, to postpone the loss. Denial questions the diagnosis, anger asks 'why me,' and acceptance reflects a sense of peace.

q: A nurse manages symptoms for a client receiving hospice care. Which comfort-focused interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Administer scheduled around-the-clock opioids for pain control
Withhold opioids until pain is severe to avoid dependence
Reposition the client and give an anticholinergic for noisy secretions
Elevate the head of the bed and provide a fan for dyspnea
Perform frequent deep suctioning for the 'death rattle'
r: At end of life, comfort is the priority: opioids are given on a schedule and not withheld, secretions are managed by repositioning and anticholinergics, and dyspnea is eased with an elevated HOB and moving air. Deep suctioning is distressing and generally avoided.

q: A parent asks about a child newly diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder. Which findings are consistent with ASD? Select all that apply.
o: Impaired eye contact and not responding to own name
Delayed or absent language, sometimes with echolalia
Repetitive movements such as hand-flapping and rocking
Strong preference for routine with distress at change
A consistent drive to initiate reciprocal social play with peers
r: ASD features deficits in social communication (poor eye contact, not responding to name, language delay, echolalia) plus restricted, repetitive behaviors and insistence on sameness. Seeking reciprocal social play is not characteristic.

q: Which nursing interventions support a school-age child with ADHD? Select all that apply.
o: Provide a consistent daily routine and structure
Give clear, simple, one-step directions
Reduce environmental stimuli during tasks
Use positive reinforcement for desired behavior
Schedule the last stimulant dose at bedtime
r: Structure, simple directions, low stimulation, and positive reinforcement help the child with ADHD succeed. Stimulants are given early in the day; a bedtime dose causes insomnia.

q: A nurse plans care for a child with Tourette's disorder who has frequent motor and vocal tics in the classroom. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Apply a consequence each time a tic occurs to reduce the behavior
Educate the family and school that tics are involuntary and reduce the child's stress
Restrain the child during episodes of vocal tics
Isolate the child from peers until the tics fully resolve
r: Tics are involuntary and worsen with stress, so they should never be punished. Education, stress reduction, and support protect the child's self-esteem; medication is added for disabling tics.

q: A client's home is destroyed in a hurricane. The nurse identifies this as which type of crisis?
o: Maturational
Situational
Adventitious
Anticipatory
r: An adventitious crisis is not part of everyday life and results from a natural disaster, crime, or other traumatic community event, such as a hurricane.

q: A newly retired client reports feeling lost and without purpose. The nurse recognizes this stressor as which type of crisis?
o: Situational
Maturational
Adventitious
Reactive
r: A maturational (developmental) crisis arises from an expected life-stage transition such as marriage, a new baby, or retirement.

q: Which statement best reflects the primary goal of crisis intervention?
o: Restructure the client's personality
Provide long-term insight-oriented therapy
Return the client to at least the pre-crisis level of functioning
Prevent the client from ever experiencing anxiety again
r: Crisis intervention is short-term and directive; the goal is to restore the client to at least their baseline (pre-crisis) level of functioning, not to change the personality.

q: A nurse is providing crisis intervention. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Assess for suicidal or homicidal risk first
Take an active, directive role
Focus on the immediate, here-and-now problem
Explore unresolved childhood conflicts in depth
Help mobilize the client's support systems
r: Crisis intervention is reality-based, short-term, and directive: assess safety first, take an active role, focus on the present problem, and mobilize supports. Deep exploration of past conflicts is not appropriate during acute crisis.

q: A client with severe depression suddenly appears calm and cheerful. What is the nurse's priority interpretation?
o: The client is improving and precautions can be reduced
The client may have finalized a suicide plan and needs increased observation
The antidepressant has reached therapeutic effect
The client no longer requires monitoring
r: A sudden, unexplained calm or lift in mood in a severely depressed client is a warning sign that the person may have decided on suicide and feels relief. The nurse should increase, not reduce, observation.

q: A nurse suspects a client is suicidal. Which is the most therapeutic action?
o: Avoid mentioning suicide so as not to plant the idea
Ask directly whether the client is thinking of killing themselves
Wait for the client to bring up the topic
Focus only on the client's sleep and appetite
r: Asking directly about suicidal thoughts, plan, and means does not plant the idea. It conveys concern and is the priority assessment.

q: Which client has the highest priority risk for suicide?
o: States hopelessness but has no plan
Has a specific plan, a firearm at home, and a prior attempt
Reports feeling sad after a recent breakup
Has vague thoughts of death but strong family support
r: The highest lethality risk combines a specific plan, available and lethal means, and a prior attempt (the strongest single predictor).

q: A client is admitted on suicide precautions. Which nursing interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Provide continuous 1:1 observation, including in the bathroom
Remove belts, shoelaces, sharps, and cords from the environment
Rely on a signed no-suicide contract to ensure safety
Dispense medications in limited amounts and check for cheeking
Encourage the client to verbalize feelings
r: Safety measures include 1:1 observation, removing means, controlling medications, and encouraging expression of feelings. A no-suicide contract is not evidence-based and never substitutes for observation.

q: A client is pacing, clenching fists, and speaking loudly. Which is the nurse's best initial action?
o: Immediately place the client in physical restraints
Use a calm voice, maintain personal space, and offer PRN medication
Confront the client firmly about the behavior
Turn away to give the client privacy
r: During early escalation, verbal de-escalation is most effective: remain calm, maintain a safe distance, and offer PRN medication. Restraint is a last resort.

q: When is the use of restraint or seclusion justified?
o: When the unit is short-staffed
When the client is imminently dangerous to self or others and less-restrictive measures have failed
When a client refuses to attend group therapy
As routine punishment for rule violations
r: Restraint and seclusion are a last resort, used only for imminent danger after less-restrictive interventions fail. They are never used for convenience or punishment.

q: A provider orders restraints for an adult client. Within what time frame must the provider conduct a face-to-face evaluation?
o: Within 15 minutes
Within 1 hour
Within 4 hours
Within 8 hours
r: A face-to-face evaluation by the provider is required within 1 hour of initiating restraint or seclusion.

q: Which are legal or safety requirements for restraint and seclusion? Select all that apply.
o: A provider order is required (obtained ASAP if started in an emergency)
PRN or standing orders for restraint are acceptable
Continuous monitoring of circulation, vitals, hydration, and toileting
Release the client as soon as behavioral criteria are met
Use the least-restrictive effective intervention first
r: Restraint requires a provider order, continuous monitoring, prompt release when criteria are met, and use of the least-restrictive option. PRN or standing restraint orders are never permitted.

q: The nurse suspects intimate-partner violence. The partner insists on staying in the room. What is the nurse's priority?
o: Interview the client with the partner present to save time
Find a way to interview the client alone
Confront the partner about the suspected abuse
Document that abuse is confirmed
r: The suspected victim must be assessed alone, separated from the accompanying person, so they can disclose safely. The nurse does not interview with the suspected abuser present.

q: A nurse suspects an older adult in a care facility is being neglected. Which action is legally required?
o: Wait until abuse is proven before acting
Report the reasonable suspicion to Adult Protective Services
Discuss it only with the family
Take no action unless the client requests it
r: Nurses are mandated reporters for suspected abuse of children and vulnerable/dependent elders. Reasonable suspicion is enough; proof is not required.

q: An abused client says, 'Maybe I should just leave him tonight.' What is the nurse's best response?
o: 'Yes, you must leave immediately for your safety.'
'Let's work together on a safety plan for whatever you decide.'
'Why did you stay with him this long?'
'You should confront him about the abuse first.'
r: Leaving is the most dangerous time, and the decision belongs to the client. The nurse supports autonomy and helps develop a safety plan rather than directing the client to leave.

q: Which findings would increase the nurse's suspicion of child physical abuse? Select all that apply.
o: Injuries inconsistent with the reported mechanism
Multiple fractures in various stages of healing
A single bruise on the shin of an active toddler
Spiral fractures or patterned burns
The child appears fearful of the caregiver
r: Red flags for child abuse include injuries that don't match the story, injuries at different healing stages, spiral fractures or patterned burns, and fear of the caregiver. A single shin bruise on an active toddler is a normal finding.

q: A sexual-assault survivor asks whether she should report to police. What is the nurse's best response?
o: 'You are required to report this to the police.'
'This is your decision, and I will support whatever you choose.'
'You should report so he does not hurt anyone else.'
'It is too late to report now.'
r: Care is survivor-centered. Reporting is the survivor's choice; the nurse provides support and information without pressuring the survivor's decisions.

q: A survivor arrives at the ED after an assault and wants to shower before the forensic exam. What should the nurse explain?
o: Showering is fine and will not affect the exam
Showering, douching, or changing clothes may destroy evidence, so it is best to wait
The survivor must have the exam regardless of consent
Evidence is unimportant compared with comfort
r: To preserve evidence and chain of custody, the survivor should avoid showering, douching, voiding, brushing teeth, or changing clothes before the forensic exam, if possible, while still respecting their choices.

q: A sexual-assault survivor appears calm and emotionally flat. How should the nurse interpret this?
o: The client is probably fabricating the assault
A controlled, calm response is a normal acute reaction
The client was not seriously affected
The client is refusing care
r: In the acute phase of rape-trauma syndrome, both an expressed (crying, distressed) and a controlled (calm, flat) reaction are normal. The nurse should never judge credibility by emotional display.

q: Which actions reflect survivor-centered care after sexual assault? Select all that apply.
o: Obtain informed consent before any exam or evidence collection
Remain nonjudgmental and let the survivor control decisions
Pressure the survivor to press charges
Offer STI prophylaxis and emergency contraception
Store evidence-containing clothing in a plastic bag
r: Survivor-centered care means informed consent, nonjudgmental support, survivor-driven decisions, and offering prophylaxis. Never pressure decisions; evidence clothing goes in paper bags, not plastic, to preserve it.

q: A nurse is reinforcing teaching with a group of adolescents regarding identifying behavioral indicators of depression. Which of the following manifestations should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Grandiosity
Euphoria
Irritability
Isolation from peers
Decreased energy
r: Adolescents with depression often present with irritability (rather than sadness), isolation from peers, and decreased energy. Grandiosity and euphoria are manifestations of mania.

q: A nurse is discussing group therapy with a client who has a depressive disorder. Which of the following benefits of group therapy should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Gaining support and encouragement from other group members
Developing social skills
Decreasing feelings of isolation
Focusing on the management of symptoms
Assisting the client in choosing an antidepressant
r: Group therapy provides support and encouragement from peers and decreases isolation. Choosing an antidepressant is the provider's role, and symptom management is addressed individually rather than being the purpose of the group.

q: A nurse is collecting data from an adolescent client who has anorexia nervosa. Which of the following findings should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
o: Hypokalemia
Amenorrhea
Altered body image
Tachycardia
Erosion of teeth
r: Expect hypokalemia, amenorrhea, and altered body image. Anorexia typically causes bradycardia (not tachycardia); tooth erosion is a purging finding associated with bulimia nervosa.

q: A nurse is collecting data from a client who is taking chlorpromazine. Which of the following findings should the nurse identify as extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS)? Select all that apply.
o: Sexual dysfunction
Fidgeting behavior
Impaired gait
Fluctuating vital signs
Muscle contractions of the neck
r: EPS include akathisia (fidgeting/restlessness), pseudoparkinsonism (impaired/shuffling gait), and acute dystonia (muscle contractions of the neck). Sexual dysfunction is an adverse effect but not EPS; fluctuating vital signs suggest NMS.

q: A nurse is collecting data from a client who is experiencing alcohol withdrawal delirium. Which of the following findings should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
o: Hypotension
Grandiosity
Paranoid delusions
Visual hallucinations
Tremors
r: Alcohol withdrawal delirium causes paranoid delusions, visual hallucinations, and tremors, along with hypertension and tachycardia — not hypotension. Grandiosity is a manic finding.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who is experiencing acute anxiety. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Speak to the client using a high-pitched voice
Validate the client's feelings
Avoid eye contact when addressing the client
Identify the cause of the anxiety
Establish rapport with the client
r: Validate feelings, identify the cause, and establish rapport. Use a calm, low-pitched voice and maintain appropriate eye contact.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has dementia. When performing a mental status examination (MSE), the nurse includes which of the following? Select all that apply.
o: Level of consciousness
Long-term memory
Presence of suicidal thoughts
Level of orientation
Ability to perform calculations
r: The MSE includes level of consciousness, thought content (including suicidal thoughts), orientation, and calculation ability — per this ATI item, long-term memory is not the indicated component here.

q: A nurse in a long-term care facility is performing a mental status examination (MSE) for a newly admitted client who has dementia. Which of the following data should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Long-term memory
Grooming
Affect
Presence of pain
Support systems
r: The MSE covers memory, appearance/grooming, and affect. Pain and support systems belong to the broader nursing assessment, not the MSE itself.

q: A nurse is preparing for an in-service with nursing staff to discuss substance use disorders. Which of the following should the nurse include as etiological factors of addictive disorders? Select all that apply.
o: Asian ethnicity
Family history of addiction
Low self-esteem
Poor educational resources
Lack of support system
r: Family history, low self-esteem, poor educational resources, and lack of support are etiological factors. Asian ethnicity is associated with lower risk (ALDH variant causes a flushing reaction that discourages drinking).

q: A nurse on an inpatient unit is caring for a newly admitted client who has anorexia nervosa. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Offer specific privileges for sustained weight gain
Monitor the client's weight daily after first voiding
Stay with the client during meals and for 1 hr afterward
Give the client a weight gain goal of 4 to 5 lb per week
Encourage the client to keep a diary of daily food intake
r: Behavioral rewards, daily post-void weights, meal supervision (during + 1 hr after, to prevent purging), and a food diary are standard. A realistic goal is 1–2 lb/week — 4–5 lb risks refeeding syndrome.

q: A nurse is contributing to the plan of care for a client who has signs of alcohol intoxication. Which of the following interventions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Check the client's pupil reactivity
Obtain a blood sample
Prepare the client for a CT scan
Perform a developmental screening test
Obtain a prescription for as-needed restraints
r: Check pupil reactivity (neuro status), obtain a blood sample (blood alcohol level), and prepare for a CT scan to rule out injury. Developmental screening is irrelevant, and PRN restraint prescriptions are not permitted.

q: A nurse is collecting data from a child who has autism spectrum disorder. Which of the following findings should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
o: Spins a toy repetitively
Delayed language development
Consistent limit-testing
Short attention span
Ritualistic behavior
r: ASD features repetitive motions, delayed language, and ritualistic behavior. Limit-testing suggests oppositional defiant disorder; short attention span suggests ADHD.

q: A nurse is discussing the possible physical effects of alcohol withdrawal with a newly licensed nurse. Which of the following effects should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Illusions
Nystagmus
Seizures
Polyphagia
Tremors
r: Alcohol withdrawal causes illusions, seizures, and tremors. Nystagmus is associated with intoxication/Wernicke encephalopathy, and polyphagia is not a withdrawal effect.

q: A nurse is discussing comorbidities associated with eating disorders with a newly licensed nurse. Which of the following comorbidities should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Schizophrenia
Depression
Obsessive-compulsive disorder
Anxiety
Breathing-related sleep disorder
r: Depression, OCD, and anxiety commonly co-occur with eating disorders. Schizophrenia and breathing-related sleep disorders are not typical comorbidities.

q: A nurse is assisting with a community health education class about suicide prevention. Which of the following should the nurse identify as risk factors for suicide? Select all that apply.
o: Age greater than 45 years
Substance use disorder
Female gender
Currently married
Schizophrenia
r: Age > 45, substance use disorder, and schizophrenia increase risk. Male gender carries higher completed-suicide risk, and marriage is generally protective.

q: A nurse is collecting data from a client who reports that he has obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). Which of the following findings should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
o: Perfectionist behavior
Irrational fear of certain objects
Unaware of compulsions
Rule-conscious behavior
Difficulty relaxing
r: Expect perfectionism, rule-conscious behavior, and difficulty relaxing. Clients with OCD are aware their compulsions are irrational; irrational fear of objects describes a specific phobia.

q: A nurse is assisting with an educational session for caregivers of older adult clients who have dementia. Which of the following topics should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Available community resources
Legal services
Maladaptive responses to grief
Actions to reduce stress
Social support systems
r: Caregiver teaching covers community resources, legal services (advance directives, power of attorney), stress reduction, and social support. Maladaptive grief responses are not a standard caregiver-education topic.

q: A nurse is collecting data from a newly admitted client who has bipolar disorder and is displaying manic behavior. Which of the following findings should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
o: Reports sleeping for long periods of time
Reports spending large sums of money
Talking in rapid, continuous speech
Interacting with others in a flirtatious way
Exhibiting clang associations
r: Mania features excessive spending, pressured speech, flirtatious/disinhibited behavior, and clang associations. Clients in mania have a decreased need for sleep.

q: A nurse facilitating a group therapy session is listening to clients discuss coping strategies. Which of the following statements indicate adaptive coping? Select all that apply.
o: "I sleep in in the mornings."
"I isolate myself in my room for a few hours when things get overwhelming."
"I call a friend who makes me smile and laugh."
"I think about being on my favorite beach vacation."
"I tense and release my muscles, starting with my feet."
r: Calling a supportive friend, guided imagery (beach visualization), and progressive muscle relaxation are adaptive. Oversleeping and isolating are avoidance — maladaptive.

q: A nurse is collecting data from a client who is taking clozapine. Which of the following findings indicate the client is experiencing adverse effects? Select all that apply.
o: Muscle rigidity
Tinnitus
Elevated temperature
Bradycardia
Drooling
r: Muscle rigidity + elevated temperature suggest NMS; elevated temperature can also signal agranulocytosis-related infection. Drooling (sialorrhea) is a known clozapine effect. Clozapine causes tachycardia, not bradycardia.

q: A nurse in a mental health facility is caring for a client who was involuntarily admitted. Which of the following client statements should the nurse recognize as accurate? Select all that apply.
o: "Before I agree to any treatment, you must tell me about my alternatives."
"My wife put me here, and now you can tell her anything I say."
"I am going to kill myself, and there is nothing you can do about it."
"I do not have to take any medications."
"I have the right to ask the court to decide if I can be held here involuntarily."
r: Involuntarily admitted clients retain informed consent (including alternatives), the right to refuse medications, and the right to a court hearing. Confidentiality still applies to family, and staff must intervene to prevent suicide.

q: A nurse is caring for a school-age child who has a history of conduct disorder. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Place the child in a vest restraint when disruptive behavior occurs
Shorten a reading activity when the child appears to become frustrated
Introduce some humor during interactions with the child
Redirect with physical activities when the child's disruptive behavior begins
Explain to the child the need to pick up crayons when thrown on the floor
r: Shorten frustrating activities, use humor, redirect to physical activity, and hold the child accountable for behavior (picking up thrown crayons). Restraints are never used for disruptive behavior alone.

q: A nurse is assisting with a psychosocial assessment of an adolescent client. Which of the following factors indicate a potential risk for suicide? Select all that apply.
o: Sudden decline in school performance
Death of a parent at a young age
Recent or impending move
Sense of responsibility to family
Low parental expectations
r: Risk factors: declining school performance, early parental death, recent/impending move, and low parental expectations. A sense of responsibility to family is protective.

q: A nurse is teaching newly licensed nurses about the progressive nature of Alzheimer's disease. Which of the following are manifestations of the moderate stage? Select all that apply.
o: Inability to perform common tasks
Inability to recognize family members
Exhibits wandering behaviors
Inability to find commonly used items
Difficulty remembering how to swallow
r: Moderate stage: inability to perform common tasks and wandering. Failing to recognize family and forgetting how to swallow occur in the severe stage; misplacing common items is an early finding.

q: A nurse is reviewing the medical record of a client who attempted suicide. Which of the following findings should the nurse identify as risk factors for suicide? Select all that apply.
o: Access to firearms
Pregnancy
Unemployment
Diagnosis of major depressive disorder
Recent marriage
r: Access to firearms, unemployment, and major depressive disorder are risk factors. Pregnancy and recent marriage are generally protective.

q: A nurse is preparing to assist with the care of a client who is to undergo electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). Which of the following equipment should the nurse set up in the room prior to the treatment? Select all that apply.
o: Flexible sigmoidoscope
Electrocardiogram (ECG) monitor
Portable x-ray machine
Oxygen saturation monitor
Electroencephalogram (EEG) monitor
r: ECT requires ECG (cardiac monitoring), pulse oximetry, and EEG (to confirm seizure activity). A sigmoidoscope and x-ray machine are not part of ECT setup.

q: A nurse in an acute mental health center is performing a physical assessment on a client. Which of the following findings should the nurse document under the integumentary system? Select all that apply.
o: Needle tracks
Ecchymosis
Skeletal deformities
Numbness
Alopecia
r: Needle tracks, ecchymosis (bruising), and alopecia are skin/hair findings. Skeletal deformities are musculoskeletal; numbness is neurological.

q: A nurse on an inpatient psychiatric unit is caring for a client who has generalized anxiety disorder (restlessness, irritability, insomnia, isolating, missing work). Which of the following actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Stay with the client
Encourage the client to join the other clients in the dayroom
Instruct the client to sit and take 6 to 12 breaths into a paper bag placed over the nose and mouth
Offer the client high-calorie snack food
Administer acetaminophen to the client
Provide the client detailed instructions regarding daily activities
Speak to the client in a relaxed manner
r: Stay with the client (safety, reduces anxiety), use paper-bag rebreathing for hyperventilation, offer high-calorie snacks (anxiety burns energy), and speak in a relaxed manner. The dayroom adds stimulation, acetaminophen is unindicated, and detailed instructions overwhelm an anxious client.

q: A nurse in a long-term care facility is admitting a client who has dementia (nighttime confusion, poor appetite, forgetfulness, agitation). Which of the following interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
o: Obtain the client's weight weekly
Offer the client finger foods for meals
Speak loudly when addressing the client
Give one task at a time to the client
Turn the client's TV on at night when they are unable to sleep
Encourage the client to take deep breaths when feeling agitated
Assess the client's memory every shift
r: Weekly weights (poor appetite), finger foods, one task at a time, and deep breathing for agitation are appropriate. Speak in a calm normal tone, keep the environment quiet at night (TV worsens sundowning), and every-shift memory checks are unnecessary.

q: A 14-year-old client with anorexia nervosa is in the ED after fainting; the client has been refusing to eat and exercising for hours daily. Which of the following 5 findings require immediate follow-up by the nurse? Select all that apply.
o: Magnesium level
Sodium level
Phosphate level
Blood pressure
Respiratory rate
Capillary refill
Glucose level
r: Priorities: electrolytes (Mg, Na), blood pressure (hypotension caused the syncope), capillary refill (perfusion), and glucose (starvation hypoglycemia). Per this item's key, phosphate and respiratory rate are not the five priority findings.

q: A client in the ED reports "passing out" at school (BP 84/48, HR 48). The nurse collects data for manifestations of anorexia nervosa. Which of the following findings should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
o: Client has soft, unpigmented hair on their arms
Client's hair appears brittle and thin
Client reports preoccupation with thoughts about food
Client comments that they are too thin and need to gain weight
Client reports being "too tired" and lacking interest in daily workouts at the gym
Client reports consuming around 600 calories per day
r: Expect lanugo, brittle thinning hair, preoccupation with food, and severe caloric restriction. Clients see themselves as fat despite being underweight and typically exercise excessively.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has borderline personality disorder taking naltrexone and fluoxetine. Which of the following findings in the health record require immediate follow-up? Select all that apply.
o: Sexual behaviors
Financial status
Frequency of hospitalizations
BUN level
Sodium level
Increased use of mood-altering substances
Hepatitis viral study (HAA) results
Hgb level
Loss of parent
r: Follow up on impulsive sexual behaviors and financial problems (impulsivity/self-harm risk), sodium (SSRIs can cause hyponatremia), substance use (relapse risk on naltrexone), hepatitis results (naltrexone is hepatotoxic), and loss of a parent (abandonment triggers in BPD).

q: A client with anorexia nervosa (BMI 17, vomiting after meals, laxative/diuretic use, excessive exercise) — which of the following findings in the EHR require follow-up by the nurse? Select all that apply.
o: WBC count
Magnesium level
Body temperature
Potassium level
Heart rate
Sodium level
Blood pressure
ECG
r: Follow up on hypothermia, potassium (purging causes hypokalemia), heart rate (bradycardia/dysrhythmias), blood pressure (hypotension), and the ECG (electrolyte-related dysrhythmias are the leading cause of death).

q: A client who has bipolar disorder reports 3 days of diarrhea, upset stomach, irritability, confusion, and a new right-hand tremor. Which of the following 6 items require immediate follow-up? Select all that apply.
o: Lithium level
Acetaminophen
Sodium level
Lithium dosage
BUN level
TSH level
Levothyroxine dosage
White blood cell count
Blood pressure
r: The findings suggest lithium toxicity: check the lithium level and dosage, sodium (hyponatremia raises lithium levels), BUN (renal excretion), and TSH/levothyroxine (lithium causes hypothyroidism, and thyroid status affects presentation).

q: An outpatient client (BMI 20.1) reports overeating with self-induced vomiting every weekday evening and daily laxative/diuretic use. Which of the following findings indicate the client has bulimia nervosa? Select all that apply.
o: BMI of 20.1 (within the expected range)
Erosion of teeth and numerous dental caries
Overeating with subsequent episodes of induced vomiting; daily laxative and diuretic use
Frequent premature ventricular contractions (PVCs)
Potassium 3.2 mEq/L
Reports a good relationship with family
r: Bulimia nervosa typically presents at a normal weight, with tooth erosion from vomiting, the binge–purge cycle itself, and purging complications: hypokalemia and resulting dysrhythmias (PVCs).

q: A client is admitted by court order after a DUI arrest, with a history of criminal behavior since their teens. During group therapy the nurse observes the client. Which findings are consistent with antisocial personality disorder? Select all that apply.
o: Sitting in a rigid posture at the beginning of group
Attempts to intimidate other clients during group therapy
Failure to pay rent
Expresses that they feel empty inside
Requests to lead the group discussion
r: ASPD findings: tense/rigid hostile posturing, intimidation of others, and disregard for financial obligations (unpaid rent). Chronic emptiness is characteristic of borderline personality disorder.

q: A client has borderline personality disorder, alcohol use disorder, and suicidal ideation. Which of the following nursing actions are anticipated for this client? Select all that apply.
o: Initiate suicide precautions
Maintain the same staff members caring for the client
Instruct the client to avoid foods with tyramine
Apply wrist restraints
Offer sympathy and attention in response to maladaptive behavior
Encourage the client to talk about feelings prior to maladaptive behavior
Offer the client opportunities for physical exercise
Explore feelings of abandonment with the client
r: Anticipate suicide precautions, talking through feelings before acting out, physical exercise, and exploring abandonment. Rotating (not fixed) staff prevents dependence/splitting; tyramine teaching is for MAOIs; restraints and rewarding maladaptive behavior with attention are contraindicated.

q: A client with bipolar I disorder (multiple hospitalizations, drinks up to 5 energy drinks/day) is admitted in acute mania and is aggressive. Which of the following prescriptions/orders are anticipated? Select all that apply.
o: Ensure the client's room is brightly lit
Verbally confront the client
Apply wrist restraints
Administer olanzapine 10 mg IM stat
r: For dangerous aggression, anticipate IM olanzapine and, if less restrictive measures fail, restraints. Bright lighting increases stimulation and confrontation escalates mania — both contraindicated.

q: A client has type 2 diabetes mellitus, binge-eating disorder since age 14, and obesity. Which of the following interventions are anticipated? Select all that apply.
o: Request a potassium supplement for the client
Instruct the client to weigh themselves daily
Encourage the client to eat small, frequent meals
Recommend the client journal about their feelings
Instruct the client to plan meals ahead
r: Anticipate small frequent meals, journaling (links feelings to eating), and meal planning. Potassium supplements are for purging disorders, and daily self-weighing reinforces preoccupation with weight.

q: A withdrawn client with depression is started on new prescriptions; on day 3 the client eats an aged cheddar omelet with smoked salmon. Which of the following prescriptions should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
o: Hydrocodone/acetaminophen 5/325 mg PO every 6 hr PRN headache
Paroxetine 20 mg PO daily
Lorazepam 2 mg PO every 8 hr as needed for anxiety
Nifedipine 10 mg PO once
r: The tyramine-rich meal (aged cheese, smoked fish) in a client on an MAOI risks hypertensive crisis — anticipate nifedipine to lower BP and PRN lorazepam. Opioids are avoided, and adding an SSRI (paroxetine) to an MAOI risks serotonin syndrome.

q: A client has antisocial personality disorder and cocaine use disorder. Which of the following orders are anticipated? Select all that apply.
o: Provide rewards for positive behavior
Use bargaining to improve behavior
Maintain a low-stimuli environment
Ignore escalating behavior
r: Reward positive behavior and keep stimulation low. Bargaining lets the client manipulate limits, and escalating behavior must be addressed early — never ignored.

q: A nurse in the ED is caring for a client in acute mania who has a history of bipolar disorder, cholecystitis, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Which of the following 3 interventions should the nurse implement? Select all that apply.
o: Offer the client finger foods
Stay with the client
Place the client in a room close to the nurses' station
Offer the client a caffeinated beverage
Weigh the client daily
r: Finger foods allow eating while moving, staying with the client maintains safety, and daily weights track nutrition. Caffeine worsens mania, and rooms near the nurses' station add stimulation — per this item's key, a quiet room away from activity is preferred.

q: A client on an increased dose of sertraline who also took several doses of sumatriptan presents restless, irritable, diaphoretic with diarrhea and chills. Which of the following 4 findings should the nurse monitor that indicate serotonin syndrome? Select all that apply.
o: Potassium level
Temperature
Respiratory rate
Medications the client is taking
Blood pressure
Abdominal pain
White blood cell count
r: Serotonin syndrome: monitor temperature (hyperthermia), the serotonergic medication combination (SSRI + triptan), blood pressure (labile/hypertension), and GI symptoms (abdominal pain, diarrhea, hyperactive bowel sounds).

q: A client with bulimia nervosa (tooth erosion, parotid swelling, calluses on hands, peripheral edema) is being treated in an outpatient clinic. Which of the following 4 assessments indicate a therapeutic response to the treatment plan? Select all that apply.
o: Laxative abuse
ECG report
BUN level
Potassium level
Overeating/purging cycle
Coping skills
r: Therapeutic response is shown by decreased laxative abuse, a normalizing ECG, a normal potassium, and improved coping skills — per this item's key.

q: A client lost their partner of 30 years four weeks ago, was unable to be at the bedside, and is experiencing prolonged grief. Which of the following 3 findings indicate the client is progressing? Select all that apply.
o: Plans for the future
Feelings of guilt
Activities with others
Sleep pattern
Weight
r: Progress is shown by making future plans, acknowledging and working through guilt, and resuming activities with others — per this item's key.

q: A client on an inpatient unit is escalating: shouting at clients and staff, refusing redirection, medication, and de-escalation. The client is placed in seclusion. Which of the following 3 actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Allow the client to return to the dayroom immediately following seclusion
Complete neuromuscular checks every 15 min
Escort the client to the restroom as needed
Speak to the client in a calm, matter-of-fact manner
Obtain a PRN prescription for restraints
Offer the client food and liquid every 4 hr
r: During seclusion/restraint: circulation and neuromuscular checks every 15 min, toileting as needed, and a calm, matter-of-fact approach. PRN restraint prescriptions are prohibited, reintegration is gradual, and food/fluids are offered more frequently (about every 2 hr).

q: A client with acute mania received 5 mg IM midazolam in the ED; 45 minutes later the client is responsive only to painful stimuli. Which of the following 3 prescriptions should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
o: Administer IM naloxone
Administer activated charcoal
Administer 0.9% sodium chloride IV
Monitor the effects of IV flumazenil
Prepare the client for intubation
Begin chest compressions
Prepare the client for electroconvulsive therapy
r: Benzodiazepine oversedation: give IV fluids, reverse with flumazenil (a benzodiazepine antagonist — naloxone reverses opioids), and prepare for intubation in case of respiratory depression.

q: A client taking lithium is admitted with 3 days of vomiting and diarrhea, muscle twitching, slurred speech, and drowsiness. Which of the following interventions should the nurse recommend for the plan of care? Select all that apply.
o: Withhold the next dose of lithium
Initiate seizure precautions
Request a dietary consult for a low-sodium diet
Discuss the need for hemodialysis with the client
Notify the provider of potential medication interactions
r: These are signs of lithium toxicity: hold the lithium, start seizure precautions, and notify the provider of interactions. Clients on lithium need consistent, normal sodium intake (low sodium raises lithium levels); hemodialysis is reserved for severe toxicity and is a provider decision.

q: A client with major depressive disorder, a family history of suicide (mother), 10 years of psychotherapy, and 4 years of sobriety is admitted. Which of the following findings should the nurse identify as risk factors for suicide? Select all that apply.
o: Family history of suicide
Low feelings of self-worth
Access to lethal means
Limited support systems
Engagement in ongoing mental health treatment
Abstinence from alcohol for 4 years
Good physical health
r: Risk factors: family history of suicide, low self-worth, access to lethal means, and limited support. Ongoing treatment, sobriety, and good physical health are protective factors.

q: A 44-year-old client with anorexia nervosa gains 5 lb in one week of admission; the nurse notes an anxious affect, "tightness" in the feet when walking, bilateral +1 pitting edema, BP 96/50, HR 122, and RR 24. Which findings indicate the client is not progressing or has a potential problem? Select all that apply.
o: Weight gain from 145 lb to 150 lb in one week
Compliance with bathroom observation after meals
Anxious affect with foot "tightness" and bilateral +1 pitting edema
Participation in group therapy sessions
BP 96/50 mm Hg, HR 122/min, RR 24/min
r: Gaining 5 lb in a week is too rapid and, with peripheral edema and unstable vital signs (hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnea), suggests refeeding syndrome — a life-threatening complication. Bathroom observation compliance and group participation show progress.

q: A client with a 5-year history of an eating disorder and excessive laxative use lost 20 lb and reports depression. Which of the following prescriptions should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
o: Haloperidol 2 mg PO every 4 hr PRN agitation
Bisacodyl 5 mg 2 tablets PO daily
Calcium carbonate 1 g 2 tablets PO daily after meals
Multivitamin 1 tablet PO daily
Mirtazapine 7.5 mg 1 tablet PO at bedtime
r: Anticipate calcium and a multivitamin (replace nutritional deficits) and mirtazapine (treats depression and promotes appetite/weight gain). A stimulant laxative (bisacodyl) is contraindicated with laxative misuse; haloperidol is nonessential.

q: First-generation (typical) antipsychotics like haloperidol are effective against which symptoms of schizophrenia?
o: Positive symptoms only (hallucinations, delusions, agitation)
Negative symptoms only (flat affect, avolition)
Both positive and negative symptoms
Cognitive symptoms only
r: 1st-gen = positive symptoms only. Strong D2 (dopamine) blockade quiets hallucinations, delusions, and agitation — but does nothing for negative symptoms. That's the 2nd-gen job. The trade-off for strong D2 blockade: high EPS risk.

q: A client is prescribed chlorpromazine (low-potency 1st-gen). Compared to haloperidol, the nurse should expect MORE:
o: Extrapyramidal symptoms
Sedation, orthostatic hypotension, and anticholinergic effects
Prolactin elevation
Tardive dyskinesia
r: Potency rule: HIGH-potency (haloperidol, fluphenazine) = high EPS. LOW-potency (chlorpromazine) = more sedation, orthostatic hypotension, anticholinergic effects, photosensitivity — but lower EPS. Teach: wear sunscreen, rise slowly.

q: A client receiving fluphenazine asks why they must return to the clinic regularly. The best response addresses that fluphenazine:
o: Requires weekly blood counts
Is available as a long-acting depot injection — injection appointments must be kept
Requires monthly ECGs
Must be taken with food
r: Fluphenazine (and haloperidol) come as long-acting depot injections — great for clients who struggle with daily pills. The teaching that matters: keep your injection appointments. Also watch for high EPS and tardive dyskinesia with long-term use.

q: A nurse suspects neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) in a client taking haloperidol. Which findings support this? Select all that apply.
o: Lead-pipe muscle rigidity
High fever
Elevated creatine kinase (CK)
Diarrhea and hyperactive bowel sounds
Onset within minutes of the first dose
r: NMS = lead-pipe rigidity + high fever + ↑CK (from muscle breakdown), developing over days. Treatment: STOP the drug, give dantrolene. Recovery takes 7–10 days after stopping — fatal if untreated. (Hyperactive GI + rapid onset = serotonin syndrome, the look-alike.)

q: Which client statement shows correct understanding of haloperidol teaching?
o: "I'll stop the drug if I feel stiff."
"I'll report stiffness, fever, or tremor to my provider and rise slowly from sitting."
"I can drink alcohol in moderation."
"This will help my lack of motivation."
r: Teach clients on haloperidol to report stiffness, fever, tremor (early NMS/EPS warning signs) and rise slowly (orthostatic hypotension). Never stop abruptly on their own, avoid alcohol, and remember: it treats positive symptoms — not motivation (a negative symptom).

q: A client is starting a second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic. Which parameters should the nurse plan to monitor for metabolic syndrome? Select all that apply.
o: Weight and BMI
Waist circumference
Blood glucose and A1c
Lipid panel
Serum sodium
r: 2nd-gen antipsychotics = metabolic syndrome risk. Monitor weight, BMI, waist, glucose/A1c, lipids, and BP. In exchange they treat positive AND negative symptoms with less EPS (D2 + 5-HT2A blockade).

q: Which second-generation antipsychotic carries the WORST risk for weight gain and metabolic effects?
o: Aripiprazole
Ziprasidone
Olanzapine
Asenapine
r: Olanzapine = worst metabolic offender — monitor glucose, A1c, lipids, weight closely. The most weight-neutral options: aripiprazole (partial D2 agonist) and ziprasidone.

q: Which atypical antipsychotic is MOST likely to cause EPS and elevated prolactin?
o: Quetiapine
Risperidone
Clozapine
Aripiprazole
r: Risperidone is the atypical that acts most like a typical — highest EPS and ↑prolactin (galactorrhea, menstrual changes) of the 2nd-gen group. It also comes as a long-acting injectable.

q: A client taking ziprasidone should be taught to:
o: Take it on an empty stomach
Take it with food and report palpitations or fainting
Avoid all dairy products
Expect significant weight gain
r: Ziprasidone: take WITH food (absorption) and watch for QT prolongation — report palpitations, dizziness, syncope. Bonus: it's weight-neutral.

q: A client is prescribed sublingual asenapine. Which instruction is correct?
o: Swallow the tablet whole with water
Do not eat or drink for 10 minutes after the dose
Take with a high-fat meal
Chew the tablet thoroughly
r: Asenapine is sublingual — it absorbs through the oral mucosa, so no eating or drinking for 10 minutes after. Oral numbness is an expected effect. Swallowing it destroys the dose.

q: A client with treatment-resistant schizophrenia is starting clozapine. Which points should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Mandatory regular ANC monitoring for agranulocytosis
Call the provider immediately for sore throat and fever
It is the only antipsychotic shown to reduce suicidality
Seizures, myocarditis, and drooling (sialorrhea) are possible adverse effects
It is a first-line agent for newly diagnosed schizophrenia
r: Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia — never first-line — because of agranulocytosis (mandatory ANC checks; sore throat + fever = call NOW). It also risks seizures, myocarditis, and sialorrhea. Its superpower: the only antipsychotic that ↓suicidality.

q: The memory hook "E-F-S-P-C" for SSRIs stands for Effective For Sadness, Panic & Compulsion. Which administration teaching is correct?
o: Take PRN when feeling sad
Take in the morning; expect 2–6 weeks for full effect
Take at bedtime with a snack
Effects begin within 24 hours
r: SSRIs are first-line, taken daily in the AM (they can disrupt sleep), and need 2–6 weeks to work. Complications hook: S-S-S — Stomach upset, Sexual dysfunction, Serotonin syndrome.

q: Why does fluoxetine require a 5-week washout before starting an MAOI, when other SSRIs need only 2 weeks?
o: It is the most anticholinergic
It has the longest half-life
It is the most sedating
It causes the most weight gain
r: Fluoxetine has the longest half-life of the SSRIs — it lingers, so the MAOI washout stretches to 5 weeks (vs. the usual 14 days). Overlap risks serotonin syndrome.

q: A client wants to stop paroxetine abruptly. The nurse's best teaching point:
o: Paroxetine can be stopped anytime
Paroxetine causes the worst discontinuation syndrome of the SSRIs — it must be tapered slowly
Paroxetine has no withdrawal effects
Switch to double doses every other day
r: Paroxetine = most anticholinergic/sedating SSRI with the WORST discontinuation syndrome — dizziness, electric-shock sensations, irritability. Always taper slowly. Also watch GI upset early and monitor ↑ suicidal thoughts, especially under age 25.

q: A client taking citalopram asks why their dose is capped at 40 mg/day. The reason is the risk of:
o: Hepatotoxicity
QT prolongation at higher doses
Agranulocytosis
Priapism
r: Citalopram prolongs the QT interval at higher doses — hence the 40 mg max. Report palpitations or fainting.

q: Which findings indicate serotonin syndrome (memory hook: SHIVERS)? Select all that apply.
o: Shivering
Hyperreflexia and myoclonus
Increased temperature
Vital sign instability
Bradycardia with hypotension
Restlessness and sweating
r: SHIVERS: Shivering, Hyperreflexia/myoclonus, Increased temp, Vital instability, Encephalopathy, Restlessness, Sweating — onset within hours. Vitals go UP, not down. Treatment: stop the drug → cyproheptadine.

q: A client on venlafaxine (SNRI) needs which parameter monitored that is less of a concern with SSRIs?
o: Blood pressure
Platelet count
Potassium
Urine output
r: Venlafaxine raises norepinephrine → raises BP. Monitor blood pressure, especially at higher doses. Never combine with TCAs or MAOIs. Duloxetine's bonus: also treats neuropathic pain and fibromyalgia.

q: Why is amitriptyline dispensed in limited quantities for a client with depression and suicidal ideation?
o: It causes dependence
TCAs are extremely lethal in overdose — cardiac dysrhythmias, seizures, coma
It is a controlled substance
It loses potency after 2 weeks
r: TCAs are VERY POTENT — lethal in overdose (even a 1–2 week supply). Limit the quantity dispensed. Side-effect hook: anticholinergic — "can't see, can't spit, can't pee, can't poop" — plus orthostatic hypotension.

q: A client taking phenelzine (MAOI) must avoid which foods to prevent hypertensive crisis? Select all that apply.
o: Aged cheese
Cured and fermented meats
Red wine and tap beer
Fresh apples
Yeast extract and overripe fruit
r: MAOI + tyramine = hypertensive crisis: severe (occipital) headache, stiff neck, fever, dilated pupils — REPORT immediately. Avoid aged/cured/fermented anything, aged wine, tap beer. Fresh foods are fine. MAOIs take ~4 weeks to work and need a 14-day washout around other antidepressants.

q: Which antidepressant is best for a client who wants to quit smoking and is worried about sexual side effects — and who has no seizure history?
o: Paroxetine
Bupropion
Amitriptyline
Trazodone
r: Bupropion: NO sexual side effects + aids smoking cessation (also used in ADHD). The catch: it lowers the seizure threshold — contraindicated in seizure disorders and eating disorders.

q: Mirtazapine is a good antidepressant choice for a client who has:
o: Obesity and hypersomnia
Insomnia and poor appetite/weight loss
Hypertension
A seizure disorder
r: Mirtazapine causes sedation + weight gain — turn those "side effects" into benefits for depressed clients with insomnia and cachexia/poor appetite. Take at bedtime.

q: A male client taking trazodone must be taught to seek emergency care for:
o: A headache lasting 2 hours
An erection lasting more than 4 hours (priapism)
Dry mouth
Vivid dreams
r: Trazodone → priapism — an erection >4 hr is a urologic emergency that can cause permanent damage. Trazodone is usually given low-dose for sleep.

q: Which teaching points are correct for a client taking lithium? Select all that apply.
o: Keep salt intake consistent — do not start a low-salt diet
Drink 2–3 L of fluid daily
Avoid NSAIDs and thiazide diuretics
Expect levels to be drawn every 1–2 months once stable
A fine hand tremor, mild thirst, and mild nausea early on mean the drug must be stopped
r: Lithium follows sodium: low sodium or dehydration → lithium climbs → toxicity. So: consistent salt, 2–3 L fluid, no NSAIDs/thiazides, levels q1–2 months. Fine tremor, thirst, mild N/V, weight gain are EXPECTED — coarse tremor is the toxic one.

q: A client is starting valproate for acute mania. Which labs/risks should the nurse monitor? Select all that apply.
o: Liver function tests (hepatotoxicity)
Platelets (thrombocytopenia)
Amylase/lipase (pancreatitis)
Pregnancy status (teratogenic — neural tube defects)
Sodium level
r: Valproate risks: liver, platelets, pancreas, pregnancy. Monitor LFTs, platelets, ammonia, and drug level. It's teratogenic (neural tube defects) — verify contraception/pregnancy status.

q: A client taking carbamazepine and oral contraceptives should be advised that carbamazepine:
o: Increases contraceptive effectiveness
Is a CYP450 inducer that decreases oral contraceptive effectiveness
Has no drug interactions
Doubles estrogen levels
r: Carbamazepine induces CYP450 → oral contraceptives fail. Use backup contraception. Also monitor CBC and LFTs — carbamazepine can cause agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, and SJS.

q: A client taking lamotrigine calls to report a new rash. The nurse should instruct the client to:
o: Apply hydrocortisone cream and monitor
Stop the medication and contact the provider immediately — any rash may be Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Take diphenhydramine and continue the drug
Ignore it if not itchy
r: Lamotrigine rule: ANY rash → STOP and CALL. Stevens-Johnson syndrome is life-threatening. Prevention: titrate the dose slowly. Lamotrigine is the maintenance mood stabilizer (lithium = long-term; valproate/carbamazepine = acute mania).

q: Why are chlordiazepoxide and diazepam the go-to medications for alcohol withdrawal?
o: They cure alcohol cravings
They are long-acting benzodiazepines that prevent fatal withdrawal seizures
They cause aversion to alcohol
They block opioid receptors
r: Alcohol withdrawal can kill via seizures — long-acting benzos (chlordiazepoxide, diazepam) taper the CNS down safely. Benzo overdose antidote: flumazenil. Never combine benzos with alcohol/opioids (respiratory depression).

q: A client with panic disorder is prescribed alprazolam. Which point is most important?
o: It is safe for years of daily use
It has high dependence potential — short-term use only, taper to stop
It takes 4 weeks to work
It has no sedative effects
r: Alprazolam: fast relief, high dependence. Short-term only, taper off — abrupt cessation risks rebound anxiety and seizures.

q: A client asks why buspirone isn't 'working' after 3 days of PRN use. The nurse explains:
o: The dose is too low
Buspirone takes 3–4 weeks and must be taken on a schedule — it does not work PRN
It should be taken with grapefruit juice to boost levels
It only works for panic attacks
r: Buspirone = long-term GAD drug: no dependence, no sedation, but 3–4 weeks to work and useless PRN or for acute panic. (And avoid grapefruit juice — it raises levels.)

q: Propranolol may be prescribed in mental health for performance anxiety or antipsychotic-induced akathisia. Before giving it, the nurse checks:
o: Temperature
Heart rate and blood pressure — hold if low
Pupil size
Deep tendon reflexes
r: Propranolol is a beta blocker: it blunts the physical symptoms of anxiety (tremor, tachycardia) and treats akathisia — but causes bradycardia and hypotension. Check HR/BP and hold if low.

q: A client taking zolpidem should be taught to:
o: Take it right before getting into bed, with 7–8 hours available for sleep
Take it with dinner
Drive only short distances after a dose
Take it PRN during the night as often as needed
r: Zolpidem: take immediately before bed with 7–8 hr to sleep. Watch for complex sleep behaviors — sleep-driving, sleep-eating — which can be dangerous; report them and stop the drug.

q: Which anxiolytic is appropriate for a client with anxiety and a history of substance use disorder who needs something without dependence risk?
o: Alprazolam
Diazepam
Hydroxyzine or buspirone
Zolpidem
r: Hydroxyzine (antihistamine) and buspirone have no dependence potential — ideal with substance use history. Hydroxyzine's trade-off: sedation and dry mouth.

q: A school-age child is starting methylphenidate. Which teaching should the nurse provide to the caregiver? Select all that apply.
o: Give the last dose before 4 PM to prevent insomnia
Monitor height and weight — appetite and growth suppression can occur
Give with caffeine to boost the effect
Avoid MAOIs and OTC cold medicines
Expect full benefit immediately
r: Stimulants: dose before 4 PM (insomnia), monitor growth/appetite/HR/BP, avoid caffeine, MAOIs, and OTC cold meds (sympathomimetics stack). Amphetamine mixtures: same rules, ~6 weeks for full response, abuse potential.

q: Atomoxetine differs from stimulant ADHD medications because it:
o: Works faster
Blocks norepinephrine reuptake and has no abuse potential
Is given only at bedtime
Cures ADHD
r: Atomoxetine = non-stimulant NRI, no abuse potential — good when diversion is a concern. Watch: weight loss, GI upset, hepatotoxicity, suicidal ideation; max effect ~6 weeks. Not a cure — pair with behavioral therapy.

q: A client taking guanfacine (alpha-2 agonist) for ADHD stops it abruptly. The nurse should monitor for:
o: Rebound hypertension
Hypoglycemia
Priapism
Neutropenia
r: Alpha-2 agonists (guanfacine, clonidine): never stop abruptly → rebound hypertension. Expected effects: sedation and hypotension. Especially useful for ADHD with tics or aggression.

q: A client starting disulfiram must avoid which products? Select all that apply.
o: All alcoholic beverages
Mouthwash containing alcohol
Hand sanitizer
Cooking sauces and extracts made with alcohol
Aged cheese
r: Disulfiram = aversion therapy: ANY alcohol → violent illness. That includes hidden alcohol — mouthwash, sanitizer, sauces, extracts. Start ≥12 hr after the last drink; effects persist ~2 weeks after stopping. Monitor LFTs. (Aged cheese is the MAOI list — don't mix them up!)

q: Before starting naltrexone for opioid use disorder, the client must be:
o: On a stable opioid dose
Opioid-free first — otherwise it precipitates acute withdrawal
Alcohol-free for 6 months
Taking methadone concurrently
r: Naltrexone blocks the reward of alcohol AND opioids — but given to someone with opioids on board, it slams them into withdrawal. Client must be opioid-free first.

q: A client received naloxone for an opioid overdose and is now alert. Twenty minutes later they become drowsy with slow respirations again. Why?
o: The overdose is psychological
Naloxone is short-acting — it can wear off before the opioid does, so repeat dosing is often needed
Naloxone causes sedation
The client took a benzodiazepine
r: Naloxone reverses opioid respiratory depression but is SHORT-acting — the opioid can outlast it. Keep monitoring and repeat doses as needed. It may also precipitate acute withdrawal.

q: Methadone and buprenorphine are used in opioid use disorder as:
o: Aversion therapy
Replacement (maintenance) therapy to prevent withdrawal and cravings
Overdose reversal agents
Sleep aids
r: Methadone/buprenorphine = maintenance therapy — a controlled opioid replacement that prevents withdrawal and cravings so the client can stabilize. Acamprosate plays the parallel role for alcohol: it reduces cravings, started after withdrawal (~12 hr+ sober).

q: A family asks if donepezil will cure their parent's Alzheimer's disease. The accurate response:
o: "Yes, with consistent use."
"It preserves acetylcholine and may slow decline, but it does not cure or reverse the disease."
"It regenerates brain tissue."
"It only treats agitation."
r: Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) preserve acetylcholine → slow the decline. They do NOT cure or reverse. Watch: bradycardia and GI effects (N/V/diarrhea) — take with food.

q: Memantine is added for a client with Alzheimer's disease. Memantine is indicated for:
o: Mild, early-stage disease only
Moderate to severe Alzheimer's — it regulates glutamate via NMDA antagonism
Vascular dementia only
Delirium
r: Memantine = NMDA antagonist for MODERATE-to-SEVERE Alzheimer's; it regulates glutamate and can be combined with a cholinesterase inhibitor. (Donepezil = the acetylcholine drug; memantine = the glutamate drug.)

q: A nurse in an outpatient mental health clinic is preparing to conduct an initial client interview. When conducting the interview, which of the following actions should the nurse identify as the priority?
o: Coordinate holistic care with social services.
Identify the client's perception of their mental health status.
Include the client's family in the interview.
Teach the client about their current mental health disorder.
r: Assessment is the priority action. Identifying the client's perception of their mental health status provides important information about the client's psychosocial history.

q: A charge nurse is discussing mental status examinations with a newly licensed nurse. Which of the following statements by the newly licensed nurse indicates an understanding of the teaching? (Select all that apply.)
o: "To assess cognitive ability, I should ask the client to count backward by sevens."
"To assess affect, I should observe the client's facial expression."
"To assess language ability, I should instruct the client to write a sentence."
"To assess remote memory, I should have the client repeat a list of objects."
"To assess the client's abstract thinking, I should ask the client to identify our most recent presidents."
r: Counting backward by sevens assesses cognitive ability. Observing facial expression assesses affect. Writing a sentence indicates language ability. Remote memory is tested by asking the client to state a verifiable fact from their past (date of birth). Abstract thinking is tested by asking the client to interpret something.

q: A nurse is planning care for a client who has a mental health disorder. Which of the following actions should the nurse include as a psychobiological intervention?
o: Assist the client with systematic desensitization therapy.
Teach the client appropriate coping mechanisms.
Assess the client for comorbid health conditions.
Monitor the client for adverse effects of medications.
r: Monitoring for adverse effects of medications is a psychobiological intervention. Systematic desensitization is cognitive/behavioral. Teaching coping mechanisms is counseling/health teaching. Assessing for comorbid conditions is health promotion and maintenance.

q: A nurse is planning a peer group discussion about the DSM-5-TR. Which of the following information should the nurse include in the discussion? (Select all that apply.)
o: The DSM-5-TR includes client education handouts for mental health disorders.
The DSM-5-TR establishes diagnostic criteria for individual mental health disorders.
The DSM-5-TR indicates recommended pharmacological treatment for mental health disorders.
The DSM-5-TR assists nurses in planning care for clients who have mental health disorders.
The DSM-5-TR indicates expected data collection findings of mental health disorders.
r: The DSM-5-TR establishes diagnostic criteria, assists nurses in planning care, and identifies expected findings. It does not contain client education handouts or recommended pharmacological treatment.

q: A nurse is told during change of shift report that a client is stuporous. When assessing the client, which of the following findings should the nurse expect?
o: The client arouses briefly in response to a sternal rub.
The client has a Glasgow Coma Scale score less than 7.
The client exhibits decorticate rigidity.
The client is alert but disoriented to time and place.
r: A stuporous client requires vigorous or painful stimuli to elicit a response. GCS less than 7 and decorticate rigidity occur with comatose clients.

q: A nurse hears a newly licensed nurse discussing a client's hallucinations in the hallway with another nurse. Which of the following actions should the nurse take first?
o: Notify the nurse manager.
Tell the nurse to stop discussing the behavior.
Provide an in-service program about confidentiality.
Complete an incident report.
r: The greatest risk is invasion of privacy through sharing confidential information in a public place. The first action is to tell the nurse to stop discussing the client's hallucinations in a public location.

q: A nurse in an emergency mental health facility is caring for a group of clients. The nurse should identify that which of the following clients requires a temporary emergency admission?
o: A client who has schizophrenia with delusions of grandeur
A client who has manifestations of depression and attempted suicide a year ago
A client who has borderline personality disorder and assaulted a homeless man with a metal rod
A client who has bipolar disorder and paces quickly around the room while talking to themselves
r: A client who is a current danger to self or others is a candidate for a temporary emergency admission.

q: A nurse decides to put a client who has a psychotic disorder in seclusion overnight because the unit is very short-staffed, and the client frequently fights with other clients. The nurse's actions are an example of which of the following torts?
o: Invasion of privacy
False imprisonment
Assault
Battery
r: Secluding a client for the convenience of the staff is false imprisonment.

q: A client tells a nurse, "Don't tell anyone but I hid a sharp knife under my mattress in order to protect myself from my roommate, who is always yelling at me and threatening me." Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
o: Keep the client's communication confidential, but talk to the client daily to convince him to admit to hiding the knife.
Keep the client's communication confidential, but watch the client and his roommate closely.
Tell the client that this must be reported to the health care team because it concerns the health and safety of the client and others.
Report the incident to the health care team, but do not inform the client of the intention to do so.
r: The information is a serious safety issue the nurse must report to the health care team, using the ethical principle of veracity.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who is in mechanical restraints. Which of the following statements should the nurse include in the documentation? (Select all that apply.)
o: "Client ate most of their breakfast."
"Client was offered 8 oz of water every hr."
"Client shouted obscenities at assistive personnel."
"Client received chlorpromazine 15 mg by mouth at 1000."
"Client acted out after lunch."
r: Documentation must include how much water was offered and how often, a description of the client's verbal communication, and the dose and time of medication. Intake and behavior must be objective and specific.

q: A charge nurse is conducting a class on therapeutic communication. Which of the following aspects of communication should the nurse identify as a component of verbal communication?
o: Personal space
Posture
Eye contact
Intonation
r: Intonation (tone of voice) is a component of verbal communication. Personal space, posture, and eye contact are nonverbal.

q: A nurse is communicating with a client. The client states, "I can't sleep. I stay up all night." The nurse responds, "You are having difficulty sleeping?" Which of the following therapeutic communication techniques is the nurse demonstrating?
o: Offering general leads
Summarizing
Focusing
Restating
r: Restating repeats the main idea expressed by the client, which encourages the client to continue.

q: A nurse is talking with the caregiver of a child who has demonstrated recent changes in behavior and mood. When the caregiver asks the nurse for reassurance about their child's condition, which of the following responses should the nurse make?
o: "I think your child is getting better. What have you noticed?"
"I'm sure everything will be okay. It just takes time to heal."
"I'm not sure what's wrong. Have you asked the doctor about your concerns?"
"I understand you're concerned. Let's discuss what concerns you specifically."
r: This reflects and accepts the caregiver's feelings and allows them to clarify. Option a interjects the nurse's opinion. Option b is false reassurance. Option c avoids the concern and indicates disinterest.

q: A nurse is communicating with a client admitted for a substance use disorder. Which of the following communication techniques should the nurse identify as a barrier to therapeutic communication?
o: Offering advice
Reflecting
Listening attentively
Giving information
r: Offering advice is a barrier to therapeutic communication. Reflecting, listening attentively, and giving information are therapeutic.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who smokes and has lung cancer. The client reports, "I'm coughing because I have that cold that everyone has been getting." The nurse should identify that the client is using which of the following defense mechanisms?
o: Reaction formation
Denial
Displacement
Sublimation
r: Denial is pretending the truth is not reality to manage the anxiety of acknowledging what is real.

q: A nurse is providing preoperative teaching for a client informed of the need for emergency surgery. The client has a respiratory rate of 30/min and says, "This is difficult to comprehend. I feel shaky and nervous." The nurse should identify which level of anxiety?
o: Mild
Moderate
Severe
Panic
r: Moderate anxiety decreases problem-solving and may hamper the ability to understand information. Vital signs may increase somewhat and the client is visibly anxious.

q: A nurse is caring for a client experiencing moderate anxiety. Which of the following actions should the nurse take when trying to give necessary information to the client? (Select all that apply.)
o: Reassure the client that everything will be okay.
Discuss prior use of coping mechanisms with the client.
Ignore the client's anxiety so that she will not be embarrassed.
Demonstrate a calm manner while using simple and clear directions.
Gather information from the client using closed-ended questions.
r: Discussing prior coping mechanisms helps the client identify effective coping. A calm presence promotes security and relaxation. Clients with moderate anxiety benefit from the direction of others.

q: A nurse is talking with a new client at risk for suicide following their partner's death. Which of the following statements by the nurse explains the purpose of milieu therapy?
o: "Milieu therapy is focused on creating a safe, healing, therapeutic environment."
"Milieu therapy is the scheduled activities focused on improved client socialization."
"Milieu therapy consists of scheduled group sessions addressing common mental health needs."
"Milieu therapy's primary focus is on client education based on individual treatment goals."
r: Milieu therapy creates an environment that is supportive, therapeutic, and safe.

q: A charge nurse is discussing the characteristics of a nurse-client relationship. Which of the following characteristics should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)
o: The needs of both participants are met.
An emotional commitment exists between the participants.
All encounters are goal-directed.
Positive behavior changes are encouraged.
Promotes balance of client autonomy and safety.
r: A therapeutic relationship is goal-directed, encourages positive behavioral change, and balances autonomy and safety. It focuses on the client only; an emotional commitment characterizes an intimate/social relationship.

q: A nurse is planning care for the termination phase of a nurse-client relationship. Which of the following actions should the nurse include?
o: Discussing ways to use new behaviors
Practicing new problem-solving skills
Developing goals
Establishing boundaries
r: Discussing ways to incorporate new healthy behaviors is a termination-phase task. Practicing new problem-solving occurs in the working phase; developing goals and establishing boundaries occur in orientation.

q: A community mental health nurse is planning care to address depression among older adults. Which of the following interventions is a method of tertiary prevention?
o: Educating clients on health promotion techniques to reduce the risk of depression
Performing screenings for depression at community health programs
Establishing rehabilitation programs to decrease the effects of depression
Providing support groups for clients at risk for depression
r: Rehabilitation programs are tertiary prevention (preventing further problems in those already diagnosed). Options a and d are primary; option b is secondary.

q: A nurse is working in a community mental health facility. Which of the following services does this type of program provide? (Select all that apply.)
o: Educational groups
Medication dispensing programs
Individual counseling programs
Detoxification programs
Family therapy
r: Community mental health facilities provide educational programs, medication dispensing, individual counseling, and family therapy. Detoxification is provided in a partial hospitalization program.

q: A nurse is planning care for several clients attending community-based mental health programs. Which of the following clients should the nurse visit first?
o: A client who received a burn on the arm while using a hot iron at home
A client who requests a change of antipsychotic medication due to new adverse effects
A client who reports hearing a voice saying that life is not worth living anymore
A client who reports severe anxiety before and during a job interview
r: This client is at greatest risk for self-harm and should be seen first.

q: A nurse is assisting with discharge planning for a client who has a severe mental illness and requires supervision. The client's partner works all day but is home by late afternoon. Which of the following strategies should the nurse suggest?
