o: Receiving daily care from a home health aide.
Having a weekly visit from a nurse case worker.
Attending a partial hospitalization program.
Visiting a community mental health center on a daily basis.
r: A partial hospitalization program provides daytime treatment while allowing the client home at night with a responsible family member present. The other options do not provide adequate supervision.

q: Which of the following clients should a nurse consider for referral to an assertive community treatment (ACT) group?
o: A client in an acute care facility who has fallen several times while running down the hallway
A client who lives at home and keeps "forgetting" to come in for a scheduled monthly antipsychotic injection for schizophrenia
A client in a day treatment program who reports increasing anxiety during group therapy
A client in a weekly grief support group still missing a partner who died 3 months ago
r: An ACT group works with clients nonadherent with traditional therapy, such as the client who keeps "forgetting" their injection.

q: A nurse is teaching a client scheduled to begin classical psychoanalysis. Which of the following client statements indicates understanding?
o: "Even if my anxiety improves, I will need to continue this therapy for 6 weeks."
"The therapist will focus on my past relationships during our sessions."
"Psychoanalysis will help me reduce my anxiety by changing my behaviors."
"This therapy will address my conscious feelings about stressful experiences."
r: Classical psychoanalysis focuses on past relationships to identify the cause of the disorder.

q: A nurse is discussing free association with a client who has major depressive disorder. Which of the following client statements indicates understanding?
o: "I will write down my dreams as soon as I wake up."
"I might begin to associate my therapist with important people in my life."
"I can learn to express myself in a nonaggressive manner."
"I should say the first thing that comes to my mind."
r: Free association is the spontaneous, uncensored verbalization of whatever comes to mind. Option a is dream analysis, b is transference, c is assertiveness training.

q: A nurse is preparing to implement cognitive reframing techniques for a client who has an anxiety disorder. Which of the following techniques should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)
o: Priority restructuring
Monitoring thoughts
Diaphragmatic breathing
Journal keeping
Meditation
r: Cognitive reframing uses priority restructuring, monitoring thoughts, and journal keeping. Diaphragmatic breathing and meditation are behavioral therapy.

q: A nurse is caring for a client with a new prescription for disulfiram for alcohol use disorder. Informing the client that this medication causes nausea and vomiting when alcohol is consumed is an example of which type of treatment?
o: Aversion therapy
Flooding
Biofeedback
Dialectical behavior therapy
r: Aversion therapy pairs a maladaptive behavior with an unpleasant stimulus to promote change.

q: A nurse is assisting with systematic desensitization for a client with an extreme fear of elevators. Which of the following actions should the nurse implement?
o: Demonstrate riding in an elevator, then ask the client to imitate the behavior.
Advise the client to say "stop" out loud every time they feel an anxiety response related to an elevator.
Gradually expose the client to an elevator while practicing relaxation techniques.
Stay with the client in an elevator until the anxiety response diminishes.
r: Systematic desensitization is planned, progressive exposure while using relaxation to suppress anxiety. Option a is modeling, b is thought stopping, d is flooding.

q: A nurse wants to use democratic leadership with a group learning conflict resolution. The nurse implements this leadership by demonstrating which action?
o: Observes group techniques without interfering with the group process
Discusses a technique and then directs members to practice the technique
Asks for group suggestions of techniques and then supports discussion
Suggests techniques and asks group members to reflect on their use
r: Democratic leadership supports group interaction and decision making. Option a is laissez-faire; options b and d are autocratic.

q: A nurse forms a group focused on self-management of medications. At each meeting, two members conspire to exclude the rest of the group. This is an example of which concept?
o: Triangulation
Group process
Subgroup
Hidden agenda
r: A subgroup is a small number of people within a larger group who function separately from the group.

q: A nurse is conducting a family therapy session. The younger child tells the nurse about plans to make the older sibling look bad to earn more freedom and privileges. The nurse should identify this dysfunctional behavior as which of the following?
o: Placation
Manipulation
Blaming
Distraction
r: Manipulation is using dishonesty to support an individual agenda.

q: A nurse identifies various member roles in a group. Which of the following should the nurse identify as an individual role?
o: A member who praises input from other members
A member who follows the direction of other members
A member who brags about accomplishments
A member who evaluates the group's performance toward a standard
r: Bragging about accomplishments is an individual role that does not promote group progress toward goals.

q: A nurse is discussing acute vs. prolonged stress. Which of the following effects should the nurse identify as an acute stress response? (Select all that apply.)
o: Chronic pain
Depressed immune system
Increased blood pressure
Panic attacks
Unhappiness
r: Depressed immune system, increased blood pressure, and unhappiness are acute stress responses. Chronic pain and panic attacks are responses to prolonged stress.

q: A nurse is preparing a seminar on stress. Which of the following information should the nurse include?
o: Excessive stressors cause the client to experience distress.
The body's initial adaptive response to stress is denial.
Absence of stressors results in homeostasis.
Negative, rather than positive, stressors produce a biological response.
r: Distress results from excessive or damaging stressors, such as anxiety or anger.

q: A nurse is teaching about stress-reduction techniques. Which of the following client statements indicates understanding?
o: "Cognitive reframing will help me change my irrational thoughts to something positive."
"Progressive muscle relaxation uses a mechanical device to help me gain control over my pulse rate."
"Biofeedback causes my body to release endorphins so that I feel less stress and anxiety."
"Mindfulness allows me to prioritize the stressors that I have in my life so that I have less anxiety."
r: Cognitive reframing restructures irrational thoughts in a more positive, realistic way. Option b is biofeedback, c is physical exercise, d is priority restructuring.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who states, "I'm so stressed at work because of my coworker. I am expected to finish others' work because of their laziness!" Which of the following client statements to the coworker indicates understanding of effective communication?
o: "You really should complete your own work. I don't think it's right to expect me to complete your responsibilities."
"Why do you expect me to finish your work? You must realize that I have my own responsibilities."
"It is not fair to expect me to complete your work. If you continue, then I will report your behavior to our supervisor."
"When I have to pick up extra work, I feel very overwhelmed. I need to focus on my own responsibilities."
r: This is assertive communication—stating feelings about the behavior and promoting change. Option a can prompt defensiveness, b implies criticism, c is aggressive and threatening.

q: A nurse is teaching a client scheduled to receive ECT for major depressive disorder. Which of the following client statements indicates understanding?
o: "It is common to treat depression with ECT before trying medications."
"I can have my depression cured if I receive a series of ECT treatments."
"I should receive ECT once a week for 6 weeks."
"I will receive a muscle relaxant to protect me from injury during ECT."
r: A muscle relaxant (succinylcholine) reduces injury risk during the induced seizure. ECT is used when medications are ineffective, does not cure depression, and is typically given 2-3 times/week for 6-12 treatments.

q: A nurse is assessing a client immediately following an ECT procedure. Which of the following findings should the nurse expect? (Select all that apply.)
o: Hypotension
Paralytic ileus
Memory loss
Polyuria
Confusion
r: Transient short-term memory loss, nausea, and confusion are expected after ECT. Blood pressure usually elevates after ECT; paralytic ileus is not a finding.

q: A nurse is leading a discussion about indications for ECT. Which of the following indications should the nurse include?
o: Borderline personality disorder
Acute withdrawal related to a substance use disorder
Bipolar disorder with rapid cycling
Dysphoric disorder
r: ECT is indicated for bipolar disorder with rapid cycling.

q: A nurse is planning care for a client following surgical implantation of a VNS device. The nurse should monitor for which of the following adverse effects? (Select all that apply.)
o: Voice changes
Seizure activity
Disorientation
Cough
Neck pain
r: Voice changes, cough, and neck pain are potential adverse effects of VNS. Seizure activity and disorientation are associated with ECT.

q: A nurse observes a client who has OCD repeatedly applying, removing, and reapplying makeup. The repetitive behavior is due to which of the following underlying reasons?
o: Narcissistic behavior
Fear of rejection from staff
Attempt to reduce anxiety
Adverse effect of antidepressant medication
r: Clients with OCD demonstrate repetitive behaviors to suppress persistent thoughts/urges that cause anxiety.

q: A nurse is caring for a client experiencing a panic attack. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
o: Discuss new relaxation techniques.
Show the client how to change the behavior.
Distract the client with a television show.
Stay with the client and remain quiet.
r: During a panic attack, the nurse should quietly remain with the client to promote safety and reassurance without additional stimuli; the client cannot concentrate on new information.

q: A nurse is assessing a client who has generalized anxiety disorder. Which of the following findings should the nurse expect? (Select all that apply.)
o: Excessive worry for 6 months
Impulsive decision making
Delayed reflexes
Restlessness
Sleep disturbance
r: GAD is characterized by uncontrollable excessive worry for more than 6 months, restlessness, and sleep disturbance, along with procrastination and muscle tension—not impulsivity or delayed reflexes.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has body dysmorphic disorder. Which of the following actions should the nurse plan to take first?
o: Assess the client's risk for self-harm
Instill hope for positive outcomes
Encourage the client to participate in group therapy sessions
Assist the client to participate in treatment decisions
r: The greatest risk for a client with an anxiety or obsessive-compulsive disorder is self-harm or suicide, which should be assessed first.

q: A nurse is assessing a client who has acute stress disorder (ASD). Which of the following client behaviors should the nurse expect?
o: The client remembers many details about the traumatic incident.
The client expresses heightened elation about what is happening.
The client remembers first noticing manifestations 6 weeks after the traumatic incident.
The client expresses a sense of unreality about the traumatic incident.
r: ASD often involves dissociative manifestations including a sense of unreality. Clients usually cannot remember details and react with negative emotions; manifestations occur immediately to a few days after the event.

q: A nurse is involved in a serious and prolonged mass casualty incident. Which of the following strategies should the nurse use to help prevent developing a trauma-related disorder? (Select all that apply.)
o: Avoid thinking about the incident when it is over.
Take breaks during the incident for food and water.
Debrief with others following the incident.
Avoid displays of emotion in the days following the incident.
Take advantage of offered counseling.
r: Taking breaks for food and water, debriefing, and using counseling help prevent a trauma-related disorder.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has PTSD. Which of the following findings should the nurse expect? (Select all that apply.)
o: Difficulty concentrating on tasks
Obsessive need to talk about the traumatic event
Negative self-image
Recurring nightmares
Diminished reflexes
r: PTSD includes inability to concentrate, guilt/negative self-image, and recurring nightmares. Clients avoid talking about the event and are hypervigilant.

q: A nurse is planning care for a client who has dissociative fugue. Which of the following interventions should the nurse add to the plan of care?
o: Teach the client to recognize how stress brings on a personality change.
Repeatedly present the client with information about past events.
Make decisions for the client regarding routine daily activities.
Work with the client on grounding techniques.
r: Grounding techniques help clients with dissociative disorders experiencing derealization. Option a is for dissociative identity disorder; flooding should be avoided; the nurse should encourage the client to make their own decisions.

q: A nurse is admitting a client who has major depressive disorder and comorbid anxiety disorder. Which of the following actions is the nurse's priority?
o: Assess the risk of self-harm
Assisting the client to perform ADLs
Encouraging the client to participate in counseling
Teaching the client about medication adverse effects
r: The greatest risk is injury from self-harm; assessing self-harm risk is the highest priority.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has major depressive disorder. Which of the following should the nurse identify as a risk factor for depression? (Select all that apply.)
o: Male sex
History of chronic bronchitis
Recent death in client's family
Family history of depression
Personal history of panic disorder
r: Stressful life events, family history of depression, and comorbid anxiety/personality disorder are risk factors. Depression is twice as common in females; chronic bronchitis is not a recognized risk factor.

q: A nurse is interviewing a client who has a new diagnosis of persistent depressive disorder. Which of the following findings should the nurse expect?
o: Wide fluctuations in mood
Report of a minimum of five clinical findings of depression
Presence of manifestations for at least 2 years
Inflated sense of self-esteem
r: Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) is milder, with early onset lasting at least 2 years in adults. Wide mood fluctuations occur in bipolar; five findings occur in MDD; self-esteem is decreased, not inflated.

q: A charge nurse is discussing the care of a client who has major depressive disorder (MDD). Which of the following statements by the newly licensed nurse indicates understanding?
o: "Care during the continuation phase focuses on treating continued manifestations of MDD."
"The treatment of MDD during the maintenance phase lasts for 6 to 12 weeks."
"The client is at greatest risk for suicide during the first weeks of an MDD episode."
"Medication and psychotherapy are most effective during the acute phase of MDD."
r: The client is at greatest risk for suicide during the acute phase. Continuation focuses on relapse prevention; maintenance lasts a year or more; medication/psychotherapy are used during continuation.

q: A nurse is discussing relapse prevention with a client who has bipolar disorder. Which of the following information should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)
o: Use caffeine in moderation to prevent relapse.
Difficulty sleeping can indicate a relapse.
Begin taking your medications as soon as a relapse begins.
Participating in psychotherapy can help prevent a relapse.
Anhedonia is a clinical manifestation of a depressive relapse.
r: Sleep disturbances and anhedonia can indicate relapse; psychotherapy helps prevent relapse. The client should limit caffeine and take medications consistently to prevent relapse.

q: A nurse is planning care for a client experiencing a manic episode. Which of the following interventions should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)
o: Encourage the client to participate in group therapy.
Instruct the client to avoid napping during the day.
Offer the client high-calorie finger foods frequently.
Decrease the client's daily fiber intake.
r: Avoiding daytime napping promotes nighttime sleep. Frequent high-calorie finger foods address the inability to sit for meals and prevent weight loss/dehydration.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has bipolar disorder. The client states, "I am very rich, and I feel I must give my money to you." Which of the following responses should the nurse make?
o: "Why do you think you feel the need to give money away?"
"I am here to provide care and cannot accept this from you."
"I can request that your case manager discuss appropriate charity options with you."
"You should know that giving away your money is inappropriate."
r: This matter-of-fact, concise response is therapeutic. Option a is a "why" question, c does not recognize poor judgment, d offers disapproval.

q: A nurse is caring for a client experiencing extreme mania. Prior to administration of lithium carbonate, the client's lithium blood level is 1.2 mEq/L. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
o: Administer the next dose of lithium carbonate as scheduled.
Prepare for administration of aminophylline.
Notify the provider for a possible increase in the dosage of lithium carbonate.
Request a stat repeat of the client's lithium blood level.
r: During a manic episode the therapeutic lithium level is 0.8-1.4 mEq/L, so administering the next dose as scheduled is appropriate.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has schizophrenia and reports auditory hallucinations. Which of the following interventions should the nurse include?
o: Promote the use of music to compete with the client's auditory hallucinations.
Inform the client that the auditory hallucinations are not real.
Avoid asking the client if they are experiencing auditory hallucinations.
Instruct the client on the use of voice recognition regarding the auditory hallucinations.
r: Music can compete with hallucinations. The nurse should not argue about them but may focus on feelings, and should ask directly about hallucinations.

q: A nurse speaking with a client who has schizophrenia notices the client stop focusing and begin looking at the ceiling and talking to themselves. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
o: Stop the interview and resume later when the client can concentrate.
Ask the client, "Are you seeing something on the ceiling?"
Tell the client, "You seem to be looking at something on the ceiling. I see something there, too."
Continue the interview without commenting on the client's behavior.
r: The nurse should ask directly about the hallucination to identify needs and assess for risk of injury.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has schizophrenia and is experiencing psychosis. Which of the following findings indicates a potential psychiatric emergency?
o: The client reports command hallucinations.
The client exhibits a flat affect.
The client demonstrates echolalia.
The client has delusions of grandeur.
r: Command hallucinations instruct the client to perform an action (harm self or others), indicating a potential psychiatric emergency.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who began taking a conventional antipsychotic yesterday. Which of the following findings indicates the nurse should administer benztropine 2 mg IM?
o: Shuffling gait
Involuntary arm movements
Continual pacing
Severe spasm of the tongue, neck, face, and back
r: This describes acute dystonia, requiring rapid treatment with an antiparkinsonian agent such as benztropine. Shuffling gait is pseudoparkinsonism, involuntary arm movements are tardive dyskinesia, continual pacing is akathisia.

q: A charge nurse is preparing a staff education session on personality disorders. Which of the following characteristics associated with all personality disorders should the charge nurse include? (Select all that apply.)
o: Difficulty in getting along with other members of a group
Belief in the ability to become invisible during times of stress
Display of defense mechanisms when routines are changed
Claiming to be more important than other persons
Difficulty understanding why it is inappropriate to have a personal relationship with staff
r: Difficulty with relationships, maladaptive stress response (defense mechanisms when routines change), and difficulty with personal boundaries occur in all personality disorders. Options b and d do not.

q: A client who has borderline personality disorder says, "The nurse on the evening shift is always nice! You are the meanest nurse ever!" The nurse should recognize this as which defense mechanism?
o: Regression
Splitting
Undoing
Identification
r: Splitting is the inability to see positive and negative qualities at the same time—seeing a person as all good or all bad.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has avoidant personality disorder. Which of the following statements is expected?
o: "I feel like people won't like me if I speak up."
"I'll go to group therapy if you'll let me smoke."
"I need to feel that everyone admires me."
"I sometimes feel better if I cut myself."
r: Avoidant personality disorder involves fear of rejection and social inhibition. Option b is antisocial, c is narcissistic, d is borderline.

q: A nurse manager is discussing the care of a client who has a personality disorder. Which of the following statements by the newly licensed nurse indicates understanding?
o: "I can promote my client's sense of control by establishing a schedule."
"I should encourage clients who have a schizoid personality disorder to increase socialization."
"I should practice limit-setting to help prevent client manipulation."
"I should implement assertiveness training with clients who have antisocial personality disorder."
r: Limit-setting helps prevent manipulation. The nurse should seek client input rather than imposing a schedule, avoid pushing socialization on schizoid clients, and use assertiveness training for dependent/histrionic clients.

q: A nurse is performing an admission assessment for a client who has delirium related to an acute urinary tract infection. Which of the following findings should the nurse expect? (Select all that apply.)
o: History of gradual memory loss
Family report of personality changes
Hallucinations
Unaltered level of consciousness
Restlessness
r: Delirium causes rapid personality changes, perceptual disturbances (hallucinations), and restlessness. It has rapid onset with altered consciousness; gradual memory loss is dementia.

q: A nurse in a long-term care facility is caring for a client who has major neurocognitive disorder and attempts to wander out of the building, stating "I have to get home." Which of the following statements should the nurse make?
o: "You have forgotten that this is your home."
"You cannot go outside without a staff member."
"Why would you want to leave? Aren't you happy with your care?"
"I am your nurse. Let's walk together to your room."
r: Introducing oneself and redirecting calmly promotes reality. Option a is argumentative, b is negative, c is a "why" question.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has early stage Alzheimer's disease and a new prescription for donepezil. Which of the following statements should the nurse include when teaching about the medication?
o: "You should avoid taking over-the-counter acetaminophen while on donepezil."
"You should take this medication before going to bed at the end of the day."
"You will be screened for underlying kidney disease prior to starting donepezil."
"You should stop taking donepezil if you experience nausea or diarrhea."
r: Donepezil has a long half-life and is given once daily at bedtime. Clients should avoid NSAIDs (not acetaminophen), be screened for heart/pulmonary disease, and not abruptly stop the medication.

q: A home health nurse is assessing the home of a client who has Alzheimer's disease for safety. Which of the following suggestions should the nurse make to decrease the risk for injury? (Select all that apply.)
o: Install extra locks at the top of exit doors.
Place rugs over electrical cords.
Put cleaning supplies on the top of a shelf.
Place the client's mattress on the floor.
Install light fixtures above stairs.
r: Door locks that are hard to open reduce wandering; a mattress on the floor and lights above stairs reduce falls. Rugs are a fall hazard; cleaning supplies should be in locked cupboards.

q: A nurse is planning a staff education program on substance use in older adults. Which of the following information should the nurse include?
o: Older adults require higher doses of a substance to achieve a desired effect.
Older adults commonly use rationalization to cope with a substance use disorder.
Older adults are at an increased risk for substance use following retirement.
Older adults develop substance use to mask manifestations of dementia.
r: Retirement and other life-change stressors increase substance use risk in older adults.

q: A nurse is assessing a client who has alcohol use disorder and is experiencing withdrawal. Which of the following findings should the nurse expect? (Select all that apply.)
o: Bradycardia
Fine tremors of both hands
Decreased blood pressure
Vomiting
Restlessness
r: Fine tremors, vomiting, and restlessness are expected in alcohol withdrawal. Withdrawal causes tachycardia and hypertension, not bradycardia/hypotension.

q: A nurse is planning care for a client experiencing benzodiazepine withdrawal. Which of the following interventions should the nurse identify as the priority?
o: Orient the client frequently to time, place, and person.
Offer fluids and nourishing diet as tolerated.
Implement seizure precautions.
Encourage participation in group therapy sessions.
r: The greatest risk is injury; implementing seizure precautions is the priority.

q: A nurse is teaching the family of a client who has a substance use disorder. Which of the following statements by a family member indicates understanding? (Select all that apply.)
o: "We need to understand that our sibling is responsible for their disorder."
"Eliminating codependent behavior will promote recovery."
"Our sibling should participate in an Al-Anon group to assist with recovery."
"The primary goal of treatment is abstinence from substance use."
"Our sibling needs to discuss personal feelings about substance use to help with recovery."
r: Eliminating codependent/enabling behavior, abstinence as the primary goal, and the client discussing feelings support recovery. The client is responsible for recovery, not the disease; Al-Anon is for family members.

q: A nurse is obtaining a nursing history from a client who has a new diagnosis of anorexia nervosa. Which of the following questions should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)
o: "What is your relationship like with your family?"
"Why do you want to lose weight?"
"Tell me about your current eating habits."
"At what weight do you believe you will look better?"
"Let's discuss your feelings about your appearance."
r: Assessment should include family/interpersonal relationships, current eating habits, and the client's perception. Option b is a "why" question and d promotes cognitive distortion.

q: A nurse is performing an admission assessment of a client who has bulimia nervosa with purging behavior. Which of the following is an expected finding? (Select all that apply.)
o: Amenorrhea
Hypokalemia
Yellowing of the skin
Slightly elevated body weight
Presence of lanugo on the face
r: Hypokalemia and normal/slightly elevated weight are findings of bulimia. Amenorrhea, yellowing of the skin, and lanugo are findings of anorexia.

q: A nurse is planning care for a client who has anorexia nervosa with binge-eating and purging behavior. Which of the following actions should the nurse include?
o: Allow the client to select preferred meal times.
Establish consequences for purging behavior.
Provide the client with a high-fat diet at the start of treatment.
Implement one-to-one observation during meal times.
r: Close monitoring during and after meals prevents purging. The nurse should provide a structured milieu, a positive approach, and limit high-fat foods.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has bulimia nervosa and has stopped purging. The client expresses fear of gaining weight. Which of the following responses should the nurse make?
o: "Many clients are concerned about their weight. However, the dietitian will ensure that you don't get too many calories in your diet."
"Instead of worrying about your weight, try to focus on other problems at this time."
"I understand you have concerns about your weight, but first, let's talk about your recent accomplishments."
"You are not overweight, and the staff will ensure that you do not gain weight while you are in the hospital. We know that is important to you."
r: This acknowledges the concern then refocuses on accomplishments to promote self-esteem and self-image. Options a, b, and d minimize/generalize the concern.

q: A nurse is discussing risk factors for somatic symptom disorder. Which of the following risk factors should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)
o: Age older than 65 years
Anxiety disorder
Childhood trauma
Coronary artery disease
Obesity
r: Anxiety disorder and childhood trauma are risk factors for somatic symptom disorder; a younger age (16-25) is a risk factor. Coronary artery disease and obesity are not.

q: A nurse is assessing a client who has illness anxiety disorder. Which of the following are expected findings? (Select all that apply.)
o: Obsessive thoughts about disease
History of childhood maltreatment
Avoidance of health care providers
Depressive disorder
Narcissistic personality
r: Obsessive thoughts about disease, childhood maltreatment, avoidance of providers, and depression are expected. Low self-esteem, not narcissism, is expected.

q: A nurse is developing a plan of care for a client who has functional neurological symptom disorder. Which of the following actions should the nurse include?
o: Encourage the client to spend time alone in their room.
Monitor the client for self-harm once per day.
Allow the client unlimited time to discuss physical manifestations.
Discuss alternative coping strategies with the client.
r: The nurse should discuss alternative coping, encourage communication with others, continuously monitor for self-harm, and limit time discussing physical manifestations.

q: Which of the following client statements should the nurse identify as expected for factitious disorder imposed on another?
o: "I had to pretend I was injured in order to get disability benefits."
"I know that my abdominal pain is caused by a malignant tumor."
"I needed to make my child sick so that someone else would take care of them for a while."
"I became deaf when I heard that my partner was having an affair with my best friend."
r: Factitious disorder imposed on another involves consciously injuring/sickening another for a personal need. Option a is malingering, b is illness anxiety disorder, d is conversion disorder.

q: A charge nurse is reviewing the Kübler-Ross Five Stages of Grief. Which of the following stages should the charge nurse include? (Select all that apply.)
o: Disequilibrium
Denial
Bargaining
Anger
Depression
r: Denial, bargaining, anger, and depression (plus acceptance) are Kübler-Ross stages. Disequilibrium is a stage of Bowlby's model.

q: A nurse is working with a client who has recently lost a guardian. Which of the following factors influence a client's grief and coping ability? (Select all that apply.)
o: Interpersonal relationships
Culture
Birth order
Religious beliefs
Prior experience with loss
r: Interpersonal relationships, culture, religious beliefs, and prior experience with loss influence grief and coping. Birth order does not.

q: A nurse is discussing normal grief with a client who recently lost a child. Which of the following statements indicates understanding? (Select all that apply.)
o: "I may experience feelings of resentment."
"I will probably withdraw from others."
"I can expect to experience changes in sleep."
"It is possible that I will experience suicidal thoughts."
"It is expected that I will have a loss of self-esteem."
r: Resentment, withdrawal, and sleep changes are normal grief. Suicidal ideation and loss of self-esteem are associated with maladaptive grief.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who lost a parent to cancer last month. The client states, "I'd still have my guardian if the doctor would have made a diagnosis sooner." Which of the following responses should the nurse make?
o: "You sound angry. Anger is a normal feeling associated with loss."
"I think you would feel better if you talked about your feelings with a support group."
"I understand just how you feel. I felt the same when my guardian died."
"Do other members of your family also feel this way?"
r: This acknowledges the client's emotion and educates about normal grief. Option b offers advice, c minimizes feelings, d takes the focus off the client.

q: A nurse is performing an admission assessment on an adolescent who has depression. Which of the following findings are expected? (Select all that apply.)
o: Feelings of hopelessness
Inflated self-esteem
Appetite changes
Irritability
Pressured speech
r: Hopelessness, appetite changes, and irritability are expected in adolescent depression. Inflated self-esteem and pressured speech are associated with mania.

q: A nurse is assisting guardians of a school-age child who has oppositional defiant disorder to identify strategies to promote positive behavior. Which of the following should the nurse recommend? (Select all that apply.)
o: Allow the child to choose which behaviors are unacceptable.
Use role-playing to act out unacceptable behavior.
Develop a reward system for acceptable behavior.
Encourage the child to participate in school sports.
Be consistent when addressing unacceptable behavior.
r: Reward acceptable behavior, encourage physical activity, and set consistent limits. The parents should not allow the child to choose which behaviors are unacceptable.

q: A nurse is teaching guardians about manifestations of conduct disorder. Which of the following findings should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)
o: Bullying of others
Threats of suicide
Law-breaking activities
Narcissistic behavior
Flat affect
r: Bullying, suicidal ideation, and law/rule breaking are expected in conduct disorder, along with low self-esteem and irritability.

q: A nurse in a pediatric clinic is caring for a preschool-age child who has a new diagnosis of ADHD. Which of the following statements should the nurse include when teaching the parent?
o: "Behaviors associated with ADHD are present prior to age 3."
"This disorder is characterized by argumentativeness."
"Below-average intellectual functioning is associated with ADHD."
"Because of this disorder, your child is at an increased risk for injury."
r: Inattentive/impulsive behavior increases injury risk. ADHD behaviors are present before age 12; argumentativeness is ODD; below-average intellect is intellectual development disorder.

q: A nurse is assessing a client who has major depressive disorder. Which of the following client statements is an overt comment about suicide? (Select all that apply.)
o: "My family will be better off if I'm dead."
"The stress in my life is too much to handle."
"I wish my life was over."
"I don't feel like I can ever be happy again."
"If I kill myself then my problems will go away."
r: Overt statements talk directly about suicide and the wish to no longer be alive. Options b and d are covert statements.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who states, "I plan to commit suicide." Which of the following assessments is the priority?
o: Client's educational and economic background
Lethality of the method and availability of means
Quality of the client's social support
Client's insight into the reasons for the decision
r: The greatest risk is self-harm from carrying out a plan; the priority is determining lethality, availability of means, and the detail of the plan.

q: A nurse is developing protocols to address suicide attempts in the community. Which of the following interventions is a primary intervention? (Select all that apply.)
o: Conducting a suicide risk screening on all new clients
Creating a support group for family members of clients who died by suicide
Informing high school teens about suicide prevention
Initiating one-to-one observation for a client who has current suicidal ideation
Reinforcing teaching middle-school educators about warning indicators of suicide
r: Primary interventions include screening to identify those at risk and community education. Option b is tertiary; option d is secondary.

q: A nurse is caring for a client on suicide precautions. Which of the following interventions should the nurse include?
o: Assign the client to a private room.
Document the client's behavior every hour.
Allow the client to keep perfume in her room.
Ensure that the client swallows medication.
r: Ensuring the client swallows medication prevents hoarding for an overdose. Suicidal clients should not have a private room, should be documented every 15 minutes, and should not keep perfume (alcohol) in the room.

q: Which of the following events is an example of a client experiencing a maturational crisis?
o: Rape
Marriage
Severe physical illness
Job loss
r: Marriage is a maturational crisis (a naturally occurring life event). Rape is adventitious; severe illness and job loss are situational.

q: A nurse in the emergency department is caring for a client who sustained minor injuries in a motor vehicle crash. The client's spouse was killed in the accident. Which of the following actions should the nurse take first?
o: Determine if the client has thoughts of self-harm.
Ask the client how the accident occurred.
Assist the client in setting short-term treatment goals.
Instruct the client on use of coping strategies.
r: Safety is the priority; clients in crisis may be suicidal, so assessing for self-harm is first.

q: A nurse is caring for a client in an inpatient mental health facility who gets up and throws a chair across the day room. Which of the following is the priority nursing action?
o: Encourage the client to express feelings out loud.
Maintain eye contact with the client.
Move the client away from others.
Tell the client that the behavior is not acceptable.
r: The client is at greatest risk for harming others; the priority is to move the client away from others.

q: A nurse is caring for a client experiencing a crisis. Which of the following medications might the provider prescribe? (Select all that apply.)
o: Lithium carbonate
Paroxetine
Risperidone
Haloperidol
Lorazepam
r: SSRIs (paroxetine) and benzodiazepines (lorazepam) may be prescribed to decrease crisis-related anxiety. Mood stabilizers and antipsychotics are not typically useful for crisis anxiety.

q: A charge nurse is leading a discussion about family and community violence. Which of the following statements by a group member indicates understanding?
o: "Children older than 5 are at greater risk for abuse."
"Substance use disorder does not increase the risk for violence."
"Entering an intimate relationship increases the risk for violence."
"Pregnancy increases the risk for violence from a spouse or partner."
r: Pregnancy increases the likelihood of intimate-partner violence. Children younger than 3 are at increased risk; substance use increases risk; risk increases when a vulnerable person tries to leave.

q: A nurse is preparing to assess an infant. Which of the following is an expected finding of abusive head trauma? (Select all that apply.)
o: Sunken fontanels
Respiratory distress
Retinal hemorrhage
Altered level of consciousness
Increase in head circumference
r: Respiratory distress, retinal hemorrhage, altered LOC, and increased head circumference are expected in abusive head trauma. Bulging, not sunken, fontanels are expected.

q: A nurse in an emergency department is assessing a preschool-age child who reports abdominal pain. Which of the following findings should alert the nurse to possible abuse? (Select all that apply.)
o: Abrasions on knees
Round burn marks on forearms
Mismatched clothing
Abdominal rebound tenderness
Areas of ecchymosis on torso
r: Round burn marks (cigarette burns) and ecchymosis on the torso/back/buttocks suggest abuse. Minor injuries on arms/legs and mismatched clothing are common; rebound tenderness suggests appendicitis.

q: A nurse is preparing a community seminar about family violence. When discussing types of violence, the nurse should include which of the following?
o: Refusing to pay bills for a dependent, even when funds are available, is neglect.
Intentionally causing someone to fall is an example of physical violence.
Striking a sexual partner is an example of sexual violence.
Failure to provide a stimulating environment for normal development is emotional abuse.
r: Physical violence directs physical pain or harm toward another. Option a is economic maltreatment, c is physical violence, d is neglect.

q: A nurse is caring for an adult client who has injuries resulting from spousal violence. The client does not wish to report the violence. Which of the following nursing actions is the highest priority?
o: Advise the client about the location of safe houses and shelters.
Encourage the client to participate in a support group for survivors of abuse.
Implement case management to coordinate community and social services.
Educate the client about the use of stress management techniques.
r: The greatest risk is injury from intimate partner abuse; the priority is helping develop a safety plan that includes safe places to live.

q: A community health nurse is leading a discussion about rape. Which of the following statements by a citizen indicates understanding?
o: "Rape is a crime of passion."
"Acquaintance rape often involves alcohol."
"Young adults are the typical victims of sexual assault."
"The majority of rapists are unknown to the victims."
r: Alcohol and other substances are often associated with date/acquaintance rape. Rape is a crime of violence and power; people of all ages and sexes are affected; most perpetrators are known to the victim.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who was recently raped. The client states, "I never should have been out on the street alone at night." Which of the following responses should the nurse make?
o: "Your actions had nothing to do with what happened."
"You should focus on recovery rather than blaming yourself for what happened."
"You believe this wouldn't have happened if you hadn't been out alone?"
"Why do you feel that you should not have been alone on the street at night?"
r: This uses restating, promoting reflection and verbalization of feelings. Option a offers opinion, b indicates disapproval, d is a "why" question.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has borderline personality disorder. Which of the following goals is the priority when planning care?
o: The client will refrain from self-mutilation.
The client will express feelings of anger.
The client will participate in group therapy.
The client will take medications as prescribed.
r: Safety is the priority for a client with borderline personality disorder; self-mutilation poses a risk of injury.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has antisocial personality disorder and is receiving behavioral therapy through operant conditioning. Which of the following client behaviors indicates effectiveness of the therapy?
o: Refrains from manipulating others to earn dining room privileges
Attends group therapy sessions regularly
Takes medications as prescribed
Reports improved mood
r: Operant conditioning uses positive rewards for positive behavior; refraining from manipulation to earn privileges indicates effectiveness.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who is experiencing a panic attack. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
o: Assist the client with deep-breathing exercises.
Discuss new relaxation techniques.
Show the client how to change the behavior.
Distract the client with a television show.
r: Assisting with deep-breathing exercises helps the client regain control and reduce anxiety during a panic attack.

q: The primary purpose of the Community Mental Health Center Act of 1963 was to
o: get better treatment in larger, more urban areas.
move clients to their home communities for treatment.
provide former clients with employment opportunities.
remove the stigma of living in an institution.
r: The Community Mental Health Centers Construction Act of 1963 initiated deinstitutionalization — the deliberate shift from institutional care in state hospitals to community-based facilities closer to clients' homes, families, and support networks.

q: Managed care is designed to
o: control health care costs by limiting access to care.
keep health care costs from increasing over time.
limit the amount of money paid to physicians and hospitals.
maintain a balance between the quality and costs of health care.
r: Managed care aims to balance quality with cost — not simply to cut costs or restrict access. It uses utilization review and case management to ensure appropriate care is delivered efficiently.

q: Hospitals established by Dorothea Dix were designed to provide
o: asylum.
confinement.
therapeutic milieu.
public safety.
r: Dorothea Dix (1802–1887) advocated for asylum as a safe refuge — offering shelter, nutritious food, and warm clothing to the mentally ill who had previously been jailed or mistreated.

q: Hildegard Peplau is best known for her writing about
o: community-based care.
humane treatment.
psychopharmacology.
therapeutic nurse–client relationship.
r: Hildegard Peplau pioneered the interpersonal/therapeutic nurse–client relationship in nursing. She described the phases of the nurse–client relationship (orientation, working, resolution) and is considered the mother of psychiatric nursing.

q: Mental health parity laws ensure
o: better quality mental health treatment.
equality in insurance coverage for mental illness.
mental health treatment without stigma.
that persons receiving treatment really need it.
r: Mental health parity laws require insurance companies to cover mental health services on equal terms with physical health services — same copays, deductibles, and coverage limits.

q: The nurse is teaching a client taking an MAOI about foods with tyramine that they should avoid. Which statement indicates that the client needs further teaching?
o: "I'm so glad I can have pizza as long as I don't order pepperoni."
"I will be able to eat cottage cheese without worrying."
"I will have to avoid drinking nonalcoholic beer."
"I can eat green beans on this diet."
r: Pizza crust and sauce are generally low in tyramine, but many pizza toppings and aged cheeses (like parmesan) are high. The statement "as long as I don't order pepperoni" reflects a misunderstanding — aged/fermented cheeses on pizza are the real concern. Cottage cheese (A), avoiding nonalcoholic beer (B), and green beans (C) are all appropriate. Answer A is the incorrect statement requiring further teaching.

q: A client who has been depressed and suicidal started taking a tricyclic antidepressant 2 weeks ago and is now ready to leave the hospital to go home. Which is a concern for the nurse as discharge plans are finalized?
o: The client may need a prescription for diphenhydramine (Benadryl) to use for side effects.
The nurse will evaluate the risk for suicide by overdose of the tricyclic antidepressant.
The nurse will need to include teaching regarding the signs of neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
The client will need regular laboratory work to monitor therapeutic drug levels.
r: TCAs are lethal in overdose and only a 7-day supply should be given at a time to a suicidal client. With a history of suicidality, the priority concern at discharge is the risk of intentional overdose. NMS (C) is associated with antipsychotics, not TCAs. Routine lab monitoring (D) applies to lithium, not typically TCAs. Benadryl (A) is not a routine discharge concern.

q: The signs of lithium toxicity include which?
o: Sedation, fever, and restlessness
Psychomotor agitation, insomnia, and increased thirst
Elevated WBC count, sweating, and confusion
Severe vomiting, diarrhea, and weakness
r: Lithium toxicity (serum level ≥ 1.5 mEq/L) presents with GI symptoms (severe N/V/D), neurological symptoms (confusion, tremor, ataxia), and in severe cases seizures and coma. Answer A describes serotonin syndrome, B describes early lithium side effects (not toxicity), and C describes agranulocytosis.

q: Which is a concern for children taking stimulants for ADHD for several years?
o: Dependence on the drug
Insomnia
Growth suppression
Weight gain
r: The priority long-term concern with stimulants in children is growth suppression due to appetite suppression — the nurse should monitor height and weight at every visit. While insomnia and appetite suppression are side effects, they are manageable. Weight gain is not associated with stimulants (they suppress appetite).

q: The nurse is caring for a client with schizophrenia who is taking haloperidol (Haldol). The client complains of restlessness, cannot sit still, and has muscle stiffness. Of the following prn medications, which would the nurse administer?
o: Haloperidol (Haldol), 5 mg PO
Benztropine (Cogentin), 2 mg PO
Propranolol (Inderal), 20 mg PO
Trazodone, 50 mg PO
r: The client is exhibiting akathisia (restlessness, inability to sit still) and parkinsonism (muscle stiffness) — both extrapyramidal side effects (EPS) of haloperidol. Benztropine (Cogentin) is an anticholinergic agent used to treat EPS. More Haldol (A) would worsen EPS. Propranolol (C) treats akathisia but not the full EPS picture described. Trazodone (D) is unrelated.

q: Client teaching for lamotrigine (Lamictal) should include which instructions?
o: Eat a well-balanced diet to avoid weight gain.
Report any rashes to your doctor immediately.
Take each dose with food to avoid nausea.
This drug may cause psychological dependence.
r: Lamotrigine carries a risk of Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS), a life-threatening skin rash. Clients must report ANY rash immediately so the drug can be discontinued. Weight gain is not a major concern with lamotrigine. Food administration and dependence are not the priority teaching points.

q: Which physician order would the nurse question for a client who has stated, "I'm allergic to phenothiazines?"
o: Haldol, 5 mg PO bid
Navane, 10 mg PO bid
Prolixin, 5 mg PO tid
Risperdal, 2 mg bid
r: Prolixin (fluphenazine) is a phenothiazine antipsychotic. A client with a phenothiazine allergy should not receive it. Haldol (haloperidol) is a butyrophenone, Navane (thiothixene) is a thioxanthene, and Risperdal (risperidone) is an atypical/second-generation antipsychotic — none are phenothiazines.

q: Clients taking which type of psychotropic medications need close monitoring of their cardiac status?
o: Antidepressants
Antipsychotics
Mood stabilizers
Stimulants
r: Antipsychotics — particularly first-generation agents like haloperidol — can cause QTc prolongation and cardiac dysrhythmias. Second-generation agents (clozapine, ziprasidone) also carry cardiac risks. Cardiac monitoring is a priority nursing concern with antipsychotics. TCAs also affect cardiac conduction, but among the listed options antipsychotics is the best answer.

q: A 7-year-old boy is active in sports and has received a most-improved player award at his baseball tournament. According to Erikson, what describes this client's developmental task assessment?
o: Autonomy
Identity
Industry
Initiative
r: Industry vs. Inferiority is Erikson's stage for school-age children (ages 6–12). This stage focuses on developing competence through achievement and skill-building. Receiving an award demonstrates successful resolution of this stage. Autonomy (ages 1–3), Identity (adolescence), and Initiative (preschool, ages 3–6) do not fit a 7-year-old's developmental task.

q: According to Maslow's hierarchy of needs, which of the following client actions would be considered most basic?
o: A client discusses the need for order in his or her life and freedom from fear.
A client feels lonely and is seeking to share life experiences.
A client begins to realize his or her full potential.
A client is role-playing a situation with a nurse to practice assertiveness skills.
A client seeks shelter at a center for battered women.
r: Seeking shelter addresses physiological and safety needs — the most basic levels of Maslow's hierarchy. Safety needs (freedom from fear/order = answer A) come next, then love/belonging (answer B), then esteem (answer D), and finally self-actualization (answer C). Shelter is the most fundamental survival need.

q: Which of the following are examples of primary prevention in a community mental health setting? (Select all that apply)
o: Providing ongoing assessment of individuals at high risk for illness exacerbation.
Teaching physical and psychosocial effects of stress to elementary school students.
Referring for treatment those individuals in whom illness symptoms have been assessed.
Monitoring effectiveness of aftercare services.
Teaching a class on child-rearing skills for a group of new parents.
r: Primary prevention targets the general population BEFORE illness occurs — health promotion and risk reduction. Teaching stress management to students and parenting classes are primary prevention. Assessment of high-risk individuals (A) and referring symptomatic clients (C) are secondary prevention. Monitoring aftercare (D) is tertiary prevention.

q: In the emergency department, the nurse assesses a client who is aggressive and experiencing auditory hallucinations. The client states, "The CIA is plotting to kill me." To which mental health setting would the nurse expect this client to be admitted?
o: Long-term, inpatient facility
Day treatment
Short-term, inpatient, locked unit
Psychiatric case management
r: A client who is aggressive, experiencing active hallucinations, and expressing paranoid delusions poses a danger to self and others — requiring immediate stabilization in a short-term inpatient locked unit. Long-term facilities (A) are for chronic, refractory cases. Day treatment (B) and case management (D) are appropriate after stabilization.

q: A client has been fired from work because of downsizing. Although clearly upset, when explaining the situation to a friend, the client states, "Imagine what I can do with this extra time." Which defense mechanism is this client using?
o: Denial
Intellectualization
Rationalization
Suppression
r: Intellectualization is detaching emotion from a painful event by focusing on abstract, rational thinking — the client reframes job loss in intellectual/practical terms ("extra time") rather than feeling the pain. Rationalization (C) uses logical-sounding justifications. Denial (A) is refusing to acknowledge the problem. Suppression (D) is consciously pushing feelings aside.

q: Which best exemplifies an individual's use of the defense mechanism of compensation?
o: A woman feels unattractive but decides to pursue fashion design as a career.
A shy woman who abuses alcohol tells others that alcohol helps her overcome her shyness.
A poorly paid employee consistently yells at his assistant for minimal mistakes.
A teenager injures an ankle playing basketball and curls into a fetal position to deal with the pain.
r: Compensation means making up for a perceived weakness by emphasizing a strength in another area. The woman who feels unattractive channels that into fashion design — compensating for the deficit. B is rationalization (using logic to justify substance use). C is displacement (venting frustration onto a safer target). D is regression (returning to a childlike position).

q: Which best exemplifies the use of the defense mechanism of sublimation?
o: A child who has been told by parents that stealing is wrong reminds a friend not to steal.
A man who loves sports but is unable to play decides to become an athletic trainer.
Having chronic asthma with frequent hospitalizations, a young girl admires her nurses. She later chooses nursing as a career.
A boy who feels angry and hostile decides to become a mental health therapist to help others.
r: Sublimation channels unacceptable impulses (anger, hostility) into socially acceptable activities. Becoming a therapist to help others redirects aggression constructively. A is reaction formation. B is compensation (making up for inability to play by coaching). C is identification/role modeling — not sublimation because the drive (admiration) is not unacceptable.

q: A client is admitted to the emergency department after a car accident but does not remember anything about it. The client is unconsciously using which defense mechanism?
o: Undoing
Rationalization
Suppression
Repression
r: Repression is the UNCONSCIOUS blocking of painful memories or thoughts from awareness. The client has no memory of the accident — this is not a conscious choice (that would be suppression). Undoing involves symbolic acts to cancel a wrongdoing. Rationalization uses logic to justify behavior.

q: Which situation reflects the defense mechanism of denial?
o: When his twin brother excels in golf, the client begins lessons with a golf pro.
After a mother spanks her child for misbehaving, the child pulls the cat's tail.
After years of excessive drinking, the client fails to acknowledge a problem.
The client tells his family that 50% of people with his diagnosis survive.
r: Denial is refusing to acknowledge a painful reality — the client with years of excessive drinking who denies having a problem is the textbook example. A is compensation (improving in the same area as a rival). B is displacement (redirecting anger to the cat). D is rationalization or intellectualization (using statistics to cope with a diagnosis).

q: An 88-year-old client on an inpatient psychiatric unit states, "My children are refusing to visit me. I feel like giving up." This client has a deficit in which of Erikson's stages of development?
o: Initiative versus guilt
Industry versus inferiority
Identity versus role confusion
Integrity versus despair
r: Integrity vs. Despair is Erikson's final stage (late adulthood, 65+). It involves reflecting on life with acceptance (integrity) or regret (despair). An 88-year-old feeling abandoned by family and wanting to give up reflects despair — the unsuccessful resolution of this stage. The other stages apply to childhood and adolescence.

q: A client states, "I don't know what the pills are for or why I am taking them, so I don't want them." Which is an example of the therapeutic communication technique of "giving information"?
o: "You must take your medication to get better."
"The doctor wouldn't prescribe these pills if they were harmful."
"Do you feel this way about all of your medications?"
"This medication will help to improve your mood."
r: Giving information means providing facts the client needs in a clear, direct, non-coercive way. "This medication will help to improve your mood" directly informs the client about the drug's purpose. A is coercive/threatening. B is defending the doctor (non-therapeutic). C is a question that avoids answering the client's actual concern.

q: A depressed client discussing marital problems with the nurse says, "What will I do if my husband asks me for a divorce?" Which response by the nurse would be an example of therapeutic communication?
o: "Why do you think that your husband will ask you for a divorce?"
"You seem to be worrying over nothing. I'm sure everything will be fine."
"What has happened to make you think that your husband will ask for a divorce?"
"Talking about this will only make you more anxious and increase your depression."
r: This is the technique of exploring — delving further into the subject to better understand the client's concerns. "What has happened…" invites the client to describe the situation in detail. A uses "why" (non-therapeutic; judgmental). B offers false reassurance and dismisses feelings. D discourages the client from expressing feelings — non-therapeutic.

q: A client states to the nurse, "I'm thinking about ending it all." Which response by the nurse would be an example of therapeutic communication?
o: "Your attitude will hamper your recovery."
"Wasn't your wife just here during visiting hours?"
"Why would you want to do something like that?"
"You must be feeling very sad right now."
r: This response uses "translating words into feelings" — reflecting what the underlying emotion likely is (sadness) to open further communication. This validates the client's experience without reinforcing suicidal ideation. A is disapproving/judgmental. B changes the subject (non-therapeutic avoidance). C uses "why" which is non-therapeutic and may feel accusatory.

q: Which of the following therapeutic communication exchanges are examples of "reflection"? (Select all that apply)
o: Client: "I get sad because I know I'm going to fail in school." Nurse: "So you start feeling down every time a new semester begins?"
Client: "I forgot to get my prescription refilled." Nurse: "It is important for you to take your medication as prescribed."
Client: "I hate my recent weight gain." Nurse: "Have you considered Overeaters Anonymous?"
Client: "I'm happy that I poisoned my husband." Nurse: "You're happy to have poisoned your husband?"
Client: "I really don't know why I'm here. My stupid husband is behind this." Nurse: "You seem angry at your husband for bringing you to the hospital."
r: Reflection directs the client's thoughts, feelings, and actions back to them. Example A reflects and paraphrases the feeling of sadness. Example E reflects and names the emotion (anger) implied in the client's statement. B gives a directive/advice (non-therapeutic). C offers unsolicited advice. D is restating (repeating exact words) — technically not the same as reflection, which identifies underlying feelings.

q: Which of the following are examples of the therapeutic communication technique of "clarification"? (Select all that apply)
o: "Can we talk more about how you feel about your father?"
"I'm not sure what you mean when you use the word fragile."
"I notice that you seem angry today."
"How does your mood today compare with yesterday?"
"Can you help me understand what you mean by a 'difficult' childhood?"
r: Clarification seeks to make unclear or vague communication more understandable — asking the client to explain what they mean by specific words or concepts. B and E both ask the client to define vague terms. A is exploring (broader topic invitation). C is making an observation. D is encouraging comparison.

q: The client states, "I'm not sure that the doctor has prescribed the correct medication for my sadness." Which would be a therapeutic nursing response?
o: "A lot of clients are nervous about new medications. I'll get you some information about it."
"So you think that this medication is not right for you?"
"Why do you think that this medication won't help your mood?"
"Your doctor has been prescribing this medication for years, and it really does help people."
r: This response uses reflection/restating — repeating the client's concern back to them in the nurse's words to validate the feeling and encourage further exploration. A generalizes the client's experience ("a lot of clients") and is mildly non-therapeutic. C uses "why" (non-therapeutic). D defends the doctor (non-therapeutic) and dismisses the client's concern.

q: Which of the following are examples of nontherapeutic communication blocks? (Select all that apply)
o: "You acted out in group. It made the other clients uncomfortable."
"Why did you refuse your medication this afternoon?"
"I'm so sorry you feel that way. It is a feeling typical of hospitalized clients."
"You just think that you are not getting better. You'll see. Everything will work out."
"What I am hearing you say is that everyone is out to get you."
r: B uses "why" — non-therapeutic because it is judgmental and may put the client on the defensive. C belittles the client's feelings by generalizing ("typical of hospitalized clients"). D offers false reassurance ("Everything will work out") — dismisses real feelings. A is making an observation (therapeutic, neutral feedback). E is a paraphrasing/reflection technique (therapeutic).

q: A client on a psychiatric unit tells the nurse, "I'm all alone in the world now, and I have no reason to live." Which response by the nurse would encourage further communication by the client?
o: "You sound like you're feeling lonely and frightened."
"Why do you think that suicide is the answer to your loneliness?"
"I live by myself and know it can be very lonely and frightening."
"Just hang in there and, you'll see, things will work out."
r: This response uses "translating into feelings" or reflecting — naming the emotions behind the client's words (lonely and frightened). This validates the experience and invites further sharing. B uses "why" (non-therapeutic). C is sympathizing/self-disclosure that shifts focus to the nurse's experience. D is false reassurance that dismisses feelings.

q: Which of the following are examples of therapeutic communication techniques? (Select all that apply)
o: "Tell me about your drunk-driving record."
"How does this compare with the time you were sober?"
"That's good. I'm glad that you think you can stop drinking."
"I think we need to talk more about your previous coping mechanisms."
"What led up to your taking that first drink after 5 years of sobriety?"
r: B uses encouraging comparison — comparing the current situation with a previous state. D uses focusing — directing the client to a specific important topic (coping mechanisms). E uses placing events in time/sequence — exploring the sequence of events leading to relapse. A is probing (can feel invasive). C gives approval ("That's good") — non-therapeutic as it implies the nurse is judging the client.

q: On a substance abuse unit, a client diagnosed with cirrhosis of the liver tells the nurse, "I really don't believe that drinking a couple of cocktails every night has anything to do with my liver problems." Which is the best nursing response?
o: "You find it hard to believe that drinking alcohol can damage the liver?"
"How long have you been drinking a couple of cocktails a night?"
"If not by alcohol, explain how your liver became damaged."
"Everyone knows that increased alcohol consumption can damage your liver."
r: This response uses paraphrasing — briefly restating the client's message in the nurse's own words. This technique validates the client's difficulty accepting the connection while keeping the door open for further discussion without confrontation. B is data-gathering but misses the emotional component. C is confrontational and challenging (non-therapeutic). D is stereotyping/using clichés (non-therapeutic).

q: A client who takes sertraline for depression tells the nurse she has also started taking St. John’s Wort because “it is natural.” Which of the following is the nurse’s priority concern?
o: Reduced effectiveness of the sertraline
Development of serotonin syndrome
Increased risk of photosensitivity
Elevated liver enzymes
r: St. John’s Wort has serotonergic activity. Combined with an SSRI, SNRI, TCA, MAOI, or triptan it can cause serotonin syndrome — agitation, diarrhea, shivering, then hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, and hyperreflexia. That is the life-threatening risk, so it is the priority. Photosensitivity is real but not the priority.

q: A nurse is reviewing supplements with a client scheduled for surgery in 3 weeks. Which of the following should the nurse instruct the client to stop because of bleeding risk? (Select all that apply.)
o: Ginkgo biloba
Garlic
Saw palmetto
Vitamin E
Ginger
Melatonin
r: The bleed-risk group is the 4 G’s + E + O: garlic, ginger, ginkgo, ginseng, vitamin E, omega-3. All supplements should generally be stopped 2–3 weeks before surgery, but the ones asked about for bleeding are those. Saw palmetto is for BPH and melatonin is for sleep.

q: A client reports taking kava daily for anxiety. Which of the following laboratory results should the nurse review most closely?
o: Serum creatinine
Liver function tests
Serum potassium
Hemoglobin A1C
r: Kava is hepatotoxic — that is its signature adverse effect and the reason it is banned in several countries. Black cohosh is the other commonly tested hepatotoxic herbal.

q: A client who takes metformin for type 2 diabetes asks about starting ginseng for energy. Which of the following responses is most appropriate?
o: “Ginseng is safe to take with any diabetes medication.”
“Ginseng can lower your blood sugar, so we need to watch for hypoglycemia.”
“Ginseng will raise your blood sugar and worsen your diabetes.”
“You should stop the metformin while taking ginseng.”
r: Ginseng can cause hypoglycemia, and combined with an antidiabetic agent that risk increases. Glucosamine does the same thing. Never tell a client to stop a prescribed medication on their own.

q: A nurse is completing a medication history. Which of the following actions best ensures supplement use is captured?
o: Ask the client to list all prescription medications
Ask specifically about vitamins, supplements, and herbal products
Review the pharmacy profile for filled prescriptions
Ask whether the client takes anything for pain
r: Clients frequently do not consider supplements to be “medication” and will not volunteer them. You have to ask about vitamins, supplements, and herbals by name. They will not appear on a pharmacy profile either.

q: A client taking warfarin reports starting a daily garlic supplement. Which of the following assessment findings requires immediate follow-up?
o: Mild garlic odor on the breath
Bleeding gums when brushing teeth
Occasional heartburn after meals
A 1 kg weight gain over 2 weeks
r: Garlic is in the bleed-risk group and adds to warfarin’s effect. Bleeding gums is early bleeding — follow up, check the INR. The other findings are not urgent.

q: A nurse is teaching a client who has a new prescription for buspirone. Which of the following adverse effects should the nurse identify as the most common?
o: Insomnia
Photophobia
Dizziness
Weight gain
r: Dizziness is the most common adverse effect of buspirone. Insomnia is also on the list, which is exactly why it is such a good distractor — but when the stem asks for the most common or expected effect, choose dizziness. Teach the client to rise slowly because of the fall risk.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has been taking buspirone for 2 weeks. The client reports a dry, sticky mouth. Which of the following is the nurse’s best response?
o: “This means the medication dose is too high.”
“Xerostomia is an expected effect. Sip water and try sugarless gum.”
“Stop the medication and notify the provider today.”
“This is an early sign of an allergic reaction.”
r: Xerostomia (dry mouth) is an expected adverse effect of buspirone. It is managed, not treated as an emergency — sip water, sugarless gum or hard candy, good oral hygiene. Other expected effects: dizziness, headache, nausea, insomnia.

q: A nurse is teaching a client who has a new prescription for buspirone. Which of the following statements should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)
o: “Take this medication every day, not just when you feel anxious.”
“It may take 2 to 4 weeks before you notice the full effect.”
“Rise slowly from sitting or lying down.”
“Avoid grapefruit juice while taking this medication.”
“This medication can be habit-forming, so we will taper it.”
“Use this medication when you feel a panic attack starting.”
r: Buspirone is a scheduled daily medication with a 3–4 week onset (ATI), so it is not PRN and not for acute panic. Rise slowly — dizziness is the most common effect. Grapefruit juice raises buspirone levels. Buspirone is non-addictive — that is its main advantage over benzodiazepines.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has been taking thioridazine for 3 weeks. The client has hand tremors, drooling, and rigid extremities. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
o: Administer diazepam
Withhold all further doses permanently
Administer propranolol
Administer benztropine
r: Tremor, drooling, and rigidity = pseudoparkinsonism, an extrapyramidal symptom. Treat with an anticholinergic — benztropine (or diphenhydramine, trihexyphenidyl, amantadine). A benzodiazepine is the distractor: benzos help akathisia, not motor-slow rigidity. Propranolol is for akathisia.

q: A nurse is planning care for a client who has major depressive disorder with vegetative signs of depression. Which of the following interventions should the nurse include?
o: Limit snacks between meals
Schedule regular naptimes during the day
Weigh the client once monthly
Provide decaffeinated beverages
r: Vegetative signs are the physical symptoms of depression — sleep, appetite, activity, bowel, libido. Decaffeinated beverages support sleep. Naps worsen night insomnia. You encourage snacks in depression, not limit them. Weighing should be daily or weekly, not monthly.

q: Which of the following are vegetative signs of depression? (Select all that apply.)
o: Insomnia with early-morning waking
Anorexia and weight loss
Auditory hallucinations
Psychomotor retardation
Constipation
Decreased libido
r: Vegetative = somatic/physical: sleep disturbance, appetite and weight change, psychomotor change, fatigue, constipation, decreased libido, amenorrhea. Hallucinations are a psychotic feature, not a vegetative sign.

q: A client who has alcohol use disorder states, “I’ve read that problems with substances can have a variety of predisposing factors.” The nurse should identify this statement as which of the following defense mechanisms?
o: Rationalization
Denial
Intellectualization
Projection
r: Intellectualization — the client uses academic language and theory (“predisposing factors”) to avoid the emotion. The tell is textbook vocabulary with no feeling words. Rationalization gives an excuse; denial refuses the problem; projection blames someone else.

q: A client who has opioid use disorder states, “I was just using the medication for my back. I can stop whenever I want.” Which defense mechanism is the client using?
o: Denial
Intellectualization
Sublimation
Reaction formation
r: Denial — refusing to accept the reality of the problem. This is the answer that trips people up on intellectualization items: it is a refusal, not a lecture. No facts, statistics, or theory appear here.

q: A nurse teaches stress-management techniques to a parent who has verbally abused their children. This intervention is an example of which level of prevention?
o: Tertiary prevention
Secondary prevention
Primary prevention
Quaternary prevention
r: The abuse has already occurred, so the goal is rehabilitation and preventing recurrence — that is tertiary. The same class taught to a parent who has not abused would be primary. Ask “has the problem already happened?” before choosing.

q: Which of the following are examples of tertiary prevention in mental health nursing? (Select all that apply.)
o: A halfway house for clients leaving inpatient care
A suicide-prevention hotline
Alcoholics Anonymous after completing detox
A stress-management class at a high school
Vocational rehabilitation for a client who has schizophrenia
Partial hospitalization for a client recovering from a manic episode
r: Tertiary = rehabilitation after the problem occurred. A hotline is secondary (crisis detection and prompt intervention). A high-school stress class is primary (education to a well population).

q: A nurse is reviewing the laboratory results of a client who has been taking risperidone for 6 months. Which of the following findings should the nurse identify as an adverse reaction to the medication?
o: Elevated blood glucose
Decreased serum sodium
Elevated serum calcium
Decreased serum creatinine
r: Second-generation antipsychotics cause metabolic syndrome — hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia, and weight gain. Monitor fasting glucose, A1C, lipid panel, weight, and waist circumference. You got this one right on Dynamic Quizzing — keep it.

q: A nurse is teaching a client who has a new prescription for a tricyclic antidepressant. Which of the following statements should the nurse include?
o: “You should feel better within 2 to 3 days.”
“Stop the medication as soon as your mood improves.”
“It can take 6 weeks to achieve the full therapeutic effect.”
“This medication works only if taken when you feel sad.”
r: All antidepressants take 2–6 weeks for full effect — TCAs included. Never stop abruptly (discontinuation syndrome) and never dose PRN. You got this one right — keep it. Also remember TCAs are the antidepressants that are lethal in overdose (cardiac + anticholinergic).

q: A client is brought to the ED by law enforcement after 4 days of little sleep, rapid pressured speech, and grandiose statements. Which findings should the nurse recognize as cues requiring priority follow-up? (Select all that apply.)
o: Has slept about 2 hours total in 4 days
Has not eaten or had fluids since yesterday morning
Superficial lacerations on both wrists
Wearing bright, mismatched clothing and heavy makeup
Speech is rapid and jumps between topics
r: This is the miss pattern that cost you 5 of 9 Clinical Judgment points. Appearance and thought process are documented, not prioritized. Maslow and ABC put the physiologic and safety cues first: sleep deprivation, dehydration/no intake, and self-injury. Bright clothing and flight of ideas confirm mania but are not the urgent cues. When a mania stem lists both, pick the body finding, not the behavior finding.

q: Which hypothesis should the nurse identify as the priority for a client in acute mania who has bilateral wrist lacerations, has skipped meals for 2 days, and touched a staff member without consent?
o: Insufficient nutritional intake
Risk for violence toward self and others
Disturbed sleep pattern
Ineffective coping
r: You chose insufficient nutritional intake on Practice Test A. The key is risk for violence. Two pieces of hard evidence outrank the nutrition problem: wrist lacerations (self-directed violence, already happened) and non-consensual touching (other-directed). Nutrition is urgent but not lethal today; injury already is. Actual harm beats potential deficiency.

q: A client in acute mania is admitted to the inpatient unit. Which actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)
o: Provide finger foods and high-calorie fluids the client can carry
Place the client in a quiet, low-stimulation room
Set firm, consistent limits on intrusive behavior
Encourage the client to attend all group activities to burn off energy
Monitor lithium level and hydration status
