r: Manic clients cannot sit to eat — portable, high-calorie finger foods solve intake. Reduce stimulation; do not add it. Group activities are over-stimulating during acute mania — that was the distractor. Firm consistent limits plus monitoring the lithium level and hydration complete the plan.

q: A client in acute mania has a lithium level of 0.2 mEq/L after 5 days of treatment and continues to be intrusive and hyperverbal. How should the nurse interpret this?
o: The lithium is working; expect improvement soon
The level is toxic; hold the next dose
The level is subtherapeutic — the client is not being treated
The level is therapeutic but the dose needs more time
r: Therapeutic lithium is 0.6–1.2 mEq/L for maintenance (up to 1.5 in acute mania). 0.2 is subtherapeutic — it explains why nothing has changed. On Practice Test A you read this as 'progressing.' It is not. Toxic is >1.5; early toxicity 1.5–2.0 = N/V, diarrhea, coarse tremor, slurred speech.

q: Which finding indicates that a client's acute mania is not improving?
o: Sleeping 5 hours at night
Eating 60% of meals at the table
Continues to insist there is nothing wrong and refuses medication
Speech is slower and easier to follow
r: Impaired judgment and insight (anosognosia) is the outcome you missed on Q38. Sleep, intake, and speech are all improving markers. 'Nothing is wrong with me' = the illness is still driving the behavior. Return of insight is the marker of real improvement.

q: Which task is appropriate for the nurse to delegate to a licensed practical nurse (PN) on a mental health unit?
o: Recording the intake of a client who is experiencing mania
Reinforcing teaching about medications for a client who has depression
Creating a care plan for a client who has schizophrenia
Completing the admission assessment on a newly admitted client
r: You picked the intake option — that is the AP's range of function, not the PN's. Reinforcing teaching the RN already started is squarely PN scope. Creating a care plan and admission assessment are RN-only (planning and assessment never delegate). Read the verb first: assess/plan/teach-new/evaluate → RN. Reinforce/monitor/give meds → PN. Measure/move/wash/feed/record I&O → AP.

q: Which tasks may the nurse delegate to an assistive personnel (AP)? (Select all that apply.)
o: Obtaining vital signs on a stable client
Recording intake and output
Assisting a client with bathing and grooming
Reinforcing medication teaching
Performing 1:1 observation as assigned
Evaluating whether a client's anxiety decreased after an intervention
r: AP = measure, move, wash, feed, record. Reinforcing teaching is PN scope and evaluating is RN-only. The Five Rights of Delegation: right task · right circumstance · right person · right direction/communication · right supervision/evaluation. You can delegate the task; you can never delegate accountability.

q: A client tells the nurse she does not understand what the provider said about her treatment and feels pressured to sign the consent. Which action by the nurse best demonstrates client advocacy?
o: Explain the procedure to the client so she can sign
Tell the client she can refuse and leave the form unsigned
Stop the process and notify the provider that the client needs more information before consenting
Document that the client is noncompliant with the treatment plan
r: Advocacy = make sure the client's voice reaches the decision, not substitute your voice for the provider's. Informed consent is the provider's duty; the nurse's role is to witness the signature and to stop the process when consent is not informed. Explaining the procedure yourself oversteps; simply telling her to refuse abandons her.

q: Which nursing actions demonstrate the role of client advocate? (Select all that apply.)
o: Ensuring the client has the information needed to make a decision
Supporting a client's decision the nurse personally disagrees with
Reporting suspected abuse of a client
Making the decision the nurse believes is medically best for the client
Referring the client to a case manager for community resources
Speaking up when a client's stated wishes are being ignored by the team
r: Advocacy protects autonomy — it does not mean deciding for the client. Supporting a decision you disagree with is the hardest and most heavily tested piece. Ethical principles in play: autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice, fidelity, veracity.

q: A client has been in behavioral restraints for agitation. Which finding indicates the nurse should discontinue the restraints?
o: The provider's order has 2 hours remaining
The client is calm, follows directions, and states a plan to stay safe
The client has fallen asleep
The unit is now fully staffed
r: The order is a ceiling, not a duration. Release as soon as the client meets behavioral criteria — calm, oriented, cooperative, and able to contract for safety. Time remaining on the order is irrelevant. Sleep is not release criteria — that may be chemical sedation, not restored control. Staffing is never a restraint rationale in either direction.

q: Which are requirements for the use of behavioral restraints? (Select all that apply.)
o: A provider order obtained within 1 hour of initiation
Documentation of less restrictive measures tried first
Face-to-face provider evaluation within 1 hour
Continuous or every-15-minute monitoring per policy
Use as a consequence when a client refuses medication
Release at the earliest possible moment the client meets criteria
r: Restraint is never punishment, never for staff convenience, never for short staffing. Least restrictive first, documented. Orders are time-limited (adults up to 4 hr, ages 9–17 up to 2 hr, under 9 up to 1 hr) and never PRN. Four raised side rails and a locked-in wheelchair also count as restraint.

q: Which findings increase an older adult's risk for maltreatment? (Select all that apply.)
o: Cognitive impairment or dementia
Dependence on others for ADLs
Social isolation with few visitors
Incontinence and disruptive nighttime behavior
An independent client who drives and manages her own finances
Female sex and advanced age (75+)
r: Risk rises with dependence, cognitive impairment, isolation, and behaviors that exhaust the caregiver. Independence is protective. Caregiver-side risks matter just as much: caregiver substance use, mental illness, financial dependence on the client, being the sole unsupported caregiver, and a personal history of being abused.

q: An older adult has bruises in various stages of healing. The caregiver refuses to leave the room and answers all questions for the client. What should the nurse do first?
o: Report the suspicion to Adult Protective Services
Ask the caregiver to step out and interview the client alone
Ask the client directly whether the caregiver is hurting her, in front of the caregiver
Document the bruises and reassess next visit
r: Separate them first. You cannot get a truthful history with the suspected abuser present, and asking in front of them can escalate the danger. Interview privately, then report. Nurses are mandatory reporters — a reasonable suspicion is enough. You do not need proof and you do not need the client's permission.

q: Which behaviors during an assessment should raise the nurse's suspicion of older adult maltreatment? (Select all that apply.)
o: Injuries that do not match the explanation given
Delay in seeking treatment for an injury
The caregiver answers for the client and is hostile toward the client
The client is fearful, withdrawn, or flinches when touched
Unexplained weight loss, dehydration, or untreated pressure injuries
The client's medications are refilled on schedule
r: The tell is mismatch — story vs injury, injury vs healing stage, delay vs severity. Add financial signs (missing money, unpaid bills despite income, a new name on the accounts) and neglect signs (soiled clothing, dehydration, missed appointments).

q: Which psychotherapy should the nurse anticipate for a client who has a specific phobia of elevators that prevents her from working?
o: Psychoanalysis
Systematic desensitization
Interpersonal therapy
Token economy
r: Specific phobia → graded exposure with relaxation (systematic desensitization), or flooding. Match the client to the therapy: depression → CBT or IPT · borderline PD → DBT · phobia → exposure · family conflict → family therapy · relapse prevention in SUD → group + motivational interviewing · child behavior on a unit → token economy.

q: The nurse is teaching the family of a client who has moderate Alzheimer's disease about home safety. Which instructions should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)
o: Install complex locks high or low on all exit doors
Lower the water heater temperature and remove stove knobs
Remove throw rugs and clutter; add night lights and grab bars
Rearrange the furniture regularly to provide new stimulation
Register the client in a wandering-response program and keep a current photo
Store medications and cleaning products in a locked cabinet
r: Rearranging furniture is the distractor — familiarity and consistency are what keep a client with dementia safe. Keep the environment the same, reduce hazards, and plan for elopement before it happens. Teach the primary caregiver before discharge, in writing, and re-teach as the disease progresses — the safety plan escalates with the stage.

q: The family of a client who has dementia asks how to handle the client's repeated questions about a spouse who died years ago. Which response is appropriate?
o: Remind the client each time that the spouse has died so she stays oriented
Redirect the client to a comforting activity and validate the feeling behind the question
Tell the client the spouse will visit later
Ignore the question so the behavior is not reinforced
r: In moderate to severe dementia, repeated reality orientation causes distress without producing learning. Use validation and redirection — respond to the emotion, then redirect. Do not lie (the spouse will visit) and do not ignore. Reality orientation still has a place in early dementia and in delirium.

q: A client admitted 8 hours ago with a blood alcohol of 0.28% now has BP 168/98, HR 112, tremors, and diaphoresis. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Administer thiamine and folic acid
Administer the prescribed lorazepam and initiate seizure precautions
Offer oral fluids and a high-protein snack
Reorient the client and reduce environmental stimuli
r: Benzodiazepine + seizure precautions is the priority in active withdrawal — untreated withdrawal can be fatal. Use CIWA-Ar to score and dose. Vitamins matter but are not the emergency. Timeline: minor withdrawal 4–12 hr · withdrawal seizures 12–48 hr (peak 24) · alcoholic hallucinosis 12–24 hr · delirium tremens 48–72 hr, and DT carries real mortality.

q: Which are priority nursing actions for a client experiencing alcohol withdrawal? (Select all that apply.)
o: Score withdrawal severity with CIWA-Ar on a schedule
Administer thiamine before any glucose-containing IV fluid
Maintain seizure precautions and a quiet, well-lit room
Monitor vital signs, electrolytes, and hydration
Restrain the client preventively because withdrawal causes agitation
Provide reorientation and a calm, consistent staff approach
r: Thiamine before glucose — glucose first can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, nystagmus/ophthalmoplegia), which can progress to irreversible Korsakoff (memory loss, confabulation). Preventive restraint is never correct. Long-term, after detox: disulfiram, naltrexone, acamprosate plus AA and relapse-prevention counseling.

q: A client who has bipolar disorder has been taking lithium for 3 weeks and reports nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and a coarse hand tremor. Which action should the nurse take?
o: Reassure the client these are expected initial effects
Hold the lithium and notify the provider; obtain a lithium level
Encourage a low-sodium diet to reduce fluid retention
Administer the next dose with food
r: Coarse tremor + GI upset = early lithium toxicity (1.5–2.0 mEq/L). A fine tremor is expected; a coarse tremor is not. Hold, notify, draw a level. A low-sodium diet raises the lithium level — that is the opposite of what you want. Teach a consistent sodium intake and 2–3 L of fluid daily.

q: Which client teaching points should the nurse include for lithium therapy? (Select all that apply.)
o: Keep sodium intake consistent day to day
Drink 2 to 3 liters of fluid daily
Avoid NSAIDs, thiazide diuretics, and ACE inhibitors
Take extra doses on days you feel more irritable
Use caution in hot weather and with heavy exercise
Report vomiting, diarrhea, coarse tremor, or unsteady gait immediately
r: Anything that loses sodium or water — sweating, vomiting, diarrhea, fever, low-salt diet, NSAIDs, thiazides, ACE inhibitors/ARBs — raises the lithium level. Never self-adjust the dose. Baseline and ongoing monitoring: lithium level, BUN/creatinine, TSH, electrolytes, pregnancy test (lithium is teratogenic — cardiac defects).

q: Which prescription should the nurse question for a client newly diagnosed with bipolar I disorder who is currently depressed?
o: Lithium carbonate
Quetiapine
Sertraline as the only medication
Lamotrigine
r: Never give an antidepressant alone in bipolar disorder — it can trigger a switch into mania or rapid cycling. An antidepressant is only used with a mood stabilizer. Lamotrigine is the mood stabilizer of choice for bipolar depression; watch for Stevens–Johnson syndrome — any rash, stop the drug and call the provider.

q: A client with anorexia nervosa is admitted at 77.1 kg, down from 84 kg one month ago. Which findings should the nurse expect? (Select all that apply.)
o: Bradycardia and hypotension
Amenorrhea
Lanugo and dry, yellow-tinged skin
Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia
Intense fear of gaining weight despite weight loss
Insight that the body image perception is distorted
r: Starvation physiology: bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, amenorrhea, lanugo, dry yellow skin, constipation, electrolyte depletion. Absent insight is the hallmark — the client does not believe the body image is distorted. Bulimia looks different: normal or slightly above weight, eroded enamel, Russell's sign on the knuckles, parotid swelling.

q: Which interventions should the nurse include when planning care for a client hospitalized with anorexia nervosa? (Select all that apply.)
o: Weigh the client daily at the same time, after voiding, in the same clothing
Remain with the client for 1 hour after meals
Set a target weight gain of 1 to 2 lb per week
Allow the client to choose which meals to skip to build autonomy
Monitor electrolytes closely for refeeding syndrome
Focus conversation on feelings and coping rather than food and weight
r: Structure is the treatment — the client does not get to negotiate intake. Refeeding syndrome is the deadly complication: rapid drops in phosphorus, potassium, and magnesium → cardiac arrhythmias, heart failure, seizures. Refeed slowly and monitor labs. Staying after meals prevents purging and hidden food.

q: A client with schizophrenia says, "The voices are telling me the staff put poison in my food." Which response by the nurse is therapeutic?
o: "There is no poison in your food; the kitchen prepared it safely."
"I don't hear any voices, but I can see this is frightening for you. You are safe here."
"What exactly are the voices saying about the staff?"
"Try to ignore the voices and focus on eating your meal."
r: Do not argue with the delusion and do not pretend to share it. Present reality gently ("I don't hear them"), then acknowledge the feeling and offer safety. Arguing entrenches the belief. Asking for detail feeds it. Telling the client to ignore it dismisses real distress. Do ask directly about command hallucinations — those are a safety assessment, not delusion exploration.

q: Which are negative symptoms of schizophrenia? (Select all that apply.)
o: Flat or blunted affect
Auditory hallucinations
Avolition (lack of motivation)
Alogia (poverty of speech)
Delusions of persecution
Anhedonia and social withdrawal
r: Negative = something taken away (the 5 A's: affect flat, avolition, alogia, anhedonia, asociality). Positive = something added (hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech/behavior). Antipsychotics treat positive symptoms in 2–6 weeks; negative symptoms respond more slowly and less completely — that is why functional recovery lags.

q: A client taking haloperidol develops a temperature of 39.4°C (103°F), severe muscle rigidity, altered mental status, and BP 88/50. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Administer benztropine IM
Stop the haloperidol and notify the provider immediately
Encourage oral fluids and recheck in 1 hour
Administer the next scheduled dose with food
r: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome — fever, lead-pipe rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability, ↑ CPK. Life-threatening. Stop the antipsychotic, cool, hydrate, notify the provider; treat with dantrolene or bromocriptine. Benztropine treats EPS (acute dystonia, pseudoparkinsonism), which has no fever — that is the discriminator.

q: A client with narcissistic personality disorder tells the nurse, "The other nurses are incompetent. Only you understand me — you should be in charge of this unit." Which response is best?
o: "Thank you, I do try to give my clients extra attention."
"You should tell the nurse manager how the other nurses treat you."
"I am part of the same team, and we all follow the same plan of care for you."
"It sounds like the other nurses have been unfair to you."
r: This is splitting/idealization, and the correct move is a consistent team message with firm, matter-of-fact limits. Accepting the flattery accepts the split. Agreeing that others are unfair reinforces it. Key traits: grandiosity, need for admiration, lack of empathy, entitlement, exploiting others, and fragile self-esteem underneath — criticism produces rage or humiliation. Set limits without arguing and avoid countertransference.

q: A client asks why buspirone is not helping her anxiety after taking it PRN for 4 days. Which explanation should the nurse give?
o: "The dose is probably too low and needs to be increased."
"Buspirone takes 3 to 4 weeks to work and must be taken on a schedule, not as needed."
"Take it with grapefruit juice to raise the level and speed it up."
"Buspirone only works for panic attacks, not generalized anxiety."
r: ATI's number is 3 to 4 weeks (your guide said 2–4 — it is corrected now). Buspirone is scheduled daily, not PRN, and not for acute anxiety or panic. It is also not a controlled/scheduled medication, causes no dependence, and needs no taper when stopped. Avoid grapefruit juice — it inhibits CYP3A4 and raises the level.

q: Which statements about buspirone are accurate? (Select all that apply.)
o: It is not a controlled substance and does not cause dependence
It does not cause withdrawal and does not require tapering
Dizziness is the most common adverse effect
It should be avoided with grapefruit juice
It provides rapid relief during an acute panic attack
It causes significant sedation and respiratory depression
r: Buspirone is the anti-benzodiazepine: slow, safe, non-addictive, no sedation, no respiratory depression, no taper — and useless in an emergency. Adverse effects, ranked: dizziness (most common), xerostomia, headache, nausea, insomnia, restlessness. Teach: take with food, rise slowly, sip water/sugarless gum.

q: A client has been taking sertraline for 5 days. Which findings should the nurse report to the provider immediately? (Select all that apply.)
o: Agitation, confusion, and diaphoresis
Muscle rigidity with hyperreflexia and tremor
Serum sodium 128 mEq/L
Headache, lethargy, and new confusion
Heart rate 88/min
Mild nausea that improves when taken with food
r: Two dangerous clusters, and they are the whole question. Serotonin syndrome = agitation, confusion, hyperreflexia, rigidity, tremor, diaphoresis, fever, unstable vitals — often within hours to days. SIADH/hyponatremia = Na <135, headache, lethargy, confusion, seizures — more common in older adults. On Practice Test A you added heart rate; 88/min is normal — that was over-reach. Mild nausea is expected and self-limiting.

q: Which teaching should the nurse include for a client starting sertraline? (Select all that apply.)
o: Full therapeutic effect takes 4 to 8 weeks
Do not stop abruptly — taper to avoid discontinuation syndrome
Report any increase in suicidal thoughts, especially in the first weeks
Avoid St. John's wort, triptans, tramadol, and MAOIs
Expect sexual dysfunction, which often persists and should be reported
Take a double dose if you miss one
r: SSRI package: 4–8 weeks for full effect, taper to stop (abrupt stop → dizziness, flu-like symptoms, insomnia, irritability), ↑ suicide risk in the first weeks and under age 24, and a long serotonergic interaction list. MAOI washout is 14 days in both directions (5 weeks after fluoxetine). Never double a missed dose.

q: A client on the mental health unit tells the nurse, “You're the only one here who actually cares. The night nurse is cruel and should be fired.” Which response is appropriate?
o: “Thank you. I'll make sure you're assigned to me.”
“The night nurse follows the same plan I do. Let's talk about what happened last night.”
“I'll speak to the night nurse about how she treats you.”
“You shouldn't say that about a coworker.”
r: This is splitting — the hallmark of borderline PD. The client cannot hold good and bad in one person, so staff get sorted into all-good and all-bad. Reinforce that the whole team follows the same plan, then redirect to the actual feeling or event. Accepting the praise or agreeing to a special assignment feeds the splitting; scolding her shuts down the conversation.

q: Which characteristic distinguishes schizoid personality disorder from avoidant personality disorder?
o: The client with schizoid PD has hallucinations
The client with avoidant PD desires relationships but fears rejection
The client with schizoid PD is highly emotional
The client with avoidant PD has no insight into the problem
r: Do they want people? Avoidant (Cluster C) wants connection but is paralyzed by fear of criticism and rejection. Schizoid (Cluster A) is genuinely indifferent — no desire for relationships, unmoved by praise or criticism. Neither has hallucinations.

q: Which nursing actions are appropriate for a client who has borderline personality disorder? (Select all that apply.)
o: Set clear, consistent limits that every staff member enforces identically
Assess directly for suicidal ideation and self-harm each shift
Renegotiate a limit if the client becomes tearful and upset
Document the plan so the client cannot get different answers from different staff
Reinforce dialectical behavior therapy skills such as distress tolerance
Share a personal experience to help the client feel understood
r: Consistency, limits, safety, DBT. Renegotiating a limit teaches that distress works, so the behavior escalates. Self-disclosure crosses a boundary and sets up the “you're the special one” dynamic. Borderline PD carries the highest completed-suicide rate of any personality disorder (~8–10%) — ask directly, every shift.

q: A client insists on being seen only by the department chair, calls the assigned nurse “unqualified,” and demands a private room. Which personality disorder should the nurse suspect?
o: Histrionic
Narcissistic
Antisocial
Obsessive-compulsive
r: Narcissistic PD — grandiosity, entitlement, need for admiration, and devaluing others, with fragile self-esteem underneath. Nursing approach: matter-of-fact, don't argue with the grandiosity and don't feed it, set limits on demands, avoid power struggles, and expect rage after any criticism.

q: Which finding differentiates obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD) from obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD)?
o: OCPD involves rituals performed to relieve anxiety
The client with OCPD believes the behavior is correct and appropriate
OCD begins in adolescence and OCPD begins in childhood
OCPD responds to SSRIs and OCD does not
r: OCPD is ego-syntonic — perfectionism, rigidity, and control feel right to the client, and there are no true obsessions and no rituals. OCD is ego-dystonic — intrusive thoughts the client hates, plus compulsive rituals performed to relieve the anxiety. Nursing for OCPD: give control where it's safe, use written schedules, don't rush her.

q: A client who has paranoid personality disorder is newly admitted. Which nursing approach is most appropriate?
o: Be warm, friendly, and physically affectionate to build trust
Use a neutral, matter-of-fact manner and give clear, honest explanations
Encourage immediate participation in group therapy to reduce isolation
Avoid eye contact so the client does not feel threatened
r: Excessive warmth backfires — the client reads friendliness as a trick. Be neutral, honest, consistent, and predictable; explain everything simply and in writing; keep every promise; and never whisper or talk quietly near the client, because it confirms the suspicion that people are conspiring.

q: Which statements about personality disorders are accurate? (Select all that apply.)
o: The pattern must be evident by adolescence or early adulthood
Clients are usually ego-syntonic and see the problem as external
No medication is FDA-approved to treat a personality disorder itself
Personality disorders typically resolve within weeks of starting therapy
Dialectical behavior therapy is first-line for borderline personality disorder
Antisocial personality disorder requires a history of conduct disorder before age 15
r: PDs are enduring and inflexible, not episodic — treatment is long-term psychotherapy, and improvement is measured in months to years. Medications target symptoms only: SSRIs for mood and impulsivity, mood stabilizers for lability, low-dose atypical antipsychotics for transient stress-related paranoia or dissociation.

q: A client with borderline personality disorder has superficial cuts on her forearm and tells the nurse, “I just needed to feel something.” Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Tell the client that self-harm will not be tolerated on the unit
Assess the wounds and the client's current suicidal intent
Explain that cutting is a maladaptive coping mechanism
Document the behavior and notify the provider at the end of shift
r: Assess before you teach and before you set the limit. Self-injury in borderline PD is often to relieve emptiness or numbness rather than to die — but you cannot assume that. Care for the wound and ask directly about intent and plan, then address coping skills and safety planning. Never dismiss self-injury as “only attention-seeking.”

q: A client with dependent personality disorder asks the nurse to choose her meals, her clothing, and whether she should attend group. Which response supports the plan of care?
o: Make the choices for the client to reduce her anxiety
Tell the client she must decide everything herself starting today
Ask the client which option she prefers and support the decision she makes
Refer the client to a family member to make the decisions
r: The goal is graded independence. Making choices for her reinforces the dependency; demanding total self-sufficiency overwhelms her and she fails. Require the decision, then support it — plus assertiveness training and clear limits on clinging. Do not do for the client what the client can do herself.

q: The nurse notices the treatment team is divided — two staff members defend a client with borderline personality disorder while two are angry with her. Which actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)
o: Recognize that the client's splitting has extended to the staff
Address the disagreement in team report and clarify one consistent plan
Ask the client which staff members she trusts and honor that preference
Document the agreed limits so every shift responds the same way
Confront the client for causing conflict among the staff
r: Staff splitting is a symptom, not a personnel problem. Fix it in report and on the care plan, not with the client. Honoring the client's staff preferences deepens the split, and blaming her for the team's conflict is punitive and non-therapeutic.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has schizophrenia and is prescribed haloperidol. Which of the following adverse effects should the nurse anticipate as most likely with this medication?
o: Excessive sedation and orthostatic hypotension
Extrapyramidal symptoms such as muscle rigidity and tremor
Severe anticholinergic dry mouth and urinary retention
Significant weight gain and hyperglycemia
r: Haloperidol is a high-potency first-generation antipsychotic, so it carries a high risk of extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) and a low risk of sedation, anticholinergic effects, and hypotension. Sedation and orthostasis are typical of low-potency agents such as chlorpromazine. Weight gain and hyperglycemia are hallmark of second-generation agents like olanzapine, not haloperidol.

q: A nurse is providing teaching to a client who is starting chlorpromazine. Which of the following statements should the nurse include?
o: "Use sunscreen and wear protective clothing when outdoors."
"Take this medication only when you hear voices."
"You should expect your urine to turn bright red."
"Stop the medication as soon as your symptoms improve."
r: Chlorpromazine causes marked photosensitivity, so sun protection is essential to prevent severe sunburn. Antipsychotics are scheduled, not PRN, because steady blood levels are needed to control psychosis. Chlorpromazine may cause harmless pink-to-brown urine discoloration, not bright red, and abrupt discontinuation after symptom improvement leads to relapse.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has schizophrenia and repeatedly stops taking oral medication after discharge. Which of the following interventions should the nurse anticipate the provider will prescribe?
o: Increase the oral dose and add a bedtime reminder
Fluphenazine decanoate IM every 2 to 4 weeks
Chlorpromazine oral concentrate three times daily
Discontinue antipsychotics and begin psychotherapy alone
r: Depot (long-acting injectable) antipsychotics such as fluphenazine decanoate are indicated for clients with poor adherence because one injection maintains therapeutic levels for weeks. Increasing the oral dose or switching to another oral form does not solve nonadherence. Psychotherapy alone does not control the positive symptoms of schizophrenia.

q: A nurse is planning care for a client who is starting olanzapine. Which of the following assessments should the nurse include for metabolic monitoring? Select all that apply.
o: Weight and BMI
Fasting blood glucose
Serum lipid profile
Waist circumference
Serum ammonia level
Blood pressure
r: Second-generation antipsychotics cause metabolic syndrome, so baseline and ongoing weight/BMI, fasting glucose, lipids, waist circumference, and blood pressure are all required. Serum ammonia is monitored with valproate-related hepatic dysfunction, not with olanzapine, and has no role in metabolic screening.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has bipolar disorder with psychotic features and a history of obesity and type 2 diabetes. Which of the following antipsychotics should the nurse expect the provider to select as most weight-neutral?
o: Olanzapine
Quetiapine
Ziprasidone
Clozapine
r: Ziprasidone and aripiprazole are the most weight-neutral second-generation antipsychotics, making ziprasidone appropriate for a client with obesity and diabetes. Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest risk of weight gain and new-onset diabetes, and quetiapine also causes substantial weight gain and sedation.

q: A nurse is reviewing the ECG of a client who is prescribed ziprasidone. Which of the following findings should the nurse report to the provider immediately?
o: Heart rate of 88/min
QT interval prolongation
Sinus rhythm with occasional premature atrial contractions
PR interval of 0.16 seconds
r: Ziprasidone carries the greatest risk of QT prolongation among second-generation antipsychotics, which can progress to torsades de pointes and sudden death, so this must be reported immediately. A heart rate of 88/min and a PR interval of 0.16 seconds are within normal limits, and occasional premature atrial contractions are benign and do not require urgent reporting.

q: A nurse is caring for a female client who has been taking risperidone for 3 months. The client reports amenorrhea and breast tenderness with milky nipple discharge. Which of the following explanations should the nurse provide?
o: "These are signs of an allergic reaction to the medication."
"This medication can raise your prolactin level, which causes these changes."
"These findings mean the medication is no longer working."
"This is an early sign of tardive dyskinesia."
r: Risperidone raises prolactin more than other second-generation agents, producing galactorrhea, amenorrhea, gynecomastia, and sexual dysfunction; the provider may switch to a prolactin-sparing agent such as aripiprazole. These are endocrine effects, not allergy or treatment failure, and tardive dyskinesia involves involuntary movements of the face and tongue, not lactation.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has treatment-resistant schizophrenia and is starting clozapine. The client reports a sore throat and has a temperature of 38.4 C (101.1 F). Which of the following actions should the nurse take first?
o: Administer an antipyretic and reassess in 4 hr
Encourage warm saline gargles and increase fluids
Hold the medication and obtain an absolute neutrophil count
Document the findings and continue the medication as prescribed
r: Sore throat and fever in a client taking clozapine are classic signs of agranulocytosis, a potentially fatal adverse effect, so the priority is to hold the dose and obtain an ANC immediately. Treating the fever or providing comfort measures delays recognition of a life-threatening blood dyscrasia, and continuing the medication could be fatal.

q: A nurse is providing teaching to a client who is starting clozapine. Which of the following information should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Regular blood tests to monitor the absolute neutrophil count are required
Report any sore throat, fever, or flu-like symptoms right away
Excessive drooling, especially at night, may occur
This medication may lower the seizure threshold at higher doses
Report chest pain, shortness of breath, or fast heartbeat immediately
This medication has no effect on suicidal thinking
r: Clozapine requires ongoing ANC monitoring for agranulocytosis, and clients must report infection signs immediately; sialorrhea, dose-related seizures, and myocarditis (chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia) are all expected teaching points. The last option is false because clozapine is the antipsychotic proven to reduce suicidality in schizophrenia.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who received the first dose of haloperidol 6 hr ago and now has severe neck twisting, jaw spasm, and difficulty swallowing. Which of the following medications should the nurse expect to administer?
o: Diphenhydramine IM
Propranolol PO
Haloperidol additional dose IM
Lithium PO
r: These findings indicate acute dystonia, an EPS emergency that can progress to laryngospasm; IM diphenhydramine or benztropine provides rapid relief. Propranolol treats akathisia rather than dystonia, an additional antipsychotic dose would worsen the reaction, and lithium is a mood stabilizer with no role here.

q: A nurse is assessing clients for extrapyramidal symptoms. Which of the following statements about EPS are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Akathisia presents as inner restlessness and an inability to sit still
Pseudoparkinsonism includes bradykinesia, shuffling gait, and pill-rolling tremor
Tardive dyskinesia typically appears after months to years of therapy
Tardive dyskinesia is reliably reversed by adding benztropine
The AIMS scale is used to screen for tardive dyskinesia
r: Akathisia (restlessness), pseudoparkinsonism (bradykinesia, shuffling gait, tremor), and late-onset tardive dyskinesia are all EPS, and the AIMS tool screens for TD at regular intervals. Anticholinergics such as benztropine treat dystonia and pseudoparkinsonism but do not reverse TD and may worsen it, which is why early detection and discontinuation of the offending drug are essential.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has been taking fluphenazine for 5 days. The client has a temperature of 40 C (104 F), severe muscle rigidity, altered level of consciousness, and blood pressure of 172/98 mm Hg. Which of the following actions should the nurse take first?
o: Administer the next scheduled dose of fluphenazine
Stop the antipsychotic and notify the provider immediately
Apply a cooling blanket and recheck the temperature in 1 hr
Encourage oral fluids and ambulation
r: Hyperthermia, lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability, and altered mental status indicate neuroleptic malignant syndrome, a medical emergency; the first action is to stop the antipsychotic and notify the provider so cooling, hydration, dantrolene, and bromocriptine can be started. Giving another dose would be lethal, and cooling alone or delayed reassessment postpones definitive treatment.

q: A nurse is comparing neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) with serotonin syndrome. Which of the following findings is most characteristic of serotonin syndrome rather than NMS?
o: Lead-pipe muscle rigidity
Hyperreflexia, myoclonus, and clonus
Onset over days to weeks after starting therapy
Markedly elevated creatine kinase
r: Serotonin syndrome produces hyperreflexia, myoclonus, and clonus with rapid onset, usually within 24 hr of a dose increase or the addition of a second serotonergic drug, and is managed by stopping the drug and giving cyproheptadine. NMS is distinguished by lead-pipe rigidity, slower onset over days to weeks, and markedly elevated creatine kinase from muscle breakdown.

q: A nurse is providing teaching to a client who is starting sertraline for major depressive disorder. Which of the following statements indicates the client understands the teaching?
o: "I should feel completely better by tomorrow morning."
"It may take 2 to 4 weeks before my mood improves."
"I will take this only on days I feel sad."
"I can stop this medication abruptly once I feel well."
r: SSRIs require 2 to 4 weeks for mood improvement and up to 8 weeks for full effect, so the client must continue the drug through the lag period rather than concluding it does not work. SSRIs are scheduled rather than PRN, and abrupt cessation causes discontinuation syndrome with dizziness, flu-like symptoms, and irritability, so tapering is required.

q: A nurse is caring for a 19-year-old client who started escitalopram 8 days ago. Which of the following findings should the nurse report to the provider immediately?
o: Report of mild nausea after the morning dose
Statement that "everyone would be better off without me"
Difficulty falling asleep for the past two nights
Report of decreased sexual desire
r: SSRIs carry a black box warning for increased suicidal ideation in clients under 25, and risk is highest in the first weeks because energy and motivation return before mood lifts, so any suicidal statement requires immediate reporting and safety measures. Nausea, transient insomnia, and sexual dysfunction are common adverse effects that are managed but are not emergencies.

q: A nurse is teaching a client about adverse effects of SSRI therapy. Which of the following findings should the client be taught to report? Select all that apply.
o: Agitation, diaphoresis, tremor, and confusion
Sexual dysfunction that is distressing to the client
Increased thoughts of self-harm
Unusual bruising or bleeding
Dry mouth on the first few days
Weight gain of 0.5 kg (1 lb) over 6 months
r: Agitation with diaphoresis, tremor, and confusion suggests serotonin syndrome; sexual dysfunction, worsening suicidality, and abnormal bleeding (SSRIs impair platelet aggregation) all warrant contacting the provider. Transient dry mouth and a 0.5 kg change over 6 months are minor, expected effects that do not require reporting.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who is being switched from fluoxetine to phenelzine. Which of the following instructions should the nurse reinforce?
o: "Start phenelzine tomorrow to prevent relapse."
"Wait 5 weeks after stopping fluoxetine before starting phenelzine."
"Take both medications together for 7 days."
"Wait 24 hours after your last fluoxetine dose."
r: Fluoxetine has an exceptionally long half-life with an active metabolite, so a 5-week washout is required before starting an MAOI to prevent fatal serotonin syndrome. Other SSRIs, SNRIs, and tricyclic antidepressants require about a 14-day washout; overlapping the drugs or waiting only 24 hr is dangerous.

q: A nurse is reviewing the medical record of a client who has a prolonged QT interval and is prescribed an antidepressant. Which of the following medications should the nurse question?
o: Citalopram 40 mg daily
Bupropion 150 mg daily
Mirtazapine 15 mg at bedtime
Duloxetine 30 mg daily
r: Citalopram causes dose-dependent QT prolongation, and doses above 20 mg daily are not recommended for older adults or clients with existing QT prolongation, so the nurse should question 40 mg. Bupropion, mirtazapine, and duloxetine are not primarily associated with QT prolongation, though each carries other distinct risks.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who is prescribed venlafaxine. Which of the following assessments is the priority for this medication?
o: Serum sodium every 3 months
Blood pressure at each visit
Serum amylase monthly
Visual acuity every 6 months
r: Venlafaxine increases norepinephrine at higher doses and causes dose-dependent hypertension, so blood pressure must be monitored regularly and before each dose increase; the other SNRI, duloxetine, is also used for diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain and fibromyalgia. Amylase monitoring applies to valproate-induced pancreatitis, and routine visual acuity screening is not indicated.

q: A nurse is providing teaching to an older adult client who is starting amitriptyline. Which of the following adverse effects should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Dry mouth and blurred vision
Constipation and urinary retention
Orthostatic hypotension with risk for falls
Excessive salivation
Sedation
r: Tricyclic antidepressants block muscarinic receptors, producing anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention), plus alpha-blockade causing orthostatic hypotension and antihistaminic sedation, all especially hazardous in older adults. Excessive salivation is not a TCA effect; it is associated with clozapine and cholinesterase inhibitors. TCAs also have a narrow therapeutic index and are highly lethal in overdose, so quantities are limited for at-risk clients.

q: A nurse is providing dietary teaching to a client who is prescribed phenelzine. Which of the following foods should the nurse instruct the client to avoid? Select all that apply.
o: Aged cheddar cheese
Salami and pepperoni
Fresh chicken breast
Soy sauce and fermented bean paste
Draft beer and red wine
White rice
r: MAOIs block breakdown of tyramine, so aged cheeses, cured or smoked meats, fermented soy products, and draft beer or wine can precipitate a hypertensive crisis. Fresh, unfermented protein such as chicken and plain starches like white rice contain negligible tyramine and are safe.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who takes tranylcypromine and reports a severe occipital headache, palpitations, and neck stiffness. The client's blood pressure is 210/118 mm Hg. Which of the following actions should the nurse take first?
o: Administer the next scheduled MAOI dose
Notify the provider and prepare to administer an antihypertensive such as phentolamine
Encourage the client to lie flat and rest
Obtain a 12-lead ECG and reassess in 30 min
r: These findings indicate a hypertensive crisis from a tyramine interaction, a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate provider notification and rapid-acting IV antihypertensive therapy such as phentolamine. Giving another dose worsens the crisis, and rest or delayed reassessment allows progression to stroke; the client should be positioned with the head elevated, not flat.

q: A nurse is reviewing the medication list of a client who is starting bupropion. Which of the following findings in the history is a contraindication?
o: History of bulimia nervosa
History of tobacco use
Report of decreased libido on a previous SSRI
History of seasonal affective disorder
r: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and is contraindicated in clients with eating disorders such as bulimia and anorexia because electrolyte disturbances further increase seizure risk. Tobacco use is actually an indication, since bupropion aids smoking cessation; bupropion is often chosen for clients with SSRI-induced sexual dysfunction and is used in seasonal affective disorder.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has depression, insomnia, and a 4.5 kg (10 lb) unintentional weight loss. Which of the following medications should the nurse expect the provider to prescribe?
o: Fluoxetine in the morning
Mirtazapine at bedtime
Bupropion twice daily
Phenelzine at bedtime
r: Mirtazapine causes sedation and increased appetite with weight gain, effects that are therapeutic for a client with insomnia and weight loss when dosed at bedtime. Fluoxetine and bupropion are activating and suppress appetite, which would worsen both problems, and phenelzine requires strict dietary restriction and is not first-line.

q: A nurse is providing teaching to a male client who is prescribed trazodone for insomnia. Which of the following adverse effects should the nurse instruct the client to report immediately?
o: Dry mouth
A persistent, painful erection
Mild morning drowsiness
Metallic taste
r: Trazodone can cause priapism, a urologic emergency that can lead to permanent impotence if not treated promptly, so the client must seek care immediately. Dry mouth, residual drowsiness, and taste changes are common, non-urgent effects.

q: A nurse is reviewing the laboratory results of a client who has bipolar disorder and takes lithium. The lithium level is 2.1 mEq/L. Which of the following findings should the nurse expect?
o: Fine hand tremor and mild thirst only
Ataxia, blurred vision, and coarse tremor with confusion
No symptoms because this level is therapeutic
Mild nausea that resolves with food
r: The therapeutic range is 0.6 to 1.2 mEq/L; a level of 2.1 mEq/L indicates moderate to severe toxicity with ataxia, blurred vision, coarse tremor, confusion, and risk for seizures and dysrhythmias. Fine tremor, mild thirst, and transient nausea are expected effects seen at therapeutic levels, not at this level.

q: A nurse is providing teaching to a client who is starting lithium carbonate. Which of the following instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Drink 2 to 3 L of fluid each day
Maintain a consistent daily sodium intake
Avoid NSAIDs such as ibuprofen unless approved by the provider
Notify the provider before starting a thiazide diuretic
Restrict all salt from the diet
Have blood levels drawn as scheduled
r: Lithium is excreted by the kidneys and competes with sodium, so adequate fluid intake, consistent sodium intake, avoidance of NSAIDs and thiazide diuretics (both raise lithium levels), and scheduled level monitoring are essential. A low-sodium or salt-restricted diet causes lithium retention and toxicity, so it must be avoided.

q: A nurse is caring for four clients who take lithium. Which of the following clients should the nurse assess first?
o: A client who reports a fine hand tremor and increased thirst
A client who has had vomiting and diarrhea for 2 days
A client who reports a 1.4 kg (3 lb) weight gain over 2 months
A client who reports a metallic taste in the mouth
r: Two days of vomiting and diarrhea cause dehydration and sodium loss, which sharply raise the lithium level and can precipitate acute toxicity, making this client the priority. Fine tremor, thirst, gradual weight gain, and metallic taste are expected effects of therapeutic lithium and do not indicate immediate danger.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who takes valproic acid. Which of the following laboratory findings should the nurse report to the provider?
o: Platelet count 78,000/mm3
Hemoglobin 14 g/dL
Sodium 139 mEq/L
WBC 7,200/mm3
r: Valproate causes thrombocytopenia, and a platelet count of 78,000/mm3 is well below the normal 150,000 to 400,000/mm3, placing the client at risk for bleeding. The hemoglobin, sodium, and WBC values are all within normal limits; the nurse should also monitor liver enzymes and amylase or lipase for hepatotoxicity and pancreatitis.

q: A nurse is providing teaching to a client of childbearing age who is prescribed carbamazepine for bipolar disorder. Which of the following information should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Report sore throat, fever, bruising, or unusual bleeding
This medication can make oral contraceptives less effective
Report any spreading rash with blistering or mouth sores immediately
Routine blood counts will be needed during therapy
Grapefruit juice increases the risk of toxicity
r: Carbamazepine can cause agranulocytosis and aplastic anemia (report infection and bleeding signs; monitor CBC) and Stevens-Johnson syndrome (report blistering rash). It is a strong CYP450 inducer that decreases oral contraceptive effectiveness, so a backup method is needed, and grapefruit juice inhibits its metabolism, raising levels toward toxicity. All five statements are correct teaching.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who started lamotrigine 2 weeks ago and now reports a new spreading rash on the trunk. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
o: Instruct the client to apply hydrocortisone cream and continue the medication
Instruct the client to withhold the next dose and contact the provider immediately
Reassure the client that rash is expected and resolves in a few days
Advise the client to take diphenhydramine and follow up at the next scheduled visit
r: Any rash during lamotrigine therapy may herald Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis, so the client must stop the drug and contact the provider immediately; slow titration reduces but does not eliminate this risk. Topical steroids, reassurance, or antihistamines with continued dosing allow a potentially fatal reaction to progress.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has taken alprazolam daily for 2 years and abruptly stopped it 3 days ago. Which of the following findings should the nurse identify as the greatest concern?
o: Report of vivid dreams
Tonic-clonic seizure activity
Mild rebound anxiety
Increased sweating
r: Abrupt withdrawal from benzodiazepines can cause seizures, delirium, and death, which is why these drugs must always be tapered. Vivid dreams, rebound anxiety, and diaphoresis are uncomfortable withdrawal symptoms but are not life-threatening.

q: A nurse is providing teaching to a client who is prescribed lorazepam for short-term anxiety management. Which of the following instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Avoid alcohol while taking this medication
Do not combine this medication with opioid pain medications unless directed by the provider
Avoid driving until you know how the medication affects you
Do not stop this medication abruptly
Take a double dose if your anxiety feels worse than usual
r: Benzodiazepines potentiate CNS depression, so alcohol and opioids must be avoided because the combination can cause fatal respiratory depression; driving is unsafe until sedation is known, and the drug must be tapered rather than stopped abruptly. Self-doubling the dose increases toxicity and dependence and is never appropriate.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has generalized anxiety disorder and is prescribed buspirone. Which of the following statements by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
o: "I will take this every day, even when I feel calm."
"I will take an extra tablet when I feel a panic attack starting."
"It may take a few weeks before I notice a difference."
"This medication is not habit-forming."
r: Buspirone requires 2 to 4 weeks for effect and is dosed on a scheduled basis, so it is useless for aborting acute panic and must not be taken PRN. The other statements are accurate: it is taken daily regardless of symptoms and carries no dependence or abuse potential, unlike benzodiazepines.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who is taking risperidone and reports an urgent need to keep moving and an inability to sit through a meal. Which of the following medications should the nurse expect the provider to prescribe?
o: Propranolol
Hydroxyzine
Zolpidem
Memantine
r: These findings describe akathisia, which responds to a beta blocker such as propranolol and sometimes to benzodiazepines. Hydroxyzine is an antihistamine used for anxiety and pruritus, zolpidem is a hypnotic, and memantine treats Alzheimer's disease; none treat akathisia.

q: A nurse is providing teaching to a client who is prescribed eszopiclone for insomnia. Which of the following instructions should the nurse include?
o: "Take the medication with a high-fat snack to improve absorption."
"Report any episodes of sleepwalking, sleep-driving, or eating while asleep."
"Take an additional dose if you awaken during the night."
"You may drink one glass of wine at bedtime with this medication."
r: Zolpidem and eszopiclone carry a boxed warning for complex sleep behaviors such as sleepwalking, sleep-driving, and sleep-eating, and the medication must be discontinued if these occur. Food delays absorption and reduces effect, repeat dosing increases next-day impairment, and alcohol potentiates CNS depression.

q: A nurse is providing teaching to the parent of a school-age child who is starting methylphenidate. Which of the following instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Give the last dose before 4 PM to reduce insomnia
Monitor the child's height and weight at regular intervals
Give the dose after meals to limit appetite suppression
This medication must not be taken with an MAOI
Keep the medication in a secure place because it has abuse potential
Double the dose on school days when focus is needed most
r: Stimulants cause insomnia (dose before 4 PM), appetite suppression and growth delay (give after meals; track height and weight), and are Schedule II drugs requiring secure storage; combining them with an MAOI can cause hypertensive crisis. Parents must never adjust the dose themselves, which risks toxicity and cardiovascular effects.

q: A nurse is caring for an adolescent client who has ADHD and a history of stimulant misuse. Which of the following medications should the nurse expect the provider to prescribe?
o: Dextroamphetamine
Atomoxetine
Methylphenidate extended release
Lisdexamfetamine
r: Atomoxetine is a nonstimulant selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor with no abuse potential, making it appropriate when misuse is a concern; it requires up to 6 weeks for full effect and monitoring for hepatotoxicity and suicidal ideation. The other three options are all controlled stimulants with abuse potential.

q: A nurse is reviewing general pharmacologic principles with a group of nursing students. Which of the following statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: A drug with a narrow therapeutic index requires close serum level monitoring
Half-life determines how often a medication must be dosed
An antagonist blocks a receptor and prevents the usual response
A partial agonist produces a weaker effect than a full agonist at the same receptor
Drugs with extensive first-pass metabolism are more effective when swallowed than when given sublingually
r: Narrow-therapeutic-index drugs such as lithium require serum monitoring, half-life guides dosing frequency, an antagonist blocks receptor activity, and a partial agonist such as buprenorphine or aripiprazole produces a submaximal response. The final statement is reversed: extensive first-pass metabolism destroys much of an oral dose, so sublingual or parenteral routes bypass the liver and preserve the drug.

q: A nurse is providing teaching to a client who is starting disulfiram for alcohol use disorder. Which of the following statements should the nurse include?
o: "You may have one drink per week without any reaction."
"Avoid all sources of alcohol, including mouthwash, cough syrup, and aftershave."
"This medication will reduce your cravings for alcohol."
"Take this medication only on days you plan to drink."
r: Disulfiram inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, so any alcohol exposure, including hidden sources such as mouthwash, cough syrup, sauces, and topical aftershave, causes flushing, throbbing headache, vomiting, tachycardia, and hypotension. Disulfiram works by aversion, not craving reduction (that is naltrexone and acamprosate), and it must be taken daily; the reaction can occur up to 2 weeks after the last dose.

q: A nurse is admitting a client who has alcohol use disorder and a last drink 10 hr ago. Which of the following medications should the nurse expect the provider to prescribe? (Select the best option.)
o: Chlordiazepoxide and thiamine
Disulfiram and naltrexone
Haloperidol and lithium
Methadone and clonidine
r: Chlordiazepoxide is used with CIWA-Ar scoring to prevent withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens, and thiamine is given to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy from vitamin B1 deficiency. Disulfiram and naltrexone are for maintenance of abstinence after withdrawal is complete, antipsychotics and lithium do not treat withdrawal, and methadone is used for opioid rather than alcohol withdrawal.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who is starting buprenorphine and naloxone for opioid use disorder. Which of the following statements by the nurse is accurate?
o: "Buprenorphine is a partial agonist, so it eases withdrawal with a lower risk of respiratory depression."
"Buprenorphine is a pure antagonist that blocks all opioid receptors."
"You may continue using short-acting opioids while taking this medication."
"This medication should be swallowed whole with water."
r: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist at the mu receptor, relieving craving and withdrawal with a ceiling effect that limits respiratory depression; the added naloxone deters injection misuse. Naltrexone, not buprenorphine, is the pure antagonist; continued short-acting opioid use can precipitate withdrawal, and the combination product is given sublingually because of first-pass metabolism.

q: A nurse is caring for a client who has Alzheimer's disease and is prescribed donepezil. Which of the following findings should the nurse report to the provider immediately?
o: Heart rate of 48/min
Report of mild nausea with the first dose
Loose stool once daily
Vivid dreams
r: Cholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine increase acetylcholine and can cause bradycardia, syncope, and heart block, so a heart rate of 48/min must be reported immediately. Nausea, diarrhea, and vivid dreams are common cholinergic effects that are typically managed with dose timing rather than urgent intervention; memantine, an NMDA receptor antagonist, is often added in moderate to severe disease and does not cause bradycardia.

q: A nurse is preparing a client for electroconvulsive therapy. Which of the following medications should the nurse expect to be administered to prevent musculoskeletal injury during the induced seizure?
o: Atropine
Methohexital
Succinylcholine
Diphenhydramine
r: Succinylcholine is a short-acting neuromuscular blocker that relaxes skeletal muscle so the seizure does not cause fractures or dislocations. Methohexital is the short-acting anesthetic that induces unconsciousness, atropine is given to reduce secretions and prevent bradycardia, and diphenhydramine has no role in ECT.

q: A nurse is reviewing reversal agents and antidotes with a group of nurses on a behavioral health unit. Which of the following medication and indication pairings are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Flumazenil for benzodiazepine overdose
Naloxone for opioid overdose
Benztropine for acute dystonia
Acetylcysteine for acetaminophen overdose
Physostigmine for severe anticholinergic toxicity
Naltrexone for lithium toxicity
r: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines (use cautiously because it can precipitate seizures), naloxone reverses opioids, benztropine relieves acute dystonia, acetylcysteine is the antidote for acetaminophen overdose (critical in intentional overdose), and physostigmine treats severe anticholinergic toxicity. There is no antidote for lithium toxicity; treatment is fluids, electrolyte correction, and hemodialysis at high levels.

q: A client asks the nurse, "What exactly is a neurotransmitter?" Which response is most accurate?
o: They are hormones released by the adrenal glands during stress
They are chemical substances made by neurons that carry information from one nerve cell to the next
They are the electrical impulses that travel down the spinal cord
They are proteins in the blood that carry medication to the brain
r: Neurotransmitters are chemicals manufactured by neurons that cross the synapse to relay information throughout the body. They are not electrical impulses — the impulse triggers release of the chemical, and the chemical carries the message across the gap.

q: A client is prescribed a benzodiazepine for severe anxiety. The nurse explains that this class of drug works by increasing the function of which neurotransmitter?
o: GABA
Dopamine
Acetylcholine
Glutamate
r: Benzodiazepines enhance GABA, the inhibitory transmitter — more inhibition → less anxiety and more sedation. Dopamine is the wrong target; blocking dopamine treats psychosis, not anxiety.

q: Antipsychotic medications reduce hallucinations and delusions primarily by blocking receptors for which neurotransmitter?
o: Serotonin
Dopamine
GABA
Histamine
r: Psychosis is linked to excess dopamine activity, so antipsychotics block dopamine receptors. Serotonin is the distractor to rule out — a serotonin deficit is tied to depression, not to hallucinations.

q: A client with major depressive disorder asks which brain chemical is involved in his illness. Which neurotransmitter deficit is most associated with depression?
o: Dopamine
GABA
Serotonin
Glutamate
r: A shortage of serotonin is the classic neurochemical link to depression, which is why antidepressants target serotonin. Dopamine is the confusable one — dysregulated dopamine points to psychosis and mania instead.

q: A client says, "I got sick after months of caregiving with no sleep, and then the depression started." Which proposed cause category of mental illness does this reflect?
o: Genetics and heredity
Infection and viral theory
Stress and immune function (psychoimmunology)
Receptor blockade from medication
r: Psychoimmunology proposes that prolonged stress and a compromised immune system contribute to the development of mental illness. Genetics is the tempting alternative, but nothing in the statement points to a familial or inherited pattern.

q: Besides psychosis, dysregulation of dopamine is most associated with which additional problem?
o: Hypertensive crisis
Chronic diarrhea
Movement problems
Peripheral allergic reactions
r: Dopamine governs movement as well as thought, which is why dopamine-blocking antipsychotics produce extrapyramidal (movement) symptoms. Allergic responses belong to histamine, not dopamine.

q: A nurse wants to address the esteem needs of a client with chronic mental illness. Which intervention is most appropriate?
o: Ensure the client receives three meals a day
Place the client in a room near the nursing station for observation
Praise the client for correctly managing his own medications this week
Encourage the client to attend a community social hour to make friends
r: Esteem needs involve competence, achievement, and respect from self and others — recognizing a mastered skill directly meets that need. The social hour is tempting but targets love and belonging, the level below esteem.

q: Which services are part of psychiatric rehabilitation? Select all that apply.
o: Teaching independent living and life skills
Work-readiness and vocational skills training
Social skills development
Linkage to community-based supports and housing
Managing medications and disease symptoms only
Long-term involuntary confinement in a locked setting
r: Psychiatric rehabilitation goes beyond managing the disease and medications — it builds life, work, and social skills and connects clients to community supports and housing, which is critical for the homeless mentally ill population. Medication management alone and involuntary confinement are not rehabilitation.

q: During the termination phase a client says, "You'll forget all about me once I'm discharged." Which response is BEST?
o: I could never forget you — you've been my favorite client.
Let's review your medication list one more time before you go.
Why would you say something like that?
Ending our work together stirs up a lot of feelings. Tell me what you're feeling about leaving.
r: In termination the nurse reviews progress and discusses feelings about the relationship ending. Calling him a favorite crosses a boundary and is false reassurance; jumping to the medication list changes the subject to a task and avoids the emotion.

q: A nursing student asks why every clinician on the psychiatric unit uses the DSM-5. Which statement best describes a purpose of the DSM-5?
o: It provides a standardized nomenclature so all mental health professionals use the same language
It lists the medication protocol required for each psychiatric diagnosis
It ranks psychiatric disorders from least to most dangerous
It replaces the clinical interview with a scored symptom checklist
r: The DSM-5 exists to standardize the language and diagnostic criteria used by all mental health clinicians. It does not prescribe treatment — it describes disorders and the criteria used to diagnose them.

q: Which of the following are stated purposes of the DSM-5? Select all that apply.
o: Provide a standardized nomenclature and language for all mental health professionals
Present defining characteristics that differentiate one diagnosis from another
Assist in identifying the underlying causes of disorders
Establish the legal criteria for involuntary commitment
Include relevant medical, psychosocial, and environmental problems
Specify the first-line medication for each disorder
r: The four purposes are standardized language, defining characteristics that differentiate diagnoses, help identifying underlying causes, and inclusion of medical, psychosocial, and environmental problems. Commitment law comes from state statute and drug choice from the prescriber — neither comes from the DSM.

q: Which outcome concerns the nurse most when a community holds strong stigma toward mental illness?
o: People delay or avoid seeking mental health treatment
Clients demand more medication than they need
Clinicians overdiagnose mental illness
Families overuse outpatient services
r: Stigma is the most common reason people do not seek help, so illness progresses untreated. Overuse of services is the opposite problem and is not what stigma produces.

q: Which activities fall within the basic-level functions of the registered nurse in mental health? Select all that apply.
o: Counseling and crisis intervention
Milieu therapy
Health teaching and health promotion
Prescribing psychotropic medications
Case management
Providing individual psychotherapy as the primary treatment
r: Basic-level RN functions are counseling, milieu therapy, self-care activities, psychobiologic interventions, health teaching, case management, and health promotion/maintenance. Prescribing and psychotherapy are advanced-practice functions.

q: Which services are part of psychiatric rehabilitation for a client with chronic mental illness? Select all that apply.
o: Independent living and self-care skills training
Work-readiness and vocational skills
Social skills training
Linkage to community-based supports and housing
Acute medical detoxification
Permanent involuntary institutional placement
r: Psychiatric rehabilitation goes beyond managing the disease and the medications to build living, work, and social skills plus housing and community supports — key resources for the homeless mentally ill. Permanent institutionalization is the opposite of the least-restrictive-environment principle.

q: Four clients are waiting on the psychiatric unit. Which client does the nurse assess first?
o: A client who says he has been saving his pills and plans to take them all tonight
A client who is upset about the dinner menu
A client requesting a PRN medication for insomnia
A client who missed morning group therapy
r: Safety first: suicidal ideation with a method and a plan requires immediate assessment and protection. The other concerns are real but none of them threatens a life in the next few minutes.

q: A client states, 'I know I can manage my own medications and get myself to my appointments.' This belief in one's own ability to determine outcomes is called:
o: Stigma
Countertransference
Self-efficacy
Milieu therapy
r: Self-efficacy is the belief in one's own ability to influence outcomes, and it is a key protective factor supporting recovery and resilience. Stigma is the opposite kind of belief — that one is flawed and shameful.

q: A client waiting for an intake interview drums his fingers on the table and repeatedly taps his foot. The nurse documents this repetitive purposeful behavior as:
o: An automatism, often seen with anxiety
Waxy flexibility
Tardive dyskinesia
Psychomotor retardation
r: Automatisms are repeated purposeful behaviors such as finger drumming and commonly signal anxiety. Tardive dyskinesia is involuntary lip smacking and tongue protrusion from long-term antipsychotic use, not purposeful tapping.

q: A client tells the nurse, "The night staff keep frenzling my medications so I can't sleep." The nurse documents the use of:
o: Neologisms
Word salad
Loose associations
Ideas of reference
r: Neologisms are invented words that have meaning only to the client. Word salad would be a string of unconnected words with no meaning at all, but this sentence has intact grammar and one made-up word.

q: Which client statement indicates the poorest insight?
o: "There is nothing wrong with me — my wife lied to the doctor to get me locked up."
"I know I get paranoid when I skip my medication."
"I need to call my case manager when I stop sleeping."
"Drinking makes my depression worse, so I stopped."
r: Insight is understanding the true nature of one's situation and accepting responsibility for it. Blaming others entirely for the hospitalization shows absent insight; the other statements show the client recognizing his illness and his own role in managing it.

q: Which findings indicate impaired insight or judgment? Select all that apply.
o: The client stopped his medication because "the pharmacy is poisoning it"
The client plans to drive himself home despite a seizure yesterday
The client says, "I need to keep taking my medication even when I feel well"
The client blames his employer entirely for losing his third job this year
The client identifies early warning signs of his illness
The client will cancel all follow-up appointments because "nothing is wrong with me"
r: Impaired insight = denying the illness and blaming others; impaired judgment = choosing an unsafe or unsound action, such as driving after a seizure. Recognizing warning signs and the need for ongoing medication are signs of intact insight.

q: A nurse tells a client, "If you don't take this medication, I will have staff hold you down and give you a shot." The nurse has committed:
o: Battery
Assault
False imprisonment
Defamation
r: Assault is threatening harm and creating fear of it — no contact is required. It becomes battery only if the staff actually touch or inject the client.

q: A competent voluntary client refuses his oral medication. Two staff members hold his arms while the nurse gives it by injection. The nurse has committed:
o: Assault
Negligence
False imprisonment
Battery
r: Battery is actual harmful or unconsented touching — forcing medication into a competent client who has refused. Assault would be only the verbal threat without contact.

q: Which client most clearly meets criteria for involuntary commitment?
o: A client who refuses to attend group therapy
A client with active suicidal intent and a plan who refuses admission
A client with an odd but harmless belief that aliens visit his garden
A client who has stopped his antidepressant against advice
r: Involuntary commitment requires danger to self, danger to others, or grave disability (unable to provide food, shelter, clothing, or basic safety). Refusing treatment or holding unusual beliefs is not grounds — psychiatric clients keep their rights.

q: A client is pacing, raising his voice, and clenching his fists in the hallway. Which action should the nurse take first?
o: Call for staff to apply four-point restraints
Place the client in seclusion
Obtain an order for restraints from the provider
Approach calmly, offer to talk in a quieter area, and offer the PRN medication
r: The law and policy require the least restrictive intervention first — verbal de-escalation, reducing stimuli, a walk, or a PRN medication. Restraint and seclusion are used only after less restrictive measures fail and the client is imminently dangerous.

q: Which findings would support involuntary commitment? Select all that apply.
o: Active suicidal intent with a plan
Threatening to kill a specific neighbor
Refusing to take prescribed medication
Living outdoors, not eating, and unable to arrange food or shelter
Having a diagnosis of schizophrenia
A family's request that the client be admitted
r: The three grounds are danger to self, danger to others, and grave disability. A diagnosis, medication refusal, or family preference is never sufficient — psychiatric clients do not lose their rights because they are mentally ill.

q: A client in crisis asks how long this will go on. Which response is most accurate and most therapeutic?
o: 'A crisis state is time-limited and usually resolves within a few weeks — our work right now is keeping you safe and rebuilding your coping.'
'Most people stay in crisis for a year or more.'
'That depends entirely on which medication you are given.'
'Don't worry about it — try not to think that way.'
r: A crisis is time-limited: no one sustains that level of disequilibrium for long, which is why early intervention determines whether the person comes out functioning better, the same, or worse. 'Don't worry about it' is false reassurance and shuts the client down.

q: Which measures help maintain safety in the inpatient milieu? Select all that apply.
o: Position the nursing station for easy observation of and access to clients
Design the environment to prevent self-harm and harm to others
Restrict access to locked areas and monitor visitors
Have a staff action plan for de-escalating violence
Allow clients unsupervised access to the medication room
Eliminate recreation areas and meeting rooms
r: A therapeutic milieu is supportive, therapeutic, and safe: open sight lines, an environment built against self-harm, controlled access and visitors, and a rehearsed de-escalation plan. Removing recreation and meeting spaces strips the milieu of the therapeutic function that makes it more than a locked room.

q: A client on the unit is shouting obscenities, has thrown a chair, and no longer responds to staff direction. Which phase of the aggression cycle is this client in?
o: Triggering
Escalation
Crisis
Recovery
r: Crisis means the client has lost control and staff must take charge for safety. In escalation the behavior is moving toward loss of control but the client can still be redirected — that is where talking and PRN medication still work.

q: During which phases of the aggression cycle are nursing interventions most likely to prevent physically aggressive behavior?
o: Triggering and escalation
Crisis and recovery
Recovery and postcrisis
Crisis and postcrisis
r: Prevention happens before control is lost — triggering and escalation are the windows for calm talking, movement, limit setting, and PRN medication. By the crisis phase the goal is no longer prevention but containment and safety.

q: A client in the crisis phase is swinging at staff in the day room. What is the nurse's key action?
o: Explore with the client what triggered the anger
Take charge of the situation to protect the client, staff, and other clients
Offer a PRN medication by mouth and wait for it to take effect
Ask the client to sign a no-harm contract
r: In crisis the client cannot problem-solve, so the nurse takes charge and directs the team for safety. Exploring triggers and offering an oral PRN belong to the triggering and escalation phases — once crisis begins, those interventions are too late.

q: Which factor is the best predictor that a client will become violent again?
o: Paranoid delusions
A history of childhood trauma
Refusal to take prescribed medication
A previous episode of violence
r: Past violence is the single strongest predictor of future violence. Paranoid delusions, medication refusal, and childhood trauma are all real risk factors, but none of them outranks a documented history of violent episodes.

q: Which combination of medications is most commonly given intramuscularly as a chemical restraint for an acutely aggressive client?
o: Lithium, sertraline, and buspirone
Haloperidol, lorazepam, and diphenhydramine
Donepezil, memantine, and risperidone
Clozapine, carbamazepine, and valproate
r: The classic IM chemical-restraint combination is haloperidol (Haldol) + lorazepam (Ativan) + diphenhydramine (Benadryl) — antipsychotic, sedative, and an anticholinergic to blunt EPS. The other combinations are maintenance drugs that do nothing for acute aggression.

q: What is the primary goal of giving a chemical restraint?
o: To treat the client's underlying psychiatric disorder long term
To improve the client's insight into the aggressive behavior
To prevent extrapyramidal side effects
To sedate the client so the aggression subsides and everyone stays safe
r: A chemical restraint is an emergency safety measure — a benzodiazepine plus an antipsychotic given to sedate and stop the aggression. It is not long-term treatment, and insight work only becomes possible after the client is calm.

q: An older adult with dementia is given lorazepam for agitation and becomes more agitated and combative. How should the nurse interpret this?
o: A paradoxical reaction — benzodiazepines can disinhibit and increase aggression in dementia
An allergic reaction to lorazepam
Evidence the dose was too low and should be doubled
The first sign of tardive dyskinesia
r: In clients with dementia, benzodiazepines can cause a paradoxical increase in aggression through social disinhibition. Doubling the dose would worsen it; the nurse should hold further doses and notify the provider.

q: A client is pacing, speaking loudly, and clenching his fists after a difficult phone call. Which nursing action is best?
o: Approach calmly and in a non-threatening manner, invite him to talk or walk, and offer the prescribed PRN medication
